en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Dukanipāta (The Book of Twos) in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
1. The First Fifty-Section (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Punishment (Kammakāraṇavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Faults (Vajjasuttavaṇṇanā)
1. In the first [story] of the *Dukanipāta*, "for the purpose of accomplishing a blow" means for the purpose of successfully inflicting a blow with a staff.
"Kañjiya" is that which is produced from fermented rice-gruel; it is sour gruel (*āranāla*), also called *bilaṅga*.
That vessel into which this is poured is a "kañjiya-ukkhali," or a "bilanga-thālī. A cause similar to that is "bilanga-thālika. [The term refers to] the skull.
"Having torn out" means having made an opening the size of a red-hot iron ball.

"The punishment of being shorn like a conch shell" is the punishment consisting of shaving the head until it resembles a conch shell. "The punishment of the mouth of Rāhu" is a punishment resembling the sun when it has entered the mouth of Rāhu.
"The garland of fire" is a punishment involving a garland of flames. "The torch in the hand" is a punishment consisting of lighting a torch with the hand.
“Erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ” means the infliction of punishment by tearing away the skin from the body in strips resembling eraka-grass mats.
“Cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ” means the infliction of punishment by clothing the person in strips of skin torn from the body.
When performing this, just as they would cut a rope starting from the neck and place it around the waist, so too [they tear the skin] starting from the ankles.
Having cut [the skin] starting from the waist, they place it upon the waist itself. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"Having cut it starting from the waist, they place it upon the ankles. "The execution of the *eṇeyyaka*" means an execution like that of the *eṇi* deer.
"Having put on iron bracelets" means having fastened iron bracelets. "They strike with iron spikes" refers to the joints of the knees and elbows.
They drive iron stakes [into him]. "That being" refers to the sentient being who has committed such deeds.
"The fish-hook flesh-tearer" refers to the act of tearing out the flesh with fish-hooks. "The penny-cutter" refers to the act of cutting [the body] into pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa coin.
"They hack" means they cut. "The salt-scraper" refers to the act of scraping [the skin] and sprinkling it with salt.
*Palighaparivattikaṃ*: the act of turning [the body] like a crossbar (*paligha*).
They make it into a single solid mass by hammering it with iron spikes. *Palālapīṭhakaṃ*: the act of twisting the body like a straw mat (*palālapīṭha*).
*Kāraṇikā*: those who carry out the execution. *Katvā palālavaṭṭiṃ viya*: just as those making a straw mat arrange the straw...
Having made a roll, they wrap it again by way of twisting; the meaning is that they act in this manner.
"By hungry dogs" means by small, well-bred dogs; for they are powerful, swift, and brave. "A thousand-fold bundle" means a bag containing a thousand [coins].
"Yāham" means "I who"; "yaṃ" is a word expressing a reason. Therefore he said, "by whom I. "With its root cut" means with its root completely severed because the root of craving has been uprooted.
The commentary on the Vajjasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Padhānasutta:

In the second [sutta], "resembling the entering of a battle arrayed on both sides" means resembling the entering into the midst of a fourfold army drawn up in ranks on both sides for the purpose of combat.
"Generosity and battle are said to be equal"—how, then, are these two equal?

For one who fears the loss of life is unable to fight, and one who fears the loss of wealth is unable to give a gift. Indeed, one who says, "I will protect my life; I will fight," does not fight at all;
for it is by relinquishing attachment to life that one fights, thinking, "Let there be the cutting off of hands, feet, and so forth."
Whether it be life or death, one fights with resolve, thinking, "I shall seize this sovereignty.

Even one who says, "I will protect my wealth and I will give gifts," does not actually give; however, having cast away attachment to wealth, one gives with resolve, thinking, "I will give a great gift.
Thus, giving and fighting are equal. And what is more—though [the wealth] be small...

The few conquer the many: just as in battle even a few heroic men conquer many cowardly men, so too one endowed with faith and other virtues, while giving even a small gift, overcomes the manifold types of greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, wrong view, doubt, and so forth—which are its opposites—and attains a great result through the ripening of that gift. Thus, both giving and battle are alike.
It is the same. Therefore he said: “Even if one gives with little faith, by that alone one becomes happy in the next world.

That which is beneficial for the household—such as farming, cattle-rearing, and so forth—is *agāriya*; because that is absent therein, it is *anagāriya*, meaning the state of going forth (*pabbajjā*). Thus he said: “The state of going forth, which is the absence of the household life...
[and so on]... the state of going forth. Regarding the phrase “for the sake of relinquishing all acquisitions (*upadhi*”), here there are four...

The *upadhīs* are: the *upadhi* of sensual desire (*kāmupadhi*), the *upadhi* of the aggregates (*khandhupadhi*), the *upadhi* of defilements (*kilesupadhi*), and the *upadhi* of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārupadhi*).

For sensual desires (*kāmā*) are also called an *upadhi* because pleasure is established therein—according to the statement: "Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures"—either as the basis for that pleasure or for the suffering that has that gratification as its cause.
In this sense of the word, they are called "upadhīs" (substrata). The aggregates are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates;

the defilements are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the woeful states; and volitional formations are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for the suffering of existence.
That in which there is the relinquishing and abandoning of all upadhīs is "the relinquishing of all upadhīs."
Nirvana. Therefore he said: “For the sake of all the aggregates, acquisitions... [etc. ...for the sake of Nirvana.
The commentary on the Padhāna Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Tapanīya Sutta.

3. Regarding the third [verse], "things that cause burning" (*tapanīyā*): here, the suffix *-anīya* has the sense of the agent; thus he says, "They burn, therefore they are 'things that cause burning'.

"They burn" means they afflict or torment—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "burning" (*tapana*) is suffering (*dukkha*); because they lead to its production and provide support for it both in the present life (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) and in future lives (*abhisamparāya*), they are "things that cause burning. Or else, "they burn by means of them."
The meaning is burning (*tapana*), remorse (*anutāpa*), and regret (*vippaṭisāra*). Because they are the cause of that [remorse], they are called "to be burned" (*tapanīya*).

One "sorrows after" (*anusocati*) means that, having become regretful, one sorrows by following after what was done and what was left undone. For sorrow arises both from what has been done and from what has not been done;
it is explained exactly thus in the Canon (*pāḷi*). Since the cases of the yakkha Nanda and others are well known, they are not shown here.
Showing the story of the two brothers, he said, “It is said that they...,” and so forth. Therein, “they” refers to the two brothers.
“What again do you seek? means: what else do you desire?
The commentary on the *Tapanīya-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Upaññāta-sutta*.
In the fifth [sutta], "this pair of qualities" refers to the pair of qualities consisting of non-contentment with wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) and non-laxity in striving (*padhāna*).
"By this" means by the statement, "non-contentment with wholesome states. "He illuminates this" means...
“‘As long as he did not arise, for that long I was not satisfied’”—this indicates the limit up to which the meaning of what is about to be said will be explained.
“In striving” means in the exertion of energy (*vīriya*). “This matter” refers to the matter stated by the passage beginning with “And in striving.
When the flow of energy is proceeding, turning back midway, retreating, or resisting—that [resistance] belongs to him; thus it is called *paṭivāna*.

"Resistance" (*paṭivānī*) means opposition; "non-resistance" (*appaṭivānī*) means the absence of resistance. Its state is "non-resistiveness" (*appaṭivānitā*), which he explains as "non-retreating" (*appaṭikkamanā*) and "non-shrinking back" (*anosakkanā*).

In this context, "non-shrinking back" means non-turning-back. "The path leading onward" (*āgamanīyapaṭipadā*) refers to the preliminary practice consisting of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). For it is by means of this that one comes [to the goal].
It is called *āgamanīyā* because one attains distinction (*visesa*) by means of it, or because the attainment of distinction comes about through it;

that very thing, being something to be practiced, is the "way" (*paṭipadā*), hence it is the "way leading onward" (*āgamanīyapaṭipadā*). "Irreversible striving" (*appaṭivānapadhāna*) means striving free from falling back;
the meaning is that it is the energy exerted without faltering in the interim.
The commentary on the *Upaññāta-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta*. Regarding the sixth [sutta]:

"Those things which are conducive to fetters (*saṃyojaniya*) by way of being a favorable condition for the fetters" refers to the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence. Therefore, he said:
“Of the ten fetters,” and so forth. One who contemplates with their virtue the gratification in things that are subject to fettering is one who contemplates gratification (*assādānupassī*);
the state of being such is *assādānupassitā*. The same principle applies here for *nibbidānupassitā* (contemplation of disenchantment).

“By way of disenchantment” means by way of becoming disenchanted with the phenomena of the three planes that are subject to fettering. Birth (*jāti*) is the act of being born; it is the manifestation of the aggregates (*khandha*).
He said: "By birth, because of the production of the aggregates. The meaning is: because the aggregates are produced again and again in this or that state of existence (*bhava*).

The maturation of the aggregates is the agedness of the aggregates included within a single state of existence. The breaking up of the aggregates here is death, by way of the severance of the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) included within a single state of existence;
thus he said: "By death, because of the breaking up of the aggregates. Internal reflection...
“Torment of mind. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outburst of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such calamities.

Since it originates from sorrow (*soka*), he says: “by lamentations characterized by that [sorrow] and by wailing (*lālappita*). Wailing is verbal outburst; and in its essential meaning, it is simply sound. “Suffering (*dukkha*):
here, bodily suffering is intended; thus he says: “by sufferings that oppress the body. “By mental distress and dejection (*domanassa*):”
[It is] by means of the mental distresses that cause the mind's frustration. For mental distress has the function of frustrating the mind through association with ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Intense exertion is *upāyāsa* (despair), just as [in the expression] "intense grasping is *upādāna*" (clinging).

And in its actual meaning, it is simply hatred manifested as extreme mental suffering in one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. For it is through the exertion of body and mind that it is indeed hatred.
The mode of occurrence [of suffering] is called "distress" (*upāyāsa*), which is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Some say that it is a distinct mental factor (*cetasikadhamma*) other than the fourteen unwholesome mental factors; others call it "despondency" (*visāda*).
The commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Kaṇha Sutta:

Regarding the seventh [sutta], just as in expressions such as "a black cow," one is called "black" because it is endowed with the color black, the phenomena are not called "dark" (kaṇha) by virtue of being black in color;
rather, they are so called because they are the cause for producing a dark rebirth.
Or, showing that they are called "dark" (*kaṇhā*) because they cause a state of little radiance, he said, "not by way of black color," and so forth.
"By way of darkness" (*kaṇhatāya*) means by way of dark rebirth (*kaṇhābhijātitā*). "Dark rebirths" (*kaṇhābhijātī*) refers to the states of misery (*apāya*) and misfortune among humans.

"By its own nature" (*sarasena*) means by its intrinsic character (*sabhāvena*). One who is not ashamed and does not feel modesty is "shameless" (*ahirika*); this refers to a person, a mind, or the aggregate of mental factors associated with it.
Regarding the term *ahirika*: it should have been called *ahirikka* (the state of that), but by eliding one *ka*-sound, it is stated as *ahirika*;

thus he says, "Non-shame (*ahirika*) is the state of non-shame (*ahirikabhāva*). One who does not feel dread is a non-dreadful person (*anottāpī*), whether an individual or the aforementioned collection of factors;
its state is non-dreadfulness (*anottappa*); thus he says, "The state of being non-dreadful (*anottāpibhāva*)."
The commentary on the Kaṇhasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Sukkasutta:
In the eighth [sutta], the quality of "white" (sukka) in phenomena is not due to the whiteness of their color—as in the case of the phrase "a white cloth," for instance—but rather—

Showing that it is due to its being a noble birth of purity and because it produces a state of radiance, he said, "Not for the sake of white color," and so forth. "For the sake of whiteness" means for the sake of a noble birth of purity.
Because shame (*hirī*) feels disgust upon seeing evil states as if they were excrement, he said, "Shame has the characteristic of disgust for evil.
Because fear-of-sin (*ottappa*) sees them as if they were fire and fears them on that account, [he said...].
It is said: “The characteristic of shame (*hirī*) is fearfulness. Furthermore, this sense of shame and dread of blame (*ottappa*) are mutually dissociated and function as a turning away from evil;
therefore, this is their distinction: shame originates internally, while dread of blame originates externally.

Shame has oneself as its dominant influence, while dread of blame has the world as its dominant influence. Shame is established in the nature of modesty, while dread of blame is established in the nature of fear.
Moral dread (*ottappa*). Modesty (*hirī*) has the characteristic of having a sense of shame; moral dread has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy.
Therein, one arouses modesty, which originates from within oneself, by means of four reasons:
by reflecting on one’s birth, one’s age, one’s courage, and one’s great learning. How so? “This doing of evil is not for those endowed with noble birth... [and so forth].
"Kamma [is the factor]; this is the work of those of low birth, such as fishermen and the like;
it is not fitting for one like me, endowed with noble birth, to do this"—thus, by first reflecting on birth in this way, one who refrains from evil arouses a sense of shame (*hirī*). Likewise:
"This performance of evil is a task to be done by the young; it is not fitting for one like me, established in middle age, to do this."
Reflecting thus, "It is not fitting," one who refrains from evil arouses a sense of shame (*hirī*).
Likewise, reflecting on one's own courage, thinking, "This doing of evil is the work of those of weak nature;
it is not fitting for one such as me, endowed with courage, to do this," one who refrains from evil arouses a sense of shame. Likewise, [reflecting on] evil action...

"This is the work of blind fools, not of the wise; it is not fitting for a wise and learned person such as myself to do this"—thus, by reflecting on his great learning (*bāhusacca*), he who refrains from evil arouses a sense of shame (*hiri*).
In this way, one arouses the internally arisen sense of shame through four reasons; and while arousing that shame, one—
Relying on this, one does not commit an evil deed.
How is it that moral dread (*ottappa*) originates externally? It is by reflecting: "If you commit an evil deed, you will become an object of reproach among the four assemblies;
consequently, virtuous fellow-practitioners will shun you. Thus one reflects.
Relying on shame that originates externally, one does not commit an evil deed. Such is shame that originates externally.
How is it that moral dread has oneself as its dominant influence? Here, a certain son of good family, making himself his own dominant influence and leader, thinks:
"It is not fitting for one like me—one who has gone forth out of faith, who is learned, and who maintains the ascetic virtues—to commit an evil deed. Thus, he refrains from evil... [and so on].
One does not do it. Such is moral shame (hirī) with oneself as its governing principle. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Making himself alone his governing principle, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he preserves himself in purity.”
What is moral dread with respect to the world as authority (*lokādhipati-ottappa*)? Here, a certain son of good family, making the world his authority and his elder, thinks:

"If you were to commit an evil deed, your fellow celibates would know of it, as well as the ascetics and brahmins in the world who possess great power and majesty, and the deities; therefore, it is not fitting for you to do evil. Thus, [he refrains] from evil action.
He does not do so. As it is said: "Great indeed is this world-dwelling;
and in this great world-dwelling there are recluses and brahmins who possess psychic power, divine vision, and knowledge of the minds of others.
They see even from afar, while those nearby are not seen; they know the mind with their own minds, and they will know me thus: 'Look!'"
"Friends, this son of good family, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
There are deities who possess psychic power, who have the divine eye, and who know the minds of others;
they see even from afar, yet remain unseen when near, and they know the mind with their own minds—they too will know me.
“Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
… [as before] … “It is by making the world itself his authority that he avoids what is unwholesome.
Thus is moral dread with respect to the world.
Regarding the phrase "established in the nature of shame": here, *lajjā* means the state of being ashamed; *hirī* is established in that very nature.
*Bhaya* means the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*); *ottappa* is established in that very nature.
Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil. In this regard, it is like two iron balls: one might be cold but smeared with excrement, while the other is hot and glowing.
Among these, just as a sensible person does not take up cool excrement because he loathes it due to its being smeared with filth, nor does he take up the other [hot substance] for fear of burning,
so too the wise man does not commit evil out of shame, loathing it through *lajjā*, nor does he commit evil out of dread of the states of misery through *ottappa*.
Thus, *hirī* is established by the nature of shame, while *ottappa* is established by the nature of fear.
How is it that *hirī* has the characteristic of having a sense of deference, while *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is to be feared due to dread of blame?

For a certain person possesses the characteristic of having a sense of deference therein through a sense of reverence arising from four causes: reflection on the greatness of one’s birth, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life. Thus it has the characteristic of having a sense of deference.

Having aroused a sense of shame (*hiri*), one does not commit evil. Another person, by means of four causes—namely, the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy rebirth—establishes the characteristic of moral dread (*ottappa*) which consists in seeing fear in what is blameworthy;
having thus manifested it, one does not perform an evil deed. And herein, the internal origination and so forth of shame and moral dread [are to be understood].
These have been described as being manifest in various instances, yet there is never any mutual dissociation between them;
for there is no shamelessness that is devoid of fear, nor is there any fear of evil that is devoid of shame. Thus should the detailed commentary on the meaning here be understood.
The commentary on the *Sukkasutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Cariyā Sutta 9.
Regarding the ninth [verse]: "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "They uphold" means they maintain it by way of upholding proper conduct (*ācāra*).

"They establish" means they establish it within the bounds of moral limits (*mariyādā*). "They protect" means that having established it within those limits by upholding proper conduct, they guard it.
"By way of treating [her] with respect, she would not be recognized"—this means that by way of making her an object of respect in the mind, she would not be recognized;
this conduct would not be permissible. Regarding the phrase "or as a maternal aunt," here the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth.
By this, it includes "or as a maternal uncle's wife," "or as a teacher's wife," or "or as the wives of those who are venerable. In that context, a mother's sister is a "maternal aunt" (*mātucchā*).

The wife of one’s maternal uncle is *mātulānī*. The wives of those who occupy the position of a teacher (*garu*), such as the mother’s brother, the father’s younger brother, the elder brother, and so forth, are likewise [included]. This is the summarized meaning:

just as goats, sheep, and other animals—being devoid of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*)—proceed everywhere in promiscuity, having broken the bounds of propriety and not perceiving their mothers as such, so too does this world of humans.
If the qualities of a world-protector did not exist, everything would proceed with total disintegration.
But because these qualities of a world-protector protect the world, there is no such disintegration.
The commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Sutta In the tenth [sutta], "not laid down" (*apaññattā*) means not permitted or not prescribed. "The rains" (*vassa*) is said with reference to the rainy season;
"the cold season" (*utu-vassa*) refers to the winter. "Harming a one-facultied living being" refers to perceiving life in trees, creepers, and so forth.
They spoke thus. Thinking that there is a "single faculty," namely the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*), they say so. "Bringing about a collision" means bringing about destruction.
"They will live in seclusion" means they will dwell in a fixed residence with few concerns. Regarding the phrase "to be approached on the day after Āsāḷhī has passed":
here, "on the day after [Āsāḷhī] has passed" (*aparajjugatā*) means "having gone on the following day"; [the meaning is] "of that day after it has passed."
"Having passed" means on another day; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as that it is to be entered upon on the first day (pāṭipada) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷha.
"When the month has gone" means: it has gone for a month, thus it is "month-gone" (māsagatā);
when that month-gone [period] has passed, the meaning is that the month is complete. Therefore, from the full moon of Āsāḷha...
The meaning should be understood as: "It is to be entered on the first day (pāṭipada) immediately following the full-moon day.
The commentary on the *Vassūpanāyika-sutta* is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Kammakāraṇa-vagga* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇavagga) 11.
In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "does not waver through lack of reflection" refers to the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*);

this is a name for the wisdom of investigation (*upaparikkhanapaññā*). The power that arises in one who develops the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) by means of the head of energy (*vīriya*) is the power of development (*bhāvanābala*). By means of the support of energy...

For when the development of wholesome states (*kusalabhāvanā*) arises as powerful and firm, those seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) that have arisen thus as a powerful development of the wholesome are also called "the powers.
In terms of their actual meaning, the seven factors of enlightenment are headed by the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*).
And this has been said: "In this context, what is the power of development? It is the cultivation and development of wholesome states."
"Abundant practice—this is called the power of development (bhāvanābala). Even the seven factors of enlightenment are the power of development.

"In the sense of being unshakable" means in the sense of being incapable of being shaken by opposing states. "In the sense of being difficult to overcome" means in the sense of being hard to be surpassed.
"In the sense of not being crushed" means in the sense of not being overwhelmed after having overcome [the opposition]. "These" refers to these aforementioned [powers].

"Two powers": this is what is recorded as "foremost. The meaning here is that it is recorded as foremost in this way: "Bhikkhus, of these two powers, this is the foremost, namely, the power of development (bhāvanābala).
In the second [case], "dependent on seclusion" means supported by seclusion; or alternatively, it refers to jhāna that proceeds by way of seclusion.
It is said, “born of seclusion”; thus, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that proceeds by way of seclusion should be understood as “dependent on seclusion.
And the sense of dependence should be understood through the function of insight and the paths, which [constitute] the paths and fruits;

or, even though there is no temporal sequence of prior and posterior, it is like the production by way of a condition in the case of “dependent origination,” due to the operation of phenomena that are inseparable.

“Dependence arises through development. Having stated that [the enlightenment factors] are “dependent on separation by means of limb-by-limb eradication and escape,” the reason for not mentioning their dependence on “tranquility-separation” is that the enlightenment factors to be developed here have already been stated in the passage beginning with “he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
For one who has developed the enlightenment factors, there are the power-enlightenment factors to be realized; of these—
The duty is the seclusion of subsiding. As for "from inclination": it is from the inclination that occurs in the thought, "I shall realize Nibbāna.

For even though at the moment of insight (vipassanā) the mind has conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as its object, once one has seen the danger in those conditioned phenomena, because of the inclination toward Nibbāna—which is their opposite—the mind becomes dependent on the seclusion of escape, just as one who is overcome by heat [seeks a cool place].
It is like a person’s state of mind being inclined toward cold.

Having stated, “Some say that rapture is based on five kinds of seclusion,” the phrase beginning with “For those [two]” was spoken in order to extract and show two other types of seclusion distinct from the three types of seclusion already mentioned.
Therein, first, at the moment of jhāna, it is based on the seclusion of suppression by way of its function.

At the moment of insight (vipassanā), one should say that one develops [the path] based on the seclusion of subsiding (paṭippassaddhi-viveka) out of one's own inclination (ajjhāsaya), thinking, "In this way I shall enter and dwell in the unsurpassed liberation," because of the inclination directed toward that state. Therefore he says, "Therefore, according to their opinion," and so forth.
By the mention of the kasiṇa-jhānas below, the inclusion of the formless attainments (āruppa) should also be understood.
Therefore, by the phrase "of these jhānas," their inclusion should also be understood.

Since dispassion (virāga) and cessation (nirodha), like the discipline of abandoning (pahānavinaya), are in meaning not distinct from the seclusion intended here, it was said: "This method applies to [the terms] 'dependent on dispassion' and so forth.
Thus he said: "For dispassion and the rest have precisely the same meaning as seclusion."
The word *vossagga* has the sense of relinquishing and the sense of leaping forward; thus, the twofold nature of relinquishing (*vossagga*) is stated.
For relinquishing (*vossajjana*) is indeed abandoning by way of the state of having let go, and it is also the leaping forward toward cessation.

Therefore, at the moment of insight, there is relinquishing through the factor of substitution (*tadaṅga-vasena*), and at the moment of the Path, there is relinquishing through the total eradication (*samuccheda-vasena*) of the opposing side. Likewise, at the moment of insight...

Relinquishment (*vossagga*) should be understood as the state of having abandoned its own inherent nature by way of being inclined toward that [object] and by taking it as an object at the moment of the path.

the Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha has practiced rightly—thus it occurs therein.
Faith in the Triple Gem is "faith in it" (*tappasāda*); that very Triple Gem is "venerable to him," thus it is "veneration for it" (*taggaru*);

the state of being so is "veneration for it" (*taggarutā*). Faith in it and veneration for it together constitute "faith and veneration for it" (*tappasādataggarutā*). By means of those—faith and veneration for it—one has shaken off views, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so forth, and is thus "one whose defilements have been destroyed. That very [object] is the Triple Gem.
"Refuge, resort, protection, and shelter"—thus, when there is such an occurrence, the arising of consciousness that functions with the aspect of being intent upon that [Buddha] is "going for refuge.
It is called "refuge" because one goes by means of it. "One who possesses that" means one endowed with that aforementioned arising of consciousness.
"Thus he approaches" means he resorts to, cultivates, and honors [the Buddha]; or else, he thus knows and awakens.
The meaning should be understood in this way.
Here, by the mention of "serene confidence" (pasāda), he refers to mundane going for refuge, for that is characterized primarily by serene confidence.

By the mention of "veneration" (garutā), he refers to the supramundane. For the Noble Ones, through their direct knowledge of the qualities of the Triple Gem, regard even a stone parasol with affection and veneration.
Therefore, it should be connected thus: by means of devotion to him, one whose defilements are dispelled through suppression [attains the goal];

and by means of reverence for him, one whose defilements are eradicated through their total cutting off, because the causes for showing disrespect are severed. Furthermore, "having him as one's supreme resort" here means having him as one's final destination;
by this, the fourfold going for refuge that is about to be explained should be understood as being included. Or, alternatively, it refers to confidence and reverence without distinction.
By the mention of "confidence" (*pasāda*) as "illumination" (*joti*), both verified confidence (*aveccapasāda*) and the other [ordinary] confidence are included;
likewise, by the mention of "reverence" (*garutā*), both types of going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*) should be connected.
The construction is: "It succeeds at the moment of the Path. By the phrase "having become one whose object is Nibbāna," the realization of the Four Noble Truths is indicated by way of its meaning.

This shows that there is likewise a supramundane going for refuge. For therein, the Dhamma of Nibbāna is established as a refuge only when it is penetrated by way of the clear realization of realization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), and the Dhamma of the Path is established as such only when it is penetrated by way of the clear realization of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*).

However, the qualities of the Buddha that fall within the sphere of disciples, as well as the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha, are established [as a refuge] by way of the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).
Therefore he said: "In terms of its function, it succeeds with respect to the entire Triple Gem. And that which is succeeding succeeds all at once;
the intention is that it is penetrated by a penetration free from delusion, and not successively, as is the case with the mundane.
However, those who say: "The going for refuge does not proceed having Nibbāna as its object; rather, because the Path has been attained, it is [the Path] itself that is attained..."

If it were the case that for some—such as those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijjā) and so forth—the refuge-taking were merely mundane, like their worldly sciences and the like, then their going for refuge would be exclusively mundane and not supramundane;
and that would be improper, because both types [of refuge] are intended to be accepted.

"That" refers to the mundane going for refuge. "The acquisition of faith" occurs through such statements as, "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth. They are "rooted in faith."

Preceded by faith as previously described. Right view is so called because it sees, by means of correct method and through the power of mundane awakening, the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice.

By the statement “right view is rooted in faith,” he shows that mundane going for refuge is wisdom characterized as previously stated, which has faith as its proximate cause. Therefore, he says: “It is the straightening of view.”

“It is so called. Because it is the view itself that is made straight by its own conditions, it is called *diṭṭhijukamma* (straightening of views); or, because the view is made straight by means of this, it is *diṭṭhijukamma*.

It is the arising of consciousness proceeding in such a manner. And by taking it thus, this statement—“the arising of consciousness proceeding in the mode of having that as its ultimate resort”—is also supported; for there is the inclusion of right view preceded by faith.
However, it should be understood that this is because the arising of consciousness has that [faith] as its primary factor.

By the phrase "the acquisition of faith," he shows the going for refuge associated with knowledge, which is like that of children and others who are encouraged by their mothers and so forth; by the phrase "right view," he shows the going for refuge associated with knowledge.
That is mundane going for refuge. "Surrendering of self" (*attasanniyyātana*) means that by this [act], one surrenders, alienates, and relinquishes oneself;
it is the rectification of views as previously described. One who has that Triple Gem as his ultimate resort and refuge is "one who has that as his resort" (*tapparāyaṇo*);
whether this refers to a person or a state of consciousness, the abstract quality of being such is "the state of having that as one's resort" (*tapparāyaṇatā*), as previously described.

It is simply the rectification of one’s view (*diṭṭhijukamma*). "Approaching" (*saraṇa*) means that by means of this, one enters into the state of a student (*sissa*) or the state of a pupil (*antevāsika*);
thus it is "approaching the state of a student. "Prostration" (*paṇipāta*) means that by means of this, one bows down with the very intention of going for refuge.

In all instances, the meaning should be understood solely through the aforementioned rectification of view. "Relinquishing oneself" (*attapariccajana*) is for the sake of escaping the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The relinquishing of one’s own state of welfare. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

The restriction “only for the Buddhas and so forth” should be stated in each instance regarding the surrendering of oneself and the other acts; for in this way, the exclusion of others is established.
Having thus shown the surrendering of oneself and the rest by way of one mode, [the author] now shows them by way of other modes as well.

The passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) is commenced. By this, he demonstrates that even through other methods, the surrendering of oneself (*attasanniyyātana*) is indeed performed, because the meaning is not different.
Regarding the phrase “of Āḷavaka and others,” the word “others” (*ādi*) should be understood as including Sātāgiri, Hemavata, and so forth.

Now, since these individuals such as Āḷavaka and the rest attained refuge by means of the Path itself, how can their going for refuge be characterized as having that [the Dhamma] as their ultimate resort?
Is it so stated? It is stated thus because even by those who have gone for refuge through the path, it was proclaimed that they would wander with him as their supreme resort, saying:
“I shall wander... [as far as] the state of being well-taught; we shall wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain...
[as far as] the state of being well-taught. Thus it was stated.
Regarding the phrase "so panesa ñāti... pe... vasenā" (and so he [acts] by way of relatives... etc., by way of):

here, the word "by way of" (*vasena*) should be applied to each term—namely, by way of relatives, by way of fear, by way of teachers, and by way of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). In that context, "by way of relatives" means by way of the state of being a relative. The same applies to the others.

"By prostrating to those worthy of offerings" means by prostration caused by their worthiness as objects of offerings. "By the others" refers to those [attitudes] proceeding from the state of being a relative and so forth.
By means of the three prostrations. With the words "By the others," etc., the meaning stated in brief is shown in detail;

thus, the passage beginning with "Therefore" was spoken. "He pays homage" is a statement defining the characteristic of prostration. "Of such a kind" refers to that which pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
For one who expects instruction—whether leading to liberation (*niyyānika*) or not—expects only the prostration toward those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
The intended meaning is "it performs. "The classification of going for refuge" means the analysis of going for refuge.
Since the noble path itself is the supramundane going for refuge, he said, "the four fruits of recluseship are the fruit of ripening.
"The destruction of all suffering" means the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra. "This" refers to "the four noble truths."
The vision of the Noble Truths is thus described as: “one sees with right wisdom.
“By way of not approaching [them] as permanent,” etc., means by way of not grasping [them] as permanent, and so forth. “An impossibility” (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause.
“A lack of occasion” (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition. By both of these, he negates the very reason. “Yam” means “by which reason.”
"One endowed with right view" means a stream-enterer who possesses the vision of the Path.

"Any conditioned phenomenon" refers to even a single conditioned formation among the conditioned formations belonging to the four planes of existence. "To approach as permanent" means to grasp it as permanent.
"To approach as pleasant" means, by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), to think: "The self is absolutely happy and free from disease after death."

This was said with reference to grasping [something] as pleasant. However, when his mind is dissociated from wrong views, the noble disciple approaches some formation as pleasant for the sake of allaying his fever, like a man pursued by a rutting elephant who approaches a dung-hill, or like a clean brahmin approaching a latrine.
In the section on the self, instead of saying "a formation," it is said "some phenomenon" (dhamma) in order to include the designations such as the kasiṇas and so forth.
In these instances as well, the delimitation should be understood either by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes.
For whatever a worldling grasps by way of clinging, from each of those the noble disciple undoes that clinging.

Regarding the terms "mother" and so forth: the mother is the biological mother; the father is the biological father; and the "arahant" is intended to mean one who has become a human being and has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava).
"But could a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) take the life of another? This is impossible;
however, this was said for the purpose of showing the great culpability of the state of an ordinary person (puthujjana) and for the purpose of showing the fruit of the state of a noble one.
"With a corrupt mind" means with a murderous mind. "He would shed blood" means [blood] from a living body.

He might cause even as much blood as can be drunk by a small fly to flow. "He would split the Saṅgha" means he would split the Saṅgha—those who share the same communion and reside within the same boundary—by means of the five methods mentioned:
namely, by means of a formal act (*kamma*), a recitation (*uddesa*), an announcement (*vohāra*), a proclamation (*anussāvana*), and the distribution of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).
"Another teacher" means another founder of a religious sect (*titthakara*). "This..."
The meaning is that it is impossible for them to accept [the claim] thus: "He is my teacher.
"They will not go to states of misery" means that those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha will not, on account of that, go to an unhappy destination;
rather, the meaning is that they will fill the hosts of devas. "By ten grounds" means by ten reasons. "They surpass" means they overcome.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the Velāma Sutta and others": here it refers to eighty-four thousand golden plates, silver plates, and bronze plates, each measuring one-fourth of a *karīsa* in size;
these were filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion, and were adorned with every kind of ornament;
as well as eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, and eighty-four thousand chariots.
By way of relinquishing eighty-four thousand cows, eighty-four thousand maidens, eighty-four thousand couches,
eighty-four thousand millions of garments, and immeasurable food consisting of various kinds of hard and soft edibles,
he continuously offered the Velāma Great Almsgiving for seven years and seven months.
A gift given to a single stream-enterer yields greater fruit than that. Greater still than a gift given to a hundred stream-enterers is a gift given to a single once-returner;
greater than that to a single non-returner; greater than that to a single arahant; greater than that to a single paccekabuddha;
greater than that to a perfectly enlightened Buddha; and greater still than a gift given to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

This is according to the Velāma Sutta, which elucidates this meaning: "Then, building a monastery for the Saṅgha of the four quarters; then, going for refuge is more fruitful than that. For it is said therein:
"Householder, compared to the gift, the great gift, which the brahmin Velāma gave, he who would feed one person endowed with right view—this is more fruitful than that," and so forth.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "the Velāma Sutta, etc.," the inclusion of the *Aggappasāda Sutta* and others is to be understood.
Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the non-knowing of the qualities of the Triple Gem; it is delusion regarding them.

Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is uncertainty, such as "Is he a Buddha or not? and so forth. Wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is a perverted grasp, consisting in the conceptualization of those qualities as being non-qualities.
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of those who lack respect and reverence.
"Not of great radiance" means not brilliant; the sense is that it is impure and unpurified. "Not of great expansion" means not sublime. "Blameworthy" means tainted by views, craving, and so forth.
Worldly going for refuge, like the undertaking of the training rules, has no fixed time limit and lasts only as long as life.
Because it exists, it is said that there is no destruction for him through the dissolution of the aggregates; thus he says, "The passing away is blameless.
"It" refers to the division of taking refuge, which is blameless. Although it is blameless, it does not have a desirable fruit;
thus he says, "fruitless. Why? Because it is without karmic ripening (*avipāka*). For that [refuge] is not unwholesome (*akusala*).

"Who is a lay follower? is a question concerning the specific nature [of the term]; therefore, it is equivalent to asking, "What is the characteristic of a lay follower? "Why? is a question concerning the cause.
By this, he shows by what basis for its application (pavattinimitta) the word "lay follower" is conventionally established for that person.
Thus he said, "Why is one called a 'lay follower'? The denotation of a word is the basis for its application; it is the cause for the existence of that state in the object of its meaning.
"What is his virtue? means: what kind of virtue does this lay follower have; by how much virtue does he come to be called "one endowed with virtue"?
"What is his livelihood? means: what is his right livelihood? Since that arises through the avoidance of wrong livelihood, that too is analyzed.
"What is failure? means: what is the failure of virtue, or the failure of livelihood? Of the immediately following...
For there is either an injunction or a prohibition. "What is the attainment?"—here too the same method applies.
"Whoever" means anyone among the kṣatriyas and so forth. This shows that here the sole cause is the going for refuge, not distinctions such as birth and so on.
"From attendance" means by means of that very going for refuge, through performing the task with diligence and being endowed with respect, reverence, esteem, and so forth.

From attending upon. "Abstentions" (*veramaṇiyo*): "Enmity" (*vera*) refers to misconduct such as the destruction of life; they are called "abstentions" because of the avoiding, the slaying, and the destroying of that [enmity].
These are the five abstinences (*virati*), because abstention is the primary factor of that virtue. For this very reason, it is said:
"He is refrained."
"Wrong trade" means not right trade; it is an improper trade, an unsuitable trade. "Having abandoned" means having relinquished by simply not engaging in it.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means not departing from the Dhamma; by this, he rejects any other livelihood that is contrary to the Dhamma.
"Justly" means without injustice; by this, having avoided misconduct such as bodily injustice, one practices good conduct through bodily justice and so forth.
He demonstrates right livelihood. "Trade in weapons" means the sale of weapons, whether one has made them oneself, had them made, or obtained them as they were already made.
"Trade in living beings" means the sale of human beings. "Trade in meat" means raising deer, pigs, and so forth—like butchers and others—and then selling the meat once it has been prepared.
"Trade in intoxicants" means the preparation and sale of any kind of intoxicant.
Trade. "Poison-dealing" means the trade of poison, whether by compounding it or by purchasing it. Among these, the trade in weapons is said to be improper because it is a cause for harming others;
the trade in living beings because it deprives them of their independence; the trade in meat and poison because it is a cause for slaughter;
and the trade in intoxicants because they are a basis for negligence.
"Of that very same" refers to both the virtue characterized by the five abstinences and the livelihood characterized by the five wrong modes of trade.
"Failure" means breach and provocation. "By which" means by which practice. "Outcaste" refers to an outcaste among lay followers (*upāsaka*). "Dirt" refers to the dirt of a lay follower.
"Despised" refers to one who is base among lay followers. [This applies] regarding the Buddha and others, as well as regarding karma and the fruits of karma.
Lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) is the opposite of faith (*saddhā*); it is wrong resolve (*micchā-adhimokkha*). One who possesses the aforementioned lack of faith is "faithless" (*assaddha*).
One who, by way of the aforementioned failure in virtue (*sīla-vipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīva-vipatti*), is immoral is "unvirtuous" (*dussīla*).

[One who is deluded] by means of the auspiciousness seen, heard, sensed, or cognized—which is reckoned as the "superstitious excitement" (*kotūhala*) imagined by foolish people, thinking, "By this view and so forth, such-and-such is an auspicious sign."* (*The asterisk indicates a note in the original source.)*

He is possessed of [the view] that omens and auspicious signs are [the cause of success]. "He believes in auspicious signs" means he believes only in auspicious signs categorized as seen-auspiciousness and so forth.
"Not in karma" means he does not believe in the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā*).

"Outside of this" means outside of this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, in the systems of outsiders (*bāhiraka*). "He seeks out those worthy of offerings" means he perceives as deserving of offerings those who have practiced wrongly.
He seeks out [worthy recipients]. He performs prior service means he first performs wholesome deeds such as giving and honoring.
Here, by treating the seeking of those worthy of offerings and the performance of prior service as one, five factors are to be understood.
Success should be understood as the opposite of what was stated regarding failure. However, this is the distinction: for all four assemblies...

In the sense of producing delight, a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is itself a jewel; thus, he is a "lay-follower-jewel" (*upāsakaratana*). By virtue of the fragrance of his qualities, beauty, fame, and reputation, a lay follower is himself a lotus;
thus, he is a "lay-follower-lotus" (*upāsakapaduma*). Likewise, he is a "lay-follower-white-lotus" (*upāsakapuṇḍarīka*).

The word "in the beginning" (*ādimhi*) has the sense of "from the beginning. "At the limit" (*koṭiyam*) means at the ultimate boundary. "By way of the dwelling" (*vihāraggena*) means by way of the section of the chamber; [as in the passage]: "In this..."
The meaning is: "by way of each respective place of residence," as in the passage beginning, "for those dwelling in the womb, this fruit is attained.
*Ajjatan* means simply "today.
By the phrase "endowed with life-breaths" (*pāṇehi upetaṃ*), he demonstrates that going for refuge lasts until the end of one's life, saying: "as long as my life..."
Having spoken these words beginning with “it proceeds,” he then spoke the passage beginning with “For I...
in order to clarify the intention that had arisen in the brahmin— that he would protect his taking of refuge by honoring those three objects even at the cost of his life—
expressing how he honors that triad of objects even with his very life, meaning as long as his life-breaths endure, and how he approaches them not merely with words.

The meaning here should be understood as follows: it is not by a single arising of the thought alone, but rather that one approaches [the precepts] for as long as life lasts by way of relinquishing living beings. 17–19.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "Jāṇussoṇī": this is not a name given to him by his parents; rather, it was obtained upon his attainment of a particular position.
Pointing this out, he said: “*Jāṇussoṇī* is, it seems, a title,” and so forth. “One office” means one position as a domestic chaplain (*purohita*).
They say that he received it along with the *uṇhīsa* (the turban) and other regalia, and that it was granted to him by the king.

Therefore, he said: “Because he had received the honor of *Jāṇussoṇī* in the presence of the king. The rest here is self-evident. There is nothing further to be said regarding the eighth and ninth [chapters].
20–21. "Ill-placed" (*dunnikkhitta*) means it has been poorly placed, having been fixed in the mind by reversing the sequence of words and phrases.
A "word" (*pada*) is so called because meaning (*attha*) is reached (*pajjati*) or known through it; a "phrase" (*byañjana*) is so called because it manifests or makes clear the meaning;
it is simply a word. For this very reason, he said: "In reverse order... [etc. ...it is called a phrase. Apart from the collection of words, [there is nothing] separate...

He said, "There is no such thing as *pāḷi*," [meaning] "Both of these are indeed called *pāḷi*. For the very foundation (*āḷi*) of the series of words that have been well-proclaimed (*pakaṭṭha*) is called *pāḷi*.
The rest here, including the eleventh [section], is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the Chapter on Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇavagga*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Chapter on the Foolish (Bālavagga) 22–24.
The first, second, and third [suttas] of the third [chapter] have their meanings already explained. 25.
Regarding the fourth, "should be led" (netabbo) means that he must be brought [to understanding] by being fetched from elsewhere; the sense is that he must be enlightened and made known [the truth].
27. In the sixth [case], "even if they do not conceal while committing" means that even if those who commit acts such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*) do so without concealment.
It is called "concealed" precisely because it is worthy of concealment due to its being a state censurable by the wise.
As for the specific locations such as Avīci and the beings reborn there, they are included under the term "hell" (*niraya*).
He said: "Hell refers to the aggregates (khandhas) together with their locations. Since there is no separate, distinct region called the animal realm (tiracchānayoni), he said:
"In the animal realm, only the aggregates are found.

Regarding the tenth [section], the meaning is as follows: it is the fruit (phala); because its existence is dependent upon that [fruit], it has mastery (vasa) over it, thus it is "the mastery of the meaning" (atthavasa); he said "the mastery of the meaning" to mean the cause (hetu).
“Causes. Regarding “forest-dwelling places” (*araññavanapatthāni*): these are forest-dwelling places that have attained the characteristics of a forest.
For the word *vanapattha* also applies to a thicket-like cluster of trees; therefore, the term “forest” (*arañña*) is included [in the compound].

It is called a “forest” (*vana*) because it is frequented (*vanīyati*) by those desiring seclusion, or because it is sought out (*vanute*) like one begging for a place to dwell for the sake of one’s own welfare. They are established there.

In this context, "forest-dwelling" (*vanapattha*) refers to a dwelling place in the forests or in dense thickets, so called because those desiring seclusion seek it for the sake of attaining the specific qualities intended therein.
The phrase "even though" (*kiñcāpi*) is a particle used in the sense of granting permission or expressing esteem. What does it grant permission for?

It grants that, in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*), the state of being a forest is "outside the village. Therefore he said, "in the non-figurative sense," and so forth. What does it express esteem for?
The state of accomplishing the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññakaṅga*). For that which accomplishes the forest-dweller’s practice should specifically be called “the forest.
Therefore he said: “That which is five hundred bow-lengths,” and so forth. “Having gone out beyond the threshold-stone” (*indakhīla*) means having gone out from the threshold-stone;
the meaning is: starting from outside of that. Or, “beyond the threshold-stone” refers to where two or three [houses]...
"Gateposts": from outside the gatepost in that case. Where there is none, they say it is "from the place where it [the gate] is located.
"Vicinity of a village" means near a village. "A place not within the precincts" means a place that need not be frequented for daily duties;
therefore he said, "where neither plowing nor sowing is done."
"And my own dwelling in happiness in this very life": by this, the Teacher proclaims his own delight in seclusion.
Therein, "this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammo*) refers to this manifest personal existence; "dwelling in happiness" (*sukhavihāro*) refers to the well-being of the four postures.
For when one is alone in the forest, even including the performance of such functions as defecation and urination, all postures are [comfortable].
They are conducive to ease; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "a pleasant abiding in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra*).
And "out of compassion for future generations": how is it that future generations are shown compassion by dwelling in the forest?
Is it so? For when sons of noble family who have gone forth out of faith see the Blessed One’s dwelling in the forest, they will think:
"The Blessed One himself does not abandon forest lodgings—even he for whom there is nothing to be fully understood, nothing to be abandoned, nothing to be developed, and nothing to be realized;
how much more so, then, must we? Thinking thus, they will consider that they must certainly dwell there. In this way, very quickly...
“They will become those who bring an end to suffering. Thus, the later generation is shown compassion.
Demonstrating this point, he said: “Compassionate toward my later disciples. 32.

In the eleventh [verse], “conducive to true knowledge” (*vijjābhāgiya*) means they partake of true knowledge; it also means they function within the sphere of true knowledge, that is, within the constituent parts of true knowledge.
"Conducive to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*). "It cuts off the foothold" means it cuts off the support of the path-consciousness;
the meaning is that it does not allow the path-consciousness to be established. "Having eradicated" means having pulled out by the roots through complete severance.
"In eight places" means in the eight objects, such as the Buddha and so forth. "By the fading away through the destruction of lust" means by the fading away characterized as the destruction of lust.
"By means of dispassion" means by bringing about the state of non-arising for passion; thus it is said.
The commentary on the Bālavagga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Samacittavagga.

33. In the first [verse] of the fourth [chapter], it is called *bhūmi* because things are established (*patiṭṭhahanti*) therein. The "ground of bad persons" (*asappurisabhūmi*) is the ground belonging to bad persons;
the same method applies to the "ground of good persons" (*sappurisabhūmi*). One who does not recognize what has been done is "ungrateful" (*akataññū*);

this is an *asamattha-samāsa* (a compound where the members do not govern each other) because the meaning is understood, just as in the case of "those who do not look at the sun" (*asūriyapassā*) and so forth. Therefore he said, "one who does not recognize what has been done. Regarding the term "one who acknowledges what has not been done" (*akatavedī*), here too...

The same method applies here. "Having made it public, he does not know" means that having made it known in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, and so forth—thinking, "This and this was done by him to me"—he does not know;
what is meant is that he does not proclaim it. "Upaññātaṃ" (known by approach) means known by way of praise.
Therefore he said, "Vaṇṇitaṃ" (praised), and so forth.
34. "One whose lifespan is measured by a hundred years" means a hundred-year-lived one (*vassasatāyuka*).

And that state of being a hundred-year-lived one occurs only for one born during the time when the lifespan is a hundred years, not for anyone else; thus he said, "born during the time when the lifespan is a hundred years.

"One who lives for a hundred years by virtue of his conduct" means a hundred-year-living one (*vassatajīvī*). And "a hundred years" is used in the accusative case to express continuous duration (*accantasamyoga*). Therefore he said, "the entire hundred years."

Regarding the phrase “while living”: because the mother is even more helpful than both parents, and because she is the one who must be repaid by virtue of her preeminence, they speak of the right shoulder-blade.
“Having given the blood of the heart” refers to milk; for blood indeed undergoes transformation into the state of milk.
“Tyāssa” means “those of his. The rest here is self-evident.

35. Regarding the phrase "In the third [case], he approached him": in order to reveal and demonstrate the specific intention with which that brahmin approached the Blessed One, the text says, "For that brahmin...
and so forth. Regarding the phrase "a question on missing the mark" (*virajjhana-pañha*):
it refers to a kind of question such that, when asked, one answers by missing the point, being unable to provide a correct and unerring response.
The meaning is as follows. A "question with two points" (*ubhatokoṭika-pañha*) is a question joined by both sides.
For instance, when asked, "What does Master Gotama profess?", one might say either "I am a proponent of action" (*kiriyavādi*) or "I am a proponent of non-action" (*akiriyavādi*).
Therefore, in answering this question, "I am a proponent of action" constitutes one side and "I am a proponent of non-action" constitutes the second; thus, it is joined by these two sides.
This is the question. To "spit out" (*uggilitun*) means that being unable to speak after having released two alternatives, one will not be able to take it outside or remove it from its meaning.
For by releasing the two alternatives, one indeed takes it outside.

To "swallow down" (*niggilitun*) means that being unable to extract [the answer] by pointing out a fault in the question, one will not be able to make it enter. In that regard, having pointed out a fault...
For "carrying away" means he causes [the object] to enter by making it disappear, as if having swallowed it. "What-doctrine-holding" (*kiṃladdhika*) means what-view-holding (*kiṃdiṭṭhika*).
It is called a "doctrine" (*vāda*) because they speak by means of it; thus, it is a view. "What-doctrine-possessing" (*kiṃvādī*) means:

what is his doctrine? "What-proclaiming" (*kimakkhāyī*) means what-expounding; that is, what kind of discourse on the Dhamma. Therefore he said: "He asks: 'What indeed... and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.

36. In the fourth [verse], they are "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*) because they deserve offerings (*dakkhiṇa*). "Sacrificial gift" (*āhuna*) refers to giving; they are "worthy of sacrificial gifts" (*āhuneyya*) because they deserve that. 37.
Regarding the fifth [verse], [the question] "How was this woman named Migāramātā born?
is answered with "For she," and so forth. "Of the eldest son" means of the son born first among her own children. It is because she shares the same name as the merchant Ayyaka.
Because he had the same name as the merchant Migāra. It is said that on the day of the naming ceremony for his eldest son, they gave him the very same name as his grandfather, the merchant Migāra.
"Not living in a fixed residence" means not having a permanent stay in one particular monastery.
"Constantly used" means regularly utilized. [Objection: But did the Blessed One not sometimes go on tour?
He departs; how then does he enjoy those lodgings as a permanent use? To this he says: "Even after wandering during the season and the rains," and so forth.
Therein, "the season and the rains" refers to the winter and summer.
"Leaving aside the path" means leaving aside the path by which the Elder was coming. "Hot clouds" refers to those that give rise to masses of clouds serving as conditions for the hot season.

These are the sons of the gods (*devaputta*). It is said that at the very moment such a thought arises in them, a mass of clouds—neither too thick nor too thin—that pervades the desired location with heat, courses through the sky covering it from here to there. This same principle applies to the clouds of cold and the clouds of rain.
However, the cloud-deities (*abbhavalāhaka-devatā*) are those who produce merely a layer of clouds, without the cold, heat, or rain.
[The clouds] are to be understood [in this way]. Or rather, they belong solely to the wind; for that reason, the deities are called "wind-clouds" (*vātavalāhakā*).
And herein, whatever cloud arises during the rainy season and the cool season is merely of natural origin, produced by the seasons.
But as for that which arises from within the clouds—a "super-cloud" (*atiabbha*)—which covers even the sun and moon for seven days and creates total darkness;
And as for the cloud that appears during the months of Citta and Vesākha, it should be understood that this cloud has arisen through the power of deities.
As for the natural winds of the north, south, and so forth that occur in their respective seasons, these are temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
Among winds, there is also what is called a "gale," which shatters the trunks and branches of forest trees; this, as well as any other unseasonable wind, [is also temperature-originated].
And this [heat] has arisen through the power of a deity. That which is heat in the summer is merely ordinary, being temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhānika*).
However, that which is excessively hot even during the heat, and the heat that arises during the cold season, have arisen through the power of a deity.
That which is cold in the rainy season and in winter is merely temperature-originated. But that which is excessively cold even during the cold [season],...
The cold that arises in the summer is produced through the power of the deities. The rain that falls during the four months of the rainy season is produced solely by the seasonal element;
however, the excessive rain that falls even during the dry season, as well as the rain during the months of Cittā and Vesākha, is produced through the power of the deities.
The story is this: It is said that a certain rain-cloud deity approached a senior monk (*thera*) who was a dweller of Mount Tagara and had destroyed all taints (*khīṇāsava*).
Having paid homage, he stood before him. The elder asked, "Who are you? "I am a rain-cloud deity, venerable sir," he replied.
"Is it true, venerable sir, that the rain-god rains according to your mind? "Yes, venerable sir. "Then we wish to see him."
“Venerable sir, will it rain? “The sound of clouds or thunder is not heard; how shall we get wet?
“Venerable sir, the rain falls by our own thought. You may enter the leaf-hut.
“Very well, divine son,” he said, and having washed his feet, he entered the leaf-hut. As soon as he had entered, the divine son sang a song.
He raised his hand, and for a distance of three leagues all around, there became a single mass of cloud. The Elder entered the leaf-hut while it was still half-flooded.
Although the deities mentioned below are indeed the Cātumahārājika gods, they were previously described according to their specific distinctions;
now, however, referring generally to other sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) gods of the first dhyāna level, he says "the Cātumahārājikas."
The Cātumahārājikās are those who belong to the four Great Kings known as Dhatarattha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera;
they reside in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among them, some dwell upon the mountains and some dwell in the sky.
Their lineage extends down to the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. [Also included are] the Khiḍḍāpadosikas, the Manopadosikas, and the divine son Candima.
"Sūriya" (the Sun) and "Devaputta" (the Son of the Gods)—all these belong specifically to the realm of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*).
"Tāvatiṃsa" is the name of the Thirty-three Gods; they too are both mountain-dwellers and sky-dwellers, their lineage extending as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.
The same applies to the Yāma gods and the others. For even within a single divine world, there are many gods.
There is no succession that does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.

Therein, having passed away together with the young brahmin Māgha in the village of Macala, thirty-three who performed meritorious deeds were reborn here; thus, that place where they dwelt together is called "Tettiṃsa" (the Thirty-Three).
That very place is "Tāvatiṃsa," and because these [gods] have that as their dwelling, they are called "Tāvatiṃsā. For this reason...

Furthermore, the six sense-sphere heavenly worlds (chakāmāvacara-devaloka) exist in all other world-systems as well. For this has been said: "A thousand [worlds] of the Cātumahārājika devas, a thousand of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is merely a conventional designation (nāmapaṇṇatti) for those heavenly worlds.

They are called Yāma because they have gone away from suffering (dukkha). They are called Tusita because they have gone to, or reached, satisfaction (tusa) through their own glorious success. Regarding Nimmāna...
Those who delight in these [creations] are the *Nimmānaratin* (Delight-in-Creation). The "deities who exercise power over others' creations" are the *Paranimmitavasavatti* gods;
they are called *Paranimmitavasavatti* because they exercise power (*vasaṃ vattenti*) over enjoyments created by others.
One is a *Brahmā* because one has been expanded (*brūhita*) and grown great through various distinguished qualities such as the jhānas. Because of possessing beauty...
Because he possesses great longevity and is a "great Brahmā" due to his status as a Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā) among those such as the Brahmapārisajjas, he is called Mahābrahmā.
Those who exist in his retinue are the Brahmapārisajjas. Those who stand in the position of his chaplain are the Brahmapurohitas.
Because they possess limited radiance compared to the Ābhassarās, they are the Parittābhās. Because they possess immeasurable radiance, they are the Appamāṇābhās.
They are called *ābhassara* (radiant) because light issues forth from their bodies, streaming and flashing like the flame of a lamp;
or alternatively, they are *ābhassara* because they have the nature of shining (*ābhāsana*) with the aforementioned radiance. *Subhā* means beautiful radiance.

For *subhā* refers to a body-radiance that is compact and motionless; since they possess such limited (*paritta*) beauty, they are the *parittasubha* (Limited Beauty). They are *appamāṇa* (immeasurable).
"These are beautiful" means "immeasurably beautiful" (*appamāṇasubhā*).

Because they are strewn and overspread with beauty—that is, with the radiance and color of their bodies—being a single mass as magnificent as a glowing lump of gold placed inside a golden casket, they are called "overspread with beauty" (*subhakiṇṇā*).
In this context, although it should be stated as *subhākiṇṇā* ("strewn with beautiful radiance"), the vowel *bhā* is shortened [to *bha*] due to the final [syllable].

By changing the letter *ṇ* to *h*, it is stated as "Subhakiṇhā. They have abundant fruit; thus they are "Vehapphalā" (Abundant-Fruit). Furthermore, they have the fruit of abundant, peaceful happiness, beauty, and so forth.
Because they do not abandon their own station for even a short time, they are "Avihā" (Unabandoning).

Because they cannot be tormented by anyone, they are "Atappā" (Untormentable). Because they can be seen with ease and pleasure due to their delightful appearance, they are "Sudassā" (Beautiful-to-See).
They are called *sudassī* because they see rightly through their virtue due to the state of being perfectly pure in vision.
They are called *akaniṭṭhā* because, owing to their connection with superior attainments, there is no attainment lower than theirs among them.

"By body-witnesses" means by those who have become witnesses by way of receiving the teaching through the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "Halāhala" means a tumultuous noise. "With a sublime mind" means with a mind of direct knowledge based on the fourth jhāna.
But is it not improper to say, "The internal is sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), and the external is fine-material and immaterial existence (rūpārūpabhavo)"?
For it is appropriate to say that the existence in which beings dwell for a longer period of time is their "internal," while that in which they dwell for a shorter period of time is their "external.
And in the fine-material and immaterial existences, beings dwell for a much longer time.

Since there is less [time] in the existence of sense-desire (kāmabhava), he asks why it was said, "The internal is the existence of sense-desire; the external is the existence of form and the formless," by saying "Even though...
and so forth. "The fourth division itself" refers to the fourth incalculable eon (asaṅkhyeyyakappa) known as the period of stabilization following evolution (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi).

"In the others" refers to the three other incalculable eons consisting of the periods of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa), the stability following dissolution (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyi), and the period of evolution (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi).
“Ālaya” means attachment. “Patthanā” is the aspiration: “How indeed might we be reborn there? “Abhilāsa” is the desire to be reborn there.
With the words “Therefore,” etc., he concludes the matter as it has been stated.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: because no defilement whatsoever has been suppressed, even by way of mere suppression in any manner...

The unliberated state of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), which functions as a specific condition for the grasping that proceeds by taking the self as its object and referring to internal apprehension, is called "internal" (*ajjhatta*).
In this context, "bondage" refers to the internal fetter (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*); one who is bound by that is "possessed of internal fetters" (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*).
By way of its opposite, one is "possessed of external fetters" (*bahiddhāsaṃyojana*).

Having shown the internal fetter and the external fetter by way of lustful passion alone, he now says, "Or the lower-tier [fetters]," etc., in order to show them also by way of the lower-tier and higher-tier fetters.
"Lower" (oraṃ) refers to the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu); they are called "lower-tier" (orambhāgiyāni) because they partake of that lower realm as a condition for rebirth-linking.

In this context, they are called *saṃyojanāni* (fetters) because they yoke (*saṃyojenti*) the result of kamma to a being through suffering. These are: personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), and aversion (*paṭigha*).

The "upper" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpadhātu*). According to the method already stated, those which partake of that upper realm are the "higher-fettering" (*uddhambhāgiya*) fetters. These are:

lust for the form realm (*rūparāga*), lust for the formless realm (*arūparāga*), conceit (*māna*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and ignorance (*avijjā*). Alternatively, the "lower part" (*orambhāga*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), as opposed to the existence of the form and formless realms.
Because they belong to the lower [realms] and because they serve as conditions for rebirth therein, they are "favourable to the lower part" (*orambhāgiya*), just as one says "a calf-tethering rope.
The "upper part" (*uddhambhāga*) refers to the sublime state (*mahaggatabhāva*); those favourable to that are "favourable to the upper part" (*uddhambhāgiya*).
Like a stone tied to one's feet, the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojana*) have the characteristic of dragging one downward.
The five higher fetters (pañcuddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) have the appearance of pulling upwards, like tree branches grasped by the hands.

For those who have not abandoned personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and the other [fetters], even if they are reborn in the Peak of Existence (bhavagga), these [fetters] pull them back down and cause them to fall right into the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).
Therefore, these five prevent one from going forward and bring back again that which has already gone. [The same applies to] the five beginning with attachment to the fine-material realm (rūparāga).
They do not prevent one who is departing, yet they do not allow one to return.
Since the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) become negligible when the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) have been severed and the necessary conditions are met,
this is stated not by way of classifying even those ordinary persons (puthujjana) for whom [the fetters] still obtain, but rather by way of the application of the noble ones (ariya).
Desiring to analyze [the matter], he said, "And both of these," and so forth. Therein, "of the great mass of people dependent on the round" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"Dichotomized" means divided into two modes by way of the realms of sense-desire, fortunate rebirths, and the form and formless existences.
The simile of the calf and the *sāla* tree is self-evident in its meaning. However, in the application of the simile, because no defilement has been suppressed in anyone [among them],...
In some way or another, sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) is "internal" because it is a specific condition for internal grasping;
for these beings, it is called "inside" in the sense of being within them. Form and formless existence (*rūpārūpabhava*) are, by contrast, "external.

For indeed, one whose lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) have not been abandoned is said to possess internal fetters; whereas one whose those have been abandoned [is said to possess external fetters].

Thus, he is one whose fetters are directed outward. Therefore, because the bonds within have not been severed and because the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds externally, he is said to be "bound within and lying outside.
