For the designation "lying" is used by way of the continuous flow of the life-continuum. Granted that their external bonds are also unsevered, it is stated thus because the internal bond is the very root [of the problem].
Therefore he said: "But their fetter is bound only to the sense-sphere realm. By this method, the meaning should be understood for the remaining three [realms] as well.
And to this extent, the particle *kira* has the sense of indicating disapproval; by it, he demonstrates his own lack of approval for the teacher’s doctrine (*ācariyavāda*).
"Virtuous" (*sīlavā*) is taken as a concise designation for virtue, because it is grasped through its general commonality without specifying particular distinctions.
Regarding the phrase "and that is fourfold," the Elder Teacher (Ācariyatthera) said, "having recited the fourfold purification-sīla. "Therein" means within the fourfold purification-sīlas.
"The foremost sīla" means the preeminent sīla. "In both cases" refers to the enumeration (uddesa) and the exposition (niddesa);
the intention is that even in the enumeration, as in the exposition, only the restraint of the Pātimokkha was spoken of by the Elder when he said "one who is virtuous" (sīlavā).
For in the Canon, the taking up of virtue is presented solely by way of restraint according to the Pātimokkha. Therefore, he said, "It is precisely the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.
Therein, by means of this restriction, he illustrates that the other three [types of virtue] are included within the Pātimokkha at least in part.

For instance, in the case of looking at what should not be looked at, transgressing a training rule for the sake of one's livelihood, or using requisites for the sick without due reflection—[these are instances where the other virtues are partially subsumed].
"And 'offense is prescribed'": "Three" refers to the virtue of restraint of the faculties and so forth.
Regarding the statement "there is a place where virtue is mentioned," is there any place where they are included under the synonym of "virtue" in some sutta, such as "restraint by the Pātimokkha"?

By saying "not granting permission," he speaks as if asking by way of a formal inquiry (*upacāra*), since he does not reject [the question] in the presence of the teacher. Therefore, he said: "without granting permission."
"Merely guarding the six doors" refers to its lightness, because it returns to its natural state by means of mere mental resolve (*cittādhiṭṭhāna*).
The same method applies to the other two [guarding the mind and guarding the faculties]. "Mere arising of conditions" shows the cause by means of the fruit;
for the arising of conditions has production as its cause. "This purpose" means this motive for the utilization of this condition.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). By the phrase "not figuratively" (*nippariyāyena*), he shows that the three [other types of virtue], such as restraint of the sense faculties, are called "figurative virtue" (*pariyāyasīla*) because they function as the preservation of the primary virtue (*padhānasīla*).

Now, in order to clarify through a simile—both by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) and by way of agreement (*anvaya*)—the status of the *pātimokkhasaṃvara* (Pātimokkha restraint) as the primary virtue, he says "Of whom," and so forth. Therein, "that" refers to the *pātimokkhasaṃvara*.
The remaining [virtues] are the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth.

"Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the virtue of the training rules (sikkhāpada-sīla) known as the *pātimokkha*—so called because it protects (*pāti*) and guards (*rakkhati*), and because it releases (*mokkheti*) or liberates (*moceti*) one from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth. Furthermore, that...
Because one who is thus constituted is said to be "endowed" with that, it is therefore stated: "endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

Another method: because of the powerful nature of the defilements, because evil deeds are easy to perform, and because meritorious deeds are difficult to perform, the worldling (puthujjana) is prone to falling repeatedly into the states of misery; thus he is a "pātī. Due to impermanence...

Or, because it wanders and moves without stability—like a potter’s wheel driven by the force of karma through states of existence such as birth and so on—it has the nature of going, and thus is a *pāti*.
Alternatively, it is a *pāti* because it has the nature of casting down (*pātana*) the individual self (*attabhāva*) into various classes of beings through death;
that is, the continuum of beings, or simply the mind itself. That which releases (*mokkheti*) this *pāti* from the suffering of saṃsāra is the *pātimokkha*.
For by the liberation of the mind, a being is said to be "liberated. Indeed, it is said:
"Through the purification of the mind, they are cleansed," and "The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Alternatively, one is called a *pāti* because, by means of causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*), one falls, goes, or wanders in *saṃsāra*. [Regarding] "those hindered by ignorance..."

For it is said: "Of beings who wander and transmigrate, bound by craving. It is the *pātimokkha* because by means of this there is liberation (*mokkha*) for that being who is falling (*pātino*) from the three defilements, beginning with craving.
Its formation as a compound should be understood in the same way as in terms such as *kaṇṭhekāḷo*.
Alternatively, it is *pāti* because it causes one to fall (*pāteti*), casts down (*vinipāteti*), or brings suffering; that is, the mind. For it has been said:
“The world is led by the mind, by the mind it is drawn along.

Because liberation comes through this for one who goes forward, it is the *pātimokkha*. Or else, it is a *pāti* because by means of it one falls into the suffering of the states of woe and the suffering of *saṃsāra*;
that is, the defilement consisting of craving and so forth. For it is said: “Craving leads a person about; craving is a person’s companion,” and so forth.
It is called *pātimokkha* because liberation (*mokkha*) falls away from it.
Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because things fall into it; that is, the six internal and external sense bases. For it is said:
"The world has arisen in the six; in the six it forms intimacy."
Therefore, it is the *pātimokkha* because it is liberation (*mokkha*) from what is called the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
Alternatively, it is *pātī*, meaning "falling," because falling (*pāta*)—that is, the miserable states (*vinipāta*)—exists within it; thus, *saṃsāra*.

Liberation from that is the *pātimokkha*. Or else, the Blessed One, as the Lord of Dhamma due to his sovereignty over the entire world, is called "Patī"; [the *pātimokkha*] is so named because one is liberated by means of this.
It is liberation (*mokkha*); it is the liberation that is foremost (*pati*), hence it is the *pātimokkha*, because it is prescribed by that [liberation].
Or else, because it is the root of all virtues, it is "foremost" (*pati*) in the sense of being supreme, and it is "liberation" (*mokkha*) in the sense already stated;
thus it is *patimokkha*, and *patimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*. For it has been said: "‘Pātimokkha’—this is its beginning, this is its mouth, this is its pre-eminence," and so on in detail.

Alternatively, *pa-* is the syllable *pa*; *ati* is a particle in the sense of "absolute. Therefore, it is called *pātimokkha* because it absolutely releases (*mokkheti*) by means of various ways (*pakārehi*).

For this virtue (*sīla*) itself releases or liberates absolutely through its own nature as a factor of that stage (*tadaṅga*), and—when accompanied by concentration and wisdom—it releases or liberates absolutely through suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*).
Or else, it is called *pātimokkha* because there is release (*mokkha*) for each and every one (*pati pati*).
The meaning of *pātimokkha* is "liberation from each respective fault of transgression. Thus, *pātimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, *mokkha* means Nibbāna; it is called *pātimokkha* because it is a reflection (*paṭibimba*) of that liberation.
For the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) is the arising of Nibbāna, like the dawn preceding the sun; it is its counterpart, because it extinguishes the defilements as appropriate.
*Pātimokkha*: it is *paṭimokkha*, and *paṭimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*.

Alternatively, it is *paṭimokkha* because it leads toward liberation (*mokkha*), or it is *paṭimokkha* because it is directed toward liberation; thus, *pātimokkha* is simply *paṭimokkha*. In this way, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* should be understood here.

"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*) means endowed with conduct consisting of non-transgression in body and speech, and with a resort consisting of not frequenting prostitutes and the like.
“Endowed with resort” means endowed with conduct and resort. “In trifling matters” means in minor matters that do not lead to an offense;

others say it refers to mere *dukkaṭa* and *dubbhāsita* offenses. “In blameworthy things” means in censurable things. Since these are exclusively of an unwholesome nature, he says “in unwholesome states.
“Seeing fear” means one whose nature it is to see [things] as fearful, even [those that are] merely atomic.
One who is of a fearful nature, having made even a minor fault as large as Mount Sineru. "Having properly undertaken" means having properly, respectfully, and in its entirety undertaken it.
Regarding the phrase "in the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*), this is the locative case used in the sense of selection;

thus, showing that it is a selection from a part of the whole, he states the meaning as: "having undertaken this or that particular training rule among the training rules, one trains. It refers specifically to the training rule itself.

The intention is that [these] must be undertaken and trained in. "Whatever among the training rules" means whatever is to be trained in, categorized as the original formulations (*mūlapaññatti*), subsequent formulations (*anupaññatti*), universal formulations (*sabbatthapaññatti*), partial formulations (*padesapaññatti*), and so forth, within the divisions of the training.
Furthermore, the virtue (*sīla*) which is to be practiced and fulfilled is of only two kinds by way of its doors; thus he said: "bodily..."

"Or verbal. In this interpretation of the meaning, "in the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*) is the locative case used in the sense of a substratum (*ādhāre*), because no separate category of training is mentioned.
Therefore he said, "all that. "A certain divine assembly" (*aññataraṃ devaghaṭaṃ*) means a certain class of devas.

"One who comes back" (*āgāmī hoti*) means one whose nature it is to come by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The same method applies here for the term "one who has come" (*āgantā*). "By this factor" (*iminā aṅgena*) means by this reason.
Since one who practices dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) for the most part applies himself to the meditation subject by way of the analysis of the four elements, he says:
"for the bhikkhu practicing the meditation subject of the elements, who is a practitioner of dry-insight. Concluding by summarizing the point already stated, he says:
"By the first factor," and so forth.
"The subtlety of the mind here should be understood as having reached a state of mere pleasure"; thus he said, "For all those," and so forth.

"By way of the lineage" means solely for the purpose of establishing the textual tradition, not for the sake of producing any path or fruit for the Elder, nor for the purpose of enjoining him to right practice; this is the intended meaning.
38. Regarding "Mahākaccāna" in the sixth [case]: in his time as a householder, he was the son of the royal chaplain of Ujjenī; he was handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and golden-hued.
As for the tree named Varaṇa, because the city was situated not far from it, it too is referred to by the word "Varaṇa";
thus it is said, "there is a city named Varaṇā. The dual compound is to be connected with each term individually.
By joining the word *hetu* (cause) individually with each term while explaining that they "occur," he says: "due to the cause of adherence to sensual lust," and so forth.
To show the meaning that arises when [the word] is connected with the term *hetu*, he says: "this is what is meant," and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase "because one has adhered through sensual lust," he elucidates the meaning of the expression "due to the cause of adherence to sensual lust."

Likewise, by the words "bound" (*vinibaddhattā*) and so forth, [the text refers to] the causes such as being bound by sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Facing toward that" (*tato mukho*) means directed toward that.
"Measures" (*māna*) refers to measuring vessels such as the *āḷhaka*. The rest here is self-evident. 39.
In the seventh [verse], "at Madhurā" means at Uttaramadhurā. "In Gundāvana" means in Kaṇhagundāvana; "in Kāḷapippalivana" means...
The meaning is as follows: "Worn out by old age" means worn out by aging (*jarā*), not like one worn out by illness and so forth, nor one overcome by untimely aging.
"Advanced in years" means that because he is worn out, he has reached an advanced stage of life through the growth of virtue and other qualities.
"Great in birth" means great due to the greatness of his lineage—that is, being of long standing—not on account of wealth, retinue, and the like.
The meaning is as follows. Regarding the term *addhagata*, the word *addha* here signifies a long period of time; thus he says, "having passed over a long duration of time.

Regarding *vaya*, this is an analysis [of the compound] by eliding the first member of the word; thus he says, "the later stage of life" (*pacchimavaya*). The meaning is that one has reached the later stage of life, which consists of the third division of a hundred years.
It is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) because the fruit exists therein, as it depends upon it for its existence; thus he says, "by which cause," and so forth, to indicate the reason.

"Fully matured" (*paripakka*) means transformed, the sense being that it has reached a state of growth. "Fruitlessly old" (*mogha-jinna*) means one who is old in name only, due to the absence of internal qualities that provide stability.
Since even a young child is called "tender" (*dahara*), [the author] uses this term to distinguish [the subject] from such a person.

"Youthful" is what was said. Since beings whose first stage of life has already passed naturally have grey hair, the phrase "with very black hair" was used to show that he is established in the first stage of life. "With noble" means with desirable;
for some, even though they are young, are one-eyed or suffer from some other deformity such as a crooked limb, and thus are not endowed with noble youth.

[He] is so called. Furthermore, one who is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with every excellence, and who—adorned with whatever ornaments and attire he desires—moves about like a son of the gods, is said to be "endowed with noble youth.
It is for this very reason that it says, "endowed with that youth," and so forth.

"In whom truth and the Dhamma": in that person, because the fourfold truth has been penetrated in sixteen ways and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma has been realized through knowledge, these exist. "Non-violence" is merely a designation;
the meaning is that in whom there is the cultivation of all four kinds of immeasurables. "Restraint and self-control" refers to virtue.
And there is restraint of the sense faculties. "One who has vomited out impurity" means one whose defilements have been extracted by means of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*).
"The wise one" (*dhīra*) means one endowed with fortitude (*dhiti*). "An elder" (*thera*): the meaning is that he is called an elder because he is possessed of these causes for stability.
40. In the eighth [verse], having extracted the phrase "the thieves are powerful," [one should explain] by what causes they are powerful.
To demonstrate their possession of these [qualities], he said, "endowed with wings," and so forth.
In this context, "endowed with a place of residence" means possessing mountain fastnesses and the like. "To enter within" (atiyātuṃ) means to go inside, that is, to enter;
however, since such entry into the interior occurs for one who has previously gone outside for some reason, he said, "having wandered abroad through the countryside," and so on.

“Niyyātuṃ” means to go out. And since that going out occurs when there is something to be done outside, he said, “Thieves are plundering the countryside,” and so forth. “Anusaññātuṃ” means to wander about. The rest here is self-evident. 41.
Regarding the phrase “the cause for the legal issue of wrong practice”: here, the prefix *adhi* is meaningless; thus he said, “of wrong practice.”
"...the instrumental cause. "One who does not accomplish" means one who does not achieve or fulfill [it].

It is called *ñāya* (method) because it goes toward Nibbāna by way of penetration; that very thing, in the sense of supporting one who possesses it from falling into the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*), is *dhamma* (the teaching/principle);
thus it is *ñāyadhamma*, the Noble Path. However, since it is intended here together with insight (*vipassanā*), he said: "together with insight."
“Path. *Ārādhanā* means accomplishment; however, since that is desired through fulfillment and completion, it is therefore said: “to fulfill and to complete. 42.
In the tenth [case], “by those wrongly grasped” means by those wrongly grasped in both meaning and phrasing, by way of deficiency, excess, perversion, repetition of words, and so forth.

The meaning is: "having grasped them in reverse order. However, this mention of "grasping in an inverted sequence" is merely illustrative, since a wrong grasp can also occur by way of deficiency, excess, and so forth.
For this very reason, he said: "showing the meaning and the text of the suttas wrongly grasped by themselves as being superior."
The commentary on the Chapter on Even-mindedness is finished.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on the Assembly. 43.

Regarding the first [offense] of the fifth [chapter]: "Possessed of restlessness" means [the perception of what is] allowable in what is unallowable, and [the perception of what is] unallowable in what is allowable.
[It arises] through the perception of what is improper as proper, the perception of what is blameless as blameworthy, and the perception of what is blameworthy as blameless;

it is characterized by restlessness. For those who are ignorant of the Vinaya, unskilled in the phenomena that lead to defilement and purification, who act with possessiveness and are full of remorse—in them, restlessness that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases further.
It reaches fullness. Because it is hollow due to the absence of core substance, it is like a reed; thus it is called a "naḷa. He says, "unnaḷā means 'upraised reeds.
Therefore he says, "those with upraised, hollow conceit. For conceit is especially hollow when it occurs in the form of thinking oneself superior to one who is superior, or equal to one who is equal.
By "cāpallena" is meant by way of fickleness; the sense is "by one greedy for craving. "Mukhakharā" means harsh in speech.
The meaning is "one who speaks harshly.
"One of scattered speech" means one whose words are incoherent, whose speech is boundless due to idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). Therefore he said, "one of unrestrained speech," and so forth.
"Those of neglected mindfulness" means those devoid of mindfulness. Even if mindfulness is present, its function as mindfulness is absent due to a deficiency in the necessary conditions.
It is said thus because of their inability to act. "Not being fully aware" means they are *asampajānā*;

this negative particle (*a-*) is used here to denote the absence of that quality (the yoke), as in "rootless phenomena" (*ahetukā dhammā*) or "a residence without a monk" (*abhikkhuko āvāso*); thus he says "devoid of wisdom" (*nippaññā*), meaning they are lacking in wisdom.
In the Pāḷi, *vibbhantacittā* means with minds wandering astray. This is due to restlessness (*uddhacca*) which has found an opportunity through the absence of concentration (*samādhi*).
The minds of those who lack concentration wander among various objects like a monkey in a forest among the branches of the trees.

"With unguarded faculties" means that, due to the absence of restraint, their faculties are wide open just as they were in the time of being householders. Therefore he said, "by those remaining in their natural state," and so forth.
"Wide open" means unrestrained.
44. In the second [case], "quarrel" (*bhaṇḍana*) is said to be the preliminary stage of a dispute.
Thus, "quarrel" refers to abusive speech that serves as the cause for a dispute, as well as similar undesirable actions. Regarding the phrase "those who have given rise to quarrels" (*kalaha-jātā*):

the meaning here should be understood as those in whom a dispute has reached its culmination through such means as the seizing of hands and so forth. "Contradictory speech" (*viruddha-vāda*) refers to: "This..."
“Dispute” refers to a conflict consisting of contradictory assertions, such as “This is the Dhamma; this is not the Dhamma.
Since speech is dependent upon the mouth, it is intended here by the word “mouth”; thus he says, “Ill-spoken words are called the ‘weapon of the mouth.
The fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha is called a “unified act” (ekakamma) because it must be performed collectively by the regular monks within the boundaries of the monastery zone.
[The term] *nāma*. Even the fivefold recitation of the *Pātimokkha* is called a "single recitation" (*ekuddesa*) because it must be recited together as one.
Furthermore, the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that has been laid down is called "equal training" (*samasikkhatā*) because it must be trained in equally by all modest individuals (*lajjīpuggala*).
In the text, the phrase "become like milk and water" means that just as milk and water blend with one another and do not remain separate...
It becomes as if it were a single unity. For although the two groups are distinct in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), their diversity is difficult for ordinary people to discern;
they remain as if completely merged together, like milk and water mixed.

Thus, because they have attained unity through their harmony, like states of consciousness that have reached oneness, they are said here to have "become like milk and water" (*khīrodakībhūtā*); such is the meaning in this context.
It should be looked upon. "With eyes of loving-kindness" means with eyes that look while having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
For those [eyes] are called "eyes of affection" because they manifest a state of endearment.
45. In the third [verse], regarding the word *aggavatī*: here the word *agga* is a synonym for "supreme"; by this, [it refers to] a distinguished person.
Since it is the undertaking of a distinguished practice that is intended here, he said: "Possessing the foremost means possessing the supreme person," and so forth.

Because they take up various requisites in great abundance due to not being free from craving, they are called *bahulā* (those who have much); those who are *bahulā* are themselves *bāhulikā* (those devoted to abundance), just as one is called a *venayika* (one devoted to discipline).
Furthermore, they are so called because they are constantly engaged in efforts for the sake of having an abundance of requisites.
Therefore, he said: "They have set out for an abundance of robes and so forth. Because they lack reverence and respect for the training, they grasp it loosely and without firmness;
thus they are called "slack" (*sāthalika*). Furthermore, *sithila* is a neuter abstract noun;

alternatively, the formation of the word *sāthalika* should be understood by way of the word *sāthala*, which has the same meaning as *sithila*. [The term is used] in the sense of "not understanding" (*avagamana*).

The meaning is: "in the sense of going downwards," that is, by way of being part of the lower realm (*orambhāgiya*). "In seclusion from acquisitions" (*upadhiviveke*) means in a state secluded from acquisitions due to the relinquishing of all acquisitions.
"Laid down the burden" (*oropitadhurā*) means having abandoned the effort. "Both kinds of energy" (*duvidhaṃ pi vīriyaṃ*) refers to both bodily and mental energy. 46.
In the fourth [sutta], this is stated for the purpose of showing that the Noble Truth of Suffering has not been grasped through direct experience as "this is suffering."
It is said [thus]. The phrase "only this much is suffering" is for the purpose of showing that it has been grasped after being delimited.
The phrase "there is no suffering beyond this" is for the purpose of showing that it has been grasped without remainder.

"They do not understand according to its true nature" means they do not penetrate it through non-delusion by means of penetrating its own inherent characteristic (*sarasalakkhaṇa*). And penetration through non-delusion is as follows:
When that knowledge is active, there is no delusion regarding the discernment of form and so forth as suffering; such is its mode of occurrence.
"Absolute destruction" (*accantakkhaya*) refers to Nibbāna, which is the cause for absolute destruction. The same principle applies here to "non-arising" (*asamuppatti*).
It is by resorting to that Nibbāna, which serves as the causal basis for the Path in the sense of being its object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), that both of these [delusions] cease.
The non-arising of that [suffering] is called Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. 47.
In the fifth [verse], because the qualifier has been placed last, it is said "a dregs-like assembly" (*parisākasaṭo*); thus he says "a dregs-like assembly" (*kasaṭaparisā*), and so forth.
For while one should have said "a dregs-like assembly," it is stated as "a dregs-like assembly. This same [principle] applies here in the case of "the cream of the assembly" (*parisāmaṇḍo*).
This is the method. The rest here is self-evident.

48. In the sixth [case], "profound" means bottomless and difficult to fathom. By the phrase "by way of the text," he refers to that quality of profundity which is the domain of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).
For because the penetration of phenomena is difficult to achieve, it is by way of the text of the phenomena...
The state of being profound is due to its depth of penetration into suffering.

Having stated that it is "profound by way of the text (*pāḷi*)," it is said to be "like the Salla-sutta" because its profundity by way of the text is found in such passages as "the signless, not-yet-known," for therein those verses remain in a form difficult to comprehend.
Indeed, that which is difficult to comprehend is "deeply penetrated" by means of knowledge.

Having been made thus, it is called "profound. Furthermore, because some verses here are difficult to comprehend due to their sequence of prior and subsequent parts, they are indeed hard to penetrate;
therefore, that is described as "profound by way of the text" (*pāḷivasena*).

By this same method, the meaning should also be understood in the phrase "profound by way of the meaning" (*atthavasena*). The profundity by way of the meaning of the Mahāvedalla Sutta is indeed easy to understand.

It transcends the world, thus it is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*); this refers to the ninefold immeasurable state (*appamāṇadhamma*). Because these [states] possess that which has become their objective referent, they are "supramundane.
Therefore, he said: "They illuminate the supramundane objective referent.
"Empty of a being, merely a mere phenomenon" means empty of a being—that is, of a self—and is merely a mere phenomenon. It should be grasped as such.
Regarding the phrase "to be mastered," he says, "and in what is to be learned and mastered," because it was stated with a reversal of gender and number (*liṅgavacanavipallāsa*).
Poetry (*kavitā*) is the work of a poet (*kavi*). Since that which is its work is said to be "made by him," he says, "poetry (*kavitā*) means made by poets (*kavīhi katā*).
The other term is *kāveyya*; it is what is called *kābya*. And *kābya* [is so called] by a poet...
The meaning is "spoken. Therefore he said, "a synonym for that very [term].
"With variegated syllables" means with syllables of diverse forms that are communicative. "Outside of the teaching" means not belonging to the scope of the Dispensation.
"By their disciples" means by the disciples of anyone whatsoever who are not known as disciples of the Buddhas. "And they do not question one another" refers to those who teach [the texts].
And those who hear it do not inquire about its meaning and so forth from one another; they are satisfied merely by the recitation and hearing alone.

"They do not go on tour" means that because of the absence of such a person and because of his internal contradictions, they do not go on tour to ask, "Is there [such a thing]? regarding the meaning and so forth known to exist in a certain place.

"How should it be planted? means in what manner should it be established? Since the meaning (attha) is known—known correctly—by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), its connection (anusandhi), its relation (sambandha), its sequence (pubbāpara), and its beginning and end, he asks, "What is the meaning? and so forth.
"Not made explicit" (anuttānīkataṃ) means not made explicit by means of the arrangement of syllables and so on. "Doubt" (kaṅkhā) refers to uncertainty (saṃsayassa).
49. In the seventh [case], it is called *āmisa* because it is to be touched by the defilements; the four requisites are this very thing.

Since these are what is heavy (*garu*)—that which is to be valued—and not the Dhamma, it is called *āmisagarū*. Therefore he said: "an assembly that remains having taken the supramundane Dhamma as inferior.
One who is liberated from both parts is *ubhatobhāgavimutto*. He is liberated twice, by means of two parts: through wisdom...
"Liberated" means liberated by the wisdom of the supreme path, independent of reliance on serenity (*samatha*). Therefore, he said:
"a dry-insight practitioner whose taints are destroyed. "By the body" means by the mental body (*nāmakāya*).

"Having touched the contact of jhāna" means having touched the contact of jhāna known as the eight attainments by way of realization. Afterwards, he realizes with the mental body the cessation that is Nibbāna, exactly as it was observed.
A body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*). But he is not yet "liberated" because some taints (*āsava*) have not been fully exhausted. "One who has reached the end of seeing" (*diṭṭhantaṃ patto*):

the "end of seeing" (*diṭṭhanta*) refers to the immediate period following what has been seen; the meaning is that he has reached the state immediately subsequent to the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated as "seeing.
For from the first fruit up to the supreme path, one is "one who has reached vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*). Therefore he said: "These..."
“Both are found in six places.
By the phrase “one who has faith is liberated,” this demonstrates that even for one who is not liberated in every respect, there is a state of liberation by means of mere faith;
thus, it clarifies that one liberated by faith is indeed a trainee (*sekha*). Alternatively, “liberated by faith” (*saddhā-vimutta*) means “not liberated apart from faith” (*saddhāya avimutto*).
The meaning is as follows. "In six places" means in six stages starting from the first fruit (sotāpatti-phala).
"He recollects the Dhamma" means he recollects the Dhamma comprised of the wisdom of the first path. "He recollects faith"—the same principle applies here as well.
Both of these belong only to one who stands on the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Why are these included? Because they are exclusively praiseworthy.
When noble ones are being selected, why do they take this which is utterly censured, wretched, and immoral?
Even when all things are available and identical in every respect, no distinction is perceived;

however, only when there is a dissimilarity does a distinction become apparent, as in the case of a mind-cloth compared to an ordinary cloth. Thus he said, "But among some," and so forth. "Bound" means tied fast. "Infatuated" means...
They have fallen into a swoon and a state of delusion. "For the purpose of drawing away desire and lust" means for the sake of removing desire and lust.
"By wisdom of escape" means devoid of the wisdom that brings about escape from that [state].
"By the burden of wisdom" means by way of the application of insight (*vipassanā*). "Engaged" means having entered the path of insight. In that...

"At the moment" means at the moment of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). One is called a "follower by Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*) because of following the stream of the Noble Path by means of the Dhamma, which is to say, wisdom.
One is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*) because of realizing *nibbāna*, which is to be realized by the mental body (*nāmakāya*).

This occurs twice, by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*). [One is liberated] from the form-body (*rūpakāya*) by means of the formless jhānas, and by the highest path (*aggamagga*)—

"From the remainder-body" (*sesakāyato*) is an ablative construction with two senses. "One who has reached vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*): because he has reached vision, or because he is one who has reached [it], he is "one who has reached vision.
In that context, "one who has reached vision" means one who has reached immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated as "seeing.
"Because of having seen" refers to the cessation [of suffering] by means of the wisdom designated as the seeing of the Four Noble Truths.
Because it has been seen. One who is liberated by means of that very preeminent wisdom which is devoid of jhāna-contact is called "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta).
The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained. 50.
In the eighth [case], "not equal" means unequal. Because bodily actions and so forth are unequal, for that very reason there is stumbling therein.
He said, "It is easy [to obtain] in the sense of 'stumbling' (*sapakkhalana-ṭṭhena*). "In the sense of 'not stumbling' (*nippakkhalana-ṭṭhena*)" means by way of the absence of stumbling.
"Contrary to the Dhamma" (*uddhammāni*) means departed from the Dhamma. "Contrary to the Vinaya" (*ubbhinayāni*): here too, the method is the same. 51.
In the ninth [section], "unrighteous" (*adhammikā*) means engaged in what is not the Dhamma. Therefore he said, "devoid of the Dhamma" (*niddhammā*), meaning lacking the Dhamma.

52. "They take up" means they cause [the matter] to proceed. "And they do not make each other understand" means that from the very beginning, they do not correctly make one another aware of how that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be settled.
When there is an assembly for the purpose of making oneself understood, one must act appropriately and suitably therein to achieve such understanding; those [who fail to do so]...

But they do not assemble for the purpose of reconciliation. "They do not cause [the matter] to be seen" means they do not cause that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) to be examined from its very root by one another.
"Those whose strength lies in non-reconciliation" means those whose strength consists solely in their own faction which they have taken up through a lack of reconciliation.
"They do not deliberate in such a way" means they do not deliberate in accordance with the truth because of their state of clinging to their own views, being obstinate and difficult to release.
Therefore he said, "With persistence," and so forth. The meaning is plain, as it should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding the dark side (kaṇhapakkha).
The commentary on the Chapter on the Multitude (Parisavagga) is finished.
The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) is finished.
2. The Second Fifty (6) 1.
Commentary on the Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga) 53.
In the first [sutta] of the Second Fifty, by the mention of "welfare" (hita), loving-kindness (mettā) is expressed, not compassion (karuṇā); by the mention of "pity" (anukampā),...
However, because compassion (*karuṇā*) was included together with the wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattin*), it was not stated as "out of compassion for the world.

In the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), what is called "compassion for the world" depends upon the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "Two" refers to the two types of excellence by way of human and divine success.
Those two, together with the excellence of *nibbāna*, make three.

54. In the second [explanation], they are called "practiced people" (*āciṇṇamanussa*) because such people have not been practiced among or active in the world many times before. They are called "extraordinary people" (*abbhutamanussa*) because their birth in the world occurs only at certain times, having never happened before. 55.
In the third [explanation], he causes distress throughout ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷasahassa*) because that constitutes a single Buddha-field (*buddhakhetta*). 56.
In the fourth [explanation], they are "suitable for the stupa" (*thūpassa yuttā*), meaning they are suitable for being placed within and for the construction of a stupa.
57. In the fifth [verse], "by his own power" means by means of his self-enlightened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*). "Buddhas" means those who have awakened. 58.
In the sixth [verse], "he does not fear because [defilements] have been abandoned" means that he does not fear due to the absence of attachment to self (*attasineha*).
Here, the mention of the view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is merely illustrative; for fear arises through attachment to self, aversion (*paṭigha*), and the delusion associated with them.
"He does not fear" means that because those [factors] have been abandoned, he does not fear; otherwise, there would have to be fearlessness for stream-enterers and the like.
Regarding "due to the strength of the view of a personal body" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), it should be stated here that the delusion of the "I-maker" (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth are also strong.
59. In the seventh [verse], they write *assājānīyo*, but the reading *usabhājānīyo* is correct.
61. "Therein, in the ninth [case], 'there' means in the marketplace (*antarāpaṇa*). 'One' refers to one of the two *kiṃnara*s.
'And he saw the fruit of the *ambilikā*' connects with 'having brought it. They say that 'fruit of the *ambilikā*' is the fruit of the *tintiṇī*; others call it 'fourfold sourness' (*caturambla*).
'Two meanings' refers to the two meanings stated in the Pāḷi."

62. In the tenth instance, when a task has been undertaken and is currently underway, to turn back midway is "resistance" (*paṭivāna*). Since there is no such resistance for him, he is "unyielding" (*appaṭivāna*). In that regard, he has reached a state free from shrinking back. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "not weary," and so forth. 63.
In the eleventh instance, "dwelling together" (*sannivāsa*) means living together.

Just as unwholesome persons, when living together, show disrespect and lack of deference toward one another, this discourse should be understood as primarily demonstrating the practice of respect among wholesome persons by way of contrast.
64. "In both sides" (dvādasame dvīsupi pakkhesu) means in both factions of the monks who have fallen into dispute.

"Wandering about" (saṃsaramānā) means occurring or proceeding. "Contempt for views" (diṭṭhipaḷāso) is contempt based on views, a grasping at opposing positions. "Harassing" (āghātentō) means striking or afflicting.
"By way of non-delight" (anabhirādhanavasena) means by way of the lack of delight in the welfare of both the one in whom it arises and others.
"All this" refers to the entire cycle of verbal expression. This is to be connected by supplying the words "in one's own mind and in the minds of the assembly.
The commentary on the Chapter on Persons is finished.
(7) 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Happiness.

65. In the first [section] of the second [chapter], "the happiness rooted in the fulfillment of all desires" refers to sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*), which has as its cause the production of objects for complete enjoyment and utilization. "The happiness rooted in renunciation" refers to the bliss of seclusion (*pavivekasukha*) caused by going forth (*pabbajjā*). 66.
In the second [section], "desires" (*kāma*) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), or else to all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

For it has been said: "All phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence are 'desires' in the sense of being desirable. "Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) is said to be going forth from the bonds of the household life.
Because of having gone forth. Or rather, it is *nibbāna* itself—according to the verse:
“Going forth, the first *jhāna*, *nibbāna*, and insight;
all wholesome states are called ‘renunciation’ (*nekkhamma*).”
Thus it was said. 67.

In the third [case], "substrata" (upadhī) refers to the five aggregates of clinging; the happiness dependent upon them is "happiness based on substrata" (upadhisukha). By contrast, "happiness without substrata" (nirupadhisukha) is supramundane happiness. 68.
In the fourth [case], happiness included within the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) is "cyclic happiness" (vaṭṭasukha); happiness having Nibbāna as its object is "unbinding happiness" (vivaṭṭasukha).
69. In the fifth [verse], "defiled" (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) means that which is subject to defilement. Therefore, he said: "the happiness of one who goes in the round of existence" (*vaṭṭagāmisukha*).

"The happiness of turning away from the round" (*vivaṭṭasukha*) is the happiness associated with the path and its fruition (*maggaphala*). 70. In the sixth [verse], "noble happiness" (*ariyasukha*) is the happiness belonging exclusively to the noble ones (*ariya*); it is called "noble happiness" because it is both noble and happiness. "Ignoble happiness" (*anariyasukha*) is the happiness belonging exclusively to the ignoble; it is called "ignoble happiness" because it is both ignoble and happiness. 71. In the seventh [verse], "that" (*tanti*) refers to mental happiness (*cetasikasukha*).
72. In the eighth [jhāna], that which proceeds together with rapture (*pīti*) is "with rapture" (*sappītika*), meaning pleasure accompanied by rapture.

That pleasure from which rapture has departed both by its own nature and by way of fading away is "without rapture" (*nippītika*). In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, only the jhāna-pleasure itself is mentioned here; accordingly, it is said: "The mundane pleasure without rapture is superior to the mundane pleasure with rapture."
For even mundane rapture (*nippītika*) can indeed be attained as the highest; thus, its status as "highest" should be understood by breaking through the different planes of existence (*bhūmantara*).
73. In the ninth [jhāna], "pleasure-pleasure" (*sātasukha*) is pleasure whose very nature is agreeable (*sāta*), not pleasure whose nature is neutral like equanimity-pleasure (*upekkhāsukha*).
Although here, even that accompanied by body-consciousness is indeed pleasure-pleasure, in the Commentary it is stated simply as "pleasure" in the case of the three jhānas.

74. In the tenth [case], pleasure associated with concentration is "concentration-pleasure" (*samādhisukha*). Pleasure not associated with concentration is "non-concentration-pleasure" (*asamādhisukha*).
75. In the eleventh, this is a discourse on the Suttantas; thus it is said: "the two jhānas accompanied by rapture" (*sappītika*). 77.

In the thirteenth, "form-jhāna" (*rūpajjhāna*) is [derived] by eliding the final member of the compound *rūpa-jjhāna*; that which has form as its object is "having form as its object" (*rūpārammaṇa*).
The inclusion of the fourth jhāna, moreover, is intended to show that it possesses a capacity for application equal to its counterpart.
"Whatever form" means whatever form characterized by the quality of being affected (ruppana). By way of its opposite, the non-material (arūpa) is to be understood.
The commentary on the Chapter on Happiness is finished.
(8) 3. Explanation of the Chapter on "With a Sign" (Sanimittavagga), §§ 78–79.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: that wherein the fruit is fixed, as if being cast in by the remaining conditions, is called a "sign" (*nimitta*);
thus he says, "with a sign" means "with a cause" (*sakāraṇā*). "In the second and so forth" means in the second sutta and the others. It is exactly the same.
By the word "nayati" (leads), he demonstrates that even the terms such as "nidāna" (cause) signify a synonym for "cause. It is called *nidāna* because it lays down (*nidadāti*) the fruit;

it is called *hetu* because by means of it the fruit goes forth (*hinoti*) and is established; it is called *saṅkhāra* because it conditions (*saṅkharoti*) the fruit; it is called *paccaya* because the fruit comes (*eti*) depending upon it (*paṭicca*);
and it is called *rūpa* because the fruit is affected (*ruppati*), destroyed (*niruppati*), or found therein. Thus, even for the terms such as *nidāna*, [the meaning is the same].
The manner of the cause should be understood.
84. In the seventh [case], "being a condition" means being a co-nascent or other type of condition. 87.
In the tenth [case], "conditioned" (saṅkhata) means that which is made by conditions having come together and combined; a conditioned phenomenon is the object (ārammaṇa).
These have conditioned things as their object. At the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), they are said not to exist because they are being abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "they do not exist" (nāhesuṃ), the word "are called" (vuccanti) must be supplied here. This is because the teaching was given up to the stage of Arahatta, and at the conclusion of each respective sutta, it is stated that "they do not exist."
The commentary on the Chapter on Having Signs is finished.
(9) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Dhamma. 88.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter], "concentration as fruit" (*phalasamādhi*) refers to concentration within all four noble fruits (*ariyaphala*). Likewise, "wisdom as fruit" (*phalapaññā*) should be understood in the same way.
89. It is "grasping" (paggāha) because it grasps the associated states in the second [jhāna]. It is "non-distraction" (avikkhepa) because it does not waver. 90.

In the third [jhāna], it is "name" (nāma) in the sense of bending (namana), and "form" (rūpa) in the sense of being affected (ruppana). Because the practice of comprehension (sammasanacāra) is intended here, it is stated simply as "the four immaterial aggregates. Therefore, he said: "The knowledge consisting in the discernment of the categories of phenomena (dhamma-koṭṭhāsa-pariccheda-ñāṇa) has been explained. 91.
In the fourth [jhāna], it is "true knowledge" (vijjā) in the sense of understanding (vijānana), and "liberation" (vimutti) in the sense of being freed (vimuccana).
92. In the fifth [pair], "existence" (*bhava*) means eternalism, because it exists forever; the view that arises by way of eternalism is the "view of existence" (*bhavaditthi*).
"Non-existence" (*vibhava*) means annihilation, in the sense of destruction; the view that arises by way of non-existence is the "view of non-existence" (*vibhavaditthi*).
Their meaning is obvious, as they follow the method explained below.
95. In the eighth [case], "one of difficult speech" (*dubbaca*) refers to a person who is difficult to speak with, who is contrary, disagreeable, and disrespectful.
The action of such a person is "difficult speech" (*dovacassa*). The volition that proceeds from the disrespect of such a person of difficult speech is [the basis for this term].
The state of that is "difficult speech-ness" (*do-vacassatā*). And the phrase "the state of that" refers to the aforementioned state of being difficult to speak with.
In its essential meaning, the state of being (atthibhāva) is simply the quality of being difficult to speak to (dovacassatā). In detail, however, this is defined in the Abhidhamma as:

"In that regard, what is the quality of being difficult to speak to? It is the state of being difficult to speak to when one is being addressed according to the Dhamma. In its essential meaning, it belongs to the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Alternatively, they say that this is a designation for the four aggregates when they occur in this particular manner.

One who has evil persons—those lacking faith and so forth—as friends due to association with evil is an "evil friend" (*pāpamitta*); the state of being such is "association with evil friends" (*pāpamittatā*).
In detail, however, this is as follows: "In that regard, what is association with evil friends? Those persons who are without faith, immoral, of little learning, stingy, and lacking wisdom.
Whatever associating, frequenting, thorough associating, attending upon, close attendance upon, and devotion toward them [is association with evil friends]."
"Association with evil friends is crookedness in that regard"—thus it is stated. In terms of its meaning, this too should be regarded as being like "difficult-to-speak-to-ness" (*dovacassatā*).
For that volition by which a person becomes known as "one who is crooked through evil association," or those four immaterial aggregates occurring in that mode, constitute "evil friendship."

96. In the ninth [verse], the meaning should be understood through the reverse of what was stated in such passages as "a person who is easy to speak to" (*subbaco*)—referring to one who is pleasant in speech, respectful, compliant, and amiable—and "one who has virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitto*), referring to one whose friends are persons possessing faith and other such virtues. 97.

In the tenth [verse], the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) and so forth, as well as the pleasure element (*sukhadhātu*) and the desire element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, are included within these very [elements]; thus, it is said: "in these."
When skill regarding the [first] eighteen is demonstrated, skill regarding those [remaining ones] is also demonstrated; thus it is said, "the eighteen elements.
By the phrase "elements are knowing," the wisdom of hearing, retaining, reflecting, and penetrating—which defines the intrinsic nature of the eighteen elements—is stated.

Among these, the wisdom of hearing and retaining the elements consists of wisdom born of hearing (*sutamaya-paññā*), while the others consist of wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-paññā*). Furthermore, among those, the wisdom of reflection...

It is mundane. For that [insight] is mundane, while the other is supramundane. Attention (*manasikāra*) is the act of bringing to mind by way of characteristics and so forth, and by way of impermanence and so forth;

skill in that is "skill in attention" (*manasikārakusala-tā*). Skill in attention is the wisdom (*paññā*) consisting of comprehension, penetration, and reviewing regarding the eighteen elements themselves;
it is divided into three types according to its beginning, middle, and end. For thus, comprehension-wisdom...
Its beginning is [the wisdom of] the undertaking, its middle is the wisdom of penetration, and its end is the wisdom of reflection.
98. In the eleventh [section], the offenses themselves are the classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
Since there are five when intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*) are not included, and seven when they are included, he says: "of the five and seven classes of offenses. "Knowing" means...

“Knowing: ‘These are the offenses, there are this many offenses, and such is the way they are incurred’—this wisdom consisting of knowing in these three ways is indeed what is called skill in regard to offenses (*āpattikusalatā*).
The formal act (*kamma*) consists of the words employed for the purpose of emerging from an offense;
such are the words of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). [One knows]: ‘By means of this formal act, emergence from this offense occurs.’”

"Does it occur at the first or the third proclamation when the syllable *yya* is reached, or when the phrase ‘I shall restrain myself’ has been completed?"—thus, the wisdom that knows the limits for emerging from each respective offense is skill in emerging from offenses.
And "emerging" (*vuṭṭhāna*) means the bringing about of the absence of obstacles in whatever way necessary for the offense as it was incurred. Thus, by the very mention of "emerging,"...
Inclusion is also established by way of the teaching.
The commentary on the Dhamma-vagga is finished.
(10) 5. Commentary on the Bāla-vagga.
99. Regarding the first part of the fifth [section]: "He bears the burden of the future" means he bears a burden that has not yet reached him.
Being himself a *thera*, he bears the burden that must be borne by *theras*, such as the duty of fanning, taking the water-vessel, and seeking alms;

this is how the meaning should be understood here. In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated that because the ninefold preliminary duties, such as sweeping and so forth, are performed only when one is commanded...

The Pātimokkha must be recited only by one who has been authorized; therefore, to show that one who performs all these duties without such authorization is said to be "bearing a burden for the future," it is stated: "the broom, the lamp," and so forth.
For this is what has come down in the Canon (Pāḷi) in the manner of the passage beginning, "I allow you, monks, to sweep the Uposatha hall," and so on, as well as in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the ‘preliminary duties’ (pubbakaraṇa) for the Uposatha. The declaration of consent,
the purity [of the monks], the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation.”
"These are called the 'preliminary duties' (pubbakicca) for the Uposatha.
Thus, the ninefold preliminary duty has been shown by these two names; it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha without having performed it.
Therefore, [the Buddha said]: "I allow you, monks, that a senior monk should direct a junior monk."

According to the instruction of the Elder, a monk who is not ill must sweep the Uposatha hall, set out drinking water and water for washing, prepare a seat, and provide a lamp; if he fails to do so, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The Elder, having recognized that it is appropriate, must give the command; and the one giving the command, while performing whatever task is required, must always...

Only one person—whether it be Kālamegha, the bearer of burdens, or anyone among the reciters or preachers of the Dhamma—should not be commanded to sweep the Uposatha hall; however, the rest should be commanded in turn.
If the one so commanded does not even obtain a temporary broom, he should sweep by making a "branch-broom" (sākhābhaṅga) allowable.
If he does not obtain even that, it becomes allowable for him once it has been obtained. Regarding the preparation of a lamp, he should be instructed in the same manner as previously described;
and by the one giving the instruction, he should say: "In such-and-such a place there is oil or a vessel; take that and prepare it.
If oil and so forth are not available, they must be sought after. If, having sought them, he does not obtain them, it becomes allowable for him once they have been obtained.
Furthermore, a fire must be kindled in the potsherds. Regarding the instruction to prepare the seats, it should be ordered in the same manner already described;
and when so ordered, if there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, they should be brought from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, arranged, and then returned.
In the absence of seats, it is permissible to arrange even straw mats or wooden planks; and upon these as well—

If branches are not available, they should be prepared as *kappiya* (permissible) and then set out. For one who does not obtain a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things permissible), what has been obtained by another becomes permissible for him. Regarding "consent and purity" (*chandapārisuddhi*):
here, when the Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of performing the Uposatha, [the consent] is given by performing the Uposatha outside [the boundary].
Having arrived, one who has gone to the assembly place but does not grant physical presence must give his consent (*chanda*).
Even one who is ill or occupied with duties must, when giving formal purity (*pārisuddhi*), give his consent. How should it be given?
In the presence of another monk, the meaning is expressed as: "I give my consent; take my consent; announce my consent."
It must be communicated by means of body, speech, or both. In this way, consent (*chanda*) is given.

However, one who has not performed the *uposatha*, or who is ill, or who is occupied with duties, must give their purity (*pārisuddhi*). How is it to be given? In the presence of a single monk, one says:
"I give my purity; carry my purity [to the assembly]; announce my purity"—this is the meaning.
It must be communicated either by body, by speech, or by both. In this way, the purity (pārisuddhi) is given.
Furthermore, when giving it, one's consent (chanda) must also be given. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"I allow you, monks, on the Uposatha day, when giving purity, to give consent as well, if there is business for the Saṅgha. In that context, the giving of purity...
One accomplishes the performance of the Uposatha for both the Saṅgha and oneself, but not the remaining duties of the Saṅgha.
The giving of consent (chandadāna) accomplishes both the performance of the Uposatha and the remaining duties for the Saṅgha alone; however, one's own Uposatha remains unperformed.
Therefore, by one who gives formal purity (pārisuddhi), consent must also be given.
"Announcement of the season" means the proclamation of the seasons, such as "so much of the winter season and so forth has passed, and so much remains.
"Counting of the monks" means the counting of the monks, such as "this many monks have assembled in the Uposatha hall.
Having performed both of these, the Uposatha must be carried out. "Exhortation" refers to the exhortation of the nuns; for [the Uposatha] is not [performed] by the nuns.
It is permissible to perform the Uposatha without announcing the exhortation (ovāda) that was requested.

For the nuns, having arrived [on the previous day] thinking, "The Uposatha is tomorrow," and having asked, "Is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?", they arrive again on the Uposatha day and say:
"Venerable sirs, the Sangha of nuns pays homage at the feet of the Sangha of monks and requests the approach for the exhortation."
"May the community of bhikkhunīs, noble sir, receive the invitation to come for the exhortation"—in this way they request the exhortation.
Apart from one who is ignorant, ill, or pregnant, no other person—even if he is a forest-dweller—is permitted to refuse it.
Therefore, the monk by whom it has been accepted must speak thus to the monk who recites the Pātimokkha at the Uposatha hall:
“Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests the opportunity to approach for instruction;
may the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, venerable sir, receive the opportunity to approach for instruction.
The reciter of the Pātimokkha should ask: “Is there any bhikkhu appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs? If...
If there is a certain monk who has been appointed as the instructor of the nuns, he should then say to them:
"The monk named so-and-so has been appointed as the instructor of the nuns; let the community of nuns approach him.
If there is no such person, then he should ask: "Which venerable one is able to instruct the nuns? If someone is able, [he should appoint him].
And he too, being endowed with eight qualities, should be appointed right there as the receiver of the exhortation, and it should be said:
"The monk named so-and-so has been appointed as the exhorter of the nuns; let the community of nuns approach him.
But if no one volunteers, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say: "There is no monk..."

“Having been appointed as an exhorter of the bhikkhunīs, may the bhikkhunī-saṅgha be accomplished through inspiring confidence. For up to this point, the entire Dispensation, comprised within the three trainings, has been announced.
That bhikkhu, having accepted with the words “Very well,” should announce it to the bhikkhunīs on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*).
Regarding the Pātimokkha as well: “Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be recited by one who has not been requested.”
Because of the statement, "Whoever should recite it [without being authorized] commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one should not recite it without authorization.
For because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha is the domain of the Elder," the Elder of the Saṅgha may recite the Pātimokkha;
and because of the statement, "I allow you, monks, that the Pātimokkha be the domain of whichever monk there is who is competent and capable," a junior monk may also do so.
Or he was instructed by the Elder. The second and subsequent sections have meanings that are self-evident.
109. In the eleventh [case], "one who feels remorse when one should not feel remorse" means one feels remorse regarding what is not fit to cause remorse.
Having obtained pork, one feels remorse thinking it is "bear meat"; even while knowing it is "pork," one [feels remorse] thinking it is "bear meat."
"He feels remorse" means that he does not consume it. Thus, he feels remorse regarding deer meat thinking it is "panther meat";

regarding meat that is actually available at the right time, thinking "it is not the right time"; regarding not being invited, thinking "I have been invited"; regarding food where no dust has fallen on the bowl, thinking "it has fallen [with dust]";
and regarding fish or meat that was not prepared specifically for him, thinking "it was prepared for me."
“Not feeling remorse where one ought to feel remorse” means that he does not feel remorse where it is appropriate to feel remorse.
Having obtained bear meat, he does not feel remorse thinking it is “pig meat”; even though he knows it is “bear meat,” he does not feel remorse thinking it is “pig meat.
This implies that he crushes it and transgresses [the rule]. Likewise with leopard meat as “deer meat,” and so forth.
The meaning here should be understood as follows: when fish or meat has been prepared specifically for oneself, one does not feel remorse thinking, "This was prepared for me.

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "That which should not be regretted means that the non-designation and non-investigation of what is the property of the Saṅgha is called 'that which should not be regretted,' yet he regrets it. That which should be regretted refers to that very same [property]."
Only this much was said: "The setting forth [of property] and the deliberation [thereon] do not give rise to remorse.

In that context, "the Saṅgha’s property" refers to fields, lands, reservoirs, and so forth, given for the purpose of the Saṅgha’s enjoyment of the four requisites, as well as the grain, gold, and other assets produced from them—the property of the Saṅgha.
"Not setting forth" means not making arrangements; hence he says, "not deliberating. "Of that very [property]"...
[This refers to] the very same property of the Saṅgha as previously described.
The commentary on the Bālavagga is finished.
The Second Fifty is finished.
3. The Third Fifty (11) 1.
Commentary on the Chapter on Difficult-to-Abandon Desires (Āsāduppajahavagga) 119.

In the first [chapter] of the Third Fifty, those things which must be abandoned through suffering are "difficult to abandon" (*duppajahā*). This also applies to terms such as "difficult to overcome" (*duccaja*) and so forth.
The same method applies here. How is the difficulty of abandoning the two hopes to be understood?

First, the difficulty of abandoning the hope for gain is clarified by the passage beginning with "by the hope for gain. "Arrayed on both sides" means gathered together from both sides for the purpose of battle.
"Rushing forward" means entering into it. The difficulty of abandoning the hope for life is clarified by the passage beginning with "the hope for life is hard to give up."
120. In the second [verse], *dullabhā* means not easily obtained. *“Iṇaṃ demīti saññaṃ karotī”* means that he acts as if making the recognition, “I am giving a debt.

And here, “one who acts first” (*pubbakārī*) is one who performs a service first. “Grateful and mindful of what has been done” (*kataññū katavedī*) is one who, having recognized what was done by the other, acts afterwards.
Among these, the one who acts first makes the recognition, “I am giving a debt”; afterwards...
Only this much is stated here: "The doer forms the perception, 'I shall repay this. However, in the *Puggalapaṇṇatti-saṃvaṇṇanā*, it says:
"One who acts first (*pubbakārī*) is one who acts at the very beginning. One who knows what has been done (*katavedī*) experiences what was done; he makes known—that which is understood—manifest.

These should be illustrated by means of householders and those who have left the household life. For among householders, mother and father are called 'those who act first,' while sons and daughters..."
Furthermore, those who care for their mother and father and perform such acts as saluting them are called "grateful.

Among those who have gone forth into homelessness, teachers and preceptors are called "those who act first," while pupils and co-residents—who care for their teachers and preceptors and perform such acts as saluting them—are called "grateful.
To illustrate this, there are the examples of the Elder Upajjhāyaposaka Soṇa and others.
The bases should be explained.

Another method: one who performs a service for another even when no service has been rendered by that other, and without regard for any service done to himself, is a "first-doer" (*pubbakārī*), such as parents, teachers, and preceptors. Such a person is rare among beings because they are overwhelmed by craving.

One who acts in accordance with a benefit conferred by another, recognizing and feeling the benefit performed for oneself as a benefit, is "grateful and appreciative," just like one who practices rightly toward parents, teachers, and preceptors. Such a person is also rare among beings because they are overwhelmed by ignorance.
Furthermore, there is the one who is affectionate without cause, the benefactor; and the one who is affectionate with cause, the requiter of kindness.
One who is grateful and appreciative of what has been done. One whose actions are independent of such motives as "He will do for me" is one who does first;

one whose actions depend on such motives as "He will do for me" is grateful and appreciative of what has been done. One who is headed from darkness toward light is one who does first; one who is headed from light toward light is grateful and appreciative of what has been done.
The teacher is one who does first; the practitioner is grateful and appreciative of what has been done. In the world with its devas, the Arahant...
It is said: "The Perfectly Enlightened One is one who acts first; the noble disciple is grateful and appreciative.
In this context, one whose heart is inclined toward doing good without a specific cause is "kind without a motive" (*akāraṇavacchalo*).
One who, looking toward a future purpose with the thought "he will do for me," first undertakes [an act] based on such a deed already performed, is indeed "grateful" (*kataññū*).

The phrase "one who will do it for me" and so forth is stated with the intention that such a person is "one who recognizes what has been done and is grateful," because they depend on such reasons for their action rather than being a benefactor from the outset.
One who is "devoted to dispelling darkness" and performs meritorious deeds without depending at all on the fruits of merit is called a "benefactor from the outset.
For one who depends on the fruit of merit stands on the side of those who recognize what has been done.
121. In the third [verse], "satisfied" (*titta*) means well-nourished, fulfilled, and free from anxiety due to having completed one's task.
For here, "satisfied" refers to one who is full through the perfection of qualities and has obtained as much as is needed. "Satisfying others" means causing others also to be satisfied.

Regarding the statement that both the *paccekabuddha* and the *tathāgata-sāvaka* (disciple of the Tathāgata) who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) are "satisfied," the *paccekabuddha* is so called by virtue of the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*).
He himself is quenched and fulfilled, yet he is unable to quench others.
For while there is no realization through his discourse on the Dhamma, there is realization for immeasurable gods and humans through the Dhamma discourse of his disciples.
Even so, when they teach the Dhamma, they do not speak by making it their own words; rather, they speak according to the Buddhas.
Having given his word, he speaks; and the assembly seated to listen also shows respect, thinking, "This bhikkhu speaks of the Dhamma realized by himself.
Thus, that respect belongs to the Buddhas alone. In this way, it is the Perfectly Enlightened One alone who is called the "Satisfier" therein.
For just as when a king says, "Give such-and-such to a person named so-and-so," [the command is fulfilled].
Even though they bring and give [the goods] because they have been commanded, nevertheless the king alone is the donor therein.
And those by whom it has been obtained take it thinking, "A position of rank has been granted to us by the king; power and wealth have been bestowed," and not [thinking], "By the king's men.
This should be understood as being of such a nature.
122. In the fourth [case], "difficult to satisfy" means it cannot be satisfied by anyone.
For one who lives depending on a family of supporters or a family of kinsmen, when his robes have become worn out, he sets aside the robe given by them and does not use it;
even when given again and again, he takes it and sets it aside. And whoever, in that same manner, receives [robes]...

One who gives away what has been obtained, gives it to another, and does the same even with what is obtained again and again—these two persons cannot be satisfied even by one who provides requisites by means of carts; thus they are "difficult to satisfy.
In the fifth [case], "does not give away" means that he does not give to another without having used it for himself; however, when there is a surplus, he does not...
He sets it aside and gives it to another. For this reason, it is said: “He does not give anything at all to others,” and so forth. This is what is meant:
“If a bhikkhu, having obtained a worn-out cloth or a garment from a family that supports him or from a family of his kinsmen, makes it into a robe and uses it, he does not set it aside;
even if he puts it on after fastening it with a pin, should it be given to him again, he [takes it] hastily.”
"He does not accept it. And he who, whatever he has obtained, consumes for himself and does not give to others—these two can both be satisfied with ease; thus they are 'easy to satisfy.
124–127. The sixth and seventh [sections] have their meaning already explained.
The commentary on the Chapter on Difficulties to Abandon is finished.
(12) 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Entreaties. 131.
"A bhikkhu endowed with faith" means a bhikkhu possessed of faith. A bhikkhu who [is accompanied] by Sāriputta and Moggallāna...
He aspires to a state of equality; he should desire for himself those very qualities by which Sāriputta and Moggallāna were established as the foremost.
Thus he said, "Just as the Elder Sāriputta is in wisdom," and so forth. To aspire beyond this would be a wrong aspiration;
therefore, [the text specifies] those qualities such as wisdom that are found in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and nothing superior to them.
One who aspires would aspire wrongly. For the boundary of the qualities of a disciple is defined by the qualities of the Chief Disciples;
among those qualities of a disciple, there are none higher than the qualities of the Chief Disciples. It is for this reason that it was said:
"Because one aspires for that which does not exist. The rest here is self-evident.
135. Regarding the fifth [type], one whose virtues (*guṇa*) are cut and impaired is said to be "cut and impaired.

Thus he says, "Because of the cutting of virtues," and so forth. "Cutting" (*khatatta*) means being severed. "Impairment" (*upahatatta*) means being lost. Therefore he says, "The meaning is: one whose virtues are severed and whose virtues are lost.
The term "progeny of demerit" (*apuññassa pasavo*) means, in substance, its acquisition; thus he says, "he procreates" (*pasavati*).
"Obtains" means he causes it to arise within his own continuum. "Without having entered into" means without having penetrated by means of knowledge.
The rest here, including the sixth and subsequent sections, is easy to understand.

(13) 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Giving (Dānavagga). 142.
Regarding the first [term] of the third [section]: it is called *dāna* because "it is given" (*dīyati*); this is a designation for the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*).

Or, it is called *dāna* because "one gives by means of it" (*dīyati anena*); this is a designation for the volition of relinquishment (*pariccāgacetanā*). He said [this] because both of these two meanings are intended here.

“Gifts by way of what is given,” and so forth. Therein, “by way of what is given” means by way of that which is to be given. “The path to the attainment of the Deathless” means the right practice that serves as the cause for attaining the Deathless. §§143–151.
The second and subsequent sections are indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the Dānavaṅga is finished.
(14) 4. Commentary on the Saṇṭhāravaṅga 152.
In the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter], regarding the lack of gain of both material goods and the Dhamma, between oneself and another...
A "spread" (*santhāra*) is the covering, closing, and encompassing of a gap, an opening, or a fissure that has arisen.
For this worldly existence is "gapped" by two things: by material gain and by the Dhamma, both of which are difficult to obtain.
Just as a seat-cover conceals the gaps of a bench so they are no longer visible, so too [the spread] conceals that gap by means of material gain and the Dhamma.

"Spreading out" (*santharaṇa*) and "gathering together" (*saṅgaṇhana*) is what is called "spreading out" (*santhāra*). In this context, the gathering [of people] by means of material gifts is called "material spreading out.
When performing this, it is permissible to give even without selecting the foremost among parents, those who act as attendants for monks, kings, and thieves.
However, kings and thieves may cause harm when [gifts] are given after having been touched [by them].
They even bring about the destruction of life. They are satisfied by what is given without being touched;
stories such as that of the thief-nāga should be told here. These are explained in detail in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Providing recitations with care, commenting on the Pāḷi, and delivering discourses on the Dhamma—this is called "support through the Dhamma" (*dhammasanthāra*).
153–163. The second and subsequent sections have their meanings already explained.

(15) 5. Commentary on the Samāpatti-vagga.

164. Regarding the first of the five [kinds of skill], skill in attainment (*samāpatti-kusala-tā*) is the wisdom that understands the delimitation of absorption together with its preliminary work (*parikamma*), knowing: "Prior to this, the preliminary work occurred; after this, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); in between is the attainment.
Skill in emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-kusala-tā*) is the state of being skilled in emerging. It should be understood here that the meaning is: "How much more so the knowledge that delimits the emergence!"
165. In the second [term], *ujju-bhāva* (the state of being straight) is *ajjava*. Its meaning is straightforwardness, lack of crookedness, and lack of curvature.
It is also stated in the Abhidhamma: “In this context, what is *ajjava*? That which is straightness, lack of crookedness, lack of curvature, and lack of bending—this is called *ajjava*.
And *anajjava* (lack of straightness) should be understood as the opposite of *ajjava*. It is like the curvature of a cow’s urine or the curvature of the crescent moon.
Indeed, there are three kinds of crookedness: the crookedness of the ploughshare-tip, and so forth.
For a certain bhikkhu, in his youth, middle age, and old age, wanders among the twenty-one improper searches and the six improper resorts;
this is called "cow’s urine crookedness," because of the crooked state of his practice from beginning to end. Another [wanders] in his youth and old age...
One fulfills the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), being modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training; in middle age, he is like the previous [type].
This is called "crookedness like the crescent moon" (*candalekhāvaṅkatā*), because of falling into a state of crookedness in the middle stage of practice.
Another fulfills the fourfold pure virtue in both early and middle age, being modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, but in late age...
This is called "crookedness like the tip of a plough," because it results in a state of crookedness at the end.
One person, having abandoned all this crookedness throughout the three stages of life, is amiable, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training;
his state of uprightness is what is called "straightforwardness" (*ajjava*), because it establishes uprightness in every respect.

In this context, some read "modesty" (*lajjava*) as "gentleness" (*maddava*). The meaning here is as follows: "In that regard, what is one who has modesty (*lajjava*)? One who feels shame where there should be shame, who feels shame regarding the attainment of evil, unwholesome states—this is called one who has modesty. Thus, the state of being modest is what is termed "modesty. This, however, is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) for it: *Madhu-maddava-lajjānam, majjatīti ca maddavo; Lajjatīti ca lajjāti, lajjatīti ca lajjavo.* [One is called] *maddava* because one softens (*majjati*) like honey (*madhu*) or is gentle (*maddava*); [one is called] *lajja* because one feels shame (*lajjati*); and [one is called] *lajjava* because one feels shame (*lajjati*). Thus, the meaning is: "That which softens like honey or is gentle is *maddava*; that which feels shame is *lajja*; and that which feels shame is *lajjava*. This is the etymological derivation.
