"One who feels shame is *lajjī*; one who possesses moral dread (*hirimā*); the state of that is *lajjavaṃ*, which means moral dread (*hirī*).
Alternatively, one who has shame is *lajjī*, just as [one is called] *mālī* (garlanded) or *māyī* (deceitful); the state of that is *lajjibhāvo*, which is simply that same shame. 166.
Regarding "patience as endurance" (*adhivāsanakhanti*) in the third [verse], here "endurance" (*adhivāsana*) is said to mean "forbearing" (*khamana*). For that [refers to] others'...
“Adhivāsana” (forbearance) is so called because one bears [offenses] upon oneself by not reacting with opposition to what is wrong (dukkata) or ill-spoken (durutta).
Patience characterized by such forbearance is “adhivāsanakhanti. “Soracca” is purity of virtue. For it is a delight in beautiful deeds.
Or, it is the state of being well-restrained from evil; thus he says “suratabhāvo” (the state of being well-restrained). For this very reason, it is also said in the Abhidhamma:

“In this context, what is gentleness (*soracca*)? That which is non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, and non-transgression by both body and speech—this is called gentleness; indeed, the entire restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) is gentleness. Thus it is handed down.

In the fourth [case], one who is *sakhila* is said to be one whose speech is gentle; its state is *sākhalya*, which is the quality of gentle speech. Therefore he said: “The state of being friendly by way of gentle speech.
For, in the case of a person who is friendly by way of gentle speech...
"Kindness" (bhāva) means gentleness of speech. For this very reason, it is said in the Abhidhamma:

"In that regard, what is gentleness? It is that speech which is not harsh, not rough, not bitter to others, not offensive to others, not bordering on anger, and not conducive to lack of concentration;
having abandoned such speech, it is that speech which is refined, pleasant to the ear, endearing..."
"Speech that goes to the heart, urbane, pleasing to many people, and agreeable to many people—such speech as this is spoken;
therein, what constitutes gentleness of speech, kindly speech, and non-harsh speech, this is called *sākhalya* (courtesy)," so it is said.
In this context, "galls" (*aṇḍaka*) refers to a mass of resin on a tree with a wound, or growths such as mushrooms that have arisen.
They say that "eggs" (*aṇḍaka*) are lumps of powder or knots that arise like eggs from a tree trunk when it is heated.
However, here speech is called "eggs" because its nature is similar to a thorn in its harmfulness and harshness.
It should be understood as harsh speech that enters and strikes the ear like the stalk of a lotus. It is produced by anger.
Its attendants are the states bordering on anger (*kodhasāmanta*). "Cultivated speech" (*porī*): it is like a woman who has been raised since childhood;
just as she is delicate and soft, so too is this speech called "cultivated. By the phrase "one whose speech is gentle," etc., he shows that speech proceeding in such a manner.
168. In the fifth [chapter], only this much is stated here: "Non-violence is the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*)," according to the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.

In the commentary on the *Saṅgītisutta*, however, it is stated: "Non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) refers both to compassion (*karuṇā*) and to the preliminary stage of compassion. In the Abhidhamma as well, it is recorded:

"In this context, what is non-violence? That which is compassion toward beings, the state of being compassionate, the state of having been compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called non-violence. For here too, any kind of compassion is termed "compassion," as is the liberation of mind through compassion.
However, it has indeed reached absorption (*appanā*).
Having formed the suffix *yak* from the word *suci* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and having substituted the letter *u* for the letter *i*, this is the explanation; thus he said:
"That which is to be purified (*socabya*) is the state of purity (*sucibhāva*). And here, "that which is to be purified" is stated by way of virtue (*sīla*). (From the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*)
In the commentary on the *Saṅgītisutta*, however, it is stated: “Purity (*soceyya*) is the state of being pure by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and that which precedes loving-kindness.
For this very reason, even in the Abhidhamma, the definition is given: “In this context, what is purity?

That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the act of loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called purity. For here too, [the same applies].

By the words beginning with “loving-kindness” (*mettī*), whatever kind of loving-kindness has been mentioned, it is specifically the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*) that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
169–171. The sixth, seventh, and eighth [factors] follow the same method as explained below.

172. In the ninth [factor], although stability among the associated mental states is indeed the sense of strength, it is stated—by the phrase “through unshakability in heedlessness,” etc.—that being unshakeable by opposing factors is the preeminent sense of strength.
173. In the tenth [section], because it is the pacification of opposing states, it is called "tranquility" (*samatha*); thus he said: "Tranquility is one-pointedness of mind.

Because it sees and contemplates through various modes such as impermanence and so forth, it is "insight" (*vipassanā*), which is wisdom (*paññā*); thus he said: "The knowledge that discerns formations. 174.
In the eleventh [section], "immorality" (*dussīlya*) is the transgression that breaks the morality one has undertaken. "Failure in view" (*diṭṭhivipatti*)...
“Wrong view is that which corrupts right view,” he says, because wrong view is the corruption of right view—which functions according to the method beginning with “there is what is given.
(175) In the twelfth [section], “perfection of virtue” (*sīlasampadā*) means the state of being complete, the absence of deficiency in every respect regarding that [virtue].
Here, the word *sampadā* has the sense of fulfilling. For this very reason, he says “the state of having fulfilled virtue. “Perfection of view” (*diṭṭhisampadā*)...

Knowledge that proceeds by way of the fulfillment of right view, beginning with the view of self-existence (*atthikadiṭṭhi*); and since that [knowledge] is fivefold by way of the right view of the ownership of action (*kammassakatā*) and so forth, he said, "By that, the ownership of action... (176).

In the thirteenth [chapter], "purity of virtue" (*sīlavisuddhi*) refers to virtue capable of bringing about purification; it is for the sake of the higher purifications, beginning with purity of mind (*cittavisuddhi*).
This means that it is "pure virtue capable of being a condition. For only perfectly pure virtue serves as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*). Therefore, he said:

"Virtue that brings about purification by means of the purifications of virtue. Here too, "bringing about purification" should be understood to mean bringing about the higher purifications, such as the purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) and so forth. However, in the Abhidhamma, this...

“In this context, what is purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*)? Non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, and non-transgression by both body and speech—this is called purification of virtue. Thus it is analyzed.

As for “purification of view” (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*): the knowledge of vision capable of bringing about purification is the purification of vision; it is the purification of the ultimate truth (*paramatthavisuddhi*).
The meaning is: right vision, such as the knowledge of one's own karma (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*), which is capable of leading and bringing one to Nibbāna. Therefore he said:
"Right view is fivefold, leading to purification... and so forth.
Here too, "leading to purification" means leading to the purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*) and to the ultimate purification known as Nibbāna.
The meaning should be understood in this way. In the Abhidhamma, however, this is stated as follows: "In that regard, what is purification of view?
It is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, the knowledge conforming to the truths, the knowledge of the path and of one possessing the path, and the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.
And here, [purification of view consists in] discerning through contrast and agreement that "this unwholesome kamma is not one's own," whereas "this kamma is one's own."
And the knowledge that understands one's own ownership of kamma is the "knowledge of kamma-ownership.

For the three kinds of misconduct—whether committed by oneself or by another—are not called "one's own kamma" because they destroy one's welfare; whereas good conduct is called "one's own kamma" because it generates welfare.
Furthermore, insight-knowledge accords with conventional truth, yet it does not [accord] with ultimate truth.
It is called "knowledge in conformity with truth" because it does not contradict truth.

For when insight-knowledge begins for the purpose of penetrating the characteristics, it conforms to the conventional truth expressed in words as "impermanence, suffering, and non-self," since it penetrates them in exactly that way.
Furthermore, it does not contradict nor does it fail the ultimate truth, Nibbāna, because it leads to it exclusively.
177. In the fourteenth [chapter], "Purification of View" refers to the right view of the first path.
And "exertion according to what has been seen" refers specifically to the energy associated with that [view]. For this very reason, it is said in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Purification of View is explained as knowledge-and-vision; and 'exertion according to what has been seen' is precisely the energy associated with that."
It has been said. For here, "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*) means vision that consists of knowledge; by this, he refers to the path of vision.
"Energy associated with that" refers to the energy associated with the first path. Furthermore, "purification of view" is the right view of the path in its entirety.
And "exertion according to what has been seen" is precisely the energy associated with that [view]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:
Furthermore, it is said: "By the first phrase, the knowledge of the four paths is meant; by the second phrase, the energy associated with that.
Alternatively, "purification of view" refers to all right view, including the knowledge that one's own actions are one's own property (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*) and so forth.
And "the striving of one who has such a view" refers to the mental application of energy... [as described] ...which is right effort. This alone accords with the canonical text.
For in the Abhidhamma, this dyad is analyzed as follows: “Now, as for ‘purification of view’: it is wisdom, understanding... [etc. ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
And for one who has such a view, ‘exertion’ is the arousal of mental energy... [etc. ...right effort.
It is for this very reason that in the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā*, it is explained by means of the phrases beginning with “that which is wisdom, understanding,” and so forth. Below...
The four kinds of knowledge beginning with the knowledge of ownership of action (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*) have been explained and analyzed.

It is stated that the energy indicated by the phrases “whatever mental exertion of energy” and so forth is included; it is mundane when in a mundane state and supramundane when in a supramundane state.
Here too, the right view of the four paths that brings about purification, or all fivefold right view, is called purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).

With this underlying intention, it is said: “Purification of view is precisely right view that brings about purification. However, regarding the phrase “the energy associated with the lower paths,” he speaks with the intention of stating:
“And the striving of one who has seen [according to truth]—this refers to the energy associated with the first path.
And here, this difference in the commentary arises from the difference in the opinions of various reciters.
One should not suspect a mutual contradiction among the words of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

As for the question, "If it is said that 'exertion belongs to one who has such a view,' why is it stated that the energy associated with the lower paths is [meant]? he says: "Because it is suitable for that view," and so forth.
In this context, "for that view" means for the view associated with the lower paths. "Of one who has such a view" means of one who possesses a corresponding view.

They explain the meaning here as follows: for one who possesses a wholesome view, or for one who has produced a view of such a kind, or for one who has produced a view corresponding to the exertion to be undertaken, or for one whose activity proceeds in accordance with that view.
(178) Satisfaction (*tussana*) is contentment (*santuṭṭhi*); there is no contentment for this person, thus it is "lack of contentment" (*asantuṭṭhi*).
The state of one who is not content is "non-contentment" (*asantuṭṭhitā*). This is a designation for the desire for more in the cultivation of wholesome states by one who is not content.
For a person endowed with that [quality], having fulfilled ethical conduct, arouses meditative absorption;
having attained meditative absorption, undertakes insight; and being one who has undertaken insight, [attains] Arhatship.
Having grasped [the goal], one does not come to rest midway; one does not fall into despondency, thinking, "Enough with this much, enough with what has been done.
Therefore he said: "The state of non-contentment with wholesome states, other than the path to arahantship.
In that context, "other than the path to arahantship" means excluding the attainment of the path to arahantship. And "non-retrogression in striving."
Since this follows the method already explained below, its meaning is self-evident and thus it is not analyzed. 179.
One whose mindfulness (*sati*) is lost or gone is "one of confused mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassati*); the state of such a person is "confusion of mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassacca*).
Thus he says: "Confusion of mindfulness means the state of confused mindfulness. And the "state of confused mindfulness" is a phenomenon that is the opposite of mindfulness.
It is not merely the absence of mindfulness. "Lack of clear comprehension" (*asampajañña*) refers precisely to ignorance (*avijjā*), as it is stated:
"What is lack of clear comprehension? It is that which is non-knowing, non-seeing... [and so on]... the blindfold of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root.

For ignorance is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*), since it is to be abandoned by true knowledge; likewise, lack of clear comprehension is the opposite of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). Furthermore, because it is the opposite of clear comprehension...
Because of its presence, there is an absence of knowledge; therefore it is said, "the state of non-knowing. 180.

In the seventeenth [definition], mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away (*apilāpana*). That by which the mind remains upon an object as if floating on water like a gourd—without plunging into it—is "floating" (*pilāpana*). Not floating is "non-floating" (*apilāpana*); that is its characteristic.
Its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is thus: it has the characteristic of non-floating (*apilāpana*).
The commentary on the Chapter on Attainments (*Samāpattivagga*) is finished.
The Third Fifty (*Tatiyapaṇṇāsaka*) is finished.
1. The Code of Anger (Kodhapeyyāla) 181.

In the subsequent sections beginning with the Chapter on Anger, "characterized by resentment" means that, through the act of becoming angry, it has the characteristic of binding the mind with thoughts such as, "He abused me, he struck me," and so forth. It binds and fastens upon anger belonging to a previous time.
It forms and construes a mode of anger; because it binds the mind as if with a basis for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), subsequent anger is called *upanāha*.
A "well-done cause" is a beneficial deed (*upakāra*);
the "smeared over" of that quality characterized by prior kindness is like wiping away water from the body with a cloth—it is the wiping away, the destruction [of that kindness].

"Having this as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of smearing well-made virtues. For in that way, it is called "smearing" (*makkho*) in the sense of smearing over the virtues of others.

He said this because of the malice (*palāsa*) that arises in the form of a grasping for equality, such as when they overwhelm even a person of great learning with the thought, "Even for one so learned, the [five] indeterminate offenses have been committed; what difference is there between you and me? and so forth.
“Palāsa has the characteristic of seizing by the yoke. In this context, “seizing by the yoke” means seizing an equal burden;

it refers to taking up even that which is unequal by making it equal to oneself. It is called *palāsa* because one “bites”; the meaning is that having bitten the virtues of others with one’s teeth, as it were, one cuts them away and makes them equal to one’s own virtues.

“Envy has the characteristic of disparaging others” means it has the characteristic of finding fault with the honors and so forth received by others. Stinginess is the state of being stingy (*macchariya*).
Since that is fivefold—namely, stinginess regarding dwelling and so forth—it is said: “Stinginess is the state of the five kinds of stinginess.
“The characteristic of begrudging” means the characteristic of being unable to endure others sharing in one’s own prosperity.
"Characterized by concealing what has been done" means characterized by concealing evil deeds that have been committed.
"Deceit is that which arises through the state of being a kerāṭika," he says; thus, "deceit is characterized by the state of being a kerāṭika.
They say that a person who reveals themselves in one way is a kerāṭika, a crooked trader. For a kerāṭika person is like the fish Ānanda.
187. "As one who is deposited according to what was brought" means that just as someone is brought and placed [somewhere], so too he is deposited in hell by his own karma;
he is simply placed there—this is the meaning. 2. The Series on the Unwholesome (Akusalapeyyāla) 191–200.

"Dukkhavaḍḍhikā" means those for whom there is an increase of suffering. For those who increase suffering, who cause it to arise again and again, there is an increase of suffering; thus it is said. The same method applies here to the term "sukhavaḍḍhikā."
3. Vinayapeyyāla 201.

"For the sake of benefit" (*atthavasā*) means for the sake of a particular excellence, that is, a particular advantage. Since these [rules] are the causes for the formulation of the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*), it is said:
"with reference to two reasons. Alternatively, "benefit" (*attha*) itself is "for the sake of benefit" (*atthavasa*); thus it is stated: "two benefits" means "two reasons."
It exists. Alternatively, "atthavaso" means that which has purpose (attha) as its fruit (phala), and because it functions in dependence upon that, it is under its control;

thus, "cause" (kāraṇa) is how the meaning should be understood here. Just as when it is said, "non-covetousness is a foot of the Dhamma," the meaning is that non-covetousness is a single constituent part of the Dhamma, so too here, "training rule" (sikkhāpada) means a constituent part of training, a single portion of the training.
"One should understand that 'a portion' (padeso) is the meaning here," he said, explaining: "The training rule has been laid down means a section of the training has been established.

"Conducive to the welfare of the Saṅgha" (saṅghasuṭṭhu) refers to the state of being well-disposed toward the Saṅgha; it is like the sense of "well done, O King" found in other passages, or the manner of accepting a statement by saying, "Well, venerable sir.
Therefore, he said: "'For the sake of the Saṅgha’s welfare' means for the sake of the Saṅgha’s state of being well-disposed," and so forth.
“For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct”: those called “difficult to correct” are persons of immoral conduct.
They are so called because even when they fall into misconduct, they do so with difficulty; or, having committed a transgression, they feel no shame.
For their restraint—for if there were no training rule (sikkhāpada), [they would ask], “What have you seen? What have you heard? What have we done? In what [have we offended]?”

Thinking, "Having charged us with some offense regarding a matter, they will harass the Saṅgha," [the Saṅgha]—when there is a training rule—will show them that training rule and restrain them in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
Therefore it is said: "For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct."
"For the comfort of well-behaved bhikkhus" means for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of those bhikkhus who are well-behaved and of pleasing virtue.

For bhikkhus of pleasing virtue, not knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and the proper time and limits, become weary while striving for the perfection of the three trainings and are oppressed;
however, [knowing] what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and the proper time...
Knowing the boundary and striving for the fulfillment of the three trainings, they do not become weary, nor are they oppressed.
Therefore, the proclamation of the training rules leads to their comfortable dwelling. Or rather, the very restraint of individuals who are difficult to manage is their comfortable dwelling;
for indeed, the Uposatha does not stand firm by relying on a person of immoral conduct.
The invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) does not take place; communal legal acts (*saṅghakamma*) do not proceed; there is no harmony;
and the monks, being distracted, are unable to apply themselves to the recitation of the scriptures, formal questioning, meditation subjects, and so forth.
However, when those who are immoral have been restrained, all this calamity ceases, and consequently, the well-behaved monks dwell in comfort. Thus, for the sake of the well-behaved...
Regarding the phrase "for the comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus," the meaning here should be understood in two ways.

In the passage, "Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma for the sake of the restraint of taints (*āsava*) pertaining only to the present life," the defilements that constitute the root of dispute are referred to as "taints. [In contrast, elsewhere it is said:
"By which one is reborn as a god, or becomes a gandhabba, or a bird..."
“Those by which one might go to the state of a *yakkha*, or fall back into the human state—those taints (*āsava*) of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.

Here, this refers to karma belonging to the three planes and all remaining unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). In this context, however, it refers to [the taints consisting of] reviling others, remorse, being slain, being bound, and so forth.
And because various kinds of calamities, which are themselves states of suffering in the realms of misery (apāya), are called "taints" (āsava), he said:

“Of those to be obtained in this very life, in this very selfhood, by reason of transgression,” and so forth. For if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rules (sikkhāpada), then there would have arisen from the causes of indulging in unrighteous conduct, taking what is not given, killing living beings, and so on, the censures of others and the like.

This was said with reference to various kinds of harm pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), as well as those kinds of harm consisting in the experience of great suffering—such as the fivefold bonds and judicial punishments—for one who is reborn in the hells and other realms solely on account of those [present-life actions].

"For the restraint of the taints (*āsava*) pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives" was said. "The present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) is said to be that which is directly perceptible (*paccakkha*).

The personal existence (*attabhāva*); the states existing therein are those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). Because one must depart and go away from it, it is called the "hereafter" (*samparāya*), meaning the world beyond;
the states existing therein are those pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).

Regarding "unwholesome enmities" (*akusalaverānaṃ*): these refer to the five types of misconduct, beginning with the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*). They are called "enmities" because they are the causes of enmity.

Furthermore, regarding the hostilities arising among individuals, or those very things previously mentioned as "states of suffering" such as killing, imprisonment, and so forth—it was for the purpose of cutting off their faction that a training rule similar to the rule on eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*) was laid down for those of evil desires.
"Of wise people" refers to those who are worldly examiners; for it is they who [rely] upon the laying down of the training rules.
Having understood the formulation of the training rules, or having seen monks practicing in accordance with what has been prescribed, they develop confidence, thinking:
"Indeed, those things in the world that are grounds for the common people's passion, hatred, and delusion—far removed from these are these recluses, the sons of the Sakyans;
they perform what is difficult to do; they perform what is weighty."
It is like a brahmin possessed by wrong view who, upon seeing a book in the Vinaya Piṭaka, [becomes suspicious].
"For the sake of producing ever-increasing confidence" means for the purpose of generating faith more and more.

For even those sons of good family who have confidence in the Teaching, having either learned the formulation of the training rules or seen the bhikkhus practicing according to what has been prescribed, [exclaim]: "Oh, how these masters perform difficult deeds!"
They become increasingly confident [in the thought]: “Those who maintain the practice of eating once a day, the holy life, and the restraint of the Vinaya for as long as life lasts.

For the sake of the long endurance of the True Dhamma means: for the sake of the long endurance of the threefold True Dhamma—the True Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma*), the True Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*), and the True Dhamma of realization (*adhigama-saddhamma*). In that regard, all that is included within the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*)...
The word of the Buddha is called the True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-saddhamma).

The thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), the fourteen rules of conduct from the Khandhaka, the eighty-two major rules, and virtue, concentration, and insight—this is called the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma).
The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is called the True Dhamma of realization (adhigama-saddhamma). That...
Because, when there is the laying down of training rules, all monks master the training rule, its analysis (*vibhaṅga*), and other words of the Buddha for the purpose of clarifying its meaning;

and by practicing according to what has been laid down, they fulfill that practice and thereby attain the supramundane state (*lokuttara-dhamma*) to be attained through practice. Therefore, with the laying down of training rules, there is long-term endurance.
"Of the fivefold discipline" means of the discipline that is of five kinds by way of discipline as the removal of the cause (*tadaṅgavinaya*), and so forth. In the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, however,
when there is the promulgation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-pannatti*), all fourfold discipline— namely, discipline as restraint (*saṃvaravinaya*),
discipline as abandoning (*pahānavinaya*), discipline as settling disputes (*samathavinaya*), and discipline as formal rule (*paññattivinaya*)— is assisted, supported, and well-supported.

Therefore it was said: "For the support of the Vinaya. In this context, *saṃvaravinaya* (the discipline of restraint) refers to the fivefold restraint—namely, the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*), the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*), the restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*), and the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*).

It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains those things that ought to be restrained and those things that ought to be disciplined, such as bodily misconduct; and it is called "discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines them.

"Discipline as abandoning" (*pahānavinaya*) refers to the fivefold abandoning—namely, abandoning by way of its own constituent part (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*)—because it is "abandoning" in the sense of relinquishing and "discipline" in the sense of disciplining;

therefore, it is called "discipline as abandoning. "Discipline as settlement" (*samathavinaya*) refers to the seven principles for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*). "Discipline as formulation" (*paññattivinaya*)...

It is the training rule (sikkhāpada) itself. For since a training rule can only come into existence when the promulgation of that training rule already exists, the "discipline of promulgation" (paññattivinaya), which is synonymous with the training rule, is supported by the promulgation of the training rule. 202–230.
"Five for the bhikkhus": this refers to the five [categories] by way of the detailed recitation of the Nidāna, Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Aniyata, and Vitthāra.
The recitations for the bhikkhus. Regarding "four for the bhikkhunīs": this refers to the remaining four, excluding the *aniyata* (undetermined) recitation from among those stated for the bhikkhus.
Ordination by the formula "Come, bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhūpasampadā*) is the ordination established by the mere utterance of the words "Come, bhikkhu.

For the Blessed One, upon seeing a person endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) for the state of being an "Come-bhikkhu," [would look] from within his saffron-colored rag-robe at one of golden complexion...
Extending his right hand and uttering a Brahma-voice, he says: "Come, monk; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.

With these very words of the Blessed One, his lay appearance vanishes, his going-forth and full ordination are established, and he becomes shaven-headed, clothed in saffron robes—thus, one [is ordained].
Having dressed himself, putting on one robe and placing another over his shoulder— with a clay bowl, the color of a blue lotus, resting against his left shoulder—
he [recited]: “The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle, together with the water-strainer—
these eight are the requisites of a bhikkhu devoted to yoga.”

When these eight requisites had been fastened upon his body, he stood there, endowed with the four postures like a monk of a hundred years’ standing, following the Teacher’s way and having the Buddha as his preceptor, while paying homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One.

“Ordination by going for refuge” (*saraṇagamanūpasampadā*) is the ordination authorized by the three goings for refuge, spoken three times by breaking the silence in the manner beginning with, “I go for refuge to the Buddha. “Ordination by instruction” (*ovādūpasampadā*) is the ordination consisting in the reception of the instruction.

And she said: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'A keen sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing. In this way, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, all of it..."
“Making that my goal, attending to it, and applying my whole mind, I shall listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear”—thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself.

Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “May mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by joy, not be abandoned by me. Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. By means of this acceptance of the exhortation...
The ordination permitted for the Elder Mahākassapa.

The ordination by answering questions is the ordination permitted for Sopāka. It is said that while the Blessed One was walking back and forth in the Eastern Monastery, he addressed the novice Sopāka:
"Sopāka, is this the perception of a bloated corpse, or is it the perception of form?"... [and so on]... these... [and so on]... Sopāka.
"Are phenomena (dhammas) of different meanings and different expressions, or are they of one meaning with only the expression being different?
Thus he asked ten questions concerning the foul (asubha). The other answered them. The Blessed One, having given him his approval, asked:
"How many years old are you, Sopāka? "I am seven years old, Blessed One. "Sopāka, having compared you with my own omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa)..."
"Having answered the question," he said, "with a mind inclined [toward it], he authorized full ordination (*upasampadā*). This is the full ordination by answering a question.
The full ordination known as "by a motion and a third proclamation" (*ñatticatuttha*) is the current method of ordination for monks.

Full ordination by the "heavy rules" (*garudhamma*) means full ordination through the acceptance of the heavy rules; and that occurred for Mahāpajāpatī through her acceptance of the eight heavy rules.

It is permitted. "Full ordination from both Saṅghas" means that for a bhikkhunī, the eightfold formal act of ordination is permitted by two legal procedures: one consisting of a motion and three proclamations from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and one consisting of a motion and three proclamations from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
"Ordination by messenger" refers to the permission granted for the ordination of Aḍḍhakāsī, the courtesan.
"A formal act by proclamation (*ñattikamma*) proceeds to nine matters. What are the nine matters to which it proceeds? It proceeds to:

reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), the Uposatha, the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*), authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), receiving (*paṭiggaha*), postponement (*paccukkaḍḍhana*), and the ninth is the very characteristic of the formal act itself.
It proceeds to these nine matters thus described. Therein: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs..."
“Such-and-such a person is seeking full ordination from the Venerable such-and-such; he has been instructed by me.
If it is opportune for the Saṅgha, let such-and-such come; he should be told, ‘Come. This is the formal introduction of one seeking full ordination;
this is what is called “introduction.”
“Venerable sirs, listen to me. This monk named so-and-so is a preacher of the Dhamma; neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga occurs to him.
Without discerning the meaning, he misinterprets the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing.
If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us have the monk named so-and-so removed, and the rest of us shall deal with this legal issue.”
"Let us settle [this] through pacification"—thus, the removal of a monk who delivers a Dhamma discourse during a formal decision by a committee is called "removal.

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the Uposatha day of the fifteenth. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha"—thus, a motion (ñatti) established by way of the Uposatha ritual is called "Uposatha."

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the fifteenth day, the Pavāraṇā. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā. This motion established by way of the Pavāraṇā procedure is called a Pavāraṇā-ñatti.
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: such-and-such a person desires ordination from the Venerable such-and-such.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, may I instruct such-and-such a person,” and, “If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha...”
“May [so-and-so] instruct [so-and-so],” “If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha,
may I question [so-and-so] regarding the obstructive factors,” “If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha,
may [so-and-so] question [so-and-so] regarding the obstructive factors,” “If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, may I [question] [so-and-so] regarding the Vinaya.”
[The motion should be made: "If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let so-and-so ask so-and-so about the Vinaya";
"If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, when asked by so-and-so about the Vinaya, I shall answer";
"If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let so-and-so, when asked by so-and-so about the Vinaya, answer. Thus...
A motion (*ñatti*) established for the purpose of appointing either oneself or another is called an appointment (*sammuti*).
“Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs: this robe-cloth, which was to be forfeited by the monk so-and-so, has been relinquished to the Sangha.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, let the Sangha [deal with] this robe-cloth for the monk so-and-so...”

"Should they give it? or "Venerable sirs, when it is appropriate for you, may you give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so"—giving things such as robes that have been relinquished in this manner is called "giving.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so remembers an offense; he discloses it and makes it clear."

He acts and declares: "If it is timely for the Saṅgha, may I accept the offense of the bhikkhu named so-and-so," or, "Venerable sirs, if it is timely for you, may I accept the offense of the bhikkhu named so-and-so.

He should then be asked, "Do you see [the offense]? If he replies, "Yes, I see it," [the other says], "You should exercise restraint in the future. In this way, the acceptance of an offense is called an "acceptance."
“Venerable residents, listen to me. If it is appropriate for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha;

we shall perform the Pavāraṇā at a later time. If those monks who are quarrelsome, argumentative, and creators of legal disputes in the Saṅgha should continue to dwell there at that time, the resident monk who is competent—
The resident monks should inform those capable of doing so: "Venerable sirs, let the resident monks hear me.
If it is timely for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the following bright fortnight.
This is what is called the postponement of the Pavāraṇā once it has been arranged.
Everyone must assemble together in one place. Having assembled, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. While we were living in a state of quarreling, disputing, and contending, much that is unbecoming of a recluse was practiced and spoken by us. If we [should confess] these offenses..."
"We shall deal with one another; this legal issue might lead to harshness, violence, and schism.

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha settle this legal issue by means of the 'covering over as with grass,' setting aside grave offenses and setting aside matters connected with householders. Thus is the settlement by the "covering over as with grass" established.
The motion that is first of all and encompasses everything is called the characteristic of a formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*).
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) proceeds to seven points. What are these seven points?

Restoration (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), revocation (*uddharaṇa*), confession (*desana*), and the characteristic of a formal act itself as the seventh—thus it is.

He goes to the seven places that have been mentioned. Therein, the expulsion (nissāraṇā) spoken of in the Khandhaka by way of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi’s overturning of the bowl, and the reinstatement (osāraṇā) spoken of by way of his righting of the bowl, should be understood.

[Also] the formal authorization of a boundary (sīmā-sammuti), the formal authorization for not being separated from the three robes (ticīvara-avippavāsa-sammuti), the formal authorization for a rug (santhata-sammuti), the designator of meals (bhattuddesaka), the distributor of lodgings (senāsanaggāhāpaka), and the storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika).

Formal authorization (*sammuti*) should be understood by way of these authorizations: the authorization for the receiver of robes, the distributor of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, the distributor of solid foods, the dispenser of minor items, the one who causes the *sāṭiyā* robe to be taken, the one who causes the bowl to be taken, the supervisor of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), and the supervisor of novices (*sāmaṇera*).
Giving should be understood by way of the giving of the *kaṭhina* robe and the giving of a robe as a gift from the deceased (*mataka-cīvara*).
The lifting [of the kaṭhina] should be understood by way of the removal of the kaṭhina. The teaching should be understood by way of the designation of the site for a hut and the site for a monastery.

Furthermore, regarding the settlement by "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka), having set aside three motions—the motion that encompasses all [faults] and one motion for each side—there is again one motion on one side and [one] on the other side.

One or two *kammavācās* consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) have been stated; the characteristics of the formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*) should be understood by way of these.
It is said that a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*) goes to seven points. What are those seven points?

They are: reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), censure (*niggaha*), admonition (*samanubhāsana*), and the characteristic of the formal act itself as the seventh.
Thus he goes to the seven places mentioned. Therein, "expulsion" (nissāraṇā) should be understood by way of the seven formal acts (kamma), beginning with the act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma);
"readmission" (osāraṇā) should be understood by way of the pacification of those very same formal acts.

"Consent" (sammuti) should be understood by way of the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs. "Bestowal" (dāna) [should be understood] by way of the granting of probation (parivāsa) and the granting of the trial period (mānatta).
It should be understood [in this way]. Discipline is to be understood by way of the formal act of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanakamma*).

Exhortation is to be understood by way of these eleven exhortations: the followers of one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattaka*), the eight cases of "up to the third time" (*yāvatatiyaka*), Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷī—these are the "up to the third time" cases.
The characteristic of the formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*) is to be understood by way of the formal act of ordination (*upasampadakamma*) and the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhānakamma*).

Regarding the phrases "presence of the Dhamma" and so forth: by whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever teaching of the Teacher the Saṅgha performs an act—this is the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, and the presence of the Teacher’s teaching.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the factual basis; "Vinaya" refers to both the formal charge and the reminder; and the "teaching of the Teacher" refers to the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*).
And there is the perfection of the proclamation. As many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived;
the consent of those who are entitled to give their consent has been brought forth; and those present do not protest—this is "presence before the Saṅgha.
The presence of the individual for whom the Saṅgha performs the formal act is "presence of the person. The rest here is of obvious meaning, as it follows the method already stated.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Unexpounded Meanings in the Commentary on the *Dukanipāta* of the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the Commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,
Chapter on Threes (Tikanipāta),
Part One: The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka)
1. Bālavagga 1.
Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā 1.
In the first [sutta] of the Tikanipāta, regarding the word *bhaya* (fear), he says it is "the terror of the mind" (*cittutrāsa*), meaning the agitation of the mind. *Upaddava* (calamity) means...
An obstacle (*antarāya*). Because it causes distraction, it is called "the mode of non-one-pointedness. An affliction (*upasagga*) means being afflicted;
it refers to falling into a state of distress due to an unremediable calamity, such as harassment by deities.
Since that [affliction] is a cause of despondency for one who is being tormented by the absence of a remedy and is thus unable to act, it is therefore called "the mode of clinging here and there."
"When they do not come on the day specified" means when they do not arrive on the day fixed for their arrival after having been deceived.
"Having set fire to the door" means having set fire to the door so that they could not go outside.
"Covered and concealed with reeds" means having covered the top with reeds by way of a thatched roof and [further] with those very same [reeds].

It is also covered all around according to the method for a wooden hut (*dārukuṭika*). By the phrase "this is the same principle," he extends [the rule] by analogy to the roofing with grass and the fact that the remaining materials are made of wood.

"The widow’s son" is an elliptical expression (indicating those who possess such characteristics). For they are devoid of passion, undisciplined, unrestrained, and do whatever they please. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Bhayasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Lakkhaṇasutta:

In the second [sutta], it is called *lakkhaṇa* because by means of it a fool is characterized (*lakkhīyati*) or known; that which has this as its characteristic is "characterized" (*lakkhaṇa*). It is a kamma. Thus [the term is explained].

“Characterized by action” means “action proceeding through the door of the body, etc.”; thus he said. It is called *apadāna* because by it faults are removed (*apa-dīyanti*), protected, or because it is plucked (*lūyanti*) and cut away;
it refers to the application of beings’ conduct, whether right or wrong. Because one shines by means of that, it is “shining with *apadāna*” (*apadānasobhanī*).
Therefore he said, “Wisdom indeed,” and so forth. “By one’s own conduct alone” means precisely by one’s own behavior (*cariyā*).
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the Cinti Sutta and others.
3–4. In the third [verse], “by these” (*etehi*) refers to ill-considered thoughts and so forth. By this, he expresses that the word *lakkhaṇa* has the sense of a refuge (*saraṇattha*).
“Those very ones” (*tāneva*) refers to the characteristics themselves. “Of him” (*assa*) means of the fool (*bāla*).

They are called “signs of the fool” (*bālanimittāni*) because by them the fool is measured, defined, or recognized. “Apadāna” is said to mean a well-known deed; and ill-considered thoughts and so forth are [the deeds] of the fool.
These are renowned for their uncommon nature. Therefore, it is said: "The misdeeds of a fool.

That which is thought with a mind corrupted and defiled by covetousness and so forth is "ill-thought"; one who thinks such things is a "thinker of ill-thoughts. That which is spoken with a mind corrupted by greed and so forth, such as false speech and the like, is "ill-spoken";
one who speaks such things is a "speaker of ill-spoken words. Because of those very [defilements], there is "wrong-action" (*dukkaṭa-kamma*) to be performed, such as the taking of life and so forth.
"One who does what is wrong" is one who performs unwholesome actions. Therefore, he said "thinking," and so forth.

"In accordance with what was stated" means by way of recollecting the meaning of the statement beginning with "This person is a fool," according to the sequence already mentioned, such as "He is characterized by these [qualities] as 'a wise man,'" and so on.
"By way of good mental conduct, etc. refers to the passage beginning with "Thinking, he thinks only what is well-thought-out by way of non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view," and so forth.

These [terms] should be applied by way of the three good conducts, beginning with good conduct of mind. The fourth [discourse] has its meaning already explained because it follows the method stated previously.
The commentary on the *Cinti-sutta* and others is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the *Ayoniso-sutta* and others.
5–10. "In the fifth [section], how many bases for recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna) are there? and so forth will be made clear in the sixth [section].

"Thus it was thought" means it was improperly thought (ayoniso). "He spoke of what was not a question as a question" means he answered while thinking, "This is not a question at all, yet it approaches as a question.
"Without losing the tenfold analytical power of phrasing (byañjanabuddhi)"—
“Lax and forceful, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized (niggahīta);
connected, distinct, and released—thus is the tenfold classification according to the intellect regarding phonemes.
Without omitting this tenfold classification of phonemic intelligence thus described.
In this context, a syllable to be pronounced with the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the places of formation (*karaṇa*) made relaxed is "relaxed" (*sithila*);
a syllable to be pronounced with those same [points and places] made firm is "firm" (*dhanita*). A long vowel has the duration of two measures (*matta*);

a short vowel has the duration of one measure. "Heavy" (*garuka*) refers specifically to the long vowel, or that which follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), such as in the phrase: "of the venerable Elder Buddharakkhita."

When it is spoken by making [the preceding vowel] short, it is called "light" (*lahuka*); or rather, it is that which is spoken by making it subordinate to the following word, as in: “of the venerable elder Buddharakkhita.
A "consonant cluster" (*niggahīta*) is that which should be uttered with the mouth not opened, nasalized, having restrained (i.e., suppressed) the articulating organs without releasing them.
A "compound" (*sambandha*) is that which is connected with a subsequent word, such as: “be silent” (*tuṇhassā*).
It is called *vavatthita* when, having made no connection with the following word, one speaks with a pause, saying "be silent.
It is called *vimutta* when it is spoken without restraining the vocal organs, releasing them, with the mouth open, and without nasalization.
Thus, there is a tenfold classification of the understanding of phonemes (*byañjana-buddhi*) according to the manner of articulation, such as the relaxed (*sithila*) and so forth.
The classification of the consciousness that produces syllables is tenfold.
For all syllables are mind-originated, and they are called "phonemes" (*byañjana*) because they express the intended meaning.

This will be clarified in the *Pañcaka-nipāta* (Fives) in the passage beginning, “It is impossible, friend Sāriputta. Furthermore, this will be clarified in the *Chakka-nipāta* (Sixes) in the passage beginning, “How many, Ānanda, are the bases for recollection? There is nothing further to be said regarding the sixth and subsequent groups.
The commentary on the *Ayoniso-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Bāla-vagga* is finished.
2. The *Rathakāra-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the Ñātasutta 11.
Regarding the first [verse] of the second [section], because it is known (*ñāta*) that it is indeed well-known (*paññāta*), he said “known, well-known. To the question “Of what is it not conformable?
he said “of the Dispensation (*sāsana*); the meaning is: not conformable to, and unsuitable for, the Dispensation. Now, regarding the word *ananulomika*:
Showing the etymology, he said: "It does not conform, thus it is 'non-conforming' (ananulomika).
Alternatively, "of the teaching" (sāsanassa) means "the teaching" (sāsana). The connection here should be understood as: "it does not conform to the teaching, thus it is non-conforming.

"Similar or dissimilar" refers to being similar or dissimilar by way of gender. He said "with regard to persons," meaning he spoke without distinguishing them by their common gender. [The term] "insanity" (ummādaṃ)...

"He reached [the goal]," it is said, because after he had resolved upon virtue (*sīla*), he sat upon the surface of his bed inside a room with its doors closed and cultivated loving-kindness (*mettā*) directed toward his wife.
Blinded by the passion (*rāga*) that arose through that practice of loving-kindness, and desiring to go to his wife's presence, he failed to notice the door;
instead, striking against the wall out of a desire to break through it and exit, he reached [his goal].
He fought against the wall throughout the entire night. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Ñāta Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta.
12. In the second [case], the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is likewise dependent upon the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
By this, it is shown that immediately upon entering the going-forth, the fourfold purification of virtue is also undertaken.

"They are dependent upon the Path" means that because one must practice for the sake of attaining the Path, the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa* meditations and so forth are indeed dependent upon the Path; therefore, by the mention of the Path alone, [they are included].
Their inclusion should also be understood, for the intention is that without them, the attainment of the path is impossible.

Because the penetration of non-delusion reaches its culmination through the attainment of the supreme path, there is an especially superior non-delusion regarding the dhammas of the fruit just as there is regarding the dhammas of the path;
thus it is said, "by direct higher knowledge" (*sayam abhiññā*), meaning "having known by oneself. Such knowing—
Its realization is the act of making it personally manifest; thus it is said, "having realized. Therefore he says:
"having made it manifest by means of one's own most distinguished wisdom. Likewise, its realization is the acquisition of it within oneself;
thus it is said, "having attained," as he says: "having acquired."
The commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Āsaṃsa Sutta: 13.
Regarding the third [verse], "He who is at peace" (*santo*): here, the word *santa* refers to the state of being weary, as in such expressions as "a weary yojana-long journey."
In such passages as, “This applied thought (*vitakka*) and this sustained thought (*vicāra*) have become peaceful (*santa*) and stilled,” it refers to the state of having ceased.
In such passages as, “This Dhamma has been realized by me—profound, hard to see, difficult to awaken to, peaceful (*santa*), sublime,” it refers to being the objective domain of peaceful knowledge.

In such passages as, “Of one who is ever peaceful and mindful,” it refers to the subsiding of the defilements. In such passages as, “The peaceful indeed proclaim [the Dhamma] among the virtuous,” it refers to... [the state of being peaceful].
In the passage beginning, “Bhikkhus, these five great thieves exist and are found among us,” it refers to their existence. Here too, it refers precisely to their existence;
thus he says, “‘Existing’ means they are present and are found. In that context, “exist” (*atthi*) means they are found in accordance with worldly convention.
For here, because it is spoken in connection with a person, “existence” (*atthibhāvo*) should be understood solely by way of worldly common usage.
Not in the sense of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). This word "exists" (*atthi*) should be understood as a particle (*nipāta*), as in such passages as "there are head-hairs in this body.
"Existing" (*saṃvijjamāna*) means being found (*upalabbhamāna*). For whatever exists is found; therefore he said, "'Existing' is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Without hope" (*anāsa*) means devoid of longing. Therefore he said, "one who does not long. "He hopes" (*āsaṃsati*) means he longs.
*Āsaṃso*. Weavers (*vilīvakārakā*) are those who make vessels such as baskets using bamboo, rattan, and other materials.
Hunters (*nesādā*) are those who kill deer, fish, and so forth; they include deer-trappers, fishermen, and the like. Carpenters (*rathakārā*) are those who fashion leather straps for chariots;
they are also called fletchers (*dhammakārā*). *Pūti* is a name for excrement; those who remove it are *pukkusā*, namely, scavengers of flower refuse.
“Ugly” (*dubbaṇṇo*) means deformed. “A dwarf” (*okoṭimako*) means one who is low due to the absence of height; the meaning is that his body is short. Thus he said, “a *lakuṇḍaka*.
For a *lakuṇḍaka* is one who moves or exists like a *laku* (a small jar);
that is, he is short. “One-eyed” (*kāṇo*) means he blinks or has a closed eye. As for that blinking, it may be with one eye or even with both; thus he said, “one-eyed in one eye.”
"Or one who is blind in both eyes. *Kuṇa* means "mutilation"; a deficiency of the hand. One who has that is called *kuṇī*. A *khañja* is said to be one deficient in foot.
One whose side—a portion (*pakkha*) of the body consisting of the lower part—is struck or impaired is called *pakkhahata*.
Therefore he says, "a cripple on a stool" (*pīṭhasappī*). That which is to be carried or led toward a lamp or illumination is *padīpeyya*; it refers to requisites such as oil and so forth.

“He does not make an aspiration” means that at the time of the royal consecration, the younger brother does not make an aspiration because, when there is an elder brother, the younger brother lacks the entitlement. One who is worthy of consecration is “worthy of consecration” (*abhisekāraho*); one who is not worthy of consecration due to being afflicted by defects such as blindness or lameness is “not worthy of consecration.
There is no such thing as a “bad” virtue; therefore, he said “unvirtuous” (*nissīlo*) to show that the prefix *du-* here has the sense of non-existence.

He said “one of base character” (*lāmakadhammo*) because, as in the passage “Evil is easily done by the evil,” the word *pāpa* is a synonym for what is inferior. [This refers to] the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*).
Or, he is immoral (*dussīla*). He is of evil character (*pāpadhamma*) due to a failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*).

Alternatively, he is immoral through the breach of restraint in body and speech, and he is of evil character through the breach of mental restraint or the breach of mindfulness-restraint and so forth. He is immoral due to impure application (*asuddhappayoga*), and he is of evil character due to impure intention (*asuddhāsaya*).

He is immoral by being devoid of wholesome virtue (*kusalasīla*), and he is of evil character by being possessed of unwholesome conduct (*akusalasīla*). "By means of impurities" (*asucīhi*) means by means of those that are not purified (*aparisuddha*).
“Conduct that is to be suspected by others” means conduct that is to be suspected by others through their doubts, thinking, “I suppose this is his deed.
Therefore he said, “some [deed],” and so forth. Alternatively, “conduct that is to be suspected by oneself” shows by this as well that the word *saṅkassara* has the sense of an object (accusative).
By one’s own doubt, one suspects—that is, harbors suspicion regarding—the conduct and actions of others.
"He runs about" (*vidhāvati*) is also [the meaning of] "one of suspicious conduct" (*saṅkassarasamācāro*); thus, here too, it should be understood as having the sense of the agent (*kattusādhanatā*).
For when he sees two or three people talking, thinking, "I suspect they are speaking of my fault," he remembers and runs toward their conduct out of suspicion.

"One who has made such a claim" (*evaṃpaṭiñño*) refers to when, in the counting of how many monks are in the monastery during the distribution of voting sticks (*salākaggahaṇa*) and so forth, the count has begun with "How many monks are in the monastery? and [he says], "I too..."
Having given his word, “I am an ascetic; I too am an ascetic,” he performs such acts as taking voting tickets; thus he is one who professes himself an ascetic, thinking, “I am an ascetic.

“One who carries a Sumbhaka bowl” means one who carries a clay bowl. “Internally rotten through his actions” means through defiled action; or, because of being devoid of virtue, he is internally rotten due to being lacking the essence of virtue.
“He has become a mass of filth” means that he has become, has been produced as, such a thing.
He says, "born from filth" (*kasambujāta*), meaning "one in whom the refuse of lust and so forth has arisen. Alternatively, *kasambu* refers to water mixed with putrid, decaying matter;
and in this teaching, one who is immoral is like such water because he is loathsome.

Therefore, he is "born from filth" because he has arisen like that filth. [This is said] because of the absence of the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). Where...
It is stated because of the breaking of that foundation upon which one might be able to attain *arahantship*.
"In the fulfillment of the great virtue" means: in the fulfillment of that wherein one might be able to reach *arahantship* by being established.
The commentary on the Āsaṃsasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Cakkavattisutta: 14.
In the fourth [sutta], "by means of the four bases of sympathy" refers to those known as generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.

By means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahakāraṇa*). "He turns the wheel" means he sets in motion the wheel of authority (*āṇācakkam*). Alternatively, here "wheel" should be understood as the jewel-wheel (*ratanacakkam*).

For this word *cakkam* is seen used in the sense of prosperity, a characteristic mark, a chariot part, a mode of deportment, giving, and in reference to the jewel, the Dharma, the hoof, the wheel, and so forth. "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels; endowed with which..."
In such passages as “of gods and humans,” it is seen in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*). In “wheels have appeared on the soles of the feet,” it refers to a mark (*lakkhaṇa*).
In “like the wheel of one who draws [a plough],” it refers to a part of a chariot (*rathaṅga*). In “four-wheeled, nine-gated,” it refers to the modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).
In “Give and enjoy; do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion for all living beings,” it refers to giving (*dāna*).
In the phrase “the divine wheel-treasure appeared,” it refers to the wheel-treasure (*ratanacakra*). In the phrase “the wheel set in motion by me,” it refers to the wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakra*).
In the phrase “for the person struck by desire, the wheel revolves upon his head,” it refers to the razor-wheel (*khuracakra*).

In the phrase “with a wheel whose edge is like a razor,” it refers to the weapon-wheel (*paharaṇacakra*). In the phrase “a thunderbolt-wheel,” it refers to the circle of the thunderbolt (*asanimaṇḍala*).
Furthermore, this [wheel-turning monarch] is to be seen here in the context of the Wheel-Treasure (*ratnacakra*). To what extent, then, is one called a wheel-turner?

Even by only a finger’s breadth or two finger-breadths, the Wheel-Treasure rises up into the air and proceeds. For indeed, from the seat where all wheel-turners have risen, the Wheel-Treasure approaches.
Having gone there, he raises a golden water-pitcher with a spout like an elephant’s trunk, sprinkles it with water, and says, "May your majesty, the Wheel-Treasure, conquer!
Immediately upon these words, the Wheel-Treasure rises into the air and sets in motion;
at the very moment it sets in motion, that king becomes known as a Cakkavatti.
"Dhamma" refers to the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action, or the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).

One who is devoted to these ten kinds of wholesome dhammas or to the irreproachable royal duties is "righteous" (*dhammika*). Because he gladdens the entire world by means of that dhamma, he is a "righteous king" (*dhammarāja*).
Alternatively, he is a righteous king because his sovereignty was obtained through dhamma. [He is so called] by the wheel-turning monarchs through dhamma...

He attains sovereignty through the right method, not through unrighteousness. "By the tenfold conduct of a wheel-turning monarch" means by the conduct of wheel-turning monarchs which is divided into ten types.
But what is that tenfold conduct of a wheel-turning monarch? It is said:
“But what, sire, is that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch? In that case, dear son, relying on the Dhamma alone—
honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, esteeming the Dhamma, worshipping the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma—
with the Dhamma as your banner, the Dhamma as your standard, and the Dhamma as your authority, provide righteous protection, defense, and security.”

Be mindful toward your inner circle, your army, the kshatriyas, your followers, the brahmins and householders, the people of the towns and countryside, the ascetics and brahmins, and even the beasts and birds.
And, dear son, let no unrighteous conduct prevail within your realm. Furthermore, dear son, you should provide wealth to those in your realm who are destitute. Those who...

And furthermore, dear son, in your realm there are recluses and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and negligence, who are established in patience and gentleness, and who tame themselves alone, calm themselves alone, and bring themselves alone to final nibbāna.
You should approach them from time to time, question them, and examine them: "Venerable sirs, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?"
"What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated?
What, being done by me, would lead to harm and suffering for a long time? Or what, being done by me, would lead to welfare and happiness for a long time?
Having heard this from them, you should avoid whatever is unwholesome and practice whatever is wholesome.
"Having undertaken it, you should practice it. This, dear son, is that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.

Thus, according to the method set forth in the *Cakkavatti-sutta*, [one should appoint] one for the household and the army, one for the nobles, one for the followers, one for the brahmins and householders, one for the townspeople and countryfolk, one for the recluses and brahmins, and one for the wild animals and birds.
One [duty] is the prohibition against acting unrighteously; one is the bestowing of wealth upon the destitute;
and one is approaching recluses and brahmins to ask questions—thus, in this way, that duty of a wheel-turning monarch consists of ten kinds.
However, for one who includes householders and those born as birds separately, it consists of twelve kinds.
Because that phenomenon does not allow one to act otherwise, it is the basis for this; thus, it is "that-basis" (*tad-adhiṭṭhāna*).
By means of that mind which has that as its basis, "honoring" means performing an act of respect. Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth.
"Holding in high esteem" means holding it in high esteem by way of regarding it with weight, like a stone parasol. For this very reason he said, "through the arising of reverence toward it."
By the phrase "by way of having arrived at the state where the Dhamma is sovereign," he shows that, due to the preeminence of the aforementioned Dhamma,

[the practitioner] has previously accumulated [merit] with great care throughout successive existences. And by the phrase "by performing all activities through the influence of the Dhamma alone," he shows that in standing,
sitting, and so forth, there is a state of being inclined, leaning, and bent toward the aforementioned Dhamma.
"Assā" means for the sake of protection, shielding, and guarding. "Protecting another" means protecting another from harm pertaining to this present life and so forth.
By that very quality of patience and the like which accomplishes the protection of others, one protects oneself from that same harm. "Mettacittatā" means by way of a mind of loving-kindness.
Clothing, upper garments, houses, and so forth constitute a "shield" (āvaraṇa) by warding off cold, heat, and other such conditions.

“In those within the household” means among the people belonging to the inner circle, such as children and wife. By the phrase “establishing them in the restraint of virtue,” he shows protection (*rakkhā*).
By the phrase “giving him clothes, perfumes, garlands, and so forth,” he shows concealment (*āvaraṇa*); by the other [phrase], guarding (*gutti*).
With the word “also” (*pi*) in the expression “also by providing gifts,” he includes establishing them in the restraints of virtue and the rest. This same method applies to others as well.

Regarding the inclusion of the word *pi* (also): those whose residence (*nivāsa*) is in a market town (*nigama*) are called *negamā*. Thus, he said "likewise those dwelling in market towns" and so forth.

Arranging (*saṃvidahana*) and establishing (*ṭhapana*) bodily actions and so on for the sake of protection, defense, and guarding is precisely what is meant by "instruction" (*upadesa*); therefore it is said "having explained.
"Among these" refers to the recluses (*samaṇa*) and others mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). It is impossible to turn back those who have reached the end of defilements (*khīṇa*).
Because the defilements do not arise again. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sacetana Sutta.
15. Regarding the fifth [section], it is called *Isipatana* because seers (*isi*) fall and gather there; thus he said, "of those reckoned as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas," and so forth.
"Having prepared all the requisites" means that on the very day the king gave his command, all the requisites—the tools for felling and stripping trees, and so on—were prepared.
It is called *nānākaraṇa* because by means of it one is made distinct; it is a state of distinction (*nānābhāva*), as he said.

Regarding the term “nānatta”: he says “na esa” because this is a grammatical exposition (niddesa) formed by the elision of the *sa* sound from *nesaṃ*. Likewise, regarding “atthesaṃ,” he says “atthi esa” because the same applies here as well.
*Abhisaṅkhāra* is the volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*) for the sake of setting [the mind] in motion;
its *gati* is its rapid occurrence. With reference to that, he says “payogassa gamanaṃ.”
“With swellings” (sagaṇḍā) means with various small swellings. Therefore he said, “joined with places that are high and low. “With their own exudations” (sakasāvā) means with their own pus.
Therefore he said, “with putrid cores,” and so forth. Thus, they have fallen through the falling away of their qualities;

just as that wheel did not stand firm because of the defects of its hub, spokes, and rim, so too some individuals, due to the defects of bodily crookedness and the like, fall away through the falling away of their qualities.

Once fallen, they do not remain in their own place. Furthermore, it should be understood that even harsh speech and the like, which lead to the states of misery (*apāya*), are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) alone.
The commentary on the *Sacetana-sutta* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. 16.
In the sixth [verse], the act of becoming dispassionate is like undertaking the "infallible practice" (*apaṇṇakappayoga*), because it is something to be undertaken later;
however, the act of not becoming dispassionate is "not deficient," because it is not to be undertaken later. Such is the person endowed with that [practice].
The state of being *apaṇṇaka* is called *apaṇṇakatā*; thus he said, “*Apaṇṇakapaṭipadā* means ‘the practice that is not failed’,” and so forth.

Because it is categorical (*ekaṃsikā*) in accomplishing the intended goal, leading out from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and because therein it is joined with reasoning, free from essencelessness, non-contradictory due to its lack of opposition, conformable, and in accordance with the Dhamma, therefore it is said, “the categorical practice,” and so forth.

"Neither by grasping at reasoning nor by grasping at method" means that one has not practiced by grasping at reasoning, nor has one practiced the "unerring path" (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā) by grasping at method.

In this context, "by grasping at reasoning" means by one's own mere exercise of reasoning, such as thinking, "In this way, there will be a happy rebirth for me, or Nibbāna," without having obtained a teacher. "By grasping at method" means through direct perception (*paccakkha*).
"By seeing" means by grasping through inference based on the method. "Having practiced after grasping in this way" means one who has practiced either by mere reasoning or by grasping the method.
The construction is: "Like a wise caravan leader, he does not fall away from his attainments.
"With reference to which it was said" means that both falling away and non-falling away were spoken of in the Jātaka with reference to this. Now, here is this [verse]:

The explanation of the meaning of the verse: "The unerring position"—the cause that is not contradictory and the cause that leads to liberation—was accepted by certain wise men headed by the Bodhisatta.

However, those logicians headed by the foolish caravan leader’s son took the second [position], which is faulty, non-conclusive, and a cause that does not lead to liberation; they have entered upon the dark path.
In this context, the bright course of practice is a course that leads to non-decline, while the dark course of practice is a course that leads to decline.
Therefore, those who have entered upon the bright course of practice are non-declined and have attained safety;
whereas those who have entered upon the dark course of practice are declined and have fallen into ruin and disaster. This is the meaning that the Blessed One [taught] to Anāthapiṇḍika.
Having addressed the householders, he further said this: “Knowing this, the wise man should take that which is ‘unerring’ (apaṇṇaka).
In this context, “the wise man knowing this” refers to a clansman endowed with that pure, supreme wisdom known as *medhā*.
Regarding these two—the state of being unerring and the second [state]—which consist respectively of non-conjectural apprehension and conjectural apprehension:
The meaning is: having understood the advantages and disadvantages, the increase and decrease, and what is beneficial and what is harmful in various situations.

"One should take that which is infallible" means one should take only that which is infallible, certain, reckoned as the white practice, the practice of non-decline, and the cause of deliverance. Why? Precisely because of its being certain and so forth.
But one should not take the other. Why? Precisely because of its being uncertain and so forth.
“Yoni” is so called because as many beings as are there, though unmixed, appear as if mixed due to their commonality of birth.

In its actual sense, however, it is a specific mode of the partial manifestation of the aggregates (khandhas) distinguished by the place of origin such as eggs and so forth; thus he said, “A portion of the aggregates is what is called ‘yoni.

It is called “yoni” in the sense of a cause, for that [cause] is difficult to penetrate in its distinctions by those who have not accumulated the requisites of knowledge regarding each respective fruit.
"It is as if mixed": because of the principle of oneness (*ekattanaya*), fools hold the wrong view that "this is that very same thing.
The path of excretion is called the "womb" (*yoni*); because beings are connected by way of that womb, they are said to be "mixed.
[The qualities] are "grasped" through non-negligence and "perfected" through repeated cultivation.

In the passage beginning with “By the eye as well,” although there is the occurrence of wholesome states and so forth within the cognitive processes (vīthi) of eye-consciousness and those mental consciousnesses that follow them, it is only the taints of sensual desire and the rest that flow out like pus from a wound in the sense of being impure substances;
therefore, they alone are called “taints” (āsava). For the word *āsava* refers here to that which flows out as a leaking impurity.
"Established" (*nirulha*): This is said because from the level of the "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) up to the paths and fruits, they do not proceed further.

For these, proceeding through phenomena by way of making them their object, do not go beyond that point. If it is asked, "Do they not proceed beyond that to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth?"—No;
for even those [subsequent states] possess the quality of being subject to taints (*sāsava*) with respect to the mundane phenomena previously apprehended as objects.

Because it is included therein and because there is no state subsequent to it. And here, by the term "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*), one should understand that the preliminary work (*parikamma*) which precedes the change-of-lineage, the inspiration (*vodāna*), the fruit (*phala*), and the attainment (*samāpatti*) are all expressed. Alternatively, only the change-of-lineage that precedes the first path is taken as the illustration of the limit;

however, beyond that, due to its similarity to the paths and fruits, [the same applies] to other paths, whether in the cognitive process of the path (*maggavīthi*) or in the cognitive process of attainment (*samāpattivīthi*).
It should be understood that the flow of the taints (*āsava*) is obstructed both in the fruits (*phala*) occurring immediately after cessation (*nirodha*) and in *nibbāna*.
"Flow" (*savanti*) means they go; the meaning is that they proceed by way of making [an object] their cognitive support (*ārammaṇa*).

The letter *ā* has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*), and limits are twofold: distinguished as exclusive (*mariyādā*) and inclusive (*abhividhi*). Among these, the exclusive limit functions by excluding the action from the boundary.
For example: “It has rained as far as Pāṭaliputta. However, an all-pervasive sense (*abhividhi*) proceeds by extending over an action, as in:
