“The fame of the Blessed One extends as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). And it is stated that this prefix *ā-* is taken here in the sense of inclusion (*antokaraṇa*), thus: “the sense of inclusion.”
In the phrase "liquor, etc.," the word "etc. should be understood as including rock salt, *kādambarikā*, *kapotikā*, and so forth.

"The state of having been stored for a long time" means the condition of having been kept for a long duration or its antiquity. Regarding the phrase "ignorance was not, etc.," the word "etc. here includes the following sutta:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit is discerned of the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*). [This refers to] the taints of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) and existence (*bhavāsava*).
By the demonstration of the long-standing cessation [of the taints], the long-standing cessation of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*),

which arises with that very state as its nature, is likewise demonstrated. Furthermore, while other aforementioned phenomena such as conceit (*māna*) exist and proceed by taking space and objects as their basis,
the similarity to a taint (*āsava*) consists in their pervasiveness through the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self," and their quality of producing intoxication.

And it should be understood that the term *āsava* (taint) is established specifically for these [three], and not for others; thus, it is restricted to these alone. Because they are beginningless, they are "long-extended" (*āyata*).
They "flow forth" (*pasavanti*) means they "bear fruit. For there is no suffering of saṃsāra whatsoever that could arise without the taints.
And "the first among these" refers to the first three out of these four alternative meanings. "In which" (*yattha*) means in those portions of the Suttas and Abhidhamma.
In this context, [the term] applies only to the defilements (*kilesa*), because the three meanings previously stated are possible only there.

"The latter also applies to karma": the latter etymology, namely "they flow and pour forth the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*," also applies to karma, because the pouring forth of suffering is common to both defilements and karma.

"Visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the aggregates (*khandha*) that have become directly manifest; "pertaining to visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhammika*) means existing within those visible phenomena.
"Being the root of dispute" means being the fundamental cause of dispute: namely, anger, resentment, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, vehemence, pride, and arrogance.
"By which one would be reborn among the gods" means by which kind of karma, defilement, or underlying tendency (*āsava*) there is rebirth or arising among the gods.
"May it be mine" is the connection [of the words]. Or, having changed the case ending, one should construe it as "may he be a gandhabba, a bird, or a sky-walker.
And here, all deities other than yakkhas and gandhabbas are included by the term "deity.
*Naḷa* means "root"; therefore, *vinaḷīkata* means "made rootless," that is, made devoid of roots. The remainder...
"And unwholesome states" (*akusalā dhammā*): the connection is that those unwholesome states remaining over from unwholesome kamma are what are referred to as "taints" (*āsava*).

"For the sake of warding off" (*paṭighātāya*) means for the sake of prevention. Regarding "reproach by others... calamities": this refers to those things that would arise if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), namely, those resulting from the causes of indulging in unrighteous conduct, taking what is not given, killing living beings, and so forth.
This was said with reference to various kinds of harm pertaining to the present life, such as verbal abuse from others, as well as the various forms of suffering experienced—
such as the fivefold punishments for criminals— for one who is reborn in hell and other realms solely on account of those very same causes.
Furthermore, "these" refers to these outflows (*āsava*), which consist of the defilements such as sensual lust, the kamma of the three planes, and the calamities such as verbal abuse.
"Where" (*yattha*) means in that portion of the Vinaya or other Pāḷi texts. "How" (*yathā*) means by which two kinds of ways and so forth;
the connection is that [the taints] have come down in three ways in the remaining Suttantas as well. "Leading to hell" (*nirayagāminiyo*) means those that go to hell.
"In the Chakkanipāta" refers to the *Āhuneyyasutta* in the Chakkanipāta; for there, the taints (*āsava*) have come down in six ways.

"Sarasa-bheda" (the breaking of the essence) refers to momentary cessation (*khaṇika-nirodha*). "The state of being exhausted" (*khīṇākāra*) refers to absolute exhaustion. It is called "the destruction of the taints" (*āsava-kkhaya*) because by means of it, the taints are destroyed and abandoned;
thus, it is the Path (*magga*). It is called "the destruction of the taints" because it arises at the time of the destruction of the taints; thus, it is the Fruit (*phala*).

It is called "the destruction of the taints" because it is to be attained through the destruction of the taints, and the taints are destroyed therein; thus, it is Nibbāna. This has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therefore, that should be understood there according to the method stated in the commentary (*Saṃvaṇṇanā*).

By the word "thus" (*tathā*), he refers back to what has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. They are called "obstructive" (*āvaraṇīya*) because they obstruct and prevent the arising of the wholesome.
"By way of previous occurrence" means prior to falling asleep, [with regard to] the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

By way of its occurrence. "Having set aside" means that, as if setting aside something already in one's hand, one falls asleep while attending to the meditation subject itself, having set it aside by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension;
like one who has attained jhāna, waking up at the very time predetermined, one is said to "wake up" only while grasping the meditation subject at the very place where it was set aside. By that—
It is said: “Therefore... [etc. ... it is called... Regarding “the original meditation subject”: this refers to the meditation subject being maintained from the very beginning.
“By way of the meditation subject that is to be attended to” means by way of the attention given to the meditation subject being attended to by one who is about to go to bed.
To show that this must be done by way of attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra), the passage beginning with “For this” was stated.
The commentary on the Apaṇṇaka-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Attabyābādha-sutta:

Regarding the seventh [sutta], it says: “‘For one’s own affliction’ means for one’s own suffering,” because affliction (*byābādhana*) is the causing of pain. It says “they are indeed not excluded” because even the arising of the consciousness of the path and its fruits is included within the category of bodily good conduct and so forth.
The commentary on the Attabyābādha Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Devaloka Sutta: 18.

In the eighth [sutta], *iti* is a particle used to illuminate the smoothness of the connection between words and syllables—that is, the semantic coherence of preceding words with succeeding words, or the euphonic smoothness of the syllables and sentences.
The commentary on the Devalokasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the First Pāpaṇikasutta. 19.
In the ninth [verse], "having opened" means having opened both the door to the shop and the bundles of merchandise. "He does not resolve" means...
He does not personally engage in various kinds of buying and selling. "At midday" means at the time of noon.

He is "without a master" because he does not receive the gains obtainable at the three [other] times. A night-quarters is a place free from wind-related ailments. A day-quarters is a place well-supplied with shade and water.
Insight meditation is also appropriate; it is specifically for one engaged in the work of insight. For by that as well, the faculties are [developed] in nine ways...

One who causes [the mind] to enter three times should grasp the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*) and the sign of insight (*vipassanānimitta*) through the observation of the mode of concentration.
The commentary on the First Merchant Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Merchant Sutta.
20. "One of distinguished burden" (*visiṭṭhadhura*) means one who exerts a distinguished burden, being endowed with energy (*vīriya*).
For the accomplishment of goals depends upon wisdom and energy. Therefore he said, "one of supreme burden," and so forth. "Merchandise for sale" (*vikkāyikabhaṇḍa*) means goods that ought to be sold.

"By means of deposited wealth" (*nikkhittadhanena*) refers to wealth that has been set aside by way of being stored away. "By way of daily use" (*vaḷañjanakavasena*) refers to [wealth used] day after day.
By way of giving and enjoyment, that is, by way of wealth to be utilized. "With articles for enjoyment and use" means with the requisites for enjoyment and use.
"They cause to fall" means they cause them to fall; they make them subject to falling through the seizure of their own wealth.

Therefore he said, "they entice. "By the power of knowledge" means by the stability of knowledge. "By the prowess of knowledge" means by energy accompanied by knowledge. For [knowledge] is divided into that pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate truth.

That learning by which one succeeds is called "learning" (*suta*). Showing this according to the highest description, he said: "One who knows a single *nikāya*... [and so on]... one who is well-versed.
"Arrived" means well-arrived due to being well-mastered; therefore he said: "Proficient and practiced.

Since the phenomena (*dhammā*)—divided into categories such as the wholesome aggregates and so forth—which are contained in the Abhidhamma, also descend into the Sutta Piṭaka, it is said: "Bearers of the Dhamma" means bearers of the Sutta Piṭaka.
It has been said. For without the status of an Abhidhammika, a thorough mastery of the Suttanta Piṭaka in its direct sense is not possible.

Regarding the phrase "one who masters the two mātikās," they say this refers to one who masters the two mātikās by way of the Bhikkhu-mātikā and the Bhikkhunī-mātikā; however, it is more appropriate to say "one who masters the mātikās of the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma.
"He inquires" means he asks about everything that ought to be asked. Therefore he said: "the meaning and the non-meaning, the reason and the non-reason..."
"‘He examines’ means he investigates.
‘The meaning should not be understood in this way’ means that the meaning should not be grasped according to the sequence of the teaching.
For the sequence of the teaching is one thing, as it proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained, while the sequence of practice is another. Or, [it refers to] the lower limit."

Regarding the three divisions known as virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), one should understand the delimitation of the teaching in some cases by the lower method through virtue, in some cases by the upper division through wisdom, and in some cases by both divisions through virtue and wisdom.
Having stated that in this sutta, however, the delimitation should be understood by the upper division, he says "Therefore," etc., in order to demonstrate that.
Or rather, because the Blessed One, first showing the spiritual friend according to the inclinations of those to be trained, proclaimed arahantship;
then, showing that "this arahantship comes about through this kind of initiated energy," he proclaimed the arousal of energy;
and finally, showing that "this arousal of energy comes about by relying upon this spiritual friend," [he taught].
It should be understood that the excellence of the support (*nissayasampatti*) is explained in accordance with the examples shown below.
The commentary on the second *Pāpaṇika-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Rathakāra-vagga* is finished.
3. Puggalavagga 1.
Samiddhasuttavaṇṇanā 21.

Regarding the first of the third [section]: “It pleases me” refers to the fact that among the types of persons such as the body-witness (kāyasakkhi) and others, [this person] possesses a state that is exceedingly more beautiful and more sublime.

He asks: "How was that which produces delight in the mind brought about? Considering that the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) was the primary factor—that is, the "burden" (*dhura*) of faith at the emergence of the path—he asks how the remaining faculties were so;

thus he says, "The rest," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "one who has penetrated the path": all three elders spoke only of their own penetration of the path of Arahatship; therefore, it is not easy [to determine the specific faculties].

"It cannot be answered categorically that 'this... pe ... is more excellent. He spoke by way of the distinction of planes: "Among these three types of persons, only one who stands on the supreme path is more excellent.
The commentary on the Samiddha Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Gilāna Sutta 22.
In the second [verse], "beneficial" (*hitāni*) means suitable. "Conducive to growth" (*vuddhikarāni*) means conducive to the growth of health and so forth.

"Appropriate" (*anucchavikaṃ*) means suitable for the act of nursing. "By the disease of wind and wasting" (*vātāpamārarogena*) means by the disease of wind (*vātaroga*) and the disease of wasting (*apamāraroga*), or by that which has wind as its cause.
Or by the disease of epilepsy. "A sick person who has reached the end" means a sick person who has reached the conclusion that "one will die before long because of this illness.
"Khipitaka" refers to the disease of vomiting. "Kacchū" is the affliction of severe scabies. "Tiṇapupphaka fever" is a fever resulting from contact with irregular winds.
"Of which" means of whichever diseases. "By nursing" means merely by providing medical treatment.
"Phāsuka" refers to the physical well-being resulting from the subsiding of disease. One is "wise" (paṇḍita) through knowing the causes and origins of the disease;
"skilled" (dakkha) through acting appropriately in providing the remedy; and "unlazy" (analasa) through the perfection of exertion and energy.

A person who is "merely a master of words" (padaparama) is described as being unfit for entering the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma). Thus, not obtaining [the Dhamma] proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
He enters upon the way that is right for wholesome states—the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya, the certainty of liberation, and the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
"Yanti" means "from which. "Having received instruction" refers to the mere instruction regarding the conduct of the higher life (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*);

for even this much brings him benefit. "Depending on that" means he depends specifically on one who is to be known through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), because such a person must be instructed again and again due to his fitness for entering the certainty of the right way.
The commentary on the Gilānasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Saṅkhārasutta 23.
In the third [sutta], because it afflicts in various ways, affliction (byābādha) itself is "afflictive" (byābajjha); that is, both bodily and mental.
It is suffering (*dukkha*). It exists together with affliction (*byābajjha*), thus it is "with affliction" (*sabyābajjha*). Therefore he said, "accompanied by suffering" (*sadukkha*).
The "mass of volition" (*cetana-rāsi*) refers to the mass of prior volitions and so forth. One who causes volition to proceed again and again is said to "make a mass" or "make a heap.
"Accompanied by suffering" means uninterrupted suffering. Therefore he said, "afflicted and devoid of gratification" (*sābādha nirassāda*). "There is" (*atthi*) means directly.

It is stated because it cannot be said that "painful feeling does not exist. Because its intrinsic nature is undesirable and its object is undesirable, it should be regarded as belonging to the side of suffering (*dukkha*).
For there are no unwholesome-resultant states that are called "desirable," and as for wholesome-resultant equanimous feeling, it has little scope there.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), because of the abundance of suffering in hell—
It is said that because suffering is powerful there, it stands in a state beyond conventional designation (*abbōhārika-ṭṭhāna*).
Having provided a simile, he stated a distinction as if it were like the generality [of the example], such as "like forms adhering to a lump of iron.
"Similes of counterparts" means similes of reflections. "Not taking those" means not taking [the beings] in the lower Brahma-world. "Mixed pleasure and pain" means mixed pleasure and pain.
Because it is mixed with the yellow [color]. "Kamma" refers to unwholesome kamma; he speaks of the fruit by way of the headword "kamma.
Although the phrase "he is reborn into a world free from affliction" occurs here, the statement "they touch with unafflicted contacts" includes supramundane contacts as well;
thus it is said that "the three types of good conduct are explained as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane."
The commentary on the *Saṅkhāra-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Bahukāra-sutta*. 24.

In the fourth [sutta], "gone for refuge" means: "He has gone for refuge, thinking, 'I have a refuge'—a protection from the suffering of the round of existence"—by way of the sequence of going for refuge.
"He has approached" means he has come near. "Together with the scriptures" (*satantika*) means together with the Dhamma of the formal teachings (*pariyatti*).
"For one who has not previously taken refuge" means for one by whom refuge was not previously taken. It is stated by way of one who has not formed a resolve;

that is, it is said in reference to one by whom no resolve to go for refuge had been made in that particular existence (*attabhāva*). Granted, a teacher who bestows refuge was mentioned previously as well, but...

The one who grants the going-forth (pabbajjā) is indeed the one who grants the refuges (saraṇa). However, previously, the one who grants the refuges was intended in the sense of being the one who establishes one in the status of a lay follower (upāsaka).

This, moreover, is the going for refuge by one who has already received the going-forth; for the going-forth is a particularly distinguished form of going for refuge, and thus the one who grants the going-forth is mentioned again.
"These" refers to the ones who grant the going-forth and so on. They are "delimited in two ways," meaning they are the ones who bring about mundane states (lokīya-dhamma).
"He who brings about the supramundane Dhamma" is delimited in two ways: either by way of having formed a resolve or not having formed a resolve.
"Above" means above the first path. "He is not able" means that because of the great power of the assistance rendered by the teacher, he is unable to offer any recompense for it.
The commentary on the Bahukāra Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vajirūpama Sutta:
In the fifth [verse], *aru* refers to an old, malignant sore; the syllable *ka* functions as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhi*), thus forming *arukūpamaṃ* (resembling a sore).
"One whose mind is like an ulcer" (*arukūpamacitta*) means one who cannot endure even the slightest suffering.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "By a flash of light for a short duration" means that the duration is merely brief due to the absence of the radiance of knowledge.

"It clings" means that a person, becoming agitated through the attachment of anger, clings when face-to-face by saying things such as "What are you saying?", and clings from behind by way of reproaching.
It is not by way of attachment through craving (*taṇhā*). "Is provoked" means it becomes angry. "Becomes corrupted" means the mind becomes impaired.

It attains a state of rigidity because there is not even a moment’s absence of hardness. "A malignant sore" refers to a malignant ulcer that, due to the corruption of the flesh and blood, has abandoned its natural state.
They also read "duṭṭhārutā"; in that case as well, the letter *t* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
"Of him" means of one who has broken out in sores. "Flowing" refers to the oozing of impurity. "Like one bloated" means like one who is steaming upward and upward due to anger;
it is because of the non-release of the distress of anger. "Of one who is fierce" means of one who is provoked.
And here, although the defilements are still subject to destruction by the lower paths, they have been brought to a state where they are no longer liable to arise [in that person] by those [paths].
Although they are cut off, because the supreme path has not yet arisen in that continuum,

it should be understood that the defilements have not been abandoned there; thus, those knowledges are described as being like lightning, not because of the existence of defilements already abandoned by those paths.
The commentary on the Vajirūpama-sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sevitabba-sutta: 26.
In the sixth [verse], "should be approached" means one should approach from time to time. "Should be drawn near" means [to stay] in the shade.
It should be absorbed through cultivation as if it were one's own; it should be attended to repeatedly, meaning one should sit near him frequently.

"Compassion" refers to the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "It is fitting to approach him" means that for the sake of being helpful—thinking, "Through this [approach], his virtue will increase"—such things as attending upon him are appropriate.
"It will not be obstructed" means that because there is no refusal—such as saying, "Go away, what is the use of this?"—due to their dear virtue, it will not be obstructed.
"It will be comfortable" means that when two virtuous people are together, if one speaks in praise of virtue, the other rejoices;
thus their conversation is both comfortable and productive. But when there is one who is immoral, [the conversation of] the immoral person...
A discourse on virtue is poorly delivered; it is not a discourse on virtue, it is not comfortable, and it does not proceed effectively.

For a person of immoral conduct, a discourse on virtue will indeed be uncomfortable. The meaning stated for the discourse on virtue is extended by analogy to the discourses on concentration and wisdom:
"The same method applies to the discourses on concentration and wisdom. For two people who have attained concentration and possess wisdom [would find such a discourse appropriate].
And while they were engaged in a discourse on wisdom, they did not even realize that night or day had passed.

"I shall assist here and there with wisdom" means: "In each of those instances where one is to be assisted, purified, or developed by wisdom, I shall assist by means of the wisdom arisen based on superior virtue (adhikasīla). And as for that assistance:
Having abandoned those things that are unsuitable and unhelpful for virtue, it comes about through the cultivation of their opposites; thus he said, "In what is unsuitable for virtue," and so forth.
Those things called unsuitable and unhelpful for virtue are improper conduct, improper resort, and the like;
their opposites should be understood as helpful factors. "In each respective place" means in the locus of each specific section of the training. It assists.
"By name" means he favors them by treating them as undifferentiated and undefiled.
"In a lye-strainer" refers to the cloth used by dyers for straining alkaline substances such as soda ash. "Declines" means one falls away from virtue and so forth.
"The most excellent person" refers to a person who is superior, more exalted, and supreme in qualities such as virtue.
The commentary on the *Sevitabba-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Jigucchitabba-sutta*. 27.

Regarding the seventh [verse], in the phrase "he rises up" (*abbhuggacchati*), with reference to the prefix *abhi*, the word "not" (*na*) is in the accusative case in the sense of the genitive (possessive).
He said, "It is so," as in such passages as "But that, sir... and so forth. "An evil report" refers to a report that must be spoken of as being base.
"Like a cesspool, [so is] immorality"—by this he shows that the immoral person is indeed similar to excrement. "Speech" means undesirable speech.
"In the same manner as before" refers to the previous statement, "Immorality is like a cesspool," and so on.

In the manner already stated. "Sucimitta" means one whose friends are pure due to the purity of their virtue and conduct. They are called "companions" (*sahāya*) because they go together and proceed together; thus he says "those who go along with.
The commentary on the *Jigucchitabba-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Gūthabhāṇī-sutta*.
28. In the eighth [verse], "one who speaks dung" (gūthabhāṇī) is so called because his speech is like dung.
For just as dung is undesirable to the great multitude, even so the speech of this person is undesirable to gods and humans.

"Foul-smelling talk" (duggandhakathā) refers to talk that emits a foul odor, like dung, due to being defiled by the impurity of the defilements (kilesa). "One who speaks flowers" (pupphabhāṇī) is so called because his speech is like a beautiful flower.

One who speaks like flowers (*pupphabhāṇī*). Just as blossoming jasmine or *adhimuttika* flowers are desirable and pleasing to the great multitude, even so the speech of this person is desirable and pleasing to gods and humans.
"Like flowers" means like fragrant flowers such as the *campaka* and *sumana*. "Fragrant discourse" means discourse that causes a pure fragrance to waft forth.
Because of the absence of the foul odor of defilements (*kilesa*). Regarding the term *madhubhāṇī*, some also read it as *mudubhāṇī*.
In both cases, however, the meaning is "one whose speech is sweet.

For just as that which is called the "fourfold sweetness" is sweet and refined, even so the speech of this person is sweet to gods and humans. The phrase *madhurakathaṃ* means because it is pleasant to the ear and endearing.
And it is a discourse of sweet nature both in its sound and its meaning. "For one's own sake" means for the sake of having one's own hands, feet, and so forth cut off or carried away.
"For the sake of another" follows the same principle here as well; therefore he said, "for one's own," and so on.
Because it is stated in the Sutta, "‘Nelaṅga,’ venerable sir, is a designation for virtues," it is said that "the virtue mentioned here..."
"Viya" means it fulfills the perfection of qualities. "Sukumārā" means soft and delicate due to their lack of harshness.
Regarding "purassa," the word *pura* here should be understood as denoting those who dwell therein, as in expressions such as "the village has arrived. Therefore he said, "of the city-dwellers.
It nourishes and increases the mind (*mano*), thus it is "manāpā"; therefore he said, "causing the growth of the heart."
The commentary on the Gūthabhāṇīsutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Andhasutta:
Regarding the ninth [sutta], in the scriptural passages beginning with "blind," the first [term] refers to the eye of wisdom that acquires wealth pertaining to the present life.
The second person is also called "blind" due to the absence of the eye of wisdom that accomplishes welfare both in this life and in future lives;
however, the third person is called "two-eyed" because he possesses both of these. "Eye of wisdom" refers to the eye of wisdom consisting in skill regarding acquisition (*āyakosalla*).
Therefore, it is said: "he should increase. "In the low and the high" means in what is inferior and what is superior. "By way of their opposites" means...
By way of the existence of the opposite. "Having a white counterpart" means one should know them as having counterparts in the form of white phenomena that abandon [them].
"Having a black counterpart" means one should know them as having counterparts in the form of black phenomena that are to be abandoned.
"Of such a nature" means that by which one makes oneself happy together with one's children, wife, retinue, kinsmen, friends, and relatives.

"He does not satisfy" means that even such enjoyments do not exist for him. "And he does not perform meritorious deeds" means he does not perform meritorious deeds by way of satisfying ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the needy, and beggars. To show the analysis of the compound *ubhayattha* as meaning "in both worlds" or "for both purposes," he said, "In this world," and so forth. 10. Commentary on the *Avakujja-sutta*.

30. In the tenth [verse], "one of downcast wisdom" means one of overturned wisdom; thus he says, "one of downward-turned wisdom. "Initial setting" (*pubbapaṭṭhapanā*) refers to the first commencement.

"Resolution" (*sanniṭṭhāna*) refers to the conclusion of the discourse. "Absorption" (*appanā*) refers to the completion of the teaching. Or, it should be construed as "many connections" (*anusandhiyo*).
In the phrases beginning with "or concentration," the supramundane states (*lokuttaradhammā*) are the Dispensation (*sāsana*) in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*).

The concentration that grasps that meaning is called its "beginning"; insight is [called its beginning] because it is proximate to it; and the path is [called its beginning] because it constitutes a part of it by way of being its root.

To show that the "perfections and purities" of the Dispensation are established precisely according to the system taught by the Teacher, yet should be understood here according to the method of one who explains them, he says: "teaching without omission," and "teaching without confusion."
And it has been said. Therein, "without tangles" (*nijjaṭa*) means without knots, unconfused. "Without knots" (*niggaṇṭhi*) means having made it free from knotted places and easy to understand.
"Heaped up" (*ākiṇṇāni*) means placed by being scattered and mixed together; hence he said, "deposited.
A person of "lump-like wisdom" (*ucchaṅgapañña*) is to be seen as one whose wisdom is like a lap; thus, due to having wisdom resembling a lap, he is called "one of lump-like wisdom. Thus...
Just as wisdom is, so too is the person like a lap; this is said with the intention that therein phenomena do not remain for long.
And just as wisdom is similar to a lap, it should be understood that wisdom is also similar to an overturned jar.
"By means of planning wisdom" means by means of planning each respective purposeful task, thinking: "When this is done, such-and-such will come to pass."
He is devoid of the wisdom of investigation that possesses the capacity [for discernment]. "Superior" (*seyyo*) means best or praiseworthy.
"The preliminary practice" (*pubbabhāgapaṭipada*) refers to the preliminary course of training for the attainment of the Noble Path, beginning with the purification of mind.
The commentary on the *Avakujja Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Individuals is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Messengers of the Gods. 1. The Commentary on the Sutta with Brahmā.

31. In the first [section] of the fourth [chapter], "together with Brahmā" (*sabrahmakāni*) means together with the best (*saseṭṭhakāni*). "Of whom" (*yesaṃ*) refers to those families. "Of sons" (*puttānaṃ*):
because of its connection with the word "honored" (*pūjita*), this genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "By that" (*tena*) refers to food and so forth.
"Attended to" (*paṭijaggitā*) and "protected" (*gopitā*) means they were looked after by giving whatever was appropriate at the proper time and by performing services for them.
And they are protected by warding off harm that has already arisen. "Of them" means of the mother and father. "For the purpose of accomplishing the state of being Brahmā and so forth" means:
because those qualities exist, one is called "Brahmā" in the world, one is called "Teacher," and one is called "Worthy of Offerings";
it is for the purpose of accomplishing their status as Brahmā and so forth, by way of showing that they obtain a child from the mother and father.
Having stated, “They are very helpful,” the passage beginning with “producers” was spoken in order to demonstrate their helpfulness in various ways.
For parents are the producers of their children’s lives, the nourishers of their bodies, the teachers of proper conduct and behavior, and the revealers of this entire world.
Therefore he said, “For children,” and so forth. First, regarding a desirable object:
How can they show an undesirable object? That too must indeed be shown for the purpose of making known its status as something to be avoided.
They are "not abandoned" because the meditation is not abandoned, owing to the fact that by means of that meditation the Brahmās have arisen in the Brahma-world.
The inclusion of the term "hundredfold" is for the purpose of showing that in the first youth, which is the age most prone to lust, an extreme state of softness has been reached.

"Separately" means individually. "By this reason" means by the reason already described, namely, the transgression committed toward one's children and the resulting arising of loving-kindness and so forth.
"The craft of weaponry" refers to the skill in weapons such as the sword, spear, javelin, and shield. "Finger-counting" refers to [calculation] by means of the contraction of fingers and so forth.

Counting by means of hand gestures (*hatthamuddā*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of counting on the fingers (*pāṇa*) and so forth is intended. Regarding "subsequent practice" (*pacchācariyā*):

it should be connected with the phrase "first of all, they are called teachers" (*sabbapaṭhamaṃ ācariyā nāmāti*), taking it to mean the causing of an individual—who has already learned the duties of a householder in the presence of his mother and father—to acquire their respective crafts, such as manual skills and the like.
"Offered" (*āhutaṃ*) means brought and offered; it is that which has been offered in various ways (*pakārehi hutaṃ*).
“Prepared” (*pāhutaṃ*) is a synonym for that very same term “prepared” (*abhisaṅkhataṃ*).
“One should pay homage” means that having gone to attend upon [the recipient] morning and evening, one should pay homage, thinking, “This is my supreme field of merit.
In the phrase “by means of that service” (*tāya naṃ pāricariyāya*), the word *naṃ* is merely a particle; it means “by means of the aforementioned service.”

The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, "by means of service" refers to the fivefold attendance consisting of providing sustenance, performing duties, maintaining the family lineage, paying off debts, and so forth. For this has been said:
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a son attend upon his mother and father as the eastern quarter:
'I shall support those who supported me; I shall perform their duties; I shall maintain the family lineage; I shall offer them their inheritance..."
‘I shall practice [the path], or else I shall provide offerings for the deceased ancestors.
Householder’s son, when parents are attended to by their son in these five ways, they in turn show compassion toward their son in five ways:
they restrain him from evil, establish him in what is wholesome, have him trained in a craft, ... [and so on].”

“They unite them with suitable wives and deliver their inheritance to them at the proper time. Furthermore, one who serves his parents by making them confident in the three bases [of faith], or establishing them in the precepts, or encouraging them to go forth into homelessness—this person should be known as the foremost among those who serve their parents. Now, this service consists of: [The following section details the types of service: 1. Service by bodily action; 2. Service by verbal expression; 3. Service by mental intention; 4. Service by providing requisites; 5. Service by honoring; 6. Service by protecting; 7. Service by fulfilling wishes; 8. Service by acting as a counselor. Service by bodily action is the performance of tasks such as massaging the parents’ limbs, bathing them, dressing them, and attending to their physical needs. Service by verbal expression is speaking to them with words that are gentle, affectionate, and pleasing. Service by mental intention is serving them with a mind free from resentment, full of love and respect.

Service by providing requisites is supplying them with food, clothing, shelter, medicine, and other necessities. Service by honoring is rising from one’s seat, saluting them, and showing deference. Service by protecting is guarding them against dangers from fire, water, thieves, or enemies. Service by fulfilling wishes is granting whatever they desire when it is appropriate and not contrary to Dhamma. Service by acting as a counselor is advising them on what is beneficial and restraining them from what is harmful. This is the nature of service. It should be understood that the Buddha has declared this service to be the highest form of merit for a layperson. As it is said: “There is no gift equal to the gift of Dhamma, no friendship equal to friendship in Dhamma, and no merit equal to the merit of serving one’s mother and father. Thus, one should strive to perform this service with diligence.
To show that [filial duty] brings benefit and happiness to a son in both worlds, it is said: "In this very world they praise him;
having passed away, he rejoices in heaven. "They praise him" means: "This person is devoted to his mother and father;
he fulfills the practice that leads to heaven"—thus they praise him right here in this world. "He rejoices" (*āmodati*) means he attains joy from the very beginning. "He exults" (*pamodati*).
[This was] for the sake of the occurrence of various kinds of joy.
The commentary on the *Sabrahmakasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Ānandasutta*.

32. "Of such a nature" (*tathājātiko*) means having such a characteristic (*tathāsabhāvo*). "Attainment of one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatālābho*) means the realization of one-pointedness of mind.
"The sign of form" (*rūpanimittaṃ*) is so called because form itself is the cause for the arising of defilements. This same method applies to the others as well. "The sign of eternalism, etc.

(*sassatādinimittaṃ*) means the sign of the states of eternalism and annihilationism. "The sign of the person" (*puggalanimittaṃ*) means the sign of the adherence to a person. "The sign of phenomena" (*dhammanimittaṃ*)...
The sign known as the mental object (dhammārammaṇa). When asked by the Elder, “Could it be so, Bhante?
the Blessed One replied, “It could be,” with reference to the attainment of supramundane concentration. For that [concentration] indeed views Nibbāna as peaceful and sublime.
Therefore he said, “In this case, Ānanda,” and so forth.

"Entering into the attainment [of fruition] with the thought ‘Nibbāna is peace’" means having inclined toward the thought ‘Nibbāna is peace’ and entered into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
By the phrase "even for a day," etc., he demonstrates the state of being absolutely peaceful, sublime, and so forth, regarding the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). It is eightfold:
"peaceful, sublime, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving... [and so on].
“Dispassion, cessation, nibbāna”—thus, regarding these eight kinds of attention known as *ābhoga*. This locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
In this context... [as it is said] "...it is indeed found," referring to the passage in the Sutta that begins, "In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu thinks thus":
even if there is only one instance of attention characterized by *ābhoga*, all eight instances of attention characterized by *ābhoga* are included.
They are indeed obtainable for those who apply their attention, because they are conducive to welfare.
"Having known by means of knowledge" means having known by means of path-knowledge accompanied by insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
"The other and further sense-bases," such as the eye and so forth. "By way of tranquility" means by way of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*). "Free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and the like."

Bodily misconduct and so forth are "smoke" in the sense of being a source of burning; he is devoid of that. "Free from distress" means sinless. Since birth and aging are mentioned, illness and death are necessarily included as well;
thus it is said, "because their existence depends on the existence of those [former states].
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta. 33.

In the third [verse], by saying, "Sāriputta, it is not easy even for one such as you to understand the Dhamma taught by me in brief," he speaks with the intention that the Elder’s knowledge transcends all else. And those who understand are rare.
Indeed, by including even the Elder Sāriputta within this general statement, he shows that even for him his own teaching was difficult to penetrate.
"Samma" means by way of cause or reason; therefore he said, "by means of the method," and so forth. "Mānābhisamaya" means the realization through the vision of conceit.
The "clear realization of abandoning" (*pahānābhisamaya*) and the "clear realization of seeing" (*dassanābhisamaya*) are said to be the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).
For the path of arahantship, by way of its function, sees conceit for the sake of accomplishing the task of full understanding;

what is meant is that it does so by way of penetration through non-delusion—this is its clear realization of seeing. And the clear realization of abandoning is seen by means of that clear realization of seeing. By means of the clear realization of seeing...

For it is precisely through the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) that [the defilements] are abandoned. This clear realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) is like the life of beings who have been struck by the poison of wrong view.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), because the clear realization of abandonment follows immediately upon the clear realization of seeing (*dassanābhisamaya*), it is stated simply as "by the clear realization of abandonment.
For when the clear realization of abandonment is grasped, the clear realization of seeing is already grasped.

"He has made an end of suffering": because conceit has been abandoned by means of the path of Arahantship, he has reached the "end" (anto) described as the limit of the body-belt, namely, "it wears out at the end of the body-belt or the hem of the garment";
the "end" (anto) described as the lowly limit, namely, "this, monks, is the end of livelihoods"; and the "end" (anto) described as a section, namely, "personality-belief is one end."
"‘This indeed is the end of suffering, the destruction of its conditions’—thus, there are four limits (antā) spoken of as such divisions.
Among these, he made that which is reckoned as the fourth limit the end of all the suffering of saṃsāra;
he made it its boundary, its enclosure; what is meant is that he left behind only the final arising of suffering. Therefore he said:
“He made an end of the suffering of saṃsāra.
But has not Nibbāna been mentioned in the exposition of this term “abandoning”?

Here, however, what is called the fruit of Arahantship—characterized as the abandoning through subsiding—is spoken of; therefore, he said “But in the exposition... and so forth, because this commentary would otherwise contradict that exposition.
In that regard, "those terms have come down" means that in that exposition, terms such as "abandoning," "stilling," and "relinquishing" have been handed down.

By the phrase "preceded by reflection on the nature of things" (*dhammatakkapurejava*), he refers to the liberation of Arahantship attained after standing in that fourth-jhāna liberation and contemplating the factors of jhāna.
For in the liberation of Arahantship, there is that which is comprised of right intention associated with the path.
Reasoning about the Dhamma is a precursor.
The commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta.
34. “For the purpose of making a heap” means for the purpose of forming a mass by way of accumulation. “Unbroken” means not shattered even in part;
for from the moment it is broken, a seed is no longer fit for the function of a seed.
“Unrotted” means not having reached a state of decay through soaking in water; for a rotten seed is no longer fit for the purpose of a seed. Therefore he said:
“By not having reached seedlessness through putrefaction. “Not destroyed by wind or sun” means they have not been ruined by wind or sun;
they have not been rendered devoid of nutritive essence (*niroja*). For a husked seed that is devoid of nutritive essence is not fit for the purpose of a seed.
“Capable of taking up the core” means they are capable of taking up the core of the grain. For a seed that lacks a core is not fit for the purpose of a seed.

Therefore he said, "having grasped the essence," which means having established the essence. "Lying comfortably due to being stored" means they were lying comfortably according to the manner of being placed in a storehouse for four months.
"Analysis of action" (kammavibhatti) means the classification of action. "The seen state" (diṭṭhadhamma) refers to the present personal existence that has become manifest to direct perception.

In this context, karma whose fruit is to be experienced in the present life is *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*. Karma whose fruit is to be experienced immediately after the present existence is *upapajjavedanīya*.

"To be experienced in another turn" (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*) refers to karma whose fruit is to be experienced in a future turn of existence—that is, in a subsequent change of personal identity—other than the present life or the life immediately following it. [Regarding] the opposites...
The first impulsion volition (paṭhamajavana-cetanā), which has attained a state of strength through its unassailability and the excellence gained by way of specific conditions,
and which proceeds with particular intensity due to the influence of a corresponding prior formation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra),

is called "kamma to be experienced in this very life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma) because it yields its fruit within that very same personal existence (attabhāva). For it is powerful in the manner described.

In the mental continuum of a javana, because it proceeds by way of being either beneficial or non-beneficial toward those endowed with specific qualities, and because it lacks the acquisition of repetition (*āsevana*) and possesses only a minor result, the first javana volition does not—like the other two [subsequent javanas]—depend on the cessation of the active continuum nor depend on the acquisition of a new opportunity;
thus, it yields its fruit right here as a mere occurrence-result, like a mere flower. Likewise...
"Unable to give" means that the giving of the result of karma occurs only through the convergence of other conditions, such as the application of a physical basis (*upadhi*) and so forth;

therefore, because of the absence of those [conditions], it is "unable to give its result in that very same personal existence. "Karma that has been" (*ahosikamma*) is to be understood as karma that simply "has been," such that its result "has not been, is not, and will not be. This is the type of karma to be known.
“Accomplishing the purpose” means that which brings about the purpose of giving and so forth, or of killing and so forth. If one asks, “What is that? he says:

“The volition of the seventh impulsion. For that is the determining volition; having acquired distinction by the method already stated, and being accompanied by the repetition gained from the preceding impulsions, it yields its result in the immediately following existence and is called “kamma to be experienced upon rebirth. It is just like the previous simile.
It is by way of the simile of the deer-hunter.

By the phrase "when there is the occurrence of saṃsāra," he demonstrates that when there is no occurrence of saṃsāra, [the action] stands on the side of "ineffective" (ahosikamma), because there is no opportunity for it to ripen.
"That which is grave" refers to unwholesome [kamma] that is highly blameworthy, and likewise wholesome [kamma].

Karma of great potency: whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, that which is heavy—such as the karma of matricide and so forth, or sublime (mahaggata) karma—that alone ripens first. Therefore he said, "But among the wholesome and unwholesome," and so on.
"That which is habitual" means that which has been frequently performed and repeatedly cultivated. Therefore he said, "But among the wholesome and unwholesome..."
"That which is frequent," and so forth. Regarding "that which is proximate," this refers to the karma remembered at the time of death;

however, as for that performed at the time immediately preceding death, there is nothing further to be said, hence he says, "But whichever among the wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] is proximate at the moment of death," and so forth.
"To be remembered" means to be remembered with clarity.
"In their absence" means in the absence of those three types of karma, beginning with the weighty (*garuka*).

"It gives its result anywhere" means it gives its result by way of producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); for the fourfold set of karmas beginning with the weighty is stated in terms of producing rebirth-linking.
Among these, the weighty ripens first; in the absence of the weighty, that which has been frequently practiced (*bahulīkata*) [ripens]. In its absence...
When that [kamma] is absent, whichever is proximate ripens; when that is absent, it is said that "the kamma performed in previous births" (*kaṭattā*) ripens.

Furthermore, among those that are frequent, proximate, and performed in the past, one must understand their relative strength and weakness. Among these, evil performed repeatedly after an interval from evil, and good performed repeatedly after an interval from good, [are strong].
From among those, even if a great amount of kamma was performed in the past and so forth, a small amount [of kamma] may ripen through the power of frequent recollection.

Because it generates remorse and the like, because its opposite is incomplete, and because of a specific transformation in the continuity of existence due to the non-exhaustion of the ripening of a commenced karma or a residual karma to be experienced in a subsequent life—
by these various causes, that which has accumulated as a fruit ripens first. This was stated by the general of King Videha in the *Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka*.
The firebrand, the seed-sowing slave, and Rucā the princess are the illustrations here. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who here is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...up to wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell. Or else, that evil kamma has been performed by him previously..."
“Either he has performed an evil deed that is to be experienced as painful, or that evil deed to be experienced as painful was done by him later on,
or at the time of death he held a wrong view that was fully adopted and embraced; because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death,
he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.”
And so on. The entire *Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta* should be recited in detail. Why say more?

This is the domain of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma: namely, that the prior and subsequent ripening of each respective kamma is established according to its specific cause.

Now, analyzing the fourfold classification of kamma beginning with the "productive" (janaka), he says: "That which is called 'productive'... and so forth. "Does not produce occurrence" means it does not produce the resultant of occurrence (*pavatti-vipāka*).

Since, in the first method, productive kamma was stated to give only the rebirth-linking result (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*), he says "another method" and so forth, while also allowing for its giving of the resultant of occurrence. Therein, by way of giving rebirth-linking and so on—
The productive [kamma] is that which brings about the arising of the continuum of karmic result (vipāka).

The supportive [kamma] is that which serves as the cause for the longer persistence of the continuum of pleasure and pain, or of the succession of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Therefore it was said: "It supports pleasure and pain;
it causes them to proceed for a duration. The obstructive [kamma] is that which, while the succession of pleasure and pain is proceeding, [causes it to proceed] very slowly.
It causes one to fail. Therefore he said: "It oppresses and afflicts pleasure and pain; it does not allow [the body] to proceed for the duration [of a lifetime].
Regarding the statement that an old man with black spots from wind cannot kill thieves:
it is said that in his old age he is unable to cut off a head in a single stroke; striking two or three times, he merely exhausts the men. For this reason, they spoke thus to him.
"Having obtained conformable patience" means having obtained the conformable patience prior to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
"He was crushed and brought to the end of his life by a cow with a young calf" refers to a certain *yakkhinī* who came in the guise of a milch-cow, struck him on the chest, and killed him;
it is with reference to this that it is said. That which exists in the city is "urban" (*nāgariya*).
"Having destroyed" means having cut off. Since the cutting off of karma is precisely the warding off of its result, he said, "having warded off its result.
And since that [warding off] provides an opportunity for the arising of one's own result, it is stated, "he makes room for his own result.
Karma that has been given an opportunity to ripen is indeed called "ripened."
He said, "But when such a space has been created by karma, that result is said to have arisen.

The obstructive (upapīḷaka) [karma] cuts off the result of another, but does not itself give its own result. However, the destructive (upaghātaka) [karma], having cut off a weak karma, produces its own result;
this is the distinction between them. [This occurs] due to the convergence of certain conditions, such as being subject to much illness and so forth.
It is obstructive (*vibādhaka*) and suppressive (*upapīḷaka*) of the fruition; likewise, it is interruptive (*upacchedaka*) of the fruition itself.
However, when obstructive karma (*upaghātakakamma*) has caused obstruction and, by making way for its own fruition, that fruition occurs, it becomes merely productive (*janaka*).

Since the status of being productive and so forth is intended with respect to the fruition and not with respect to the karma, it is as if it is logical that it is the fruition itself that is subject to obstruction.
It is seen; it should be investigated.
Another method: That action, when performed, brings about the arising of resultant and kamma-produced matter both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, is "productive" (*janaka*).
However, that action, when performed, [brings about] a desirable or undesirable fruit produced by another [action]...

Through the non-arising of obstructing or interrupting conditions and through the arising of strengthening conditions, there occurs a purity and a much longer continuity in accordance with the capacity of the producer; that is the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka*).

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome fruit produced by the producer is obstructed by a contrary factor—by way of being a sign of disease, elements, or disharmony—that [factor is the obstructing condition].

That is the "oppressive" (upapīḷaka). However, that karma by which a fruit—though it would otherwise be capable of a long-continued succession through the power of its productive capacity—is impaired or interrupted by the arising of a condition that causes such interruption, is the "destructive" (upaghātaka); this is the essential point here.
In this regard, some [maintain] the wholesome nature of the second [karma] by way of its leading to freedom from illness and long life for one who has reached this present state.
The unwholesome nature of the latter two is described by way of their leading to much affliction and a short lifespan.
And so it is said in the commentary on the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya:
"There are four kinds of kamma: obstructive (upapīḷaka), interruptive (upacchedaka), productive (janaka), and supportive (upatthambhaka). By powerful kamma..."
For that which has already been produced in the course of existence (pavatta) speaks thus in substance when it arrives as an oppressor (upapīḷaka):
"If I had known beforehand, I would not have allowed you to be born here; I would have caused you to be reborn in the four states of misery (apāya).
Very well; wherever you may be born, I shall oppress you with my so-called 'oppressive karma' until you are rendered devoid of essence."
"I shall make it a dregs-filled residue. From that point on, he acts accordingly. What does he do?
He brings about danger and destroys wealth.
"In this regard, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother's womb, there is neither enjoyment nor happiness for the mother..."
There is no [benefit], and distress arises for the parents. Thus he brings about danger.
Furthermore, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, the household wealth perishes through kings and others, like salt falling into water;
cows that yield a jar of milk no longer give milk; and gentle oxen become fierce, one-eyed, or lame.
Disease breaks out in the cattle-pens; slaves and others do not obey one's word; the sown crop does not grow;
what is kept in the house perishes in the house, and what is taken into the forest perishes in the forest; gradually, even mere food and clothing become difficult to obtain;
there is no protection for the womb; at the time of birth, the mother’s milk ceases; and the child [fails to receive] sustenance.
When it does not obtain [its object], being oppressed, it becomes sapless, juiceless, and dregs-like. This is called "oppressive karma" (*upapīḷaka-kamma*).
Furthermore, for one reborn through a long-lived karma, an interrupting karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) arrives and cuts off the life-span.
Just as if a man, having made a run of eight cubits, were to shoot an arrow, and another person were to strike it with a club the very moment it was released from the bow—
Having struck it, one would cause it to fall right there; in the same way, the obstructive kamma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) cuts off the life-span of one reborn through long-lived kamma.
What does it do? It causes [the being] to enter a forest of thieves, to descend into the waters of predatory fish, or to lead them to some other dangerous place.
This is called obstructive kamma. It is also called "injurious" (*upaghātaka*).
This is its very name. However, the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is called "productive karma" (*janaka-kamma*).

For one born into a family with little wealth and so forth, the karma that provides support by bringing about the attainment of wealth and the like is called "supportive karma" (*upatthambhaka-kamma*).

Even for that which is produced by limited karma, during the course of existence (*pavatta*), the karma consisting of abstaining from killing and so forth comes along and, in terms of its actual function (*attha*), [provides support].
He speaks thus: "If I had known first, I would not have allowed you to be reborn here;

I would have caused you to be reborn in the world of the gods. Be it as it may; wherever you are reborn, I shall provide you with support through what is called 'supportive kamma'. What does he do? He destroys dangers and procures wealth.
“In that regard, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, the parents experience only happiness and satisfaction.
Whatever dangers there may be from humans or non-humans by nature, they all depart. Thus he destroys danger.
Furthermore, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, there is no limit to the wealth in the house.”
There are no [obstacles], and treasure-pots enter the house, turning around both from the front and from behind.

Parents come face-to-face with wealth placed by others; cows yield much milk, oxen are of easy temperament, crops flourish in the place of sowing, and there is either an increase in profit or temporary gain.
Or, wealth given [in marriage] is brought and offered by themselves even without being asked; servants and others become easy to speak to; their work does not decline;
the child receives maintenance from the moment of conception; and female physicians are always present.

One born into a householder family attains the status of a merchant prince (*seṭṭhi*); one born into the families of ministers and so forth attains the status of a general (*senāpati*) and other such positions.
In this way he produces wealth. Being secure and possessing wealth, he lives long.

This is what is called "supporting kamma. Among these four types, the first two are exclusively unwholesome; the productive [kamma] may be either wholesome or unwholesome; and the supporting [kamma] is exclusively wholesome.
Here, with the intention that "obstruction" and "destruction" are not applicable to the fruition of wholesome kamma, it is said: "the first two are exclusively unwholesome."

It has been stated. However, for those such as Devadatta, for nāgas and others, and for hungry ghosts (petas) who have not yet received a new existence from this world, there exist in the hells and other realms factors that sustain, press down upon, and destroy unwholesome kamma-results.

Thus, the wholesome or unwholesome nature of all four [kinds of kamma] is not contradicted. And having established this, even when many acts of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) have been committed, [the result accrues] to one who has taken rebirth by means of even a single one.
It is said that for others, there is the providing of support to that [kamma], and that too is capable.
Having analyzed the eleven types of kamma according to the method of the Suttanta, he now shows that which is included in the Abhidhamma by presenting the text of the Vibhaṅga, beginning with:
"There are certain undertakings of evil kamma. Therein, "obstructed by the excellence of destination" means:
They are warded off, prevented, and prohibited by the excellence of destination (*gatisampatti*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
In this context, "excellence of destination" refers to a perfected destination, namely the world of the devas and the world of humans.

"Failure of destination" (*gativipatti*) refers to a ruined destination, namely the four states of misery (*apāya*). "Excellence of acquisitions" (*upadhisampatti*) refers to the perfection of the personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Failure of acquisitions" (*upadhivipatti*) refers to the inferiority of the personal existence.

“Perfection of time” (*kālasampatti*) refers to a favorable time characterized by good kings and virtuous people. “Failure of time” (*kālavipatti*) refers to an unfavorable time characterized by bad kings and wicked people.
“Perfection of effort” (*payogasampatti*) is right application. “Failure of effort” (*payogavipatti*) is wrong application.
Now, in order to show the meaning of the aforementioned passage, he says “In that regard,” and so forth. Therein, [it refers to] those who are fit for experiencing undesirable objects...
"Only when karma exists" shows the presence of evil karma caused by the experience of undesirable objects. "That karma" refers to that evil karma.

For indeed, even though much evil karma exists as a cause for the experience of undesirable objects, it ripens only for one who remains in a state of miserable rebirth (gativipatti). But if he, by means of a single...

If one should be reborn among gods or humans through a wholesome deed (*kalyāṇakamma*) in a state of excellence of destination (*gatisampatti*), there is no opportunity for unwholesome [kamma] in such a place;
it is exclusively wholesome. Thus, that kamma, being obstructed by the excellence of destination, does not ripen.
"Being obstructed" means being hindered. "In the prosperity of personal existence" (*attabhāvasamiddhi*) means in the excellence of the body. "Of defiled kamma" (*kiliṭṭhakammassa*).
The work of elephant trainers, horse grooms, cowherds, and so forth. "At a time suitable for fleeing" means at a time when one encounters enemies such as elephants and the like.
"He gives a bribe" means he gives it thinking, "In this way, my oppression by others will not come under their control.

"At a time suitable for theft" means at a time when the strength of one's faction and other factors are available. "In an intermediate aeon" means in an intermediate aeon that has reached its conclusion.
Having analyzed sixteen types of kamma according to the method of the Abhidhamma, and twelve types of kamma according to the exposition in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, he said, "Furthermore...

and so forth, in order to show them. Therein, having taken as an example the ripening of the result of kamma performed in past existences occurring only in those same past existences, it was stated: "There was kamma; there was the result of that kamma. Thus he said: "Whatever kamma..."
“In the past, it was accumulated,” and so forth. “The section on fruition” (*vipākavāra*) means the occasion for ripening, the section concerning fruition.
By the phrase “he obtains the section on fruition,” the very same meaning stated [previously] is further elucidated by the words “he produces rebirth-linking” (*paṭisandhiṃ janesi*), and so forth.

In that context, by the phrase “he produces rebirth-linking,” it is also stated that the karma which gives rebirth-linking likewise gives fruition during the course of existence (*pavatti*). This is because it is precisely the fruition of the course of existence...

But he speaks of the donor by way of the "head" (the primary factor) that produces form. This refers to the unripened result (*avipākavipāka*) of that very same past karma—whether to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) or to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*)—which, due to a deficiency in conditions, remains unripened even within past existences;

and it refers to the karma of one who has attained final nibbāna (*parinibbūta*) in those very past lives, whether that karma was to be experienced in the present life, to be experienced upon rebirth, or to be experienced in a subsequent period (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*).
And taking up the case where the ripening has not yet matured, he said, "It is stated that 'the action existed, but the ripening of the action did not exist,'" beginning with the words,
"But that which does not obtain a section on ripening," and so forth.
This refers to an action of the past whose ripening has not yet matured, which is ripening in the present existence due to the presence of favorable conditions.
Having taken up the ripening [of karma], it was said, “There was karma; there is the ripening of karma. Therefore he said, “But that which was accumulated in the past,” and so forth.
Having taken up the non-ripening ripening of past karma alone—whose time for ripening has passed—and of one who is attaining final nibbāna in the present existence, it was said, “There was karma;
there is no ripening of karma. Therefore he said, “The section on not having obtained the ripening,” and so forth.

Showing that it was said, "There was action; there will be the ripening of action," because one takes up the ripening that is to ripen through the attainment of conditions in a future existence for a past action whose ripening has not yet matured, he said, "But that which was accumulated in the past," and so forth.
And [this refers] to a past action whose time for ripening has already passed.

Having included both that which is to be extinguished in a future existence (*parinibbāyitabba*) and that whose ripening is not yet to mature (*avipaccitabba-vipāka*), it was stated: "There was action, but there will be no ripening of that action. Therefore, he said: "That which will not obtain its turn for ripening in the future," and so forth.
Thus, first of all, past action has been shown in six ways, by way of past, present, and future ripening and non-ripening.

Now, taking as an example the ripening of a result to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) that was performed in the present existence and which ripens right here, [the author] says, "There is karma, there is the ripening of karma," in order to demonstrate this. Then,
with the words "But that which does not obtain a stage of ripening at present," etc., he shows that for that very same present karma, due to a deficiency of conditions...
Here, by taking both the karma that does not ripen and the ripening [of karma] for one who attains final nibbāna in this very life,
it is shown that the statement “there is action, there is no ripening of action” was spoken. This refers to the ripening that must ripen in a future existence for present karma—
both that which is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and that which is to be experienced in a subsequent period (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*).

Having taken this up, he said, "It is stated that 'there is karma, there will be the ripening of karma,'" and so on, with the words: "But that which has been accumulated now and will receive its turn for ripening in the future," etc.

This refers both to present karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) that fails to ripen in a future existence due to a deficiency in conditions, and to karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*) for one who is destined to attain final nibbāna in that future existence.
And having taken the result that is not to be ripened, it was said, "There is karma, but there will be no ripening of karma";
thus he said, "But that which will not obtain a section on ripening," and so forth.
And having thus shown present karma in four ways—by way of present, future, ripening, and non-ripening results—he now...
Having grasped the ripening result that must ripen in the future for a deed performed in a future existence, it is said, “there will be karma; there will be the ripening of karma.
Demonstrating this, he said, “But as for that which one will accumulate in the future,” and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding that very same future karma, there is that which need not ripen due to a deficiency of conditions, and that which is to lead to final nibbāna in a future existence.
And having taken the result as something that need not ripen, it was said, "there will be karma, there will be no ripening of karma";
thus he said, "But that which will not obtain a section on ripening," and so forth. In this way, future karma has been shown in two ways: by way of future ripening and non-ripening.
With the words "In this way," etc., he concludes the twelve types of karma as previously stated.
Now, among all the aforementioned classifications of kamma, those sixteen types of kamma analyzed according to the method of the Abhidhamma,
as well as the twelve types of kamma analyzed by way of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, are all included within the eleven kinds of kamma analyzed according to the method of the Suttas;

and these are included within [the categories of] kamma to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), kamma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*).
Showing that they are indeed included within those three, he said, "Thus these very... and so forth.

Therein, "having fallen away from one's own position" means having declined from one's own aforementioned position, which is divided into twelve or sixteen types; what is meant is that one has abandoned each of those specific divisions.
"There are only eleven actions" refers to the fact that there are twelve types of actions precisely because of their intrinsic natures.
He spoke thus because [the action] was described by dividing it into sixteen ways.

Since the eleven types of actions mentioned may be either to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), or to be experienced in some subsequent period (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*), it was therefore stated: "There are only three kinds of action.
There is no transference (*saṅkamana*) among them; that is, there is no transference among those [actions] such as being experienced in this very life and so forth. Transference...
[They do not undergo] the state of being experienced upon rebirth (upapajjavedanīya) and so forth. Therefore he said, "they remain in their very own place";

the meaning is that they remain in their respective places, such as the state of being experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya). For indeed, the first impulsion volition (paṭhamajavana-cetanā) is only experienced in the present life;

the seventh impulsion volition is only experienced upon rebirth; and the five in between are only experienced in subsequent lives (aparapariyāyavedanīya). Thus, there is no mutual confusion among them.
Because of this inclusion, [kamma] remains as it is, according to its own specific nature—whether to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and so forth.
For that very reason, the Blessed One presented three alternatives: "either in the present life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
It is for this same reason that he said, "kamma to be experienced in the present life," and so on. Therein, "either in the present life" refers to the Teacher...
“He would not speak”: in the absence of a fixed rule (niyāma), he would not speak.
However, because there is no transference between them—since they possess a determined nature—the Teacher said, “either in this very life,” and so forth.
“In the bright side”: in the wholesome category (kusalapakkha) as it occurs in such passages as, “non-greed is the source for the arising of kamma. “Ceased”: [ceased]...

"By means of the attainment of the Noble Path, [the kamma] is ceased through non-arising cessation. "Made like a palm stump" means that just as nothing remains in the place where a palm tree has been cut down, so too, when kamma is abandoned, nothing remains; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, a "palm stump" refers to a palm tree cut off at its very top, because of the absence of leaves, fruit, buds, thorns, and so forth. For that very reason, it is of a nature not to grow again.
Thus the continuum of the being has abandoned its karma. Therefore he said, "like a palmyra tree with its crown cut off.
It has been rendered "without further existence" because of the absence of the subsequent arising of phenomena. Therefore he said, "just as," and so forth.

"Like the time when [the seed] has been rendered non-arising" means like the time when the arising of seeds has been completely brought to an end. "Of those whose roots are severed" refers to the root of the defilements having been completely [severed].
"Because they are cut off, their roots are cut off. For the defilements (*kilesa*) are indeed the roots of the aggregates (*khandha*).
"To be felt" means it should be understood as such. "There is no other basis" means there is no other foundation.

Even that which is designated as a "good destination" (*sugati*) is, at its lowest limit, not exempt from the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*); therefore, it is said to be "all miserable destinations" (*duggatiyo*).
The meaning here should be understood in this way: because greed (*lobha*) exists as its cause, it is "greed" (*lobha*), namely, karma that has greed as its sign.
The same applies to "hatred" (*dosa*). Therefore, he said: "Under the heading of greed and hatred, only karma born of greed and born of hatred is indicated.
"The round and the unravelling of the round" (*vaṭṭavivaṭṭa*) means both the round (*vaṭṭa*) and the unravelling (*vivaṭṭa*).
The commentary on the Nidāna Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta: 35.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "in Āḷavī" means in the province of Āḷavī, not in the city of Āḷavī. Therefore he said: "In Āḷavī means in the province of Āḷavī."
Now, *atha* is a particle used in the sense of continuity (*avicchedatthe*). In this context, the meaning is: "precisely because the Blessed One’s sitting was uninterrupted.

That is why he said, "Thus" (*eva*), and so forth. "From hand to hand" means: having gone from the hand of the yakkha Āḷavaka to the hand of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and from there to the hands of the king’s men.
“Of Māgha” means of the month of Māgha. The same applies here to “of Phagguṇa. Mud rises up from within the hoof-prints and remains;
thus, “mud rises up from within the hoof-prints and remains. The wind blowing from the four directions is called the *veramba* wind because it resembles the *veramba* wind.

“The body of the five doors” means the aggregate of consciousness that occurs by way of the five doors. “Agitating” means agitating by way of the agitation of the defilements, thereby causing disturbance to the mind.
“Mental factors” (cetasika) are those dependent upon the mind-door consciousness; hence he said, “agitating the mind-door.
“That lust” refers to lust similar to it, for there is indeed a designation of one thing by the name of another similar to it.

Just as it is said, “That very same tittiri bird; those very same medicinal herbs. For the passion that arises in one person is exactly the same as that in another, due to the commonality of the nature of passion.
Therefore it is said, “passion of such a kind,” and so forth.

Through the failure to obtain what is desired, or through the cessation of objects that provoke passion, the arising of grief should be understood as the origin of the fever of hatred (*dosa-pariḷāha*).

He does not smear [himself] because his mind is unstained. He has become cool because all his fevers have been extinguished. "Attachments" (*āsattiyo*) refers to cravings in the sense of being fastened here and there. "Distress" (*daratha*) means the arising of fever. "Of the mind" (*cetaso*) is a genitive case.
The commentary on the *Hatthaka-sutta* is finished. 6. Commentary on the *Devadūta-sutta*.
36. Regarding the sixth [verse], it is said that the term "devadūtā" was spoken by means of a grammatical shift in gender; thus he says, "the divine messengers.
Alternatively, this word possesses both genders; therefore, the demonstration of the meaning is made in the masculine gender for what was spoken in the Canon in the neuter gender.
"The god" refers to Death (maccu), because in the sense of overcoming, the King of Death brings sentient beings under his own power.
