He is called a "deva. For just as a deva overcomes ordinary beings, so does Death (maccu) overcome all beings; therefore, because he is like a deva, he is a deva.

Having said, "His messengers," [the text] now speaks the words beginning with "By means of old age, sickness, and death" in order to clarify his messengers and their status as messengers. Because they have the sense of an exhortation, they are "deva-dūtā" (messengers of the deva), meaning they are like the messengers of a deva.

He shows this: they are called "messengers" (dūta) because they are like messengers who carry out the commands of the God of Death, saying, "I shall come to crush so-and-so; you must seize him by the hair and not let him go.
Now, showing that they are "God-messengers" (devadūta) in the sense that they are like gods (deva) in respect of being trustworthy, he says, "messengers like gods," and so forth.
In this context, the phrase "adorned and prepared" is stated for the purpose of showing that she stood there having manifested her own divine majesty.

The prophecy of a deity is exactly like that of a human; for before long, old age, sickness, and death are bound to occur. "Purified deities" refers to *brahmās* whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
For they [behold] the various states of Bodhisattvas in their final existence, such as being aged and so forth.

They appear; therefore, it should be understood that the designation [of "seeing"] is established by way of a figurative sense (*pariyāya*), since it applies not only to those Bodhisattvas in their final existence who were attended upon by the Pure Abode Deities (*visuddhideva*), but also to others who were not so attended.
"Having seen" means having seen them as presented by the Pure Abode Deities; for this very reason, they are called the messengers of the Pure Abode Deities.
Why is it begun? The intention is that [the Buddha] did not show the messengers of the gods (*devadūta*) themselves in their actual form.
Showing that it was spoken in that way because it was the means for seeing the messengers of the gods, he said: "The messengers of the gods... interrogates.
In that context, "for the purpose of showing the messengers of the gods... means for the purpose of showing the action that leads to the place where one is interrogated by the messengers of the gods.
"Some elders" refers to those who maintain the doctrine of consciousness (viññāṇavādins), such as the Andhakas and others.
"Hell-wardens" (nirayapālā) means they guard those in hell by preventing them from escaping; thus they are called hell-wardens.

Alternatively, they are called hell-wardens because, by virtue of being hell-wardens, they are sufficient—that is, capable—of enveloping the denizens of hell with the suffering of hell. "That" refers to the statement: "There are no hell-wardens."

[This is] the statement. "It has indeed been refuted" means it has been refuted in the Abhidhamma by way of such passages as, "There are hell-guardians in the hells, and there are torturers," and so forth. The intention is that if those called hell-guardians did not exist, there would be no infliction of karmic punishments;
for when there is a torturer, there must necessarily be the infliction of punishment. Therefore he said, "Just as... and so forth. Herein, it is asked:
“But are these hell-wardens beings belonging to hell, or are they not? What is the point here?
If, first of all, they were beings belonging to hell, produced by karma leading to hell, then they too would experience the suffering of hell;
and that being so, they would be incapable of inflicting punishment upon other beings in hell. [Thus one could not distinguish: “These are the beings in hell; these are the hell-wardens.”

And there would be no fixed determination [of their roles]. Furthermore, those who kill others would not experience fear or terror from others who were identical to them in appearance, strength, and stature.

If, on the other hand, they were not hell-beings (*anairayika*), how could they possibly exist there? It is said: the hell-wardens (*nirayapāla*) are hell-beings produced by karma that leads to rebirth in hell;
for they are produced by a specific karma distinct from the karma that leads to the actual birth in hell itself.
They are reborn through their own karma because they belong to the class of *rakkhasas*. For thus say the Sabbatthivādins:
"Those who are wrathful, performers of cruel deeds, likewise delighting in evil, and who rejoice in those who suffer—they are born as *yama-rakkhasas*."
In this regard, as for what some say— that they would experience the suffering of torment, or else that they would kill one another, and so forth— this is without substance,
because the hell-wardens themselves lack the very nature of hell-beings. Even if the hell-wardens were not hell-beings,
as they wander about upon the hellish ground made of iron, blazing, aflame, and glowing with fire...
How is it that they do not experience the suffering of burning? It is through the power of their karma.

For just as those possessed of psychic power who have attained mastery over the mind, such as Mahāmoggallāna and others, when they approach the realms of hell out of compassion for the denizens of hell, are not afflicted by the suffering of burning by the power of their *iddhi*, so too should this case be understood.

If it is argued that this is because the domain of supernormal power (*iddhi-visaya*) is inconceivable, this too applies equally to the ripening of kamma (*kamma-vipāka*), which is also inconceivable.
For by such a type of kamma they are produced so that, while remaining entirely unafflicted by the suffering of hell, they yet slaughter the denizens of hell;
and it is not on account of this alone that the absence of external objects is untenable, since the quality of being desirable or undesirable exists individually even in the guards of the gates.

Because their intrinsic natures are distinct. For instance, what is desirable for one door and for one person may be undesirable for another, and what is undesirable for one may be desirable for another.
By establishing it thus, the claim made by some—that there is no scorching of others by fire through the power of karma—is refuted. As for what they say regarding those in the Avīci hell:
"How could their birth occur there?"—because of the existence of the various tortures for those in hell.
For karma that produces a personal existence (attabhāva) suitable for the tortures of hell-beings arises only in the location of hell itself, being directed toward such a specific place.
Indeed, those [beings] have greater strength, height, and girth than the hell-beings; they are extremely terrifying to behold and possess even more cruel modes of action.
And they do exist. By this very fact, it should be understood that the existence of tormenting crows, dogs, and so forth, which arise there for the denizens of hell, has been described.
Nor should it be said that beings of one destiny cannot torment those of another destiny, because such a thing is seen elsewhere as well.
As for what some say— that in hell the hell-wardens and the dogs and so forth are indeed devoid of a sentient nature—
this is merely their own opinion, because such a thing is not seen elsewhere.

For no such occurrence of phenomena has ever been observed that is devoid of a sentient nature and yet accomplishes a functional purpose without being instigated by presently existing sentient beings.
There is no distinguishing factor between the presence and absence of men who prevent the thirsty from drinking or who carry clubs and weapons in their hands;
therefore, what need is there to speak of the evil consequences when such persons are actually present?

Even a dream-attack is not an insufficient cause for accomplishing a purpose, since that purpose is achieved merely by the sight [of the attacker] and so forth. For instance, in a dream, one does not [require] the consumption of food and the like.

As for the accomplishment of purpose (*atthasiddhi*) and the form created by supernormal power (*iddhinimmānarūpa*), an answer has already been found here because the domain of supernormal power is inconceivable.

If it is argued that here too the ripening of kamma (*kammavipāka*) is inconceivable, that is not so, because it is unproven. It is only established that the ripening of the kamma of those in hell consists of the hell-guardians (*nirayapāla*);
and according to the method already stated and from the Canon itself, their status as sentient beings (*sattabhāva*) alone is established. It is possible...

Indeed, it is right to say that the occurrence of phenomena designated as "beings" and known as hell-wardens is like a continuous succession of ogres (rakkhasa) who subsist on vital essence (ojāhāra), because they possess the actual function of harming others intentionally.

Furthermore, their acting with prior intention cannot be denied, since they kill by means of various such intentions. For this very reason, [they are not included] among the mountain-like aggregates (saṅghātapabbata).

This is inconclusive. As for those who say, "It is merely specific elements that, possessing particular qualities such as color and shape and having a terrifying appearance, receive the designation 'hell-guardians' (nirayapāla)," that is unproven; for the statement in the Pāḷi, "There are hell-guardians in hell," has been established quite directly.

Furthermore, just as in the Noble Discipline (ariyavinaya) the existence of hell-wardens as mere primary elements (bhūtamatta) is not established, so too for one who maintains that things are mere designations (paññattimattavādin), the existence of primary elements is not established, because he does not admit the existence of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) in any way whatsoever.

For him, what are called "primary elements" do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha). If he were to employ conventional expression by grasping at the ultimate sense, then why [does he not admit them]?
"Does he deny the eye, visible forms, and so forth? Let this line of reasoning—characterized by instability and based on those who have not abandoned their perversions—stand aside.
Thus, one must reach the conclusion that hell-guardians do indeed exist.
Furthermore, even if they were present, the argument that there is a fixed location and so forth for them in hell, despite the absence of external objects, is not established.
However, it should be understood that the restriction of place and so forth applies only when an external object exists.
Because he leads (*yameti*) or directs (*niyameti*) beings toward their accumulated meritorious deeds by means of the arrival of the messengers of Yama, he is called *Yama*.
Since he is the king of the *vemānika* (intermediate) *petas*, he is the "King" (*rañño*). Thus it was said: "The one named King Yama is the king of the *vemānika* *petas*."

"Kamma-vipāka" refers to the result of unwholesome kamma. For the *vemānika-petas* (displaced ghosts), having performed mixed kamma—both dark and bright—they take rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through bright kamma, just like the deities of the lower realms (*vinipātika-devatā*). Thus, they even partake in the paths and fruits;
however, during the course of existence (*pavatti*), they experience the fruit of merit at times and the fruit of demerit at other times, in accordance with their kamma.
However, it should be understood that for those in whom the Noble Path arises, from the moment of attaining that Path onwards, only the fruit of merit arises.
Others say that the fruit of demerit is no longer as bitter as before, but becomes as mild as it was for those remaining in the human state.
Regarding the phrase "a righteous king," his righteousness here is that of a son of a righteous deity (*dhammadevaputta*).
It should be understood as a natural law (dhammatā) by which [the result] necessarily arises accordingly. "At the gates" means at the four gates of the Avīci Great Hell.
"Brahmins whose taints are destroyed" is said according to the highest description.
"The duty of inquiry" refers to the conduct that must be observed once an inquiry has been made. "Imposing" means causing [another] to perform it; [referring to] one's own question.
He asks by causing [the other] to give a reply directed toward [him]. For one who wishes to know another’s intention asks by employing a means conducive to that end.
"Adherence" (laddhi) means a conviction (gāha). "Establishing" means causing [the other] to maintain it there at all times.
"Asking for the reason" means asking for the logical justification (yutti). "Rebukes" (samanubhāsati) means [addressing] the matter as it has been investigated.
Having set aside [the literal meaning], he speaks as follows:

"Worn out" means worn out by the arrival of old age. He shows that some people, from their youth onward, resemble those who are worn out due to their bodies being overcome by diseases such as jaundice, but this [person] is not worn out in that way by the arrival of old age. "Crooked like a rafter."

It is "crooked" like a crooked rafter; for a straight rafter is not taken as an illustration of the state of being crooked. "Broken" means one whose body is broken due to the body being broken at the waist.
Therefore he said: "By this too, it is his very state of being crooked that is illustrated.
"Dependent on a staff" means that for him, the staff is the support in standing and walking; thus he is "dependent on a staff."
Because he is unable to exist without it, he said, "with a staff as his companion" (*daṇḍadutiya*). "Afflicted by old age" (*jarātura*) means one whose body is parched and exhausted by old age.
"With a large bald head" (*mahākhallāṭasīsa*) refers to a head that is entirely covered with wrinkles, like a great leather bag.

"Having wrinkles grown all over" (*sañjātavali*) means having wrinkles produced on every side. "Subject to old age" (*jarādhamma*) means one whose nature is conditioned by old age. Therefore he said, "the state of being old age" (*jarāsabhāva*). Nature (*sabhāva*).
And because it never ceases, just as heat does not depart from the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), he said, "not yet liberated from old age," and so forth.
The meaning is this: although he did not actually speak these words aloud, by the very implication of the sense, he was as if speaking them to the wise.
"I was young, endowed with youth. One who possesses the strength of the thighs is called *ūrubalī*.
By this, he shows the capacity for traveling to and from afar, leaping, and so forth; by the term "bāhubalī" (possessing arm-strength), he shows the capacity to perform tasks with the hands;
and by the mention of "speed," he shows the capacity for rapid movement. "Antarahitā" means vanished. And herein, the passage beginning with "But I am not yet...
is a demonstration that old age is a messenger of the gods. Therefore, he said: "Thus, this is a messenger of the gods."
"...is called 'born'. Because of the existence of affliction (*ābādha*), one is "afflicted" (*ābādhika*). It is called "disease" (*byādhi*) because it brings forth various sufferings (*dukkha*);

or, it is called "disease" because one is specifically bound (*ādhiyati*) by it; one in whom disease has arisen is "sick" (*byādhita*). This same method applies here to the term "pained" (*dukkhita*) as well.

Regarding the second "messenger of the gods," the meaning should be understood in the very same manner already stated. "Stricken by disease" means afflicted by disease; the sense is that he is oppressed.
“Of discolored appearance” means of discolored blue appearance. For wherever it was previously grasped, there it becomes pale-colored;
in places where the flesh has protruded, it is red-colored; and for the most part, it is as if covered by a blue cloth.
Therefore it is said: “of discolored blue appearance.”

The investigation beginning with “Who then has done much evil? and so forth is undertaken by way of those who have indeed reached hell, considering the question: “Who gains [the opportunity for release], and who does not gain it?
“Has done much evil” (*bahu pāpaṃ kataṃ*) means that evil was committed many times; by this, he speaks of the frequent repetition of that evil. Alternatively, “much” (*bahu*) means great.
For the word *bahu* is also seen to mean “great,” as in such passages as “Oh, much indeed has been done by him.”
"Weighty" (garuka) is what is meant. Having committed a weighty or frequent evil, one who remains [in that state] is reborn in hell itself;
he is not led into the presence of Yama by the messengers of Yama.

"Limited" (paritta) means limited by way of its magnitude and limited by way of its duration. In the first sense, the meaning is "not weighty"; in the second, it is "not frequent. Regarding the meaning as stated above...
The phrase beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was spoken in order to illustrate by means of a simile. "Doing what ought to be done" means they carry out the punishment itself.
"Having investigated" means having examined. "A place of adjudication" means a place for legal proceedings. "Those with minor evil karma" means those with weak evil karma.
"By their own nature" means that even when not reminded by others, they remember [their offenses] through their own inherent nature.
For they remember it both by their own nature, because evil kamma has become weak and because the accumulated wholesome kamma—
which is worthy of opportunity— has become powerful; and even when reminded by others, meaning even when others remind them, "This is the specific meritorious deed you performed."
The "Ākāsa-cetiya" (Sky Shrine) is a shrine constructed on a mountain peak in an open, exposed area.
"With a red cloth" means he made an offering by fashioning it into a banner (*paṭāka*) using a red-colored cloth.

"Hearing the sound of the fire-flames" means that upon hearing the sound of the fire-flames crackling in the hell, he immediately recollected the cloth he himself had offered; at that time, the sound of the wind striking the banner served as the sign (*nimitta*).
Because he had grasped it, he recollected the cloth he himself had offered, thinking: "At that time, at Ākāsacetiya, I heard the sound of the cloth being worshipped.
"With a jar of *sumana* flowers" means with a heap of *sumana* flowers the size of a jar. Some say it was "ten thousand jars plus ten *nāḷis*," while others say it was "five *ambaṇas*.
He did not remember even these three things, being utterly deluded by his powerful evil karma. [He remained] silent.
"He was silent" means that, seeing no way to provide a remedy there, thinking "this man deserves punishment," he remained silent.
"By those as large as the roof-covering of a single side" means by the size of the roof-covering of a house of medium dimensions. "Having struck it with thread" means having applied black thread.
Just as a chariot made entirely of iron would be ablaze, so too were its yokes and other parts.
"They were indeed blazing and aflame," thus he said, "having yoked [the chariots] together... with the chariots.
"The size of a great gabled house" means the size of a seven-storied great gabled house.
"Divided" means divided by the common evil karma of sentient beings. "An inferior body" means an inferior class of beings.
"Or an inferior selfhood. Regarding "clinging" (*upādāna*), there are four kinds of clinging. As for its meaning, however, it is the grasping of craving and views;
thus he said, "in the grasping of craving and views. It is called "origination" (*sambhava*) because aging and death originate through it;
thus he said, "the six causes of birth and death. "Without clinging" (*anupādā*) means not having clung. Therefore he said, "without clinging."

"Having transcended all the suffering of saṃsāra": because, through the cessation of the final consciousness, neither the suffering of saṃsāra nor even the defilements can possibly arise, they have transcended all the suffering of saṃsāra.
The commentary on the *Devadūta Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Catumahārājasutta 37.

In the seventh [verse], they are called *amaccā* (ministers) because they attend together (*amā saha vattanti*) upon their respective duties; thus they are "companions. They are called *pārisajjā* (councillors) because they exist within the assembly (*parisati bhavāti*);
that is, they occupy the position of a retinue and are included within the assembly. Therefore, he says "the attendant deities" (*paricārikadevatā*). "O dear ones" (*tātā*):
Addressing: in the manner stated as “Are there many people? and so forth. Eight times: four times in one half-month and likewise in the other;
thus, eight times. They resolve: they determine. They keep watch: they remain vigilant each time.
For beings who perform merit are said to be “keeping watch,” because they are intent upon the duties that ought to be done.
But others are said to sleep because they are devoid of concern for their own welfare or the welfare of others.
Just as one follows the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, one cannot go out to meet the Uposatha on the fifteenth day because there is no daylight.
"From here and there" means from various places. "Depending upon that" means depending upon those respective villages, market towns, and royal capitals. "Inhabiting" means...
The deities residing in parks, groves, trees, and so forth. "They" refers to those deities. "He speaks with reference to them" means the Blessed One speaks.
"It is said" means it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary).

"Constantly and regularly" refers to the Uposatha; because it must be observed and performed year after year, it is called the "Fortnight of Marvels. "By the factors of virtue" means by the factors of the Uposatha.

"Having dwelt" (*vutthavāsa*) means having lived the life of purity (*vusita-brahmacariya*). "The duty to be performed" (*kattabba-kicca*) refers to the duties such as full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding suffering and the other truths.
"Having cast off" (*otāretvā*) means having abandoned. "One whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed" (*parikkhīṇa-bhava-saṃyojana*) means one whose bonds to existence are entirely exhausted.
"Having known by means of a cause" (*kāraṇena jānitvā*) means having known the Four Noble Truths through the wisdom of the Path accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
"Knowing" means knowing the virtue of the Uposatha ritual thus: "This is the practice of emulating the Arahants, namely, the proper observance of the Uposatha.
"By such [a ritual]" means by the Uposatha ritual that consists in emulating the Arahants, which is the kind of Uposatha state prescribed for the Blessed One.
It is possible for one who is resolute, having exerted himself in insight (vipassanā), [to attain the goal].
In order to attain the perfection of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). The eighth [section] is self-evident, as it follows the method already stated in the seventh.
The commentary on the *Catumahārāja-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Sukhumāla-sutta*.

39. In the ninth [verse], "free from suffering" (*niddukkho*) means being devoid of bodily and mental suffering. For one who is beset by suffering and affliction has no opportunity for refinement due to their delicacy;
therefore, one who is happy is called "delicate" because of that freedom from suffering. Because his delicacy has reached the highest excellence, it is said "supremely delicate" (*paramasukhumālo*).
The meaning is "extremely delicate. "Beyond the limit" (*antamatītaṃ*) means "absolute" (*accantaṃ*). [This applies] at all times.
"He is delicate" means "always free from suffering. "At the time of his conduct" refers to the period when he was practicing the conduct of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
"By him" means by the Bodhisattva. Elsewhere, however, *paduma* refers to a red lotus, while *puṇḍarīka* is said to be white.
"The others" refers to the other ponds. The passage beginning with "It is said that for the Bodhisattva... is a demonstration of the origin of those ponds.
"Kuddālakammakārā" means diggers. "Pokkharaṇiṭṭhānāni" means places suitable for digging lotus ponds. "Gaṇhāpesi" means he had them dug.
Here, the word *pokkharaṇi* should be understood as established in the sense of such a reservoir of water, just like words such as *paṅkaja* (lotus).

"Sopānabāhukānaṃ matthakaṭṭhānaṃ uṇhīsaṃ" refers to the topmost part of the handrails of the stairs. "Udakasecananāḷikā" means water-sprinkling pipes or mechanical devices for discharging sprays of water.
"Fivefold" is according to color and according to species.

"Now, moreover" (*kho pana*) is merely a particle. It should be understood that the word *kāsika* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) for very soft, fine, and costly cloth, but it also occurs by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) for other things of that same kind. Therefore he said: "sandalwood that is not from Kāsi."
A dwelling for the winter is a *hemanta*; that which is fit for the winter is *hemantika*, as in the case of a palace.
Having stated, "The same principle applies to the others as well," the passage beginning with "In this regard, the *hemantika*" was spoken in order to demonstrate what those [palaces] are fit for.
"With lattices" means having windows with lattices; "water-fountains" means mechanisms for the discharge of streams of water. "On the top of the palace" means on the upper open terrace of the palace.
"Having bound" means having bound the dried hide of a non-violent (deer) that had been fastened to the machine.
"Having turned the machine around" means having turned the machine—which had been set in operation for the purpose of throwing up stones and again for the purpose of releasing them—around.
"They release it upon that" means they release it onto the dried hide of a non-violent deer that was bound to the surface of the roof-covering.

“Of thousandfold strength” means possessing the power of a thousand men; it is capable of bearing a load that must be carried by a thousand men. “Seated upon a couch” means seated exactly as he was on a couch made of jewels.
“With wings raised as if to fly” means as if they had risen up and remained suspended.
“While striking the bowstring” means while making contact with the bowstring. “The sound of the bowstring’s stroke” means the sound produced by the impact of the bowstring.
"Fastened to a machine" means placed there after being secured by a mechanical device. "Within earshot" means within the range of hearing for a man of medium strength.
A *kosa* is also called the fourth part of a *gavyūta*; it is a distance measured by two thousand staff-lengths.
"All places" refers to all those various dwelling places of a Great Man. "Tied to the crest" [refers] to the very nature of a man.
This is specifically a demonstration. "It is not for the purpose of causing excitement" means that he did not speak on the subject known as causing excitement;
for in his case, the demolition of the bridge occurred right at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Precisely because of that" means precisely because it illustrates the characteristic of heedfulness.
"Transcending himself" means he grieves without considering his own arrival at old age. But this...
"It was abandoned by the path" means that at that time, the path had not yet been attained. "Having rejected the training" means having abandoned the training as it had been undertaken.
"Being of the very nature of disease and so forth" means being exclusively of the nature of disease and so on.
"Thus dwelling in loathing" means for one who dwells thus, dwelling in a state of loathing for the entire suffering of saṃsāra. "Thus loathing" means...
"Thus [there was] loathing for another. "Not loathing another" means not loathing another by way of exercising compassion.

"I am a conqueror" means I am one who has overcome. "Zeal arose" means that there was indeed energy endowed with four factors and the fourfold energy of right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*), by which he became one whose ultimate goal is the holy life of the Path (*mārgabrahmacaryaparāyaṇa*).
The commentary on the Sukhumāla-sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Ādhipateyya-sutta: 40.
In the tenth [sutta], that which is dominant in the sense of prevailing after having overcome is the "overlord" (adhipati); it is any kind of preeminent thing, not a creator or a self.
Taking "lord" (adhipati) as the sense, the self itself is the lord; that which has come from that is "having the self as its lord" (attādhipateyya).

Therefore he said, "the self," and so forth. "The world" (loka) refers to the world of sentient beings (sattaloka). And this is intended specifically as one endowed with distinguished qualities such as the various supernormal powers (iddhividha), because it is the state of being a lord that is intended here.

"The ninefold supramundane dhamma" is stated by way of an exalted description. "Thus, existence" (iti bhavo): *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full passage would typically continue with a definition of "existence" (bhava) as the five aggregates.*
Thus there is existence as success (*sampattibhava*), and therein, thus, there is growth.

"The cause of existence as success" means the cause for each respective existence as success and for the growth therein. Because the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*)—which is the sign of birth—has been performed and accumulated, birth enters within.
This same method applies to aging and the rest, because the establishment of the fruit follows from the establishment of the cause.
"Unlanguid" means not having reached a state of contraction. "Established" means established by way of clearly discerning the specific nature of the body and so forth.
"Unconfused" because of the absence of delusion. "Unagitated" because of the suppression of agitation and its causes.
"One-pointed" because the state of being distracted has been cast far away. "Having made stainless" refers to the stains of lust and so forth.
"By removing" means having made it free from impurity. "He guards" means he protects it from the harm of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
"This one" refers to the bhikkhu who practices in this way. "He maintains himself in purity" because even the defilement that constitutes impurity is absent.

"You think you have surpassed me" means you think you have overcome me. "Born of that craving" means consisting of it, being subject to craving. "The state of that" is *tammayatā* (the state of being made of that); by the absence of that *tammayatā*. "He does not decline" because he has attained the full development of qualities such as wisdom (*paññā*).
The commentary on the Ādhipateyya Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Devadūta Vagga is finished.
5. The Cūḷa Vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Sammukhībhāva-sutta* 41.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "one is present" (*sammukho bhavati*) by means of that which is presence (*sammukhībhāvo*); it is the state of being existing in front.

Therefore, it is called "from presence" (*sammukhībhāvā*). "Meritorious action" (*puññakamma*) refers to meritorious action consisting of giving (*dāna*). "Two things are easily obtained" (*dve dhammā sulabhā*)...
Because they are external, they are obtained through the convergence of their respective conditions. Faith, however, is difficult for ordinary people to obtain because its function is unstable.
For this very reason, he said, "of the worldling," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Sammukhībhāva-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Tiṭṭhāna Sutta 42.
In the second [verse], "the stain of stinginess" (*macchariyamala*) means stinginess itself is the stain.

It is called "free from the stain of stinginess" (*vigatamacchariyamala*) because the stain of stinginess has departed from it, since stinginess causes the mind to take on a stained nature. Even when someone gives something there due to the absence of greed...
He does not withhold his proximity [to others], yet this person is not like that; thus it is said, "one whose generosity is unrestrained.
He is like one with soiled hands due to the absence of purity of mind. He is like one with washed hands because he accomplishes the task that must be done by means of washed hands.
Therefore it was said: "When the mind is pure, they are purified"—so spoke the Great Seer. He is worthy of being entreated by supplicants.

"From the fulfillment of desires. Because he is well-engaged by supplicants who are unable to provide for themselves, he is "devoted to it" through that very state of possession, not merely by thought alone; thus he said, "One who gives... is called devoted.
Having said, "It is too high, venerable sir," one might think, "This person is speaking to me from too high a position"; therefore, [the Buddha] said again, "You are not too high."
He said: the intention is "with the body. "Of dark-blue color" means having a blue luster. "He asked" means he asked the bhikkhus.

"He remained drawing a line on the ground" means that after first lying down on the couch and then rising, he remained drawing a line on the ground with the thought, "Let there be the conceit that [he] has not yet exhausted the taints (*akhīṇāsrava*).
For thus the king [described] one named an "exhausted-tainted-one" (*khīṇāsrava*)... [and so forth].
He turned back. "With their banners raised" means with their banners already hoisted.

"The site of the stone cetiya" refers to the place made of stone located between the Thūpārāma and the Mahācetiya. [The Buddha] stood at the cetiya... [thinking], "This gabled hall belongs to a disciple.
"To the rear" means behind the elder who was preaching the Dhamma. "Gonasa" means a hooded snake (*maṇḍalasarpa*). An obstacle to hearing the Dhamma.
Thinking, "May it not become an obstacle for many to attain the path to heaven," he resolved, "I shall not create an obstacle to hearing the Dhamma.
"Having suppressed the poison" means having suppressed the force of the poison by the heat of his insight (vipassanā).
"A thousand verses" means possessing a thousand verses. "By the *Paṭṭhāna*-verse" means by the introductory verse, that is, the opening verse.

The meaning is as follows. He established [the recitation] starting from the *Paṭṭhāna*... pe ...up to the very final verse, because his body was exhausted; he did not [recite] what was spoken in between. The recitation was the evening Dhamma talk.
"She grasps" (*paggaṇhāti*) means she receives it by making it manifest before her eyes; the meaning is that she listens attentively.
On the day of the Dhamma talk, faithful lay followers [act] for the sake of the Dhamma-preachers not becoming weary.
They give wholesome food and honey-drinks for the sake of the sweetness of the voice, as well as medicinal herbs such as ghee, madhuka, oil, and so forth.
Therefore he said, “I shall speak of the noble lineages,” and so on. “Having bitten with four fangs” is a demonstration of the state of having firm teeth.
“I shall move about” means I shall attend properly; the sense is that I shall listen with due care. “Having crushed” means having rubbed away; the sense is having removed.
The commentary on the *Tiṭṭhānasutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Atthavasasutta*: 43.

In the third [sutta], "benefit" (*attha*) means the fruit; that which has this as its basis (*vasa*) is "basis of benefit" (*atthavasa*). It is the cause; it is called "basis of benefit" because it possesses this benefit.
"It is the meaning, and it is just that," he said; thus, "three meanings, three reasons.
Teaching the Dhamma, in the highest sense, is the manifestation of the Four Noble Truths; therefore, he said, "he manifests the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"He experiences the commentary with wisdom" means he is one whose nature is to experience each word of the Pāḷi through the wisdom of exposition. "This..."
“...the meaning of this statement. By this, he expresses the function of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

“Experiencing the textual doctrine (*pāḷidhamma*)” means one whose nature is to experience each and every instance of the textual tradition, its progression, and the word-by-word commentary. By this, he expresses the function of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
The commentary on the *Atthavasasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kathāpavatti Sutta 44.

In the fourth [verse], "proceeding" (*pavattinī*) means proceeding without interruption until the conclusion of the intended meaning. It is "unobstructed" (*appaṭihatā*) due to the absence of resistance. It is "leading out" (*niyyānikā*) and "possessing proof" (*sappāṭihīrakā*).
The commentary on the Kathāpavatti Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Paṇḍita Sutta 45.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "established by the wise" (*paṇḍitapaññattāni*) means first established by the wise.

"Spoken" (*kathitāni*) means spoken as something superior. "By great beings" (*mahāpurisehi*) refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) refers to the liberation of mind through compassion (*karuṇā-cetovimutti*). "The preliminary stage" (*pubbabhāga*)...
Its proximate cause is self-control (*dama*). It is called "self-control" because it is the taming of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth.

"Taming of oneself" means the taming of the mind. Furthermore, patience (*khanti*) is also called "self-control," because in the *Puṇṇovāda* it is said: "Puṇṇa, you will indeed be able [to cross] by means of this self-control and tranquility.
And in the *Āḷavaka Sutta*, it is spoken of in the verse: "Truth, self-control, and generosity..."

In this sutta, it is appropriate to say that wisdom (*paññā*) is also "taming" (*dama*). Protection, guarding, and care consist of: protection from dangers caused by humans and non-humans on the part of parents;
guarding against misfortunes such as disease and the like; and caring through the performance of services such as providing food and clothing.
One is called "peaceful" (*santo*) because of the subsiding of all the distress and fever of the defilements (*kilesa*), and because of the tranquility of one's bodily and verbal conduct.
"In the highest sense, 'peaceful' means peaceful in the sense of being excellent through such qualities as filial duty toward one's mother (*mātṛtva*).
'In this world, by performing these very three things' means by performing and bringing about the three things mentioned in this discourse.
'These... are the causes' refers to these two: service to one's mother and service to one's father."
The causes of the supreme persons. For it is by performing the highest duties that those who attend upon their mother and father are called "supreme persons.
Therefore he said: "Mother and father... [as stated]. It is secure because it is free from calamity.
The commentary on the *Paṇḍita-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sīlavanta Sutta (46).

Regarding the sixth [verse], "a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane": here, because it is stated without distinction that "human beings generate merit," one should understand that the possibility of the supramundane exists as well, since it includes merit consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*).
The commentary on the Sīlavanta Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Characteristics of the Conditioned (Saṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta) 47.
In the seventh [verse], "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) means that which is made by conditions having come together and combined.

"Signs" (*nimittāni*) means signs for the purpose of recognition. "Arising" (*uppāda*) is the occurrence in the convergence of causes and conditions; it is the acquisition of self-existence. "Decay" (*vaya*) is dissolution. "Of that which stands" (*ṭhitassa*)...
It is that which has reached the moment of presence after the moment of arising.
Since this state of it is distinct from the state of arising, it is called "aging" (jarā) as a state of alteration.

Because a phenomenon breaks up at the very moment it arises, if that were so, arising and dissolution would be simultaneous; however, that is not tenable. Therefore, the state facing dissolution is distinct from the state of arising.
Aging is to be understood [in this way]. As for those who say, "There is no stability of formations," their position is wrong.

For just as the state of dissolution is accepted as distinct from the state of arising of that very same phenomenon—otherwise one would fall into the view that "one thing arises and another ceases"—so too, phenomena that are in the process of arising and are facing dissolution [are distinct from those already arisen].
It should be desired. And that is the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇo*). For it cannot be understood that "what is arising is breaking up.

"Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) refers to phenomena belonging to the three planes, because they have arisen from conditions. If this is so, one might ask how the states of the Path and its Fruits are [conditioned];

thus he says, "But as for the Paths and Fruits," and so forth. For the discussion of characteristics (*lakkhaṇakathā*) is intended solely for the purpose of full comprehension (*sammasana*). At the moment of arising...

[Arising occurs] at the moment of arising, not at the moments of presence or dissolution. Why? Because the moment of arising and the moment of arising itself are mutually delimited. For just as the moment of arising is delimited by the modification termed "arising," so too is the arising delimited by the moment of arising.
The same principle applies to the other two [moments]. Time, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, exists only by way of conventional worldly designation.
It has been said: "The characteristic is not conditioned; the conditioned is not the characteristic"—this shows their distinction.
For the states are distinct from that which possesses the states. Regarding the term "delimited": let it be granted that the conditioned is delimited by arising and passing away;
but how is it said to be delimited by aging? It is not said that there is a delimitation merely by way of the prior and posterior limits.
Now, this fault does not apply because of the distinction in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). A collection of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammajāta*) is delimited;
that very same collection of phenomena is known as "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) precisely because Nibbāna is characterized and recognized by the absence of those [conditioned qualities].
Now, with the words beginning "Just as," he clarifies the aforementioned point through similes.
The commentary on the Saṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta 48.

In the eighth [sutta], "of the unconditioned" (*asaṅkhatassa*) means that which is not conditioned (*na saṅkhatassa*), according to the method already stated. Therefore he said, "by conditions," and so forth. Just as...

Just as the category of conditioned phenomena is recognized as "conditioned" by virtue of the existence of arising and so forth, so too Nibbāna is recognized as "unconditioned" by virtue of the non-existence of those [characteristics].
The commentary on the *Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇa Sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Pabbatarāja Sutta 49.
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: here the word *sāla* is used as a general term for trees, not as a term for a specific species of tree;
thus he says, "Great *sāla* trees" means great trees. "The head of the clan" (*kulajeṭṭhaka*) means one who is the eldest and the master in that clan. It was made of stone, not of earth.

And [the phrase] "and what belongs to a village. Excluding both the village and the vicinity of the village (*gāmūpacāra*), everything is called "forest" (*arañña*); thus he said, "In the forest" means "in a place devoid of villages.
The construction is: "a great mountain, a rock.
The commentary on the *Pabbatarājasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Ātappakaraṇīya Sutta 50.
In the tenth [sutta], "of those arisen in the body" (*sarīrasambhavānaṃ*) means arisen within the body. "Pains" (*dukkhānaṃ*) means undesirable things.
"Thick" (*bahalānaṃ*) means not sparse due to their continuous occurrence. "By way of burning" (*tāpanavasena*) means by way of causing suffering. "Intense" (*tibbānaṃ*) means cruel.
The abandoning of those aforementioned painful feelings that must be abandoned through endurance is indeed "patience" (khamana);
thus he says, "for the sake of patience. "Having commanded" means having issued the Buddha's injunction: "Ardor should be practiced.
It is described as being both mundane and supramundane because it speaks of the path-factors together with their requisites.
The commentary on the Ātappakaraṇīya Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Mahācora Sutta: 51.
Regarding the eleventh [sutta], he said that a thief possessing great strength is a "great thief" (*mahācora*), meaning "a great, powerful thief. As for "powerful thief":
And it is to be understood by way of his great majesty, his large retinue, and his capability for the work of a great thief.

"The plundering of great villages and market towns" is *mahāvilopa*. "Including this or that reason" means taking each respective non-doing as the reason itself, and including it within the discourse connected thereto.
"They will explain the meaning" refers to each of those [cases].
And they will explain the meaning. "Carrying away" means removing or taking away. "Based on the ten grounds" means based on the ten grounds such as "the world is eternal.
"Views that stand by grasping an extreme" means views that stand by grasping that very extreme, such as eternity, and not relinquishing it.
The commentary on the Mahācorasutta is finished.
The commentary on the Cūḷavagga is finished.
The First Fifty is finished.
2. The Second Fifty (6) 1.
The Chapter on Brahmins 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Two Brahmins (*Paṭhamadvebrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā*)

52. In the first [sutta] of the Brāhmaṇa-vagga, "worn out by old age" (*jarājiṇṇa*) means worn out by virtue of aging, not worn out because of illness and so forth, though they resemble those who are worn out.
"Advanced in years" (*vayovuddha*) means grown old through having reached the increase of years, not through the growth of virtue and so forth.
"Great in birth" (*jātimahallaka*) means great in birth due to having known [the world] for a long time. "Having passed three stages" (*tayo addhe atikkanta*)...
The three periods—past, present, and future—are the first, middle, and last.
"Having reached the third period" means having reached that very last period. Regarding the phrase "those who have not performed the protection against fear":

here, "protection against fear" refers to merit that protects one from the fear of an unhappy rebirth; since they have not performed this, they are "those who have not performed the protection against fear. "A foundation for action" is that which brings about a foundation known as a happy rebirth.
Kamma. "Is brought forth" (upasaṃharīyati) means it is led toward [its result]. It is said, "It is led near" (upanīyati); to the question "What is led near by what?", he says:
"For this [world] is led near to old age by birth," and so forth. "This" refers to the world. One who is born does not remain in the state of being born alone;
rather, after that, one is led toward old age, and by old age, one is led toward sickness. In this way, one is led further and further toward suffering alone.
"In the sense of protecting" means in the sense of guarding. "In the sense of a place of concealment" means by way of being a place where one hides.

"In the sense of a foundation" means by way of being a basis. "In the sense of a refuge" means by way of being something to be relied upon. "By way of the supreme goal" means by way of being the highest destination.
The commentary on the first two *Brāhmaṇa* suttas is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Two Brahmins (Dutiyadvebrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā). 53.
In the second [discourse], it is a "vessel" (*bhājana*) in the sense of being shared and in the sense of being distributed among others; that is, household goods.
The commentary on the Second Discourse on Two Brahmins is concluded.
3–4. Commentary on the *Aññatarabrāhmaṇasutta* and others, 54–55.

In the third [sutta], it is shown how, through the non-abandonment of lust and the other [defilements], there arises for a person self-affliction and so forth, while through their abandonment, these do not arise;
thus, the noble Dhamma that abandons lust and the rest is of great majesty and great benefit.
"It is to be seen by oneself" means it is directly visible (*sandhiṭṭhika*). In this manner, the remaining terms should also be explained, drawing out their meanings as appropriate.
As for the literal meaning of the words, it should be understood according to the method set forth in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*. The fourth [term] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the *Aññatarabrāhmaṇasutta* and others is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Nibbutasutta 56.
In the fifth [sutta], "not to be attained at another time" means that since it is to be obtained at the very moment of the penetration of the Truths, it is not to be attained at some other time.
Because it is to be brought near by means of path-knowledge, it is "to be brought near" (*upaneyya*). That which is to be brought near is itself "the state of being brought near" (*opanayika*).
He said: "It should be approached through practice.
The commentary on the *Nibbāna Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Paloka Sutta*.
57. In the sixth [verse], “of the teachers of teachers” (*ācariyapācariyānaṃ*) means of the teachers’ teachers.

It is “continuously crowded” (*nirantaraphuṭo*) because of the great number of those who have committed the karma leading to hell among the beings in hell. “Both of these” (*ubhayampetaṃ*) refers to the two meanings as previously stated.

“Dense habitation” (*ghananivāsaṃ*) refers to the dense clustering of villages. It is “entirely unrighteous” (*ekanteneva adhammo*) because, being caused by improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), it is a cause of harm.

And it is *adhamma* by necessity. It is stated that "lust for what is not the Dhamma" (*adhammarāga*) is not intended [here] because, like lust for the requisites of others, it is not considered a great offense.
For indeed, lust directed toward one's own requisites—unlike improper greed—is not invariably productive of rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).
It is only because lust arising for the requisites of others possesses the quality of being a great offense that it is designated as "lust for what is not the Dhamma."
There is no such thing as a "simultaneous time" for greed, because—unlike bodily misconduct and the like—it does not arise from improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
"This" refers to this evil state. It is "equal greed" because it lacks the characteristic of being unequal.

For indeed, the activity arising from that [greed] is not called sexual misconduct. "By way of what is reckoned as the resorting to a place" refers to that which is approved by worldly people as virtuous.
The basis for lust is the object; [lust arises] through the act of enjoyment toward an object other than that.
"Various crops" refers to various kinds of crops such as rice, paddy, and so forth. "Spoiled crop" is a crop defiled by a defiling agent (*paccaya-dūsa*).
"While it is developing" means even before the time of growth in the womb, because it is already coming into being. "Vermin" refers to insects such as locusts and the like.
“They fall” means they fall upon the tops of the crops. “It becomes merely like a tally-stick” means it becomes incapable of growing further or taking root.
“They” refers to the predatory non-human beings (*vāḷamanussa*). “Having gained the opportunity” means having gained the opportunity because they were permitted by the lords of the *yakkhas*.
The commentary on the Paloka Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Vacchagotta Sutta 58.
In the seventh [sutta], "mahāvipāka" means having a sublime fruit and great result. "Dhamma" refers to the discourse spoken, based on the principle that "it reveals and clarifies the meaning.
"Anudhamma" refers to the counter-discourse, based on the principle that "it is the dhamma that follows after that."
“Saha dhammena” means *sahadhamma*; that which belongs to it is *sahadhammika*.
Since the word *dhamma* here is used in the sense of a cause, he says “with its cause. “Of the argument” means of the speech. “Anupāto” means subsequent occurrence.
It stands in the way, thus it is *pāripanthika*. Because he stands on the path and seizes the property of others, he is a highwayman (*panthadūhana-cora*).

If it is reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), how is it "of one beyond training" (*asekkha*)? He says: "Because it occurs in one beyond training. "The others" refers to the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.
In the phrase "itself also," the word "also" (*pi*) includes the meaning "and because it occurs in one beyond training.

"Free from guile" (*nivisevana*) means devoid of guile, having departed from a state of crookedness. "They do not examine" means they do not investigate. "Births" (*jātiyo*): it goes to or approaches birth (*jāti*), which is its arising; thus the meaning is "one who is born. Therefore he said: "in whatever family one is born."

“Kevalī” means one who possesses the absolute (kevala); the meaning is “perfection. Therefore he said, “endowed with the state of being complete. This is the word *kevalī*. “The further shore of direct knowledge” (*abhiññāpāra*) means the limit of higher knowledge.

One who has gone to the end because of having reached the boundary is a “one who has gone to the further shore” (*pāragū*). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “By hearing the determination of the field” means:
“These [persons], endowed with qualities such as virtue, are a field for merit in the world including the devas.”
"Then there is no other field"—thus they are devoid of hearing such a determination regarding the field.
The commentary on the Vacchagotta Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Tikaṇṇa Sutta.
59. "Difficult to approach" (*durāsada*) means difficult to draw near. "He will be released from censure" means: "If I speak thus, the ascetic Gotama might say something in response;
in this way, I shall be released from even the mere reproach that 'he has not obtained even my word'.
"Wise" (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom. "Steadfast" (*dhīra*) means possessed of fortitude. "Clever" (*byatta*) means [endowed] with the capacity to crush the arguments of opponents.
“Endowed with proficiency”: possessed of great learning (*bāhusacca*). “Orators”: skilled in the methods of debate.

“Esteemed”: highly regarded as virtuous by many people. “The discernment of the modes such as wisdom” means the discernment of the modes such as the wise character of those who possess the three Vedas (*tevijja*).
The word *ākāra* (mode) is a synonym for cause (*kāraṇa*), and the word *pariccheda* (discernment) has the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*); thus he says, “by this much cause.”
“Yathā” means in whatever manner or by whatever cause; thus he said, “‘Yathā’ is a word for a cause.
Having stated, “By both sides,” he spoke “from the mother’s side and from the father’s side” in order to show those sides in their specific form.
To demonstrate his noble birth by way of those two sides, he said, “Whose mother,” and so forth, [referring to] the state of being the progenitor and the progenitress.

In the world, the designation "mother" is seen even in the absence [of biological relation]; however, here it is intended specifically in the sense of a biological son (*orasaputta*), as indicated by the term "one who has conceived from a pure womb" (*saṃsuddhagahaṇika*).
That which conceives—that is, bears—the embryo is the *gahaṇī*; this refers to the region of the mother’s womb known as the seat of the embryo.
It is called the *gahaṇī* because it receives and does not discard the food that has been eaten by digesting it; thus, it is the element of bodily heat born of karma (*kammaja-tejo-dhātu*).
The father and the mother are the parents; the fathers of those parents are the grandfathers;

their generation is the grandfather-generation (*pitāmahayuga*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "as far back as the seventh grandfather-generation, the seventh pair of grandfathers.

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, without taking the word "pair" (*dvanda*), it is stated: "'Generation' (*yuga*) refers to the measure of the lifespan. And this is the sense of the word *yuga* according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

It is shown that "the grandfather himself is the grandfather-generation. Regarding the term *pubbapurisa* (forefathers), it should be understood here that the inclusion of the word *purisa* (man/person) is made by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*).
For in this way, the scriptural expression *mātito* (on the mother’s side) is properly accounted for.

*Akkhitta* means thrown away. *Anavakkhitta* means not thrown away or discarded among things such as offerings of faith or *thālipāka* (boiled rice) oblations. *Jātivādena* [is used] in the sense of a cause (*hetumhi*).
The phrase beginning with “for what reason” was stated in order to show that it is an instrumental expression. Here, by the words “from both sides...
[down to] the lineage of grandfathers,” the absence of any defect in the Brahmin’s birth is shown through the praise of his pure descent.
By the word “uncensured,” the absence of any transgression in his conduct is indicated; for even beings of pure birth fall into reproach due to a transgression of action.

“Unreproached”: by this is meant the absence of improper association. For it is in dependence upon improper association that beings—even those of pure birth and free from any fault in their conduct—receive abuse.

*Taṃ*: that word of reproach. “He recites the mantras”: he rehearses the Vedas; the meaning is that he masters them. “He bears the mantras”: having made the mantras as they were learned not forgotten, he places them in his heart.
"By way of the manner of striking with the lips" means by way of determining the meaning (*atthāvadhāraṇavasena*). Regarding the phrase "together with the *Nighaṇḍus* and *Keṭubhas*":
here, it is called *nikhaṇḍu* because it cuts, breaks, and shows the meaning and the word by dividing them through the relationship of the signified and the signifier;

that very term is spoken of here as "*nighaṇḍu*" by changing the letter *kha* to *gha*. It is called *keṭubha* because it moves (*kiṭati*) or causes one to go through the divisions of grammatical action and so forth, or because it exhausts them without remainder.

It is called *keṭubha* because it fills up (*pūreti*) the gaps. It is "that which elucidates synonyms" (*vevacanappakāsaka*), meaning it reveals multiple synonymous expressions for each single meaning.
This is merely an illustration, for that treatise functions also by way of revealing how many different meanings can be expressed by a single word.
It is so called because by means of it, action—characterized by the differentiation of speech and so forth—is conceived (*kappīyati*) and analyzed (*vikappīyati*).
The *kiriyākappa* (the section on verbal formations) is, however, a vast section due to its divisions such as phonemes, word-connections, and word-meanings;
therefore, it is called the "expansion of the *kiriyākappa*. And this is said with reference to the *Mūlakiriyākappa* treatise.

For that is a work of great scope, consisting of a hundred thousand [verses], and includes various treatises such as the *Nāmācariya*. Phonemes are analyzed according to their divisions of place and organ of articulation, as well as according to their etymological derivations.
"By these" refers to the classifications of syllables, the grammars, and the etymologies. "Of these" refers to the four Vedas.

A "word" (*pada*) is of four kinds or five kinds; one who "embodies" (*kāyati*) that word is a "knower of words" (*padaka*), or alternatively, one who embodies those very Vedas word by word is a *padaka*.
"The remainder thereof" refers to the sentences remaining after what has been mentioned. Up to this point is the exposition of phonology (*saddabyākaraṇa*).
Having spoken thus, he further states that "exposition" (*byākaraṇa*) refers to the exposition of meaning. It is called "exposition" because it explains or expounds various words and their meanings;
thus, it is the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). Because people do not strive or exert themselves for future welfare through it, it is called *lokāyata*.
For, relying on that treatise, sentient beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds.
The eighty great disciples were: Aññā-Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, Assaji, Nāḷaka, Yasa, Vimala, Subāhu,
Puṇṇaji, Gavampati, Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, Gayākassapa, Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna,
Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāna, Mahākoṭṭhita, Mahākappina, Mahācunda, and Anuruddha.
Kaṅkhārevata, Ānanda, Nandaka, Bhagu, Nandiya, Kimila,
Bhaddiya, Rāhula, Sīvali, Upāli, Dabba, Upasena, Kaṅkhārevata of the Khadiravana grove, Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, Puṇṇa of Sunāparanta,
Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, Soṇa Koḷivisa, Rādha, Subhūti, Aṅgulimāla, Vakkali, Kāḷudāyī, and Mahāudāyī.
Pilindavaccha, Sobhita, Kumārakassapa, Raṭṭhapāla, Vaṅgīsa, Sabhiya, Sela, Upavāṇa, Meghiya,
Sāgata, Nāgita, Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, Mahāpanthaka, Cūḷapanthaka,
Bākula, Kuṇḍadhāna, Dārucīriya, Yasoja, Ajita, Tissa-Metteyya, Puṇṇaka, Mettagu, and Dhotaka.
Upasīva, Nanda, Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa, Jatukaṇṇī, Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, Posāla, Mogharāja, and Piṅgiya—these are known as the eighty great disciples (mahāsāvaka).
But why are these elders specifically called "great disciples"? Because of the greatness of their initial resolve (abhinīhāra). Likewise...
Indeed, even the two Chief Disciples are included among the Great Disciples.

For although they stand in the foremost position among disciples due to their attainment of the supreme state through the perfection of the knowledge of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), they are also called "Great Disciples" because of their commonality in the greatness of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*).
As for the others, however, they possess a resolve that is even more exalted than that of ordinary disciples. Thus, regarding Padumuttara...

Having made their aspirations during the time of the Blessed One, they consequently attained mastery over the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti) to an extraordinary degree, and possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

Granted, all Arahants alike, having perfected the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) and the other stages, with minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as they truly are, exhaust the defilements (kilesa) without remainder through the sequence of the paths; yet...
Although they all establish themselves in the supreme fruit, nevertheless, just as there is a distinction in the cultivation of the path— achieved through specific distinctions in prior cultivation—
between one who has attained vision compared to one liberated by faith, and between one who is doubly liberated compared to one liberated by wisdom; so too,

because they have produced a preeminent distinction of qualities within their own mental continuities due to the greatness of their initial resolve and the greatness of their prior practice, these disciples are "great" by virtue of their qualities such as virtue and the rest.
The great disciples. Furthermore, among those very [disciples], it was because of their right practice—which was performed with care, continuously, and over a long period of time;

which was brought forth by a corresponding application of effort; and which served as the cause for the production of the extraordinary power of function regarding right view, right intention, and so forth, which were preeminent among the factors conducive to enlightenment—that they attained, respectively, excellence in wisdom and concentration.
Sāriputta and Moggallāna stand pre-eminent among all virtuous qualities due to their attainment of the highest perfection (*ukkaṭṭhapāramippatti*).

The other seventy-eight elders are called "great disciples" (*mahāsāvaka*) because they do not occupy the foremost position among all disciples at the pinnacle of disciple-perfection (*sāvakapāramī*).

Ordinary disciples (*pakatisāvaka*), however, [are so called] because of the absence of greatness in their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) and the absence of greatness in their prior application (*pubbayoga*).
And they are called "disciples of the Teacher. However, they are not limited in number like the chief disciples or the great disciples;
rather, they number many hundreds and many thousands.
"Vaya" means age; [this refers to those] who, throughout the beginning, middle, and end, do not grow weary nor expand [unnecessarily] regarding those texts.

“Santāneti” means “he leads forth. To show that two negations return to their original state, it says “there is no deficiency (avayo),” and then, in order to demonstrate what that deficiency is, it states:
“Deficiency is called... [etc. ...he is not able.
“Here” means in this sutta. “This” refers to the statement beginning with “quite secluded from sensual desires. For the attainment of the third true knowledge—
The sequence of practice has been explained in great detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, because of the desire not to repeat that here, and because of the desire to speak briefly—as was done in such discourses as the *Bhayabherava Sutta*—it is stated simply as "the two knowledges" (*dvinnaṃ vijjānaṃ*).
"Knowledge" (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of seeing through the mass of delusion (*mohakkhandha*) that conceals past lives; for delusion is a concealer by its very nature.
It is called "darkness" (*tama*) because it is like darkness. It is "to be done" (*kātabba*) because it must be performed;

thus, "making light" (*obhāsakaraṇa*) means that which is to be produced as the state of light by its own conditions—this is the meaning. "This is the meaning" refers precisely to this intended sense.
"A word of praise" is a term of eulogy for that very meaning, [referring] to the specific modes of activity that dispel opposing factors.
"By way of awakening. "The connection" refers to the connection between the words spoken by way of praise and the word spoken by way of showing the meaning.
By the phrase "ignorance is destroyed," it should be understood that this also illustrates the meaning that "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of "seeing.
Because "clear knowledge has arisen," its opposite, ignorance (*avijjā*), is indicated; and its being an opposite is due to its state of being something to be abandoned.
And he shows that it is by means of knowledge acting as the abandoner. "In the other two phrases as well" refers to the two phrases: "darkness is dispelled" and "light has arisen.
"The same method applies" extends this same construction [to those cases]. Herein, this is the construction:
for one who has thus attained knowledge, darkness is dispelled, shattered. Why? Because light has arisen—the light of wisdom.

"Manifested" means: "of one whose mind has been sent forth," that is, of one who has relinquished the mind for the attainment of the accomplishment of the intended goal; it is said to mean "of one whose mind has been sent forth for the sake of attaining the first stage of true knowledge (vijjā).
By the phrase "the basis for insight," he expresses the state of that jhāna-consciousness as being conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). Insight is threefold.

By way of the classification of individuals who possess insight (*vipassaka-puggala-bhedena*). For the insight of Great Bodhisattvas and Pacceka-Bodhisattvas has become self-originated knowledge (*sayambhu-ñāṇa*) because it is developed through knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*);
for others, however, it is born from the instruction of another because it is developed through knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

That [insight] is manifold, as stated in such passages as: "Having emerged from any one of the remaining fine-material or immaterial jhānas, with the exception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... and so forth.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, the discernment of the four elements has been elucidated through various methods in manifold ways,
by means of either the method of the formless door or any one of the specific methods for grasping the elements that have been explained therein. However, for the Great Bodhisattvas,
it possesses a manifold method due to its progression through twenty-four million billion doors, which serves as the support for omniscient knowledge.

There arises the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) which is supremely profound, exceedingly subtle and delicate, and not shared by others; it serves as the womb for the preliminary knowledge that provides the foundation for the knowledge of the Noble Path, and it reaches full maturity.
This is what is called "the Great Thunderbolt Knowledge" (mahāvajirañāṇa) in the commentaries. And according to its analysis in terms of occurrence, it is divided into twenty-four million types.
When practiced as a basis for attainment (*pādakabhāvena*), these are called the daily attainments of the Teacher, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand billion;
this mode of insight practice (*vipassanācāra*) of the Buddhas has been shown in the *Paramatthamañjūsā*, the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*, and should be taken from there by those who seek it.
Here, however, with reference to the insight practice of the disciples (*sāvaka*):
It is said, “that which establishes insight.

Granted that even the knowledges of the lower paths are indeed knowledges that exhaust the taints (*āsava*), yet their exhaustion without remainder occurs only through the knowledge of the supreme path;
therefore, it says, “for the sake of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. From the destruction of the taints means from the complete [destruction] of the taints.

Because it cuts off completely. Showing that "knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is knowledge regarding the destruction of the taints, he says, "And herein this knowledge," and then says, "in the destruction," using the locative case to indicate the locus (ādhāra) rather than the object, explaining, "because it is included therein.
"Directs" (abhinīharati) means he brings it forward toward [the goal], so that there may be the realization of the Path; hearing is directed toward that.
"He sets it forth. "This is suffering" is a demonstration that the Noble Truth of Suffering was then grasped by the bhikkhu through direct perception (*paccakkha*).
"So much is suffering" is a demonstration that it was grasped with its limits determined. "There is nothing more than this" is a demonstration that it was grasped without remainder.
Therefore he said, "The entire Truth of Suffering," and so forth. "By penetration of its specific characteristic" means...
By means of penetrating through non-delusion regarding the characteristic known as intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

"Penetration by non-delusion" refers to the way that knowledge proceeds so that, subsequently, there is no delusion in the discernment of the actual form and other attributes of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
For this very reason, it is said: "He understands it as it really is. That from which suffering arises is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*).
"Having reached that state" means having approached that *nibbāna* which serves as the cause by way of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for the Path.
It is stated thus with reference to the occurrence of the person who possesses both [the Path and its fruit]. Alternatively, "having reached" refers to the cause of attaining.
"Non-occurrence" means the sign of non-occurrence. Or, it is "non-occurrence" because those [defilements] do not occur therein; that is, *nibbāna*.
“Of that” means of the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*). “Perfectly excellent” means perfectly excellent by way of realization (*sacchikiriyā*).

“By way of defilements” means by way of the defilements known as the taints (*āsava*). Since the taints have a synonym for the truth of suffering because they are included within it, and the remaining truths have synonyms for its origin and so forth, it is therefore said “by way of a synonym (*pariyāyato*)”. [The author] shows this:
The construction is: "the truths. Here, the mention of the *āsava*s (taints) is because [the path] was undertaken for the sake of "knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
For indeed, by means of the liberation from the taints—starting with the words "the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire"—the liberation from all defilements is stated.
Since the mixed path is described here by such passages as "he understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,'" it is said to be "together with insight" (*saha vipassanāya*).

It is said: "He taught the path that has reached its culmination. By the phrase "of one who knows and sees," the clear realizations (abhisamaya) of full understanding (pariññā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) are stated.
By the phrase "is liberated," the clear realization of abandonment (pahāna) is stated; thus he says, "By this, he shows the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa).
Alternatively, "of one who knows and sees" is a description of the cause. The construction is: "Because of knowing which, the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava)."
For even among phenomena that are simultaneous, the relationship of condition and conditioned is found at the level of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

Here, by the inclusion of the "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*), the inclusion of the "taint of views" (*diṭṭhāsava*) should also be understood, since the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) is likewise subsumed under it, just as the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) is.

By the phrases beginning with "Birth is destroyed," [the fruit is indicated]. "Of that" refers to the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "The plane" (*bhūmi*) means the sphere of occurrence.
Explaining the intention behind the objection raised by the words “But what of her...,” he says, “Not yet has her...,” and so forth.
Therein, the intention is that “her past birth has not yet been exhausted through the cultivation of the Path. He states the reason for this:

“Because it was already exhausted previously. The construction is: “Her future birth has not [yet] been exhausted. And the term “not [yet] future” refers to the commonality of the state of being future.

Having taken [the term] in its general sense, he urges the objection. Therefore he said: "Because there is no effort regarding the future. However, what is intended here is the specific distinction of the future;
for in the exhaustion of that [future], effort is indeed obtainable. Therefore he said: "But as for the path's... and so forth.

"In the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences" is a mention of the three existences (bhava) for the purpose of showing, according to the method already stated, that birth has been exhausted without remainder. "That" refers to what was just mentioned.
"Birth. "He" refers to the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.
"Abiding in the holy life" (brahmacariyavāsa) here means precisely the bringing forth of the holy life of the Path; thus he says, "lived" (parivutta).
This is because when right view functions by accomplishing the tasks such as full understanding regarding the four truths, it also [accomplishes] the tasks of right intention and so forth.

The occurrence [of the path] in accordance with the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the truth of suffering is evident; likewise, its occurrence in the other truths by way of the realization of abandonment (*pahāna*), etc., is also manifest.
Therefore it was said: "By means of the four paths in the four truths, through the realizations of full understanding, abandonment, realization, and cultivation.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "the noble ordinary person (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), etc.," the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) are included.
"‘Itthattāya’ means: these modes are ‘itthaṃ’; their state is ‘itthattaṃ’; thus, ‘for that purpose’ is what is meant.

Now, those modes intended here are thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) and so forth, which constitute the function of the Noble Path. Therefore, he says: ‘for the sake of the state of the sixteenfold function.
For these [modes] become manifest and present themselves to one who reviews the Path through the power of the Path, among thorough knowledge and the rest."

And he says, "or for the destruction of the defilements," because the others have that as their purpose, [meaning] that abandonment itself is the exertion (*padhāna*). Or rather, this is stated by way of reviewing the defilements already abandoned.

Regarding the second alternative, he says, "from this state of being" (*itthabhāvato*), explaining that in the phrase "for this state of being" (*itthattāya*), the dative case is used in the sense of the ablative.
"The other" refers to the future. These, however, are the five aggregates comprised within the final existence (*carimakattabhāva*). "They remain fully understood" means:
By this, he shows their lack of a foundation. For a foundation is rooted in non-full-understanding (*apariññā*). As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical nutriment, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows," and so forth.
Therefore he says: "Like trees whose roots are cut," and so on.

“Of whom”: of the worldling (*puthujjana*). For his virtue sometimes increases and sometimes declines. However, even those in training (*sekkhā*) are indeed those who practice the fulfillment of the precepts;
as for those beyond training (*asekkha*), there is simply nothing further to be said. Therefore he says, “of one whose taints are destroyed,” and so forth.

“Attained to mastery” means having reached the state of mastery (*vasībhāva*). “Well-concentrated” means perfectly concentrated by means of the concentration of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-samādhi*).

“Endowed with steadfastness” means possessed of the steadfastness of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*). “Standing having abandoned death” is said because of the absence of renewed existence in the future.
To the question, “How is there an absence of renewed existence? he says: “Standing having abandoned all evil states.
Because every state to be known is included within the Four Noble Truths, it is said: “The Buddha” means one who has awakened to the Four Noble Truths. “The disciples of the Buddha”...
“Even disciple-buddhas pay homage [to him], how much more so other people. For other people pay homage even to disciples.

Having thus explained the meaning of the verses by way of the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), he now said “Or else,” and so forth, in order to show the meaning also by way of the disciple. The disciple Gotama, too, by virtue of his physical appearance...
