By means of this established connection, all noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) are called the "legitimate sons" (orasaputta) of the Blessed One.
"Nivāsa" means that which is inhabited; since it refers to the continuum of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) that has been inhabited, he says "the succession of inhabited aggregates.

By both readings—*ave* and *avedi*—he demonstrates precisely the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). This is because of the commonality of being a single body and having a single perception.
Since even those in the Vehapphala realm are included right here, it was stated simply as "six in the sense-sphere [realms] and nine in the Brahma-worlds.
As for the others, they were not mentioned because they do not exist in abundance; furthermore, their non-mention should be understood as being because they are outside the scope of certain [beings].
"Jātikkhayo" means that by this, birth is exhausted; thus he said, "he attained arahantship."
“Abhiññāya”: where it should have been said “abhiññāya,” the designation “abhiññā” was made by the elision of the letter *y*; thus he says “having known.
“By the completion of the task” means by the conclusion of the sixteenfold task to be performed by the four paths.
“Vosito” means finished; the sense is that it is brought to an end. “Endowed with moneyya” means endowed with bodily moneyya and the rest. “He speaks what has been spoken” means...
*Lapitalāpano*. By the phrase "having known through direct personal experience," he illuminates the fact that those three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) have been attained.
The commentary on the *Tikaṇṇa-sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the *Jāṇussoṇi-sutta*.

60. "In the ninth [chapter], 'this is the name of the gift' (deyyadhamma)" refers to the gift that must be given by one performing a sacrifice (*yāga*), because anything else is already included by the mention of "the gift" (*deyyadhamma*) in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

"Funeral meal" (*matakabhatta*) means food to be given in honor of the deceased; it is what is called "the rice-ball for the father" (*pitupiṇḍa*). "Of excellent men" (*varapurisānaṃ*) means of distinguished persons.
The meaning is "of supreme persons. "All this giving" refers to the various types of giving previously mentioned, such as the giving of sacrifice, faith, and so forth.
The commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta.
61. In the tenth [case], "repairing what is worn out" (*jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇa*) refers to the restoration or returning to its original state of dilapidated elephant stables and so forth;

one who performs this is a "restorer of what is worn out. "In an external system" (*bāhirasamaye*) means in the systems of other sectarians outside the Teacher’s dispensation. Regarding the phrase "by every fourfold set" (*sabbacatukkena*) and so on:
for each individual among all living beings distinguished as bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth, there are four...
A sacrifice that is to be performed by killing four living beings is called the "all-quadruple" (*sabbacatukka*).
The meaning in the remaining cases should also be understood according to this method. Regarding the phrase "of this or that," it is said to be the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative;
thus he says, "from this or from that. Regarding the expression "even so for him," he says, "even so for this," explaining that here *assa* is merely a particle.
"Causing to increase" means establishing. "The immersion of the holy life" refers to that which is the depth, the root, and the foundation of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Therefore, he said: "Of that which is reckoned as the path of Arahatship," and so forth.

It should be understood here that by way of the highest description, only the path of Arahatship is taken. It is the supreme foundation by virtue of being the object and decisive support (*upanissaya*).
“Appaṭṭhā” means that she has need (*attha*) of attendants (*veyyāvaccakara*) and others; the *ttha* sound is changed to *ṭṭha*. Therefore he said, “Where there are many,” and so forth.
“Yattha” means in which practice (*paṭipadā*). “Appasamārambho” means that for this [practice], the undertaking (*samārambha*) is slight.
“Pāsaṃsā” means worthy of praise. “Etaṃ yeva kathāpessāmī” means I shall have this very matter discussed with this brahmin.
“By drowsing” means by sleep. “By negligence” means by negligence characterized by the absence of mindfulness due to a lack of application toward wakefulness and so forth.
“By way of removing adversaries” means by way of removing opposing factors. For indeed, the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching are the sectarian teachers;
it is called a "miracle" (*paṭihāriya*) because of the removal (*haraṇa*) of them. For they [the sectarians] act by way of removing [others from] right view.
And because they are incapable of manifesting [right] view, they are carried away and removed by means of psychic power, direct teaching, and instruction.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "afterwards," as in such passages as, "When he had entered therein, another brahmin arrived.
Therefore, when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task...
"Patihāriya" means that which is to be removed later and set in motion; or, when one's own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the Path, the subsequent removal is "patihāriya.

Furthermore, the miracles of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) must be performed again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from defilements and has completed his task.
And when one's own defilements have been removed, [the miracles are performed] for other beings...
They are called "wonders" (*paṭihāriya*) because they remove defilements; a wonder itself is a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*).
Alternatively, each individual member of the collection consisting of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction—which together constitute a wonder—is called a miracle.
Or else, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "wonders" because they remove opposing factors; that which arises therein, or [the miracle] which has that as its cause or source, is likewise so called.
"Arrived" means a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*).

"By the sign of arrival" means by way of observing the mode of arrival. This same method applies to the others as well. "One king" refers to the lord of Dakkhiṇamadhura; "one pale king" refers to Paṇḍu.
"In this way your mind [is occupied]" means that your mind proceeds in this manner. In that manner...
He said, “or gladdened,” and so forth, to indicate its occurrence. This was stated with the intention that a general description is restricted to a specific instance.
Furthermore, the phrase “your mind is thus” merely shows the state of the mind being gladdened and so on;
it does not, however, show the cause by which it is gladdened or dejected. And here, by the mention of “gladdened,” those things associated with it are also included.

Lust and so forth, as well as faith and so forth, are indicated; by the inclusion of "dejection" (domanassa), hatred and so forth are indicated. "The second" refers to the phrase "even this, your mind.
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*), as in such passages as, "Kaccāna, 'it exists'—this is one extreme," and so on.
Therefore he said, "contemplating this and that meaning. The particle *pi* has the sense of including what has already been stated.

"Having heard them talking" means having heard the sound of them talking. "By means of that" means by means of that thought [of his]. "By one who acts as a judge" means by one who decides legal cases.
"He does not know the noble ones" means he does not know the minds of the noble ones—the minds of the paths and fruits.

For since he has not attained those, they cannot even be known by him through the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*); however, he certainly knows other types of mind. The lower [knowledge] [does not know] the higher.
It should be understood that statements such as "the mind does not know [itself]" are also spoken with reference specifically to the path and fruition consciousnesses.

For even stream-enterers and others are able to know, through the supernormal knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), the very path and fruition they have themselves attained when it has been produced by others, but not what they have not themselves attained. All noble ones likewise enter into their own fruition because it has been attained.

Showing this, he said, "And among these," and so forth. If noble ones enter the fruit they have themselves attained, one might suspect that those in higher stages also enter a lower fruit because it has been attained, just like worldly attainments;
to dispel such a doubt, he said, "One in a higher stage does not enter a lower one."
"Higher" refers to noble persons such as the once-returner and so forth. "Lower" refers to the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.
"Does not attain" means that even though it has been attained, one does not enter into meditative absorption (samāpatti) [upon rebirth]. If one asks why, the reason is stated: "For of them," etc.;
for those noble persons such as the once-returner and so forth, the lower and lower attainments of the fruits occur only within those respective lower noble persons.
"Not in the higher ones" is the meaning. By this, he shows that a lower fruition-consciousness does not arise for a higher one.
Why? Because it has subsided through the attainment of the state of another person (a different level).
By this, he shows that a higher noble one does not enter a lower fruition-attainment as if it were a mundane attainment, because it has already been attained by himself.
It should be understood that the cause [of distinction] as it exists is subject to deviation.
For in mundane jhānas, there is no such thing as attaining the state of another person due to the absence of any specific distinction;

however, here, because the cessation of kamma and defilements has not been eradicated, there is for a stream-enterer the attainment of the state of another person—such as a once-returner or higher—just as among ordinary worldlings (puthujjana).

Because each successive lower fruit-state has been turned back by the higher and higher path-states, as if overcome by adversaries, it has reached a state of non-occurrence. For this very reason it is said: "because of their subsidence.
Furthermore, the occurrence of wholesome functional activity is one thing, and the occurrence of fruition is another; and because [the fruition] follows immediately upon [the path],...
For the higher supramundane wholesome states are, from the perspective of the lower ones, as if they belong to another existence.
Indeed, it is by virtue of each respective fruit that Noble Ones obtain the names of stream-enterer and so forth.

If they were to possess other fruits as well, their designation as stream-enterers and so on would become indeterminate. Alternatively, because each fruit of a particular Noble One is similar [to the preceding], [the distinction is maintained].
It should be understood that even a mere trace of the lower fruit exists for one who possesses the higher fruit;

how, then, could there be the attainment of it? Furthermore, those of the lower stages, such as stream-enterers and others, do not attain the higher fruits, such as the fruit of once-returning, because they have not yet reached them.
For it is impossible to attain an attainment that has not been reached; therefore, all noble ones [are considered in this context].
One must reach the conclusion that they themselves attain the fruit.
"Causing to proceed" means being those who cause [the path] to proceed; the meaning is "by way of causing to proceed.

"Thus" refers to the reference to the manner in which [the teaching] has proceeded by way of injunction and by way of prohibition according to the instruction as it was taught. And that is indeed called "right thought."
It proceeds by way of showing the mode of occurrence of wrong thoughts.

In this context, the meaning is that it is specifically the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), and not the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*), for the purpose of distinguishing between its benefits and its dangers.

For the inclusion of the particle *eva* is intended to exclude its opposite. Here too, the meaning and the purpose of using the word *eva* should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

The same principle applies to the inclusion of this [term]. The mention of "lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" should be regarded as merely illustrative, because the abandonment of other types of lust, hatred, and so forth is intended, and because the abandonment of those [specific instances] serves as the means for the removal of other lusts, hatred, and the rest.
This is just as the removal of corrupted blood requires the excision of the previously corrupted flesh as a means. Thus it is said: "Only the supramundane state..."
The restriction (avadhāraṇa) should be understood as being intent upon the exclusion of blameworthy states (sāvajjadhamma) because it has the nature of a negation;
for there is no state of "immediate succession" (ānantariya) regarding other blameless states (anavajjadhamma) which constitute the means and benefits for attaining that [state].
By the phrase "resembling the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) charm," it is meant that there is a certain charm in the world known by the name "Cintāmaṇi."
There exists [a knowledge] by which one discerns the minds of others; thus it is explained. Regarding this, some say:

"The person who masters that science, having recited the mantra at a specific place and time, infers and declares the mental activity of another—whom he wishes to know—by means of perceiving particularities such as the appearance of their hands and so forth.
Others say: "By causing them to utter speech, one discerns it through the observation of the syllables therein."
"And all this" refers to everything occurring in the manner beginning with, "The venerable Gotama experiences various kinds of psychic power.
The commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Vagga is finished.
(7) 2. Mahāvagga 1.
Commentary on the Titthāyatana Sutta 62.
In the first [section] of the second [chapter], "ford" (*tittha*) refers to the sixty-two views, as well as any mental agitation regarding views apart from those.
Because of their non-existence. For here beings cross over, float about, and perform the act of emerging and submerging;
therefore it is called a "ford" (*tittha*). Indeed, for those who hold wrong views, there is no crossing in the sense of reaching the further shore;
for them, "crossing" consists merely in floating back and forth by way of repeated submerging and emerging right there. "Producers" refers to Pūraṇa Kassapa and the others.

"Titthiyā" means those born in a *tittha* (ford); or, they are called "titthikas" because they possess a *tittha*—namely, that which is designated as a "viewpoint" (*diṭṭhigata*) as previously described—and being *titthikas*, they are thus *titthiyas*.
"Manorame" means delightful, both because it is filled with sweet fruits and because it is free from fear in every direction.
"In these very three places" refers to the aforementioned *tittha*-stations.

By the phrase "to whomever it occurs in such a way that he knows it as such, to him it is spoken accordingly," this shows that it was stated thus according to the disposition (*adhyāśaya*) of the individual (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, the word *puggala* (individual) is common to all three natures;

therefore, the inclusion of the term *purisa* (man/person) serves to specify it from among those, just as in the expression "eight types of persons" (*aṭṭha purisapuggalā*). "He makes it known" means solely by way of knowing.
It makes [the result] known. It experiences, or it experiences that which has reached the characteristic of ripening (*vipāka*).
Regarding the phrase "caused by what was done previously" (*pubbekatahetu*), he says, "by the condition of karma done previously alone," because this is a term containing an internal restriction.
By this—that is, by the statement "all that is caused by what was done previously"—he refers to feeling co-arising with wholesome and unwholesome karma as "karma-feeling" (*kammavedanā*).

“Functional feeling” (*kiriyavedanā*) refers to the feeling that arises simultaneously with functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*), which is described as being neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma.

To show that they reject not only those feelings resulting from kamma or functional consciousness, but also those well-known in the Dispensation and in the world—such as diseases like wind-disorders (*vātābādha*) and so forth—he said, “Or these which...,” and so on. In this regard:
"Arising from bile" (*pittasamuṭṭhānā*) means produced through an excess of a disorder of bile. This same method applies to the following two [categories] as well.

"Arising from a combination" (*sannipātikā*) means born from the combination of the disorders of all three—bile and the others. "Arising from a change in the seasons" (*utupariṇāmaja*) means born from a transformation of the cold and other seasons, that is, from their irregular shifting.
"Arising from improper conduct" (*visamaparihāraja*) refers to [diseases] arising in the body by way of the practice of engaging in unsuitable food and so forth.

[It] arises from the avoidance of irregularities. "Produced by means" (*opakkamikā*) means produced by an external agent. "Born of the ripening of kamma" (*kammavipākajā*) means born from the aggregates that constitute the result of kamma.
A disorder of the elements arising from adverse conditions is a state of transformation;

or, the painful feeling resulting from those conditions is called an "affliction" (*ābādha*) in the sense of being an affliction, and that very same thing is a "disease" (*roga*) in the sense of causing injury. In this context, "that which has the characteristic of being curable..."
They say that such is a disease (*roga*), while the other is an affliction (*ābādha*).

For all of these, the respective imbalance of the elements (*dhātu*) is the proximate cause, and not the others. Furthermore, among those, the state of the elements being provoked is the proximate cause, and not the state of external conditions;
this is how it should be understood. They accept only the eighth type of affliction—that born of the ripening of kamma—as being "all caused by what was done in the past" (*pubbekatahetu*).
By way of a distorted grasp. Regarding the word "previously" (*pubbe*): because only past karma is grasped, they reject even that which is to be experienced upon rebirth;
thus it is said, "having warded off two. "They accept" means they allow for it.
"Based on what was done by oneself" refers to the cause of action performed with one's own hand. "Based on an order" refers to the act of commanding another.
"By reason of the performance of the rite. These are the three kinds of feeling.

"They ward off all" means they prevent all diseases, because it is impossible for those [diseases] to exist when there is a single sovereign creator of them all; this same principle applies to the others as well.
"They ward off everything" means they prohibit everything by way of negating causes and conditions.
"Having set forth the matrix (mātikā)" means having made a brief statement for the purpose of showing the lack of essence in all three Vedas.
"That" refers to that matrix. "Having analyzed and shown" means having shown it by way of division through the very process of pointing out its defects.

"For the purpose of establishing their own tenet (laddhi)" means for the purpose of making them profess their own tenet. "Transferring from one tenet to another tenet" means [transferring] from one root-tenet to another tenet.
They approach [the view] and profess it. By saying, "One experiences only what was done in the past as a cause," they treat even the experience of karma as the experience of its ripening (vipāka).

For those who hold such views have deluded minds; they confuse one type of karma with another, one ripening with another, and so forth, and are unable to make them known without confusion. To show that this applies to wholesome karma just as it does to unwholesome karma, [it is said:]...
“‘In this way, from the destruction of life’ and so forth was said. In that context, ‘in this way’ means:

just as those who destroy life are called such solely because of past causes and not due to a cause created by themselves now, so too, when one considers that abstaining from the destruction of life is likewise solely due to past causes, the doctrine of past-action (pubbekatavāda) turns out to be nothing other than a doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda).”
The desire characterized by the wish-to-act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) is not the desire characterized by craving (*taṇhā-chanda*). "Wish-to-act" means the desire to do.

It is called "personal effort" (*paccatta-purisakāra*) because there is no task to be performed by this or that specific person, since [the result] is accomplished solely through the cause of what was done in the past.

He does not obtain either of these two: namely, the performance of what is to be done, which is the fulfillment of good conduct, and the non-performance of what is not to be done, which is the abstention from misconduct.
He does not obtain either of these two. For even those who are ascetics (samaṇa) are such only because of past actions;

they are ascetics solely due to past actions, not through the present undertaking of restraint and so forth. Likewise, even those who are non-ascetics (assamaṇa) are such only because of past actions;
they are non-ascetics solely due to past actions, not by virtue of a breach of restraint.

Just as in the doctrine of past-action (pubbekata-vāda), there is an absence of individual human effort because of the impossibility of desire and exertion, so too in the doctrine of creation by a Lord (issara-nimmāna-vāda), since it is admitted that everything is created by the Lord alone, it is said: "It should be understood in the same manner as explained in the case of the doctrine of past-action.
This same method applies to the doctrine of causelessness (ahetuka-vāda) as well; thus he says: "Likewise in the case of the doctrine of causelessness."

With the words "Of these," and so forth, it is shown that because these sectarian systems (tīṭṭhāyatana) are empty and devoid of essence, there is an absence of even a trace of ultimate reality (paramattha), just as when threshing husks one obtains not even a grain of broken rice;
likewise, there is an absence of even a spark of fire from the light of a glowworm;
and just as a blind man in a caravan fails to find the path, they fail to find the right path by relying on mere sound through their wrong adherence.

Through its perversion, it is shown to be like a hare in the *Daddara Jātaka*. "The state of being essential" (*sārabhāva*) refers to the presence of essence by way of the perfection of the essence of virtue (*sīla-sāra*) and so forth.
"The state of leading out" (*niyyānikabhāva*) refers to the quality of bringing about an absolute departure from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Unrestrained" (*aniggahita*) means not to be restrained; hence he said, "impossible to restrain. "Uncorrupted" (*asaṃkiliṭṭha*) means devoid of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
Therefore he said, "free from defilement" (nikkileso), and so forth. "Without reproach" (anupavajjo) means that it cannot be criticized from the standpoint of the Dhamma.
Regarding "not censured" (appaṭikuṭṭho), this may mean either not being refuted or not being reviled; showing both of these, he said, "unopposed and uncensured.
"Of that Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma set forth by the words beginning with, "But this, monks... [and so on]. [The word] "question" (pañhaṃ)...
"Having asked" means having asked a question by way of a desire to speak. "In the proper sequence" means according to the order in which they were set forth in the matrix (mātikā).

"Elements" (dhātu): they are called elements in the sense of maintaining their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva). Furthermore, because they do not have the nature of desire—unlike the self, beauty, pleasure, permanence, primordial matter (pakati), stability, the soul (jīva), the body-group (kāya), and so forth, as imagined and conceptualized by craving and views—they are the bases for worldly designations such as the Udumbara flower, which are [merely] released from [the notions of] views and the like.
And because they are not merely the basis for speech, but are rather the ultimate reality of truth, he says "of their own nature" (*sabhāvā*);
the meaning is "having the nature of truth. For they are called "elements" (*dhātuyo*) because they bear their own nature.

"Manifesting the state of being devoid of soul and devoid of a living being" means manifesting the absence of a soul as postulated by outsiders, and manifesting the absence of a "being" as conceived by the common worldling. "In the sense of a mine" means in the sense of being a place of origin.
For even the place of origin is called a "source" (ākara) or a "sphere" (āyatana), as in the expression, "Kamboja is the sphere of horses.
"Mental explorations" (manopavicāra) means the various modes of movement of the mind having approached this or that object. To the question "By what [means] and where?", he says:
"By means of the feet of applied thought and sustained thought," and so forth. "In eighteen instances" refers to six instances conducive to joy, six instances conducive to grief, and...
"Six are bases for equanimity"—thus it is in eighteen instances.
"The element of support" (*patiṭṭhā-dhātu*) is the element whose nature is to serve as the support for the remaining three primary elements (*bhūta*) and for all derived matter (*upādārūpa*).

By this same method, the meaning of "the element of cohesion" (*ābandhana-dhātu*) and so forth should also be understood. Furthermore, [the element of extension] is established by its state of hardness, [providing] for co-nascent phenomena...
The state of being a support is the state of being a foundation. Cohesion, which is established through the state of fluidity, is binding.
Maturation, which is established through the state of heat, brings about softness and ripeness. Distension, which brings about a state of rigidity, is swelling.
Space is that which is devoid of form and bounded by form; it is said to be "the space element" because it is not touched by those things which constitute its boundaries.
“An element that is untouched. The perception-element is the apprehension of an object devoid of conceptualization.
It is appropriate to explain it in detail because detail is included within the brief;

however, it is not appropriate to explain it only briefly because there would be no exhaustive completion of the meaning to be explained. Therefore he said: “It is appropriate [to explain] by way of detail alone.”
"In both ways" means both in brief and in detail.

Although the space element (*ākāsadhātu*) is unconditioned (*anipphanna*), it is nevertheless called "derived matter" (*upādārūpa*) merely because it must be apprehended by depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*).

"Only those that are seen" refers to those things to be observed by way of their commonality as derived matter. Feeling (*vedanā*) that arises simultaneously with that [matter] is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Because conventional usage applied to a whole is also seen to apply to its parts— as in the expression, "the cloth is burnt" when only one part of the cloth is burnt—
[it is said that] contact and volition are the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*),

because they are predominant factors and because the aggregate of formations is primarily characterized by them. The immaterial aggregates are called "name" (*nāma*) because they bend toward the object.
And because its inclusion depends upon its name. The aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is "form" (*rūpa*) in the sense of being manifestly subject to transformation (*ruppana*).

"Condition" (*paccaya*) refers to a condition that serves as a support. By way of classification, there are forty-two. There are eighty-one types of consciousness when taking into account "the course of comprehension" (*sammasanacāra*).
One who proceeds by gradual stages—thus established in the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*)—[proceeds] with the three subsequent purifications.
Exerting oneself in the development of purification by way of accomplishment.
"Basis of contact" (*phassāyatana*) means the place of origin for contact. "Of gold and so forth" refers to gold, gems, diamonds, and the like.
It is called a "mine" (*ākara*) because [the substances] arise there as if they were crowded together. Just as the eye is a specific condition for resultant contact, [so too is the ear].
It is said, “two eye-consciousnesses,” and so forth, because the others are not like that. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
Among the thirty-two resultant contacts, excluding the two resultant contacts associated with the fivefold sense-consciousness, the remaining twenty-two resultant contacts are to be understood.
It is precisely what has been seen, because they possess an identical capacity for application (*yogakkhema*). “In brief, first of all... [is the phrase].
Although the discussion has begun as a brief account, it is said, "it should be understood from what was stated below...," because the detailed exposition here follows the same method.
That which serves as the basis for the arising of joy is the "basis for joy. Therefore, he said, "that which is the cause of joy."

"Upavicarati" means that it proceeds having approached. Because they are the causes for the arising of joy and so forth, and are the counterparts to joy and so forth, both by way of their intrinsic nature and by way of intention, he says, "or it may be desirable," and so on.
The fourth [object] is indeed what has been seen, because of its inseparable connection with that.
Regarding the term "Ariyasaccāni" (Noble Truths), this is an analysis using the elision of the latter member of the compound; thus he says, "those which produce the state of an Arahant," and so on.
The intention is that since this has already been elucidated in the *Visuddhimagga*, it need not be elucidated here.

"For the sake of easy comprehension" means for the purpose of easily understanding the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) as it is being taught. Therefore he said, "For one who," and so forth.
"Twelve factors" means having twelve factors by way of the factors such as ignorance (*avijjā*). "The round of conditions" means the continuity of conditions. He wishes to speak [of this].
It is because he wishes to show the truths by way of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).

By the phrase "descent into the womb" (*gabbhāvakkanti*), he shows the round of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) by way of the descent into the womb, starting with the words "there is a descent into the womb.

Therefore, it is said that here the round is shown specifically by way of the descent into the womb, beginning with the words "In the round of descent into the womb," and so forth. "In the round of descent into the womb": [End of excerpt]
In the continuity of phenomena that proceeds by way of rebirth in a mother’s womb. "Shown" means shown by way of the teaching.
It is said, "The first two modes of birth are more distinct due to their grossness than the others," in the passage beginning with "descent into the womb...
even for awakening. "Mere condition" refers to the mere state of being a common condition for the six elements, not something produced from them as separate parts.
The specific condition [is not stated] because it was spoken without distinction in the phrase, "From where, then, do these six elements [arise]?
Therefore he said, "This is what is meant," and so forth. [They do not arise] from the mother or the father because those elements are external to this being.

Regarding the term "of the womb" (*gabbhassa*): here, that which exists as the state of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) is the womb; it is the continuity of phenomena (*dhammappabandha*) in the stages beginning with the *kalala*.
However, because it is supported by that [womb], the continuum of beings is called a "womb" (*gabbha*), just as those supported by a bed are said to be "the beds are shouting.
Because it serves as its support, the mother's womb is called a "womb," as in such expressions as "the young man dwells in the womb.
Alternatively, it is a "womb" because it is like a womb; for just as a private chamber is called a "womb" because it is a place of residence for beings, so too is this.
Thus, for beings born from a womb, the mother’s womb is called a "womb" (gabbha) because it is the place of residence until birth.
However, here it should be understood as a "womb" in the sense previously stated. Therefore he said, "And what is called a womb," and so forth.

It is a "hell-womb" (nirayagabbha) because it is a hell (niraya) in the sense of being devoid of delight (nirati), and it is a womb in the sense already explained. This same method applies [to other terms].

In the remaining cases as well, this is the distinction: they are called *tiracchānā* (animals) because, unlike gods, humans, and others, they are not long upwards but are long and bent across (*tiriyaṃ añcitā*).

Those very beings, by virtue of being a constituent part (*khandhakoṭṭhāsabhāvena*) of a womb (*yoni*), and being a "womb" (*gabbha*) in the manner already described, constitute the "womb of animal birth" (*tiracchānayonigabbha*).
"Peta" means having departed from or being removed from what is excellent and pleasant; it refers to those who have attained that state.

“Realm” (*visaya*) means the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), the womb of hungry ghosts (*petayoni*). “Humans” (*manussa*) refers to those whose minds are developed through qualities such as courage due to the predominance of the mind, and who possess minds of exalted virtue.
“Devas” are so called because they play, sport, frolic, and shine with the strands of sensual pleasure and other such things.

The term “womb” (*gabbha*) is to be understood in the manner already stated. “Of various kinds” (*nānappakāra*) means that it is of diverse types according to what has been described and its subsequent subdivisions.
The human womb is intended here because it is well-known and directly perceptible. "Descent" (okkantī) is so called because, having entered the mother's womb, one has as if "risen" [into existence].
"Generation" (nibbatti) is the act of being produced; it is the manifestation and the clarification of arising.
To show that "conjunction" (sannipāta) refers to the absence of deficiency in both caste and other factors, it is said: "Here, the mother and father... and so forth.
"Here" means in this world of sentient beings. "Assembled" means gathered together, come together, and closely joined because of their state of union.

"In season" means fertile, having reached the time of menstruation; and this is said with reference to the proper time for conception, not merely the day of the onset of the local designation of "menstruation.
For it is in that place within the female body known as the "womb-cavity" (*gabbhāsaya*) that the child is conceived.
There, a large red swelling forms; though it has never been touched before, it bursts and flows out.
The site becomes pure because of the flowing blood and because of its healthiness.
When the site is pure and the parents have come together once, it remains as a field for seven days. Even after bathing, the site remains pure.
For a few days, because the embryo is still in a state of stabilization, it remains merely a field due to the presence of a small smear of blood.
At that time, even by touching the limbs through grasping the hands or pulling the hair, the child is indeed brought forth.
For even within the female continuum, all seven elements are indeed obtainable. Thus, for example, by the touching of the navel of a pregnant woman...
Through the Bodhisatta Sāma’s grasping at the navel of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, Maṇḍabya was reborn.

Because it approaches (abbati) by means of kamma leading to existence—which is named "gandha" because it indicates and illuminates through the manifestation of signs arising from the scent (gandhana)—it is called a *gandhabba*;
it is the being who is about to arise there. Thus it is present.
"He exists" means that one who stands nearby and waits, observing the union of the mother and father, is said to be "present";
however, the intended meaning here is that a single sentient being, driven by the mechanism of karma, is the one destined to be reborn in that place.
For at that time, the sentient being bound for that state is impelled toward that end by the "pushing mechanism" known as the karma conducive to rebirth there.
It is like a skin that has been brought forward.
In the formula "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," because consciousness is taken as the condition, it is stated as "the three formless aggregates.
Here, however, without taking consciousness as the condition, [it refers] only to the descent into the womb.

Because it is taken as a condition, it is said: "including the aggregate of consciousness. However, because the descent into a human womb is intended here, it is said: "at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born from a womb.
Because craving is taken as the nature of the truth of origination, it is said: "excluding craving. It is the illuminator of that very [craving].

It is that which brings about the arising of the aforementioned truth of suffering. Regarding the phrase "the cessation of suffering," since craving is also included by the mention of "suffering" here, he says:
"the cessation of both of these... [is] the cessation of suffering. For, without distinction, the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) belonging to the three planes is intended here as "suffering.
Alternatively, it is the non-arising and cessation of suffering, [which results from the cessation] of the craving that constitutes its very nature.
It is said that "without the cessation of non-arising, it does not exist," and thus: "For both of these... [there is] the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, "the cessation of non-arising" indicates Nibbāna as the cause for the cessation of non-arising.
Having stated, "It should be understood in the manner explained therein," he shows the difference in the mode of occurrence of the Pāḷi in both instances.
"But this is the distinction," he said. "Therein" means in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Here" means in this sutta. "But of ignorance alone" means: but of ignorance indeed.
Regarding the phrase "through the remainderless fading away and cessation": here, that by which one becomes utterly detached from formations (*saṅkhāra*) is "fading away" (*virāga*), namely the Path;
therefore, it is through the Path, designated as "fading away," that there is cessation without remainder—that is, cessation leaving nothing behind.
"Cutting off completely"—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
"Of the whole" means without remainder. Or, "of the entire" means of the pure, which is devoid of a self, a life-principle, and so forth as imagined by others.
The state of being exhausted is also called "cessation" (nirodha) in the sense of "ceasing" (nirujjhana). Thus, even Arahantship is "cessation."
It is called "cessation" (*nirodha*) because it arises at the end of cessation.

Nibbāna is also called "cessation" because it serves as the basis for the cessation of ignorance and the other [defilements], having been designated as "cessation" in the sense that "ignorance and the rest cease herein.
"By way of showing the mode of their exhaustion" means by way of showing the mode of ceasing through the non-arising and cessation of ignorance and the rest. This refers specifically to Nibbāna.

But the intention is not that it is [merely] arahantship. For the suppression of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) occurs precisely through the manifestation of their own individual essence (attasabhāva), by way of demonstrating a deficiency or excess relative to the delimitation of the aforementioned phenomena; thus he said, "suppressing," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Titthāyatanasutta* is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Bhayasutta 63.
"By way of being capable of protecting" means by way of being capable of guarding against arisen fear.
"Amātāputtikāni" (those that do not protect mother and son) means those things which lack the capacity to protect one another, namely mother and son; they are thus called "amātāputtikāni."
Therefore he said, “There is none here,” and so forth. Regarding the word *yaṃ*, it is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; thus he said, “at which time.

The intention is that even the mother does not obtain the opportunity to see her son, nor is she able to protect him. The same principle applies here to the phrase “even the son [does not see] his mother.
Fear is simply the terror of the mind; hence, “fear of mental terror. By this, [he excludes] shame, fear of censure, and the like.
He turns back. By the mention of the "forest" (*aṭavi*), those dwelling in the forest are meant, as in expressions such as "the whole village has arrived";
thus he said, "And here, by 'forest,' one should understand the bandits dwelling in the forest. "These" refers to the bandits dwelling in the forest.

"This was stated" means that this [phrase], "disturbance of the forest" (*aṭavisaṅkopa*), was stated. Those who possess the cycle of postures (*iriyāpathacakkasamaṅgin*)—such as standing, walking, and so forth—are those mounted upon the cycle of postures.
He said, "The term 'wheel' (cakka) applies even to the modes of deportment (iriyāpatha)," meaning that the modes of deportment themselves are called a wheel in the sense of revolving.
They "go around" (pariyāyanti), meaning they move completely toward various directions and regions. Therefore he said, "They go here and there.
Unable to go [away] due to maternal affection, one comes into their presence; this is because of the powerful nature of self-attachment (attasineha).
Even disregarding his mother, he goes thinking, "I shall protect myself alone.
Having gone and hidden in a certain place according to the method already described, he sits down in a safe spot. Regarding the phrases "on a raft," and so forth:

a *kulla* (raft) is that which carries or brings one to the further shore (*kūla*); it is bound together by making a bundle of bamboo, reeds, and other materials for the purpose of crossing. Having spread it out...
A "raft," however, refers to a vessel such as a tub or a clay pot. "Being carried away" means being led downstream by the current of the water.

It was said, "Having thus shown the dangers in a figurative sense as being 'without mother and son' with respect to the uninstructed worldling," because the three aforementioned dangers—which were originally "with mother and son"—were presented here as being "without mother and son.
The commentary on the *Bhayasutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Venāgapura Sutta* 64.
Regarding the phrase "in the country named thus" (*evaṃnāmake janapade*) in the third [sutta]: by the mention of the name, he shows that the word *Kosala* is a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*).
For instance, there were princes of the realm called the *Kosalas*, and even though they were many, the single country where they resided was also called *Kosala*.

By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*), it is called "Kosala. For etymologists (*akkharacintaka*) desire that in such instances the gender and number be as they are logically appropriate (*yutta*), according to the rule:

"In such cases, the gender and number are as they are appropriate" (*Pāṇini* 1.2.51). This is the conventional usage here, just as in other cases such as "he dwells among the Kurus" and "he dwells among the Aṅgas.
However, when the word "country" (*janapada*) is used as a qualifier for that [name], being a term denoting a genus (*jāti*), it takes the singular number, as in "among the Kosalas" (*kosalesu*).
“In the country”: *cārikā* means wandering (*caraṇa*). Alternatively, wandering is *cāra*, and that itself is *cārikā*.
Here, what is intended is travel on a journey, not merely going about in small increments; thus he said, “while traveling on a long road.
To show this by way of classification, he said, “And as for this *cārikā*,” and so forth. In that context, “even far away” means both at a distance and not too far. Suddenly...

"Gamana" means swift movement. Regarding the phrase "in [the cases of] going out to meet Mahākassapa and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the journeys undertaken for the sake of Āḷavaka and others.
For instance, when the Blessed One went out to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, he traveled three *gāvutas* of road in a single moment;
for the sake of Āḷavaka, he traveled thirty *yojanas*; likewise for Aṅgulimāla; and for Pukkusāti, he traveled forty-five *yojanas*.
For Mahākappina it was one hundred and twenty *yojanas*; for the sake of Dhaniya, seven hundred *yojanas*;
and for the novice Tissa, the forest-dweller who was the co-resident disciple of the General of the Dhamma, he traveled one hundred and eighty-three *yojanas*.
"With reference to this" means with reference to this journey made without haste.
Regarding the phrase "they perceived" (*upalabhiṃsu*), he says "through the ear-door... they knew" in order to show that the meaning here is "they perceived by way of hearing.
Since every sentence has an implicit restriction as its result, he says, "or it is a particle used merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
Furthermore, by the phrase "in the sense of restriction," he indicates that the word *kho* is employed to restrict the intended meaning.
[The commentator] shows this. Regarding the word *assosi* (he heard): when the particle *kho* is included, it becomes as if full, adorned, and embellished, and thus it is said to be "fulfilled.
By that means, the preceding and following words become well-connected; however, when it is not included, [the connection is lost]. Therefore, he says:
"By the fulfillment of the word, there is merely the smoothness of the expression (*byañjana*). The word *matta* has the sense of excluding any further qualification.
Thus, its quality of indicating a distinct meaning is shown; moreover, by the word "eva" (thus/only), its definitiveness is established through the elegance of the phrasing.
"Because evil has been stilled" means because evil has been stilled absolutely, without remainder, and along with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

For in this way, the Blessed One’s stilling of evil is distinguished from the stilling of evil by outsiders, those free from passion, and those in training or beyond training. Therefore, this name—namely, "Samaṇa"—is one acquired according to his qualities as they truly are.

He explains [the word] as "ascetic" (*samaṇa*). Since particles have multiple meanings, he says, "The particle *khalu* is used here in the sense of tradition," meaning that the sense of tradition is intended here. "Mere address" means mere words of affectionate speech;

for these are terms of endearment such as "Sir," "Friend," or "Beloved of the Gods. Regarding "by way of lineage": here, lineage (*gotta*) is so called because it protects one from going astray (*gaṃ tāyati*).
The word *gotta* (clan) is so called because it protects (*tāti*) both the speech and the intellect currently in use as "Gotama," guarding them by means of its exclusive domain.
Just as the intellect cannot function without an object that serves as its referent, so too the designation cannot exist without that which is designated;
therefore, that referent termed "clan" is said to protect and guard those two. But what is this? It is that which is not shared with other family lineages.
It should be understood that this is the common form of the ascetic (sāmañña-rūpa), which has been handed down from the first person of that clan and is shared by all members belonging to that clan.
Here, by the term "ascetic" (samaṇo), the Blessed One’s state of being highly esteemed by discerning people is shown, because it proclaims his having stilled evil.
By the term "Gotama," his birth in a noble family is illuminated among worldly people, because it reveals his descent from a distinguished and exalted khattiya lineage.
For the Sakyan royal family is the most eminent and unadulterated lineage among all kṣatriyas, beginning from the Great King Mahāsammata.
"By no loss whatsoever" means it was never overcome or eclipsed by any kind of decline, such as the loss of relatives or the loss of wealth.
Indeed, there was no such loss for that family on account of the Lord of the World.
Rather, there was only increase. Furthermore, the fact that his state of supreme prosperity in the world became even more manifest and well-known upon his Great Renunciation is evident.

The statement "he went forth from the Sakyan clan" is spoken to illustrate the Blessed One’s state of having gone forth out of faith, as it establishes that he renounced a vast circle of kinsmen and a great mass of wealth before going forth.
Regarding the phrase *itthambhūtākhyānatthe*: it means "in the sense of describing one who has become such," that is, in the sense of stating that someone has become or arisen in such a manner.
The term *upayogavacanaṃ* (accusative case) refers to the word *abbhuggato* here; the prefix *abhi-* indicates the sense of describing one who has become such.

Because of its connection with that [prefix], the expression *taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ* is in the accusative case (*upayogavacanaṃ*) in the sense of a genitive (*sāmiatthe*). Therefore, he said: "Of that venerable Gotama."
“Meaning. “Endowed with excellent qualities” means joined with excellent qualities; the intention is that he is dependent on them and has them as his object.
“Supreme”—here too the method is the same. “Fame” (*kitti*) is so called because it is to be praised;

that very thing is called “sound” (*sadda*) because it is to be heard, thus he says: “‘Fame-sound’ means fame itself. Sound proceeding by way of praise is a cry of exultation. Together with the world of devas...
"Exalted, having overspread the world" means that because it proceeds by way of qualities not shared by others,
it has risen up having overspread— that is, having overcome—
the world together with its devas. "That Blessed One" refers to him who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

The Fully Enlightened One, the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the Lord of the World—whose fame and renown are spread throughout the world with its devas due to such causes as his great fortune—is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
This term "Blessed One" is a designation for the Teacher’s name. Thus the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said: "‘Blessed One’—this is not a name [given] by a mother..."
“‘Kataṃ’ and so forth; however, ‘Bhagavā’ is the praise of his qualities.

Just as one who practices meditation on the subject of the Buddha recollects the Buddha’s qualities by joining the word *iti* to each of the nine epithets beginning with ‘Arahaṃ,’ so too does he do so by means of this brief enumeration of the Buddha’s qualities.
Thus, showing this, he said: ‘Thus indeed he is Arahant, thus indeed he is Sammasambuddha... [and so on] ...thus indeed he is Bhagavā. ‘Thus indeed this is real...’”
In this context, the word *iti*—as in such phrases as "it is thus, this is true"—has the sense of making something proximate and manifest;
the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*), and by it the multiplicity of those qualities is indicated.
Furthermore, showing that when one who is wise intends to enumerate them, they must be enumerated as having been brought directly before the mind, he said: "It means 'by this and by that reason.'"

When one praises [the Buddha] after having thus investigated him, that person develops an exceedingly great confidence in the Blessed One. "Because of being far removed" (*ārakattā*) means because of being very distant.

"Of enemies" (*arīnaṃ*) refers to the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of spokes" (*arānaṃ*) refers to the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. "Because of being struck down" (*hatattā*) means because of being destroyed. "Of requisites, etc.
(*paccayādīnaṃ*) refers both to the requisites such as robes and to specific forms of worship. "From there" (*tato*) means from the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*).
And just as [the details] are to be understood from the *Visuddhimagga*, so too their full exposition should be taken from its commentary (*Taṃsaṃvaṇṇanā*).
This phrase "this world" was not spoken merely with reference to what is before the eyes of the multitude;
rather, it was said in order to show that it includes everything without exception. Therefore, he said: "He now points out what is to be stated."

"Pajāta-ttā" means because of being produced by one's own respective kamma and defilements. The inclusion of the "five classes of sense-sphere devas" is by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*), since the others have been included by another term.
In the compound "sadevaka," the analysis is by way of its parts, while the meaning of the whole compound is the collective.

The inclusion of the "sixth class of sense-sphere devas" is by way of proximity (*paccāsattinaya*); for he was born there and resides there. By the expression "together with Brahmā" (*sabrahmakavacanena*)...
The inclusion of the Brahmās beginning with those of the Brahmakāyika realm follows this same principle.

The mention of "hostile recluses and brahmins" is merely illustrative, because even non-hostile recluses and brahmins—those who have stilled [the passions] and removed evil—are included under the term "recluses and brahmins.
Granted, by virtue of the specific qualifiers such as "together with the devas," it is understood that the word *loka* (world) refers to the domain of sentient beings.

Because this compound is found even in cases where there is no equality of connection—as in “having hair” (*salomako*) and “having wings” (*sapakkhako*)—he stated, “by the word *pajā* (progeny), the world of beings is grasped,” in order to show that [the rule] is not universally applicable.
As for the term *deva*, it receives this etymological derivation: immaterial beings, dwelling in their own imperturbable state (*āneñjavihāra*), shine (*dibbanti*), and thus they are called *devas*.

He said: "By the inclusion of 'together with the devas,' the world of the formless realm (ārūpāvacara-loka) is included. Therefore he said: "into the companionship of the devas who have attained the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana).
By the inclusion of "together with Māra," the world of the six classes of sense-sphere devas (kāmāvacara-deva) is included, because that [world] exists specifically under the sway of Māra.
By the inclusion of "together with Brahmā," the world of the form-realm Brahmas (rūpī-brahmaloka) is included, [but not] the formless-realm Brahmas (arūpī-brahmaloka).
Because they have already been included. "By way of the four assemblies" means by way of the four assemblies consisting of kṣatriyas and so forth.

However, the other four assemblies are indeed included by the mention of "together with Māra and Brahmā," etc. The remaining world of beings consists of various classes such as nāgas, garuḍas, and so on.
"In three ways" means by the three modes consisting of being accompanied by devas, Māras, and Brahmas. "In three locations" refers to [the phrases] beginning with "together with devas."
"In three places. "In that and that manner" means by way of those various modes such as being "together with devas" and so forth.
The ancient masters said, "The triple world itself is completely exhausted"—this is how the construction should be understood.
Regarding "by direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*): this is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *y*; its meaning here is "having directly known," as he says: "by direct knowledge."

"Having known by means of superior knowledge. The "rejection of inference and so forth" refers to the rejection of inference (*anumāna*), logical presumption (*arthāpatti*), and the like, because [for the Buddha] there is only a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding all things due to the unimpeded range of their knowledge in every respect.
"Supreme bliss of seclusion" is the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). Sometimes the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is even interspersed with that [bliss].

The inclusion of the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even having abandoned" (*hitvāpi*) is intended to convey this. For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, at whatever moment the assembly utters a cry of approval or reflects upon the Dhamma as it has been heard, he delimits that moment by means of a preceding interval and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*);
and having emerged from that attainment according to the previously established limit, [he continues his teaching].
He teaches the Dhamma starting from the very place where he stands. "Whether teaching little or much" means:

either teaching little by way of one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), or teaching much by way of one who gains knowledge through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) or one who is guided by instruction (*neyya*).
Since the excellence and the liberating quality of the Dhamma consist entirely in its state of being blameless, he says, "having made it indeed blameless."
"Teaching" (desanā) refers to the act of instructing and awakening [the listener] through methods such as commands directed toward those who are nearby;
this should be understood by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma). Thus he said: "First, by way of teaching, even a four-line verse... and so forth.

Since the introduction (nidāna) and the conclusion (nigama) also follow the Teacher’s own teaching, they are included therein; thus he said: "The introduction is the beginning, and 'This was said' is the end."

The "teaching" (sāsana) is the instruction given according to the nature of the person to be instructed—such as their specific offense—and the disciplining (vinayana) thereof by means of *tadaṅgavinaya* and other methods;
this should be understood as consisting of the Dhamma of practice. Thus he said, "Virtue, concentration, and insight," and so forth.
Regarding "of the wholesome" (*kusalānaṃ*), this refers to the primacy of faultless states—namely virtue, serenity, insight, and right view—because they are rooted therein.

Regarding the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhammā*): just as the Noble Path is called the "Middle Way" because it is free from the two extremes, so too the state of being intermediate among those things produced by means of right practice is called "the middle. Thus it is said: "There is, monks... [etc.]...
that which is called the Middle. The "fruit" (*phala*) is called the "conclusion" (*pariyosāna*) in the sense of having a residue remaining (*saupādisesa*). Nibbāna is the conclusion.

The name [is given] by way of the state of having no residue remaining (*anupādisesa*). Now, in order to show through scripture that both of these constitute the conclusion of the Teaching (*sāsana*), the passage beginning with "Therefore, then, you...
was spoken. Because of the statement "with its meaning and its phrasing" (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*), the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching of the Dhamma are intended;
thus he said: "Here... is intended. In each respective meaning, there is a sequence of words that marks the limit of the discourse.
The Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) is established by way of verses and by way of discourses; that is what is called "teaching" here.
Furthermore, its specific meaning consists of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; thus he said: "For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma... he shows [this].
In that context, by the mention of "virtue," virtue along with its requisites is included; likewise, by the mention of the "path."
The path together with its requisites stands having exhausted the meaning of the scriptures in its entirety by means of both [the beginning and the end].

"By that" refers to the demonstration of virtue and so forth. For here, it is the state of being "good in the beginning" and so on, in terms of the purpose (*atthavasena*), that is intended for the teaching.
"The speaker’s disposition" (*kathikasaṇṭhiti*) is the speaker’s configuration, his stable establishment through the act of speaking.
He does not teach with a meaningful purpose, because that teaching lacks the quality of leading to liberation.
"Connected with a single consonant, etc. means it is connected with consonants of only one kind or two kinds among the various types such as soft (*sithila*), etc., like the Tamil language.
Or, because they must be pronounced without touching the lips due to the openness of the vocal organs, all the consonants are labial, like the Kirāta language.
Or, because it is suitable for the relinquishing of everything, it is like the Yavana language, which has all its consonants elided (*vissajjita*);
or, because it possesses all [consonantal] traces (*anusāra*), it is like the Mleccha languages such as Pārasika, which have all their consonants suppressed (*niggahita*).
Since all of these function only by means of a portion of their phonemes (*byañjana*) and are thus considered to have incomplete phonemes, they are called "without phonemes" (*abyañjanā*).

A syllable to be pronounced with the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of articulation (*karaṇa*) made relaxed—such as the first and third consonants of the five groups (*vagga*), and so forth—is "relaxed" (*sithila*).
A syllable to be pronounced with those same points and modes made non-relaxed—such as the second and fourth consonants of the groups, and so forth—is "pressed" (*dhanita*).
That which has the duration of two measures (*matta*) is "long" (*dīgha*). That which has the duration of one measure is "short" (*rassa*). That very [short vowel] is also "light" (*lahuka*).
That which follows a conjunct consonant is long; that which is heavy is also long. The *niggahita* (the nasal stop) should be pronounced after suppressing the place and organ of articulation.
That which is joined with what follows is "connected" (*sambandha*). That which is not so connected is "determined" (*vavatthita*).
That which is pronounced with the place and organ of articulation relaxed is "released" (*vimutta*). Thus, there is a tenfold classification according to the cognition of phonemes.
Thus, there is a tenfold classification of the consciousness that produces syllables according to the perception of phonemes (*byañjana*) based on factors such as laxity.
For all syllables are mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), and they are called "phonemes" (*byañjana*) because they express the intended meaning.

"Without smearing" (*amakkhetvā*) means without defiling, without destroying, or without letting [the meaning] go; this is the sense. [The Blessed One spoke thus] in order to make known this matter...
Even when he teaches a single verse or a single sentence, he teaches that meaning through that very teaching with complete words and phonemes;
thus it is said: “Having made the phonemes complete, he teaches the Dhamma. Here, the word *kevala* signifies "without remainder," not "unmixed" or similar meanings;
hence it is called a synonym for "entirety. *Paripuṇṇa* means completely full in every respect. That...
However, because there is nothing lacking or anything superfluous, it is called "a statement that is neither deficient nor excessive" (*anūnādhikavacana*).

In this regard, its non-deficiency should be understood from the fact that it establishes the purpose for which it was taught; its non-excessiveness, however, is due to the fact that it does not establish what is contrary to that purpose.
"Entire" means possessing all parts. "Precisely complete" means completely complete in every respect. Therefore he said: "Even a partial teaching..."
“There is nothing incomplete. What is called “impure teaching” arises from the defilement of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa*). Worldly bait refers to the requisites such as robes and so forth;
one who is indifferent to worldly bait is so because of having a mind unattached to them. “By extending welfare” means by bringing about welfare.

“One whose heart is softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness” means one whose heart is softened through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) or compassion (*karuṇā*). “By that which is established in the nature of rescuing...”
The meaning is: "with a mind established in the mode of uplifting [beings] from all defilements and from the suffering of the round of existence, with a compassionate intention.
Therefore—because the entire teaching comprised of the three trainings is intended here by the term "brahmacariya"—therefore.
Demonstrating the meaning by connecting all the words in grammatical apposition with this term "brahmacariya":
"He teaches the Dhamma... reveals it"—thus the meaning should be understood here.
"Sundara" means auspicious (*bhaddaka*). And its auspiciousness is to be understood by way of bringing welfare and happiness to the one who sees it;

hence he said, "bringing welfare, bringing happiness. In that context, "bringing welfare" means bringing the welfare associated with the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
"Sukhāvahanti" means bringing about the three kinds of happiness as previously described. "Tathānurūpānan" means of those who are suitable for such [happiness].

However, showing that the Blessed One, by virtue of whatever qualities he is endowed with, is in every way absolutely inspiring to the world of the fourfold measure because they are his true nature, he says "yathārūpo" and so forth. Therein, "yathābhūta... [and so on].
By the word "arahant," it is shown that even those beings who are small in terms of Dhamma or small in terms of material goods can inspire confidence in the Blessed One;
by the other [terms], the same is shown for others. Regarding the statement "even mere sight is beneficial," the story of Kosiya should be told here.
"Belonging to both sides" means belonging to both factions by way of wrong view and right view. "Kerāṭika" means crafty.
Because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, the combination of particles *yāvañcidaṃ* indicates an exceeding measure or limit;
thus he says, "This is a statement regarding an exceeding measure and limit.
"Exceedingly clear" (*adhimatta-vippasannāni*) means clear by way of an excessive measure. And "clear" (*vippasannāni*) means clear beyond their natural state (*pakati-ākāra*). Is it not so?
And since the eye and the other sense-faculties are cognizable by the mind, how can their clarity be known by that [mind]?
To this he says: "For his... and so forth. "His" refers to the brahmin. "Their" refers to the five sense-faculties, beginning with the eye.
Even so, since the locus established by the mind-faculty has not been seen, how can the clarity of the mind-faculty be known?
"It is known by that," he says, beginning with "But because... This is the wisdom of method (*naya*) belonging to that brahmin.

It occurs only when the mind is clarified, because the clarity of the location where the eye and other faculties are established arises precisely from the excellence of the form produced by a clear mind.
He says, “of a deep red color,” because the gold of Jambūnada is indeed of a red hue.
“A bowl of Jambūnada gold” means a lump of Jambūnada gold.

By this, he shows that what is called a *nekha* is an unworked ornament made from Jambūnada gold weighing five *nekkhas*. Alternatively, a *nekha* is an ornament made from more than five measures of gold.
"Katabhaṇḍa" is what was said; for that is capable of withstanding rubbing and immersion. "Suvaṇṇa" is a designation for five *dharaṇas*;
therefore, what is intended here by "nekkha" is an ornament adorned with twenty-five *dharaṇas* of gold.
"Jambonada" is that which is produced in the river flowing from the branch of the Great Rose-apple tree (*jambu*). It is said that this jewel is red.
When the juice of a great jambu fruit has entered the earth, golden sprouts arise;
thus, the meaning is also "ornaments made from that gold. *Suparikammakataṃ* means well-prepared through processing. *Sampahaṭṭhaṃ* means properly struck;
it refers to being well-processed by means of hammering and so forth. Therefore he said: "By a goldsmith... [etc. ...the meaning is 'well-polished.'"
“Fierce forms” means these fierce forms that have been brought here. “A couch crowded with improper forms, a divan”—this is from the *Sārasamāsa*.

“Variegated with jewels” means variegated with jewels by way of wall-paintings and so forth. “Of the three types of cotton” refers to the cotton of trees, the cotton of creepers, and the cotton of *poṭaka* plants.
“Some say it is *uddalomi*”—this is the view of the masters of the *Sārasamāsa* and those of the Northern Monastery (*Uttaravihāra*). Likewise...
*Ekantalomiyaṃ*: made of silk and *kaṭṭissa* cloth; that is, made of silk and fine cotton. *Ajinacammehi*: with the skins of antelope deer.
It is said that those skins are very fine; therefore, they are sewn after being made into double or triple layers. Hence it is said: "an antelope-skin rug," and so forth.

“Obtaining at will” means obtaining according to one’s desire; hence he says, “obtaining whatever is desired. “Obtaining abundantly” means obtaining what is sublime (*uḷāra*). For “meager” (*kasira*) is said to mean limited; by its opposite, “not meager” (*akasira*) means sublime. Hence he says, “obtaining greatly,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “and having obtained, they are not allowable”:
since it is prohibited in general terms, someone might suspect that they are not allowable in every respect;
to dispel that doubt, he says, “some things are allowable,” and so forth. In this context, “pure silk cloth” (*suddhakoseyya*) refers to that which is not sewn with gems.
And here, because it is stated in the Vinaya that "pure silk (suddhakoseyya) is permitted," only this much is mentioned here as well. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"Except for the mattress (tūlikā), all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka* and others, even if sewn with jewels, are not permitted.
In that context, by the phrase "except for the mattress," it is indicated that even a mattress that is devoid of jewel-sewing [is not permitted].
He indicates that it is not permissible. By the word "from the statement," he shows that this is recorded in the Vinaya.

By the phrase "by a single method," he speaks with reference to the very method already described. If this is so, why did the Blessed One issue a general prohibition stating, "And once obtained, they are not allowable"? To this he replies: "But because they are unallowable," and so forth.
Regarding the term *pallaṅka*, here the prefix *pari-* functions in the sense of "all around" (*samantato*);
therefore, it is called *pallaṅka* because one sits having placed both thighs evenly together and joined the two feet to each other—hence the description "a seat with the thighs bound all around.
It is a sitting posture by way of binding the thighs. And as for the phrase "having folded the *pallaṅka*," it is as follows:
"Sitting cross-legged" means that both feet are placed with the legs bent; the sense is that one has positioned them in such a way.
He says "having bound them" because he makes those two feet connected in that manner.
"Holding the body erect" means having placed the upper part of the body straight, aligning the tips of the eighteen vertebrae tip-to-tip.
For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend.
Consequently, those pains that would otherwise arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise.
When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not slip away, and it attains growth and expansion. Therefore he said, "The eighteen back-vertebrae," and so forth.
“Having set the body erect” means having set the upper part of the body straight; this is the reading itself.
For the non-erect posture of the lower part of the body is already implied by the mention of “sitting. In the phrase “the body erect,” the word *kāya* refers specifically to the upper body.
Regarding the term *parimukha*, the prefix *pari* has the same meaning as the prefix *abhi*; thus he says, “facing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).”
The meaning is: having turned away from external, manifold objects and having placed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) foremost.

Here, just as a dwelling suitable for meditation was shown by the words "I enter the edge of the forest," etc., so too by the word "I sit" a posture that belongs to neither the side of lethargy nor agitation is shown;
and by the phrase "having folded the legs crosswise," [the sitting posture is further specified].
The firmness of the posture is indicated by the phrase "having established mindfulness directed to the front," which is the means for grasping the object.

"Having grasped the outlet" means having made mindfulness such that it is entirely free from confusion and has abandoned all confusion; the meaning is: having established mindfulness with supreme skillfulness (*satinepakka*).
*Parī* has the sense of grasping, as in the word *pariṇāyikā* (guide) and others. *Mukha* has the sense of an outlet.
As in the case of [the terms] “emptiness-liberation” (*suññatavimokkha*) and so forth, the meaning of “going out” (*niyyāna*) is the sense of emerging from what is opposed [to it].

Since the four fine-material-sphere jhānas are called “divine abodes” (*dibbavihāra*) because they bring about a divine state, even the walking meditation performed in their vicinity is called “divine” by way of metaphorical extension; thus he said, “For the four fine-material jhānas,” and so on. And while walking after having attained [them]...
And this [practice] is stated with reference to walking meditation performed while repeatedly entering meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and emerging from them again and again.

For it is not possible to walk while remaining in an attainment without having emerged from it. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "walking for one who walks after emerging from attainment," this refers to the intervals between emerging from attainment and [resuming] walking.
This is stated by way of one who walks while having entered [meditative absorption]. "In two abidings" refers to the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and the noble abidings (*ariyavihāra*).

The divine abidings are so called because they are abidings that have become divine—that is, supreme—due to their proceeding by way of bringing about benefit through loving-kindness-jhāna and the rest.
However, the noble abidings are so called because they are the abidings of the Noble Ones (*ariya*), being not shared with others; these are the four attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
But here, only the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) is mentioned.
The attainment of fruition is spoken of in reference to reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), because reviewing is possible for one who has emerged after entering that attainment.
"Walking and so forth" refers to walking, standing, sitting, and so on, both for one who has entered the attainment of fruition and for one who has emerged from it.
The intention is that the noble walking meditation and so forth occur for one who is not reflecting.
The commentary on the *Venāgapura Sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Sarabha Sutta*.
65. In the fourth [explanation]: it is called *Gijjhakūṭa* because there are vultures (*gijjhā*) on this peak (*kūṭa*).

It belongs to him (or it), thus it is *Gijjhakūṭa*. Alternatively, it is called *gijjha* because it is like a vulture; it is a peak (*kūṭa*). It belongs to him (or it), thus it is *Gijjhakūṭa*, the mountain. On that *Gijjhakūṭa*. Therefore he said: "Or vultures," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "not long departed" (*acirapakkanto*): here, what is intended is not departure to another place, but rather—
Showing that this refers to going forth in the Dispensation (*sāsana*), he said, "having gone forth in this Dispensation," and for that very reason it was stated, "of this Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Gain" (*lābha*) means that which is obtained; it is a designation for the four requisites.
"Honor" (*sakkāra*) means that which should be performed or given with respect. For it is the requisites themselves—whether excellent or inferior, beautiful or ugly—that are prepared and offered.
"Offerings" (*sakkāra*) is what is meant; or rather, "offering" (*sakkāra*) means a beautiful act, or the performance of respect by others toward oneself, or worship with flowers and so forth.
"Gain and offerings" (*lābhasakkāra*) refers to gain and offerings; those who have lost or abandoned these are "those whose gain and offerings are lost" (*naṭṭhalābhasakkāra*).
"Great gain and offerings arose" means that at that time, it is said, great gain and offerings arose for the Blessed One, as was the case [with other Buddhas].
This was for one who had fulfilled the accumulation of the perfection of giving over four incalculable eons. Indeed, throughout all directions, the great twin-clouds arose like a mighty flood;
as if all the perfections had gathered together, thinking, "We shall yield our fruit within a single existence," they produced a great flood of gain and honor.
From every side, [beings] came with food, drink, vehicles, clothing, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands.
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others came and sought out the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, the Lion among Men?
Even after bringing offerings in hundreds of carts, they were unable to gain entry;
they remained standing for a distance of a league all around, cart-hitching against cart-hitch, and followed after him.
And it was like that for the brahmin of Andhakavinda. As it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. And this has been said:

"Now at that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was also honored..."
"...[and] requisites.
Likewise:

"Cunda, as far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world at present, I do not see any other single Saṅgha that has attained such excellence in gain and excellence in fame as this Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Cunda."
