The gain and honor that arose for both the Blessed One and the Saṅgha became immeasurable when combined, like the waters of two great rivers; moreover, whatever gain and honor arose for the Blessed One and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha also accrued to the Dhamma.
For honor paid to those who uphold the Dhamma is indeed honor paid to the Dhamma itself.
Therefore it was said: “Great gain and honor arose for the Three Jewels.
To illustrate the meaning already stated by means of the canonical text (pāḷi), he said “As it has been said,” and so forth.
In that context, “honored” (sakkata) means one who has received honor. For he to whom one respectfully brings the four requisites—well-prepared and most excellent—is “honored.”

"Respected" (*garukato*) means that because he had reached the pinnacle of the supreme qualities that are the causes for being held in esteem, he was respected by all gods and humans with a reverence unique to him alone, like a stone parasol.
For he is "respected" in whom they offer requisites while establishing a sense of esteem. "Honored" (*mānito*) means honored through right practice, cherished and beloved in their minds. By that...
For this is pleasing to the wise. "Honored" (*pūjita*) means honored by both honor such as respect and by the offering of the four requisites;
for he to whom all these honors are performed is "honored. "Venerated" (*apacita*) means venerated by acting with humility.
Indeed, upon seeing the Teacher, people descend from the backs of elephants and the like, give way on the path, and [remove] their upper garments from their shoulders.
They take [him] away; they rise from their seats and pay homage—thus he is said to be honored by them.
"Having spread disrepute" means having spread it here and there by way of proclaiming it. "The artifice of enticement" (āvaṭṭanimāya) refers to the artifice of seizing after having enticed.
It is called "enticement" because by means of it one turns [someone] back from their previous disposition and brings them under one's own control.
*Āvaṭṭanī* means *māyā* (deception); the meaning is: having employed that deceptive deception and having muttered [the incantation].
"From the end" means starting from the final limit. Because speaking in dispraise of the Three Jewels with a stiff body and harsh speech brings about harm, it is said to be like pouring poison;
thus he says, "having poured poison. *Aññāto* means *āñāto*. Therefore he says, "known," and so forth.
*Kāyaṅga* means the body itself as a limb, or a limb of the body, such as the head and so forth.

*Vācaṅga* means a component of speech, such as the words "Be it so" or "Excellent. *Ekakena* means alone, without a companion. *Imassa panatthassa* refers to the meaning stated by the passage beginning with "when practicing the conduct.
*Yato yato garu dhuraṃ* means in whichever place the burden (*dhura*) is heavy or weighty; [whereas] other oxen...
They were unable to lift it up. Regarding the phrase *gambhīravattanī*: it is called *vattanī* because they turn (*vattanti*) upon it;
this is a name for a bad path. The meaning is that at that place, due to the great extent of mud and water, or because of the unevenly cut banks, the path becomes deep.
Then, as for the expression *tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjenti*: *assu* is merely a particle; [the sense is] "then Kaṇha..."
The meaning is "they yoke. When the burden is heavy and the path is deep, it is said that they remove the other oxen and yoke Kāḷa alone.
In the phrase "he indeed carries that burden," *assa* is merely a particle;
the meaning is "he carries that burden."
“House-fee” (*gehavetana*) means that which is to be given because of his being supported in the house.
“Kāḷaka by name”—it is said he was the color of collyrium; therefore they gave him the name “Kāḷaka. “Having approached Kāḷaka, he said”—it is said that one day Kāḷaka thought:
“My mother is in a poor state; having placed me in the position of a son, she supports me with great hardship. What if I were now...”
“By working for wages, he might free me from this state of poverty.
From that time on, he wandered about seeking employment. Then, on that day, he was grazing near there together with the village cattle.
The merchant’s son was also looking for a way to get the carts unstuck, thinking, “Is there perhaps someone among these cattle who is capable of pulling the carts out?”
Thinking, “He is a noble bull,” and seeing the Bodhisatta, he realized, “This noble bull will be able to pull my carts out. Therefore, having approached him, he spoke thus.

As for the passage beginning with “He went to the house of others…” and ending with “…he went home,” it is said that at that time village boys would come to his presence, asking, “What is this on Kāḷaka’s neck?”
Thus, having pursued him and driven him away from afar, he went into the presence of his mother; it was with reference to this that it was said.
"In the evening time" (*sāyanhasamayaṃ*) means at the time of evening. This accusative case is used in the sense of the locative; for here, absolute connection [of time] is not possible.
Regarding the phrase "having emerged from seclusion" (*paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito*), [it refers to the Blessed One] together with those various beings such as co-residents, pupils, laymen, and laywomen.
Having turned away and withdrawn from both [sensual pleasures] and mental formations such as visible objects,
his hiding away and seclusion— due to being secluded from body and mind— is "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*), namely bodily seclusion and mental seclusion.

One who has emerged from that twofold seclusion, having departed from the attainment of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and from association with fellow celibates, is said to have "emerged from seclusion."

This is the name. However, because he emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), which is the supreme among the various states of seclusion (*paṭisallāna*), it is therefore said, "from the attainment of fruition.
"We shall become bodily witnesses" means that we shall become witnesses by means of our mental bodies through the act of receiving the teaching.
But why was it said, "he sat down on the prepared seat"? [It was said] because of the heretics (*titthiya*).
Since they are indeed adversaries of the Blessed One, why would they prepare a seat for him? To this he says, "The Tathāgata, indeed," and so forth.
"Contentious talk" means talk that leads to conflict and is provocative. "You should entreat" means you should make a verbal request.
"You should long for" means you should wish for it in your mind. "You should yearn for" is a synonym for the same. "Depriving of splendor..."
“Has fallen into” means he has fallen into a state of lacking luster due to the loss of his radiance; the sense is that he has become lusterless.
For that very reason, even monks and others are unable to look him directly in the face, so he is “with shoulders drooping,” meaning with shoulders slumped. Thus it says, “with neck bent.
“In regard to the teachings shown” means in regard to the teachings already spoken. For there is only the mere mention of them for such a person, but not the actual seeing [of their truth].

Because of the non-existence of those phenomena. Or, in the case of the Blessed One himself, regarding those phenomena shown by way of another’s statement, such as “these phenomena have not been fully awakened to.
“He will evade” means he will act or proceed for the sake of concealment;
or rather, the word *carati* has the sense of concealing because verbal roots have multiple meanings—thus he says, “he will conceal. Or, “one thing by another.”
However, he says, "or by another statement," etc., to show the manner of concealment.

In that context, "another statement" means that whatever statement was spoken by the Blessed One while interrogating another person to reveal their fault, [the offender] conceals it with a different statement.
This refers to the words spoken by the accuser: "You have committed an offense."

Just as one might introduce another unrelated topic by saying, "Who has fallen into [an offense]? What has he fallen into? In what has he fallen? Who are you speaking of? What are you saying? and so forth;
so too, when asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense?", he replies, "I have gone to Pāṭaliputta.
When told again, "We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta; we are asking about the offense," [he remains evasive].
“Then I went to Rājagaha. Whether you go to Rājagaha or to the house of a brahmin, you have fallen into an offense.

By bringing up some other incidental talk instead of the words spoken by the interrogator—speaking as if saying, “I obtained pork there,” and so forth—he will deflect [the question] and lead it into confusion; for they are not satisfied with that.
“Without joy and without gladness” (*atuṭṭhā asomanassikā*) means absence of favorable conditions; this is a designation for dejection (*domanassa*).
“Not achieving what is beneficial for oneself or for others” (*anabhiraddhi*) is likewise dejection. For this very reason it is said:

“Dejection is stated by way of the absence of favorable conditions. Regarding the phrase, “For whatever purpose the Dhamma has been taught to you,” here the word *dhamma* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
He said: "For the sake of whichever path or fruit. For the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths is taught for the purpose of attaining the paths and fruits.
"Does not go forth" means does not set in motion. "That" refers to that Dhamma.
Now, in the passage "But for what purpose, indeed, was the Dhamma taught by you," the word *dhamma* indicates the Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-dhamma*), and not—
Intending to show the various interpretations of the meaning according to the sense of "the Dhamma of the Four Truths," he says, "Alternatively," and so forth.
By "five things," he refers to the grasping, hearing, retaining, mastering, and wise attention directed toward the aggregates and so on, which constitute the practice of profound knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "for the maker [of the effort] for the complete destruction of suffering," the word "rightly" (sammā) should be construed with both parts.
“For one who acts rightly, there is the right destruction of suffering. For it is only for one who practices the Dhamma rightly that the right destruction of suffering occurs.
However, as for the one who acts rightly in the manner described, his deliverance is, in actual fact, the deliverance of the Dhamma itself;
therefore, by way of its negation, he said: “That Dhamma... does not lead out, does not go forth.”

If the roar of the wild lion is called the "best roar" because it is superior to the roars of all other animals, certain humans, and non-humans, how much more so must the roar of the Tathāgata-lion be? Thus he said: "The 'lion's roar' means the best roar.

Or, if the status of the wild lion's roar as the "best roar" is desired on account of its fearlessness and lack of adversaries, this same meaning applies even more so to the roar of the Tathāgata-lion.
It is "excellent," he said, using the terms "the roar of fearlessness" and "the unopposed roar.
For this roar is called the "best roar" and the "supreme roar" because it possesses the reality of the meaning expressed by such statements as, "This is impossible, there is no occasion for this.
Indeed, the meaning of what has come to be is the supreme meaning. Furthermore, for the Blessed One who speaks this meaning, there is no fear or apprehension from any other source.
"It does not exist" is called the fearless roar. For one who speaks what is unreal, there might be fear or apprehension from some quarter;
however, since no one is able to rise up and oppose the Blessed One when he speaks thus, this roar is called the roar without a counter-roar.
*Sannitodakaṃ* means piercing or stabbing by way of suppressing from all sides; or, that by which they properly thrust or press down is *sannitodakaṃ*.
Regarding the word *vācāya*, it is used in the instrumental case as a nominative. Therefore he said: "by the goad of speech.
*Sañjambharimakaṃsu* means they made it thoroughly gathered together; all the wanderers [did so] by means of verbal goads.
The meaning is "they tore apart. Therefore he said: "Sambharitaṃ... pe... vijjhiṃsu. "Siṅgālakaṃ yeva" means "just like a jackal";
there is also a reading "segālakaṃ yeva. "Tasseva" means "of that very [sound], namely the howl of a jackal.
Alternatively, "bheraṇḍakaṃ yeva" means "just like the bird Bheraṇḍa. The Bheraṇḍa is a certain two-faced bird; it is said that its—
The sound was exceedingly distorted and unpleasant. Therefore he said: "Furthermore, it cries out with a broken voice, an unpleasant sound.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Sarabha Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Kesamuttisutta 66.

Regarding the fifth [sutta], he says "residents of the town of Kesamutta" because those for whom Kesamutta is their dwelling are "Kesamuttis. "Eight kinds of drinks" refers to the eight types of drinks beginning with mango juice (*ambapāna*).
However, in passages such as "Do not [rely] on oral tradition," one [kind of drink] has been so called from childhood onwards; thus there is this oral tradition, and it has been so for a long time.
"How could this, which is obtained through tradition (*anussuti*), be otherwise? Therefore, one accepts it as 'this is real' based on oral report (*anussava*).
Rejecting such acceptance, he said, "Not by oral report. *Anussava* means hearing repeatedly (*anu-anu-savana*). Another [explanation] is:

"This has been brought down to us through the succession of instructions from our elders, such as our fathers and grandfathers"—thus [he rejects] such talk of what has been handed down through tradition.
One might grasp [a teaching], thinking, "It must not be otherwise; therefore, this is the truth," and he says, "Do not [accept it] on tradition" (*mā paramparāya*), in order to reject that.
One might grasp [a teaching] as soon as someone says something to anyone, thinking, "This is indeed so," and he says, "Do not [accept it] on hearsay" (*mā itikirāya*), in order to prevent that.
*Piṭakasampadāna* means that the basket (*piṭaka*)—the text—is contained within it. Of the text...
One who learns. Because of that state of learning the Piṭakas, a certain person, having made such a text proficient, compares it with that [teaching] and finds it to be consistent;
therefore, he takes it as "this is real. It is with reference to this that the prohibition "not by mere conformity to the Piṭakas" is stated;
the meaning is: "Do not accept it merely because of the excellence of the text you have learned yourself. "Sametaṃ" means "consistent" (saṃgataṃ).
Someone, while reflecting on something, might grasp it as "this is real" solely on the basis of their own conjecture, thinking, "It must be so";
it is with reference to such a person that it is said, "Do not because of reasoning.
Another might grasp it as "this is real" solely through inference based on a methodological approach; rejecting that, it is said, "Do not because of a methodological approach."
He said: For someone who imagines, "This might be so," a certain reason presents itself;
he grasps it in the manner of his own imagination, thinking, "It exists. To refute that, [the Blessed One] said, "Do not by means of a conceptual investigation of modes (*ākāraparivitakkena*).
This refers to another person who, while reflecting, adheres to some object as imagined, thinking, "This is exactly so and not otherwise."

A single view arises. That which is acceptable to someone who reflects upon its cause and contemplates it as if it were directly perceived—such a person grasps it through the acceptance resulting from reflection on that view.
It is with reference to this that he said: "Do not [grasp] through acceptance resulting from reflection on a view."
"Hostility that is unwholesome" refers to the fivefold hostility beginning with the taking of life. He says "by the absence of a mind of anger" because anger is indeed a suffering of the mind.
"Of the defilement" refers to the defilement such as restlessness and remorse which afflicts and torments the mind. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Kesamutti Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta: 67.
In the sixth [verse], "pātarāsa" refers to food that is not to be eaten until morning; those by whom the morning meal has been eaten are called "bhuttapātarāsā."

"Slaves" (dāsā) means those born in the house, those purchased with wealth, those brought as captives, or those who have entered into slavery of their own accord. "Laborers hired for food and wages" (bhattavetanabhatā kammakārā) is the term used.
Regarding the word "free from hunger" (nicchāto): here, "hunger" (chātaṃ) refers to craving (taṇhā) because it is the cause of physical hunger;

he has no such thing, thus he is "free from hunger. Therefore, it is said: "one free from craving" (nittaṇho). [The phrase] "of the defilements that cause internal torment" refers to the production of distress and fever within one's own continuum.
Because of the absence of the defilements that burn within, he has become cool, tranquil, and attained to coolness; thus he is called "one who has become cool" (*sītibhūta*).
Therefore it is said: "one who has become cool. Or, because he experiences the bliss of the Path, the Fruition, and Nibbāna, he is "one who experiences bliss" (*sukhappaṭisaṃvedī*).
The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Sāḷha-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Kathāvatthu-sutta: 68.
Regarding the seventh [section], "bases for discussion" (*kathāvatthūni*) refers to the grounds upon which discussion proceeds; for without them, discussion does not take place.
Therefore, it is said, "the causes of discourse. That which moves, flows, proceeds, and continues constantly is called *addhā*, meaning time;

thus he says, "The past time (*atītamaddhāna*) is indeed a time that occurs. For although time does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*), it is nevertheless designated by that very conventional expression (*vohāra*) based on the specific state of the occurrence of those very phenomena.
It is designated by such terms as "past" and so forth; and this distinction of past and so on belongs, in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), to phenomena (*dhammā*) themselves and not to time.
Therefore, he says, "The aggregates also proceed. He extends the same principle to the other two periods by stating, "This same method applies to the future and the present as well.
Furthermore, regarding the phrases "the past period" and so on, there are two modes of expression (*pariyāya*): the mode of the Suttanta and...
And there is the method of the Abhidhamma. According to the method of the Suttanta, the period prior to rebirth-linking is called the past time;
the period after death is called the future time; and that which occurs together with death and rebirth-linking—that interval—is called the present time.
According to the method of the Abhidhamma, among the three moments, the period prior to arising is called the past time; from arising onwards...
The future period is called *addhā* (the course), and the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] are called the present period (*addhā*).

In this context, since this is a teaching given in the Suttanta style, he spoke the passage beginning with “In the past, there was one named Kassapa,” etc., showing how the subject matter of the past and so forth is presented according to the method of the Suttantas.
That which is to be answered or explained categorically is "to be explained by way of a categorical response" (*ekaṃsabyākaraṇīya*). Regarding the question, “Is the eye impermanent?”...
The statement "it must be explained categorically" is said with reference to the emphasis on the latter term (*uttarapada*), because there is not even a trace of permanence (*niccatā*) therein;
however, if the emphasis were on the former term (*purimapada*), it would be a matter of answering by way of analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīyatā*). Therefore he said:
"But when asked, 'Is the eye impermanent? and so forth. This is because the specific meaning and the general meaning are not shared [in common] between the terms "eye" (*cakkhu*) and "ear" (*sota*).

Since the similar challenge regarding those two must be answered by way of concealment alone, and must be resolved both by way of negation and by way of affirmation, he said: "As with the eye, so with the ear... this is a question to be answered by counter-question.
Regarding the question of the non-difference between the soul and the body—namely, "That which is the soul is the body"—it is that [soul] of which there is non-difference from that [body].
And because that very [person] is not found in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), it is like the description of the three jhānas as being "Metteyya";
thus, due to its being undeclared, it is called "to be set aside" (*ṭhapanīya*). For a question of this kind, since it cannot be answered in three ways, it must be set aside without giving an answer.
It is called a "basis" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands upon it, depending on it for its existence; thus he says, "in the cause and the non-cause."
"By a fitting reason" means by a corresponding reason. "Is able" means he is capable of refuting [the opponent].

"He demonstrates his own state as an eternalist" means that, having seen the fault in the doctrine of annihilationism which he himself had previously accepted, he now demonstrates his own state as an eternalist.
By the phrase "in the case of the proponent of the person (puggalavādin)," he indicates the Vatsiputriya. This is how one should proceed when questioned with a question.
The practice is the duty for those who ask questions.
"He practices" (*paṭicarati*) means he moves or proceeds by way of concealing. Or rather, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word "practices" (*carati*) has the sense of "concealing";
thus he says, "he conceals. Furthermore, "one thing by another" is a demonstration of the manner of concealment.

He said, “By another statement,” and so forth. Therein, “by another statement” means that he conceals with a statement other than that which was spoken by the accuser to reveal the fault of the one being accused.
For when it is said, “You have fallen into an offense,” he says, “Who has fallen? What has been fallen into? In what has one fallen? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?”
When asked, “Have you seen anything like this? if one says, “I have not heard of it,” and turns the ear [to listen], this is called evading with something else (*aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati*).
For evading with something else is the resorting to distraction without first answering the charge, such as by asking, “Who has committed an offense? and so forth;
whereas answering and then diverting the conversation toward an external topic is the difference between these two. Therefore he said: “An irrelevant talk...”

“While bringing [the mind] down,” and so forth. In that context, *apanāmeti* means he diverts it. *Tatra* refers to that diversion into talk about external matters. *Upanisā* is a cause because the fruit (*phala*) depends upon it;

or, it is called *upanisā* because one relies upon it by approaching it. Thus, *saha upanisāya* means “with its basis,” which is why he says, “with its support (*saupanissayo*), with its condition (*sapaccayo*).

*Ohitasoto* means having the ear directed toward the hearing of the Dhamma because of not being occupied with anything else; for that very reason, it means having the ear fixed upon that purpose. By “wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*),” the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is intended; thus he says, “the Noble Path.”
The commentary on the Kathāvatthu Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Aññatitthiya Sutta: 69.
In the eighth [section], [the topics] are "rooted in the Blessed One" (bhagavaṃmūlakā) because the Blessed One is their root cause for understanding them as they truly are. Therefore, he said:
“Indeed, it is by relying on the Blessed One that we understand and penetrate these teachings.

They said, “Our teachings,” because they are to be realized by themselves. For the knowledge of penetrating the truths as they truly are regarding what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated belongs to those who have attained them;
and these [knowledges] are rooted in the Perfectly Enlightened One, since their object is none other than Him. Therefore, he said:
“Formerly, by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa,” and so forth. “These phenomena” (*ime dhammā*) refers to these phenomena of knowledge.
“We understand” (*ājānāma*) means we know them directly and face-to-face. “We penetrate” (*paṭivijjhāma*) is a synonym for that same term;

its meaning is “we attain. “Those whose leader is the Blessed One” (*bhagavaṃnettikā*): he is their leader (*netā*). A “leader” (*netā*) is one who brings those to be trained to the phenomena that should be cultivated. A “trainer” (*vinetā*)— [is one who disciplines them].
One who leads away from the states that should not be cultivated the mental continuum of those to be trained; or one who disciplines by means of partial discipline (*tadaṅgavinaya*) and so forth.

Alternatively, one who leads specifically so that there may arise the distinction of noble knowledge and vision (*ariya-ñāṇadassana*). "One who inclines" means one who makes known for the purpose of both establishing and removing, [saying]:
"These states should be cultivated; these should not be cultivated. Therefore he said, "according to their true nature," and so forth.

It is called a *paṭisaraṇa* (refuge) because they return (*paṭisaranti*) to it; those for whom the Blessed One is the refuge are "those who have the Blessed One as their refuge" (*bhagavampatisaraṇā*).
For when they come within range [of his teaching], the Blessed One is their refuge and their place of convergence. Therefore he said, "the phenomena of the four planes," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is a *paṭisaraṇa* because one returns to it or approaches it individually by way of the penetration of its intrinsic nature; thus, the Blessed One is the refuge.
"They have the Blessed One as their refuge" means *bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā*. Alternatively, that which one goes back to (*paṭisarati*) or penetrates (*paṭivijjhati*) is a "refuge" (*paṭisaraṇa*);
therefore, because they have the Blessed One as their refuge by way of penetration, they are called "those who have the Blessed One as their refuge. For this reason he said, "Moreover," and so forth.
"By way of penetration" means by way of the state of being something to be penetrated. Even though the word [for "penetration"] is not explicitly present, it is so in terms of meaning.
"It is as if he were speaking," he said, "‘Contact comes, O Blessed One;
what is my name? For contact, as it enters the range of knowledge, is as if asking its own name, ‘What is my name?’, and the Blessed One is as if giving it a name."
Regarding the word *paṭibhātu*: here, in relation to the prefix *pati*, the form *bhagavantaṃ* is in the accusative case;
however, showing that the meaning should be understood as being in the genitive case, he says "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*). Furthermore, *paṭibhātu* means "let there be a portion.
For this teaching of the Dhamma is a portion of the Blessed One, whereas our portion is its hearing—this is the intended meaning. Thus, according to the characteristics of grammar...
It is appropriate. Some, however, state that the word *paṭibhātu* means "may it be seen," in the sense that "may it be seen by knowledge" or "may it be taught.

*Upaṭṭhātu* means "may it stand before knowledge. Regarding the phrase "What is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) in the text?"—here, the meaning is "what is the superior application (*adhikappayoga*)?"
"By way of worldly censure" means by way of that which is naturally censurable by worldly people.
"By way of the censure of its result" means by way of the censure of the result as leading to the states of misery (apāya). With the words "How?
and so forth, he shows the scope [of the offense] as being less blameworthy even by way of both types of censure. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Aññatitthiyasutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Akusalamūlasutta*: 70.

In the ninth [sutta], "he is greedy" is greed (*lobha*); "he hates" is hatred (*dosa*); "he is deluded" is delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, these—greed and the others—are [the roots] of those things that do not arise simultaneously.
They are called "roots of the unwholesome" because they serve as a decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for certain unwholesome states such as killing;

because, being associated, they cause the arising of certain co-nascent unwholesome states such as taking what is not given; and because they themselves are unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy and having painful results.
Thus it was said: "They are roots of the unwholesome, and they are themselves unwholesome. And this has also been said: "One who is lustful, friend..."
"One who is overcome by lust, whose mind is possessed, even kills a living being," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "whatever [lust]," he says, "O monks, whatever greed there is," because it was stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). Regarding the phrase "that too," he says, "that too is a root of unwholesomeness," because the same method applies here as well.
Showing the application of the meaning even without a change of gender, he says, "or a root of unwholesomeness," and so forth.
"In all cases" refers to such passages as: "Monks, whatever is hatred, that too is a root of unwholesomeness.
Regarding the term "constructs," the meaning here is "exerts effort"; and since that exertion is accomplished through the coming together of conditions, it is like a gathering or a piling up.
Thus he says: "He gathers; he makes a heap."
In the Pāli, regarding the phrases beginning with “by killing” (*vadhena*), “by killing” means either by slaying or by striking.
For the word *vadha* has the sense of harming and the sense of afflicting. “By binding” (*bandhanena*) means by means of fetters and the like. “By ruin” (*jāniyā*) means by the loss of wealth;
the meaning is: by punishment such as “seize a hundred! or “seize a thousand! “By reproach” (*garahāya*) means the shaving of the head and beard.
By performing such acts as sprinkling with cow dung and tying a *kuraṇḍaka* (a type of plant) around the neck, one causes reproach and brings about evil.
In this context, "shaving the head like Pañcasikha" means shaving it in the shape of a crow's wing. "Sprinkling with cow dung" means pouring water mixed with husks over the head.
"Tying a *kuraṇḍaka*" means tying a rope made of *gaddula* grass.
“He does not speak at the right time” means he does not speak at the appropriate moment; rather, he speaks at an inappropriate time, either before or after the time when it ought to be said.
“A speaker of what is unreal” means one who speaks of that which does not exist. Therefore, it is said: “He does not speak what is real.
“He does not speak what is meaningful” means he does not speak the reason; he is one who speaks what is based on non-reason and is fruitless. “He does not speak the Dhamma” means...

"He does not speak of what is real" means that one who speaks of what is unreal is a speaker of what is not as it is. "He does not speak of the discipline" means he does not speak of the discipline of restraint (*saṃvaravinaya*);
he is not a speaker connected with the discipline of restraint, nor is he a speaker who brings about the discipline of restraint for himself or for those listening to him—this is the meaning.

"Unreal" (*ataccha*) means an untrue matter. Therefore he said: "The other is a synonym for that. Alternatively, "unreal" (*abhūta*) means non-existent or non-occurring; "unreal" (*ataccha*) means having a nature that is not such [as it appears].

“Ayo” (prosperity) means that which comes from meritorious action (*puññakamma*) and arises; it is growth. Its opposite is “anayo,” meaning lack of growth; thus he said, “He falls into misfortune (*anaya*), which is to say he falls into lack of growth.
A *māluvā-sipāṭikā* is a long-shaped pod of the *māluvā* creeper; the meaning is a small pod containing the fruit of the *māluvā*.
“Phalitāya” means having split after drying up in the heat. [This refers to] the *vaṭa* tree and so forth.
"At the root" means near the base of trees such as the banyan (*vaṭa*). Why are they unable to remain established in their own nature?
Because of the fear of the destruction of their existence. For from a *māluva* seed fallen at the foot of a tree, a creeper arises and climbs the tree.
It possesses large leaves and many leaves, and with its branches and twigs—which are shaped like the leaves of a great *kolira* tree and even larger than those—it [envelops the tree].
It is endowed with leaves. Then, wrapping itself around that tree from the root upward and covering all its branches, it stands there creating a great burden.
When the wind blows or the rain falls, having become dense and acting as a cause for hanging beneath the torrent, it breaks all the branches of that tree and falls to the ground.
It causes it to fall. Then the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) resting upon that tree breaks apart and perishes.
Thus, those deities, out of fear of the destruction of their abode, are unable to maintain their own forms.

And in this regard, as for the celestial mansion that is supported by branches, when the branches break, it breaks right there at each point; and when all the branches have broken, [the entire mansion perishes].
It breaks apart; however, it should be understood that the tree-dwelling celestial mansion (*rukkhaṭṭhaka-vimāna*) does not perish as long as even the mere root of the tree remains.
"Having crumbled here and there" means having broken apart here and there. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Akusalamūla-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta 71.

Regarding the tenth [verse], "on that day" (*tadahū*): here, the meaning is "on that particular day," as he says, "on that Uposatha day. It is called *uposatha* because they observe the fast (*upavasanti*) there;
it is the Uposatha day. And "they observe the fast" means by means of virtue, or by fasting, or by methods such as the milk-and-nutritious-food regimen.

The meaning is: "having become endowed with [virtue], they dwell. For on the Uposatha day, those belonging to the Dispensation (sāsana) dwell having become endowed with virtue, while outsiders (bāhiraka) dwell having become endowed with the total abstention from food, or by means of such methods as the milk-elixir or honey-elixir.
Furthermore, this Uposatha day is threefold, being divided into the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth; therefore, in order to exclude the other two, [the text specifies...]
“On the day of the fifteen-day uposatha”: this is what is stated. Regarding the phrase *vavassaggatthe*, it means in the sense of verbal expression (*vacasāyatthe*).
The word *diva* is synonymous with *divasa*; since it is being used as an adjective qualifying that [day], the word *diva* illuminates its meaning more specifically.
Thus he said: “*Divassa divā* means ‘at midday’. The term *paṭicchāpetvā* refers to acceptance.

"Having caused [it] to be done. "By way of the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*)" means by way of a corresponding fruit. It does not bear great fruit because it is defiled by the immorality of mental misconduct.

"By way of the benefit of ripening (*vipākānisamsa*)" means by way of the fruit of prosperity. "By way of the radiance of ripening (*vipākobhāsa*)" means by way of the radiance of ripening known as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), which is produced by the departure of opposing factors.
It does not possess great radiance because of its impure state. "Of the expansion of ripening (*vipākavipphāra*)" means of the abundance of ripening.
Because the statement beginning with "I am nowhere" arises through the influence of wrong adherence, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "I declare this to be his false speech.
However, that which proceeds by way of seeing the emptiness of the fourfold alternative (catukoṭika-suññatā) is indeed the vision of the Noble Ones;
thus, there is no false speech therein. For this has been said:
“Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am not anywhere, in anything, belonging to anyone; nor is there anywhere anything belonging to me, in anything. And so forth.
Herein, the fourfold emptiness (*catukoṭika-suññatā*) is taught. How so? For the noble one, in the phrase “I am not anywhere,” does not perceive a self anywhere;
and in the phrase “in anything belonging to anyone,” he does not regard his own self as something to be brought into the state of being a possession for anyone else.

"He does not see" means that having imagined [the other] as a brother in the place of a brother, as a friend in the place of a friend, or as a requisite in the place of a requisite, he does not see what ought to be brought near.
Regarding the phrase "nor anywhere mine," setting aside the word *mama* for a moment, the meaning is: "nowhere does he see another's self, nor anywhere his own. Now, regarding the word *mama*:

Having brought it forth, thinking, "I have nothing whatsoever belonging to me," he does not see the self of another as existing through the state of being anything whatsoever belonging to him; he does not bring the self of another into any position— whether in the place of a brother,
in the place of a friend, or in the place of a requisite— by way of this state of being anything whatsoever belonging to him.
The meaning is "he sees. Thus, because he does not see a self anywhere, nor does he see anything belonging to another that should be brought into the state of being one's own;

and because he does not see a self of another anywhere, nor does he see a self of another that should be brought into the state of being one's own, this emptiness should be understood as having four aspects.
However, because it is impossible for those with wrong view to see things as they truly are, the vision of emptiness according to the fourfold scheme previously described is not possible for them.
Therefore, just like the statement "there is no mother, there is no father," the words "I am nowhere" and so forth were spoken by way of a false apprehension;
thus, the occurrence of false speech (*musāvāda*) here is appropriate. *Kvaci* means in a place or at a time.
Or: Now, why is it said to be "fruitless"? For by the expression "not of great fruit," only the absence of great fruit is indicated, not the total absence of fruit altogether;
thus he says, "For here the literal expression alone is incomplete," and so forth.
"In the remaining phrases as well" refers to "not of great benefit" and the others.
"By eight reasons":
"Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the gods, recited eight true praises of the Blessed One before the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
'What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa devas, as far as that Blessed One...'"

I do not perceive, even looking back into the past, any teacher who was endowed with this quality—that he practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans; nor [do I perceive such a one]... [who practiced thus for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans].
"Indeed, at present there is no one other than that Blessed One"—
by these eight reasons, such as "practicing for the welfare of the many," which were set forth in detail in the Mahāgovinda Sutta and which illustrate the majesty of the Buddha.
Now, why was it stated "by eight reasons" instead of saying "by nine reasons"?
He said: “For here... [etc. ...all the mundane and supramundane qualities of a Buddha are included. This is what is meant:
in this sutta, by the expression “Thus indeed is the Blessed One,” all the mundane and supramundane qualities of a Buddha are shown without distinction;
therefore, with reference to those qualities shown therein, it is said, “by eight reasons.”

The qualities beginning with *arahanta* (worthiness) are indicated individually; the meaning is that by each individual word beginning with "arahant," a single specific quality is indicated. "Together with the text" (*sahantika*) means accompanied by the Dhamma of the scriptures.

"The application should be made in the same manner as before" means the application should be made according to the method beginning with: "For those sporting in the festivities of the constellations do not shine when their bodies are adorned with ornaments while they are soiled [with impurities].
"Recollection of the Sangha" is indeed the recollection of its qualities; thus he said: "Of the eight types of noble persons..."

“He recollects the virtues. Regarding the phrase “heat that has been applied two or three times,” this refers to the heat applied by heating [the cloth] on the stove two or three times for the purpose of softening it.
The application [of the commentary] should be made in the same manner as before;

that is, the application should be made according to the method beginning with: “For women who have adorned themselves with ornaments while wearing soiled clothes do not shine while sporting at the festival.”
"From the time they have been abandoned... pe ...in the case of abstinence": by this, he shows that the abstinence intended here is that which has abandonment as its cause.

For it is said that Arahants are "completely abstinent from the misconduct of killing living beings" because such misconduct has been abandoned through the knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma;
this is because the abstinences consisting in abandonment by way of complete eradication (*samuccheda*) are what is intended. Although there is both abandoning and refraining...

There is no [distinction of] prior and posterior time; however, when the relationship of condition and conditionally arisen state is considered among the path-factors—namely right view and so forth, and right speech and so forth—even those that are co-nascent are apprehended as being in a relationship of condition and conditionally arisen state precisely by way of priority and posteriority.
Thus, it is by virtue of the mode of the occurrence of apprehension regarding the conditions, such as right view and so forth, that...

The term "prior time" refers to the act of abandoning with respect to the things to be abandoned (*pahāyakadhamma*), while the term "subsequent time" refers to the act of abstaining with respect to the abstinences (*virati*) that arise as conditions.
Thus, abandonment (*pahāna*) should be understood in the sense of total eradication (*samuccheda*), and abstinence (*virati*) in the sense of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).
Alternatively, "killing of living beings" (*pāṇātipāta*) is that by which a living being is killed; it is the collection of phenomena that serves as the cause for the destruction of life. What...?

But what are they? They are the defilements such as shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), and cruelty (*vihiṃsā*). For it is by abandoning and eradicating these through the Noble Path that the Arahants are said to be "utterly refraining from taking life and from immoral conduct," because when the defilements have been abandoned, the karma characterized by those defilements no longer arises.
The same principle applies to the phrases "having abandoned taking what is not given" and so forth.
By the term "viratāvāti" (abstaining), he shows that this abstention is unlimited by way of time and other factors.
For while others who have undertaken abstentions may break their undertaking due to an unsettled mind or for the sake of gain, livelihood, and so forth, the Arahants do not;
rather, because they have entirely abandoned the taking of life, the Arahants are absolutely and completely abstinent.
He said, "for the purpose of harming others," and so forth, in order to indicate the state of avoiding the infliction of harm upon others, which is designated as "punishment" (*daṇḍana*).
Regarding the term "conscientious" (*lajjī*), it should be understood that by the "conscience" (*lajjā*) mentioned here, "moral dread" (*ottappa*) is also implicitly included;
for there is no such thing as a lack of conscience that is devoid of both disgust for evil and fear of evil.

"It exists. Or rather, because of their reverence for the Dhamma and because the Dhamma is their own master, it is "shame" (*lajjā*)—which has the self as its overlord—that is being described, and not "fear of worldly censure" (*ottappa*), which has the world as its overlord. As for why it is said, "They have attained compassion and a mind of loving-kindness":
is it not the case that the word *dayā* occurs in such passages as "not devoid of compassion" (*adayāpanno*) to signify "compassion" (*karuṇā*)? True, this is so; however, this...
However, since the word *dayā* (compassion) occurs here including the sense of "protection" within its scope, it functions both as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and as compassion (*karuṇā*);
thus, it is stated here as functioning specifically as loving-kindness. It is called *mettā* because one is moistened (*mijjati*) or made tender (*siniyhati*).
That which possesses this [moistening] is *mettaṃ*. One who has a mind characterized by this is *mettacitto*. The state of being such is *mettacittatā*, which simply means loving-kindness itself.
“Compassionate and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings”: by this, he shows the boundlessness of that abstinence in terms of its manifestation.

“Toward living beings” means toward those born as living beings. “Sympathetic” means those who feel compassion; however, since loving-kindness (*mettā*) is a specific condition for compassion (*karuṇā*), it is said:
“by that very state of having become compassionate. Thus, by these qualities, there is abstinence from taking life.
It is accomplished; thus, the state of being endowed with those qualities of mere shame and compassion is shown.
"Taking what is possessed by another" means taking what belongs to another. A *thena* is called a thief; the state of such a person is *theyya* (theft).
Although it is true that the words "possessed of shame" and "endowed with compassion" are not explicitly stated here, they are nevertheless effectively stated by implication through the context.
It should be understood as follows: Just as shame and the other [virtues] are specific conditions for the abandoning of killing, so too are they for the abandoning of taking what is not given;
therefore, that passage from the Canon should also be cited here. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well.

Alternatively, by the phrase "having become pure," the possession of shame, fear of wrongdoing, and so forth, as well as the abandoning of shamelessness and the rest, has already been stated; thus, it should be understood that terms such as "the conscientious" (*lajjī*) are not mentioned again.

*Asaṭṭhacariyaṃ*: the conduct of those who are not excellent, the base; or the conduct that is not excellent, the lowly; the meaning is "lowly behavior," namely sexual intercourse. *Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ*:
he speaks of the noble, supreme practice, which is the abstention from sexual intercourse. By the phrase *ārācārī methunā*, [it is meant]:
"In this case, someone does not indeed engage in the union of two by two with a woman, but rather..."
It should be understood that by the passage beginning, "He consents to being rubbed, massaged, bathed, and anointed;
he relishes it, he desires it, and he finds satisfaction in it," the sevenfold union of sexual misconduct is shown to be abstained from.
In expressions such as "saccato thetato" (truly and firmly), the word *theta* is a synonym for "firm"; and this state of firmness arises from truthful speech.
Because it is established by way of discourse, he said, "The meaning is 'established discourse'.
"One whose discourse is not established" means that just as turmeric-dye and the like are not established because their nature is unstable, so too is his discourse not established;
thus, "one whose discourse is not established" should be construed in the same manner as turmeric-dye and the like serve as a simile for discourse. This...
The same method applies to such expressions as "like an inscription on stone" and so forth. *Saddhāyikā* means that faith (*saddhā*) goes forth or proceeds therein;

it is thus "that which possesses faith," just as one speaks of "those who follow the Vinaya" (*venayikā*). Alternatively, *saddhāyikā* means that which is to be approached by means of faith; the sense is "that which is to be believed.
The intention is that [the person] incurs the state of being subject to censure because of their deceptive nature.
“Eka-bhattaṃ” means a single meal; those for whom this exists are “ekabhattikā,” meaning those who eat only once in a single day.
Since this might also include eating at night, he said, “rattūparatā” (abstaining from food at night). Even so, they might still be “ekabhattikā” by eating in the evening;
therefore, to exclude that possibility, it is said, “viratā vikālabhojanā” (abstaining from food at the improper time). [This refers to] from the rising of the dawn...
From the time [the sun] has risen until midday—this is called the "proper time for food" (bhojana-kāla) as practiced by the Buddhas and the Noble Ones;
any other time is "improper" (vikāla). However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), because eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase, the period after midday is specifically termed "vikāla."

In brief, because the teaching of the Blessed One—proceeding in the manner beginning with "the non-doing of all evil"—is not compatible with the viewing of dancing and so forth due to its arising from desire and passion, he said: "Because it is not in conformity with the Teaching.
Dancing, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others, is referred to in the Canon by the single term *nacca* (dancing) due to the commonality of its nature as dancing.
Just as [the term "seeing"] includes what has been grasped, so too do the sounds of singing and instrumental music; thus he says, "by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), he includes singing, causing to sing, playing instruments, and causing to play instruments. Furthermore, hearing is included here under "seeing" by the method of "residual inclusion of dissimilar items" (virūpekasesa-naya);
or else, because the five types of consciousness have the nature of looking (ālocana), even the act of hearing is subsumed under the category of seeing.
It is simply stated as "seeing. Since hearing music that is not frivolous is sometimes permitted, he says, "seeing that which is frivolous.
For it is likewise stated in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*:
"Song associated with the Dhamma is permitted; the Dhamma associated with song is not permitted."
"Whatever" means any flower, whether bound together or not. "A kind of fragrance" (gandhajātanti) refers to a class of fragrant substances.
Because of the expression "whatever" used here as well, it shows that for any kind of ointment, whether perfumed or unperfumed, none is permitted.
"Ucca" is another word with the same meaning as the word "ucca. "Seti etthāti"—it is where one lies.
Regarding "sleeping": high beds and large beds are intended here as those unsuitable for a recluse; thus it says, "exceeding the proper measure and having an improper covering.
Furthermore, chairs and the like should be understood as being included under the category of "beds" (*sayana*) here.
Since, however, when the physical basis is prohibited, the activity supported by that basis is also necessarily prohibited, it is therefore stated simply as "high beds and large beds."

This has been stated. However, in terms of its actual meaning, it should be understood that the abstention from sitting and lying down on such things—which constitute the enjoyment of those [luxuries]—is what is being shown.

Alternatively, this designation is made by means of the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*) regarding the sense of "high seats and luxurious seats," just as in the expression "the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ*). Or else, it is because the act of reclining (*sayana*) is preceded by the act of sitting (*āsana*).
It should be understood that by the mention of "lying down" (sayana), "sitting" (āsana) is also included.
The word "kīvā" is a particle; it clarifies the meaning of "kittakaṃ," as he said:
"kīvamahapphalo means 'of how much great fruit'? "In the remaining phrases" refers to "kīvamahānisaṃso" and so forth. The word *ratta* is a synonym for *ratana*.
He said: "Possessing abundant red jewels" means "endowed with an abundance of what is reckoned as red jewels.

However, in the Pāḷi, the reading "possessing abundant seven-jewels" (*pahūtasattaratanānaṃ*) is also seen. "Having made it like the surface of a drum" means having made it smooth like the surface of a drum.
"One part is not worth that" means that the aforementioned universal monarch’s sovereignty is not worth even one part of that.

It is not worth even one sixteenth part of that; it is far more abundant than that. "More abundant than the glory of the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch" means it exceeds the splendor of a universal monarch's reign.
Regarding the phrase "of the gods of the Four Great Kings," etc.: the gods of the Four Great Kings dwell in the middle of Mount Sineru.
Among them, many are mountain-dwellers and many are sky-dwellers; their successive ranks extend as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains. [There are also] the *khiḍḍāpadosika* (those corrupted by play).
Manopadosika, Sītavalāhaka, Uṇhavalāhaka, Candima the son of a god, and Suriya the son of a god—all these belong exclusively to the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika).
Because thirty-three persons were born there, it is called Tāvatiṃsa.
Furthermore, it is said that "Tāvatiṃsa" is simply the name of those gods. Among them, some reside on mountains, and some...
The space-dwellers (*ākāsadvaka*); their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and so too is that of the Yāma gods and the others.

For even within a single world-sphere, there is no place where the lineage of the gods does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Therein, they are called *yāma* because they have gone (*yātā*), proceeded (*payātā*), and arrived (*sampattā*) at divine bliss.
They are called *tusita* because they are contented (*tuṭṭhā*) and delighted (*pahaṭṭhā*). [They are called *nimmānarati*] because they delight in objects beyond those that are natural or prepared...
They are called *Nimmānarati* because they create objects of enjoyment according to their own desire whenever they wish to sport, and then take their pleasure with them.
They are called *Paranimmitavasavatti* because, having understood the mental inclinations of others, they exercise mastery over the objects of enjoyment created by those others.
Among these, the lifespan of the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (*Cātumahārājika*) is nine million years by human calculation.
For the gods of the Thirty-three, it is three hundred and sixty million years.
For the Yāma gods, it is fourteen hundred and forty million years. For the Tusita gods, it is fifty-seven hundred and sixty million years.
For the Nimmānarati gods, it is two hundred million years.
Three hundred and four million years. For the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranimmitavasavatti*), nine hundred and twenty-one billion and six million years.
"With hands and feet like fists" means that from the soles of the feet up to the lower limit of the wrists, the feet are the size of a fist-cubit (*muṭṭhiratana*).
"And that [should be measured] by the hand of a man of medium size, which is now commonly known as 'the carpenter’s hand.
From the moment of undertaking the precepts, one should spend the time doing nothing else, either by listening to the Dhamma or by attending to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna);
thus he said: 'But while staying there... it should be investigated.'"

Having made a verbal resolution, one should undertake the factors of the Uposatha by setting a time limit, saying, "For this night and this day," and then taking the eight training rules together as the components of the Uposatha, saying:
"I undertake the training rule of abstaining from the destruction of life... [and so on] ...I undertake the training rule of abstaining from high and luxurious beds."
Having made such a verbal declaration as "I undertake [them]," they should be undertaken according to the text (*pāḷi*).

However, by one who does not know the text, they should be undertaken either individually in their own language, or by way of a single resolution, saying: "I resolve upon the Uposatha prescribed by the Buddha.
If no other way is found, they must be resolved upon. For even when undertaking the lay follower's precepts (*upāsaka-sīla*) oneself, [the same applies].
Whether one undertakes them in the presence of another, or undertakes them all at once, or undertakes them individually—in each case, they are indeed "undertaken.
However, for one who undertakes them all at once, there is only a single abstinence and a single volition.
Since that [volition] performs the function of all abstinences and volitions, by that means as well, all the training rules (sikkhāpada) are indeed undertaken.
However, when one undertakes them individually, various volitions of abstention arise according to their respective functions;
but when undertaking them all together, there must indeed be a verbal expression. [These are] connected with the obstruction of others and connected with the harming of others.
But surely, when "gem" is mentioned, even beryl is already included; for what purpose, then, did he say "beryl"?
“‘Beryl’... [as before] ...he shows. Having said “gem,” one should connect this with “beryl” as showing its status as a gem of noble birth (*jātimaṇi*).
“The color of a year-old bamboo” means the color of bamboo that has passed one year from birth. “Acquired” means beautiful.
“All like the moonlight and the hosts of stars” means that all the hosts of stars do not equal even a fraction of the moonlight.
"The meaning here is 'they do not experience [it]'; thus he said: 'Candappabhā' is in the nominative case in the sense of a possessor (*sāmī-atthe*).
The commentary on the Uposatha Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
(8) 3. The Chapter on Ānanda. 1.
Commentary on the Channa Sutta. 72.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter], "the wandering ascetic Channa": he was not a naked wandering ascetic. "Having plucked out and carried away the doctrine of the outsiders" means having refuted the doctrine of the outsiders and entered [the order].
Because it obstructs the eye of wisdom and thus makes one blind, it is called "blind-making" (*andhakaraṇa*); hence he said, "for whom lust arises," and so forth.

"Eye-making-not" (*acakkhukaraṇa*) is an *asamattha-samāsa* (a compound where the members do not possess the capacity for the action expressed), like in expressions such as "mouths that do not look at the sun"; hence he said, "it does not produce the eye of wisdom, thus it is 'eye-making-not'.
"The destroyer of wisdom" (*paññānirodhika*) [refers to] mundane and supramundane wisdom that has not yet arisen.

It does not allow [wisdom] to arise; however, even when mundane wisdom has arisen by way of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and the five direct knowledges (*pañcābhiññā*), it cuts it off and casts it away—thus, it should be understood here that its meaning is "the cessation of wisdom" (*paññānirodhika*).

For it is called "the cessation of wisdom" because it ceases wisdom by being the cause for the non-arising of what has not yet arisen and for the disappearance of what has already arisen. It "afflicts" (*vihanati*) and "distresses" (*vibādhati*), thus it is "affliction" (*vighāta*); he said "suffering" (*dukkha*).
“Of the affliction termed suffering”: by the phrase “the extinction of defilements” (kilesanibbāna), he refers specifically to the unconditioned extinction (asaṅkhata-nibbāna).
For that which is called the unconditioned extinction does not allow one to make it manifest; thus, [a path] that does not lead to extinction is so called.
It is described as mixed with the supramundane because the noble path belonging to the prior stage is also included in the description.
The commentary on the Channa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta: 73.
In the second [verse], "not desiring to know" means not desiring to understand at all. Therefore he said: "for the purpose of grasping."
"But having come," means for the purpose of grasping [the truth] after having delimited it with wisdom and investigated it.
"Specification of the reason" (*kāraṇāpadeso*) is a description of the cause. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta of the Sakyan Clan 74.
Regarding the third [sutta], the state of being ill is "sickness" (*gelañña*); thus he says, "because of the state of being ill.

"He illustrates" means he makes it known precisely through the sequence of the teaching. For, having first spoken of the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one in training (*sekha*), and subsequently speaking of the virtue and so forth of one beyond training (*asekha*), he illustrates this meaning.
The commentary on the Mahānāmasakkasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Nigaṇṭhasutta: 75.
Regarding the phrase "covered with a swan-patterned canopy," it means covered with a swan-patterned [canopy], in the shape of a circle of swans.
*Attha* means "meaning. That which has nothing remaining is *aparisesa*. Therefore he said, "without leaving even a small remainder.

Alternatively, because of knowing the phenomena that are without remainder, one claims the knowledge and vision designated as "without remainder"; thus the meaning here should be understood in this way.
*Satataṃ* means "constant. *Samitaṃ* is a synonym for that very same thing; therefore he said, "constantly and continuously."
"At all times, without interruption. Alternatively, since the word *satata* (constant) in the sense of "perpetual" might indicate a frequent occurrence, it is said to be "continuous" (*samita*).
By this, he shows its uninterrupted occurrence, hence he says: "at all times, without interruption.
"For the purpose of bringing about purification" refers to those whose minds are defiled by the stains of lust and so forth, as well as by covetousness, improper greed, and the like.
For the purpose of bringing about the purification of beings. "For the purpose of transcending" means for the purpose of abandoning sorrow (*soka*) and lamentation (*parideva*).
"For the purpose of reaching the goal" means for the cessation—that is, the disappearance—of these two: bodily pain (*kāyika-dukkha*) and mental grief (*cetasika-domanassa*).
Nibbāna is called *ñāya* because it proceeds with certainty; or else, it is that which is known (*ñāyati*).
It is called a *ñāya* (method) because one penetrates [reality] by means of it; thus he said, "for the sake of attaining the Noble Path.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of realizing conditionless Nibbāna": because it is devoid of conditions, it is "conditionless" (*apaccaya*); because it is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) and free from the burning of craving, it has received the name "Nibbāna.
This refers to the realization of the Deathless (*amata*), which is to say, its direct personal experience.
"Touching again and again" means reaching again and again. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Nigaṇṭha Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Nivesaka Sutta.
76. They are called *amaccā* because they are together (*sahabhāva*) in matters of duty and business (*kiccakaraṇīyesu*).
They are called *ñātī* because they know or are known thus: "This one is internal. *Sassusasurapakkhikā* means both the father-in-law and mother-in-law and those belonging to their side.
*Sālohitā* means those connected by blood. Or, they are relatives on the father’s side or on the mother’s side.
"Sālohitā" refers to relatives on the mother’s or father’s side, or relatives on the side of the mother-in-law or father-in-law.
"Aveccappasāda" (unshakable confidence) is confidence that arises after having understood the qualities of the Triple Gem as they truly are.

Because it has been brought about by the Path, it is unshakeable and invulnerable to anyone; therefore, it is described as "immovable confidence" (*acalappasāda*). "Bhāvaññathatta" means a change in one's fundamental nature.
"In twenty parts" means in those beginning with head-hairs and ending with the brain. "In twelve parts" means in those beginning with bile and ending with urine.

"In four parts" means in the four parts described thus: "that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion."

"In the six parts" means in the six parts mentioned thus: "upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds residing in the belly, winds residing in the bowels, winds circulating through the limbs and members, and in-breath and out-breath.
"Distension" is the causing of the remaining three elements to become rigid; some say it is "playful movement. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Nivesaka-sutta* is finished.
6–7. Commentary on the *Paṭhamabhava-sutta*, etc. 77–78.

In the sixth [sutta], "kamma-formative consciousness" (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) refers to consciousness co-arising with kamma. The rest here is easy to understand. In the seventh, there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the first *Bhavasutta* and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Sīlabbatasutta*: 79.
"Devotion to the practice of austerities" (*dukkarakārikānuyoga*) means devotion to the performance of difficult deeds. "Essential through attendance" means by way of the mode of attending.
“Essential. By the words “This is the best,” etc., he clarifies the manner of its manifestation. “In this”—that is, in response to this question asked by the Teacher.
The commentary on the *Sīlabbata-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Gandhajāta-sutta*.
80. Regarding the ninth [term], *mūla*: it is said that "the scent of the root is *mūlagandha*," meaning "scent having the root as its basis" (*mūlavatthuko gandho*).
That which has the root as its basis (*vatthu*) is "root-based" (*mūlavatthuko*). Now, showing that the root itself is "scent" by virtue of being associated with scent, he says:
"Or rather, the root itself, when endowed with scent, is *mūlagandha*. Of these two alternative meanings, the latter alone is more appropriate.
To demonstrate this, he said, “For its fragrance,” and so forth. “Vassika flowers, etc. refers to jasmine flowers (*sumana*) and the like.
The commentary on the *Gandhajāta Sutta* is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Cūḷanikā Sutta*.
81. Regarding the origin of the discourse in the *Aruṇavati-sutta* in the tenth [chapter]:
"Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Aruṇava. Now, monks, King Aruṇava had a royal capital named Aruṇavatī.
And it was in dependence on the royal capital of Aruṇavatī, monks, that the Blessed One Sikhī, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, resided."
...dwelt. Now, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava, a most auspicious pair.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū. This is from the Aruṇavatīsutta, as it appears in the *Brahmasaṃyutta*.
In the *Aṭṭhuppatti* (Origin of the Discourse). "Atippago" means excessively early; the meaning is "excessively morning," which implies that the meal has not yet been finished in the families.
"Ujjhāyanti" means they find fault;
they think with contempt, they think of it as something base. "Anekavihitam" (in various ways)...

"Having performed a transformation by psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbana*)" means: having performed the manifold transformations of psychic power described in such passages as, "having discarded his natural form, he displays the form of a nāga, or he displays the form of a supaṇṇa," and so forth.
"A thousandfold world-system" (*sahassilokadhātu*) refers to a thousand world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*).
"He spoke two verses" means that the Elder, it is said, [considered]: "How has this teaching of the Dhamma been taught? and so on.
Thinking, "They are dear and pleasing to everyone," and further realizing, "All sectarians and all gods and humans praise human effort according to their own respective systems;
there is no one who speaks in dispraise of energy. Therefore, I shall teach by making it connected with energy.
In this way, my teaching of the Dhamma will become dear and pleasing to all," [he proceeded] in the three...
Having searched through the Piṭakas, he spoke these two verses beginning with, “Exert yourselves!
Strive! [The question] “What light is this? means: “To whom does this light belong? [The phrase] “of those searching” means of those reflecting.
“All” refers to all the gods and humans within the world-system. “Of the assembled company” means of the limited and defined assembly that had gathered for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
"Of the assembly. "The meaning was also manifest to them" means that they did not merely hear the sound;
rather, the meaning became as clear to them as if it were within the normal range of hearing. Therefore, the intention is that [the Buddha] made himself known throughout a thousand world-systems.
"They carry around" means they circumambulate, keeping Sineru to their right. "Shining forth" means gleaming with their own radiance.
"Or shining. "The world a thousandfold": as many individual worlds as there are, reckoned as world-systems, illuminated by the moon and sun—that much is the measure of the "world a thousandfold";
the meaning is that together with this [central] world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*), it is a thousand world-spheres.
But why was this brought forth? Why was this minor world-system brought forth and taught by the Blessed One?

The purpose [of this section] is to show the delimitation of the intermediate world-system (*majjhimikā lokadhātu*), that is, to show the measure of the two-thousandfold world-system (*dvisahassilokadhātu*).
A thousandfold world-system multiplied by a thousand is a two-thousandfold world-system; by calculation of world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*), its measure is one million world-spheres.

Therefore he said: "Having counted the thousand world-spheres by way of a thousandfold division," and so forth. [This is shown] by means of the shaking [of the earth], the approaching of the deities, and so on.
The birth-field (*jātikkhetta*) is the state of security from bondage (*yogakkhema*) together with the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
That the birth-field consists of exactly that much is to be understood by way of the very nature of things (*dhammatā*); some say it is "by way of its delimitation.

They say that for all Buddhas, the birth-field is thus, and the realization of the Dhamma occurs only for the deities dwelling therein. [This applies] only to the seven [stages], beginning with the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
The mention of "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) is merely illustrative, since that trembling is also obtained at times such as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).

By stating that a thousand [worlds] calculated by dividing each into a thousand is a "middle" world-system (*majjhimikā*), he shows that a thousand of those middle world-systems is a "three-thousandfold world-system" (*tisahassilokadhātu*), and that this very system is the "great three-thousandfold world-system" (*mahāsahassilokadhātu*).
The issuing of the command occurs through his mere mental resolve (*sarasena*).
The field of authority (*āṇā-khetta*) is that which contracts and expands all at once.
"The authority prevails" means it functions by being received with bowed heads by the deities residing therein; and this occurs solely through the power of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "To whatever extent he might wish," there is nothing whatsoever that is outside the scope of the Buddhas, owing to their intention; for such is the field of their domain.
There is no measurement or limitation [to its extent]. It is called "uneven" because of the unevenness of the sun’s rising and so forth;
for this very reason, it says, "In one place the sun has risen," and so on. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Cūḷanikāsutta is finished.
The commentary on the Ānanda-vagga is concluded.
(9) 4. The Samaṇa-vagga: 1–5.
Commentary on the Samaṇa-sutta and following.
82–86. Regarding the first [training] of the fourth [precept], it is called "undertaking" (samādāna) because it is a correct taking up or grasping; thus he says, "Undertaking is said to be grasping.

Higher virtue is *adhisīla*. Since mundane virtue (*lokīya-sīla*) possesses the nature of higher virtue only figuratively, in order to show that it is so in the literal sense, he says, "Moreover, all mundane virtue," and so forth. "Because it is to be trained in" (*sikkhitabbato*).
Because it is to be cultivated. The five or ten precepts are called "virtue" (*sīla*);

the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* is called "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) because it constitutes the complete restraint of both body and mind, and because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the virtue of the Path. The eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are "mind" (*citta*);

the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*) is "higher mind" (*adhicitta*), because it serves as the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the concentration of the Path. Knowledge of the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).
Wisdom (*paññā*)—namely, insight (*vipassanā*)—is "higher wisdom" because it serves as the basis for path-wisdom.
Furthermore, even the five precepts and the ten precepts undertaken by one aspiring for *nibbāna* are indeed "higher virtue," because they serve as conditions for the attainment of *nibbāna*.
Likewise, even the eight meditative attainments entered by one aspiring for *nibbāna* are indeed "higher consciousness."
“The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil;
one experiences both of these, for the cause follows its effect.

Thus, by means of discerning the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past and the future, there arises through the state of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) a longing for liberation.

They also say that the wisdom of self-ownership (*kammassakatapaññā*), which serves as the condition, is "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*). The second, third, fourth, and fifth [discourses] are of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Samaṇasutta* and others is finished.
6. Commentary on the First *Sikkhāsutta*.
87. In the sixth [case], "one who fulfills completely" means one who is endowed with the practice in its entirety and without deficiency.
Regarding the status of the training rules as being minor or major, which is established by way of perspective, he said: "Even there, the *saṅghādisesa* is minor," and so forth.
"Teachers who utilize the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*" means teachers who maintain the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*; that is to say, reciters of the *Aṅguttara*. "Worldly offense" (*lokavajja*).

He does not incur [an offense] involving a world-transgressing training rule (*lokavajja-sikkhāpada*) because the dense thicket of defilements that accomplishes such transgression has been entirely abandoned.
He incurs only what is a transgression by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), for even in one who is unaware of the transgression of a rule, an offense may still arise.
Regarding "one who incurs [an offense] through the mind incurs the acceptance of money": he incurs it by consenting to what has been set aside [for him].
The "foundations of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyāni*) are those things that constitute the beginning of the holy life;
they are themselves the "foundational holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyakāni*), just as one says "the discipline itself is the disciplinarian. He said, "of the holy life of the Path," and so forth.

By "the four great training rules of virtue" (*cattāri mahāsīlasikkhāpadāni*), he refers to the four *pārājika* offenses. Because they cause the opposing states to flow out completely, they are called "outflows" (*sava*).

Because it is the Noble Path (ariyamagga) that is the stream, he said, "by the path known as the stream. It is called a *vinipāta* because it causes one to fall (*nipātetī*) in a distorted way, accompanied by suffering and distress;
thus, it is that which casts one into the suffering of the states of loss (*apāya*). *Dhamma* means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

One whose nature is not to fall into a state of loss is "one of a non-falling nature" (*avinipātadhamma*); what is meant is that his nature is not to cast himself into the states of loss. Why? Because of those factors (*dhammā*)...
[He is] one who goes to the states of misery, because those have been abandoned. Therefore he said: “*Avinipātadhammo* means having the nature of not falling into the four states of misery.

In that context, “having the nature of not falling” means having the nature of not arising [there]. “Fixed by the method of the stream-entry path” means fixed because the attainment of the higher paths is certain to occur.
For this very reason he said: “*Sambodhiparāyaṇo*” (destined for full enlightenment). At the very least, from the seventh existence...
Or, it is "fixed" (niyata) by virtue of the fact that [the remaining defilements] are no longer liable to arise. It is called "awakening" (sambodhi) because one awakens to it; it is the Noble Path.

Since the first path has already been attained, and the remainder is still to be attained and desired as such, it is "destined for awakening" (sambodhiparāyaṇa), meaning its further course (parā-ayana) or ultimate goal (parā-gati) is awakening—namely, the triad of the higher paths. Therefore, he said: "destined for the awakening of the triad of the higher paths."
It is called "slight" (*tanubhāva*) because of its infrequency of arising and because of the weakness of its obsession.

Indeed, this slightness should be understood by two reasons: by its occasional arising and by the weakness of its obsession. For in the case of a once-returner, the defilements do not arise frequently as they do for the common worldling who follows the cycle of existence; rather, they arise only occasionally.
They arise sparsely, like sprouts in a field that has been thinly sown.
Even as they arise, they do not appear crushing, pervading, or covering [the world] and creating darkness for the great masses of people who follow the cycle of existence;
