rather, they arise very slowly, appearing thin in form, like a layer of clouds or the wing of a fly. Regarding this, some elders say:
“Although the defilements of a once-returner arise only after a long time, they nevertheless arise in abundance;
for indeed, his sons and daughters are seen. But this is not a valid measure, for sons and daughters can exist even through the mere touching of one’s limbs and members.
His thinness of defilements should be understood by two reasons alone: by their infrequency of arising and by the mildness of their obsession.
Regarding the term *heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ*: here, "below" (*heṭṭhā*) means below the sublime plane (*mahaggatabhūmi*), that is, in the sense-sphere plane (*kāmabhūmi*).
They are called "belonging to the lower part" (*heṭṭhābhāgiyā*) because they are beneficial to the lower part by way of being its conditions;
thus, "of those belonging to the lower part" means of those taken as conditions for the lower part, namely, for sense-existence (*kāmabhava*). They fetter and bind.

Because aggregates, destinies, and states of existence arise from aggregates, destinies, and states of existence—or because karma [arises] from its fruit—they are called "fetters" (saṃyojanāni). Thus he says:
"Fetters means bonds. For one whose lust and other defilements have not been eradicated, there is currently a connection between present aggregates and so forth and future aggregates and so forth;
however, for one whose lust and other defilements have been eradicated, that connection does not exist, even regarding karmas already performed.

The sense of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) is established through the positive and negative concomitance of lust and the other [defilements] with the state of incapacity. "By complete destruction" means by total eradication. "Spontaneously born" (*opapātiko*) means one whose mode of birth is spontaneous;
it refers to one who is accomplished in the act of arising. This is a statement that excludes the other modes of birth. By this, he expresses the absence of the suffering of dwelling in a womb.
Therein, by the term "one who attains final nibbāna" (*parinibbāyī*), he expresses the absence of all remaining suffering. In that regard, the state of attaining final nibbāna...
To show that this occurs by way of the non-returning of the seed of the aggregates in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), it is said: "one whose nature is not to return" (*anāvattidhamma*).

"Only above" means only in the Brahma-world. "One whose nature is not to return" means one whose nature it is not to return again and again from that Brahma-world by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Therefore he said: "one whose nature is not to come back by way of the various wombs and destinations" (*yonigati*).

"One who practices partially fulfills a portion" means that the "portion" (*padesa*) refers to the three lower paths, which constitute a single part of the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth.
One who performs that [path] "fulfills a portion," meaning they bring to completion—that is, accomplish—the three lower fruits, which likewise constitute a single part.
Therefore, it was said: "A person who practices partially is one who has attained stream-entry," and so on. "One who practices fully fulfills the whole."

By fulfilling completely—through the aggregate of virtue and so forth, as well as the faculty of faith and so forth—the path to arahantship, which is designated as "complete," one attains and brings forth the complete fruit of arahantship; this is the meaning of "he accomplishes. Therefore it was said:
"The Arahant is called 'one who fulfills' (paripūrakārī)," and so on.
The commentary on the first training rule is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the second training rule and following, 88–91.
Regarding the seventh [rule]: "going from family to family" means going from one family to another. "Two or three [times] at most."
There are two or three existences by way of gods and humans; this is stated according to mixed existences. This expression "two or three" is merely for the sake of the teaching.

Even if one wanders in saṃsāra up to the sixth existence, one remains a *kolaṅkola* (one who goes from family to family). For this very reason it was said: "For he [remains] for two existences... [etc.]...
thus should the alternative here be understood. Or rather, in this context, the word refers to noble families.

The word *kula* means family; because he goes from family to family, he is called *kolaṅkolo*. From the moment of realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), there is no longer birth in a low family; the meaning is that he is reborn only in families of great wealth.

For the word *kula* by itself refers to a noble family, as in such terms as "son of good family" (*kulaputta*). Regarding the term *ekabījī*, here the "seed" refers to the seed of the aggregates (*khandhabīja*).

The "seed of the aggregates" (*khandhabīja*) refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). For a stream-enterer who has one seed of the aggregates remaining, there is one more taking of existence;
he is thus called "one-seeded" (*ekabījī*). Therefore it was said: "He is 'one-seeded' because he has the seed for only one more existence.
As for the phrase "human existence," this is merely a conventional designation used here in the teaching.
It is indeed appropriate to say that he "rebirths in the deva realm.
He is called an *uddhaṃsota* (one who flows upwards) because his stream of craving or his stream of the round of existence flows upwards due to its upward-moving nature;
or, he is an *uddhaṃsota* because the stream of the Path is to be attained by him after going upwards. By way of rebirth-linking, [he goes] to the Akaniṭṭha realm...
"He goes" means one who goes to Akaniṭṭha. "Anywhere whatsoever" means in any place among the Aviha realms and so forth.
"With application" means together with the application known as the volitional formations of insight-knowledge; the meaning is "with a great application of insight.
"Upahacca" (having reached) has the sense of "having approached. By this, both the passing beyond the midpoint and the departure at the time of death are included.
Because he exists [at that stage], it is said: "But he who, among those with a lifespan of a thousand eons in the Aviha realm," and so forth;

thus one who attains parinibbāna after having passed the midpoint of his lifespan is called an "upahacca-parinibbāyī" (one who attains parinibbāna after the middle). He is of three kinds: he is of three kinds according to whether his knowledge is sharp, middling, or dull.
Therefore, it was said: "Among those with a lifespan of a thousand eons," and so forth.

"Having applied oneself with faith as the primary factor" means: having applied oneself by way of the predominance of faith, thinking, "If it is possible to produce the supramundane path through faith, I shall produce it," and then establishing insight (vipassanā).

"One who has applied oneself with wisdom as the primary factor" means: having applied oneself by making wisdom the primary factor, thinking, "If it is possible through wisdom, I shall produce the supramundane path."
Extending the aforementioned eightfold classification to those who are "from family to family" (*kolaṃkola*) and "with seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*), he said:

"Likewise, there are those who go from family to family and those with seven births at most. By the method already stated, this means there are eight types of *kolaṃkola* and eight types of *sattakkhattuparama*.
In that context, "seven births at most" refers to the taking up of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) in seven future existences; beyond that, an eighth [birth] does not occur.
"One who does not take up existence again is 'one who has seven births at most' (*sattakkhattuparama*). These names were given by the Blessed One according to the very names he had assigned;
they arose for those born into the noble lineage just as names are given to children by their parents.

For it is when one has reached this much of a stage that one is called a 'single-seeded' (*ekabījī*), this much a 'family-to-family' (*kolaṅkola*), and this much a 'seven-births-at-most'—thus [it was] said by the Blessed One."

Their names have been mentioned. However, there is no fixed rule that this one is a "single-seeder" (*ekabījī*), this one is "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkolo*), and this one is "one who has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparamo*).
What, then, determines this distinction among them? Some elders say it is "the prior cause" (*pubbahetu*) that determines it;
some say it is the first path; some say it is the three higher paths; and some say it is the insight (*vipassanā*) pertaining to those three paths.

In that regard, if one asserts that "the prior cause determines [the result]," it follows that the first path has already established its decisive support (*upanissaya*), while the statement that "the three subsequent paths arise without such support" would be contradicted.

If one asserts that "the first path determines [the result]," it follows that the three subsequent paths are rendered purposeless. If one asserts that "the three subsequent paths determine [the result],"...
One would fall into the position that the three higher paths have already arisen even before the first path has arisen.
However, the statement that "insight determines the [attainment of] the three paths" is logical. For if the insight for the three higher paths is powerful, one is called an "ekabījī";
if it is weaker than that, a "kolaṃkola"; and if it is weaker than that, a "sattakkhattuparama."
For some stream-enterers have an inclination toward the round of existence and delight in the round; they repeatedly move within and are seen within that very round.

Such people include the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the female lay follower Visākhā, the divine sons Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha, the divine son Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka the king of the gods, and the divine son Nāgadatta—all these individuals had inclinations toward the round.
Those who delight in the round (saṃsāra) will, starting from the beginning, purify the six heavenly worlds, abide in Akaniṭṭha, and then attain final Nibbāna;

these are not included here. Nor are only these [excluded]; likewise, one who attains Arahantship after wandering among humans for seven more times, or one who, having been reborn in the heavenly worlds, wanders from one state to another among the gods for seven times—[these are also not included].

He attains Arahantship. These [other types] are not included here; rather, it is one who, having wandered through births among gods at one time and among humans at another, eventually attains Arahantship who is included here.

Therefore, it should be understood that the term "one who has seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparama) is stated here as the name for the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) who undergoes eight mixed existences.
Because of the statement, "Having come to this world only once," among the five types of *sakadāgāmins*, four are excluded and only one is taken.
For some, having attained the fruit of *sakadāgāmin* here, attain final nibbāna right here;

some, having attained it here, attain final nibbāna in the world of the gods; some, having attained it in the world of the gods, attain final nibbāna right there; and some, [having attained it] in the world of the gods...
Having reached this [state] and being reborn here, he attains final nibbāna. These four types are not included here.

However, it should be understood that only one who, having reached this state, dwells in the world of the devas for the duration of his lifespan and then, being reborn here again, attains final nibbāna, is included here.
Now, in order to show its classification, he said: "But in the three liberations," and so forth. Regarding this once-returner (sakadāgāmin):
What is the distinction between [the once-returner] and the one-seeded (ekabījin)? For the one-seeded there is only one rebirth-linking, while for the once-returner there are two rebirth-linkings;
this is their distinction. One whose taints are destroyed and who is liberated by the void liberation is fourfold according to the mode of practice;
likewise with the signless and the desireless liberations. Thus, there are twelve types of Arahants.
He said: “Just as it is for once-returners, so too should twelve [types] of arahants be understood. The eighth, ninth, and tenth [discourses] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the second *Sikkhā-sutta* and others is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Saṅkavā-sutta*.
92. One who bears and carries out the burden of new construction and other duties connected with the monastery is a *bhārahāra*.

For this very reason it is said: "He establishes new dwellings and maintains those that are old. Because they are to be trained in, they are *sikkhā*; or because one goes by means of them, they are *padāni* (steps). Thus, training itself as steps are "training-steps" (*sikkhāpadāni*). Therefore he said: "By those reckoned as training..."
"By means of words. "He shows" means he shows by way of direct perception; he makes it manifest and clarifies it, making it as evident as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.
"He causes to grasp" means that while those teachings are being attended to by the mind and thoroughly penetrated by view, he causes them to be taken up.
"He encourages" means he generates enthusiasm for concentration. "By means of the qualities already attained" refers to that teaching.
And by means of the personal effort (*paccattapurisakāra*) based on that, he purifies them through the qualities they have realized.

"He purifies" means he makes their mental continuum radiant by removing the stains of defilements such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). "He speaks very gently" means he speaks having made it exceedingly subtle.
"Transgression" (*accaya*) is said to mean "offense" (*aparādha*), referring to the overstepping that occurs after having crushed the good boundary (*sādhumariyāda*).
Alternatively, it is called *accaya* because one goes beyond (*acceti*) or transgresses by means of it; it is the unwholesome state (*akusaladhamma*) that causes the occurrence of transgression.

That very same thing is called "offense" (*aparādha*) because one commits an offense (*aparajjhati*) by means of it; for it proceeds by overcoming the person who is committing the offense. Therefore he said: "Having transgressed..."
"Having overcome [it], it proceeds. Regarding "let him accept," the meaning is "let him receive by way of forbearance";
thus he said, "let him endure. Regarding "the escape from the world with its devas," he is called *ariya* because he is to be sought after (*araṇīya*);
thus he said, "in the discipline of the Noble One," meaning "in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. While establishing the discourse in terms of individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), although...

The statement “this is growth” was initiated by way of a reference to the Dhamma; nevertheless, while delivering the teaching, he spoke of it as a reference to the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), saying, “he enters upon restraint. Thus is the construction.
The commentary on the Saṅkavā Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Samaṇavagga is finished.
(10) 5. The Loṇakapalla-vagga 1.
Commentary on the Accāyika-sutta.
93. Regarding the first [section] of the fifth: "atipātikāni" means they should be performed quickly.

As for "karaṇīyāni," he says "avassakiccāni" because here the suffix -anīya should be understood in the sense of necessity (avaśya). "Nikkhantasetaṅkurāni" means white sprouts that have emerged from the seed.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Accāyika-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Paviveka-sutta* 94.

In the second [sutta], "sāṇa" refers to those produced from *sāṇa* (hemp) fibers. "Mixed *sāṇa*" (*missasāṇāni*) means those that are not made of flax (*masāṇāni*). "Eraka-grass and so forth" refers to *eraka* grass and similar materials.
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of mats, *kacika*, plantain leaves, cloth, and so forth.
For garments made from *eraka* grass and the like are called "coarse rags" (*chavadussa*) because they are wretched cloths. "Kuṇḍaka" refers to a thin preparation of rice.

"The five types of misconduct" (*pañca dussīlyāni*) refers to the five beginning with the taking of life. "The four taints" (*cattāro āsavā*) refers to the four taints beginning with the taint of sensual desire.
"Attained the pinnacle of virtue" means either by virtue or having reached the pinnacle of virtue.
The commentary on the *Paviveka-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Sarada-sutta*.

95. "In the third [watch], when it has become clear" means when it has become distant. And since this state of distance occurs for the sky through the disappearance of clouds, he said, "when it has become distant through the disappearance of clouds.
For that very reason, it is said: "in the clear sky, free from clouds.
"Ascending into the sky" means reaching up toward the atmosphere; by this, the state of the young sun is shown. When it has not yet risen too high...

For "Ādicca" is a designation for the young sun. "He has no fetter of two kinds" means that for this noble disciple who has attained the first jhāna, there is no fetter of either the lower or the higher type.
But why is it said that he has no higher fetter as well? Because here, only the abandonment of the lower fetters is intended.

He said, "The other [fetters] also," and so forth; the meaning is that the other fetters belonging to the higher realm (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are said not to exist because they are incapable of bringing one back to this world by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For all Noble Ones (*ariya*) who have attained jhāna, even those reborn in the Brahma-world, do not reappear in the lower realms;
and even when they arise in progressively higher states, they do so only up to the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavagga*).
Having attained [Arahatta] there, they are not born anywhere else; having attained Arahatship right there, they attain Parinibbāna. For this very reason it was said:
"In this sutta, one who does not return by means of jhāna (jhānānāgāmī) is described. Indeed, because one does not return to the lower realms by way of jhāna, one is called a jhānānāgāmī.
The commentary on the Sarada Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Parisā Sutta 96.
In the fourth [sutta], "those who are addicted to abundance" (*paccayabāhulika*) refers to those who have set out for the sake of an abundance of requisites such as robes and so forth.

Because they have not yet abandoned craving, they take up and grasp various kinds of requisites in great quantity; thus they are "abundant" (*bahula*), and being so, they are "addicted to abundance" (*bāhulika*), just as one is called a "purifier" (*venayika*).
They are "engaged in abundance" because they are occupied with a profusion of requisites; thus, they are said to be "practicing for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth.
Because they lack reverence for the training, they grasp it loosely and not firmly; hence they are "slack" (*sāthalikā*). The term *sithila* is a neuter abstract noun.
The derivation of the word *sāthalikā* should be understood by means of the word *sathala*, which has the same meaning as *sithila*.

"In the sense of descending" means in the sense of going downwards; the meaning is "by way of being lower-fettered. "Laid down the burden" means those who have set aside their burden and abandoned their exertion.
"Seclusion from the substrata" is Nibbāna. "Both kinds of energy" refers to both bodily and mental energy.
"Those among whom strife has arisen" (*bhaṇḍanajātā*); this is stated by placing the qualifier after the noun (*paranipāta*).
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, showing the meaning by means of placing the qualifier first, it says:

"those who have given rise to brawling" (*jātabhaṇḍanā*). The same method applies here as well in the case of "those in whom strife has arisen" (*kalahajātā*), meaning that strife has arisen among them.
"The preliminary stage of strife" refers to undesirable actions that serve as the cause of strife, its counterparts, and its similitudes. "By way of seizing with the hands," and so forth.

Having become angry and grasping one another by the hands, they fall into dispute—characterized by contradictory speech such as "This is the Dhamma" and "This is not the Dhamma"—through means such as idle chatter and the seizing of property;
thus they are "fallen into dispute" (*vivādapannā*). Therefore he said, "They have fallen into contradictory speech.
Alternatively, because it resides in the mouth, speech is intended here by the word "mouth"; thus he said, "Harsh words are the arrows of the mouth."
Although there is a difference between these two groups in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), their diversity is difficult for ordinary people to discern;
rather, they remain as if extremely well-mingled, like milk and water mixed together. Thus it is said:
"The elements are like milk and water. Just as milk and water blend with one another and do not remain separate, but become a single unity—
The meaning is that mental states have reached a state of unity by way of harmony, just as [water] becomes one.

Having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), looking with eyes that are like those of a friend, he said, "with peaceful eyes of loving-kindness" (*upasantehi mettacakkhūhi*); for eyes that reveal affection are called "loving eyes.
He speaks of a powerful joy (*pīti*) caused by the condition of gladness when he says, "joy arises in one who is gladdened" (*pamuditassa pīti jāyati*).
"Fivefold rapture arises" means that rapture arises in five modes, distinguished as "slight" (khuddika) and so forth.
"With a rapturous mind" means with a mind gladdened by that rapture; the meaning is: with a mind saturated by sublime surges of rapture that bring about tranquility.
"Free from distress" means having the distress [of the defilements] stilled through their removal from a distance.
Thinking, "By what water was this mountain region split open? he said, "It is called a *kandara*," and so forth.
Because it produces a river through the flow of water following its natural slope, it is also called a "river-glen" (*nadikuñja*). The clefts are the rivers that wind along.
"For eight months" refers to the eight months of the winter and summer seasons. The small channels carrying water are like branches; thus they are called "branches" (*sākhā*).
The term *khuddakasobbha* (small pools) and *kusobbha* (little pools) is formed by changing the vowel *o* to *u*.
Those places where water, having come from a higher elevated area, both stands and flows away are *kusobbhas*, that is, small pits.
"Small rivers" refers to small streams issuing from the foothills of mountains.
The commentary on the *Parisā-sutta* is concluded.
5–7. Commentary on the first *Ājānīya-sutta* and following, §§97–99.
Regarding the fifth [sutta]: "suitable" (*anucchavika*) means fit for the king’s use. "By the symmetry of the limbs such as the hands and feet" means...
It is called the "limb of the king" because of the symmetry of its parts, such as hands and feet, or because it is a constituent part of the king's army.
It is called *āhuna* because it should be brought and offered; thus he says, "alms-food reckoned as an offering," meaning that in substance the two terms are one.
This is a designation for that which should be brought even from afar and given to those possessed of virtue. Furthermore, "alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) is merely an illustration.
“Āhuna” is a designation for the four requisites, such as robes and so forth, which are to be brought and offered.
One who is worthy of that is “āhuneyyo. Because he makes the acceptance of those things highly fruitful, he is “fit to receive” (paṭiggaṇhituṃ yutto), meaning he is suitable to accept them.
Regarding “the meal for guests”: it refers to hospitality provided for dear and agreeable kinsmen and friends who have arrived from all directions and quarters.

Regarding the food prepared for guests: setting aside such distinguished guests, it is proper to give that to the Saṅgha alone, and it is the Saṅgha alone who is fit to receive it. For there is no guest equal to the Saṅgha;
indeed, he appears only once after the passing of an entire Buddha-interval, or sometimes even after the passing of incalculable eons.
And he is endowed with qualities such as being dear and agreeable that are not intermingled [with their opposites].

Thus, he is worthy of hospitality because it is fitting to give him hospitality and fitting to receive hospitality from him; hence he is "worthy of hospitality" (*pāhuneyya*). This is the intended meaning here:
"Relatives and friends who have gone abroad meet again after no long time, and their mutual affection remains unstable; but it is not so with the Noble Saṅgha."
"Therefore, the Saṅgha alone is worthy of hospitality.
It is called *dakkhiṇā* because by means of it beings prosper with the desired attainments;
it is a gift given out of faith in the next world. It is "worthy of that *dakkhiṇā*" (*dakkiṇeyya*), or "conducive to *dakkhiṇā*," because it produces great fruit.
He is "one worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyya) because he purifies [the donor].
He is "one to whom the añjali-gesture is to be made" (añjalikaraṇīya) because it is here that those seeking merit should perform the añjali-gesture.

Alternatively, he is "one to whom the añjali-gesture is to be made" because he is worthy of the añjali-gesture performed by the entire world, placing both hands upon the head. Therefore, he said: "he is suitable for the raising of the añjali."
Although it is stated as "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in the Pāḷi, it is called "unsurpassed" because there is nothing superior to it;
and showing that there is also nothing equal to it, he said "incomparable" (*asadisa*). It protects (*tāyati*) or guards the sown seed by making it yield great fruit;
or, it is a "field" (*khettam*) because seeds are scattered (*khipanti*) or sown therein—such as a rice-paddy—and it is like a field.

A field; a field for merits, a merit-field. For just as the place where a king or a minister’s rice or barley grows is called "the king’s rice-field" or "the barley-field," so too the Saṅgha is the place where all the world’s merits grow.
Indeed, it is by depending on the Saṅgha that various kinds of welfare and happiness conducive to the world arise.
Meritorious deeds flourish [therein]; therefore, the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. The remainder is easy to understand.
The sixth and seventh [suttas] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the first *Ājānīya-sutta* and the others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta 100.
In the eighth [verse], "new" means newly woven. Therefore it is said: "It is spoken of with reference to its making.

"Cloth made of flax" refers to a garment made of flax such as hemp (*sāṇa*) and so forth. "Discolored" means faded in color. "Painful to the touch" means coarse to the touch. "It is of little value" means...
It is of little value. Even when valued too highly, it is worth only a kahāpaṇa.

"Of middling use" means it is middling by way of the time of its use; for even during the middle period of use—having passed beyond newness but not yet reached old age—it remains discolored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value.
Even when valued too highly, it is worth only half [a kahāpaṇa].
But in times of scarcity, it is worth half a māsaka or a kākāṇikā. "Wiping the mortar" means wiping the black mortar.
"New" refers to one who is below five years of ordination; even if sixty years old by birth, such a person is still considered "new.
"By way of ugliness" means by way of ugliness both in the color of the body and in the quality of one's virtues. For a person of immoral conduct lacks luster in the midst of the assembly.
Even the beauty of his physical form does not arise; as for the beauty of his virtues, there is nothing at all to be said.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that he is ugly both because of the ugliness of his physical form and because of the absence of the beauty of virtue.
"But those who [belong] to him" means those who attend upon him, such as his supporters, kinsmen, friends, and so forth.
"Of them" means of those persons who serve six teachers, like those with wrong view;
and like Kokālika and others who served Devadatta, that service leads to harm and suffering for a long time.
"Middle" refers to the period from five years up to nine years [of seniority]. "Elder" refers to [seniority] from ten years onward.
"Thera" means an elder. "Evam āhaṃsu" means they speak thus. "Kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ" means "what is the purpose of what you, a fool, have said?
"Tathārūpaṃ" means of such a kind, of such a nature, or of such a character—that which constitutes the grounds for an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
"Tīhi kappāsaaṃsūhi suttaṃ kantitvā katavatthaṃ" means a cloth made by spinning thread using three cotton fibers; that is, having taken three cotton fibers, [the cloth] spun from that thread...
Woven fine cloth—when newly woven, it is priceless; in its stage of use, it is worth twenty or thirty thousand;
when worn out, it is still worth eight or ten thousand.
"That belongs to them" means that for those such as the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who cultivate it, that cultivation leads to their welfare for a long time.
It leads to happiness. For there is no measure of the beings who have been liberated until this very day by relying on the Fully Enlightened One alone;

likewise, there is no measure of the beings who have gone to heaven by relying on the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and the remaining eighty great disciples, nor even of those beings who have followed their example until this very day.
There is indeed no measure [of its value]. "It goes to be held" means that the word of that Great Elder,
which is based on the meaning, goes to be held and established upon the head and the heart as the supreme limbs— just as Kāsika cloth goes to be held and placed within a perfumed casket.
The commentary on the Potthakasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Loṇakapallasutta 101.
In the ninth [verse], "in whatever way one performs an action" means in whichever manner one performs unwholesome actions such as the killing of living beings.
"It performs [an action]. It experiences the result"—by this restriction, it is shown that in the establishment of karma, there is no non-occurrence of its result.

For this very reason, he said, "For it is not possible," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "this being so" (*evaṃ sante*), he says "when this is so" (*evaṃ sante*) because the locative case is used in the sense of a locus.
"By the cessation of the volitional consciousness" (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇanirodhena*) means by bringing about the state of the karmic consciousness being subject to non-arising in the future.

“‘This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, not exempt from this [condition]’—by such passages, the contemplation of the body’s aspects such as impurity and impermanence is called ‘development of the body. Thus he said: ‘By that development reckoned as the contemplation of the body.
In the phrase ‘of lust and so forth,’ the word ‘and so forth’ (ādi) should be understood as including hatred and delusion. ‘Lust, friend, is a maker of measure; hatred is a maker of measure...’”

"For delusion is a cause of measurement; that has been abandoned by the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Thus it was said. For just as there is water at the foot of a mountain from a rotten leaf—appearing black to those looking down from a hundred fathoms—so too...
It appears as if very deep; even for one measuring it by taking hold of a pole or a rope, there is not even enough space to lift a foot from the ground.
In the same way, as long as lust and the other defilements have not yet arisen in a certain person, that individual cannot be identified;
he appears like a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner. But when—

When lust and the other [defilements] arise, one is then known as "lustful," "hateful," or "deluded. Thus, those states such as lust arise as if showing the measure of the person by saying, "This is how much he is";
therefore, they are called "measure-makers" (*pamāṇakaraṇā*). "To cause to live" means to make [the person] a winner of the wealth of the Conqueror (*jinadhana*).
"He" refers to the king or the high minister. "His" refers to the one who is entreating with palms joined in reverence. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Loṇakapallasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Paṃsudhovakasutta* 102.

In the tenth [sutta], "the fault of not having been scrubbed" (*anīhatadosa*) means that the large black specks have not been removed. "Not having had the stains removed" (*anapanītakasāva*) means that the fine black specks have not been eliminated. "Merely brought forth" (*pahaṭamatta*) means merely fetched.
A consciousness arisen by way of the ten courses of wholesome action is simply consciousness;

the consciousness of the eight attainments that serve as the basis for insight and the consciousness of insight itself are a consciousness superior to that [ordinary] consciousness, and thus it is called "higher consciousness" (*adhicitta*). Therefore, he says: "Higher consciousness means the consciousness of serenity and insight.
"Of one who is devoted" (*anuyuttassa*) means of one who is devotedly engaged in the sense of producing what has not yet arisen and in the sense of increasing what has already arisen.
In this context, the meaning is "one who is properly engaged. Furthermore, here, even one who goes out after having wandered for alms before the meal and returned from the alms-round after the meal,
taking his sitting mat and thinking, "I shall practice the duty of a recluse at such-and-such a tree root, forest thicket, or mountain cave," and having gone there,
[removes himself] from the place of sitting or standing by means of his hands or feet—
Even while removing grass and leaves, he is indeed devoted to higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).

But having sat down, washed his hands and feet, taken up the primary meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*), and applied himself to meditation—even before reaching absorption (*appanā*) through that meditation—he is still "devoted to higher consciousness," both because of that meaning and because of the conventional usage of that term.
He is "endowed with mind" (*cittasampanno*) because he is possessed of a mind of Dhamma.
"Of a wise nature" means having the character of a wise person.

"With reference to sensual pleasures" means with reference to objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*). Alternatively, "thought connected with sensual pleasure" (*kāmavitakka*) is thought associated with what is termed sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

"Ill will" (*byāpāda*) is so called because the mind is corrupted (*byāpajjati*) by it; it is hatred (*dosa*). "Harmfulness" (*vihiṃsā*) is that by which beings are harmed, or the act of harming itself.
Or, "this belongs to them" is *vihiṃsā*; this is a designation for that evil state which is the opposite of compassion and occurs in the manner of harming others.
"A thought arisen with reference to relatives" is a thought arisen by way of attachment rooted in the household life directed toward relatives.
"A thought arisen with reference to the country"—here too the method is the same. "O, may... [etc.]
"Thinking of me... and so on: the thought that has arisen as "Oh, may others not despise me;
may they not think of me with contempt, but rather hold me in high esteem, like a stone parasol"—this is the thought that has arisen.
"The ten thoughts that are defilements of insight" refers to the thoughts that have arisen concerning the ten defilements of insight, beginning with illumination (obhāsa).
"Having residual thought of phenomena" (*avasiṭṭhadhammavitakko*) means that for this person there remain thoughts concerning phenomena; this refers to insight-concentration (*vipassanāsamādhi*).
"Not attained to one-pointedness" (*na ekaggabhāvappatto*) means not having reached the state of one-pointedness. It is called *ekodi* because it "rises as one" (*ekaṃ udetīti*);

the meaning is that it rises as something preeminent and excellent because it is not overcome by opposing states. For even what is excellent is called "one" (*eko*) in the world, by virtue of its being concentrated upon a single object.
This is a designation for the mind that has become active. The state of being one-pointed is *ekodibhāva*; this is a designation for one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).
"Internal certainty" (*niyakajjhatta*) is a designation for one's own mental continuum. "Internal range" (*gocarajjhatta*) here refers to Nibbāna.
Therefore he said: "It stands solely within the range of Nibbāna. It sits well means [it remains] in opposition to the factors adverse to concentration (*samādhi*).
“Settling the defilements, it settles well. “It becomes one-pointed” means that through the attainment of a state free from distraction, it becomes one-pointed.
“It is rightly directed” means that it is directed rightly and properly in such a way that it is well-fixed upon the object.

Regarding the phrase “of that which is to be realized by direct knowledge,” although it should have been stated as “to be realized by direct knowledge” (*abhiññāya sacchikaraṇīyassa*), it is here simply called “direct knowledge” (*abhiññā*).
However, by the elision of the letter *ya*, the description "making manifest" (*kālakiriyā*) is established again; thus he says, "having directly known, it is to be made manifest.

Or rather, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "to be realized through direct knowledge" (*abhiññāsacchikaraṇīya*) refers to the realization through higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), such as the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*), which consists of the actual experiencing of the modes of psychic power and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "he reaches the state of being capable of witnessing," here [it refers to] that for whom there is direct perception.
There is such a person; he is a witness (*sakkhī*). The state of being capable of being a witness is "witness-capacity" (*sakkhibhabbatā*); what is meant is "the state of becoming a witness.
He is both a witness and capable, thus he is a "capable witness" (*sakkhibhabbo*). For he is capable of the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*) and the like, and he is a witness therein;
thus he is a "capable witness. His state is "witness-capacity"; the meaning is that one attains this.

Regarding the phrase "the classification of the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), etc.": here, *abhiññāpādā* means the bases for direct knowledge, and *abhiññāpādakajjhāna* means the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge.
It should be understood that by the word "etc. (*ādi*), both Arahantship and the insight (vipassanā) leading to Arahantship are included.

For this very reason, it is said in the *Madhupindika-aṭṭhakathā*: "In the expression 'mindfulness as the basis of mindfulness,' [it refers to] the cause of mindfulness. And what is the cause here? It should be understood as either direct knowledge or the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge; finally, however, it is either Arahantship or the insight leading to Arahantship that is the cause."

For that which is designated as "the state of being capable" (sakkhibhabbatā) in various instances—namely, the experience of the various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha) and so forth—has direct knowledge (abhiññā) as its cause.

Alternatively, if the experience of the various kinds of psychic power and so forth is itself direct knowledge, then the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññāpādaka-jjhāna) is its cause.
Finally, for the sixth direct knowledge, however, either Arahantship or insight (vipassanā) is the cause.

For Arahantship is the cause for one who, having established a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, thinking, "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?", brings about direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
And this [longing] is not common [to all]; however, insight (*vipassanā*) is the cause for Arahantship by way of its being common [to all].
For in this sutta, the sixth direct knowledge is stated by way of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore it was said:
"And here, 'the destruction of the taints,' etc., should be understood as stated by way of the attainment of the fruit.
The commentary on the Paṃsudhovaka Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Nimitta Sutta (103).
In the eleventh [sutta], those things by which the fruit is marked—being as if cast into the place of its arising—are the *nimittas*.
Therefore he said, "three causes. Regarding the phrase "from time to time" (*kālena kālaṃ*), here "at time" (*kālena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative.

"Kāla" is a term denoting an object of use; thus he says "at the proper time, at the proper time. "Should be brought to mind" means they should be brought to the heart, that is, they should be generated—this is the meaning.
Here, concentration itself, characterized by the mode of being composed, is called the "sign of concentration";
thus he says, "For one-pointedness is here stated to be the sign of concentration. Regarding the phrase, "That state might lead the mind to indolence": here...
“There is a possibility” is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that there exists a cause for that mind of development to lead to indolence.
Or, the meaning is that there exists a possibility—that is, a cause—for that act of attention to lead the mind to indolence.
Therefore he said, “A cause exists,” and so forth. “Speed of knowledge” refers to [the speed] regarding formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The speed of wisdom proceeding by way of impermanence and so forth.
Whatever charcoal vessel is suitable for heating gold is intended here as a "torch," hence he says "a pan of coals.
"Should prepare" means he should make ready it in such a way that the gold placed therein is heated. "Should kindle" means...
“Should take up” means “should kindle. Therefore he said: “There, [he would have them] take up coals... and so forth.
“Or he should throw it into a crucible” means he should throw it into a heated one. “He examines” means he observes.
The commentary on the *Nimitta-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Group on the Salt-Crystal is finished.
The Second Fifty is finished.
3. The Third Fifty.
(11) 1. Sambodhavagga 1–3.
Commentary on the Pubbeva-sambodha Sutta and others, 104–106.
In the first [sutta] of the third [vagga], “prior to full enlightenment” (*pubbeva sambodhā*): “full enlightenment” (*sambodha*) refers to the knowledge (*ñāṇa*) within the four paths.
“Because he awakened correctly by himself through this,” means that it was prior even to that; hence he said, “only after having attained the Noble Path.

Regarding the phrase “while he was still a bodhisatta”: just as a lotus that has emerged from the water and reached full maturity is called a “flowering lotus” because it will inevitably blossom upon contact with the rays of the sun.
Because he has thus received a prophecy in the presence of the Buddhas, he will certainly awaken after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) without obstacle;
therefore, he is a "being destined for awakening" (bodhisatta). Thus it is said: "Of one who is indeed a being destined for awakening... while still undertaking [the practice].
Or else, regarding that awakening (bodhi) which consists of the knowledge of the four paths: "When indeed shall I attain that awakening?"—[it is of such a one that this is said].
One who practices while aspiring [for enlightenment] is called a *bodhisatta* because they are attached (*satta*) or clinging (*āsatta*) to enlightenment (*bodhi*). Therefore he said:
"Of one who is indeed attached (*satta*), that is, clinging (*lagga*), to full enlightenment (*sambodhi*).

Alternatively, *bodhi* means knowledge (*ñāṇa*), in the sense that "one awakens by means of this"; thus, a being (*satta*) possessing enlightenment (*bodhi*) is a *bodhisatta*. This refers to the first term...
By means of eliding the latter member of the compound, as in the term "ñāṇasatto," the meaning is: "a being who possesses knowledge, who possesses wisdom, who is wise.
Indeed, from the moment he made his formal aspiration (abhinīhāra) at the feet of the Buddhas, that being was already wise and not a blind fool;

thus he is a "bodhisatta" (wisdom-being). This refers to one who is truly a bodhisatta by virtue of the name arising from such qualities. That which is enjoyed is "assāda" (gratification); it is happiness.
And because it has the characteristic of having the aspect of gratification, he said: "‘Taste’ means the sweet aspect.

Nibbāna is called "the removal of desire and lust" (*chandarāgavinaya*) and "the abandoning of desire and lust" (*chandarāgappahāna*) because therein desire and lust are both restrained and abandoned. Therefore, he said: "Nibbāna," and so forth.
In that context, the word "having come to" (*āgamma*) refers to the making of an object by that person who restrains and abandons lust.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). The second and third [suttas] are of plain meaning (*uttānattha*).
The commentary on the *Pubbevaṃsambodha-sutta* and others is finished.
4–9. Commentary on the *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa-sutta* and others.
107–112. In the fourth [case], "the state of recluseship" (*sāmañña*) refers to the Noble Path;

because it is to be sought after (*araṇīya*) and approached (*upagantabba*), it is the "goal of the state of recluseship" (*sāmaññattha*). Thus he said: "The goal of the state of recluseship is the fourfold Noble Fruit.

The same method applies here to "the goal of the state of brahminhood" (*brahmaññattha*). Therefore he said: "The other is a synonym for that very thing. It is simply the state of recluseship, consisting of the Noble Path.

Or, because it is worthy of being sought after (*araṇīya*), he said, "The four paths by way of the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*). The fifth and subsequent [sections] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the *Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta* and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Dutiyanidānasutta*.
113. Regarding "kamma leading to the turning away" (*vivaṭṭagāmikamma*) in the tenth [chapter], this refers to kamma that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the turning away.
Concerning the phrase "he turns back that," it is said that "that" (*taṃ*) refers to the misapprehension (*parāmāsa*) of the result (*vipāka*);
thus, "he turns back that" means he turns back by overcoming that result. Now, it is not only the result that is referred to by the word "that."
Then, it should be understood that there is a misapprehension regarding those phenomena which are the basis for desire and lust, as well as their result;
thus he said, "Or when by that," and so forth. "Those very phenomena" refers to those phenomena which are the basis for desire and lust.
"Having become disillusioned, he sees" means that having become disillusioned with the defilements, he sees them after making them manifest and clear.
The commentary on the Second Nidāna Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Sambodha Vagga is finished.
(12) 2. The Āpāyika Vagga.
1. Commentary on the Āpāyikasutta 114.

Regarding the first [verse] of the second [sutta]: because they have the habit of being reborn in the states of misery (apāya), those who go to the states of misery are called *āpāyika*. Thus it is said:
"They will go to the states of misery, therefore they are *āpāyika*. Others who lead the holy life (*brahmacārin*) are well-clad, well-dressed, and carry bowls made of *sumbhaka* clay.

Seeing those who maintain their livelihood by wandering for alms in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, he himself behaves in such a manner that he is as if giving the promise, "I am a celibate practitioner" (brahmacārī).
Thus it is said: "One who claims to be a celibate practitioner is a mere pretender to being a celibate practitioner.
Furthermore, when one says, "I too am a bhikkhu," yet enters into the Uposatha observances and so forth [only nominally], [he is likewise a pretender].
He indeed makes a declaration as a *brahmacārī*, likewise when taking property belonging to the Saṅgha. Therefore he said: “Or of them... thus declaring.
“He reviles” means he reviles him with such words as, “You are not an ascetic; you are one who merely declares himself an ascetic,” and so forth.
“He scorns” means [he says], “Do you think, ‘Let it be so, I am a shaven-headed ascetic,’ yet now I shall establish your state of being a non-ascetic,” and so forth.
He speaks while reviling.
Even the enjoyment of the defilement-desire (kilesakāma) is included within the object-desire (vatthukāma); and since their enjoyment may occur by way of the defilement-desire, he says:
"of one who indulges in object-desires through the defilement-desire. In the phrase "by the defilement-desire," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent (or instrument).
"There is no fault" means that in the enjoyment of sense objects, there is no disadvantage; the intention is that, on account of that, nothing stands as an obstacle.
"It becomes something to be drunk" means it attains the state of being enjoyed. For this word *pā* has the meaning of "enjoyment," and the suffix *-tabba* functions as an agentive;
thus, the meaning is "one enjoys according to one's desire. "It becomes something to be drunk... [and so forth].
Regarding the phrase "to be enjoyed," here too the meaning should be understood according to the agent alone.
The commentary on the Āpāyikasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Dullabhasutta.

115. In the second [verse], acting in a manner corresponding to the benefit performed by another, knowing and feeling the benefit done to oneself as a benefit, one is called "grateful" (*kataññū*) and "thankful" (*katavedī*). Thus he said, "By this, a benefit has been done for me," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Dullabhasutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Appameyyasutta*.

116. "Easily measurable" means that just as the measure of a small amount of water is easily grasped, so too, the measure of one endowed with the aforementioned unwholesome factors such as "restless" and so forth is easily grasped; thus, it is "easily measurable.
"Difficult to measure" means that just as the measure of the great ocean is difficult to grasp, [so too is the measure of one endowed with wholesome qualities].
In the same way, for one endowed with the factors of virtue shown by such terms as "unagitated," a measure is grasped through suffering;
he comes to be called "one who is a non-returner" or "one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, he is to be measured by that suffering.
"One cannot measure him" means that just as it is impossible to grasp the measure of space, so too it is impossible to grasp the measure of one whose taints are destroyed.
Because it cannot be measured by that, it is "immeasurable" (appameyya).
Because it is empty due to the absence of essence, it is like a reed; thus he says, "puffed up" (unnaḷo) means "one with a raised reed. What is meant is "one whose empty conceit has arisen.
Therefore he says, "the meaning is: standing having tossed up empty conceit. For [conceit] thinks of one who is superior as "superior."
"Sadiso" (like) refers to being empty specifically in terms of one's conduct. "By way of fickleness" means by way of a fickle nature;

the meaning is "by way of being greedy with craving. "Mukharo" means harsh-mouthed; the meaning is "one of harsh speech. "Vikiṇṇavāco" means one whose speech is scattered, one whose speech is boundless due to idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).
Therefore he said, "one of unrestrained speech," [meaning] even during the day, [he utters] meaningless speech.
"Chatterer" is what is meant. "Devoid of one-pointedness of mind" means lacking access and absorption concentration;
his activity is unstable, like a boat tied in a violent current. "With wandering mind" means having an unstable mind, like a wild animal that has escaped from a trap.
"With unrestrained faculties" means that due to the absence of restraint, his eye and other faculties are unguarded, just as they were in the time of his lay life.
The commentary on the *Appameyya-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Āneñja-sutta* 117.
In the fourth [verse], "one who goes together" (*sahabyo*) means one who moves along with; it refers to one who functions in company. The state of being such is "companionship" (*sahabyatā*).
He said, "It occurs simultaneously," meaning "it arises as a co-existent state.

Since there are statements such as, "Having exhausted the entire lifespan of those deities, he goes even to hell," it appears as if the rebirth in a state of woe (apāya) is being described for one who has passed away from the formless existence (arūpabhava).
To prevent that [misunderstanding], explaining the Blessed One’s intended meaning, he says: "This was spoken with a specific reference..."
He explains the "statement" by saying, "because they are not liberated from the hells and so forth," and so on.

For there is no unwholesome state more powerful than access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). By this, he demonstrates that for those passing away from that realm, access concentration itself is the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Adhippāyo" means that by which one exerts or applies oneself excessively; it refers to an activity to be performed with distinction.
Therefore he said, "excessive application. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Āneñjasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vipattisampadāsutta.

118. Regarding the phrase "given in the fifth [case]," it is said that "giving" is mentioned by way of the category of things to be given (*deyyadhamma*); thus he says, "He speaks with reference to the absence of fruit for what has been given.
But how does he reject the gift of material objects such as food and so forth? This same method applies to the terms "sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) and "offered" (*huta*).
A "great sacrifice" (*mahāyāga*) is a great gift common to all. A "hospitality gift" (*paheṇakasakkāra*) refers to [gifts] for guests.

"Honour should be rendered. "Fruits" refers to both the fruit of benefit (*ānisamsaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*nissandaphala*). "Ripening" (*vipāka*) refers to the fruit of similarity (*sadisaphala*).
"For one standing in the next world, this world does not exist": for one standing in the next world, this world to be obtained through kamma does not exist.
"For one standing in this world, the next world does not exist": for one standing in this world, [the next world] to be obtained through kamma...
"There is no world beyond. He states the reason for this: "All are cut off right there, right where they are.

These beings, wherever they may abide—whether in various realms of existence (*bhava*), modes of birth (*yoni*), or destinies (*gati*)—are cut off right there; they perish through the destruction of the dyad.
"By way of the absence of fruit" means by way of the non-existence of the fruit of proper or improper conduct toward one's mother and father.

When he says, “there is no mother, there is no father,” it is not because a mother and father do not exist, nor because of the absence of right or wrong conduct toward them, for they are evident to the world.
He said, “there are no spontaneously born beings,” in order to show that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble, and not preceded by a moment of destruction. Thus he spoke.
"He says that there are no beings who arise after having passed away. Regarding the phrase "proclaiming what they have realized for themselves through direct knowledge":

those who, by means of their own preeminent wisdom, have made both this world and the other world directly manifest to themselves and proclaim them—by saying "there are none," he indicates the non-existence of omniscient Buddhas.
The commentary on the *Vipattisampadā-sutta* is finished.
6–7. Commentary on the *Apaṇṇaka-sutta*, etc. (119–120).
In the sixth [sutta], "a die possessing six faces" means that there are four faces on its four sides.
"On two sides there are two surfaces"—thus, it is a special kind of die, resembling a gem, possessed of six surfaces for those intent on playing with dice.
The seventh [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Apaṇṇaka-sutta and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the First Discourse on Purity (Paṭhamasoceyyasutta-vaṇṇanā) 121.

In the eighth [discourse], "purity" (*sucibhāva*) refers to the state of being pure through the removal of the impurity of the defilements (*kilesa*), that is, the state of being undefiled; in terms of meaning, it consists of bodily good conduct and so forth.
The commentary on the First Discourse on Purity is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Purity (Soceyyasutta) 122.
Regarding the ninth [verse]: because all misconduct of body has been abandoned by way of its total eradication, it is "pure in body" (*kāyasuci*), or "purity of body" (*kāyasuci*).
Therefore he said, "In the door of the body," and so forth. "Endowed with purity" (*soceyyasampanna*) means being completely purified because the defilements have been subsided.
It is endowed with the attainment of purity. One who has washed away—meaning cleansed by the water of the supreme path—all evil is a "washed-evil-doer" (*ninhātapāpaka*);
that is, one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, he said: "Only one whose taints are destroyed is described.
The commentary on the second discourse on purity is finished.
10. Commentary on the Moneyya Sutta 123.

In the tenth [sutta], "moneyya" refers to the states of a sage (*muni*). Those qualities by which one becomes known as a sage because of his sage-like seclusion for the welfare of both [self and others]—those very factors that constitute the practice leading to the state of a sage are what are called "moneyya.
Or alternatively, these are the "moneyya" of a sage; they are the aforementioned qualities.
Thus it is. In this context, because there is the non-doing of what should not be done with the body and the doing of what should be done;
because there is the knowing of the object designated as "body" by way of such statements as "In this body there are head-hairs," and so forth;

and because there is the thorough understanding of the body exactly as it is—by way of its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—it is through such thorough understanding that [it is called "contemplation of the body"].

Furthermore, the path of insight that has arisen, the abandoning of desire and lust for the body by means of that [path], or the attainment reached after ceasing bodily formations—all these phenomena belonging to the practice of moneyya (sainthood) that proceed by way of the body are called *kāyamoneyya*.
Therefore, to demonstrate that meaning, it is asked: "What is *kāyamoneyya*? It is the threefold wrong conduct of body..."
The Pāḷi has come down thus: “The abandoning of bodily misconduct is bodily integrity (kāyamoneyya);

the threefold good conduct of body is also bodily integrity,” and so forth. Here too, demonstrating the meaning according to that same scriptural method, he said: “The abandoning of the threefold bodily misconduct is called bodily integrity,” and so on.
Now: “What is verbal integrity? The abandoning of the fourfold verbal misconduct is verbal integrity; the fourfold...”

By stating "the same method applies to verbal integrity (vacīmoneyya)" and so forth, he illuminates the meaning expressed in this passage: "verbal good conduct, knowledge of speech as an object, full understanding of speech, the path accompanied by full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for speech, and the attainment of the second jhāna through the cessation of verbal formations.
In that context, both the "coaxing speech" and the "speech of sounds" [are included].

Wisdom that arises directed toward speech is knowledge of speech. Thoroughly understanding that speech from the perspective of its origin and so forth is the full understanding of speech (*vācā-pariññā*).
“What is mental purity (*manomoneyya*)? The abandoning of the threefold misconduct of mind is mental purity; the threefold good conduct of mind; knowledge regarding the object of the mind;
the full understanding of the mind; the path accompanied by full understanding; and the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind.”
Explaining the meaning according to the method set forth in the passage, “The cessation of mental formations is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the mind’s purity,” he said, “Having understood the meaning of the mind’s purity by this same method,” and so forth.
And therein, knowledge that occurs with reference to the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness is knowledge of the mind as its object. From its origination, etc., [of that mind...]
"Thoroughly understanding" is the full understanding of the mind; this is the distinction.
The commentary on the Moneyya Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Āpāyika Vagga is finished.
(13) 3. Kusināra-vagga 1–2. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta, etc. 124–125.
In the first [sutta] of the third [vagga], "bound by the greed of craving" means bound by the fetter of craving. "By the intoxication of craving" means...
By way of craving, one falls into infatuation. "Infatuated" (*mucchita*) means having fallen into infatuation, delusion, and negligence.
"Overwhelmed" (*ajjhopanna*) means overcome. Having been surpassed by craving, one stands as if swallowed, submerged, and finalized.
Therefore he said: "‘Overwhelmed’ means occurring after being swallowed and finalized by craving. "One who does not see the danger" (*anādīnavadassāvī*)...
He does not see even a slight danger in the enjoyment [of food] through its state of being "clinging" and so forth.

"Possessing the wisdom of escape" (nissaraṇapañño) means that regarding the enjoyment of nutriment, he possesses the wisdom that effects the escape from the desire and lust bound up with nutriment—which functions by delimiting its purpose with the words, "only for the maintenance of this body," and so forth; thus he is one possessing the wisdom of escape.
The rest here is self-evident. In the second [sutta], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Kusināra Sutta and others is finished.
3. Commentary on the Gotamakacetiya Sutta.
126. In the third [case], "many" refers to approximately five hundred. It is said that five hundred brahmins, who had mastered the three Vedas, later heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma;
seeing the peril in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, they went forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
Not long after, having mastered the entirety of the Buddha’s word, they attained mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
Relying on their conceit, they said: "Whatever the Blessed One speaks, we understand it immediately.
For the Blessed One says nothing except for the three genders such as the feminine, the four cases beginning with the nominative, and the seven case-endings beginning with the first;
and when he speaks in this way, we have no knots [of doubt] whatsoever."
Having become disrespectful toward the Blessed One, from that time forth they no longer went frequently to attend upon the Blessed One or to listen to the Dhamma.
It was with reference to them that it was said: “It is said, monks, that many brahmin renunciants... do not go to listen to the Dhamma.
“Having taken their word” means having [addressed] that matter by saying, “Is it true, monks? and so forth.
Having questioned them and received the reply from those bhikkhus, "It is true, Blessed One," he accepted it;
for since it was confessed by their own mouths, it is called a "confession by mouth" (*mukhapaṭiññā*).
They did not see either the place where [the thief] had come from or the place where he had gone. Why? Because of ignorance. It is said that they [did not know] of that sleeping man...

They did not understand the meaning. For at that time, even though that discourse was endowed with various methods and the elegance of the teaching, it was as if a cloth of thick, wide silk had been tied over its face and placed before them like a forbidden meal.
And did not the Blessed One spend more than a hundred thousand eons in order to make others understand the Dhamma he himself had taught?
Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons, he attained omniscience; why then does he teach in such a way that they do not understand?
It is for the purpose of breaking their pride. For the Blessed One [thought]:

"These are incapable of realizing the path or the fruit without first uprooting this thicket of pride," and thus he acted to counteract the conceit arising from their reliance on their own learning and mastery of the scriptures.

Having established the occasion for the teaching, the Teacher, skilled in exposition, spoke the Mūlapariyāya Sutta beginning with "The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" in order to break their pride.
They thought, "The Perfectly Enlightened One speaks only that which is appropriate for his mouth, thinking, 'My discourse will lead to liberation.'"
This is stated according to the method of the *vaḷañjanaka-kathā* (the "current" or "usage" discourse) of the Aṅguttara reciters. However, the Majjhima reciters speak thus:
"Furthermore, having heard that sutta taught for the purpose of shattering conceit, those bhikkhus [thought]:
'Indeed, it is that very same earth which the one held by wrong view perceives; yet the learner, the Arahant, and the Tathāgata likewise directly know it. Why...'"
Thinking, "What is this? How is this?", they said, "Previously we understood whatever was spoken by the Blessed One immediately;
but now we neither know nor see the end or the limit of this *Mūlapariyāya*.
Oh, how immeasurable and incomparable are the Buddhas! Thus, like snakes whose fangs have been pulled out, they became humble and attended upon the Buddha.
And they went respectfully to listen to the Dhamma. At that time, the monks seated together in the Dhamma hall initiated this discussion:

"Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas! Those brahmins who had gone forth, so intoxicated by pride and arrogance, have been humbled of their pride by the Blessed One through the teaching of the *Mūlapariyāya*. Hearing this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now."
"In the past as well, I subdued these who were walking with their heads held high by pride," he said, and bringing up the past, he related:
"Once upon a time, monks, a certain world-renowned brahmin lived in Bārāṇasī;
he was a master of the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇṭu and Keta-bhā, the Sakkharappabheda, and the Itihāsa as the fifth."
He was a master of words and grammar, unskilled in none of the Lokāyata or the marks of a Great Man; he taught the mantras to about five hundred young brahmins.
"The wise young men grasp much quickly and reflect upon it well," and with such words he related the Jātaka.
Having heard this, those bhikkhus thought, "In the past too we were ruined by pride," and they became even more thoroughly humbled of their pride.

Having offered [the sacrifice], they became devoted to their own beneficial meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Then, on one occasion, while wandering through the countryside, the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī and stayed at the Gotamaka Shrine;
perceiving that the wisdom of these five hundred bhikkhus had reached maturity, he preached this Gotamaka Sutta. Having heard this sutta, those five hundred bhikkhus, right then and there—
"On that very seat, they attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

"Having directly known" means having directly known, in accordance with reality, the Dhamma to be taught—classified as wholesome and so forth, and classified as the aggregates and so forth—as well as the dispositions, latent tendencies, conduct, inclinations, and other classifications of those to be trained, and the specific manner in which it should be taught to them. These are the five aggregates...
It should be understood that the phrase "the twelve bases," and so forth, is stated here merely as an illustration. "With conditions" (sappaccaya) means having a cause;

the meaning is that it is accompanied by a sign, along with reasons and examples, either according to the inclination of those to be trained, or through a question, or through the arising of a specific occasion.
"Paṭihāriya" is the warding off of lust and the other [defilements]; that itself is a "pāṭihāriya. [The term] "with pāṭihāriya" (sapāṭihāriya) means together with such a miracle.
It is "with a demonstration" (sappāṭihāriya). For the Teacher teaches the Dhamma precisely by way of suppressing lust and the other defilements. Therefore he said:

"Having made it truly with a demonstration by means of warding off opposition. Others, however, say that it is "accompanied by the demonstrations of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction as appropriate," on the grounds that there is no teaching devoid of the demonstration of instruction. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Gotamakacetiya Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta 127.

Regarding the fourth [sutta], "at the time of Āḷāra Kālāma": this means during the lifetime of Āḷāra Kālāma. "Full understanding" (*pariññā*) refers here to the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).
For that [type of full understanding] is indeed transcendence, not the other. Therefore he said: "Full understanding is called transcendence.
And here, the first teacher should be regarded as one who has attained the fine-material-sphere attainments; the second, as one who has attained the immaterial-sphere attainments;
and the third, as the Perfectly Enlightened One. For this has been stated in the *Puggalapaññatti*:
“That teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, but does not proclaim the full understanding of forms, nor the full understanding of feelings—
such a teacher should be regarded as one who has attained the meditative absorptions of the form realm.
That teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures and the full understanding of forms, but does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings...”
“He proclaims: ‘The Teacher is one who has attained the formless-sphere absorptions; the Teacher is to be seen as such.

And this Teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings—he is the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One; he is to be seen as such.”
In that regard, the followers of other sects, knowing their own tenets, would describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures while speaking of the first jhāna;

they would describe the full understanding of forms while speaking of attachment to the formless; and they would describe the full understanding of feeling while speaking of attachment to the non-percipient realm.
Yet they do not even know: "This is the first jhāna," "this is existence in the form realm," or "this is existence in the non-percipient realm."
They do not know. Being unable to explain them, they merely say, "Let us explain.
The Tathāgata, however, explains the full understanding of sensual desires by means of the non-returner path, and the [full understanding] of form and feeling by means of the arahant path.
Thus, in this world, there are three types of teachers: two outsiders and one Fully Enlightened One.
The commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta, §128:
Regarding the fifth [verse], "abhikkanta" means "passed beyond" (atikkanta), and its meaning is "gone away" (vigata); thus he said, "it is seen in the sense of destruction. For that very reason...
For it was stated immediately after [the previous passage]: "The first watch has passed. *Abhikkantataro* means exceedingly more desirable.
And such a thing is called beautiful and auspicious; thus he said, "it is seen in what is beautiful. *Ko* means who—among whom?
Among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth. *Me* means my. *Pādāni* means feet. *Iddhiyā* means by means of this kind of divine power (*deviddhi*). *Yasasā* means...
"With such a retinue and such a following. "Shining" means glowing brightly.
"With a lovely appearance" means with an exceedingly beautiful, desirable, and handsome complexion—that is, the color of the skin and the radiance of the body.
"Illuminating all directions" means shining upon the ten directions, making them one mass of light and one mass of radiance, like the moon or the sun.
The meaning of the verse: *Abhirūpe* means in one who is of noble form, endowed with excellent form. *Abbhanumodanā* means in rejoicing. *Idha pana* refers to this phrase:
"at the end of the night" (*abhikkantāya rattiyā*). *Tenā* is because it is a beautiful expression.
Alternatively, the word *abhikkanta* here should be understood as "destruction"; thus, it is said: "at the end of the night, that is, when the night has completely perished."
In the phrase "in the case of the visible-form base and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood as including syllables and other such things.
Regarding "golden-colored," the meaning here is "having golden skin"; thus he says, "of the skin. For it has been stated: "His skin resembles gold.
"Saññūḷhā" means connected; the meaning is "knotted together. Regarding "praise" (vaṇṇa), he says "of eulogy" (thutiya), meaning "of hymn of praise" (thomanāya).

The meaning is as follows. *Kulavagga* refers to the divisions of families such as the kṣatriyas and so forth. In this context, "complexion" (*vaṇṇa*) means the skin, in the sense of being described as "clear and translucent" and so on.

"Complexion" also means praise, in the sense of describing or extolling. Furthermore, "complexion" refers to the division of families such as the kṣatriyas, in the sense of being described and established without mutual confusion.
It is called "complexion" (*vaṇṇīyati*) because by means of it, [the family] is made known (*ñāpīyati*).
Color (*vaṇṇa*) is the indicative cause. Because it appears as gross, short, and so forth through its coloring (*vaṇṇana*), it is "color," which is shape (*saṇṭhāna*).
Because it is to be described as large, small, or medium, and because it is to be measured, it is "color," which is dimension (*pamāṇa*).

It is called "color" (*vaṇṇa*) because it is colored (*vaṇṇīyati*) and seen by the eye; thus, it is the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). In this way, the word "color" (*vaṇṇa*) [applies] to each respective meaning.

The occurrence [of the term] should be understood. "Sā" refers to the word *vaṇṇa* (color). It should be regarded as the skin, because even when it is apprehended within the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it must be apprehended by way of the skin alone.
Others, however, maintain that it is the color-element residing in the skin that is grasped by the mention of "color" in the phrase "golden-colored.
"Entirely complete" means that it is complete without leaving out even a single part; this is the meaning here.
He said: "The meaning is 'without remainder'. Regarding the word *kevalakappa*: the term *kappa* is a particle used merely to fill out the meter;

the meaning is simply "entirely" (*kevalaṃ*). And since the word *kevala* denotes "abundance," he said: "The meaning is 'for the most part. However, some say: "'Kevala' means slightly incomplete, and 'kevalakappa' [means] that which is [nearly] complete.
In this context, the word *kevala* may have the sense of "without remainder," as it does not differ in meaning from "entirety."
However, the word *kappa* has been added as an expansion of the phrase: “entirely (*kevala*) and like the world-age (*kappa*), thus ‘entirely-like-the-world-age’ (*kevalakappa*).

Or alternatively, they are called *kevalakappa* because they are to be fashioned (*kappanīya*) and to be designated (*paññapetabba*) as such. Purity (*suddhatā*) is the state of being unmixed (*abyāmissatā*), that is, the absence of commingling with anything of a different nature. Non-excess (*anatirekatā*) is the state of having that as the limit (*taṃparamatā*), the absence of any further distinction.
“Entirely-like-the-world-age” (*kevalakappa*) means having made it entirely firm (*daḷhaṃ katvā*). “Entirely” (*kevalaṃ*) is said...

Nirvana is so called because it is secluded from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*). One who has attained that [nirvana] is a *kevalī* (an absolute one). He is one who has realized cessation and whose taints (*āsava*) are destroyed.
Now, this word *kappa*, whether with or without a prefix, indicates by its intended meaning the mere word *okappa* found in the term *okappaniya*;
otherwise, if the meaning of the word *kappa* were merely enumerated, the term *okappaniya* would remain unindicated.
It may be so. "By means of the conventions of a recluse" means by those designations of a recluse established by the Vinaya.

"Always" means at all times. "Designation" is a name; for this is the name of that venerable one, namely, "Kappa. "One with trimmed hair and beard" means one whose hair and beard have been cut with a razor.
"The two-finger convention" means the allowance [for shaving] once the time of midday has passed. "Pretext" means a reason.
It may happen that even a light capable of pervading without remainder might, for some reason, pervade only a single part;
however, in order to show that this [light] pervades everything, the word *kappa* was taken in the sense of "all around" (*samanta*). Thus he said: "without remainder, all around.
"Having pervaded with radiance" means having pervaded with the radiance arising from the robes, garlands, ornaments, and body. For of the deities...
The radiance of his body pervades an area measuring twelve *yojanas*. It remains even after extending further than that, as does the light emanating from his robes, ornaments, and so forth.
The commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta.
129. In the sixth [case], it is "go-yoga" because there is a connection (*yoga*) here by way of the buying and selling of cows;

or, it is "go-yoga" because those who engage in buying and selling are connected (*yujjanti*) with cows here—namely, a place for the sale of cows. A *pilakkha* tree grown there is a "go-yoga-pilakkha"; [the locative case] refers to that.
This locative form is used here in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*). Therefore he said: "in the place for the sale of cows."
“Near the Pilakkha tree that had risen up. It is called *rittassāda* because its gratification is empty (*ritta*). Therefore he said:
