“Empty of gratification due to the absence of the bliss of jhāna. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta. 131.
Regarding the eighth sutta, in the phrase "this conceit of yours," the term *mānasmiṃ* is used in the locative case as a synonym for the thing itself (*paccatte bhummavacana*).
As for the word *idaṃ*, it is expressed in the neuter gender by way of a grammatical shift (*liṅgavipallāsa*); thus he says: "This is your conceit increased in nine ways."
The same method applies to the remaining suttas as well.
The commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Paṭicchanna Sutta.
132. “An uncommon training rule” (*asādhāraṇasikkhāpada*) refers to a training rule prescribed solely for bhikkhunīs, which is not shared with bhikkhus.
“A common training rule” (*sādhāraṇasikkhāpada*) refers to a training rule prescribed for both [bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs].
The commentary on the *Paṭicchanna-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Lekhasutta 133.
Regarding the tenth [verse], "from the standpoint of firmness" means precisely from the standpoint of firmness.

One whose lines of anger produced by successive offenses are like lines carved upon stone is "endowed with the likeness of a line on stone," and is thus called "one who resembles a line on stone. The others are to be understood in the same way.

"It underlies" means it underlies by way of not being abandoned. "It does not quickly disintegrate" means it does not perish in the interim, because it perishes only through the meditation subject itself.
"In this very way" means that for such a person, anger does not come to an end in the interim—neither on the following day nor on a subsequent day—but rather it is long-lasting;
the meaning is that it comes to an end only with death. "Harshly" means excessively harshly.
"By one who cuts off the Dhamma with harsh speech. "He blends" (*saṃsandati*) means he becomes one;
"he rejoices" (*sammodati*) means he becomes continuous—thus should the meaning be understood here.
Alternatively, "he joins together" (*sandhiyati*) means that in bodily activities such as standing or walking, he attains coordination with the body, like sesame seeds and rice grains.
The meaning is that it attains a state of intermingling, as it were. "It blends" (saṃsandati) means it reaches a unification with the mind through mental activities;
the meaning is that it attains a state of oneness like milk and water. "It harmonizes" (sammodati) means it reaches a unification with speech through verbal activities such as recitation and inquiry;
even when they have gone their separate ways, it attains a state of greater affection, like a dear companion who has returned from abroad.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, it should be understood that in matters of duty and what is to be done, one "joins" (saṃdhīyati) by entering into a state of single action with them from the very beginning;
one "mingles" (saṃsandati) as long as one proceeds in the middle; and one "rejoices together" (sammodati) as long as one does not turn back until the end.
The commentary on the Lekha Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Kusinārā Chapter is finished.
(14) 4. The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga): 1.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Warrior (Yodhājīva-sutta).
134. In the first [meaning], one who fights is a warrior (*yodha*); one whose livelihood (*ājīva*) is this is a "warrior-for-livelihood" (*yodhājīva*).
Alternatively, in the sense of "one who lives by war," the derivation of the word *yodhājīva* should be understood according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*). Therefore he said:
"One who lives by war is a 'warrior-for-livelihood'. "Together... sees" refers to the stage prior [to the path], by way of the comprehension through insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
At the moment of the path, one sees by means of knowledge that is personally realized through the power of clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*).
The commentary on the *Yodhājīva Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Parisā Sutta*.
135. "Disciplined without questioning in the second case" means that the assembly was disciplined solely by means of a teaching on the Dhamma without being questioned, as in:
"Bhikkhus, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? and so forth. "A poorly disciplined assembly" means an assembly that is difficult to discipline.
"Disciplined after questioning" means [disciplined] after being questioned, as in: "Bhikkhus, what do you think? and so forth.
They are disciplined by means of taking formal consent (*anumatiggahaṇa*). "A well-disciplined assembly" means an assembly that has been easily disciplined;
for disciplining by means of taking formal consent is not difficult.
The commentary on the *Parisā-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Uppādāsutta 137.

Regarding the fourth [sutta], "Whether Tathāgatas arise" (*uppādā vā tathāgatānam*): even upon the arising of Tathāgatas, the impermanent nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) and so forth does not depend upon the arising of Tathāgatas—just as the arising of the path and its fruits occurs for individuals to be trained (*veneyyapuggala*) even when Tathāgatas have arisen;
rather, it is independent of them. Furthermore, even upon the arising of Tathāgatas...

The meaning is that even in non-arising, it is precisely this [nature] that exists. "That element remains indeed" means that this very nature of impermanence remains constant because there is no deviation;
conditioned phenomena are never not impermanent. Granted, that nature is not eternal like the unconditioned element, nevertheless, the intention is that it exists at all times.

Another method: "That element remains ever-present" means that this element, this intrinsic nature—that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent"—was not produced by the Tathāgatas, having remained unpenetrated prior to their arising and even after;

rather, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent at all times, and that element remains ever-present. It is simply because of the realization through self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) [that it is called awakening].
And because he proclaims, “This Dhamma has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,” the Tathāgata is called the Master of Dhamma, owing to his production of that which was previously non-existent.
Therefore it is said: “That element remains fixed.
He “fully awakens to” means he fully awakens to it with knowledge. He “comprehends” means he arrives at it with knowledge. He “declares” means...
He speaks. "Teaches" means he demonstrates. "Expounds" means he makes known. "Establishes" means he places [it] within the gateway of knowledge.
"Discloses" means having opened, he shows. "Analyzes" means he shows by way of division. "Clarifies" means he makes it manifest.
Alternatively, "fully awakens to" means he awakens face-to-face through direct realization; he penetrates [the truth] exactly as it is.
For that very reason, one "realizes" (abhisameti), meaning one comes face-to-face with it. Speaking from the beginning, one "explains" (ācikkhati); the meaning is that one recites (uddisati).
One "teaches" (deseti) by bringing that very recitation to its conclusion.

One "makes known" (paññāpeti) by making the matter known through various modes of illustration according to how it was recited. One "establishes" (paṭṭhapeti) by firmly setting forth this matter through various modes. [This applies] to what was recited...
He reveals and analyzes by way of providing a counter-example. Making the meaning revealed and analyzed clear through the presentation of reasons and examples, he makes it plain.
The commentary on the Uppāda-sutta is completed.
5–10. Commentary on the *Kesakambala-sutta* and others, §§138–143.

Regarding the phrase “of garments woven from thread” (*tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ*) in the fifth [sutta], he says “the genitive case is used in the sense of the direct object” (*paccatte sāmivacanaṃ*), because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word “whatever” (*yāni kānici*).
“Woven” (*vāyitānaṃ*) means “warp-woven” (*vītānaṃ*). “Lowly” (*lāmako*) means inferior; [he refers to] Makkhali, that empty man.
In this context, "Makkhali" is his name. It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground carrying an oil jar, his master said to him, "Dear boy, do not stumble (mā khalī).
He stumbled through negligence and fell; out of fear of his master, he began to flee.
His master ran after him and seized him by the hem of his garment. [The man] discarded his cloth and became a naked ascetic (acelaka).
He fled. Not even knowing how to cover himself with leaves or grass, he entered a village carrying only the gold.
When people saw him, they thought, "This ascetic is an Arahant of few desires; there is no one equal to him," and they approached him bringing cakes, rice, and other offerings.
He thought, "Because I am without a garment to wear, this has come to pass for me. Then...
From that time on, even after receiving a cloth garment, he did not wear it, and he took up the going-forth (pabbajjā) right then and there.
In his presence, five hundred other people—some here, some there—also went forth. It is with reference to him that the Blessed One said, "Makkhali the foolish man.
The sixth and subsequent points are of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Kesakambala Sutta and others is concluded.
11–13. Commentary on the First Mora-nivāpa Sutta and others. 144–146.

In the eleventh [sutta], they are called "absolute" (*accantā*) because they have transcended the limit known as destruction and decay by virtue of their unshakeable nature (*akuppadhammatā*). Thus...
Because its nature is non-declining, it has an absolute end (*accantaniṭṭha*). Therefore he said: "One whose end has transcended the limit," and so forth.
For there is no such thing as the impairment of the vision of the supramundane dhamma once it has been penetrated. "One with a stable end" (*dhuvanidḍha*) means one with a constant end.

Because he possesses absolute security from the four *yogas*, he is "one who has attained absolute security from the *yogas*" (*accantayogakkhemī*); that is, one who is permanently secure from the *yogas*.

The meaning is as follows: because he has lived the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*) and because its nature is not to be abandoned, he is an "absolute practitioner of the holy life" (*accanta-brahmacārī*);
the meaning is "a constant practitioner of the holy life. "The consummation" (*pariyosāna*) refers both to the consummation of the holy life and the consummation of the suffering of saṃsāra.
One for whom there is absolute consummation is "one whose consummation is absolute" (*accanta-pariyosāno*). The twelfth and thirteenth [verses] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the first discourse, "The Peacock’s Feeding Ground," is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on Warriors is concluded.
147–156. The Chapter on Auspiciousness is self-evident in its meaning.
The Third Fifty is finished.
(16) 6. Commentary on the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga), §§ 157–163.
Regarding the subsequent sections of the Sutta, [the commentary] explains the meaning stated as "firm" (*gāḷhā*) by using the term "harsh" (*kakkhaḷā*).
He said: "Her conduct is harsh, yet her nature is not coarse; rather, it is a firm grasping by way of craving.
Thus he said, "because of firm grasping by way of greed. Or, "the practice that is not immersed" means immersion into sensual pleasures—that is, the pursuit of sensual happiness.
"The practice that is parched" is a practice that proceeds by way of withering and wasting away the body.
The meaning is: devotion to self-mortification. "Naked" (*niccela*) means one who has cast off clothing, having entirely rejected all garments.

He is "naked" by undertaking the vow of nakedness. "He voids excrement while standing," etc., is merely an illustration, because he has also abandoned such practices as rinsing the mouth after vomiting.
"He scrapes his hand with his tongue" means he licks it.

"By water" means from the downward direction. The same method applies to the second alternative as well. When it is said, "Come, venerable sir" (*ehi, bhaddante*), the procedure consisting of approaching is called *ehibhadanta*;
one who practices that is an *ehibhadantika*. By way of its opposite, one is a *na-ehibhadantika*. This is with the intention:
"One should not act according to the words of another simply because one is called a 'recluse' (*samaṇa*)."
They "purify" that place beforehand because they arrive there earlier than others. It is said that he does not accept [alms] with the intention, "A bhikkhu may take whatever alms he desires.

He does not accept what has been prepared specifically for him, thinking, "By my presence as the intended recipient, many small creatures have met their destruction. He likewise does not consent to an invitation; thus, for them...
"The word will be accomplished. He says "a potter, a basket-maker," and so forth, because he perceives those [objects] as sentient beings even in pots and such things.
"An obstacle to the mouthful" means that for one who has stood up, there is an obstacle to both mouthfuls.

"A communal recitation" (*saṅkitti*) is that by which people gather together and chant according to their respective groups, such as a heap of rice and so forth. "Human beings" refers to men who perform services.
“Only the drinking of *surā*” means the drinking of *surā* that has reached the characteristic of being an intoxicant. By the mention of *surā* here, *meraya* (distilled liquor) is also included.
One who begs at only one house is an *ekāgārika*. One who subsists on only one mouthful of food is an *ekālopika*.
It is called a *datti* because it is given by it; it is a small vessel for receiving alms-food that holds only two or three mouthfuls. Therefore, he said, “a small bowl.”
“Ekāhika” means that which has one day (*eka-aha*) by way of fasting; it is food. That [food] is *ekāhika*.
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it refers to one who fasts for one day, thus he said, “lasting for one day. The same method applies to “dvāhika” and so forth.
Fasting for one day and then eating for one day is a “one-day turn” (*ekāha-vāra*); in terms of its actual meaning, that is simply *ekāhika*. [Fasting] for two days...

"Eating every other day" means one whose turn for eating comes every second day. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. However, the "superior" type of one who eats by turns does not eat for two days, but eats on only one day. The same method applies to the other two types as well.

Because the practice of the "crouching posture" (ukkūṭika-vata) occurs solely through the influence of wrong effort, he says, "devoted to crouching energy. "Devotion to self-mortification" (attakilamathānuyoga) [is explained as follows].
“Devotion to self-exhaustion” means a cause of bodily suffering; for here the word *atta* (self) is a synonym for the body, as in such expressions as *attantapo* (“one who torments oneself”).
“The two extremes” means both limits, that is, both inferior modes of practice.
For even what is inferior is called an “extreme,” as in such passages as: “This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods, the very bottom.”

Because they are off the path of the Middle Way (*majjhimapaṭipadā*), they are "extremes" (*anta*); that is, they are unpleasant, to be avoided, and to be known. For that very reason, they are inferior.
The commentary on the *Acelakavagga* is finished.
The commentary on the *Peyyālavagga*.
164–184. *Samanuñño* means one who has properly given his consent. Therefore he said, "one of like disposition. The rest here is self-evident.

Thus ends the Elucidation of the Meaning Not [Previously] Explained in the Commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the sub-commentary to the Exposition of the *Tika-nipāta* (The Book of Threes), titled the *Manorathapūraṇī*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Catukkanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
1. The First Fifty [Discourses]. 1.
The Chapter on the Village of Bhaṇḍa. 1–2.
Commentary on the Anubuddha Sutta and others.
1–2. In the first [section] of the Catukkanipāta, "awakening" (*anubodha*) is knowledge belonging to the prior stage, while "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization through awakening.

In this context, since penetration preceded by awakening does not occur without awakening—because a certain kind of awakening is connected with penetration, and the wandering in saṃsāra is caused by the absence of both—therefore it is said:

In the Pāḷi, it says: “Through non-comprehension... and yours. “Running” (*sandhāvana*) refers to the transition from one existence to another existence by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
“wandering” (*saṃsaraṇa*) refers to moving about through repeated death and rebirth. Thus he said, “from existence,” and so forth.
Regarding the first alternative, he said, “by me and by you,” with reference to the fact that the words *sandhāvita* and *saṃsarita* function as karmic objects (*kamma-sādhana*).
In the second interpretation, however, taking it as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), it is stated according to the literal sense as “my own and yours.

Just as a man with a rope in his hand leads a bird bound by a long cord to another place, so too the volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) leads the continuum of beings (*sattasantāna*) bound by the rope of craving (*taṇhārajjū*) to another existence (*bhavantara*). Thus it is called the “guide to existence” (*bhavanetti*). Therefore he said, “the rope of existence,” and so forth.

"One who makes an end of the suffering of the round" means one who brings about the destruction and non-existence of the entire suffering of the round within both his own continuum and the continua of others.

"Possessing the eye" means possessing the five eyes known as the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine eye, the fleshly eye, and the universal eye. Because he has utterly eradicated the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), he possesses an eminent *parinibbāna* regarding the defilements.
He has attained final Nibbāna. The second [sutta] is likewise clear.
The commentary on the *Anubuddha-sutta* and others is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the *Paṭhama-khata-sutta* and others.
3–4. *Kaliṃ* means fault or transgression. *Vicināti* means he accumulates or produces it. And by that *kali*, one does not obtain happiness;
that is, by that transgression, one does not find bliss. For the ripening result is indeed the same whether one praises those who should be censured or censures those who should be praised.
"Censuring those who should be praised" refers to its occurrence through the destruction of virtues already perfected.
Because it is a great transgression, its maturation is more bitter. But if one asks: "How is praising those who deserve blame a maturation equal to that [of blaming those who deserve praise]?

It is because, by attributing qualities that do not exist in them, it becomes a cause for both oneself and others to engage in wrong practice, and because it makes that which is praiseworthy appear as if it were actually present.
For even in the world, one who makes a coward equal to a hero is censurable; how much more so [in the case of the Dhamma]?
"Making one who has practiced wrongly equal to one who has practiced rightly. "With one's own wealth" means with one's own property.
"A very slight loss" refers to a minor offense because it pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and because it can be remedied. This...
[is] a much greater loss because it is accumulated through action, pertains to future lives (*samparāyika*), and cannot be remedied.

"Nirabbuda" is a specific numerical designation; thus he said "by the calculation of nirabbudas," meaning one hundred thousand nirabbudas. The measure of a nirabbuda should be understood through the calculation of years as follows:
just as a hundred times a hundred thousand is a *koṭi*, so too a hundred times a hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*. A hundred times a hundred thousand...
Ten million is a *koṭi*; ten billion is a *koṭipakoṭi*; ten trillion is a *satasahassakoṭipakoṭi*; ten quadrillion is a *nahuta*; ten quintillion is a *satasahassanahuta*;
ten sextillion is a *ninnahuta*; ten septillion is one *abbuda*; twenty times that is a *nirabbuda*.
"By reviling the Noble One, one is reborn in hell"—this refers to the hell known as *nirabbuda* for one who reviles the Noble One.

"He is reborn" means that there is no separate hell named Nirabbuda; rather, this is the name for a place within Avīci itself where one must be cooked according to the Nirabbuda calculation. The fourth [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the first *Khaṭasutta* and so forth is concluded.
5. Commentary on the *Anusotasutta* In the fifth [sutta], "goes with the stream" (*anusotaṃ gacchati*) means that one goes by way of being favorable to the stream of saṃsāra.

"By a practice contrary [to the stream]" (*paccanīkapaṭipattiyā*) means by a practice such as the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*), which proceeds in opposition to the stream of saṃsāra. "Of a stable nature" (*ṭhitasabhāvo*)...

One whose nature is established through the possession of unshakable confidence and so forth. For a non-returner (anāgāmī) is said to have a "stable nature" because his mind cannot be shaken by lack of faith, sensual lust, or ill will, and because he is subject to the law of not returning from that world.
"Having crossed the flood" means having transcended the fourfold flood, such as the flood of sensual desire. "Gone to the further shore" means gone to the shore of Nibbāna. "Brahmin" (brāhmaṇo):
One who has cast off evil is reckoned a brahmin; such a person is one whose taints are exhausted. Therefore it is said: "The best is the faultless one.

"The five acts of enmity" refers to the five types of misconduct, beginning with the taking of life. "Even with pain and even with grief" means even together with the suffering and mental distress that arise when there is the obsession of the defilements.
"Complete" means [complete] in even a single one of the three trainings.
"Unimpaired. "Pure" means free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*). "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the supreme conduct.
By this section, the stream-enterer and once-returner are described. But do they practice the holy life while weeping? Yes;
they are said to practice while weeping with the weeping of the defilements (*kilesa*); thus, even a worldling bhikkhu endowed with virtue is included right here.
"Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of fruition (*phalasamādhi*). "Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the knowledge of fruition (*phalañāṇa*).

"One who has gone beyond in six ways" means one who has reached the further shore, the limit, and the culmination of all phenomena through these six modes: mastery of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), mastery of full understanding (*pariññā*), mastery of development (*bhāvanā*), mastery of abandoning (*pahāna*), mastery of realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and mastery of attainment (*samāpatti*). The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Anusotasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Appassutasutta*:
In the sixth [discourse], "little learning" means that one has learned only a small portion of the Teacher’s ninefold dispensation. That very same...
In order to show the Teacher’s dispensation with its nine limbs, it was said: “Sutta, geyya,” and so forth. Therein, explaining the *sutta* and the others in detail, he said:
“The two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, the Parivāra,” and so on. But how is this classification appropriate?
For a *sutta* that contains verses is *geyya*, while a *sutta* without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*. And that which is distinct from both of these—
There is no discourse (sutta) devoid of specific designations such as Udāna and so forth that could constitute the Sutta-aṅga.
Furthermore, discourses such as the Maṅgala-sutta would not be included in the Sutta-aṅga because they consist of verses (gāthā), like the Dhammapada and other such works.

Alternatively, they might be included in the Geyya-aṅga because they contain verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. Likewise, there are verse sections within the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other texts. To this it is said:
“‘Sutta’ is the general rule; others are specific rules; they possess a formal cause due to conventional usage, and because of their association with another, not from anything else.
For indeed, “sutta” is the general rule for the entire word of the Buddha. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said:
In the *Nettippakaraṇa*, it is stated: "The investigation of the ninefold Suttanta. This much has come down as the Sutta of that Blessed One, included within the Sutta;
namely, the five hundred suttas in our own tradition, and so forth—this serves to establish this meaning.

Furthermore, the specific types [of texts] such as the *Geya* and others, which are established by their respective characteristics (*nimitta*), are the specific types found elsewhere together with their defining marks. Likewise...
For the *geyya* contains verses; that is the reason for its being so designated. Indeed, even in the world, a collection of stanzas (*cuṇṇiya-gantha*) accompanied by prose or verses is called "geyya.
However, when it is devoid of verses, the state of providing an answer after posing a question is the reason for the *veyyākaraṇa* being so designated.
For a response to a question is called "byākaraṇa" (explanation); and "veyyākaraṇa" is simply an elaboration of "byākaraṇa."
If that were so, would it not follow that even the *Sagāthaka* and other sections—which proceed by way of questions and answers—would possess the status of *Veyyākaraṇa* (Exposition)?

It does not follow, because there is no scope for the designations *Geyya* (Chanting) and so forth [in those cases], and because they are specifically qualified by the phrase "when there is an absence of verses.

For instance, in the *Dhammapada* and similar works, although they consist solely of verse compositions and thus possess the quality of being *Sagāthaka*, they are joined with verses consisting of joy and knowledge.

In connection with such statements as "For it has been said," and in specific discourses associated with marvelous phenomena (*abbhutadhamma*), the designations *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, and *abbhutadhamma* have been established respectively.

Likewise, although they consist of verse composition, those [texts] that reveal the power of the Blessed One’s conduct in past births are designated as *jātaka*; and although they consist of answers to questions, [they are designated as *pañhāpucchaka*].

Furthermore, because the term *vedalla* is established by virtue of its being accompanied by verses (*sagāthaka*) in certain discourses (*suttanta*), the designations such as *geyya* and so forth are established for those specific discourses by means of their respective characteristics, such as being accompanied by verses;
thus, the *geyya* and other categories following the *sutta* division are distinguished by their specific modes.

However, that which is devoid of the characteristics of the *geyya* division and the rest— [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...that is [the *sutta* division].* *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the structure and meaning of the preceding portion.)*
The *sutta* division [exists] because it proceeds by means of general concepts (*sāmañña-saññā*) through the avoidance of specific concepts (*visesa-saññā*).

Is it not the case that the objection—"Is it not true that a sutta containing verses is *geyya*, while a sutta devoid of verses is *veyyākaraṇa*? Thus, the *sutta* division is impossible"—remains as it was?
No, it does not remain as it was, because it has been resolved. For it was previously resolved that "in the absence of verses, there exists the nature of question and answer..."
“...the cause for that [term] in the case of a *veyyākaraṇa*.

As for what was said—that because they exist as verses (*gāthā*), the *Maṅgalasutta* and other such texts would not be included within the category of *sutta*—that is not so, because the term is conventional (*nirūḷha*).

For the status of being a *sutta* is conventionally established for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others; indeed, they are not merely collections of *dhammapada* verses like the *Buddhavaṃsa* and similar works.
They are not renowned as being by way of verses (*gāthā*), but rather precisely by way of discourses (*sutta*);

for that very reason, the name is given as "named *sutta*" in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As for what was said—"Because it contains verses, it might be included in the *geyya* division"—that too is not the case, because it is accompanied by something else.
For "containing verses" (*sagāthaka*) means "together with verses. And "being together" (*sahabhāva*) in its actual sense means [being] with another.

There is no portion of the Sutta that is devoid of verses—such as the Maṅgala-sutta and others—which could be called "with verses" (*saha gāthāhi*), nor does there exist anything called a "composite whole" (*samudāya*).
As for what was said—that "portions containing verses within the Ubhatovibhaṅga and so forth might be included under the Geyya factor"—that too is not correct, for another reason.
For those verses are indeed different, because they are comprised within the Jātaka and other such categories.

Therefore, those [two] do not constitute the Geyya factor among the Ubhatovibhaṅga and so forth. In this way, the absence of mutual confusion among the factors such as the Sutta and the rest should be understood.

This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, has been set forth by us in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā, and should be taken from that very source by those who desire it.
Regarding the phrase "having understood the meaning and having understood the Dhamma, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma," the connection here should be understood as follows:

having known both the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he does not practice the preliminary path (*pubbhāgappaṭipadā*), which is the Dhamma corresponding to the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*).
For this very reason, it was said: "Having understood the meaning and having understood the Dhamma" [refers to] the commentary...
“Having learned the Pāḷi... [and so on] ...he is not one who practices.
The commentary on the Appassuta Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sobhana Sutta.
7. In the seventh [verse], "by means of discernment" (*paññāveyyattiya*) refers to the discernment consisting in the penetration of the Truths (*sacca-sampaṭivedha*) and so forth.
"Approached discipline" (*vinayam upetā*) means having approached the disciplining of the defilements (*kilesa*) by way of their removal (*tadaṅga*) and other methods.

"By confidence" (*vesārajja*) means by confidence arising from the departure of evil states such as wrong view and doubt which cause timidity; the meaning is "free from timidity. They possess much that has been heard (*bahu-suta*) by way of the Three Piṭakas.

They are "learned" (bahussuta). They bear that very same Dhamma of the scriptures in their hearts, not allowing it to perish, but rather placing it there through its state of being well-mastered and well-recited—like lion’s milk placed in a golden vessel.
And since such persons are indeed the repositories for the Dhamma they have heard, he said: "repositories of the heard Dhammas."
The commentary on the *Sobhana-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Vesārajja-sutta*:
In the eighth [sutta], "shamelessness" (*sārajjana*) is the seeking of refuge through delusion; it is the fear of delusion. It has departed (*vigata*).
One who is confident (*visārado*) is so called because he possesses confidence; the state of being that is *vesārajja* (fearlessness).

That, moreover, is the fourfold knowledge of reflective review (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*) which proceeds by relying upon the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of specific teaching, and security. Therefore, he said, "In the four instances," and so forth.
That which belongs to a bull (*usabha*) is *āsabha*; it is the preeminent position. By virtue of professing omniscience...
They go toward him, or the eight assemblies approach him; thus he is a "bull" (*āsabha*), referring to the Buddhas of the past.
But this [term] refers specifically to the state of omniscience (*sabbaññuta*) of the Buddhas. "Even while standing" means that even without speaking, he makes his claim simply by standing.
"He approaches" means he consents.
“In the eight assemblies”: “Indeed, Sāriputta, I recall having approached many hundreds of assemblies of khattiyas...

[and so on]... assemblies of brahmins, assemblies of householders, assemblies of ascetics, assemblies of the Four Great Kings, assemblies of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, assemblies of Māra, and assemblies of Brahmā; there too, I have previously sat together with them.”

“I do not see any sign, Sāriputta, that fear or trepidation would overcome me when I have previously conversed with them and engaged in discussion with them”— thus [he speaks] regarding the assemblies mentioned.
He “roars an unafraid roar” means that he roars an unafraid roar, being confident because of the application of knowledge demonstrated by others.
"By the *Sīhanāda Sutta*" means by the *Sīhanāda Sutta* found in the Khandhaka-vagga.
By the remainder of the sutta, "The four wheels turn for devas and humans," the occurrence of the attainment of fruits such as reliance upon true persons (*sappurisa*) and so forth is stated;
that is, the occurrence of the attainment of later reliance upon true persons and so forth, based on earlier reliance upon true persons and so forth.
Or it is so stated. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it should be understood that the term *cakra* (wheel) is also included therein.

A thunderbolt shaped like a discus is itself called a *asanivicakka*. Regarding the phrase "in the breast-discs, etc.," by the word "etc.," it should be understood that the term *cakra* also applies to collections of commands and so forth;
for in such expressions as "We shall cause a schism in the Saṅgha, a *cakrabheda* (schism of the wheel)," the "wheel" refers to the command.
In such expressions as "the circle of devas" and "the circle of asuras," it means a collection.
Because it is the culmination of penetration, the knowledge of the path to arahantship is called "penetration"; thus it is said, "it is that which has arisen at the moment of the fruit.
By this, even for the knowledge of teaching that has been acquired, the accomplishment of its function occurs merely by causing another to awaken.
It is said: “The stream-entry of Aññā Koṇḍañña... [and so on]... this is called the occurrence at the moment of the fruit.
Furthermore, it should be understood that from then until his parinibbāna, the occurrence of the knowledge of teaching is the station of that very Wheel of Dhamma which had been set in motion.
Regarding the phrase “among the dhammas shown,” it means among the dhammas spoken; for there was merely the speaking of them, but not the seeing of such [a Wheel].

Because of the non-existence of such a phenomenon (dhamma). Or else, regarding those phenomena shown by another’s statement as "these phenomena have not been fully awakened to" by the Blessed One himself—the word *dhamma* in expressions such as "analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

Thus he said, "by means of the phenomenon, that is, by means of the cause. And here, "cause" should be understood as a reason for establishing a proof (*upapattisādhanahetu*), not as a creator-cause (*kārakahetu*).
Or one who brings about [the offense]. "Sign" (*nimitta*) means the cause for the accusation. In this context, it is a "cause" because the accuser (*codaka*) performs the accusation;

it is a "cause" because the Dhamma performs the accusation by means of it. Therefore he said, "The person as well," and so forth. "Secure" (*khema*) means unassailed by virtue of being unopposed by anyone.
They are "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because they possess an obstacle, or because they are connected with an obstacle. And since they are of such a nature...
They are called "obstructive" because they create obstacles; therefore, it is said: "They are obstructive because they cause an obstacle.
It is stated that "they have transgressed intentionally" because [transgressions] committed unintentionally are not considered excessively blameworthy.

The phrase "the seven classes of offenses," and so forth, is merely an illustration, since there is no deviation from the status of being "obstructive" even in the case of the other four things mentioned as such.
"But here, sexual intercourse is intended"—this was stated by way of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti), as in the case of the Ariṭṭha training rule.
Because even at that moment, if one sees the danger in sensual pleasures and abstains, one attains distinction and is not attached to sensual pleasures;
therefore it is said: "Sexual intercourse... is an obstacle. In this context, "of anyone whatsoever" means:
This applies not only to one who has gone forth, but to anyone at all; for it is said: "For one devoted to sexual intercourse, even the Teaching is lost.
Regarding the phrase "in that non-leaving dhamma":
this refers to the sign of a non-leaving dhamma as imagined by others. For here, the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (nimitta) in connection with the object (kamma).

“Upanibaddhā” means composed. Therefore, he said “abhisaṅkhatā” (constructed). “Puthubhāvaṃ” means the state of being many. Or, “puthūhi vā sitā” means composed and bound by many recluses and brahmins.
The commentary on the Vesārajja Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Taṇhuppāda Sutta.

9. In the ninth [case], by means of this, there is the state of being healthy; thus, "existence" (bhava) refers to the requisite for the sick. When existence has increased, it is "non-existence" (abhava).
For this letter *a* has the sense of increase (*vuddhi*), as in the examples "restraint and non-restraint" (*saṃvarāsaṃvara*) and "fruit and non-fruit" (*phalāphala*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "ghee, fresh butter, etc.," oil, honey, molasses, and so forth are included. Furthermore, the mention of ghee, fresh butter, and the rest is merely illustrative.

It should be understood that all requisites for the sick are included here. Alternatively, "existence and non-existence" (bhavābhava) should be understood as both the minor and the major modes of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). For this very reason, he said, "in states of success" (*sampattibhavesu*), and so forth.
Or else, "existence" (*bhava*) is success, and "non-existence" (*abhava*) is failure; "existence" is growth, and "non-existence" is decline. And it is with that as its cause that craving arises.
It is said: "or for the sake of existence after existence.

"With craving as his companion" means accompanied by craving. For craving performs the function of a companion for a being who is tormented by thirst—just like the perception of water in a mirage in a waterless desert—by providing a semblance of consolation, thereby causing that being not to become disenchanted with future existences and the like.

She causes one to wander about. For, like fishermen who do not consider the precipice and merely seek honey, she shows only the advantages while there are many dangers in the various states of existence;
thus, she causes one to wander within the net of harm. Therefore, craving is called "the second [self] of a person.
But are not other defilements and so forth also conditions for the production of existence? This is true, but—
However, craving is a specific condition (*visesa-paccaya*) in such a way that no other factor is;

for it is a specific condition for the production of existence through unwholesome states in the absence of wholesome ones, and through wholesome states of the fine-material sphere and so forth in the absence of wholesome states of the sense-sphere and so forth. Therefore, it is called the "truth of origin" (*samudaya-sacca*).

Regarding the phrase "this state and another state": "this state and another state" (*itthabhāvaññathābhāva*) is a compound consisting of "this state" (*itthabhāva*) and "another state" (*aññathābhāva*).
"That which has this" is "existence-in-this-state-and-otherwise" (*itthabhāvaññathābhāva*), which is *saṃsāra*; that is, existence-in-this-state-and-otherwise.
In this context, "existence-in-this-state" (*itthabhāva*) is human existence, while "existence-otherwise" (*aññathābhāva*) refers to the remaining abodes of beings.

Alternatively, "existence-in-this-state" is the present personal identity (*attabhāva*) of various beings, and "existence-otherwise" is their future personal identity. Or, it may be of another such kind.

“Attabhāva” (selfhood) means being thus; it is not a state of being otherwise. For this very reason, he said: “Regarding ‘being thus and being otherwise,’ here ‘being thus’ refers to this selfhood,” and so forth.
“Saṃsaraṇa” (wandering) is “saṃsāra” (the round of existence). [As it is said:
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases;”
“When the continuity is severed, it is called ‘saṃsāra’.
Therefore he said: “The succession of the aggregates, elements, and bases,” meaning the successive occurrence of the aggregates, elements, and bases by way of cause and fruit.
Regarding the phrase “having known this danger,” some read it as “having known *etaṃ* (this) danger,” referring to this entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

The meaning is: "having understood its origin, its arising, and its danger. Alternatively, "having understood such danger" means having understood the fault—the danger consisting in not transcending the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) as previously described.

It is "restrained" (*niggahaṇo*) by means of relinquishing all grasping, which consists of the four kinds of clinging; it is [so called] because of the cessation of the activity of formations through the parinibbāna of the aggregates.
"Should depart" (apagaccheyya): this is how the meaning should be understood here.
The commentary on the *Taṇhuppāda-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Yoga-sutta*.

10. In the tenth [verse], "they yoke" means that they yoke—that is, they join—kamma with its result (vipāka) to existence (bhava) and so forth, and they yoke—that is, they connect—a sentient being with suffering through other existences and so forth;
thus they are called *yogas*. It is a *kāmayoga* because it is both desire (*kāma*) in the sense of longing and a *yoga* in the sense already stated.

To show that what is called *bhavayoga* is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), it is said: "In the realms of form and formlessness," and so forth. Therein, the first [type of existence] refers to the realms of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
Lust is the second [type of clinging] among the kamma-existences; the third is that accompanied by the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*).

Just as it is called "lust" (*rāga*) in the sense of being impassioned, so too it is called "yoke" (*yoga*) in the sense of being bound. "Ignorance regarding the four truths"—this was stated in reliance on the method of the Suttas, for this is a commentary on the Suttas;
or alternatively, because the past limit (*pubbanta*) and so forth are included therein.

There are two kinds of origination: momentary origination (*khaṇika-samudaya*) and conditional origination (*paccaya-samudaya*). The moment of arising is momentary origination; the condition itself is conditional origination.
"Origination" (*samudaya*) is so called because it originates (*samudayati*) or the act of originating (*samudayana*); it is called "origination" because things originate from it (*etasmā*).
Thus, the distinction between these two types of origination should be understood even from the perspective of the meaning of the terms. One who understands conditional origination...
A bhikkhu understands the momentary arising; and while understanding the momentary arising, he also understands the causal arising.
For one who sees the arising of formations from the perspective of conditions, it is easy to see their arising from the perspective of moments;
and for one who sees their arising from the perspective of moments, it is even more so from the perspective of conditions because the conditions have been correctly grasped.
Insight (*dassana*) succeeds through ease. Here, however, showing the momentary arising (*khaṇika-samudaya*), he said:

"Arising means origination. Cessation (*atthaṅgama*) is also twofold: absolute cessation (*accanta-atthaṅgama*) and dissolution-cessation (*bhedatthaṅgama*). Absolute cessation is the cessation of non-occurrence;
some say it is Nibbāna. Dissolution-cessation is momentary cessation. Both of these [are understood] in the preliminary stage by means of study, questioning, and so forth.
When one sees a particular thing, the seeing of the other is already established.

At the preliminary stage itself, while comprehending through the object as subject to exhaustion and vanishing, one who sees its dissolution and passing away sees its absolute cessation by way of contrast, rather than through hearsay or tradition;
however, at the moment of the Path, one sees its absolute cessation from the perspective of the object.
Through non-delusion, one sees the other as well. Here, however, in order to show the dissolution through breaking apart, he says:

"Dissolution means breaking apart. By grasping the arising and breaking apart of sensual pleasures (*kāma*) here, just as the dependent origination of sensual pleasures is made manifest, so too is that of the bases of sensual pleasure (*kāmavatthu*);
thus, the impermanence, suffering, and selflessness of both are made manifest.
It should be seen. By the phrase "the state of sweetness," he shows the pleasure and mental joy dependent upon sensual desire. For it is said:
"Monks, whatever pleasure and mental joy arise dependent upon these five strands of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification in sensual pleasures.
By the phrase "the state of lack of sweetness," however, he shows the suffering and mental grief caused by sensual desire.
"Of the bases of contact" means of the eye-base and so forth, which serve as the causes for contact occurring at the six doors. Therefore he said:
"of the eye and so forth, which are the causes of eye-contact and so forth. "Punabbhava" (re-becoming) is the making of renewed existence;

this is to be understood through the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*), and the preceding member should be seen as ending in a vowel, just as in the word *mano*. Those whose nature (*sīla*) is renewed existence are [the "punnabbhaviyas"].

"Ponobhavikā. Alternatively, since the meaning [of "giving"] is already conveyed by the suffix *-ika* in the sense of "habitual practice" (*sīla*), the absence of a word expressing the action itself should be understood, just as one who has the habit of eating cakes is called an *āpūpika*.
Alternatively, they give renewed existence (*punabbhava*), they lead to renewed existence, or they produce repeated renewed existence;
thus they are "those leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā*). For the term is indicated in the plural by the designation "taddhita-suffixes" (*taddhitā*).

Alternatively, the formation of the term *ponobhavika* (leading to renewed existence) in such meanings as "giving renewed existence" and so forth should be understood either through the diversity of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) or because of the nature of verbal expression.

They are called *visaṃyoga* (disconnections) because they disjoin the person practicing the path from the yoke of sensual desire and the rest; thus, the meditations on the foul (*asubha-jjhāna*), etc., are the causes of disconnection. Therefore he said: "Disconnections are the causes of disconnection," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Yogāvacara-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Bhaṇḍagāma-vagga* is finished.
2. The *Cara-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the *Carasutta* 11.
Regarding the first [verse] of the second [sutta]: "While walking" (*carato*) means while going or while pacing up and down (*caṅkamantassa*).

"A sensual thought arises" (*uppajjati kāmavitakko vā*) means that, due to not being free from lust for sense-objects (*vatthukāmesu*), a thought associated with sensuality (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutto*) arises when such a condition is present.
"If it arises": if either a thought of ill-will (*byāpādavitakka*) or a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*) arises. The connection is as follows:
because the mind has been specifically subdued for the removal of resentment, a thought associated with ill-will toward an object of resentment arises;
or a thought associated with cruelty, in the sense of harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth, arises. "If that, the bhikkhu endures" means: [if he tolerates it].

He tolerates—that is, he allows to dwell—those aforementioned thoughts of sensual desire and so forth that have arisen in his own mind according to their respective conditions, by not subjecting them to such reflection as:
"In this way, this thought is evil; in this way, it is unwholesome; in this way, it is blameworthy; and furthermore, it leads to one's own affliction," and so on. While thus tolerating them...
And he does not abandon them by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*) and so forth; nor does he relinquish them. For that very reason, he does not dispel them;

he does not push them away from his own mental continuum, nor does he extract them. Because he does not dispel them in this way, he does not bring them to an end—that is, he does not make them reach their limit.
Being ardent and resolute, he acts so that not even a trace of them remains within him, not even a mere fragment.
The meaning is: "He acts in this way, but he does not act in that way. However, being thus [endowed with evil thoughts], he does not cause them to go to non-existence;

he does not cause them to go to non-existence little by little (*anu anu*). The meaning should be understood by connecting the word *ce* (if) with such phrases as "if he does not abandon" and "if he does not dispel.

"Being thus" means being possessed of evil thoughts such as sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth. "Without ardor" (*anātāpī*) refers to [the lack of effort] regarding the defilements (*kilesa*).

One who lacks ardor (*ātāpa*) due to the absence of ardent energy (*vīriya*) is "unardent" (*anātāpī*). One who lacks moral dread (*ottappa*) characterized by the shrinking away from evil is "undreadful" (*anottāpī*).
"Constantly, continuously, at all times, and without interruption" means perpetually and uninterruptedly.

"Lassitude, inferior energy" means one is "lazy" (*kusīta*) because of falling away from wholesome states (*dhamma*), sinking into what is base on the side of the unwholesome, and being possessed of indolence (*kosajja*); it is also due to the absence of the energy of right exertion (*sammappadhāna*).
"One of inferior energy" is said and described as one who is devoid of energy. "Of one who stands" means of one who stands having ceased walking.

Since the posture of lying down is particularly conducive to indolence, the phrase "of one who is awake" is stated to show how [mental states] arise through the cultivation of that [posture] by one who possesses it.

"In the bright fortnight, if that [thought] does not take hold of the bhikkhu": even while dwelling with energy aroused, if sensual thoughts and the like should arise due to forgetfulness of mindfulness—owing to long-term habituation throughout the beginningless cycle of existence—or due to the convergence of such conditions, the bhikkhu, having brought them back to his own mind, does not let them remain;
the meaning is that he does not allow them to remain within. Not tolerating them...
What does it do? It abandons and discards. Is it like a basket [discarding] refuse? No; rather, it dispels, pushes away, and removes it.

Is it like a goad [driving away] a bullock? No; rather, it brings it to an end and makes it vanish, making it so that not even a trace remains of them—not even a mere fragment. In this way, it acts upon them.
But how does he do so? He makes them go to non-existence; he makes them go to non-existence one by one.

What is meant is that he acts in such a way that they are thoroughly suppressed by means of suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhana-ppahāna*). Regarding the phrase "one who has become thus" (*evaṃbhūto*) and so forth:
being thus one whose disposition is perfectly purified by not tolerating sensual thoughts and the like, and by that...

Through the perfection of his disposition and the perfection of application caused by it, he is one whose virtue is purified, who guards the doors of the sense faculties, who is moderate in eating, and who is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

He is "ardent" because he is possessed of energy characterized by the tormenting of the defilements through the methods such as "by that factor" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth; and he is so called because he is endowed with a complete dread of evil.

"Always conscientious day and night": this means he is one who has exerted energy and is resolute through the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), by way of accomplishing the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhāna*), continuously and without interruption.
"He is said to have his mind directed toward Nibbāna" is the meaning of what is stated.

Regarding the verses, the phrase "dependent on the household" refers here to the fact that [the worldling] has not abandoned the household life, possesses the nature of a householder, and is subject to the conditions of the household.

Or, "home" (geha) refers to sensual desire for objects (*vatthukāma*). Alternatively, they are called "homes" because they are bound up with the home, or because they serve as the dwelling place for the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*);
since they have those [defilements] as their basis, thoughts of sensual desire and so forth are said to be "dependent on the home.

"One who has entered upon a wrong path": because covetousness and other such states, along with the factors associated with them, constitute a by-path to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), they are therefore called the "wrong path. Thus:
"One who is full of thoughts of sensual desire and the like" means one who has set out upon a wrong path.

"Infatuated with things that lead to delusion" means infatuated with, devoted to, and obsessed by forms and so forth which are conducive to delusion. "Enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of the Noble Path.
"To touch" means to reach or attain. Such a person, evil and having wrong intention as his sphere of activity, is incapable; the meaning is that he never attains it.
"Having stilled thought" means having pacified the aforementioned wrong thought by means of the power of reflective cultivation (*paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanā*).
"Delighting in the stilling of thought" means being delighted and intent upon *arahatship*—which is the absolute stilling of even the nine great thoughts—or indeed upon *nibbāna* itself.
"He is capable" refers to that person who is practicing rightly as described.

Having first, by the power of serenity and insight, stilled all discursive thoughts as appropriate through their respective factors of abandonment and so forth, and having remained thus, he further intensifies his insight;

it is such an Arahant who is capable of touching and attaining the supreme enlightenment—consisting of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and that which is termed Nibbāna—by means of the successive stages of the path. In this way, the commentary on the text should be understood.
The commentary on the Carasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sīlasutta. 12.
Regarding the second [sutta], "endowed with virtue" (*sampannasīla*): here, "endowed" (*sampanna*) is threefold, by way of being complete, possessed, and sweet. Therein—
“Kosiya, the crows eat the rice-plantation that has been fully harvested;
I inform you of this, O Brahmā, for I am unable to prevent them.
This is called “fully perfected and complete. “By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, one is endowed, fully endowed, and has arrived [at virtue].”
“Has arrived, has been reborn, has attained, is endowed with”—this is called “endowed with possession” (*samaṅgisampanna*).
“Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is endowed [with sweetness], its taste is like that of pure, dark honey”—this is called “endowed with sweetness” (*madhurasampanna*).
Here, the meaning is shown by way of being “endowed with completeness” (*paripuṇṇasampanna*).
"‘Of perfected virtue’ means ‘of fulfilled virtue,’ he said. The meaning is also appropriate in the sense of being possessed of [virtue] (*samaṅgi*) and perfected (*sampanna*);
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as either ‘having become one of perfected virtue,’ that is, ‘one of fulfilled virtue,’ or ‘having become one possessed of virtue.
In this context, she is ‘of fulfilled virtue’ because, through the complete undertaking of virtue, it has reached the state of being unbroken and so forth."
One who possesses virtue (*sīlasamaṅgin*) is so called because of not interrupting [the practice] from the moment of undertaking it.

Indeed, the state of possessing virtue should be understood as occurring through the non-arising of factors that are absolutely opposed to what has been undertaken; however, there is no need to speak of the occurrence-characteristic (*pavattilakkhaṇa*) regarding those factors such as volition (*cetanā*) which have the characteristic of moral conduct (*sīlana*).
In this context, by the phrase "perfect in virtue" (*paripuṇṇasīlā*),

the perfection of virtue through the removal of defects in virtue is stated as being like the perfection of a field through the removal of defects in a field. For just as a field is incomplete when it possesses four defects—
namely, a defect in the seed, a defect in the sowing, a defect in the water, and a defect in the soil— therein, a "defect in the seed" refers to that where...
From time to time there are seeds that are broken or rotten; wherever they fall, the crop does not grow there, and the field becomes broken—meaning it is incomplete.
A "broken sowing" is where an unskilled person, while sowing seeds, drops them here and there. For in this way, the crop does not grow everywhere.
The field is broken. A "water-broken" field is one where there is either too much water or no water at all in certain places;
for even there, the crops do not grow, and thus the field is broken.
A "salt-broken" field is one where, in a certain area, the farmer, while plowing the ground four or five times with the plow, [encounters] too deep [saline soil].
When one plows, salt arises from that [plowing]. For even there, the crop does not grow;
the field becomes broken, and such a field is neither of great fruit nor of great benefit. Even there, though much is sown, little is obtained.
But with the disappearance of these four defects, the field becomes complete; and such a field—
It is of great fruit and great benefit. In the same way, virtue that possesses four faults—being broken, flawed, mottled, and tarnished—is incomplete;
such virtue is neither of great fruit nor of great benefit.
However, with the disappearance of these four faults, virtue becomes complete; and such virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.
“Possessing virtue” (*sīlasamaṅgino*): by this meaning, it is simply said, “Dwell having become possessed of, having attained, and having been endowed with virtue.
In that regard, perfection of virtue comes about through two causes:
by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue. Both of these—

This has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding this, the Elder Suma, who lived at the Day’s Abode, said: "By the words ‘one endowed with virtue,’ the Blessed One has indicated the fourfold purification of virtue;
then, by the phrase ‘restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,’ he shows in detail the foremost type of virtue therein.
However, his pupil, the Elder Cūḷanāga, who was versed in the Three Piṭakas, said: "In both instances..."

"The Blessed One spoke of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; for restraint according to the Pātimokkha alone is virtue (sīla), while the other three are merely what is called 'places' (ṭhāna) where virtue resides.
Having said this, not granting that [position], he said: "What is called restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors;
purity of livelihood is merely the arising of requisites through the Dhamma and in accordance with justice."

It is merely the consumption [of requisites] after reflecting that they have been obtained in dependence on conditions and for the purpose of this [sustenance]. In the ultimate sense, virtue (*sīla*) is simply the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

For one whose [restraint] is broken, it is not said that he will protect the remaining [limbs], just as a man whose head is severed cannot be said to protect his hands and feet. But for one whose [restraint] is intact, he is like one whose head is unsevered.
Just as a man can protect his life by making the rest [of his possessions] ordinary,
so too, having indicated the restraint of the Pātimokkha by the phrase “perfect in virtue,” and having stated “perfect in the Pātimokkha” as a synonym for that very same thing,
he spoke the passage beginning with “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” in order to explain it in detail.

“Restrained by the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha” means that with the virtue of the training rules—known by the name *pātimokkha* because it protects (*pāti*) and releases (*mokkheti*) one who observes it from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth—the doors of body and speech are closed.
And being such, they are said to be “endowed” and “possessed” of it; thus he says, “having become endowed. [This applies] both to conduct and to range of activity.
"Endowed" means endowed with conduct (*ācāra*) consisting of non-transgression in body and speech, and not endowed with a resort (*gocara*) such as frequenting prostitutes;
thus the meaning is "endowed with both conduct and resort. "In matters of minute measure" means in those very slight matters that do not constitute an offense.
Others say: "In mere wrongdoings and verbal faults. "Faults" refers to blameworthy unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*).
"Those who have the habit of seeing [faults] as fearful" means those whose nature is to fear even a fault the size of an atom as if it were the magnitude of Mount Sineru.

"In all sections of the training" refers to the various divisions such as the original formulations (*mūla-paññatti*), subsequent formulations (*anupaññatti*), universal formulations (*sabbattha-paññatti*), and partial formulations (*padesa-paññatti*).
"Having undertaken whatever is to be undertaken" means having taken up whatever is to be undertaken among the various sections of the training, such as the original formulations and so forth.
The meaning is: having correctly undertaken, correctly, respectfully, and entirely that bodily or verbal virtue which is to be trained in, practiced, and fulfilled.
One who sees arising sees twenty-five characteristics: "With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of form" is in the sense of the arising of conditions.

He sees the arising of the aggregate of form. He sees the arising of the aggregate of form in the sense of the arising of conditions: "With the arising of craving... [and so on] ...with the arising of karma... [and so on] ...with the arising of nutriment there is the arising of form.
Even while seeing the characteristic of generation, he sees the arising of the aggregate of form. Seeing the arising of the aggregate of form, these...
He sees five characteristics. Likewise, he sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking:
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling"; with the arising of craving... [and so on] ...with the arising of kamma...
[and so on] ...with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling. This is the characteristic of production.
Even while passing by, he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. Seeing the arising of the aggregate of feeling, he sees these five characteristics;
in this manner, having stated five for each aggregate, he sees the twenty-five characteristics of arising.

When one sees "decay," one sees the twenty-five characteristics. Thus: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form"—one sees the decay of the aggregate of form from the perspective of the cessation of conditions.

"With the cessation of craving... [and so on] ...with the cessation of kamma... [and so on] ...with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form"—one sees the decay of the aggregate of form from the perspective of the cessation of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of change...
He sees the fall of the aggregate of form. Seeing the fall of the aggregate of form, he sees these five characteristics.

Through the cessation of ignorance... [and so on] ...through the cessation of craving... [and so on] ...through the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling; thus, in the sense of the cessation of conditions, he sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling.
Even while seeing the characteristic of change, he sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling.

"We see its passing away. By way of such a method as "One who sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling sees these five characteristics," one sees twenty-five characteristics of passing away, five being stated for each aggregate.
"With mind directed toward" means with the mind directed toward Nibbāna. "They speak" means that the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, describe such a bhikkhu.
“Yataṃ care” means one should proceed with effort; even while performing movements such as walking back and forth,

one should exert oneself and strive, applying the energy of striving described in the passage beginning, “He generates desire and exerts himself for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states,” in such a way that unwholesome states are abandoned and wholesome states [are established].
"They reach the fulfillment of cultivation; thus, one should proceed in this manner—this is the meaning. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"Stretching out each limb": being one who possesses the aforementioned energy, exerting oneself (*yatamāno*), one should stretch out each limb—the hands, feet, and so forth—that ought to be stretched;
the intention is that one should not abandon effort in any respect.
Now, in order to show the practice by which one who practices is called "striving with effort" (*yatam yatanto*), the passage beginning with “above” (*uddham*) was spoken.
Therein, “above” (*uddham*) means upward. “Across” (*tiriyam*) means all around; the meaning is: in every direction and sub-direction, such as the eastern quarter and so forth.
“Below” (*apācīnam*) means downward. “As far as the range of the world” (*yāvatā jagato gati*) refers to however much of the extent of the conditioned phenomena of sentient beings.

The world’s process; the meaning is "in all respects therein. Up to this point, he shows the inclusion of the entire range of the object of comprehension-knowledge (*sammasana-ñāṇa*) without exception.
"Contemplated" (*samavekkhitā*) means contemplated by way of a balanced method or principle; what is meant is that they have been seen through insight (*vipassanā*) as impermanent and so forth.
"Of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) refers to those things empty of a self. "Of aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ*) refers to the five beginning with form.
Of the aggregates. "Arising and passing away" means both arising and passing away. This is what is meant:

by means of the knowledge of arising and passing away—which is attained through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth regarding all material and immaterial phenomena comprised within the five aggregates of clinging, which are divided into past and other categories throughout the entire world encompassed in the three directions (above, across, and below)—[one contemplates] the twenty-five [aspects].
"One who has examined and clearly perceived arising through its modes and passing away through twenty-five modes.

"Conformity to mental serenity" (*cetosamathasāmīci*) refers to the purification of knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) that is appropriate for the Noble Path known as mental serenity, due to the absolute pacification of the defilements of the mind. "One who is training" means one who is practicing the way.
He is developing [it], producing a succession of knowledges. "Always" (sadā) means at all times, both by night and by day.
"Mindful" (sata) means acting with mindfulness endowed with the fourfold clear comprehension. Thus should the commentary on this verse be understood. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Sīla Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Padhāna-sutta* 13.
Regarding the third [verse], "supreme energies" (*uttama-vīriyāni*) means the best energies, because they accomplish a distinguished goal.

"The realm of Māra" (*māradheyya*) is so called because Māra dwells therein; it is the sphere of activity of the defilement-Māra, namely, the round of existence consisting of the three planes. Thus he said.
“The realm of Māra is what is known as the round of existence in the three planes. Fear born from birth and death is “fear of birth and death”;
or, because birth and death themselves are the cause of fear, they are called “fear of birth and death. Therefore he said: “Birth and death... [etc. ...of fear.
The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Padhānasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Saṃvarasutta*: 14.
In the fourth [sutta], they are called "strivings" (*padhānāni*) because one strives by means of them for the sake of accomplishing restraint and so forth. For one who is exercising restraint...

"Arisen energy" means the energy that has arisen in one who is not indolent, through the establishment of mindfulness and the closing of the eyes and so forth, in such a way that covetousness and other such states do not arise.

"Of one abandoning" means of one dispelling [them]. "Arisen energy" refers to the energy that proceeds by way of accomplishing that very abandonment. Regarding "arisen energy of one developing," it is here also...

The same method applies here. "The sign of concentration" (*samādhinimitta*) means concentration itself. For since the concentration that has previously arisen is the cause for the concentration that arises subsequently, it is called the "sign of concentration.

"Due to seclusion from the acquisitions" (*upadhivivekattā*) means due to being secluded from or detached from the acquisitions such as the aggregates (*khandha*). "Having approached that" means having relied upon that.

Nibbāna is the cause for attainment by means of the path. It is called *virāga* (dispassion) because passion and the like fade away (*virajjanti*) therein, or because they are faded away by it. Cessation (*nirodha*) should also be understood in this way.
Since it is intended here in connection with the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), it is stated:

"either by way of its object or by way of what is to be attained. In that context, "by way of what is to be attained" means by way of being inclined toward it. "Tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*) means by way of relinquishment.
The virtue of dedication consists in both the relinquishing and the leaping forward [into the goal]. Therefore, he said, "There are two kinds of relinquishment," and so forth.
Relinquishing the aggregates means by way of abandoning the defilements bound up with them;
for it should be stated that in whatever manner insight abandons the defilements, in that very same manner it abandons the aggregates which are their objective cause.
He says, "It is worthy (arahati)," [referring to the passage] "insight... completely abandons.
Because insight, upon reaching the state of leading to emergence, is said to "leap into" Nibbāna exclusively by way of its inclination, slope, and tendency;
and because the Path completely abandons the defilements and the aggregates by way of their eradication, therefore, in due order:
Through the insight paths, one should understand the plunging, the relinquishing, and the relinquishment.
"For the sake of relinquishment" means for the sake of both the relinquishment of giving and the relinquishment of plunging. "It transforms" means it relinquishes.
Furthermore, that transformation occurs through the attainment of the state of leading to emergence and the attainment of the state of the noble path.

"It is desired," he said, "because it attains both the state of insight (vipassanā) and the state of the path (magga). Regarding the "remaining phrases": this refers to the remaining sections of the factors of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga), such as "he develops the investigation-of-dhammas factor of enlightenment" and so forth.
It is "auspicious" (bhaddaka) because, by suppressing unwholesome states such as the hindrances and by the departure of lust, it is exclusively beneficial.
And it is rare, auspicious, and beautiful. For there is no other object of concentration (*samādhinimitta*) so rare that it is the direct antidote to lust.
Regarding the phrase "he guards it," guarding here means acting in such a way that there is no decline from the concentration already attained;
thus he says, "concentration," and so forth, by means of the instruction for practice and the removal of its opposites.

"Beginning with the perception of the skeleton" means beginning with the jhāna of the skeleton. He speaks of the jhāna by way of its primary characteristic, which is "perception. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Paññatti Sutta.
15. Those who possess a personal existence (*attabhāva*) are called *attabhāvino*; [the text refers to] those *attabhāvino*. Therefore he said, "of those possessing a personal existence.
King Mandhātu, it is said, enjoyed exquisite sensual pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indras;
on one occasion, he asked his own jewel of a counselor: "Is there anything more delightful than the human world?"
“[This is] the place. “Why, Your Majesty, do you speak thus? Do you not see the power of the moon and the sun?
Is their place not more delightful than this? The King, placing the Wheel-Treasure in front, went there.
Hearing that “Great King Mandhātu has arrived,” the Four Great Kings thought, “This Great King possesses such great supernormal power; he cannot [be stopped].”
“Let us ward him off by means of battle,” they said, and they offered up their entire kingdom to him. Having accepted it, he asked again:
“Is there indeed any place more delightful than this? Then they described to him the realm of the Thirty-three: “The realm of the Thirty-three, O Lord, is delightful;
there, these four Great Kings are the attendants of Sakka, the King of the Gods, at the gateway.”
They remain. Sakka, the king of the gods, possesses great psychic power and great majesty.

His places of enjoyment are these: the Vejayanta Palace, a thousand yojanas in height; the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, five hundred yojanas in height; the Vejayanta chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas long; likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa;
and the Nandana Grove, adorned with a thousand celestial trees, as well as the Cittalātā Grove.
"In the Phārusaka Grove stands the Pāricchattaka Koviḷāra tree, a hundred yojanas in height.
Beneath it is the Paṇḍukambala stone, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high, with the color of a *jayasumana* flower;
due to its softness, when Sakka sits upon it, half his body sinks into it."
Having heard this, the king, desiring to go there, launched the Wheel-Treasure. It rose into the air together with the fourfold army.

Then, from midway between the two heavenly worlds, the Wheel-Treasure descended and came to a halt upon the earth near the ground, together with the fourfold army headed by the Counsellor-Treasure. The king—

Alone, by his own power, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. When Sakka heard that Mandhātā had arrived, he went out to meet him and said, “Welcome, Great King! It is yours, Great King; command it, Great King.
Having spoken thus, he divided the kingdom into two portions and gave one portion to him, together with the celestial nymphs. Thus the king [resided] in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
As soon as he was established there, his human nature—the scent of a human being, the appearance of a human body, and so forth—vanished;

and because space had been made for karma that yields its result in the world of the gods and is to be experienced in a subsequent life, his divine nature—characterized by always appearing sixteen years of age, never fading garlands, and other such qualities—manifested.
While he sat with Sakka upon the Pandukambala stone, in the mere twinkling of an eye...
A distinction is perceived. Not noticing this, the gods are deluded regarding the distinction between Sakka and him.

While he is experiencing celestial prosperity there, during the time it takes for humans to reach thirty-six Sakkas—passing away after having been reborn with an incalculable lifespan—he exercises the sovereignty of Sakka and thinks, "What use have I for this half-kingdom?"
Unsatisfied with sensual pleasures, he passed away from there and fell into his own garden in the human world;

there, due to the harshness of the seasons and being struck by wind and heat, his body was afflicted and he died. Therefore it is said: "In the world of the gods, he enjoyed exquisite sensual pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indas."
The commentary on the *Paññatti-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Sokhumma-sutta*: 16.
In the sixth [sutta], "penetrating the subtle characteristics" means penetrating the subtle characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth.
"By means of knowledge that discerns subtle characteristics" means by means of the knowledge that discerns subtle characteristics.

"Having known them from another" means having known them as other because they are not subject to one's own control. For even when formations are desired [by thinking], "May they not break up," they nevertheless break up;
therefore, because they are not subject to one's own control, they are called "other. And this "otherness" of theirs becomes manifest upon the vision of impermanence.
