It is said: "By this phrase, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is explained. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sokhumma-sutta* is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the first *Agati-sutta* and following.

17–20. Regarding "In the seventh [verse], *chandāgatin*": here, showing that there is a elision of the vowel (*saralopa*) by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), he says, "going through desire" (*chandena agati*).
He says "by desire" (*chandenā*) because the word "desire" (*chanda*) is used in the ablative case to express a cause; the meaning is "through affection" (*pemena*).

In this context, the word "desire" (*chanda*) is a synonym for craving (*taṇhā*) or a synonym for unwholesome desire (*akusalacchanda*). "In the remaining [cases]" refers to such passages as "he goes to going through hatred" (*dosāgatin gacchati*), and so forth.
And herein, when one— out of favoritism (*chanda*) thinking, "This person is my friend," or "He is a close acquaintance," or "He is a relative," or "He gives me bribes"—
makes one who is not the owner the owner, this is called doing what should not be done through favoritism.
When one— due to a long-standing enmity thinking, "This person is my enemy," or due to anger arising at that very moment— makes an owner non-owner...

He does it; this is called doing what should not be done out of hatred (*dosa*). But he who, out of dullness or delusion, speaks whatever is improper or groundless, and makes one who is not the owner the owner—this is called doing what should not be done out of delusion (*moha*).
Furthermore, he who [thinks], "This person is a favorite of the king," or [perceives] in an unjust person such as a thief, or in unjust bodily misconduct and so forth...
Thinking, "By acting according to his instructions, he might do me harm because he relies on partiality," one who is afraid makes a master of one who has no master;
this is what is called doing what should not be done out of fear.
Furthermore, when distributing something, thinking, "This person is my friend or a close associate," one gives more out of affection...
One gives less out of hatred, thinking, "This person is my enemy. One who is deluded, not knowing what has been given or not given, gives less to some and more to others.
Or, being cold, one gives more to someone, thinking, "If this were not given to him, he might even cause me harm.
Thus, all four types of such persons proceed, in their respective order, according to favoritism (*chandāgati*) and the other [biases].
"He does what should not be done" means he performs improper actions.
"His fame diminishes" means that for one who goes on a wrong path, both his reputation (*kittiyasa*) and his following-fame (*parivārayasa*) diminish and decline.
For fame (*yasa*) is so called because it is praised (*yassati*); *kitti* is the sound of praise. It is so called because it is praised by those who walk before him and follow behind him.
It is called *yaso* because it surrounds; thus, it is a retinue (*parivāra*). The eighth, ninth, and tenth [chapters] have meanings that are self-evident.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Wanderers (*Caravagga*), is concluded. 3. The Chapter on Uruvelā (*Uruvelavagga*).
1. Commentary on the First Uruvela Sutta 21.
In the first [section] of the third [chapter], "Mahāvelā" means like a great flood; the sense is that it is like a vast sandy bank because of its abundance of sand.
Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'a great heap of sand. *Uru*, *maru*, *sikatā*, *vālukā*, *vaṇṇu*...
“Vālikā” and these words are synonymous; there is only a difference in their phonetic forms (*byañjana*). Therefore he said: “*Uru* is called *vālikā*.
“*Najjā*” means that which flows or resounds, thus a river (*nadī*); of that river, of the flowing stream—this is the meaning. Regarding “*Nerañjarāyā*”:

it should have been said “*Nelañjalāyā*,” but by changing the letter *la* to the letter *ra*, it is stated as “*Nerañjarāyā*,” meaning [the river] whose waters are free from defects such as mud, moss, and aquatic plants.
The meaning [is as follows]. Some say that where it should have been said "on the Nīlañjalā," it is "on the Nerañjarā.
Or rather, it should be understood that this is simply the name of that river. To show the place on the bank of that river where the Blessed One dwelt, it is said, "at the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree.
As for why this came to be called the Ajapāla-nigrodha, he says "of that... and so forth. However, some [say] because...
They say: "There, elderly brahmins who were unable to recite the Vedas built dwellings surrounded by walls and all resided there;
therefore, it received the name 'Ajapāla-nigrodha' (the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree). Herein, this is the etymology: they do not mutter (*na japanti*) [the mantras], thus they are *ajapā*;
the meaning is those who do not study the mantras. They take up [or frequent] the *ajapā*, hence [it is called] *ajapāla*.
"It is called Ajapāla because [the goats] dwell there (nivāsaṃ ettha). Others, however, say:
"Because at the time of midday, when the goats have entered inside, it protects (pāleti) and guards them with its own shadow, therefore the name 'Ajapāla' became established for it.
In all cases, this is the name of that tree.
"Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means "first fully awakened"; this expression is formed by the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).

For this very reason, it says: "Having become fully awakened, first of all. Furthermore, "paṭhamaṃ" is a neuter noun used adverbially; therefore, the connection here should be understood as: "Having become fully awakened, I am dwelling for the first time at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree. This is the thought.
This is the thought that occurs thus: “What if I were to... [pe] ...dwell? An elephant, a monkey, and a partridge are “elephant-monkey-partridge.
Those who honor the elders—there are three kinds of elders: the elder by birth, the elder by age, and the elder by virtue. Among these, one endowed with noble birth...
One who is aged by birth is called "aged by birth"; one established in [advanced] years is called "aged by years"; one endowed with virtues is called "aged by virtue.
Among these, it is the one aged by virtue and aged by years who is intended here by the term "the aged. "Honoring" means they worship them through the act of honoring elders.
"Skilled in the Dhamma" means skilled and proficient in the Dhamma of honoring elders. "In this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme) means in this very [existence].
"In this very life" (*attabhāve*). "Praiseworthy" (*pāsaṃsā*) means worthy of praise. "And a happy destination in the future world" (*samparāye ca suggati*):
even in the next world, which must be gone to after passing away and leaving this world, for them there is only a happy destination. This, then, is the summarized meaning here:
whether they be Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, householders, those gone forth, or even animals—whosoever [they may be].
Some beings, through the act of honoring their elders, show respect to those who are advanced in age and endowed with virtues such as moral discipline;
they receive praise, eulogy, and acclaim for being "honourers of their elders" in this very life,
and upon the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.

"In another" means in someone else. "There is no self" means there is another, a stranger. However, in this context, it does not refer to just anyone, but rather to one who occupies the position of a teacher.
Therefore he said: "without placing anyone in the position of a teacher. One who obeys, that is, accepts the command of a teacher, is "obedient" (*patissa*);
one who is not obedient is "disobedient" (*appatissa*), meaning devoid of obedience, or lacking reliance upon a teacher.
In the compound *sadevaka*, the analysis (*viggaha*) is by way of its parts, while the collective whole is the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*).

By the inclusion of "with the devas" (*sadevaka*), the deities of the five sense-sphere realms (*pañca-kāmāvacara*) are included through the principle of elimination (*pārisesa-naya*), since the others are already comprised by the other terms. By the inclusion of "with Māra" (*samāraka*), the deities of the sixth sense-sphere realm are included through the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti-naya*);
for Māra is both born there and resides there. By the expression "with Brahmā" (*sabrahmaka*), the deities of the Brahma-world such as the *Brahmakāyika* and others are included.

By the very principle of proximity (*paccāsatti-nīya*). The phrase "of the generation together with recluses and brahmins" includes the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
This is merely an illustration, because by that same expression, non-adversarial recluses and brahmins who have not yet stilled [the defilements] or abandoned evil are also included.
Granted, the word "world" (*loka*) refers to sentient beings by virtue of the qualifiers such as "together with devas."
It is understood [that this compound does not apply] because those [terms] share a common grammatical relation (*tulyayoga*);

however, since this compound is seen to occur even in cases of non-common relation (*atulyayoga*), as in the examples "having hair" (*salomako*) and "having wings" (*sapakkhako*), the word *pajā* is included. By the term *pajā*, the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is intended.

Even though Māra and Brahmā are included under the general category of "divine state" (*devabhāva-sāmañña*), the word is used to show the specific distinctions that belong to them which are not shared by the others.
Showing that the mention is separate, he said, "Māra by name," and so forth. He said, "of all," because Māra is capable of causing even the Brahmās to lose their vision.
"Above" means in the upper region. "Brahmā" refers to the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world system; thus he said, "with ten fingers," and so forth.
Here, as in the Dīgha Nikāya and others, there are also collections of texts belonging to outsiders.

He said, "by way of the single Nikāya and so forth," because it is obtained. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the sciences of site-selection, etc.," the various branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhānāni*) are included.
It is called "the generation" (*pajā*) because it is born or produced by its own respective kamma and defilements; it refers to the category of beings (*sattanikāya*).
Alternatively, by the phrase "together with devas and humans," one should understand that this includes both conventional deities (*sammutideva*) and the remainder of the human world.

Having thus explained the world by way of its divisions (*bhāgaso*) and shown the *yojana*, he now says "But here too" (*apicettha*) and so forth, in order to explain the *yojana* by taking the world without such divisions (*abhāgaso*).
They are spoken of by way of the world (*loka*) because "kamma and the fruits of kamma are found therein" (*lokīyanti ettha*).

They are spoken of by way of progeny (*pajā*) because "they are born (*pajātā*) by means of causes and conditions. Regarding the phrase "more endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampannataran*), here it refers to the state of being complete and perfected (*paripuṇṇa-sampannatā*).

It is intended [in this sense], as in such passages as “the rice-field was well-ripened. Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘more abundant. For that which is complete deserves to be called more abundant.
“Reason” means a logical justification (*yutti*). “Meaning” means the non-perverted meaning. “Increase” means the cause for excessive increase.
“By this statement” means by the statement spoken immediately following in this sutta. It is not by this alone; there is also another sutta.
Showing that [the opponent] must be brought forward and refuted, he said, "I have no teacher," and so forth.
In this context, "I have no teacher" means that regarding the supramundane Dhamma, I have no one who can be called my teacher.

Even with respect to mundane phenomena, there is no realization such as that of the Lord of the World which can be attained through the instruction of another. However, in the case of the supramundane Dhamma, [his realization is unique].
"Even these do not exist. "There is no person who is my counterpart" means there is no person who serves as a substitute for me by way of qualities such as virtue and so forth.
He said "by those who remember" because this is the nominative case used in the sense of an instrument; or alternatively, the meaning is "or by reason of remembering."
Because the suffix *-to* has the sense of the locative case (*bhumm-attha*), he said, "at which time. Those who know the nights are *rattaññū*;
they know many nights starting from the day of their own going-forth (*pabbajita*). What is meant is that they are long-ordained. The greatness of those who know the nights is *rattaññumahantaṃ*.
This designation emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*). Or alternatively, it is *rattaññumahattaṃ*.
This is the method for the remaining [terms] as well. "Vipula" (vastness) refers to the vastness of the elders, novices, and those of middle standing.

"Brahmacariya-mahantaṃ" (the greatness of the holy life) refers to the vastness of the holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings, by way of the jhānas, direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and so forth.
"Lābhagga-mahantaṃ" (the greatness of the excellence of gains) refers to the vastness of the attainment of distinguished requisites. "By way of the fourfold greatness" means...
By way of fourfold greatness. The mention of the time when the Blessed One gave the pair of cloths to Mahāpajāpatī is merely to show that it was a time when his reverence for the Saṅgha was manifest;
for the Blessed One did not dwell devoid of reverence for the Saṅgha prior to that.
The commentary on the First Uruvelā Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Uruvelā Sutta 22.
Regarding the phrase "by one of the *huhuṅka* temperament": it is said that this young brahmin Diṭṭhamangalika wandered about making the sound "huhu" out of a tendency toward views and out of anger;
therefore, he is called "one of the *huhuṅka* temperament. Some also read it as "*huhukkajātiko*," by which...
The meaning is "having come together. "Worn out by old age" means brought to a state where the teeth are broken and the hair is gray due to aging.
"Advanced in years" means having reached the limit of growth in the limbs and members of the body. "Elderly by birth" means endowed with the state of being advanced through the process of rebirth.
They are called "elders" (*mahallaka*) because they possess or take hold of greatness; they are elderly by birth, not by wealth or other such means.
"Of great age": having reached the final stage of life; "final stage of life" means the last third of a hundred years.
Or, "aged" means ancient, which is to say belonging to a lineage that has existed for a long time.
"Venerable" (vuddha) means endowed with the growth of virtues such as morality and conduct. "Elderly" (mahallaka) means possessed of greatness in wealth. "Of great fortune" (mahaddhana):
"Of great wealth. "Those who have reached the journey's end" means those brahmins who, having set out upon the path, proceed without transgressing the boundaries of ascetic practice and so forth.
"Those who have attained old age" means those who have reached the final stage of life, the state of being advanced in years.
Regarding the phrase "sutaṃ netam," the word division here is *sutaṃ no etam*. The genitive case in *no* is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus he said, "heard by us."
"At the wrong time" means at an improper time. "He speaks what is unreal" means he speaks that which does not exist.
"He speaks what is unbeneficial" means he speaks that which is based on no cause. And "based on no cause" means fruitless; for fruit is indeed dependent upon a cause.
And because it is invariably concomitant with that [absence of cause], it is said to be "based on no cause," "fruitless," and "vain."

"Speaks what is not discipline" means he speaks that which is not connected with the discipline of restraint; it is said that he speaks what does not bring about restraint for himself or for his listener.
"Unfit to be stored in the heart" means it is unfit to be stored because it has not entered the mind due to being unbeneficial and harmful.
"At an unfit time to speak" refers to one who is preaching the Dhamma.
The time when a particular meaning should be stated is prior to or subsequent to that [specific occasion]; to speak of it before or after that time is to speak at an inappropriate time.

"Devoid of a reference" means devoid of a scriptural reference (*sutta-apadesa*). "He does not speak with a reference" means he does not speak by providing a reason, such as saying, "This was said by the Blessed One in such-and-such a sutta"; thus, he does not speak by making it supported by a reference and accompanied by a reason.
"Without limit" means without boundary. Having set aside a Sutta or a Jātaka, one brings forward its application, a simile, or a narrative background;
yet, without touching upon the discourse that constitutes the very body of the Sutta or Jātaka thus set aside, one speaks only of external matters.
What has been set aside remains merely set aside as "a Sutta..."
One falls into the position of saying, "Is he now telling a Jātaka? Or is it something else? We see neither its end nor its limit.

Just as on every branch of a banyan tree where it has reached, new shoots descend, and having descended, they grow further and continue to expand, so too [the narrative] proceeds for half a league or even a full league. As it proceeds—
But as he walks, the root tree perishes, while only the roots of the secondary shoots that have grown from it remain;
in this way, he is called a "speaker on the nature of the banyan tree. Having set down each point exactly as it was set down, he proceeds carrying it along by the side.
But one who, even while speaking much, [says] "this was said for this purpose," [and thus] from the suttas already set down, [brings in] something else...
It is possible for one to make [the meaning] known by repeatedly bringing forward examples through the application of analogies;

it is appropriate for such a preacher of the Dhamma to speak extensively. "Not based on mundane or supramundane benefit" means that it does not bring about mundane or supramundane welfare for oneself or others.

The term *pāḷi* refers to the "lineage" (*āḷī*) of excellent strings of speech, so called because it awakens the meaning of virtue and other such qualities that are preeminent and sublime, and because it was spoken by the Buddhas and others according to their own nature and terminology; thus, it is the Dhamma of the scriptures.
*Anusandhi* is the connection of a subsequent meaning with a preceding meaning; however, by way of meaning, it also applies to sections of the scriptures.

There is indeed a connection (*anusandhi*). This connection is fourfold, by way of: connection through questioning (*pucchānusandhi*), connection through intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*), connection according to the subject matter (*yathānusandhi*), and so forth.

However, for each of these, one should apply them respectively according to the preceding and following passages of the respective teachings, and according to the sequence of the connections themselves.
"Mastered" (*uggahita*) means grasped higher and higher, both by way of the phrasing (*byañjana*) and by way of the meaning (*attha*), through the process of thorough mastery (*pariyāpuṇana*).
The meaning is that it has been grasped by the heart both through hearing and through thorough inquiry.

It is called "heard" (*suta*) because it is to be heard by those seeking escape from the suffering of saṃsāra; thus, it refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures. One who retains that is a "retainer of what is heard" (*sutadhara*).
For one who is a retainer of what is heard, the heard becomes established in him—well-established and healthy; therefore it is said, "the foundation of what is heard. Thus he said: "Of whom..."
"‘Hī’ and so forth. A single word, or even a single syllable, being accumulated without being lost, is called ‘accumulation’ (*sannicaya*).
That in which there is an accumulation of what has been heard is ‘an accumulation of what has been heard’ (*sutasannicaya*). ‘Having clung to’ (*ajjhosāya*) means having entered into it.

‘It remains’ (*tiṭṭhati*) means it is not forgotten. ‘Familiar’ (*paguṇa*) means it has reached the tongue. ‘Unwavering’ (*niccalika*) means it does not fluctuate. ‘Having compared’ (*saṃsanditvā*) means having compared it with others."
"Having fully grasped" means having penetrated the meaning by way of thorough inquiry. It is "like the flow of the Ganges" because there is no interruption in its continuity.
Alternatively, the reading is "like the flow of the *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum)"; the meaning is that it proceeds with natural ease.
Here, mastery through mere verbal recitation of a portion of a sutta or of the sutta alone is not intended; rather, what is intended is mastery by way of chapters (*vagga*) and so forth.

He said: "The ten suttas... [etc. ...have been recited. The meaning is that they have been recited by way of speech after having observed them as "the ten suttas have been traversed," "the ten chapters have been traversed," and so forth.
They have been examined repeatedly with the mind, contemplated in their various parts, reflected upon, and scrutinized with the mind.
It appears like a visible form (*rūpagata*); that is, it is clear to the eye like a visible form.
It is manifested after having been offered. "Well-penetrated" means it has been thoroughly penetrated according to reality by making it rootless and thornless.
"Exalted mind" (*abhiceto*) refers to the mind of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*). Its exaltation consists in its being more beautiful than ordinary sense-sphere minds;
that [beauty] is purity by way of contrast, which is why he said, "excellent, purified mind. "Higher mind" (*adhicitta*)...

He speaks of concentration. That too should be understood as access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*). He says, "he experiences the bliss of renunciation," because all four kinds of jhāna-bliss—namely, the bliss of rapture and happiness born of seclusion, the bliss of rapture and happiness born of concentration, the bliss of bodily happiness free from rapture, and the bliss of knowledge born of the purity of mindfulness—are called the "bliss of renunciation" by virtue of having emerged from their opposites.
By the phrase "capable of entering [jhāna] at any desired moment," he expresses mastery over the attainment (*samāpajjana-vasībhāva*) regarding those jhānas.

Furthermore, from the expression "one who gains them at will" (*nikāmalābhī*), it should be understood that mastery over adverting (*āvajjana*), resolving (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*) is also stated.
By the phrase "having suppressed the opposing states with ease," the state of these jhānas being easy to practice (*sukhappaṭipada*) is indicated.
And it demonstrates his quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññatā*).
"Of the vast" (*vipulānaṃ*) means of the jhānas that have been brought to fullness. "Vastness" (*vipulatā*) indeed consists in their proceeding for a longer duration due to being well-developed;
and that [vastness] should be understood as corresponding to the limit [set]. Thus, having said "of the vast," he says "to emerge according to the limit."

"‘Capable’ is what is meant," he said. For one who emerges before reaching the time of the limit is not a "gainer of what is not difficult to obtain," because of being incapable of maintaining [the attainment] for as long as desired.

Now, in order to clarify the mastery in entering and so forth as previously described by way of contrast, the passage beginning with "A certain person... was stated. In that context, the phrase "he is indeed a gainer" refers to this:
This is said by way of the mere attainment of jhāna. "Thus" means at whatever desired moment. "Obstructive" refers to states that are adverse to mastery.
However, the states adverse to the attainment of jhāna have already been suppressed; otherwise, the attainment of jhāna itself would not be possible.
"He suppresses with difficulty" means he purifies with difficulty by means of reflecting on the danger of sensual desires and so forth.

Here, "suppression" (*vikkhambhana*) and "purification" (*visodhana*) should be understood as the complete removal of other obstacles to concentration (*samādhipāripanthika*), such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth.
"A water-clock vessel" (*nāḷikayanta*) refers to a vessel for measuring time.

"One whose intention is not fixed" (*aṭṭhapitasankappo*) means one whose intention is not rightly directed (*sammāpaṇihita*). "One who has reached the further shore of direct knowledge" (*abhiññāpāragū*) [refers to] all mundane and supramundane states.
"Having reached the further shore through direct knowledge" means that he stands having known all phenomena by means of the supreme path-wisdom (*aggamagga-paññā*).

"One who has reached the further shore through full understanding" means that he has reached the further shore through the full understanding of the five aggregates; the meaning is that he stands having fully understood the five aggregates.
"One who has reached the further shore through development" means that he has reached the further shore through the development of the four paths; [the meaning is] the four paths...

The meaning is: "having developed [them], he stands. "One who has reached the further shore through abandonment" means one who has gone to the further shore by the abandoning of all defilements; the meaning is that he stands having abandoned all defilements.
"One who has reached the further shore through realization" means one who has gone to the further shore through the realization of cessation (*nirodha*);

the meaning is that he stands having realized cessation. "One who has reached the further shore through attainment" means [one who has gone to the further shore] by the attaining of all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

"Gone" means having entered and remained in all the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). "One who has reached the perfection of the holy life" (*brahmacariyassa kevalī*) means one who is endowed with that which is the entirety or completeness of the holy life;

the meaning is that he dwells in the entirety of the holy life of the four paths. Therefore it is said, "one whose holy life is complete," meaning one whose holy life of the path is fulfilled. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the second Uruvelā Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Loka Sutta: 23.
In the third [sutta], "the world" (loka) is so called in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. In terms of meaning, the two preceding Noble Truths [are intended].
Here, however, the noble truth of suffering is to be understood. Therefore he said: "The world is the truth of suffering.
"Dissociated" means unattached and not bound; the meaning is that it is completely liberated from that because all fetters have been thoroughly severed.
According to the method of the Suttas, the origin of the world is craving; according to the method of the Abhidhamma, however, it is the volitional formations.
Together with one thousand five hundred defilements. "The cessation of the world" is Nibbāna. "Realized" means made personally manifest.
"The practice leading to the cessation of the world" is the Noble Eightfold Path, which comprises the three aggregates beginning with virtue.
For it goes to—that is, it reaches—Nibbāna, the cessation of the world; it is practiced by the Noble Ones for that purpose.
And this is called the practice leading to the cessation of the world.

To this extent, the meaning of "Tathāgata" is shown as follows: he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to those things that are "thus" (tatha) and has gone according to reality (yāthāvato gata). For the four noble truths are indeed called "thus. As it is said in detail:
"Monks, these four are thus, not otherwise, not different. Which four? 'This is suffering,' monks—this is thus, this is not otherwise, this is not different," and so forth.
Furthermore, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (*gata*) to suchness (*tathā*); "gone" here means understood, transcended, attained, and practiced.

This is what is meant: because the Blessed One has gone to and understood suchness—that is, the non-erroneous state—by means of full comprehension through investigation of the entire world, therefore the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; thus he is the Tathāgata. [He has likewise understood] the origin of the world by means of full comprehension through abandoning...
Thus, he has gone to that which is thus (tathā), therefore he is the Tathāgata. He has gone to, or attained, the cessation of the world for the sake of its realization, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
He has gone to, or entered upon, the path leading to the cessation of the world, which is such and unerring, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
In this way, the meaning of this passage should be understood by way of illustrating the state of being a Tathāgata.
Thus, having manifested his own state as a Tathāgata by means of the full awakening to the Four Noble Truths, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with “Bhikkhus, that which...
in order to demonstrate that same state also by means of the full awakening to what is seen and so forth.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “Having declared his own Buddhahood by means of the four truths...”; this [refers] to the words *tathāgata* and *buddha*.
This was stated in order to show that there is no difference in meaning [between the terms]. For it is precisely in this way that the canonical text proceeds.

"Seen" (*diṭṭha*) refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) because it is to be seen. By this, everything that has been seen, that is being seen, that will be seen, and that one might see in the future is included as "seen," since no specific time period is intended, just as in the case of the word "milked" (*duddha*).
[The text] shows this. The same method applies to the terms "heard" (suta) and so forth. "Heard" (suta) refers to the sense-sphere of sound because it is to be heard by the ear.

"Sensed" (muta) refers to that which is to be apprehended by reaching and grasping [the object] while releasing its dependence upon the faculty along with its physical basis. Therefore, he said: "because it is to be apprehended after having reached [it]. "Cognized" (viññāta) means that which is to be known.
Furthermore, since that is to be cognized as distinct from what is seen and so forth, he said: "having pleasant and painful mental objects as its domain."
“Having reached” means having reached it in whatever way it may be; the meaning is that it has come into one’s hand. Therefore he said: “Whether sought after or not sought after.
“Sought after” means that which was sought for the purpose of obtaining. That, moreover, may be either already obtained or not yet obtained;
since in both cases it is indeed something sought after, he said: “Whether obtained or unobtained. By both [of these]...
This shows that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to both kinds of bowl and both kinds of seeking in their respective ways.
"Wandering through with the mind" means that, having set those [objects] aside, he wandered through them one by one with the mind alone; the meaning is that he reflected upon them.
"Yellow," and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes all portions of visible objects such as red, white, and the rest. "Sumanā" means...
"Sumana" (joyful) means joyful by way of lust, by way of greed, or by way of faith and so forth.
"Dummana" (dejected) means dejected by way of ill-will thought or by way of cruelty thought. "Majjhatta" (neutral) means neutral by way of ignorance or by way of knowledge.
This same method applies everywhere. In that context, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there are included the sound of a conch, the sound of a drum, the scent of leaves, and the scent of flowers.

The inclusion of such things as flower-juice, fruit-juice, the appropriated (*upādinna*), the non-appropriated (*anupādinna*), neutral feeling, wholesome karma, and unwholesome karma should be understood.
"Not reached" (*appatta*) means not attained by knowledge; the meaning is "not known. Therefore he said, "not realized by knowledge" (*ñāṇena asacchikata*).
"Gone by the world" (*lokena gata*) means known by the world. "Because it has gone in that very way" (*tath'eva gatattā*) means because it has been known in that very way.
Because of having attained full enlightenment (*abhisambuddhattā*), the meaning is that the root *budh* (to awaken) has a single sense with the word *gata*.
For grammarians hold that verbal roots whose primary sense is "going" (*gati*) come to have the sense of "awakening" (*buddhi*).
And as for the phrase, "O monks, that unsurpassed perfect enlightenment which the Tathāgata fully awakens to," in which...
On the night of the full moon of the month of Visākha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata— in the sense of being such as he is—
sitting upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment, having crushed the heads of the three Māras,

attained supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*) together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) and omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), because there is nothing higher than that. And on the night when [he passed away] into the realm of Nibbāna without remainder...

"He attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna" means that on the very same night of the full moon of Visākha, at Kusinārā in the Upavattana sal grove of the Mallas, between the twin sāla trees, he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
"In the interval between these two" refers to the period between these two elements of nibbāna: that with residue and that without residue.

During the period measuring forty-five years—at the first enlightenment, the middle enlightenment, and the final enlightenment—whatever Dhamma he spoke, consisting of the various divisions such as Sutta and Geyya, he declared by way of illustration, he recited by way of pointing out, and he explained by way of full exposition.
All that is exactly so; thus, all that was taught within this interval [is likewise true].

The word of the Buddha, consisting of the ninefold division beginning with the Suttas and Geyyas, is complete in both meaning and phrasing—neither deficient nor redundant—and is perfect in every aspect.
It subdues the intoxication of lust, the intoxication of hatred, and the intoxication of delusion; therein not even a hair’s breadth of error exists.
It is as if marked with a single seal, as if measured with a single measure, as if weighed on a single scale.
And it is "thus" (*tathaṃ*) because it is exactly as it was spoken for the sake of its intended purpose, since it accomplishes that purpose in one way alone and not otherwise;
therefore, it is "thus," "not otherwise," and "not different. By this, he shows that he is the "Tathāgata" because of his speaking thus.
This word *gata* has the sense of "speaking" (*gada*), with the letter *da* changed to *ta*; therefore, the meaning is "one who speaks what is thus" (*tathaṃ gadati*), hence "Tathāgata."
Alternatively, *āgada* means "speech" (*vacana*). Because his speech is not contrary [to reality], he is called the *Tathāgata*—the *da* being changed to a *ta*.
Thus should the derivation of the word be understood here. As for the phrase "one who speaks according to [reality]":
those phenomena which the Blessed One has declared, "These phenomena are unwholesome, blameworthy, censured by the wise; when fully undertaken and observed..."
When he teaches the Dhamma to others, saying, "These things lead to what is unbeneficial and to suffering," he has himself abandoned those things absolutely.
But as for those things regarding which the Blessed One says, "These things are wholesome, blameless, praised by the wise,
and when fully undertaken and practiced, they lead to what is beneficial and to happiness," he has himself [fully undertaken and practiced] those things absolutely.
He dwells having attained [it]; therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One acts as he speaks.
Likewise, because he correctly fulfills virtue and the other perfections, the Blessed One acts as he does in the right practice;
and just as he acts, so too does he speak, by means of teaching the Dhamma to others to establish them therein. For the body of the Blessed One conforms to his speech.
Speech is also [the guide] for the body; therefore, one acts as one speaks and speaks as one acts.
For one who has become thus, just as the speech has gone and proceeded, so too has the body; and just as the body, so too has the speech gone and proceeded—this is the meaning.
"The Conqueror, unconquered" means that having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, [he is victorious] across the intermediate directions...
In immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One surpasses all beings by virtue of his moral conduct, concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
there is no equal or measure for him.

He is peerless, equal to the unequaled, matchless, incomparable, without rival, unmeasured, immeasurable, unsurpassed, the King of Dharma, the God of Gods, the Sakka who excels the Sakkas, and the Brahmā among Brahmās.
He is a supreme Brahmā; for that very reason, he is not overcome by anyone. "He sees" (dakkhati) means he sees everything.

Because there is no desire for further specific terminology, the word "ten" (dasa) has as its scope the entirety [of knowable objects]. By this, it is illustrated that whatever is called "knowable" (neyya), he sees all of it as if it were an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of his hand.
He is unerring through his awakening to the underlying dispositions (*āsaya*) and so forth, and through his bringing about of welfare and so forth.
He brings beings to the knowledge of their various natures; he brings formations to the state of being led toward that [knowledge];
through mastery in practicing in every way, he brings the attainments and the mind under his control—thus, "one who exercises mastery" (vasavattī) is how the meaning should be understood here.

"Dissociated" (visaṃyutta) means dissociated from the four bonds (yoga). Therefore it is said: "dissociated by the abandoning of the four bonds. "Devoid of the fuel of craving and views" means devoid of the fuel known as craving and views throughout the entire world.
"Standing having overcome" means standing having conquered and transcended by means of the abandoning of the defilements pertaining to those objects.
"Standing having released from the four ties" means standing having released all [fetters], such as the bodily tie of covetousness, from one's own continuum.
Alternatively, he is the "releaser from all ties" because he releases them from the continua of those to be trained through the excellence of his own teaching. Of him who has touched...
"Supreme peace": by this, it should be understood that the connection here is as follows—"this Buddha, whose taints are exhausted, has touched supreme peace through the touching of knowledge.
Therefore he said, "of one who has touched," and so forth. "In Nibbāna there is no fear from anything":
because of its unconditioned nature and its absolute security, there is no fear in Nibbāna arising from any cause of fear. Therefore he said:
The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is secure and the practice that leads to security,” and so forth.
Alternatively, since there is no fear from any quarter for one who has attained Nibbāna, Nibbāna should be understood here as “fearless from every side” (*akutobhaya*).
It is not that there is fear from anywhere in this [state] once it has been realized; thus, it is called “fearless from every side,” namely, Nibbāna. This is how the meaning should be seen here.
And the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) should be understood as follows:
"Anigha" means free from suffering. "One who has reached the destruction of all karma" means one who has reached the exhaustion, the end, and the absolute cessation of all karmas.
"Upadhi-saṅkhaya" means that here the acquisitions (*upadhī*) are completely destroyed; it is Nibbāna.
He said: "In Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of the substrata (upadhi-saṅkhaya). "The Wheel" refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka).
"Set in motion" means he set it in motion with its three revolutions and twelve aspects. It is "great" because it is endowed with great qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.
"Fearless" means free from timidity due to the possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Lokasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kāḷakārāmasutta: 24.
In the fourth [verse], "you praise them excessively" means that you praise and extol those ascetics, treating them with great importance.
"What is their virtue? means "of what virtue" (*kiṃsīlā*). "What is their conduct? means "of what conduct" (*kiṃsamācārā*). "Established in the excellence of qualities" (*guṇaggasaṇṭhitā*):
the letter *m* is used for euphonic junction (*padasandhi*); it means they are established in the highest qualities (*aggaguṇe patiṭṭhitā*).
"With tranquil faculties and tranquil minds": some also read, "Their going and staying is peaceful. "Solitary" (*ekakiyā*) means alone; [they are so] in all four postures.

The intended meaning is: "dwelling alone. For this very reason, he said, "without a second. Regarding the phrase "such ascetics as these are mine," here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*). By this, [the following is implied]:
"Their bodily action is pure, their verbal action is untroubled;..."
“Those ascetics of mine have minds that are utterly purified.
Stainless like conch shells and pearls, pure both within and without,
filled with wholesome qualities— such are the ascetics of mine.”
“The world is uplifted by gain and cast down by loss;
those who are the same in gain and loss—such are my ascetics.
The world is uplifted by fame and cast down by ill-repute;”
“Those who are of one mind with fame and glory—such are my ascetics.
The world is uplifted by praise and depressed by blame;
those who remain equanimous amidst both blame and praise—such are my ascetics.”
“The world is uplifted by pleasure, and it is depressed by suffering;
those who are unshakable amidst pleasure and pain—such as these are my ascetics.
This and similar passages are included [in this category].

This is the meaning of the verse beginning with “The virtuous are far away”: “Virtuous” (*santa*) refers to the Buddhas and others who are called “virtuous” because of the pacification (*santatā*) of passion and the other defilements;

however, in this context, those beings who have performed service under previous Buddhas, whose roots of merit are abundant, and who have developed spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are intended by the term “virtuous.
“They shine forth” (*pakāsanti*): even though they stand at a distance, they come within the range of the Buddhas’ knowledge and thus become manifest.

They exist. "Like the Himalayas" means that just as the Himalayan mountain—extending for three thousand leagues, rising five hundred leagues high, and adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks—appears as if standing directly in front even to those situated far away, so too do they appear;
this is the meaning. "Those who are not present here are not seen" refers to those who value gain and disregard the world beyond.
Those who have eyes only for material gain, who have gone forth for the sake of a livelihood, and who are foolish persons—these are called "the non-existent.
Even though they are seated near the knee-circle of the Buddhas' sacrificial offering, they are neither seen nor perceived.
They are like arrows shot in the night; that is, like arrows shot into the darkness endowed with its four factors. Of such a kind...
The meaning is that they do not appear because of the absence of a prior cause (*pubbahetu*) acting as a decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"Brahmadeyya" means a gift for the best; the meaning is that it is given in such a way that it cannot be taken back again—given as something relinquished and abandoned.
"He does not conceive of what is seen": here, "seen" refers to what is seen by the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) and also what is seen by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
This is a designation for the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).

For whatever has completed the act of seeing performed by the two eyes—whether it was seen, is being seen, will be seen, or might be seen in combination—all that is stated simply as "seen" because there is no desire to specify a particular time, just as one says "milked" (*duddha*).
For this very reason, it is said: "The visible form-sphere is what is seen."
“Such statements as these” refers to expressions such as “it should be seen, it should be heard,” and so forth.

“He is the same in gain and the same in loss” means that he is just the same at the time of gain as he was at the time of loss; thus he is “of such a kind” (tādī). “Even in fame” means even when there is fame, even at a time when he has a large retinue. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta is finished.
5. Brahmacariyasuttavaṇṇanā 25. Regarding the fifth [sutta], *na-y-idam*:
here, *na* is a particle used for negation; it connects with the word *vussati*, thus forming *na vussati*.
The letter *y* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). As for the word *idam*, [it refers to]: "At one time, monks... [and so forth].
In such passages as, "I dwell at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a king of sal trees," it is used as a mere particle;
in such passages as, "This, monks, is indeed that trifling, mere morality," it occurs in the sense of what has been stated as something near at hand or directly perceived.
"For this is that Jeta’s Grove, frequented by the assembly of seers..."
"In these passages such as 'Inhabited by the King of Dhamma, which produces joy in me,' [the term] refers to what is about to be spoken and is thus proximate and evident;
here too, it should be understood as referring to that which is about to be spoken and is proximate and evident.
As for the word *brahmacariya*—
“What was your vow, and what was your holy life?
Of what well-practiced deed is this the result:
this psychic power, radiance, strength, vigor, and rebirth?”
And this, O Naga, is your great celestial mansion.
"In the world of humans, both my wife and I were faithful patrons of the gift."
My home was then like a wellspring,
for I satisfied the ascetics and brahmins.
That indeed was my vow, that was my holy life.
"This is the result of that well-performed deed:
psychic power, radiance, strength, heroism, and rebirth—
this, O Hero, is my great celestial mansion."
In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, it is introduced in the context of giving:
“By what does the hand become a giver of desires? By what does the hand have the sweetness of honey?
By what kind of holy life (*brahmacariya*) is merit accomplished in the hand?”
In this *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*, it refers to service (*veyyāvacca*).

In this *Tittira-jātaka*, it refers to the morality of the five training precepts (*pañcasikkhāpada-sīla*), [with the words]: "Thus indeed, monks, was that holy life (*brahmacariya*) called 'the partridge'.

In this *Mahāgovinda-sutta*, it refers to the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), [with the words]: "But that holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, was not for disenchantment, nor for dispassion... [etc.]... only as far as rebirth in the Brahma-world."
In this *Sallekha Sutta*, regarding the abstention from sexual intercourse, it says: “Others will be unchaste; we here shall be chaste.
And: “We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us.”
"Except for those [wives], we lead the holy life;
therefore, indeed, among us the young do not die."—
Thus [it is said] in this Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, concerning contentment with one's own wife.
“I recall, Sāriputta, that I practiced the holy life endowed with four factors, and I was indeed an ascetic,” as stated in the *Lomahaṃsa Sutta* regarding energy.
“By an inferior holy life one is reborn as a khattiya;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; and by the supreme one, one is purified.”
In the *Nimi Jātaka*, regarding the eightfold Uposatha established by way of self-taming;
and in the *Mahāgovinda Sutta* itself, regarding the Noble Path: “But this holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion... [etc. ...this very Noble Eightfold Path”;
and [regarding] that holy life which is successful, prosperous, widespread, well-known, and extensive...
"In the *Pāsādika Sutta*, [it is said]: 'well-expounded by gods and men'—referring to the entire teaching comprised of the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*).
Here too, it applies to both the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) and the Teaching (*sāsana*).
‘Is lived’ (*vussati*) means ‘is dwelt in’ (*vusīyati*); the sense is ‘is practiced. For the purpose of deceiving people: ‘Oh, this venerable one is virtuous, endowed with proper conduct...’"

"It is for the purpose of astonishing the people—that is, the world of beings—by means of such [claims] as: 'He is of few wishes, contented, possessed of great psychic power (mahiddhika), and of great majesty (mahānubhāva).

Some, however, say: "'For the purpose of deceiving' means for the purpose of astonishing the people by means of the three bases of deception—namely, the muttering of hints, the adoption of specific postures, and the use of requisites—which belong to one who is of evil desire and driven by craving. Here too, [the same applies].
This very meaning has been shown. For this reason he said: “for the sake of deceiving people by means of the three bases of hypocrisy.

The meaning is: for the sake of astonishing people. “For the sake of making people talk” means: for the sake of causing those with confident hearts to say, “What is needed? What should be brought?”—thinking, “A gift given to a noble one such as this will be of great fruit. It is also [read as] “for the sake of conversing with people.”

They recite [the following]: "For the sake of deceiving people" means that for one who possesses evil desires, it is for the purpose of winning over people through the act of flattery and the manner of speaking by means of indirect hints regarding the acquisition of requisites;
that is the meaning. For this very reason, he said: "Not for the sake of deceiving people" means "not for the sake of winning over people.
Regarding the phrase "not for the sake of the benefit of escaping censure," they also read here: "not for the sake of the benefit of gain, honor, and fame."

In this context, there is the acquisition of the four requisites, which was spoken of as a benefit of virtue in the passage: "Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should wish, 'May I be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,' let him be one who fulfills his virtue";
and there is the honor consisting of the careful giving of the four requisites, which is to say, the state of showing respect, esteem, and reverence; and that which...

The meaning is this: for those living the holy life (*brahmacariya*), the worldly benefit in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammika-ānisansa*) consists of renown—defined as the sound of one’s voice rising up through the manner of being "endowed with virtue, learned, a retainer of what has been heard, and energetic"—and so forth; that is the purpose.

However, some say it is "for the sake of the benefit of gain, honor, and renown," [meaning] that for one who possesses evil desires, due to a heavy attachment to gain and the like, there arises that which is reckoned as gain, honor, and renown.
They say this means "for the sake of producing the arising of benefits.
It is not for the sake of being honored on account of one's own existing virtues— thinking, "Let people know me thus," or "In this dwelling in the holy life,
let the world know and esteem me as 'virtuous' and 'of beautiful character'"— that this holy life is practiced.

The connection is with the word "is lived" (*vussati*). Some, however, explain the meaning here as follows: "For one who has evil desires, this holy life is not lived with the intention of being esteemed for qualities he does not possess, thinking, 'Let the world know me to be possessed of such qualities.
Yet, in all cases, the first interpretation alone is the more excellent.
Now, regarding the phrase *atha kho*: here *atha* is a particle used in the sense of "moreover" (*aññattha*), while *kho* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
By this, he shows that this holy life, monks, is lived for a purpose other than mere deception and the like. Now, pointing out that purpose, he says:

"for the sake of restraint and for the sake of abandoning. In that context, restraint is fivefold: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, [restraint by patience, and restraint by energy].

“Restraint through patience, restraint through energy. This restraint of the Pātimokkha, which is presented in such a manner as, “Thus he is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha, fully endowed with it,” is also called restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). That which is presented as, “He guards the eye-faculty;
he attains restraint over the eye-faculty,” is restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their obstruction;
I call the restraint of these streams wisdom, for by means of wisdom they are closed.
Thus comes this restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). “He is patient with cold and heat,” and so forth—by way of such passages, this restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*) comes.
This is the restraint of energy, which comes in the manner beginning with: “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire,” and so forth.
In terms of its meaning, however, it is both volition and abstinence as they occur through the abandoning of killing living beings and so on, and through the fulfillment of duties and counter-duties.
In brief, it is the entire restraint of body and speech; in detail, it consists of the seven classes of offenses.

Non-transgression is the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). Mindfulness itself is the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*), or it is the wholesome aggregates (*khandha*) in which mindfulness is predominant.

Knowledge itself is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*). Through the mode of forbearance, non-hatred (*adosa*)—or the wholesome aggregates occurring in such a way with non-hatred as their predominance—is the restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*);
some say it is wisdom (*paññā*). Energy (*vīriya*) itself, occurring through the mode of overcoming sensual thoughts and so forth, is the restraint of energy (*viriya-saṃvara*).

Vīriyasaṃvaro (restraint through energy). Among these, the first is to be understood as "restraint" because it restrains immorality consisting of bodily misconduct and so forth; the second, because it restrains forgetfulness;
the third, because it restrains ignorance; the fourth, because it restrains impatience; and the fifth, because it restrains and shuts out laziness.
Thus, for the sake of this restraint, the meaning is "for the purpose of restraint," that is, for the purpose of accomplishing restraint.
"By three kinds of abandoning" means by the three kinds of abandoning known as abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*).

It is indeed appropriate to speak of fivefold abandoning here as well. For fivefold abandoning consists of: abandoning by substitution of opposites, suppression, eradication, tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*).

Among these, that which occurs through non-greed and so forth—as the opposite of greed and so forth—by means of the light of a lamp, or through the insight-knowledges such as the discernment of name-and-form; ... [text continues] ... [the remainder of the passage is omitted as per instructions to provide only the translation].

The abandoning of each respective disadvantage is as follows: by means of relinquishment, the abandonment of the stains such as greed; by means of virtue, the abandonment of misconduct such as the taking of life;
by means of faith and the other [faculties], the abandonment of lack of faith and so forth; by means of the discernment of name-and-form, the abandonment of the personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi);
by means of the investigation of conditions, the abandonment of the views of no-cause and wrong-cause; and subsequently, by means of the overcoming of doubt regarding that very same [investigation].

By means of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), [one abandons] the state of being a skeptic; by means of the definition of what is and is not the path (*maggāmaggavavatthāna*), [one abandons] the perception of a path where there is no path;

by means of the vision of arising (*udayadassana*), [one abandons] the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*); by means of the vision of passing away (*vayadassana*), [one abandons] the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*);

by means of the vision of danger (*bhayadassana*), [one abandons] the perception of safety where there is danger; by means of the vision of disadvantage (*ādīnavadassana*), [one abandons] the perception of gratification (*assādasaññā*); and by means of the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*)...

By means of the perception of non-delight, there is the abandoning of the desire for liberation; by means of the knowledge of the desire for liberation, there is the abandoning of the lack of desire for liberation;

by means of the knowledge of equanimity, there is the abandoning of the lack of equanimity; by means of conformity, there is the abandoning of the state of opposition toward the stability of phenomena and toward Nibbāna; and by means of the change-of-lineage, there is the abandoning of the grasping at the signs of formations—this is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

Furthermore, the abandoning of various defilements such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) by means of concentration— distinguished as access and absorption— which prevents the occurrence of existence just as a blow from a water-jar [clears] moss from the surface of the water,
is called "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
That which occurs in one's own continuum for one who possesses the respective path due to the cultivation of the four noble paths (*ariyamagga*) regarding the "bases of views" (*diṭṭhigata*)...

The total eradication of the grasping at defilements—which belong to the side of origination—as described in the sequence beginning with “for the sake of abandoning,” by means of their absolute non-occurrence, is called abandonment as eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).

That which, at the moment of the fruit, consists in the subsiding of the defilements, is called abandonment as subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*). That which has abandoned all conditioned things because it is detached from all that is conditioned...
Nirvana is what is called "abandonment by way of escape. Regarding that [nirvana], the meaning here should be understood as follows:

it is for the purpose of abandoning—that is, for the sake of the abandonment—of the fivefold defilements such as lust and so forth, insofar as they are relinquished or transcended in their respective ways; or rather, it is for the purpose of being the means for that abandonment.

In this context, they say that by means of restraint (*saṃvara*), there is the prevention of the defilements from entering the continuum of the mind, and by means of abandonment (*pahāna*), there is both the prevention of entry and their total eradication (*samugghāta*).
However, it should be understood that through both, both results are appropriately accomplished.
For the very phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth are called "restraint" because they restrain, and "abandonment" because they abandon.
"Anītihaṃ": "Īti" refers to calamities, both those pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to future lives. That which destroys such calamities is "ītiha";
that which follows after (or overcomes) calamities is "anītiha"—namely, the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).

Alternatively, those things which go along with or proceed together with calamities and misfortunes are "ītihā," namely, the defilements such as craving and so forth. There are no such calamities herein; thus it is "anītiha."
*Anītihaṃ*. *Ītiha* refers to the doctrines of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya-samaya*) as previously described; because this [teaching] is their opposite, it is *anītiha*.
There is also a reading *anitihaṃ*. Its meaning is as follows: “*Itihāya*” means doubt (*vicikicchā*), so called because it involves a state of indecisive grasping regarding phenomena.

Because it is proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) and establishes freedom from doubt for those practicing according to his instructions, it is [not doubt]. Thus, it is *anitihaṃ*.
And because there is no "thus" (itihā) here, it is "not based on hearsay" (anitiha); the meaning is "not dependent on another. For this has been said:

"It is to be personally realized by the wise," and "it is not within the sphere of mere reasoning. However, for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition, they recite it as "anītihaṃ," lengthening the vowel.
To show an alternative interpretation of the meaning here, the phrase beginning with "avoiding hearsay" (itihaparivajjitaṃ) was stated.
It goes to the further shore, which is the refuge and foundation known as Nibbāna; thus it is "leading to the refuge of Nibbāna" (*nibbānogadhagāmī*).
The meaning is that, because it possesses the essence of liberation, it leads exclusively to the attainment of Nibbāna. That is the holy life (*brahmacariya*) leading to the refuge of Nibbāna.
Alternatively, the Noble Path is called "the refuge of Nibbāna" (*nibbānogadho*), because without it the plunging into Nibbāna is impossible, and because of that [path], Nibbāna...
Because it does not proceed without having taken [Nibbāna] as its object, and because it goes by means of attaining that exclusively, it is "leading to the plunge into Nibbāna" (*nibbānogadhagāmī*).
Alternatively, "leading to the plunge into Nibbāna" means that which enters into the interior of Nibbāna.

For the holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*), having made Nibbāna its object, proceeds within that very [Nibbāna]. And in order to show this alternative meaning, [the text says]: "Of Nibbāna..."

"Entering within," and so forth, is what was said. "He" refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; he taught (adesayi) [the Dhamma].
"By the great ones" means by those of great spiritual stature and noble aspirations. They seek and search for the great Nibbāna, or they seek the great aggregates of virtue and so forth.
The Noble Ones are the Great Seers, the Buddhas and so forth.
He follows and practices according to them. "Just as it was taught by the Buddha" means:

just as this holy life of the path and the holy life of the Dispensation for its sake were taught by me, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in their aspects of being to be directly known and so forth—those who practice this [path] in that manner... them.
For those who carry out my instruction and repay my counsel— teaching me, the Teacher, as is appropriate through the ultimate truths concerning both the present life and the future—
they will bring about the end, the limit, and the non-occurrence of the entire suffering of saṃsāra;
or they will realize the end of suffering, which is Nibbāna.
The commentary on the *Brahmacariya Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Kuha Sutta*. 26.

In the sixth [sutta], "deceivers" (*kuhakā*) refers to those who deceive by means of the grounds for deception such as hinting (*sāmantajappanā*), out of a desire to be esteemed for qualities they do not possess.
"Deceivers" means those who cause the ruin of others by practicing hypocrisy (*kohañña*).
"Stubborn" refers to one who is angry and full of distress, who becomes resentful, irritated, hostile, and obstinate even when addressed with only a little;

thus, it refers to anger as described therein, and to being difficult to speak to, being possessed of qualities that make one difficult to speak to, being unenduring, and being unwilling to accept instruction.

“Instruction. Thus, by means of the difficult-to-admonish nature already mentioned, and by means of the conceit (māna) categorized as the pride of birth, clan, gain, health, youth, and life—already mentioned as “pride of birth,” etc.—they wander about without showing proper respect even toward those worthy of honor, remaining unbending like those who have swallowed an iron ball. Therefore he said, “And by anger,” and so forth.
*Upalāpakā* means those who gather around families by way of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*). *Lapā* means talkers;
the sense is "talkers" (*lapakā*) by way of speech employed for the sake of requisites and by way of backbiting (*nippesikatā*). *Siṅga* means flirtatiousness (*siṅgāra*).

For that [flirtatiousness] is like a well-formed horn encircled on the head because it pierces into what is wholesome (*kusala*) and because of its firmness due to being well-practiced; thus it is like a horn (*siṅga*).
"Siṅgaṃ" is a name for the "horn" (siṅga) of defilement, which is designated as urbanity (*nāgarikabhāva*).

"Siṅgārabhāvo" means "the state of being amorous" (*siṅgāratā*), or the manner of acting in an amorous way. "Cāturabhāvo" means "the state of being clever" (*cāturatā*); likewise for "cāturiyaṃ. "Parikkhatabhāvo" means "the state of being polished" (*parikkhatatā*);
this is a name for firm amorousness that has been established after being thoroughly honed. The other term is a synonym for that very same thing. Thus...
In all these instances, it is merely the state of being adorned with the defilements that is described.
"Those who carry aloft the reed" refers to those who wander about having raised up an empty pride similar to a reed; therefore he said, "standing while raising up empty pride.
Because they do not practice rightly due to their association with hypocrisy and the like, [the Buddha thought], "They do not belong to me."

It has been said: "They have departed. Even though they have gone forth in my teaching, because they do not practice according to the instructions, they have indeed departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya; he shows that they stand far away from here. For this has been said:
"The sky is far, and the earth is far..."
"The further shore of the ocean they say is far away;
but even farther than that, they say,
is the Dhamma of the virtuous compared to that of the wicked, O King."

“They reach abundance by being spread everywhere” means that through the state of being spread everywhere, they reach abundance by means of the fulfillment of the aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and the rest.
The commentary to the Kuha Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary to the Santuṭṭhi Sutta.

27. In the seventh [verse], "faultless" (*niddosa*) means free from blame, both because of the purity of their acquisition and because they lack the state of being a basis for defilements such as bodily adornment.
Therein, by their ease of acquisition, the absence of the suffering of seeking is shown; by their scarcity, the absence of the suffering of maintaining them is shown;
and by their faultlessness—that is, their being beyond reproach—their suitability for a monk (*bhikkhu-sāruppa*) is shown. By their scarcity...

Alternatively, by their being limited, they show that greed and so forth lack a basis; by their being easily obtained, it is shown that there is the presence of wisdom regarding the seeing of danger and the means of escape, since they are blameless.
Or, because they are insignificant, gain does not produce joy and loss does not produce grief;
and because they are blameless and serve as a basis for non-remorse, they do not produce the equanimity of ignorance which is a cause for regret.
*Paṃsukūla*: It is called *paṃsukūla* in the sense of being "raised up" (*abbhuggata*) because it lies upon dust in places such as rubbish heaps;
or it is called *paṃsukūla* because it goes toward (*ulati*), that is, reaches a state of worthlessness (*kucchita-bhāva*) like dust.
It refers to a robe made by collecting rags fallen on carriage roads and other such places. *Rukkhamūla*: [The root of a tree].
“Near a tree” means any place suitable for seclusion. “Any kind of cow’s urine” means any cow’s urine whatsoever.
However, some here say that “putimutta” refers to pieces of *harītakī* fruit infused with cow’s urine.
Others maintain that “putimutta” refers to any medicinal substance that has been discarded from a shop or elsewhere due to its state of decay, being cast away and unclaimed.
*Yato kho* is an ablative form used in the sense of the relative pronoun *yaṃ*. Thus, it means "that which. By this, it refers back to the action previously mentioned:
"he is contented. *Tuṭṭho* means "satisfied" (*santuṭṭho*). *Idam assāhaṃ* refers to that contentment with the fourfold requisites as they have been described—being few, easily obtained;
this is one factor of asceticism (*sāmaññaṅga*) for this bhikkhu, consisting in any one of the restraints such as virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).

"I say that this is the cause of the state of a recluse (sāmañña). For one who is content, the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) becomes complete, and both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) reach the perfection of cultivation. Alternatively, what is called 'recluseship' is the Noble Path;
briefly, it has two factors: the external and the internal. Therein, the external is reliance upon a true person (sappurisūpanissaya)."
And there is the hearing of the true Dhamma. As for the internal factors, they are wise attention and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Among these, because these qualities—namely, fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, lack of socializing, and the arousal of energy—are, as appropriate, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma and the very roots thereof; that is to say, [qualities] such as these.
Therefore it was said: "I declare this to be one of its factors of asceticism.
"With reference to lodgings" means with reference to lodgings such as monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth, as well as beds, chairs, and the like.

"With reference to robes, drinks, and food" means with reference to robes such as lower garments (*nivāsana*) and so forth, drinks such as mango juice and so forth, and edible things such as hard foods (*khādanīya*) and soft foods (*bhojanīya*).
“Connection. “Affliction” means the state of being afflicted; the construction is: “there is no suffering of the mind.
Herein, this is the summary meaning: by going to a place where requisites can be obtained, thinking, “In such-and-such a residence, requisites are easily found”;
or by falling into disputes, thinking, “It goes to me, not to you”; or by means of performing building work and so forth regarding lodgings and other matters.
The distress that arises in the mind of those who seek and are dissatisfied due to not obtaining what they desire, etc., does not occur for one who is content therein.
"He is not obstructed by the quarters" means that because of his state of being oriented toward the four directions through contentment, he is not repelled by any direction.
For this has been said: "Being content with whatever comes his way, he is oriented toward the four directions and is unrepelled."

"Conformable to the duty of a recluse" (*samaṇadhammassa anuloma*) means they are suitable for the cultivation of serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā-bhāvanā*), or rather, for the Noble Path itself;
namely, fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth. "By a bhikkhu with a contented mind" (*tuṭṭhacittassa bhikkhuno*) means by a bhikkhu whose mind is contented.
"Are acquired" (*adhiggahitā hontī*) means they have been grasped after having overcome opposing states. "Included within" (*antogata*) means they have gone inside.
"Not excluded" means not made external.
The commentary on the *Santuṭṭhi-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Ariyavaṃsa-sutta*.

28. In the eighth [verse], the word *vaṃsa* (bamboo) occurs in such passages as “he sits having crossed over the back-bamboo,” referring to the staff that should be placed at the junction of two rafters.
“As a wide bamboo that is entangled, so too is the attachment toward children and wives.”
In such passages as, "Like the bamboo-stalk flower, unattached, let him wander alone like the rhinoceros horn," it refers to a bamboo shoot.
In such passages as, "The sound of kettledrums, the sound of tabors, the sound of flutes and cymbals," it refers to a specific musical instrument; it is also [called] *veṇu*.
It is said [in various contexts]: in expressions such as “the elephant is dead with its backbone broken,” it refers to the region in the middle of the back of elephants and so forth;

in expressions such as “I shall establish the family lineage,” it refers to the ancestral line; in expressions such as “a protector of the lineage, a guardian of the tradition,” it refers to the succession of qualities and the continuous occurrence of those qualities.
However, in this context, it refers to the qualities consisting of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation.

It should be seen in the *Pabaṃdha*. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the lineage of his clan (*kulanvaya*) and the lineage of his virtues (*guṇanvaya*) by way of illustration, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated.
Therein, "the lineage of the Khattiyas" (*khattiyavaṃsa*) means the lineage of the Khattiya family. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

"The lineage of recluses" (*samaṇavaṃsa*), however, refers to the stream of recluses (*samaṇatan-ti*) or the succession of recluses (*samaṇapaveṇī*). Regarding the phrase "of the root-fragrance, etc. (*mūlagandhādīnaṃ*), by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [fragrances such as] heartwood-fragrance and so forth are included.

Regarding "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*): in this context, the inclusion of cow’s milk and so forth is to be understood by the first [use of the] word "and so forth" (*ādi*), while by the second [use of] "and so forth," Kāsi cloth, cream of ghee, and so on are included.
The term "noble" (*ariya*) applies even to those humans whose place of residence is called a "noble region" (*ariya-āyatana*).
As it is said: "To whatever extent, Ānanda, there is a noble region. It also applies to worldly virtuous people, for...

In such passages as, "You noble ones are pure in bodily conduct; I am one among them," it is intended to show that those who have penetrated the Noble Truths and whose etymological derivation is given as "far removed from defilements" (*ārakā kilesehi*) are what is meant here.

To this end, having asked the question, "But who are these noble ones? the passage beginning with "The noble ones are called... was stated. In that context, those [who have been so for] eons due to their great aspiration...
From the time [the Buddha] set out until this present eon, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) who have arisen during that interval—

having first shown them according to their individual forms, and having included other Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Private Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas), and disciples of the Buddhas— the text beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) was stated in order to show the Noble Ones (*ariya*) without exception.
In that regard, as long as the Dispensation (*sāsana*) does not disappear, so long does the Teacher endure.
"Evam nāma" refers to this very Blessed One. The inclusion of the present tense is with reference to those who are currently disciples of the Buddha.
If it were argued that "those who exist at each respective time are 'present'," then there would be no need to mention the past and the future.
Now, just as the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle..."

“I shall proclaim the holy life (brahmacariya), which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, entirely complete and pure—namely, the six sets of six,” he thus praised the teaching on the Six Sets with eight phrases.
Likewise, regarding the teaching on the Great Noble Lineage (mahāariyavaṃsa), he spoke of the lineage of the noble ones: “Bhikkhus, these four noble lineages are the foremost...”

"Known for long, known for generations, ancient, unmixed and never before mixed, not being mixed now and not to be mixed in the future, they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins"—having brought forward these nine terms with which he spoke the praise, he said "But these indeed...
and so forth, praising them in the manner of a eulogy. They are to be known as the "foremost" among all lineages.
Because they are the most excellent state and because they accomplish the most excellent state.
They are to be known as "long-standing" (*rattaññū*) by those who know [the past], such as the Buddhas and others, because they have been practiced in that way for a long time.
They are to be known as "lineages" (*vaṃsa*); that is, they are to be known as the lineages of the noble ones, beginning with the Buddhas. "Ancient" (*porāṇa*) means old. Not...
"Recently acquired" means not newly obtained. "Unscattered" means not thrown about or discarded; therefore he said, "not removed.
"Not previously removed" means not previously discarded; because they are the means for fulfilling all three trainings, they have never been abandoned.
For that very reason, they are not being removed now, nor will they ever be removed in the future.
One is wise by virtue of discerning the intrinsic nature of phenomena. Those who have stilled evil are recluses (*samaṇa*), and those who have expelled evil are brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*).

They are neither reviled nor rejected by them. For those who are not to be reviled are not to be censured; they are not to be blamed, and because they are not to be abandoned, they are not to be rejected.
Regarding "contented" (*santuṭṭho*): here, by way of showing only the intended kind of contentment, it is said "contented" in the sense of contentment with the requisites (*paccaya-santosava-sena*).
For a bhikkhu’s state of being contented exists also by way of jhāna, vipassanā, and so forth. Regarding "with this or that" (*itarītarena*): [it means] "with this or that.
The word *itara* is a term for the indefinite; when stated twice, it functions with the sense of "whatever."
