It is said that "by whatever" means it has the same meaning [as the previous term].
Since this [term] expresses indefiniteness, just as it denotes any one among "coarse" (*thūla*) and so forth, it likewise denotes any one among "as obtained" (*yathāladdha*) and so forth.
In that regard, showing that the second alternative alone is intended here, he says "atha kho" and so on. But are not "as obtained" and the others also included among "coarse" and the rest?

Is that so? This is true; nevertheless, there is a distinction. For that contentment which exists regarding the coarse robes and so forth as they are obtained is indeed "contentment with whatever is obtained" (*yathālābha-santosa*), and not the other kind.
Indeed, that [latter] is not intended to rely merely upon the requisites themselves, but rather upon their being suitable for one's own physical strength.
All three types—the coarse, the medium, and so forth—may be obtained among the robes; the medium...
It should be understood that [the first] three contentments apply to all four requisites, whereas the last one is obtained regarding robes and lodgings.
These three contentments are stated here by way of a comprehensive method.
For those who, as later on, include the requisite for the sick within almsfood itself, there are twenty [modes] for robes, fifteen for almsfood, and fifteen for lodgings, thus making fifty in total.
Contentments are so called; all of them, according to their respective nature, are included within and converge upon these very three contentments.
"The robe should be known" means that the robe should be known by its class as "this specific robe is allowable.
"The field for robes" refers to the source from which a robe arises. "Rags from the dust-heap" refers to a rag-robe that has attained the characteristics of a rag-robe.
The meaning is that the robe should be understood. "Contentment with robes" means that all contentment obtainable regarding robes should be understood.
The ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with robes should be understood, by guarding which one is properly satisfied through contentment with robes.
*Khoma*, *kappāsika*, *koseyya*, *kambala*, *sāṇa*, and *bhaṅga* are the [types of] *khoma* and so forth. Among these, *khoma*...
*Khoma* refers to a robe made from *khoma* cloth woven from *khoma* fibers; the same applies to the remaining types. *Sāṇa* is a robe made from *sāṇa* (hemp) fibers.
*Bhaṅga*, however, is a robe made by mixing all of these—*khoma* fibers and so forth—or some of them.
Some say that *bhaṅga* is made exclusively of wool (*vāka*). "Six" indicates the limit of the number. If this is so, what other class of cloth is there besides these?

Is it not the case that [these materials] do not exist? It is not that they do not exist. However, in order to show that these are the corresponding [substitutes], the phrase beginning with “dukūla and so forth” was stated.
By the word “and so forth,” there is an inclusion of *pattuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, *cīnapaṭṭa*, *iddhija*, and *devadatta*.
Among those, *dukūla* is the corresponding material for hemp (*sāṇa*) because it is made of flax (*vāka*). *Pattuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the region of Pattuṇṇa.
For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: “*Koseyyaviseso*. Fabrics produced in the regions of Soma and Cīna are called *somāra-paṭṭa* and *cīnapaṭṭa*.
The three types beginning with *pattuṇṇa* are similar to *koseyya* because they consist of threads spun by insects.

That which is produced through psychic power (*iddhija*)—the robe generated by the merit-power of the *ehibhikkhus*—is one of the aforementioned types such as *khoma*, and is therefore similar to them.

"Given by deities" (*devadinnan*) refers to cloth given by deities; it is produced on the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) and is similar to the garment given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī.
That too conforms to linen and the like, because it is of the same nature as those.
"These" (*imāni*) is a restrictive term included within the phrase itself, meaning "these alone. This is because they are suitable for the use of the Buddhas and others.
These are the allowable robes (*kappiyacīvarāni*). Now, in order to show by way of illustration those [robes] excluded by the restrictive definition, it is said:
“a robe of *kusa* grass,” and so forth. Therein, a robe made from *kusa* grass or other similar grasses is a *kusacīra*.
A robe made from fibers such as hemp or flax is a *vākacīra*. A robe made from rectangular or triangular wooden slabs is a *phalakacīra*.
A *kesakambala* is a blanket made from the hair of humans. A *vālakambala* is a woolen blanket made from the tails of yaks (*cāmarī*), horses, and so forth.
A *potthaka* is cloth woven from the threads of hemp. *Camma* refers to any hide, such as the hide of a deer and so on.

An *ulūkapakkha* is a robe made by sewing together the wings of owls. A *rukkhadussa* is tree-cloth made from bark, leaves, and the like. *Tirīṭaka*— [Note: The provided text ends with "Tirīṭakanti," which indicates the beginning of a new term.]
This is the meaning. *Latādussa* is cloth woven from very fine creepers or creeper-fibers. *Erakadussa* is made from *eraka* grass fibers.
Likewise for *kadalidussa*. *Veḷudussa* is made from fine bamboo fibers. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), bark-cloth and other such materials are included.
These are unallowable robes because they bear the banner of the heretics.

"By way of the eight matrices (mātikā)" means by way of the eight matrices for the arising of robes that have come down in such passages as "he gives within the boundary," "he gives according to an agreement," and so forth.
For the Blessed One established these matrices with the words, "Bhikkhus, there are these eight matrices," in order to show the fields for the acquisition of robes.
They are called "matrices" (mātikā) because they are mothers (mātaro), being the progenitors of the arising of robes.
*Sosānika* means fallen in a charnel ground. *Pāpaṇika* means fallen at the door of a shop.
*Rathiya* means a rag discarded on a road by those seeking merit through a window opening. *Saṅkārakūṭa* means a rag discarded in a rubbish heap.
*Sināna* means a bathing rag, which spirit-doctors discard after bathing with their heads on, calling it a "rag of ill fortune."
They go. They stand on a "standing-rags" (titthacoḷa)—a piece of cloth discarded at a bathing place. "Burnt by fire" means a place burnt by fire; for people discard such places.
"Gnawed by cattle" and so forth are well known; for people also discard those.
"Having raised a banner" means having raised a flagstaff by those boarding a ship or entering into battle.
"Having raised it up," means that which was tied there and brought by the wind, with the intention that it had been discarded by them.

"By a monk who approves" means by a monk who consents to a householder’s robe. "Just for a month" means it is permissible to entertain thoughts regarding a robe for a period of exactly one month known as the "robe-month," but not beyond that;
for this is for the purpose of restraining all craving.
"Practice in the Dispensation": The *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearer) accomplishes this in half a month because the acquisition of his robe does not depend on others;
for the other [type of practitioner], however, since it depends on others, only a full month is permitted. This period of a month or half a month... [etc.
...is "contentment with thoughts" because one who is thinking is limited by time. Therein, the Great Elder was his own companion.
Even though he wished to go, out of profound respect he said, "Venerable sir, I shall go to the village gate.
The Elder, knowing his intention, said, "Friend, I too shall go. Thinking, "Let there be no opportunity for this monk's [unwholesome] thought," he entered the village while asking a question.
"Obstructed by excrement" means being oppressed by defecation. At that time, of the Blessed One...

Because the defilements were suppressed by the intensity of the surge of rapture and joy that arose toward the Tathāgata through the recollection of his austerities, he attained the three fruits right then and there...
[as before] ...The thought "Where shall I obtain them? is preceded by a desire for gain; therefore, it is said "without thinking thus. "Beautiful..."
What need is there to mention such thoughts as, "I shall obtain [something]," or "I shall obtain something pleasing"? As for how one should go, he says:
"Going with the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) as the foremost. By this, he shows that one should not think about anything at all regarding the robe.
He says, "a pleasant monk," because even a search for what is unlovely or unsuitable might become a condition [for attachment].

"Having taken," it is said. "Being brought" means that when a person, knowing that "these monks are wandering in search of rag-robes," brings from places such as a charnel ground a cloth that has fallen there;
[this refers to] even for one who takes what is obtained in this way.

"Even for one who takes what is obtained" means even for one who, without violating contentment with what is acquired, takes what has been found. "Only as much as is sufficient for oneself" means according to what was obtained.
For the purpose of obtaining one or two pieces of cloth from discarded rags, he should take only as much as is sufficient for himself.

By the use of the restrictive particle (*eva*), he excludes anything beyond that. For one who wanders for alms in the village, walking from house to house in regular succession like one who practices *sapadānacāra*, this is called "avoiding greed," because greed has been cast far away.
"To sustain" means to maintain one's physical existence. "By means of washing" means by way of cleansing. "Leaves" refers to leaves such as those of the mango, rose-apple, and so forth.

"Without disturbing" means without disturbing contentment. "In a manner sufficient for the purpose" means that whatever one wishes to make—such as an inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) or other garments—one takes the material, whether coarse or fine, as obtained, and makes it according to the measure sufficient for that purpose. "Merely for the covering of the three circles" means...

If the lower garment does not cover the navel-circle and the knee-circle, but rather [reaches] the throat-circle, then "the knee-circle" refers only to making it sufficient to cover those three circles.
In its actual substance, however, it must be exactly the size prescribed for the lower limit of the three robes.
Without investigating, without scrutinizing.

"At the time of sewing" means at the time of stitching after the circles have been joined. "Seven times" means seven rounds of stitching. "Contentment with what is allowable" (*kappasantosa*) is the absence of making any alteration by way of adding an allowable mark (*kappabindu*).

Since the purpose of warding off cold and so forth is established through implication, it was stated as "merely for the purpose of concealing the private parts" in order to show the primary purpose for the use of the robe.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Merely for the purpose of concealing the private parts."
It is permissible; yet, satisfaction is not disturbed merely by that, because of the failure to obtain requisites from those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
"Standing in the qualities conducive to affection" (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) means standing in the state of sharing possessions with virtuous monks.

By the words beginning with "thus" (*iti*), he shows that the first noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*) consists of the two factors of wearing rag-robes and being content with three robes, and demonstrates their causal relationship, saying: "Thus..."
"These states are mutually productive and supportive," he explains. This same method applies to those that follow.
Regarding the phrase "he is content and speaks in praise [of contentment]," four logical alternatives (catukkoṭika) are possible there;
however, the teaching was given in such a way that only the fourth alternative is praised. One person is content but does not speak in praise of contentment.

Just as the elder Nālaka; one who is not contented himself but speaks in praise of contentment, such as Upananda the Sakyan-son; one who is neither contented nor speaks in praise of contentment, such as the elder Lāḷudāyin;
and one who is both contented and speaks in praise of contentment, such as the elder Mahākassapa.
*Anesanā* means an improper search. Therefore he said, "unbecoming" (*appatirūpa*), meaning unseemly and unfit for those established in the Teaching.
"Practicing hypocrisy" (*kohaññaṃ karonto*) means practicing deception and deluding others for the sake of obtaining robes.
"Is terrified" (*uttasati*) means he trembles repeatedly due to the anxiety of craving. "Is agitated" (*paritassati*) means he is agitated all around. Just as all bodily and vocal activities—
They arise for that very purpose; thus one trembles in every respect. "Gadhita" means greedy;
here, it is intended in the sense of the characteristic of covetousness (*abhijjhā*). One who has no such greed is "agadhita"; thus he says, "free from the greed of lust.
"Mucchanti" refers to delusion by way of craving (*taṇhā*). He has not attained, nor entered, nor approached that heap of suffering.
“Unassailed” means not overcome. “Unenveloped” means not covered over by the veil of craving (*taṇhā*).
“Seeing the danger” means seeing the fault both pertaining to the present life and to future lives. That by which one escapes from enjoyment through attachment is the “escape”;

this refers to the state of having no more [craving] as its object. One who understands that is “one possessed of the wisdom of escape. Therefore he said: “To the extent that... knowing... and so forth.
"He does not exalt himself" means he neither exalts nor elevates himself, nor regards himself as superior. The passage beginning with "I am...
is a demonstration of the manner of such exaltation. "He does not disparage" means he does not revile or regard [others] as inferior.
"In that contentment with robes" refers to that twentyfold contentment with robes as previously described. Indeed, here, by the very inclusion of the aforementioned types of contentment—

Seeking [robes] through improper means (*anesanā*) and so forth are already included under "for the sake of robes" (*cīvarahetu*), because when that [seeking] exists, those [improper means] exist, and when it does not, they do not.
However, since praising oneself, exalting oneself, and disparaging others are not included, the alternative formulation "or in praising and so forth" (*vaṇṇavādādīsu vā*) was stated.
And here, "skillful" (*dakkho*) and so on refer to those qualities by virtue of which his aforementioned contentment and other traits [arise].
They succeed; that is the vision. Therein, by the phrase "one who sees," he shows the wisdom that originates them.

By "one who is not indolent," he shows the energy of exertion. By "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*), he shows the wisdom of mastery. By "mindful" (*paṭissato*), he shows conduct free from forgetfulness therein.
"Almsfood is to be understood" means almsfood is to be understood according to its classification. "The field for almsfood" is the place where almsfood arises.
"Contentment with almsfood is to be understood" means the various types of contentment with almsfood are to be understood.
Here, medicine also falls under the category of almsfood; for it is included among items such as ghee because they are things to be brought [as offerings].
The "field of alms" (*piṇḍapātakkhetta*) is a field because it is the place where alms arise, just like a [grain] field.
It is a "place of arising" (*uppattiṭṭhāna*) because [alms] arise there or by means of it. For a monk’s alms arise either from the Sangha or by way of a specific dedication (*uddissa*).
In that context, *saṅghabhatta* is food to be given to the entire Sangha. Having designated a few monks...
Food to be given by means of a list is *uddesabhatta*. Food to be given after having invited [the monks] is *nimantanabhatta*.
Food to be given by means of voting sticks is *salākabhatta*. Food to be given on one day during a fortnight is *pakkhika*.
Food to be given on every Uposatha day is *uposathika*. Food to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*) is *pāṭipadika*.

*Āgantukabhatta* (guest meal) is the meal to be given to those who have arrived as guests. *Dhurabhatta* (resident meal) is the meal to be given by setting it aside specifically for the resident quarters.
*Kuṭibhatta* (hut meal) is the meal to be given with reference to a specific hut. *Vārabhatta* (turn-based meal) is the meal to be given by those living in the village and others in rotation.
*Vihārabhatta* (monastery meal) is the meal to be given with reference to the monastery as a whole. The remaining terms are self-evident.
He reflects: "Where indeed shall I wander for alms today? When the Elder says, "Where shall we wander for alms tomorrow?
and [the other] replies, "In such-and-such a village, venerable sir," this is certainly a giving of an answer;

however, it is with reference to the specific state of mind by which one thinks before saying that he says, "having thought this much. "From then on" refers to the hall of applied thought (*vitakkamāḷaka*).
"Having stood [in that state] from the moment of initial reflection"—if one reflects beyond that point, one has fallen away from the noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*).
This should be understood with reference to all three types of those who follow the noble lineage, not only the solitary wanderer (*ekacāraka*).
For every follower of the noble lineage is permitted to reflect only once, and not beyond that. "Excluded" means being outside the state of following the noble lineage.
One’s own satisfaction with thought is not disturbed by attention to the meditation subject; rather, it becomes purified. This same principle applies to the subsequent cases as well.
For this very reason, he said: "One should proceed under the heading of the meditation subject. The word *eva* (only) is used here in the sense of exclusion (*aṭṭhānappayutta*).
It should be construed thus: "Only that which is sufficient for maintenance should be taken."
“In this” means in this receiving of alms-food. “Little” means that one should take little even from the measure required for one’s own sustenance, for the sake of pleasing the donor’s mind.
“Only according to measure” means that one should take only what is appropriate for oneself.
To show the reason why it must be taken with measure, it is said: “For in the receiving,” and so forth. “Smeared” means ruined.
It carries away; it causes one to fall into ruin and destroys by misapplying what is not the proper place. Regarding "the Teaching":

he does not act upon nor practice the Teacher’s instruction, the guidance. Just as one who goes on alms-round visits door after door in regular succession, so too is there avoidance of greed and contentment;
thus he said, "one should go door by door."
“Having removed” means having set aside what is excessive. It is called a “renunciation” (nissaraṇa) because by means of it one emerges from greed for food.
He said, “...the satisfaction of hunger,” etc., because while it is made for the purpose of dispelling hunger, the purpose of maintaining the body and so forth follows as a matter of course.
The intention is that it should not be stored away and consumed even on that very day.

In other cases, however, it is prohibited by the training rule (sikkhāpada) itself. "Standing in the qualities conducive to harmony" means standing in the state of sharing enjoyments with virtuous bhikkhus.
"With lodgings" means with beds and seats. For wherever one lies on a bed or the like, or in a monastery or the like, [that is the lodging].

That is the *senā* (bed). Wherever one sits on a chair or similar object, that is the *āsana* (seat). Having combined both together, it is called “*senāsana*” (lodging). Therefore he said, “a bed,” and so forth.
Therein, a “bed” (*mañca*) refers to a couch (*masāraka*) and the like; likewise for a “chair” (*pīṭha*). A “cushion” (*bhisi*) is of two kinds:
a bed-cushion and a chair-cushion. A “vihāra” is an entire dwelling delimited by a wall; some say it is a long-faced palace (*pāsāda*).
*Addhayoga* is a long mansion; some say it is a dwelling with a roof covering only one side. *Pāsāda* is a square mansion; some say it is a long, four-sided mansion.
*Hammiya* is a mansion with a flat roof. *Guha* is a mountain cave in its entirety. *Leṇa* is a shelter enclosed by a door.
*Aṭṭa* is a house with thick walls, which does not take in rafters but [is built] with bricks.
This is the roofing; some also say it is "constructed in the shape of a watchtower.
A *māḷa* is a specific type of dwelling with many corners, comprised of a single peak; some call it "a lodging constructed in the shape of a circle.
"In the same manner as described for alms-food" refers to [the passage beginning]: "The monk who accepts [food] thinks: 'Where shall I dwell? and so forth.

These points should be understood according to the method already explained regarding almsfood. Furthermore, everything such as, “If he thinks about anything beyond that, he has fallen away from and is excluded from the Noble Lineage;
without thinking ‘Where shall I find lodging? he should go with his meditation subject as his primary concern,” is exactly as stated in the previous method.
But why, when the Blessed One was demonstrating contentment with requisites here, did he not include contentment with the requisite of medicine?

To show that this should not be viewed in such a way, he said, "The requisite of medicine, however, is included within almsfood," the intention being that they share the common characteristic of being things to be brought forth.
If that is so, then there too—in the case of almsfood—contentment with thoughts and so forth [should also be included].
To show that "fifteen contentments are to be desired," he said, "In that regard," and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Are not only twelve ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) applied here, while the single practice of sitting continuously (nesajjikaṅga) is not applied anywhere? To this he replied:
"The practice of sitting continuously belongs to the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa) that delights in meditation. And this meaning is indeed recorded in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
Showing this, he says, "And it has also been said," and so forth.
The phrase "like one spreading out the earth" and so on demonstrates the extreme difficulty of the teaching on the Noble Lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*), because that teaching has a vast scope;
for it is adorned with a thousand methods and is extensive for the sake of attaining the Noble Path.

The teaching being expounded in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* and this discourse on the Noble Lineage of Delight in Meditation (*bhāvanārāma-ariyavaṃsa*) are indeed expounded in detail for the sake of attaining the Noble Path;
thus it is said: "He began the teaching adorned with a thousand methods... and so forth.
Because it delights by way of facing toward the destruction of opposing factors, it is called "delight" (*ārāma*); therefore he says: "The meaning is 'delightful' (*abhirati*)."
An external compound (bāhiratthasamāsa) also occurs by way of words in different grammatical cases (*byadhikaraṇa*), such as "urasiloma" (hair on the chest) and "kaṇṭhekāḷa" (a crow on the neck);
thus it says, "one for whom there is delight (*ārāma*) in meditation (*bhāvanā*) is 'delighting in meditation' (*bhāvanārāma*).

Alternatively, *ārāma* means that which is to be delighted in; thus, "one for whom meditation is the delight" is "delighting in meditation. In this way, the construction of the compound should be understood here. By the phrase "he delights while meditating,"...

This shows that for those whose delight is in cultivation (*bhāvanārāma*), there is both the status of being the agent of the accomplishment and the nature of a *kammadhāraya* compound. Because it is stated, "he delights while abandoning," the same principle applies here to the term "delight in abandoning" (*pahānārāma*).

Granted, it is said that "one resorts to the noble lineage of delighting in cultivation, which is the limb of the sitting posture (*nesajjikaṅga*)," because such practice is suitable for the application of cultivation (*bhāvanānuyoga*).

Furthermore, since for a bhikkhu who observes the practice of always sitting (nesajjikaṅga), there is a state of non-offense regarding certain offenses, [the author], including that as well, stated "of the thirteen ascetic practices" (dhutaṅga).
Then, because it is desired that one must abide by what is grave when reaching the Vinaya, he said:
"The practice by way of not abandoning effacement (sallekha) belongs only to one who stands within the Vinaya."
"...of thirteen... it is said. Granted that discourses on virtue (*sīla*) have indeed been brought forth here and there even in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas;

nevertheless, when those qualities by which the purification of virtue occurs are explained, the Vinaya Piṭaka is said to abound in discourse on virtue, while the Sutta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka abound in discourse on mental development (*bhāvanā*).
It is said that when the fourth noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa) has been explained, everything has indeed been explained; thus it is stated:

"By one who delights in development (bhāvanārāma), the remaining two Piṭakas have been explained. Because the teaching proceeds there starting from the "state of renunciation" (nekkhammapada) with the words, "He delights while developing renunciation," or because [it covers] all the phenomena of serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the path (magga) according to their respective [categories].

Because it is designated as "renunciation" (nekkhamma) due to its departure from its opposite, and because that specific reading is found therein, it is called the "Renunciation Text" (nekkhammapāḷi);
thus he said, "It should be recited by means of the Renunciation Text. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary:
"All wholesome states (dhammā) are indeed called 'renunciation'. "By way of the Dasuttara Sutta" means by way of the doctrine of the Dasuttara Sutta.
Or, the meaning is: "according to the method presented in the Dasuttara Sutta. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness. "Renunciation" (nekkhamma) refers to the preliminary stage of the first jhāna, so called because it has emerged from sensual desires;
it is described in the passage beginning with, "Having abandoned covetousness for the world," and so forth. This is the development of the preliminary stage of the first jhāna.
For these [terms] are intended here; therefore, the meaning should be understood in the same way for "non-ill-will" (*abyāpāda*) and so forth as well.
For herein the teaching proceeds by way of the eight attainments together with their methods, the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), and the four noble paths (*ariyamagga*).
Among these, "non-ill-will" is loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Perception of light" is through mental attention having made it manifest.
The perception of light is established. Non-distraction is concentration. The discernment of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*) is the determination of wholesome and other phenomena as they truly are;

some also call it "the discernment of names together with their conditions. Thus, through the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire, there arises a delight in the cultivation of the preliminary path to the first jhāna, described by the words, "Having abandoned covetousness for the world," and so forth.
Having shown the delight in abandoning, he now says "knowledge," etc., in order to show that [delight] together with its means—the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights.

For the perceptions of impermanence and so forth are accomplished for one who stands in full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), by means of distancing delusion—which acts as an obstacle to the overcoming of doubt regarding the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Likewise, it is so in regard to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and attainments.
When dissatisfaction has been dispelled there by means of gladness, which is the antidote to dissatisfaction, the attainment of the jhānas and so forth occurs;

thus, the attainment and insight are the means for dispelling dissatisfaction and shattering ignorance. Furthermore, this out-of-order presentation should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that ignorance—which is by nature an hindrance—is included among the hindrances listed below.
This is so even though [ignorance] exists right within the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna.
Suffering is abandoned even in the preliminary stage (upacāra) of the fourth jhāna; however, with reference to its complete abandonment, it is said: "The fourth jhāna [abandons] pleasure and pain.
Contemplation of the impermanent as "impermanent" is the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); it is the impermanence of the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
This is the name for the contemplation that has thus proceeded. "Perception of permanence" refers to the wrong perception that occurs regarding conditioned phenomena as permanent and eternal.
By means of the term "perception," the inclusion of views and consciousness should also be understood. This same method applies to what follows hereafter.
"Contemplation of disenchantment" is the contemplation that proceeds by way of becoming disenchanted with formations.
They delight in craving accompanied by rapture. Contemplation of fading away (*virāgānupassanā*) is contemplation occurring in the mode of fading away.
Contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*) is the contemplation of the cessation of formations.
Alternatively, contemplation of cessation is the contemplation that "those formations indeed cease; they do not arise again in the future by way of origination. For this very reason, it was said:
“Through the contemplation of cessation, it ceases and does not arise. For this desire for liberation has now reached its full strength.
Contemplation that proceeds by way of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*). This is indeed reflective discernment and composure.
“Grasping” (*ādāna*) is the apprehension [of things] as permanent and so forth; it is the grasping at unity by way of continuity, aggregates, functions, and objects.

The perception of density (*ghanasaññā*). Accumulation (*āyūhana*) is the process of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*). Transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the attainment of a particular state. The perception of stability (*dhuvasaññā*) is the grasping at a state of permanence.
A sign (*nimitta*) is the appearance of formations as having a concrete form, by way of their collective density and their delimitation of specific functions.
Aspiration (*paṇidhi*) is the aspiration for passion and so forth; in its actual meaning, however, it is the inclination toward formations by way of craving (*taṇhā*). Adherence (*abhinivesa*)...
The view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*). The investigation of all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, is higher wisdom and insight into phenomena (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*).

Clinging to the essential (*sārādānābhinivesa*) refers to the perversion of grasping at what is non-essential as being essential. The adherence that "the world arose through the creation of Īśvara" and so forth is the adherence of delusion (*sammohābhinivesa*).
Some, however, maintain that it is the occurrence of doubt, such as "Did I exist in the past? and so forth.
They say it is "adherence through delusion. Grasping at formations as a refuge or a shelter is "adherence through attachment" (*ālayābhinivesa*).

According to the statement, "Delighting in attachment, rejoicing in attachment," attachment is craving; some maintain that this very craving, by way of proceeding with adherence toward the eye and so forth, and toward forms and so forth, is "adherence through attachment.
Thus established, those formations are relinquished—this is the process.
Knowledge is the contemplation of reflection. Because it is free from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), Nibbāna is the "unfolding" (*vivaṭṭa*);
the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) is the "contemplation of unfolding" because it proceeds by means of that which is called the object within that [Nibbāna].

"Adherence through conjunction" is the settling upon formations by way of conjoining. "Associated with views" refers to those things associated with views by way of co-nascence and by way of abandonment. "Gross" means...
This was stated with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing would be grosser than those to be abandoned by the second path.
"Subsisting in a subtle state" means existing in a subtle manner. This was stated with reference to what is to be abandoned by the lower paths.
"All defilements" refers to all remaining defilements; for defilements already abandoned by the first and subsequent paths are not abandoned again.
Thus, having concluded the application of the *Nekkhamma-pāḷi* in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, he demonstrates the application according to the tenfold method beginning with the *Dīghanikāya*.

The statements, "One delights in developing one state" and "One delights in abandoning one state," are not spoken according to the sequence found in the *Dasuttara-sutta*; for there it says, "One state is to be developed..."

The teaching has come down as: “One thing is to be abandoned. Even so, because there is no difference in meaning, it is stated in the *Nekkhamma* section of the *Paṭisambhidāmaggapāli* according to its own sequence:
“Delighting in one thing, he delights; abandoning one thing, he delights. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

Having thus concluded the application by way of the "ten-plus" method (*dasuttara-pariyāya*), the passage beginning with "In the Majjhima Nikāya" is now commenced in order to demonstrate the application by way of the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta* method.
Although the application has here been made concisely by way of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) alone, it should also be applied by way of the twenty-one bases. Now...
In order to show [this] by way of the exposition of the Abhidhamma, the passage beginning with “by way of the exposition in the Abhidhamma” has been commenced.
Regarding what is to be said about “impermanence” and so forth, it should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Discontent” (*ukkaṇṭhita*) refers to discontent with higher wholesome states and with secluded dwellings; and “lack of application” (*ananuyoga*)—

The meaning is as follows: The wise, virtuous bhikkhu who fulfills the noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), not desiring the destruction of the fulfillment of the noble lineages, being concentrated and possessing insight, becomes a conqueror of both aversion and delight through the destruction of their conditions.
Thus it is said: "Bhikkhus, the wise one is a conqueror of aversion and delight. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Dhammapada Sutta: 29.
In the ninth [verse], "dhammapada" means that by means of it, the Dhamma—divided into the jhānas and so forth—is reached; thus, non-covetousness itself is the "footstep of the Dhamma."

The "footing of the Dhamma that is non-covetousness" (*anabhijjhā-dhammapada*) refers either to the state of non-covetousness itself or to a portion of the Dhamma consisting of the practice of non-covetousness.

The same applies to the remaining terms. In terms of meaning, however, the "footing of the Dhamma that is non-covetousness" is either non-greed (*alobha*), or the jhāna, insight, path, fruit, and Nibbāna attained under the heading of non-greed.

The "footing of the Dhamma that is non-ill will" (*abyāpāda*) is either loving-kindness (*mettā*), or the jhānas and so forth attained under the heading of loving-kindness. The "footing of the Dhamma that is right mindfulness" (*sammāsati*)...
"Right mindfulness" (*sūpaṭṭhitassati*) refers either to well-established mindfulness itself, or to the jhānas and so forth attained by means of mindfulness.

"The footing of the Dhamma that is right concentration" (*sammāsamādhidhammapada*) refers either to the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), or to the jhānas, insight, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna attained by means of the eight attainments.

Alternatively, the jhānas and so forth attained by way of the ten kinds of foulness (*dasaa-subha*) constitute the "footing of the Dhamma that is non-covetousness" (*anabhijjhā*). By way of the four divine abodes (*catubrahmavihāra*)...

The state of non-ill will (*abyāpāda*) has been attained as a footprint of the Dhamma. Through the ten recollections and the perception of repulsiveness in food, the state of right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) has been attained as a footprint of the Dhamma.
Through the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing, the state of right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) has been attained as a footprint of the Dhamma.
"One who is not covetous" means one whose nature is free from coveting. The root *jhe*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, has the sense of coveting. For this very reason, it is said:
“Having become free from craving”: by not abandoning one’s natural state—that is, by not abandoning the state of natural purity, which is reckoned as one’s own nature and as blameless.
For when a blameworthy state arises, the blamelessness of the mind is abandoned.
The commentary on the *Dhammapada* Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Paribbājaka Sutta 30.
In the tenth [sutta], "renowned" (*abhiññāta*) means known by way of distinctive characteristics as being "of such and such a kind. Therefore he said, "known, well-known.

Regarding the phrase "emerged from seclusion" (*paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito*): here, "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) refers to [the state] with respect to various beings, such as co-residents, pupils, lay followers, and so forth.

Having turned away and withdrawn from both the internal states and the formations consisting of visible objects and so forth, there is a shrinking back, a hiding away, a state of oneness, which is called seclusion (*paviveka*).

One who has emerged from that is said to have "emerged from seclusion. However, since the Blessed One emerged from seclusion in its highest sense—from the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*)—therefore it is said: "From seclusion..."

"Emergent" means emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Regarding sense-objects" (*vatthukāmesu*) means regarding those sense-objects, such as forms and so forth, which serve as the basis for the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).
"Intense passion" (*bahalarāga*) refers to the defilement of sensual desire that has become thickened through clinging due to its firm roots and difficulty of release.
"With reasons" (*sakāraṇā*) means with those very reasons by which they point out the faults in the doctrines of others; thus, they are "with reasons. Not...
Indeed, it is not possible to demonstrate the faults in the doctrines of others without a reason endowed with the [proper] characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādi*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes such views as, "There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings," and so on;
therefore, the meaning is that those who hold such views are proponents of the negation of causes. And herein, the view of nihilism (*natthikadiṭṭhi*)...
The view of non-action obstructs ripening; the view of no-cause obstructs action; and the view of no-cause obstructs both.
In this regard, by one who obstructs action, ripening is obstructed; and by one who obstructs ripening, action is also obstructed.
Thus, all these are in fact obstructors of both: they are proponents of no-cause as well as proponents of non-action.
And they are proponents of nihilism (*natthikavāda*).

"Having entered the fixed course" (*okkantaniyāmā*) means having plunged into the fixed course of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*). "He studies" (*sajjhāyati*) means that, having mastered the text that illustrates that view, he recites it.
"He investigates" (*vīmaṃsati*) means he examines its meaning. The phrase beginning with "of him" (*tassa*) and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of investigation. In that...

Regarding the phrase "in the object": it refers to the object of the view that proceeds in the manner of "there are no causes," etc., due to the absence of such things as the causes and conditions as they have been imagined.

"Wrong mindfulness settles" means that through long-term habituation, the mind presents itself directly in its own form—just as if with a physical grasp—by means of reflections on the nature of those objects acquired through hearsay, such as "there are no causes," and so forth.

Thus, when the Tathāgata has accepted "contemplative patience" (nijjhānakkhanti) by way of attaining a state of endurance toward such contemplation, then for one who repeatedly pursues and cultivates it in that very same way,

there arises craving accompanied by that acquisition— a craving which, being brought along by wrong thought and propped up by wrong effort, perceives what lacks the true nature as having that nature, and which has acquired the name "wrong mindfulness" (micchāsati).

It remains steady. "The mind becomes one-pointed" means that, by obtaining the aforementioned conditions such as applied thought (*vitakka*), the mind—through its stability upon that object and having abandoned distraction—becomes one-pointed as if fixed, even by way of wrong concentration (*micchā-samādhi*).
For even that [wrong concentration], when it has acquired the power of cultivation through specific conditions, can indeed sometimes perform a function similar to true concentration.
It should be understood that this refers to [the process] such as striking with a weapon.

"The impulsions impel" means that when several preceding sets of impulsions have occurred in that manner many times, seven impulsions impel in the very last set of impulsions. In the first impulse, [the condition] is curable; likewise...
"In the second [view] and so forth" is a statement regarding the nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*);
however, at that moment, it is impossible for anyone to bring about their state of being incurable. "Therein" means among those three wrong views.
"Someone falls into one view" means that for one whose adherence (*abhinivesa*) and habitual practice (*āsevanā*) have proceeded toward only one [view], he falls into that very one view. For whom...
When adherence and repetition proceed toward two or three [factors], one falls into two or three.
By this, those views which were previously established as having the purpose of warding off both [extremes] belong to the preliminary stage;

however, for those who have entered the wrong course of determination (*micchā-niyāma*), there are distinct attainments—each according to its own specific conditions and origin—which are like objects of perception that are separate from one another.

This shows that they are "scattered" because they have not arisen together as one. By stating that even when one has entered [a wrong view], or when two or three have entered, one becomes a person of fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhika*), he demonstrates that these three views share the same fruit and the same strength.
Therefore, even though three volitions arise in a single person, they provide mutual support for one another.
But is he fixed in this very same personal existence (attabhāva), or even in another? He is fixed in this very one. For this unwholesome [kamma] is weak;
it is not like wholesome [kamma], which possesses great power. Otherwise, it would be absolute, like the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma).
However, by way of repetition, one continues to take pleasure in that respective view even in another existence. Therefore, it was said:
“This being is like a stump in a whirlpool. Therefore, the illustration of the stump in a whirlpool is intended to show that the fool, once submerged, remains submerged forever;

however, it cannot be said that because this person has entered upon that vision through certain conditions, he will never again—depending on conditions that oppose it—be able to lift his head from that state of fixedness in falsehood (micchattaniyāma). For this reason it is said, “for the most part.”
“Like that” means similar to what was stated in such passages as, “They are incurable even for Buddhas.
“Out of fear of being censured by others” means out of fear of the censure that others might utter against oneself, as in the passage beginning, “And they blame you for having right view.
“Out of fear of provocation” means out of fear of thus disparaging others. “In accordance with the Dhamma” (sahadhammena).
"Criticism" (*upārambha*) is the reproach that others should direct toward oneself; "fear of criticism" (*upārambhabhaya*) is the anxiety arising from that.
However, in terms of its actual meaning, this is the fear of being slandered; thus he said, "by the fear of slander" (*upavādabhayena*).

"The removal of covetousness" (*abhijjhāvinayo*) is that by which covetousness is removed through the process of subsiding; it is the fruit of arahantship. Therefore he said, "the removal of covetousness is called arahantship."
The commentary on the Paribbājaka Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Uruvela Vagga is finished.
4. The Cakka Vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Cakkasutta* 31.
Regarding the phrase "four wheels" in the first part of the fourth [sutta]:
here, "wheel" (*cakka*) is fivefold—namely, the wooden wheel, the jewel-wheel, the Dhamma-wheel, the wheel of postures, and the wheel of prosperity. Among these, "that which... [the text continues:]
“Friend, the wheelwright’s wheel was finished six months ago, less six days”—this is the wooden wheel.
“He turns the wheel set in motion by his father”—this is the jewel-wheel. “The wheel set in motion by me”—this is the Dhamma-wheel.
“Four wheels and nine gates”—this is the wheel of postures. “Monks, these four... [and so forth].
“The wheels by which the fourfold wheel turns for gods and humans who possess them”—this refers to the wheel of success (*sampatticakka*).
Here too, this alone is intended; thus he said, “the four wheels of success turn.
“In a suitable place” means in a location appropriate for the performance of merit and right practice. “Attendance” means approaching from time to time.
“Devotion” (bhajana) means attending upon with affection. “Establishing oneself rightly” means the wise establishment of one’s own mental continuum.
He said, “If,” etc., regarding the settling [of the mind] in faith and the other [faculties].
And here, “this alone is the measure” means that this very wheel of prosperity, consisting in the merit performed in the past, is the standard among these wheels of prosperity.

Because of the causal status of the others. Therefore he said, "By which," and so forth. And that very person who has performed merit establishes himself rightly, because one who has not performed merit lacks that quality.
The commentary on the *Cakka-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Saṅgaha Sutta 32.
Regarding the second [verse], "only that should be given to him": for one who has gone forth, the requisites of a renunciant—such as the bowl and robes—should be given;
for a householder, the requisites of a householder—such as clothing, weapons, vehicles, and beds—should be given. "All" means every kind of assistance.
"Having smeared, he destroys" means remaining in a state of smearing. "He smears as with oil" means he smears as if with oil that has been washed a hundred times.
"Discourse on increasing welfare" (atthavaḍḍhanakathā) is discourse that brings benefit. Here, the mention of "discourse" is merely illustrative;
bodily application that brings benefit to others is also "conduct for the good" (atthacariyā). In the commentary, however, conduct for the good is treated specifically by way of verbal application.

It is said: “Samānattatā” means the state of being similar, or placing [the other] in an equal position. Furthermore, that placing in an equal position consists in sharing the same enjoyment (*ekasambhogatā*) by way of making them like oneself.

Because one shares the same enjoyment with them when happiness arises for oneself and when suffering arises for them—sharing in that suffering as if it were one’s own—it is called “the state of having the same pleasure and pain” (*samānasukhadukkhabhāva*). And that state of having the same pleasure and pain...
Showing that [the fault] becomes evident through sitting together with others and so forth, he said, "In a single seat," and so on.
In this regard, one who is inferior by birth but superior in wealth is difficult to manage. Indeed, it is not possible to share enjoyments with him because of his inferiority by birth.
And if one does not act accordingly toward him, he becomes angry because of his superiority in wealth; therefore—
Thus, he is difficult to associate with. Even one who is inferior in wealth but superior in birth is difficult to associate with;
for thinking, "I am of noble birth," he desires to share in the same enjoyments as one endowed with wealth, and when this is not done, he becomes angry.
One who is inferior in both is easy to associate with; for because of his low status in birth, he does not desire to share in the same enjoyments with the other.
One does not become angry when [the sharing] is not performed because of being deprived of wealth. One who is equal in both respects is indeed easy to reconcile.
This is because, by virtue of that very equality, there is an expectation of shared enjoyment with the other, and because there is no anger when such sharing is not performed.
A monk who is immoral is difficult to reconcile; for it is not possible to share in common enjoyment with him, and when it is not done—

And he does not become angry. One who is virtuous is easy to associate with. For one who is virtuous does not become angry even when some material gift is not given or when some act of conciliation is not performed;
because of his gentle nature, he does not look upon another with an evil mind even if that person does not share enjoyment with him.
For that very reason, it is easy for others to enjoy things together with him; therefore, [it is said of] a householder—

If he is a layperson, he is equal to both [the householder and the monk]. If he is one who has gone forth, he is a person endowed with virtue. Thus, he should be included through this state of equality.
For this very reason it was said: "If he is equal to the householder in birth and to the one who has gone forth in virtue, this state of equality should be established for him.
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Saṅgaha-sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Sīha-sutta: 33.
In the third [sutta], "Sīha" refers to the lord of beasts who has received the name "Lion" because he endures dangers and because he slays his adversaries.
"Four" means that although they are equal in their lion-nature (*sīhajātibhāva*), there are four lions distinguished by differences such as their color and other qualities.
Having now shown them by name, by color, and by food, the passage beginning with "grass-lion" (*tiṇasīha*) is commenced in order to clarify the specific lion intended here through its various types.
A lion whose food is grass is a "grass-lion" (*tiṇasīha*), according to the elision of the latter member of the compound in the first word, just as...
“*Sākapatthiva*” (Pāṇini 2.1.60). Because of its black color, it is a black lion; likewise, a pale lion (*paṇḍusīha*). Therefore he said:

“resembling a black *gāvī* [deer], resembling a *gāvī* the color of a withered leaf. It is called a *kesarī* because it possesses a mane (*kesara*)—that is, hair on its neck—like a red woolen blanket.
The construction is also: “with the extremities of its legs as if treated with lac.”

"By virtue of his majesty and great power, established through the influence of his past kamma, he is the king of the entire host of beasts. The passage beginning with "From the golden cave... is stated on the grounds that such is the dwelling and the behavior of a lion.
"Having set down evenly" means having placed it upon the ground so that all parts are level.

"Having drawn forward" means having dragged it toward the front. "Having carried toward" means having brought it face-to-face. "Destruction" (*saṅghāta*) means ruin. A "bull's place" (*usabhaṃ*) refers to a space measuring twenty *aṭṭhakas*.
“Like a lion” means he is like a lion in his lineage and his majesty. The phrase “I am equal” is merely a teaching; it is because of his very majesty that he does not fear.

“Because of the strength of the view of individuality” means because of the powerful state of the view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which serves as the cause for the conceit of “I,” being the sign of the overweening pride of power, thinking: “Who else is superior to us? We alone are truly mighty.”

"Because of the abandoning of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)" means that he does not fear because of the absence of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and because of the thorough eradication of attachment to a self (*attasineha*).

Having stated, "In such and such a way," meaning he described himself in various manners such as being like a lion, he spoke the passage beginning with "He is indeed a lion" in order to explain and demonstrate that meaning. As for "the state of Buddhahood which is certain to come about":

it refers to the state of Buddhahood that is absolutely destined to occur through the attainment of the certainty of enlightenment (*bodhi-niyata-bhāva*) by the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*) who possesses great resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).

Having established that the periods prior to the full enlightenment—such as the time of dwelling in the three palaces, the time of giving his promise to King Māgadha, and the time of consuming the milk-rice—are also like those of a lion, they have been shown thus.
For even the usage of the world employs the designation of what has already come to be for what is yet to be (*bhāvini bhūtūpacāra*).

Furthermore, by virtue of the commonality of being "knowledge" (*vijjā*), even other types of knowledge are taken together with the two-fold knowledge; thus, from the contemplation of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-sammasana*)...

Having treated that [knowledge] as if it were already established beforehand, he said, "having purified the three types of higher knowledge. By way of the knowledge proceeding in direct and reverse order, it is called "the churning of the knowledge of the pairs.
"While dwelling there" means while dwelling at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree. "On the eleventh day" refers to [the period] after the seven-week interval.
On the eleventh day thereafter. "The immovable seat" (*acalapaḷlaṅka*) refers to the seat upon which he sat at Isipatana for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
For that sitting, being unshakable by anyone and performed for the sake of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, is called the "immovable seat," just like the Vajirāsana.
And in this context, the phrase refers to the discourse beginning with: "Bhikkhus, these two extremes... and so forth.
And in this portion of the True Dhamma, Dhammaghosa... [and so on]... covered the ten-thousandfold world system with the resolve:
"May they hear it wherever they stand. "In sixteen ways" means: the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the development of the path;
by taking four aspects for each of the four paths, there are thus sixteen ways.

By the first method, having taken even the state prior to the full awakening (*abhisambodhi*)—which was necessarily already established—to demonstrate his likeness to a lion, the passage beginning with "Another method" is commenced in order to now demonstrate his likeness to a lion specifically during the states of full awakening. Regarding the phrase "by eight reasons":
"He is a Tathāgata because he has come thus; he is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus; [he is a Tathāgata] because of the true characteristic..."
He is called the Tathāgata because he has come; he is called the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of phenomena as they really are;

he is called the Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are; he is called the Tathāgata because of his speaking things as they truly are; he is called the Tathāgata because of his acting in accordance with what he has seen; and he is called the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.
Thus, by these eight reasons that establish him as a Tathāgata—even though the Blessed One was merely sitting on the seat of enlightenment—
He was not yet fully enlightened while sitting there; nevertheless, by sitting in that very posture, he dispelled all perils and became fully enlightened.
For this reason, it is called the "unconquered throne" (*aparājitapallaṅka*).
Therefore, not being satisfied with saying "up to the Bodhi throne," he said "up to the knowledge of the path to Arahatship."

Regarding the phrase *iti sakkāyo*, the word *iti* here has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). By this, the personal existence (*sakkāya*) is shown by way of its essential nature, its measure, and its delimitation;
thus he says, "This is personal existence," and so forth. By the words "this is personal existence," the five aggregates of clinging are shown by way of their essential nature.
By the words "so much is personal existence," they are shown by way of their measure. And of that measure...
By showing its absolute nature, it is said: "There is no identity-view (sakkāya) greater than this. "By way of individual essence" means by way of specific characteristic.

"By way of own-nature" means by way of its own function. "By way of limit" means by way of the limit of its measure. "By way of delimitation" means by way of defining the extent of the place in which it occurs.
"By way of enclosure" means by way of its occurrence at the final stage. All [these]...
The five aggregates of clinging are shown according to the aforementioned classification.
"This is called the origin of identity" (*sakkāya-samudaya*) means this is the origin of identity consisting of nutriment and so forth. Therefore he said, "To this extent," and so on.

"Cessation" (*atthaṅgama*) means destruction. By taking that [nutriment] specifically as "with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment," he includes the remaining factors under the word "etc. (*ādi*).
“Adorned with the fifty characteristics” means it is embellished by the fifty characteristics of arising and passing away, through the grasping of their origin and cessation.
“By one whose taints are destroyed” means because the taints have been completely and without remainder destroyed. For even non-returners do not experience fear or mental terror.
Knowledge of the appearance of fear is the wisdom of the appearance of fear; as for the other deities, however—
He speaks with reference to the gods whose taints are not yet exhausted. "Bho" is merely a form of polite address; it is simply a conventional mode of speaking.
"Cakra" (wheel) refers to the wheel of the Teacher’s command. Because that [command] has come forth from the Dhamma, it is the "Dhammacakka" (Wheel of Dhamma).

In this context, for noble disciples, it is the Dhammacakka because it has come forth from the Dhamma of personal realization (*paṭivedha*); for others, it is the Dhammacakka because it has come forth from the Dhamma of teaching (*desanā*).
In both types [of knowledge], wisdom is primary; thus it is stated under the heading of wisdom: “both penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and teaching knowledge (*desanā-ñāṇa*)”.
Now, in order to show that knowledge according to its specific nature, it is said: “penetrative knowledge, named...”, and so forth.
Because that knowledge has been penetrated, the Blessed One is capable of showing those sixty thousand methods (*naya-sahassa*) to those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Because it was so, those sixty thousand methods were established along with that very knowledge;
thus, showing this, he said, "He penetrated by means of sixty thousand methods. "Three turnings" (tiparivaṭṭa) means:
"This is suffering," "It is to be fully understood," and "It has been fully understood"—thus it has three turnings, and that itself consists of twelve aspects. That...
Knowledge of teaching. This Blessed One is "without a counterpart," meaning he is devoid of any person who could serve as a substitute. "Of one and the same kind" means being without variation.
The commentary on the Sīha Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Aggapasāda Sutta.
34. In the fourth [verse], "confidence in the supreme" (*aggesu pasāda*) means confidence in the best (*seṭṭhesu*). Or, "supreme confidence" (*aggā pasādā*) means confidence that has become supreme.
Here, the word *agga* is a term for "best. In the first interpretation of the meaning, the Three Jewels beginning with the Buddha are expressed by the word *agga*.
Among those, the Blessed One is [the supreme] in the sense of being peerless, in the sense of having distinguished qualities, and in the sense of being equal to the unequaled.

He is the foremost. For, beginning with the Great Resolve and the discernment of the ten perfections, he is the foremost in the sense of being incomparable to other beings by virtue of his qualities for accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, his Buddha-qualities, and his purposes.
Furthermore, because those qualities of his—such as great compassion and so forth—are superior to the qualities of all other beings, he is the foremost by way of being the supreme among all beings.

He is the foremost. Furthermore, he is the foremost in the sense of being "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*), for while the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were unequal to all beings, he alone is equal to them in terms of both the qualities of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the qualities of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*).

Likewise, the Blessed One is [foremost] because his appearance is difficult to encounter, because he possesses the marvelous human state, because he brings about the welfare and happiness of many people, and because he is peerless and without equal.
"He is called the foremost in the world. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, the manifestation of one person is rare in the world. Of which one person?
Of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Bhikkhus, when one person arises in the world, he arises..."
A person of wondrous nature. Monks, one person, when arising in the world, arises for the benefit of many people...

[as before] ...the Perfectly Enlightened One. Monks, one person, when arising in the world, arises peerless, without companion, matchless, incomparable, without rival, unequaled, equal to the unequaled, the foremost of bipeds. Who is that one person?
“The Tathāgata is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.

The Dhamma and the Saṅgha are supreme because they are incomparable with other Dhammas and Saṅghas in terms of their distinguished qualities, and because of the rarity of their manifestation and so forth.
For indeed, by virtue of their specific qualities—such as the Dhamma being well-expounded and the Saṅgha being well-practiced—they have no equals among other Dhammas and Saṅghas.
There is not even the slightest inferiority among them, so how could there be superiority? They are superior precisely because they possess qualities that are themselves distinguished.
Likewise, their nature consists in being rare to appear, marvelous, bringing benefit and happiness to many people, and being peerless companions, and so forth.
For to the same extent that the Blessed One is rare to manifest, so too are the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. This same principle applies to their marvelousness and other such qualities.
Thus, "confidence in the foremost" (*aggappasāda*) refers to confidence in those who are foremost, best, supreme, and distinguished by their qualities.
In the second sense, however, "foremost confidence" refers to the confidences that have become foremost through arising toward the "foremost" ones already mentioned, such as the Buddha and so forth.
Furthermore, those confidences based on penetration (*aveccappasāda*) that have been attained via the Noble Path are "foremost confidences" because they are exclusively of the highest order.
As it is said: “Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha,” and so forth.

Furthermore, these are called supreme confidences (*aggappasāda*) because their fruition is supreme. For this has also been stated: “For those who have confidence in what is supreme, the fruition is supreme.

In the phrases “or one without feet” (*apadā vā*), etc., the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). Just as in the case of: “The taint of sensual desire that has not yet arisen...”
In the phrase, “the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, or the arisen taint of sensual desire increases,” the meaning is “both the unarisen and the arisen.

And just as in the phrase, “for the stability of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth,” the meaning is “both of those who have come to be and of those seeking rebirth.
And just as in the phrase, “from fire, or from water, or from the breaking of friendship,” [the meaning is likewise].
The meaning is: "from fire, from water, and from the breaking of friendships. Likewise, in the passage "whether footless... [etc.
...is declared supreme," the meaning should be understood here as well through the method of combining "the footless and the two-footed. Therefore it was said:
"The word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not the sense of option (*vikappa*)."
“Material” (*rūpin*) means possessing form. “Not material” (*arūpin*) means formless. “Perceiving” (*saññin*) means possessing perception. “Non-perceiving” (*asaññin*) means lacking perception.

By all the terms beginning with “or footless,” one should understand that among the ninefold existence—namely, sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), perceiving existence (*saññibhava*), non-perceiving existence (*asaññibhava*), and neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving existence (*nevasaññināsaññibhava*)—it applies to all.

It shows all beings without exception. For here, by the mention of "beings with form" (rūpī), the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), fine-material existence (rūpabhava), five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava), and one-aggregate existence (ekavokārabhava) are shown;
by the mention of "formless beings" (arūpī), the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) and four-aggregate existence (catuvokārabhava) are shown;

while the percipient existence (saññibhava) and so forth are shown explicitly by their own names. By the mention of "the footless" (apada) and so forth, however, only a portion of the sense-sphere existence, the five-aggregate existence, and the percipient existence is shown.

But why, in this context, is the inclusion of "footless beings" and so forth made instead of simply using the term "two-footed beings," as was done in the *Adutiyasutta* where it says, "the foremost of two-footed beings"?
It is said in reply: In the *Adutiyasutta*, the inclusion of "two-footed beings" alone was made by way of their being the most excellent.
For when one who is called "foremost" arises in this world, he does not arise among footless, four-footed, or many-footed beings.
It arises only among bipeds. Among which bipeds? Among humans and among devas.
When arising among humans, he arises as a Buddha capable of bringing the entire world under his influence;
when arising among devas, he arises as a Mahābrahmā capable of bringing ten thousandfold world-systems under his influence, acting as his attendant.
Or he becomes a monastery attendant. Thus, it was stated there [in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*] that he is the foremost of bipeds by way of being superior even to those [others].
But here, it is stated thus by way of an exhaustive inclusion: "Bhikkhus, as far as beings exist—whether footless... pe...
or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared their foremost. This is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

This is a genitive expression (*sāmivacana*). The letter *ma* is for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). The word-analysis (*padavibhāga*) is: "the foremost (*agga*) is declared. For this very reason, he said: "foremost by way of qualities," and so forth.

"The result (*vipāka*) is foremost" means that for those who have faith in the Foremost One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (*Sammāsambuddha*), that faith is foremost, best, or of the highest limit;
therefore, its result (*vipāka*) is also foremost, best, of the highest limit, most exalted, and most sublime. That...
Furthermore, confidence (pasāda) is twofold, distinguished as mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Of these, first, regarding the mundane:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to the plane of misery."
Having abandoned the human body,
they will fulfill the host of devas.
"The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises, 'He is a Buddha'— "
Indeed, that rapture alone is better than even the whole of Jambudīpa.
"A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred chariots drawn by mules,
and a hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings— "
“They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single stride of one who has gone for refuge.
“It is indeed good, Lord of the Devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha;
it is because of going for refuge to the Buddha, Lord of the Devas, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, [are reborn] in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
They are reborn there. They surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine glory, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.”

Through such scriptural passages as these, one should understand the connection with the specific fruits of confidence (*pasāda*). Therefore, that [confidence] should be regarded as bestowing specific happiness within states of prosperity, along with the turning away from the suffering of the woeful states (*apāya*).

The supramundane [confidence], however, bestows the fruition of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) and turns one away from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). And all this confidence, by way of succession, indeed turns away the suffering of the round of existence. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects his own faith, at that time he does not..."
At that time, the mind is not obsessed by lust, nor obsessed by hatred...
nor obsessed by delusion; at that time, his mind is simply straight. In one whose mind is straight, gladness is born;
in one who is glad, rapture is born... [as before] ...he understands: "There is nothing further beyond this state of being."

“Dhammas” means phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). “Conditioned” (*saṅkhata*) means made by conditions having come together and combined; thus, they are phenomena that possess conditions.
That which is not made by any causes or conditions is “unconditioned” (*asaṅkhata*); it is Nibbāna, which is without conditions.
Because the conditioned things have reached their termination, the plural term “unconditioned” is used. Dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them.

Of those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, that unconditioned phenomenon which is designated as "dispassion" (virāga) is called the foremost, the best, the supreme, and the most excellent precisely because of its intrinsic nature of being subtle and delicate, its state of being more peaceful and more refined, its state of being profound and so forth, and its state of intoxicating the intoxicated and so forth.
*Yadidaṃ* is a particle; the meaning is "that which. Regarding the phrases beginning with *madanimmadano*:
All these are synonyms for Nibbāna. For this very reason, it is said: “Dispassion (*virāga*), and so forth, are names for Nibbāna itself.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “lust, pride, and so forth,” it includes pride in one’s status (*mānamada*), pride in being a man (*purisamada*), and the like.

“All thirsts” refers to all thirsts, beginning with thirst for sense-pleasures (*kāmapipāsā*). “All attachments (*ālaya*) go to total eradication” means that all attachments, beginning with attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmālaya*), reach complete destruction.
They go. "The rounds" refers to the round of kamma and the round of result. "Craving" refers to craving in all its one hundred and eight varieties.
Regarding the statement "the foremost result occurs," here too it is said:
"Whosoever have gone for refuge to the Dhamma... and so forth.
“The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises the Dhamma…” and so on;
“It is good, Lord of Devas, to go for refuge to the Dhamma; it is because of going for refuge to the Dhamma, Lord of Devas, that some here [attain] … divine tactile sensations.
Through such scriptural passages as these, the connection between confidence in the Dhamma and the attainment of specific fruits should be understood.
“Whether assemblies or groups” means all those known as assemblies or groups that exist in the world.

“The Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples” refers to the community of the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala), which is called a *saṅgha* because it is bound together by the commonality of view and virtue.
“Is declared supreme” means that, by virtue of its own specific qualities such as morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, it is the foremost among those assemblies.
"Best, supreme, excellent"—this is what is said. "Yadidaṃ" means "which are these. Regarding the "four pairs of persons":

by way of pairs, the one standing in the first path and the one standing in the first fruit constitute one pair; continuing in this manner up to the one standing in the fourth path and the one standing in the fourth fruit, these constitute one pair—thus there are four pairs of persons. "Eight individuals"—this is by way of individual persons.
One is at the stage of the first path, and one is at the stage of the first fruit; by this method there are eight types of persons (*puggala*).
And here, the words "person" (*purisa*) and "individual" (*puggala*) are synonymous, though they are stated thus according to those who are to be trained (*veneyya*).
"This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples"—these four pairs, when taken individually, constitute eight [types of individuals].
These are the individuals who constitute the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples. The terms beginning with "worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*) have already been explained in their proper context.
Here too, it is said: "Whoever has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha...
and "For one who praises the 'Saṅgha,' there arises in the body a rapture... and so forth.
“Excellent indeed, Lord of Devas, is going for refuge to the Saṅgha; by reason of going for refuge to the Saṅgha, Lord of Devas...

[and so on] ...one is endowed with celestial tactile sensations”—by means of such scriptural passages, one should understand the connection of the confidence in the Saṅgha with specific fruits and its state as the supreme maturation.
Likewise, there is the attainment of the unsurpassed, and from the seventh existence onwards, the total cutting off of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
The attainment of unsurpassed happiness and so forth should be understood as the state of supreme fruition (*aggavipākatā*) by way of producing such exalted results.
In the verses, "in the foremost" (*agge*) refers to the Three Jewels; or, it refers to those who have faith because of their preeminence.

"The foremost Dhamma" (*aggaṃ dhammaṃ*) refers to the Buddha’s excellent enlightenment, the excellent nature of the Dhamma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha—the unique qualities of the Three Jewels not shared by anything else.
Of supreme nature, or of a nature characterized by qualities such as being well-expounded and well-practiced by the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

"Vijānantānaṃ" means "of those who understand. Having thus shown the object of faith in the Supreme generally, it is now said, "In the Supreme Buddha," etc., in order to show that same object specifically and by way of classification.
Therein, "of those who have faith" refers to those with faith through verified conviction (*aveccappasāda*).
And by means of other forms of confidence, [it is] for those who are confident and resolute. "In dispassion and tranquility" (*virāgūpasame*) means: in dispassion and in tranquility;
that is to say, as the cause of absolute dispassion toward all lust and as the cause of absolute tranquility regarding all defilements. "In bliss" (*sukhe*) means:
in bliss by way of the destruction of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) and by way of the bliss of the tranquility of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārūpasama*).
"Giving to the foremost" means giving to the Three Jewels—the foremost—while relinquishing the objects of charity.
In that regard, "giving to the Buddha" refers to those who, while the Blessed One is still living, attend upon, honor, and revere him with the four requisites;
or, after the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, those who attend upon, honor, and revere shrines containing his relics and so forth, dedicating their offerings to the Buddha.

They indeed give. Thinking, "We shall honor the Dhamma," those who attend upon persons who uphold the Dhamma with the four requisites, honoring and revering them, thereby making the Dhamma long-enduring, are said to give a gift to the Dhamma.
Likewise, those who attend upon the Noble Saṅgha with the four requisites, honoring and revering them, and [giving] to others as well for their sake—
Those who practice in such a manner are said to give gifts to the Saṅgha. "Supreme merit increases":
thus, for those who, with a mind full of confidence in the Triple Gem, exercise sublime relinquishment and sublime honor and respect, supreme and sublime wholesome kamma is accumulated day by day.
Now, in order to show the preeminence of that merit through its supreme ripening:
“Supreme life,” and so forth, was said. Therein, “life” (*āyu*) means that divine or human life—supreme, sublime, and ultimate—increases and expands further and further.
