“Beauty” (*vaṇṇa*) means perfection of form. “Glory” (*yasa*) means perfection of retinue. “Fame” (*kitti*) means the sound of praise.
“Happiness” (*sukha*) means both bodily and mental happiness. “Strength” (*bala*) means both physical strength and the strength of knowledge.
A giver of gifts to the supreme Triple Gem; or alternatively, one who has performed a sublime act of giving by means of the most excellent objects of charity and has thereby cultivated merit therein.

"Composed in the supreme Dhamma" means endowed with, possessed of, and accompanied by the supreme quality of serene confidence as well as the qualities of generosity and so forth, being possessed of unwavering faith;
or [endowed] with those qualities such as being dear and pleasing to many people, which are the results of that [faith].
"Endowed. "He who has reached the summit rejoices" means that wherever he is born among the classes of beings, there he has attained the state of being foremost, the state of excellence;
or, having attained the state of being foremost—the supramundane path and fruit—he rejoices, delights, and is fully satisfied.
The commentary on the *Aggapasāda Sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta 35.

Regarding the fifth [phrase], "in the noble way" (*ariye ñāye*): because it is far removed from defilement, it is "noble" (*ariya*), faultless, pure, and by virtue of being a state of dhamma that leads to liberation.
The meaning is "in the cause" (*kāraṇe*). It is called "the way" (*ñāya*) because one definitely goes to Nibbāna by means of it, or because Nibbāna itself is known and penetrated through it.
By this, the noble path (ariyamagga) is the principle (ñāya). And that very same [path] is called the "cause" (kāraṇa) because it serves as the cause for bringing about [the goal].
However, here the noble path together with insight (vipassanā) is intended; thus he says, "in the path accompanied by insight.
In the verses, the same method applies to the phrase "the principle and the Dhamma" (ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ).
The commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta: 36.
Regarding the sixth [verse], "being carried by torches" means being carried by lamps; having lit staff-lamps, they were carried.

The meaning is that it was built while [torches] were being held aloft. For that city was constructed even at night while torches were being carried, so that the auspicious day, the favorable moment, and the propitious star might not pass by. It is called *ukkaṭṭhā* because it stands (*ṭhāti*) amidst torches;

the grammatical derivation is established through the application of the rule beginning with *mūlavibhujādi* (Pāṇini 3.2.5), meaning it is situated or firmly established while the torches are shining.

It should be understood [thus]. Or, according to the method of etymology (*nirukti*), it is called *Ukkaṭṭhā* because she remained (*ṭhitā*) while the torches (*ukkāsu*) were burning. Others, however, say:
"That city received the name *Ukkaṭṭhā* because of its association with superior qualities (*ukkaṭṭha-guṇa*)—namely, excellence of location, excellence of inhabitants, and excellence of requisites.
*Setavya* is the name of that city. Furthermore, regarding that [city] of Kassapa, the Possessor of the Ten Powers...
"Jātanagara" means "the birthplace of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa in the past.
"Vijjantarikāya" means at the moment when lightning flashes. "Antarato" means from within the heart. "Antarā" means in the interval between the commencement and the completion [of an action].
"Antarikāya" means in the intermediate space. And here, "tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya, etesaṃ antarā kappā... [refers to] "Who could know that interval, the eons between these?"
In such instances as "countless from calculation" (*gaṇanato asaṅkhyeyyā*) and "how does one arise in between?

(*antarantarā kathaṃ opapātetī*), it is the word *antara* occurring in the sense of intervals between causes that should be cited, and not the words *antara-antarika* occurring in the sense of gaps between moments of consciousness (*cittakkhaṇa*).
For this is the extraction of the meaning of the word *antara*.

However, the intended meaning here may be as follows: since the word *antara* occurs in those same instances where the word *antaras* occurs, the word *antaras*—which functions in the sense of *antarasa*—has been cited because they share the same meaning.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the word *antara* itself was pronounced with a short vowel (*rantara*) for the sake of metrical ease in the verse "yassantarato.
Furthermore, the word *antara* alone [is used] together with the suffix *-ika*.
Having extended the word, it is stated as “*antarikā*”; thus, in this case, the absence of contradiction between the example and what is to be exemplified should be understood.

If [the word] were not joined [with *antarā*], the accusative case would not be reached, because when there is the possibility of a genitive case, the accusative is desired due to its connection with the word *antarā*.
For this very reason, he said: “But because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case is employed.”
Having pacified the great dispute that had arisen throughout all of Jambudīpa,

and having settled the quarrel between the Kosiñāraka Mallas and the remaining kings— who stood surrounding Kusināra city for the sake of the relics after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, saying, "Either give us the relics or give us battle," and so forth— he, it is said...
Having heard their dispute, the brahmin thought, "These kings are quarreling over the site where the Blessed One attained final nibbāna;
this is indeed not fitting. Enough of this strife; I shall settle it.
Having gone there and stood on a high place, he recited the discourse known as the *Doṇagajjita*, consisting of two sections (*bhāṇavāra*). Regarding that, in the first section:
For that long, they did not recognize even a single word of his.
At the conclusion of the second recitation section, everyone cried out, "This is the voice of our teacher! This is the voice of our teacher!
Indeed, it is said that on the plains of Jambudīpa, there was generally no one born into a noble family who was not his pupil; thus, upon hearing his own words, he [realized this].
Knowing that they were silent and still, he spoke again:
"Listen, sirs, to my single word:
our Buddha was a teacher of patience."
For there can be no conflict regarding the bodily remains of the Supreme Person who has attained perfection. "All of you,
sirs, being united and in harmony..."
“Greeting one another, let us divide [the relics] into eight portions;
let the stupas be spread throughout the quarters,
so that many people may have faith in the One with Vision.”
Having spoken these two verses and having pacified that quarrel, he divided the relics into eight portions and gave them away;
it was with reference to this that it was said: "He will pacify the great quarrel arisen throughout all Jambudīpa and distribute the relics.
"The wheel-marks" refers to the two wheel-marks on the soles of his two feet.
"By the taint" means by the taint that has karma and the defilements as its cause. For here, both the karma of the three planes and all remaining unwholesome states are called "taints.
"Rebirth among the gods" means arising or birth among the gods. And here, all gods—excluding the *yakkhas* and *gandhabbas*—are included by the term "gods.
Alternatively, a *gandhabba* is a winged being who moves through the sky. "I" [refers to the self].
It should be construed by changing the case endings.
The commentary on the *Doṇa-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Aparihāniya-sutta*.

37. "He wanders only in the peace of Nibbāna" means that he wanders only in the peace of the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*) and the final Nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*), having determined that "he will attain it before long.

In the verse, "delighting in heedfulness" (*appamādarato*) means being delighted and fond of the non-neglect of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*); the meaning is that he passes his days and nights solely in heedfulness. [Regarding] heedlessness...
"Seeing [heedfulness] as fear" means seeing heedlessness as fear because it is the cause for the fear of rebirth in hell and other such states.
"Unable to fall away" means that one of such a nature is incapable of falling away from the qualities of serenity and insight, or from the paths and fruits.
For he does not fall away from the attainment of serenity and insight, and he reaches those other [states] which he has not yet attained.
The commentary on the *Aparihāniya-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Paṭilīna-sutta*: 38.
In the eighth [sutta], the phrase "the world is finite" is either due to grasping the kasiṇa-sign—which has been expanded on one side—as "the world," or...

Or, a view arises through mere reasoning. For one who possesses the eye of meditative absorption (*jhānacakkhu*) perceives and grasps [the object] by seeing it, whereas the other does so by means of mere reasoning.
Or, a view arises through the grasping of the kasiṇa-sign—which is immeasurable and expanded on all sides—as "the world," either by way of such grasping or by mere reasoning.
Or, a view arises that "the soul is the same as the body," meaning that the soul and the body are one and the same entity.
"Relinquished" (*vissaṭṭhāni*) means they have been let go by way of one's own renunciation. "Vomited" (*vantāni*) is stated here to show that they are not to be taken back again.
For while some might take back even what has been cast away, this [gift] is not like that; thus it is said "vomited.
Indeed, that which has been vomited by someone is not taken back by him again. Yet, something that has been vomited might still remain clinging to one's own continuum.
The term "freed" (*muttāni*) is stated for the purpose of showing that it is not merely "this [is freed]"; for this very reason, he said, "made with bonds severed.
The meaning is that they have been made with bonds severed by way of liberation from the continuity (*santati*).
Even something that is freed might remain somewhere like a fruit whose bond has been released; to show that it is not so, the term "abandoned" (*pahīnāni*) is stated. Just as...
Whatever has been relinquished poorly and then taken up again is called "re-relinquished" (*paṭinissaṭṭha*) when it is properly relinquished;

likewise, in order to show that those things relinquished by insight—which are like what was previously taken up—and which are abandoned by the Path, are called "re-relinquished," it is said: "re-relinquished.
For this very reason he said: "so that they do not ascend in the mind again."
"Thus they have been relinquished.

*Kāmesanā* means the seeking of sensual pleasures (*kāma*), or the seeking that is characterized by sensual pleasure; thus it is called *kāmesanā*. For this has been said: "In this context, what is *kāmesanā*?

It is whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, thirst for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and clinging to sensual pleasures regarding sensual pleasures."
“This is called the search for sensual pleasures (kāmesanā)”; therefore, lust for sensual pleasures should be understood as “the search for sensual pleasures.

For this very reason it was said: “The search for sensual pleasures... is abandoned by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga). The search for states of existence is the “search for existence” (bhavesanā).

And this has also been stated: “In this regard, what is the search for existence? Whatever desire for existence among states of existence... clinging to existence—this is called the search for existence.”

Therefore, craving for existence (*bhavesanā-rāga*) should be understood as the longing for existence in the realms of form and the formless. For this very reason it was said: "But craving for existence is abandoned by the path of Arahatship.

Craving for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*) is the seeking of the holy life. And that is twofold: by way of seeking the holy life of the Path and by way of seeking the holy life approved by those who hold wrong views.
Thus he said, "I shall seek the holy life," and so forth. [Regarding] that which is approved by those who hold wrong views...
For even the seeking of the holy life is called the "seeking of the holy life. And this has also been said:
"In this context, what is the seeking of the holy life? It is the view that 'the world is eternal,' or 'the world is not eternal'; or 'the world is finite,' or 'the world is infinite';
or 'the soul and the body are the same,' or 'the soul is one thing and the body another'..."

Whether "the Tathāgata exists after death," or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
any such view, any state of view, any thicket of views, any wilderness of views, any distortion of views, is [thus described].
“The writhing of views, the fetter of views, grasping, settled grasping, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false road, falsity,
the domain of sectarians, and the grasping of perversions— this is called the search for the holy life. Therefore,
it should be understood that the search for the holy life approved by those who hold to views is the “search for the holy life based on what has been seen.”
For this very reason it was said: "But the search for the holy life through views is stilled by the stream-entry path alone.
By this much, it is shown that lust and views are searches. And not only lust and views are searches; the karma associated with them is also a search.
For this has also been stated:

“In that regard, what is the search for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*)? Sensual lust and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions associated therewith—this is called the search for sensual pleasures.
In that regard, what is the search for existence (*bhavesanā*)? Lust for existence and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions associated therewith—this is called the search for existence.
In that regard, what is the search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*)? [It is] the adherence to extremes...”
“Wrong view, and the unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action associated with it—this is called the search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*).
Regarding the ninefold conceit: it refers to the ninefold conceit presented as “I am superior to one who is superior,” and so forth.

In the verse beginning with “the search for sensual pleasures” (*kāmesanā*), however, the search for the holy life is mentioned together with the search for the holy life; [this is expressed] by the elision of a case ending (*vibhattilopa*).
For this is the explanation. Or, this is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant:

“The three searches (esanā) are the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life. Among these, in order to show the search for the holy life according to its specific nature, it is said:
“Adherence to ‘this is the truth,’ the standpoints of views, the aggregates. Its meaning is as follows: “Thus,” that is, “in this way,” [is] “truth.”
“Adherence” (*parāmāsa*) means adherence to what is not true. This shows the mode of occurrence of the view: “This alone is the truth; all else is vain.
All views are “bases for views” (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*) because they are the cause of every kind of harm. For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the foremost fault.
And these very [views], through their progressive increase and by way of the accumulation of defilements such as conceit, greed, and so forth, [lead to further suffering].
And because they are accumulations through the accumulation of the suffering of saṃsāra, and because they are the causes of all harm by way of adhering falsely with the thought,
"Only this is true, the other is false," these views— which are the cause for the accumulation of the suffering of defilements— are called "the quest for the holy life. By this,
it should be understood that the quest for the holy life is shown both in terms of its mode of occurrence and its production.
"Of one who is detached from all lust" means of one who is detached from all lust for sense-pleasures (*kāma*) and existence (*bhava*).
Precisely because he is liberated in Nibbāna, which is characterized by the destruction of craving, he is "the Arahant liberated through the destruction of craving.

"Seeking has been relinquished" means that seeking for sense-pleasures and seeking for existence have been entirely relinquished and abandoned. "Bases for views have been uprooted" refers to [seeking] what is reckoned as the seeking for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
And the bases for views have been eradicated by the first path itself. In this way, the commentary on the meaning of this verse should be understood.
The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Patilīna-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ujjayasutta. 39.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "a family sacrifice" (*anukulayañña*) refers to a gift that should be given according to the family lineage (*kulānukkama*). Therefore it was said: "We...
[should] sacrifice according to the succession of families. It is the gift that must be given by descendants in the line of succession to those who have fallen into misfortune.
A family that provides regular offerings intended for virtuous persons does not cease giving even when they fall into poverty.
Here is an illustration: In the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, five hundred tickets for meals were distributed.
There were five hundred ivory tickets. Then, that family was gradually overcome by poverty. One [ticket] remained there...
In her family, the girl was unable to draw more than a single lot.
Later, she went to the kingdom of Sātavāhana, cleared the threshing floor, and gave that lot using the grain she obtained therefrom. A certain elder informed the king.
The king had her brought and installed in the position of chief queen. From then on, she once again set five hundred lots in circulation.

Regarding the *Assamedha* and other sacrifices: it is said that in ancient times during the era of kings, there were four bases of social integration (*saṅgahavatthu*)—namely, the *sassamedha*, the *purisamedha*, the *sammāpāsa*, and the *vācāpeyya*—by means of which kings won over the world.

Among these, the taking of a tenth portion from the harvested crops was called the *sassamedha*; the meaning is that one is wise (*medhāvī*) in the production of crops. [The *purisamedha* refers to] great warriors...
The provision of food and wages for a month is called the *purisamedha*; the meaning is that one is wise (*medhāvī*) in winning over men.
Taking a written bond from poor people and providing them with wealth amounting to two thousand or three thousand [coins] for three years without interest is called the *sammāpāsa*.
For it "correctly displays" (*sammā pāseti*) men, as if fixing them in their hearts; therefore—
“Right confidence” is what is meant. Furthermore, speaking with gentle words such as “Dear one,” “Uncle,” and so forth, is called *vācāpeyya*;

the meaning is that it is pleasant speech, speech that is agreeable. Thus, a kingdom consolidated by these four bases becomes prosperous and flourishing, with abundant food and drink, secure, free from calamity, and where people rejoice with gladness, fondling their children upon their chests.
They dwell with the doors of their houses left open. Because there was an absence of bolts on these house-doors, this is called "boltless" (*niraggaḷa*).

This is the ancient tradition. Later, however, during the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins—while diverting these four bases of sympathy and this prosperity of the kingdom—uprooted [the tradition] and [instituted] the horse-sacrifice, the human-sacrifice, and so forth.
They performed what were called the five sacrifices. For this was said by the Blessed One in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta:
“They fell into confusion, having seen [the world] from the subtlest atom...
[as it is described]; having composed mantras there, they approached Okkāka.”

Now, in order to show the meaning established by those [previous passages] through their re-explanation, he said, "The horse sacrifice" (*assamedha*), and so forth. Therein, "they medhanti" means they kill.
"By two *pariyaññas*" refers to the two surrounding sacrifices (*parivārayañña*) to be performed before and after the great sacrifice (*mahāyañña*).
"Of the terrifying slaughter of nine hundred and five hundred animals" refers to the five hundred animals in addition to the nine hundred.
By the slaughter of hundreds of animals, it is terrifying and brings fear to those who dread evil. For thus they say:
"Six hundred animals are yoked; in the middle sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice, there are three fewer than the prescribed number of animals."

They settle [the dispute] by means of a stick that must be inserted through the hole in the yoke. They cast [the stone], meaning they throw it. "By means of portable [vehicles]" refers to those things to be carried by carts.
It is said that formerly, while one king was performing the Sammāpāsa sacrifice, he sank away as soon as a fissure opened in the earth on the bank of the river Sarassati;
yet the blind and foolish brahmins, following one another blindly, declared, "This is the path leading to heaven for him."
In that regard, they establish the correct placement of the sacrificial offering (*sammāpāsayañña*). Therefore it is said: "starting from the place where [the fire] has been submerged.
A sacrifice (*yāga*) with no *yūpa* pillar lasts for a few days; one with a *yūpa* pillar is to be understood as lasting many days, namely a *satrayāga*.

The term *vāja* is a designation for ghee and honey prepared according to the formulas of the mantras. [This applies to] the seventeen-fold sacrificial fee (*dakkhiṇā*) consisting of gold, bullion, cattle, buffalo, and so forth.
"Niraggala" means that there is no bolt (*aggaḷa*) here in the inner chambers, storehouses, and so forth.
It is said that at such [sacrifices], one's own property is offered up entirely without concealment.

"Great undertakings" (*mahārambha*) refers to those involving the slaughter of many animals. However, since it will be stated in the commentary, "Wherein various [beings] are slain," [the term refers to the place].

“Having great duties and great tasks” is stated as the first alternative meaning. However, the second alternative meaning is commenced with the words “Moreover,” etc., with the underlying intention that the phrase “having great undertakings” refers to goats, sheep, and so forth, by way of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*).

Here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already explained. [Objection: But is it not the case that even a mere trifle of unwholesome kamma, such as the destruction of life...?
Since no fruit is obtained [therein], why was it said, "They do not bear great fruit," without stating that they are fruitless?
To this he says: "In the sense of being without remainder," and so forth. *Anukula* means a family followed;

the meaning is "one who follows the family. Those people who, without interrupting the succession from one generation to the next, maintain the constant meal and other offerings established by their ancestors—
They give; this is what is meant by "they sacrifice according to their lineage. It is for this reason that he said, "Those others who sacrifice according to their lineage," and so forth.
The commentary on the Ujjaya Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Udāyi Sutta.

40. "In the tenth [verse], 'free from the harming of living beings' means free from killing living beings. 'The wise person is reborn in a world that is unafflicted and blissful'—because it is devoid of sensual desire, ill will, and the like, it is 'unafflicted,' meaning free from suffering.

Since there is no infliction of harm upon others, nothing further needs to be said. Because of the abundance of bliss through the attainment of the jhānas, it is 'blissful,' meaning a world of absolute bliss, the Brahma-world."
Through the merit of *jhāna*, and through other merit, the wise and discerning person attains a world of happiness characterized by other forms of excellence and existence. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Udāyisutta is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Wheel-turning Monarch is finished.
5. The Chapter on Rohitassa: 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Development of Concentration.
41. Regarding the first [meditation] of the fifth [tetrad], "for dwelling in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya*):

the meaning is for the sake of dwelling in happiness within this very selfhood (*attabhāva*), that is, for the sake of dwelling in non-material happiness through the state of being free from defilements (*nikkilesatā*).

By this, the four meditative attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-jhāna*) and the form and formless meditations attained subsequent to the realization of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) by one whose taints are exhausted are described.
“For the sake of obtaining the knowledge and vision of the divine eye” means for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the divine eye.
For here, the term “knowledge and vision” (*ñāṇadassana*) refers to the divine eye-knowledge in the sense of seeing celestial and other forms.
“He attends to the perception of light” means [he attends] to the sun, lamps, moon, gems, fireflies, lightning, and so forth, by day or by night.
Light is perceived both by day and by night; he attends to the light and fixes it in his mind precisely as it was perceived.

He attends to it in such a way that, as if with a well-developed kasiṇa of light, that light stands before him at will and for as long as desired even at night, by means of which he establishes the perception of day there during the night. By day...
He becomes free from sloth and torpor as if it were day. Therefore he said: "As by day, so by night.
Just as the perception of light was attended to by day, in that very same way he attends to it by night;
just as the light was seen by day, in that very same way he attends to it by night. Regarding the second phrase: "As by night, so..."
In this sentence, "by day," the phrase "this is the method" refers by extension to the following meaning:
just as light such as moonlight was seen during the night, in that very same manner of seeing it at night, one brings that light to mind and establishes it in the consciousness during the day.
Thus, "with a mind uncovered" means with a mind that is not shut off, that is, with a mind not shut off by the covering of sloth and torpor.
This has been stated. "Uncovered" means not covered on all sides, not concealed. With the words "Even though," etc., he confirms the very point he himself has stated.
It was made like light by [the passage] beginning with "As by day, so by night.
"Of one possessing the seven bases" refers to the one possessing the seven bases as described in the passage beginning with "He acts with clear comprehension in going forward and in returning."
For the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension. "By way of having the object of the basis discerned" means by way of knowing the basis and the object as they truly are.

For just as when someone seeking a snake has discovered its lair, the snake itself is as good as found and captured, because it is easy to seize it by the power of spells and antidotes; so too, in that which is the lair of feeling...

When the basis and the object are known, even for a beginner, feeling is indeed grasped as known, both in its specific characteristic and its general characteristic, because such grasping is easy to accomplish.
This is even more so for one who has fully understood the basis and whose taints are exhausted;
for him, feeling is known and manifest at the moment of its arising, at the moment of its presence, and at the moment of its dissolution. "Those..."

"Feeling, having arisen in this way... and so forth. It is not only feeling that arises, persists, and ceases; here, the perception and other factors mentioned, as well as those not mentioned such as volition and the rest, are likewise known to arise, persist, and cease.
This mention of feeling, perception, and thought in the text is merely by way of illustration; by means of it, the arising and so forth of all phenomena without exception [should be understood].
It shows that the state [of feeling] has been understood.
Furthermore, the arising of feeling is understood, its presence is understood, and its passing away is understood.
How is the arising of feeling understood? With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of feeling; with the arising of craving...
One who sees the characteristic of origination—namely, that the arising of feeling is from the arising of contact and the arising of kamma—also sees the origin of the feeling aggregate.
In this way, the arising of feeling is known. How is the manifestation of feeling known?
For one who attends to it as impermanent, its manifestation as exhaustion is known; for one who attends to it as suffering, [its manifestation as terror is known].
When one attends to [feeling] as non-self, its manifestation as emptiness becomes known.
Thus, the manifestation of feeling becomes known. In this way, one knows it through its destruction, its fearfulness, and its emptiness.
How does the subsiding of feeling become known? With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of feeling... [and so on] ...thus the subsiding of feeling becomes known.
It is known. By this same method, the meaning here should be understood.

Regarding the phrase *iti rūpaṃ* (thus [it is] form): here, the word *iti* has the purpose of indicating the specific nature (*sarūpanidassana*) of form without remainder. By the phrase *tassa idaṃ rūpaṃ* (this is its form), it expresses the indication of the specific nature in a general sense;
by the phrase *ettakaṃ rūpaṃ* (only this much is form), it expresses it without remainder, and not beyond this.
"Beyond form there is nothing more" means that there is no other thing apart from that [form]. Thus, regarding feeling and the rest as well, the meaning should be understood as follows:
"This is feeling; this is the extent of feeling; beyond this there is no further feeling. This is perception... [and so on] ...these are volitional formations...
[and so on] ...this is consciousness; this is the extent of consciousness; beyond this there is no further consciousness. Therefore, he said: "The same method applies to feeling and the rest."
"Having known the higher and lower through knowledge. "The higher and lower" means both the higher (*parāni*) and the lower (*oparāni*).

"The superior and inferior" refers to the bodies of others and one's own body, and so forth, which are superior and inferior. "Agitation" is the flickering of craving and views. "Untroubled" means free from the troubles of passion and the like.
"He has crossed over"—such an Arahant has crossed over birth and old age.
The commentary on the *Samādhibhāvanāsutta* is finished.
2–4. Commentary on the *Pañhabyākaraṇasutta*, etc., 42–44.
Regarding the second [discourse], "of these questions": this refers to the four types of questions, beginning with those to be answered categorically (*ekamsabyākaraṇa*). In each respective [case]...
“He knows the explanation according to the occasion”: when asked, “Is the eye impermanent? it must be answered categorically, “It is impermanent.

But when asked, “Is that which is called the eye impermanent? one must answer by analyzing: “It is not only the eye; the ear, too, is impermanent. And: “As the eye is, so is the ear; as the ear is, so is the eye.”
When asked, one should counter-question: "In what sense do you ask? If he says, "I ask in the sense of seeing," one should answer, "No.
If he says, "I ask in the sense of impermanence," one should answer, "Yes. However, when asked such questions as "Is that which is the soul the same as the body?
and so forth, one should set them aside, saying, "This has not been declared by the Blessed One. This is the method for such questions.
“It cannot be declared” means that one knows it in this way. “By the attainment of the goal” (atthasamāgamena) means by the acquisition of the goal, that which is to be obtained.
*Samiti*, *saṅgati*, and *samodhāna* mean *samaya*; thus it is an acquisition. *Abhisamaya* is simply *samaya*, or *samaya* is *abhisamaya* by virtue of being directed toward [the goal];
in this way the meaning of the words here should be understood. The rest is easy to understand. The third and fourth [sections] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the Pañhabyākaraṇasutta and others is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Rohitassasutta and others. 45–46.
In the fifth [sutta], "in one place" (ekokāse) means in one location designated as the boundary of the world-system (cakkavāḷa). "Of the earth" (bhummam) refers to "where."
This is a statement concerning the earth-plane. Although it was stated in general terms as “that is the end of the world,” it refers specifically to a particular realm because of that statement.
Having said, “He is not born, he does not die,” why was it further said, “he does not pass away, he does not reappear”?
He says: “This [phrase] ‘from one state to another’... is included. “By way of going on foot” means by walking with the feet. The Teacher [refers to] the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*).
He speaks with reference to the limit, desiring to reveal everything that follows. For the limit of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*) is Nibbāna.
One who possesses a bow that is firm and strong is a *daḷhadhanvā*; he is likewise called a *daḷhadhammā*. Thus he says, "one of strong bow.
That which is called the supreme measure is the thousand-fold-strength bow. He is a "bowman" (*dhanuggaha*) because he has mastered the craft of wielding the bow.
It is not by the mere fact of being a bowman; thus he said, "A 'bowman' (dhanuggaha) is a teacher of the bow.
Having stated "bowman," when it is further said "trained," it is understood that he is trained in the science of archery.
And since training reaches its highest excellence for one who trains for such a length of time, he said, "trained in the craft of archery for twelve years. Regarding the measure of an ox:
Twenty *yaṭṭhi*s make one *usabha*; in that space measuring a *usabha*. *Vālagga* means the tip of a hair.
*Katahattha* means one whose hand is practiced. *Katasa-rakkhepa* means one who has performed the casting of arrows toward others, both at stationary targets and moving targets.
Therefore he said, "one who has demonstrated his craft"; some say it means "one who has completed his training. *Asanti etena* means...
The seat is the trunk. "Tālacchādin" means tāla-shade; that, moreover, is a cubit (ratana) in measure, or four finger-breadths (vidatthi-caturaṅgula).
"From the eastern ocean" refers to the eastern ocean within a single world-system (cakkavāḷa). By the term "ocean," he refers to the eastern rim of the world-system.
The same method applies here for the "western ocean. "Without proliferation" (nippapañca) means not made by the untamed. "In prosperity" (sampatte)—
"Having arrived by traveling with such speed. Regarding "Anotatta," the word "having arrived" (*sampatte*) is to be supplied here to complete the connection;
likewise, it is to be supplied in the phrase "the nāga-vine tooth-stick. "Tadā" means when he was a seeker of the world's end.
"A long-lived period" refers to a time when the lifespan is many thousands of years. "Of the world-system" (*cakkavāḷalokassa*) is used in its general sense.

The singular number [is used] because the meaning is "of the world-systems" (*cakkavāḷalokānam*). It is by means of the attachment established through previous familiarity with birth in this very world-system.

By saying "in the one possessing perception," he shows that it is not merely in the phenomena of form (*rūpadhamma*), but rather in the aggregate of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhasamudāya*). "One who has stilled evil" (*samitapāpa*) means one whose defiled states (*saṃkilesadhamma*) have been utterly cut off. The sixth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Rohitassa-sutta* and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Suvidūrasutta (47).
In the seventh [verse], there is the inclusion of the terms *suvidūra* and *vidūra*, which have identical meanings, in a single location.

This is because the state of being distant or near is established only through relative dependence (*apekkhāsiddhattā*). For the state of distance intended here cannot, by any means, be established in isolation.
It was said, "Having become distant in some way," and so forth, for the purpose of showing that they are not near.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Suvidūra-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the Visākhasutta 48.
In the eighth [verse], regarding "polished" (*porī*): it is called *porī* because it has fulfilled the causes for the qualities of speech through skill in verbal expression;

it exists as something polished, hence it is "polished. For this reason, he said: "of perfected speech," which means speech that is perfected in its syllables and phrases. "Unobstructed" (*apalibuddhāya*)...

"Not obstructed by bile and so forth" means not followed by such humors. "Without stumbling" (*anelagalāya*) means without stumbling (*anelāya*), without faltering (*agalāya*), faultless (*niddosāya*), and with words and phrases that do not slip away (*agaḷita-pada-byañjanāya*).
For when the Elder speaks, neither his words nor his phrases fail him.
Therefore he said: "'Without stumbling' means both faultless and without slipping," and so forth. Therein, "faultless" (*niddosāya*) refers to the meaning.
And it is free from faults both in its meaning and its phrasing. "With words and phrases that have not fallen away" means with words and phrases that are not lacking.

Alternatively, "with speech that does not dribble" (*anelagala*): it is "dribbling" (*ela*) because it flows out as a fault (*dosa*); thus, "not dribbling" (*anelagala*) means speech that is uninterrupted.
It is not like the kind of speech that slow-witted people utter while saliva drips from their mouths; rather, it is speech that is faultless.

The meaning is "possessing clear speech. Or, because speech that reveals the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is never free from the turning away, he says "included within the turning away," meaning it proceeds without abandoning the turning away.
For speech that reveals the turning away proceeds by bringing about the delimitation of the turning away.
The nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*) are "exalted" in the sense of being superior to all phenomena and in the sense of being risen above them.
And he said, “It is called ‘the banner’ (dhaja) in the sense of being uplifted,” and so forth. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Visākha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Vipallāsa Sutta.
49. In the ninth [section], the objects such as impermanence and so forth are called "perversions" (*vipallāsa*) because they do not exist in a perverted manner—as permanent and so on.
"Perversion of perception" (*saññā-vipallāsa*) refers to the perversion of perception. The same method applies to the other three as well.

Thus, these are four by way of the four objects, and twelve by way of perception and the other [mental factors] regarding those objects. Among them, eight are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).

They are abandoned. The perversion of perception and mind that takes the unattractive as attractive becomes attenuated by the path of the once-returner and is abandoned by the path of the non-returner.
It should be understood that the perversion of perception and mind that takes the painful as pleasant is abandoned by the path of arahantship.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Vipallāsa-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Upakkilesa-sutta*. 50.
In the tenth [sutta], "by making it defiled" means by making it stained. Regarding the five kinds of fermented liquor and the four kinds of...

"And *meraya*": here, there are five kinds of *surā*: *pūvasurā* (flour liquor), *piṭṭhasurā* (dough liquor), *odanasurā* (rice liquor), *kiṇṇapakkhittā* (liquor made by adding grain), and *sambhārasaṃyuttā* (liquor prepared from various ingredients).
There are four kinds of *āsava*: *puṣpāsava* (flower spirit), *phalāsava* (fruit spirit), *madhvāsava* (honey spirit), and *guḷāsava* (molasses spirit).
This is what is called the fourfold *meraya*. Among these, *pūvasurā* is that which is made by putting flour into a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and kneading it.

The same applies to the remaining types of liquor (*surā*). "Kiṇṇa," however, refers to the fermenting seed of that liquor. Those liquors which are also called "modakas" (sweetmeats) are those made by adding such ingredients; these are called *kiṇṇapakkhittā*.

Those prepared by combining various ingredients such as *dhātaki* and so forth are called *sambhārasaṃyuttā*. Flower-liquor (*pupphāsava*) is the juice of flowers such as *madhuka*, palm, and coconut, which has been aged for a long time.

Fruit-liquor (*phalāsava*) is the juice of fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*). Honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*) is the juice of grapes (*muddikā*). Sugar-cane liquor (*guḷāsava*) is the juice of sugarcane.
The commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Rohitassa Vagga is finished.
The First Fifty is finished.
2. The Second Fifty (6) 1.
The Chapter on the Outflows of Merit (Puññābhisanda-vagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on the Outflows of Merit (Paṭhama-puññābhisanda-sutta-vaṇṇanā)
51. Regarding the first [section] of the second [chapter], "streams of merit" (*puññābhisandā*) means rivers of merit.
For merits that flow continuously and constantly are called "streams of merit" in the sense of overflowing. "Immeasurable" (*aparimitaṃ*) means immeasurable by the calculation of *āḷhaka* measures;
however, it does have a measurement in terms of *yojana*. For thus, below the great earth and above—

It is possible to determine its measurement in terms of *yojanas* because it is bounded on all sides by the sky, by the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and by the various islands and mountain ranges situated therein.

"By terrifying objects" means by terrifying objects that are both animate and inanimate; for instance, that great body [is filled with] large fish, crocodiles, *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, great *nāgas*, *dānavas*, and so forth.
It is called "full of many terrors" by way of conscious objects such as the Vaḷavāmukha chasm and the like, and unconscious objects that are terrifying.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the first Discourse on the Blessing of Merit is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Overflow of Merit (Dutiyapuññābhisandasutta-vaṇṇanā) 52.
In the second [discourse], "faith" is intended as that of a stream-enterer; thus, the faith that has arisen through the path of a stream-enterer is what is intended.
The commentary on the Second Discourse on the Overflow of Merit is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the First Saṃvāsa Sutta, etc. 53–54.
In the third [sutta], they go to and approach their respective destinations according to their karma; thus, they are *ariyā*, meaning beings.
However, these are "wicked *ariyā*," that is, *kadariyā*. They are "stiffly stingy," meaning they are possessed of stiff avarice.

The meaning is this: there is nothing as loathsome, always base, or similar to stubborn stinginess as that which obstructs giving—the very foundation of all virtues and the root of all success, such as the attainment of wealth. Therefore he said: "Kadariyā means those who are stubbornly stingy.
For some, even when monks stretch out their hands in the place where they dwell, do not...
He pays homage. Having gone elsewhere and entered a monastery, he pays careful homage and offers a sweet greeting:
"Why, venerable sir, did you not come to our dwelling place? It is a well-provided area;
I am capable of serving the noble ones with rice gruel, alms-food, and so forth. The bhikkhu, thinking, "This lay follower is faithful," wins him over with rice gruel, alms-food, and the like.
Then a certain elder went to that village and wandered for alms. Upon seeing him, [the householder] would either go by another way or enter his house.
Even if he came face to face with him, he would merely bow with his hand and depart, saying, "Give alms to the noble one;
I am leaving on some business. After the elder had wandered through the entire village, he returned with an empty bowl.
He goes out. This, first of all, is what is called "soft stinginess," by which even a non-giver appears as if he were a giver.

But here, "hard stinginess" is intended. One who possesses this, when monks have entered for alms and it is said, "The elders are standing there," says things such as, "What, are my feet hurting? and remains like a stone pillar or a stump.
He stands as if stiffened and does not even perform the proper etiquette, let alone give a gift. This is what is intended here.
Therefore it is said: "stiff and miserly" means "endowed with stiff miserliness.
*Macchara*, *macchera*, and *macchariya* are one in meaning.
“Abusers” refers to those who, upon seeing monks standing at the door of a house, intimidate them with such words as, “Have you come here after plowing, sowing, and reaping?
We cannot even get enough for ourselves; how could we have anything for you? Get out quickly!
Regarding the phrase “those who understand the meaning of the beggars’ words”: although the monks standing at the door of the house may be silent...
In terms of their meaning, however, they are indeed called "noble begging" when they say, "Give alms. For this has been said:
"The noble ones stand for the sake of [giving]; this is the begging of the noble ones. In that regard, those who share out the gift, thinking, "We cook, but these others do not;
if one goes to those who cook and does not receive anything there, where will one find it?"—they are the generous ones (*vadaññū*).
They are said to "know the meaning of the words of supplicants" because, having known it, they perform what ought to be done. The fourth [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the first *Saṃvāsa-sutta* and others is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the *Samajīvī-sutta* and others.
55–56. In the fifth [case], "for the sake of favoring" means for the purpose of gathering these two: the mother of the mongoose and the father of the mongoose.
The father of the young mongoose is the "father of the mongoose. The term "mother of the mongoose" follows the same principle.
The rest here is self-evident. In the sixth, there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Samajīvīsutta* and others is concluded.
7–10. Commentary on the *Suppavāsāsutta* and others, 57–60.
In the seventh [verse], "she becomes one who obtains a portion of life" means she becomes one who obtains a segment of her lifespan. "The threefold world" refers to...
The threefold world, which consists of the seven types of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) and the receptacle world (bhājanaloka), has been made known—that is, made manifest.

Regarding the phrase "by those who know the world" (*lokavidūnaṃ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus he says, "praised by the Buddhas. The eighth, ninth, and tenth [chapters] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the Suppavāsā Sutta and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Outpouring of Merit is finished.
(7) 2. The Chapter on Worthy Deeds: 1–4.
Commentary on the Discourses on Worthy Deeds, etc.

61–64. Regarding the first [category] of the second [set]: those things which are not undesirable (*aniṭṭha*) are intended here as "desirable" (*iṭṭha*). Thus he says, “by the negation of the undesirable, they are desirable.
Whether they have been sought after or not, the meaning is that they are objects of desire (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*).

For even that which is sought after is called "desirable," but that is not what is intended here. "In the mind" means in the mental faculty (*manasmiṃ*). Or, "lovely" (*kanta*) means "to be desired" (*kamanīya*).
The meaning is "to be desired. "They increase the mind" means they augment the mind by way of its being desirable.

Since the word *bhoga* (wealth/enjoyment) is used here in the sense of an object (*kamma-sādhana*), he says, "Bhogā means 'that which is to be enjoyed,'" and so forth. "Having caused harm to the Dhamma" means having dispelled wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).
He says, "They are to be looked upon closely (*upanijjhāyitabba*)," thus [explaining] "they are called *upajjhāya* because they are to be looked upon closely in times of pleasure and pain."
The meaning is: because they are to be recollected when pleasure and pain have arisen. Regarding the phrase "by those who are seen and supported":

here, those who are merely seen coming together in various places, but are not very close friends, are "seen" (*sandiṭṭha*); those who are well-supported, affectionate, and firm friends are "supported" (*sambhatta*).

"Vast greed" (*visamalobha*) means powerful greed. "Happy" (*sukhita*) means one in whom happiness has arisen. "Satiated" (*pīṇita*) means nourished and well-fed. And since one who is in such a state possesses strength, it is therefore said: "he makes [them] possessed of strength."
One who delights in beautiful bodily and verbal action is *sūrata*; by lengthening the vowel *u*, it becomes *soracca*.

Its state is *soracca* (gentleness), which consists in the non-transgression of body and speech. In terms of meaning, however, this is the state of being well-disciplined (*susīlabhāva*). Thus he said:

"Established in patience and gentleness" means established in both the patience of endurance (*adhivāsanakkhanti*) and in the state of good character (*susīlatā*). "A single self" means a single mind.

For the taming and so forth of lust and the other defilements in their preliminary stages must be undertaken individually; they are not abandoned all at once through the means of reflective contemplation as they are at the moment of the Path.
Or, "one's own self" (*ekamattānaṃ*) refers to the self alone, solitary by virtue of its seclusion.
For this very reason, he said: "one's own single personal existence," and so forth. "In the higher and higher planes" refers to those comprised within the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure.

"In the successive planes of sense-sphere existence" (*uparūparikāmabhūmīsu*). The fruit of kamma is called "supreme" (*agga*). However, it is said here that this [kamma] "goes upwards" (*uccagāmī*) because "its path is upward" (*uddhamaggassa*).

"Sovaggikā" means either "connected with a good destination" (*suvagge niyuttā*) or "having a good destination as its purpose" (*suvaggappayojanā*). "Of the ten distinctions" (*dasannaṃ visesānaṃ*) refers to the specific fruits consisting of divine lifespan, beauty, fame, happiness, and sovereignty, as well as desirable forms and so forth.
And here, by the mention of "beauty" (*vaṇṇa*), one's own personal beauty (*attabhāvavaṇṇo*) is included.
By the mention of “form,” the external form-object is intended. The second, third, and fourth [sections] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Pattakamma-sutta* and others is concluded.
5. Commentary on the *Rūpa-sutta*.
65. In the fifth [verse], it is called *pamāṇa* because one measures (*paminoti*) distinctions such as its loftiness by means of it;

thus, "one whose measure is form" (*rūpappamāṇo*) means one for whom the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is the measure. For that very reason, he is "one who has faith in form" (*rūpappasanno*). Here, "sound" (*ghosa*) refers to the sound of praise. "Coarse" (*lūkha*) refers to the coarseness of the requisites.
By "qualities" (*dhamma*), the qualities of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth are intended. Now, regarding these four types of persons...
The distinction [between these types of persons] is found in the Pāḷi itself. For it is said:
"And what kind of person is one who has form as his measure and is devoted to form?
Here, a certain person, having seen the height, or having seen the circumference, or having seen the shape, or having seen the fullness, finds his measure therein."
Having grasped it, he generates confidence. This person is called one who takes form as the measure and is confident in form.

And what kind of person is one who takes sound as the measure and is confident in sound? Here, a certain person, having taken the measure from the praise of others, the eulogy of others, the laudation of others, or the extolling of others, generates confidence therein. This person is called...
A person who takes sound as the measure and has faith in sound.
And what is the person who takes coarseness as the measure and has faith in coarseness?

Here, a certain person, having seen the coarseness of a robe, or having seen the coarseness of a bowl, or having seen the coarseness of a lodging, or having seen some kind of various ascetic practice...
Having seen it there and having grasped its measure, he generates confidence. This person is called one who has the coarse as his measure and is confident in the coarse.

And what kind of person is one who has the Dhamma as his measure and is confident in the Dhamma? Here, a certain person, having seen virtue, or having seen concentration, or having seen wisdom, grasps its measure therein and generates confidence. This—
“It is said that a person has the Dhamma as their measure and is devoted to the Dhamma.
In this context, “height” refers to tallness; and that should be understood as being proportionate at each respective time.
“Circumference” refers to fullness by way of being neither too thin nor too thick. “Proportions” refers to the well-formed arrangement of those various limbs and members.
"In places endowed with long, short, round, and so forth" means [perceiving] the state of being such as that.

"Fullness" (pāripūri) means the completeness and lack of deficiency in all the parts of the body. "Taking the measure therein" means taking the state of being a standard of excellence regarding the perfection of form within that physical appearance.
"Generates confidence" (pasādaṃ janeti) means it generates and produces resolute conviction (adhimokkha).
“By praising another” means by speaking of another’s virtues, saying, “Such-and-such a person is like this and like that.
“By extolling another” means by means of praise that produces admiration for another in their absence;
it is said to be extolling through the expression of praise formulated in verses and so forth. “By commending another” means by recounting another’s virtues in their absence.
"By taking away another's praise" means by taking away another's praise through a succession—that is, by introducing the sound of another's eulogy through a series.
"Therein" refers to that sound of praise.

"Coarseness of the robe" refers to the roughness of a robe due to its being thick, old, or made of many patches, and so forth. "Coarseness of the bowl" refers to a bowl [conditioned] by having many knots, dents, and so forth.
"Austere state" (*lūkhabhāva*) refers to various difficult practices (*dukkarakārika*), such as the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"Or, having seen virtue" (*sīlaṃ vā passitvā*) means: having seen with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) the purity of good conduct of body and speech through the fulfillment of virtue;

or, having seen the purity of concentration consisting in the attainment of jhāna and so forth, or the wisdom (*paññā*) known as insight and direct knowledge (*vipassanā-abhiññā*). This is the meaning.
Thus, in this world-system measured by these four standards, those who lack faith in the Buddhas are few, while those who have faith are many.

For among all things measured by form, there is no form more conducive to inspiring faith than the physical form of a Buddha. Among all things measured by sound, there is no sound more conducive to inspiring faith than the sound of the renown of the Buddhas.
Among all things measured by coarseness, there are no garments more costly than those of Kāsi silk.

Apart from the coarse [robes] of the Buddha, the Blessed One— who had abandoned magnificent palaces suited to all the perfections for the three seasons and instead utilized rag-robe garments, stone bowls, the foot of trees, and so forth as his lodgings—
there is nothing else more coarse that could bring such faith. For the Tathāgata,

who is the standard of the Dhamma in the world with its devas and possesses extraordinary qualities such as virtue, there is nothing that brings greater faith than his own virtues of virtue and the rest.
There is no other quality such as virtue (sīla) and so forth. Thus, the Blessed One stands as if holding this fourfold measure of the world’s habitation in his fist.

"They measured" means they took its measure. "He does not know its internal quality" means he does not know the virtue of morality and so forth occurring within its interior. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Rūpasutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Ahirājasutta: 67.
In the seventh [verse], by the restrictive term "only those with venom in their fangs," he excludes those with venom in their gaze and so forth. [This refers to] Kaṭṭhamukha and others.

Indeed, there are four kinds of venomous snakes—those whose venom is in the bite, those whose venom is in the sight, those whose venom is in the touch, and those whose venom is in the breath—and since each of these is of four types, sixteen are mentioned according to the variations in the force of their venom.
Among these, he shows that only those with venom in the bite are included here, and not the others. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Ahirājasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Devadattasutta* 68.
In the eighth [sutta], "when the time had arrived" means when the time for birth had arrived because the fetus had reached full maturity. "A young one" (*potaka*)...

The son of a mare. Regarding the verse beginning with “The fruit indeed destroys the plantain,” he said, “The fruit indeed destroys the plantain,” because the production of fruit leads to the destruction of the plantain, as its flowering and the growth of its leaf-sheaths have already been cut off by the *kukkujaka*.
*Kukkujaka* refers to the flowering stalk of the plantain. Likewise, because the ripening of fruit marks the end of medicinal herbs, [it is said] “the fruit...”
"Bamboo and reed" is what was said. This, however, is the summarized meaning here:

just as its own fruit destroys the plantain, bamboo, and reed, and just as the embryo destroys the mule, so too does honor, which is one's own kamma, destroy the person who is not a true man (*asappurisa*).
The commentary on the Devadatta Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Padhānasutta* (69).

Regarding the ninth [verse]: they are called "strivings" (*padhānāni*) because one strives by means of them. They are the supreme efforts, the best efforts, because they accomplish a distinguished goal.
"For the purpose of restraining the defilements" means so that covetousness and the other [unwholesome states] do not arise. Thus...

"By the establishment of mindfulness" means for the purpose of restraining the defilements. "For the purpose of abandoning" means for the purpose of dispelling sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth.
"Exertion" (*padhāna*) is the energy that operates by way of accomplishing that very abandonment.

"For the purpose of increasing wholesome states" means for the purpose of increasing the wholesome states comprised of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). "Exertion" refers to that very same [energy].
Energy that proceeds by way of accomplishing growth.
The commentary on the *Padhāna Sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Adhammika Sutta*.

70. In the tenth [verse], this is a *bhāvanapuṃsaka* (neuter present participle). Therefore he says, "having become uneven" (*visamā hutvā*). "At an improper time" (*asamayena*) means at an unseasonable time.
This instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. Those for whom the straight path (*añjasa*) is prominent or principal are *pañjasā*;

or alternatively, those who have gone toward or entered upon the straight path are *pañjasā*, meaning those who proceed along the natural path. Those who are not *pañjasā* are *apañjasā*, meaning those who have not entered the path.
Since they are, however, said to have "departed from the path," it is therefore stated: "departed from the path," and so forth.
In the verses, the connection here should be understood as follows: *Gonam ce taramānānam* means "when the cows are crossing a great flood.
*Jimham gacchati pungavo* means "if the bull, the leader of the herd, goes crookedly. All...
"They go crookedly" means that all those cows go only in a curved manner. Why? Because when the leader goes crookedly, it is due to his curved course;
for he is their authority and the one who removes their misfortune. "In just this way" means:
just as this is so, even so, if among humans he who is esteemed as a leader should be one who acts contrary to the Dhamma (*adhammacārī*), then those who depend upon him—
All [the people] become unrighteous as well. For the attainment of material goods brings about the attainment of natural prosperity.
Since this is so, therefore the entire kingdom suffers, if the king is unrighteous.
The commentary on the *Adhammika-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Deeds Done is finished.
(8) 3. The Chapter on the Inevitable: 1–2.
Commentary on the Discourse on Exertion, etc.
71–72. In the first [sutta] of the third chapter: *yoni* means that by which the fruit is, as it were, mixed together;
it is the decisive cause. *Assa* refers to the aforementioned bhikkhu. *Paripuṇṇaṃ* means complete, without deficiency or remainder.

*Āsave khepeti* means "he exhausts the taints," which is the supreme path (*aggamagga*). However, here the fruit of arahantship is intended, hence he says, "for the sake of arahantship. The second [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Padhānasutta* and others is finished.
3–5. Commentary on the *Sappurisassutta* and others, 73–75.
In the third [sutta], "led forward for the sake of questioning" means led face-to-face for the purpose of posing questions. *Alambitaṃ*.
*Katvā* means having made it an object; or this reading itself is *vipalambaṃ katvā*, meaning "without making it an object. *Avajānāti* means he treats with contempt;
the meaning is that he reviles. Regarding the fourth and fifth [suttas], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Sappurisa-sutta* and others is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta 76.
Regarding the sixth [paragraph]: "Upavattana" means that by which they approach and proceed; it is so called because those desiring to enter the city proceed from the park.
For just as one must go from the Kalamba River to the Thūpārāma via the gate of the Royal Mother’s Monastery, so too...
From Pārimatīra on the Hiraññavatī River there was a Sāla grove park;
just as the Thūpārāma is to the south-west of Anurādhapura, so that park is to the south-west of Kusinārā.
Just as the road from the Thūpārāma enters the city through the southern gate, proceeding eastward and then turning northward, even so from the park [proceeds] the row of Sāla trees.
Having gone facing east, they turned back toward the north; therefore, it is called "Upavattana" (the Turn-back).
"In between" means in the middle of two *sāla* trees. For when the bed was being prepared there, one row of *sāla* trees was at the head-end and one at the foot-end.
Even there, one young *sāla* tree was close to the head-end, and one...
Of one quarter-part. Furthermore, they also say that the so-called *yamakasālā* are *sālā* trees standing with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves interlaced with one another.
"Doubt" (*dveḷhaka*) means a twofold apprehension; the meaning is a lack of certainty. "Uncertainty" (*vimati*) means falling into doubt; thus he said, "to decide."
"Incompetence. "I say this to you" means: I say this to you, referring to that bhikkhu who possesses doubt.

"Making manifest the state of being free from doubt" refers to the omniscient knowledge itself, which stands having penetrated that matter exactly as it is, making manifest the state of those bhikkhus' freedom from doubt regarding the Buddha and the others. "In this" means: in this matter.
The commentary on the *Kusināra-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Acinteyya-sutta* (Sutta 77) 77.

In the seventh [sutta], "speculation about the world" (*lokacintā*) refers to inquiry connected with the arrangement of the world. Therefore, he said: "By what means, indeed, do the moon and sun... and so forth.
The phrase "coconuts and so forth" includes, by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of medicinal herbs, grasses, forest trees, and other such things not explicitly mentioned.
"Worldly concerns of this kind" refers to these aforementioned matters as well as others similar to them.
The commentary on the Acinteyya Sutta is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Dakkhiṇa Sutta (Sutta 78).
Regarding the eighth [sutta]: "Of the offering (dakkhiṇā) known as giving" means of the offering known as the object to be given.
"Purification" means great radiance. Furthermore, that should be understood by way of its great fruitfulness; thus he said, "by way of its state of great fruitfulness."
"Is purified" means it is not defiled; the meaning is that it becomes stainless, of great radiance, and of great expansion.
"Pure by nature" means having a pure essence through the removal of the impurities of passion and so forth. "Base by nature" refers to a lowly essence due to evil deeds;
for unwholesome states are exclusively base. A usurer is not virtuous nor of good nature; [this applies] to that Great Bodhisattva himself...
The gift of children reached its culmination in the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), becoming capable of shaking the great earth.

Regarding this quality of the donor, he said: "The Great King Vessantara must be told," and so forth. "He rescues" means that he generally rescues [beings] from the states of ruin (vinipāta) that would otherwise be incurred due to evil karma;
therefore, the intention is that there is nothing else for his mind to be concerned with.

“*Petadakkhiṇan*”: an offering that is to be given in dedication to the departed (*petas*). “At the very time it is presented” means at the very moment it is presented to the recipient by way of dedicating it, saying, “May this gift be for such-and-such a *peta*.
“*Assa*” means of the *peta*. “It reaches him” means it reaches him by way of causing him to obtain the perfection of the fruit [of the merit].
For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) regarding a gift dedicated to a *peta*. At that time, of King Kosala...
With reference to his extreme inclination toward giving by way of relinquishment, and with regard to the excellence and distinction of the qualities of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha,
he said, "The incomparable gift should be told.
The commentary on the Dakkhiṇāsutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the *Vaṇijjasutta* and others (79–80).
In the ninth [sutta], "similar to that" (*taṃsadisa*) means: whatever kind of trade was undertaken, whether it turns out otherwise than intended or something else altogether, it is similar to that.
"It goes to ruin" (*chedaṃ gacchati*) means it reaches destruction. It is superior to the intention.
This refers to the intention of another. For this very reason, it is said: “It yields a fruit greater than one’s own aspiration.
“You should speak to me with requisites such as robes” means you should speak to me for the sake of requisites like robes, or you should desire them for me. Alternatively, the meaning is:
when there is need for requisites such as robes, then you should ask me for them. The rest is easily understood. The tenth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Vaṇijja-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Apaṇṇaka-vagga is finished.
(9) 4. The Macala-vagga.
1–6. Commentary on the *Pāṇātipāta-sutta* and others (81–86).
The first [sections] of the fourth [chapter] have their meanings already explained.

In the fifth, one is called a "dark person" (*tamo-puggala*) because they are possessed by darkness (*tama*); "darkness" (*tama*) is so called because it overcomes them through the state of being little light, as expressed in the passage beginning with "reborn into a low family. For it is thus:
Because of that [quality], a person receives that designation, just as one is called "miserly" because of being joined with miserliness (*macchera-yogato*).
Therefore, *tamo* means one who has become dark through the state of non-illumination, like darkness itself; or the meaning is that he has reached the state of darkness.
That which has darkness—characterized as described above—as its successive course, destination, and end is *tamaparāyaṇo*. By both [terms] containing the word "darkness,"...

The "darkness of the aggregates" (*khandhatama*) is spoken of, not the "darkness of gloom. By "darkness of the aggregates," one should understand simply the occurrence of the aggregates when they are devoid of excellence.

Because he shines by way of being manifest through such qualities as "being reborn in a high family," he is a "light" (*joti*); thus, all [the terms] such as "one who has light as his destination" (*jotiparāyaṇa*) should be understood according to the method already stated.

"The other two" refers to the other two types of persons: the one whose destination is both light and darkness (*jotitama-parāyaṇa*), and the one whose destination is both light and light (*jotijoti-parāyaṇa*).
Those who work with bamboo, cane, and other such materials to make baskets, boxes, and various vessels are "basketwork-makers" (*vilīvakārakā*).

Those who kill deer, fish, and so forth for the sake of hunting are "hunters" (*nesādā*), such as deer-stalkers and fishermen. Those who make chariots by lacing them with leather are "chariot-makers" (*rathakārā*), that is, leather-workers.
"Pūti" is a name for excrement; those who remove it are "scavengers" (*pukkusā*), namely flower-throwers. "Dubbaṇṇo" means...
“Virūpa” means deformed. Because he lacks height, reaching only to the ankles (*okoṭima-koṭi*), he is “low” (*heṭṭhima*); the meaning is that his body is short. Therefore, it is said: “a *lakuṇḍaka*.
He moves or proceeds like a *laku* (a small stick) or a *ghaṭikā* (a small staff), thus he is a *lakuṇḍaka*; he is short. He grinds or blinks, thus he is “one-eyed” (*kāṇa*).
As for that blinking of his, it may be with one eye or even with both; therefore, it says: “one-eyed (*ekacchikāṇa*) or two-eyed (*ubhayacchikāṇa*).”
“Or” (vā). *Kuṇa* means contraction; it is a deficiency of the hand. One who has this is *kuṇī*. A *khañja* is said to be one deficient in the feet.
One whose side (*pakkha*)—meaning a portion of the body designated as the lower part—is damaged is a *pakkhahata*. Therefore, he says “a cripple” (*pīṭhasappī*).
That which is to be carried or led in a lamp or for lighting is *padīpeyya*, namely the equipment such as oil, a bowl, and so forth. “Stated” means stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

“Failure in arrival” (*āgamanavipatti*) refers to failure by way of the place of arrival, based on the sense that “arrival occurs here. “Failure in previously arisen conditions” (*pubbuppannapaccayavipatti*) refers to a reversal by way of the first-arisen conditions;
for his parents, who are outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and so forth, are the first-arisen conditions.

“Failure in conditions during the course of existence” (*pavattapaccayavipatti*) refers to failure in pleasant conditions during the course of existence. Even though one has been born into such a low-born family...
Someone might be endowed with wealth, but this person is poor and ill-favored. "Failure in the means of livelihood" refers to failure by way of the means for sustaining life.
For he lacks the skills of elephant-training and so forth, which serve as the means to maintain a livelihood with ease;
instead, he sustains his life by performing work such as throwing away flowers and pounding stones. Therefore, it is said: "in a life of hardship."

"Failure of personal existence" means failure of the substrata (*upadhivipatti*). "Conjunction with the causes of suffering" means the coming together of conditions for the arising of bodily and mental suffering.
"Failure of the causes of happiness" means the loss of the conditions for happiness. "Failure of enjoyment" means the destruction or non-attainment of the happiness derived from enjoyment.
Both "light" and "the state of having light as one's destination" constitute the bright side (*sukkapaṅkha*). The sixth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Pāṇātipātasutta* and others is finished. 7. Commentary on the *Puttasutta* 87.

In the seventh [verse], the letter *ma* functions as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*), as in the case of “*aññamañña*” and similar forms. “A firm ascetic” (*niccalasamaṇo*) means a steadfast ascetic. “One who is to be sprinkled” (*abhisiñcitabbo*) is called an “ablution” (*abhiseko*); thus, the word *abhiseka* is used in the sense of the action (*kamma-sādhana*). Therefore, he said: “fit to perform the ablution.”

“Like the Elder Bākulatthera”: for that elder was of great renown; his sons, daughters, grandsons, and great-grandsons had robes made from fine cloths, dyed them, placed them in baskets, and sent them [to him]. At the time of the elder’s bath, they would set them out in the bathing shed.
The elder would both put them on as an inner robe and wear them as an upper robe. It is for this reason that it was said.

Regarding the Elder Sīvali on the road to Khadiravana: it is said that when the Teacher set out upon that path, the deities thought, "We shall pay honor to our noble Elder Sīvali. Having built a monastery at every *yojana*, they did not allow him to travel further than one *yojana*.
Rising early in the morning, they took celestial rice-gruel and other offerings, thinking, "Our..."
“Where is the noble Elder Sīvali sitting? they asked as they wandered about. The Elder gave what had been brought for him to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Thus the Teacher, together with his retinue, traversed the thirty-league wilderness while experiencing the fruit of the merit of the Elder Sīvali. It was for this reason that it was said.

"Like the Elder Ānanda in the *Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta*": it is said that a householder from Aṭṭhakanāgara, having gained confidence through the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, built and gave him a monastery worth five hundred [pieces]. It is with reference to this that this was said.

"Like the Elder Pilindavaccha": it is said that, through the power of the Elder’s supernormal abilities (*iddhānubhāva*), people who had gained confidence brought many medicines such as clarified butter (*sappi*).
Furthermore, by his very nature, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was a recipient of the five [requisites].
Whatever medicine he received, he would distribute it among the assembly. Therefore, this was said:
"Like the Elder Pilindavaccha with regard to the requisite of medicine.
"Produced by the combination of all three" means they are born from the combination of the three humors—bile and the rest—when they are in a state of imbalance.
"Transformation of the seasons" means by way of being excessively cold and so forth; thus he said, "arisen from excessively cold or excessively hot weather.
A transformation of the season (*utupariṇāma*) is a season dissimilar to the previous one; "arisen from that" means *utupariṇāmajā*, which is to say, arisen from a discordant season.
For those living in a dry (*jaṅgala*) region who dwell in a marshy (*anūpa*) place, a discordant season arises; and for those living in a marshy place [who dwell in a dry place], the same applies.
Regarding "in a forest region": in this way, even due to factors such as Mount Malaya or the seashore, a discordance of the seasons (*utu-visabhāgatā*) indeed arises.
Those [diseases] born from that are called "born of seasonal change" (*utu-pariṇāmaja*).
Those born from an improper maintenance of the body through a deviation from its natural mode of conduct are "born of irregularity" (*visama-parihāraja*). These...
However, they are to be understood through such factors as overeating and standing for too long; thus he says, "caused by overeating, standing too long, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes carrying heavy loads, pounding lime, walking at improper places or times, and other such activities.

"Caused by external means" (*opakkamikāni*) refers to those produced from another's assault—such as the assault of being beaten with the knees, shanks, clubs, and so on, after having been seized as a thief or an adulterer.
The meaning is: "arisen by making a condition. Therefore he said: "produced by means of such efforts as killing, binding, and so forth.

"Kevalaṃ" means exclusively, without depending on any external condition; the sense is "without that [external cause]. Therefore he said: "born solely through the power of the ripening of previously committed kamma.
The commentary on the *Puttasutta* is finished.
8–10. Commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* and others (88–90).

Regarding the eighth [sutta]: because he possesses unshakable faith (*acala-saddhā*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) cannot be shaken by the four winds—that is, by the doctrines of others—just like a gatepost;
having gained a firm footing in the Teaching, he is called a "steadfast ascetic" (*samaṇamacala*). Thus it is said: “Because he has gained a firm footing in the Teaching,” and so forth.
Because the defilements that cause rigidity have been completely eradicated— due to the total absence of the higher-fettered defilements that cause rigidity of the mind—
he is called "the delicate ascetic" (*samaṇasukhumāla*) because he has attained a state of delicacy.
The ninth and tenth [stages] are indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Macala-vagga* is finished.
(10) 5. The *Asura-vagga*.
1–2. Commentary on the *Asura-sutta* and others. 91–92.
The first and second [sections] of the fifth [chapter] are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the *Asura-sutta* and others is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Second Samādhi Sutta 93.
Regarding the third [sutta], because the designation *appaṭivānī* emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*), it is said to mean "the state of not turning back" (*anivattanatā*).
Although one might expect the form *appaṭivānitā*, it is stated as *appaṭivānī*. For while the stream of energy (*vīriya*) is proceeding, there is no returning midway.
