But does he know or not know other sounds—namely, nouns, verbs, prefixes, and suffixes? To the same extent that, having known sound, he knows "this is conventional terminology" and "this is non-conventional terminology," to that same extent he will also know those [other types of words].
However, having rejected that [knowledge of grammar] on the grounds that "this is not the function of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*),"...
This story is told:
it is said that the Elder Tissa-datta took a golden needle at the Seat of Enlightenment and announced, "In which of the eighteen languages shall I speak?
However, he made this announcement based on his own mastery of learning, not on the basis of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
By one who is established [in mindfulness]. For he, through his great wisdom, having caused various languages to be spoken and having mastered them, invited [the monks] in this way:
"Beings indeed learn language. Having said this, the following is explained here:
For when children are young, their parents place them on a couch or a chair and, while performing various tasks, speak various words. The children—
They establish each respective language, thinking, "By this [person], this was said. As time passes, they come to know every language.
If the mother is a Tamil and the father is an Andhaka, the son born to them will speak the Tamil language if he first hears his mother’s speech;
if he first hears his father’s speech, he will speak the Andhaka language.
He will speak [in Māgadhī]. Furthermore, even one who does not hear the speech of either [the human or non-human worlds] will speak in the Māgadhī language.

Even one born in a great wilderness where no village exists and where there is no one else to speak, when he utters words according to his own natural disposition, will speak only in the Māgadhī language.
[This applies likewise] in hell, in the animal realm, and in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
In the human world and in the deva worlds, the Māgadhī language alone is predominant everywhere;
the remaining eighteen languages—such as those of the Oṭṭas, Kirātas, Andhakas, Yonakas, and Damilas—undergo change, becoming otherwise over time and eventually perishing.
This one language alone, known as the *yathābhūta-brahmavohāra* (the speech of Brahmā as it truly is) and the *ariyavohāra* (the noble speech), the Māgadhī language, does not undergo change.
For although that [earth] may shift in some places at some times, it does not shift everywhere, at all times, or in every way;

even at the destruction of an eon, it remains just as it is. Indeed, when the Perfectly Enlightened One was committing the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas to the oral tradition (tanti), he committed it specifically in the Māgadhī language.
Why? Because it is easy to transmit in this way. For in the Māgadhī language—

For the word of the Buddha that has been committed to the *tanti*, even its coming within the range of hearing for those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) is a mere elaboration (*papañca*).
By the mere fact of its being compiled, the meaning presents itself through hundreds and thousands of methods.
Having purified what has been committed to the *tanti* in another language, it must be mastered; yet, even after mastering much, for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), [the meaning remains obscured].
There is no non-attainment of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), nor is there any noble disciple who has not attained the analytical knowledges.

The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding eloquence, capable of performing the functions of observing, clarifying, and defining the various distinctions of inspired speech.
For among the three types of knowledge concerning the objects of meaning, phenomena, and so forth, [one knows]: "These knowledges illuminate this meaning."

This is a designation for knowledge that has proceeded in such a manner. Furthermore, it should be understood that these four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) undergo differentiation in two stages and become purified by way of five causes. In which two stages?
In the stage of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) and the stage of the adept (asekha-bhūmi). In this regard, [it was so for] the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and the Elder Mahākassapa...

The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of eighty great elders, including the Elder Mahākaccāyana and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, have reached differentiation within the stage of those beyond training (*asekkha-bhūmi*).
The analytical knowledges of the Elder Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli,
the female lay follower Khujjuttarā, and others like them, [have reached differentiation] within the stage of those in training (*sekkha-bhūmi*).

"Attaining differentiation" means that they attain differentiation within these two planes. "Differentiation" refers to the attainment of differentiation regarding the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) acquired through the paths.
By what five causes do the analytical knowledges become clear? By realization, by study, by hearing, [by reflection, and by cultivation].
Through thorough inquiry and prior application. In this context, "attainment" refers to Arahantship; for one who has reached that state, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear.
"Hearing" refers to hearing the Dhamma; for one who listens attentively, the analytical knowledges become clear.
"Thorough inquiry" refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); for one who explains the meaning of the memorized Canon, the analytical knowledges [become clear].
They become clear. "Former practice" (pubbayoga) means being engaged in former practice, that is, having mastered the meditation subject by way of taking it up and bringing it back.
For one engaged in former practice, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) become clear.
Among these, however, study, hearing, and interrogation—these three are the powerful causes for the differentiation [of the knowledges].
Prior application is a powerful condition for attainment. Does it exist or not as a condition for analysis?
It does exist, but it is not a powerful condition for analysis in the same way it is for attainment.

For whether there was prior study, hearing, and interrogation or not, the attainment of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) occurs through prior application—both previously and now—even without the contemplation of formations (*saṅkhārasammasana*).
There is no [separate] name for them. However, these two, when combined together, support the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and thus become clear.
The commentary on the Vibhatti-sutta is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika-sutta and others.

173–4. Regarding the phrase "in the third [section], of the bases of contact" (*phassāyatanānaṃ*): here, the word *āyatana* has the sense of a "source" (*ākara*). Thus he says, "of the sources of contact," and so forth.
In such expressions as "a gold mine" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or "a silver mine" (*rajatāyatana*), the word *āyatana* is used in the sense of a source;

however, the meaning of *āyatana* is also obtained in the senses of "birthplace," "convergence," and so on. The particle *mā* is a prohibitive indeclinable. This [particle] applies to the six bases of contact.
"Thinking that there is no other statement whatsoever regarding the remainderless fading away and cessation," he said, "Do not speak"—this is the meaning.
"The five bases of contact have ceased" is said with reference to the absence of the eye and so forth therein. "Of the sixth" refers to the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
In the fourth [case], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika Sutta and others is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta and others. 175–6.

In the fifth [sutta], "by means of clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the threefold knowledge consisting of the divine eye, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).

Or by means of the eightfold clear knowledge (*vijjā*). For even this eightfold clear knowledge is stated as being comprised within the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) together with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and the supernormal power of the mind-made body (*manomaya-iddhi*). "Endowed with conduct consisting of fifteen factors" refers to:
restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, faith (*saddhā*), moral shame (*hirī*), and moral dread (*ottappa*).
He is endowed with the qualities of conduct consisting of fifteen divisions: erudition, energy, mindfulness, wisdom, and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
Indeed, these very fifteen factors are called "conduct" (*caraṇa*) because by means of them the noble disciple conducts himself and proceeds toward the deathless state.
There is nothing further to be said regarding the sixth [chapter].
The commentary on the Upavāṇa-sutta and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Rāhula-sutta: 177.
In the seventh [verse], "only the earth element" refers to this [element] being twofold by way of its rigidity, hardness, and roughness.
"The earth element has a single characteristic" thus he shows by joining the internal with the external. Why?
Because the insentient nature of the external earth element is evident, whereas that of the internal is not;
therefore, for one who grasps it as being exactly like the external—namely, as purely insentient—it is easy to comprehend. How is this so? As in the case of a tamed ox.
When an untamed horse is yoked together with [a trained one], it neighs and kicks for only a few days, and then before long it comes under control; likewise,
for one who perceives the internal as being exactly like the external, the internal appears to be insentient after only a few days,
and then before long its insentience becomes manifest through the vision of it as being merely elements (dhātu).

"This is not mine... [etc. ...it should be seen as it really is" means that both of these should be seen with right wisdom (*sammappaññā*) as they truly are: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "As it really is" means according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāva*). For that [nature] has impermanence and so forth as its characteristic;
therefore, the meaning is that it should be seen as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Because "this is not... [etc.]... [the rest of the passage follows].
Seeing, "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self," one does not see a self anywhere,

nor does one see that [self] as something to be brought into the state of being a possession for another, nor does one see another's self as something to be brought into the state of being a possession for oneself;
therefore it is said, "The so-called emptiness of the fourfold limit has been explained."
The commentary on the Rāhulasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Jambālīsutta 178.
In the eighth [verse], "peaceful" (santa) means lovely and captivating due to both the peace of its factors and the peace of its object.
"Deliverance of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the deliverance of mind pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. For this very reason, it is said: "any one of the eight attainments.
"Smeared with a coating" means smeared with lac. "Without having cleared away the obstacles" means without having cleared away the obstacles such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
For one who has not thoroughly suppressed sensual desire through the contemplation of the dangers of sense-desire and so forth—
Without having thoroughly calmed grossness by means of bodily tranquility,

without having properly dispelled sloth and torpor by means of attention to the element of initiative and so forth, without having eradicated restlessness and remorse by means of attention to the sign of serenity and so forth,
and without having properly cleared away other factors obstructive to concentration, one enters into jhāna.
Just like a bee that has entered an unclean dwelling, or like a king who has entered an impure park, he quickly departs.

However, he who enters into jhāna after having thoroughly purified the states that obstruct concentration is like a bee that has entered a well-purified dwelling, or like a king who has entered a perfectly clean park.
And for the entire duration of the day, he remains within meditative absorption itself.
"Inlets" (āyamukhāni) means the paths of approach from rivers, ponds, caves, footprints, and so forth. And since these are indeed caves, he says, "four caves of entry.
"Outlets" (apāyamukhāni) means the paths of departure. For they are called outlets because by means of them one goes away (apenti), departs (apagacchanti).

The states of misery (*apāya*) themselves are the "mouths" [of water], thus they are called "the mouths of misery. And since these are the openings through which water flows out, he says "the openings for draining away";
the meaning is that they are the openings for the flow-out of water designated as "states of misery. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Jambālī Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Nibbāna Sutta 179.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "in the manner stated in the Abhidhamma":
"What is wisdom partaking of decline? For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by sensual desire..."
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by decline occur, wisdom partaking of decline stands firm; when mindfulness that conforms to that [state] persists, wisdom partakes of stability.
When perceptions and acts of attention unaccompanied by applied thought occur, wisdom partakes of distinction.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion occur, wisdom partakes of penetration.”
The meaning should be understood in this way according to the method explained in the Vibhaṅga starting with the word "Ādi.
Therein, "one who has obtained the first jhāna" refers to one who has acquired the first jhāna that is not yet fully mastered.

"Perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by sensual desire occur" means that, having emerged from that state, perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by sensual desire arise by way of the object.
Having been abandoned, perceptions and mental applications arise, strike at him, and urge him on.

Through the influence of those perceptions and mental applications that leap toward sensual desires, his wisdom of the first jhāna declines and diminishes; therefore, it is called "wisdom partaking of decline.
"Conforming to that" means having a nature corresponding to that. "Mindfulness settles" refers here to wrong mindfulness.

It was said, not right mindfulness. For when, having seen the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime because its intrinsic nature conforms to the first jhāna, a person experiences gratification and delight, and attachment arises through that attachment, then their wisdom regarding the first jhāna neither decreases nor increases;
it remains at a fixed level. Therefore it is said: "partaking of stability."

"Wisdom. "Accompanied by non-thinking" means that for one who attends to the second jhāna—which is without thinking—as peaceful and sublime, there arise perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by non-thinking by way of its object.
"Occur" means that, because it is familiar, they strike and urge [the mind] away from the first jhāna for the sake of attaining the second jhāna; they leap up into the second jhāna above that.
By way of perception and attention, that wisdom of the first jhāna is called "partaking of distinction" because it serves as the proximate cause for the arising of the second jhāna,
which is distinguished from it.
"Accompanied by disenchantment" means that one who has attained that very first jhāna, having emerged from it, [is accompanied] by what is termed disenchantment...
They are accompanied by insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). For insight-knowledge becomes weary and dissatisfied while the various factors of meditative absorption (*jhānaṅga*) are occurring;
therefore, it is called "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*). "Practicing" means they prick and urge one toward the realization of Nibbāna.
"Connected with dispassion" means connected with Nibbāna, which is designated as "dispassion. For indeed, by this insight-knowledge...
Because it is set forth as "to realize Nibbāna, which is dispassion, by means of the Path," it is called "conjoined with dispassion" (*virāgūpasaṃhita*).

The perception and attention associated with that [wisdom] are likewise said to be conjoined with dispassion. By virtue of those perceptions and attentions, that wisdom of the first jhāna is called "partaking of penetration" (*nibbedhabhāginī*) because it serves as the proximate cause for the penetration of the Noble Path.
The commentary on the Nibbāna Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Mahāpadesa Sutta.
180. Regarding "the ten great bases": in a great space, there are great foundations for the establishment of the Dhamma. In these—

The Dhamma established [by the Great Authorities] is not rejected, because there is no doubt. But what are those [authorities]? They are the Suttas distinguished by their source, such as the *Uttari-manussa-dhamma* and others.
In the second interpretation, they are called *apadesā* (authoritative references) because they are cited; those which have great authoritative references are the *Mahāpadesā*.
They are the grounds for determining that a certain teaching brought forward by someone—such as "I heard this directly from the Blessed One, friends"—is indeed the Dhamma.
But what is that? It is precisely his crossing over by means of the sutta as it was brought to him. If this is so, how can there be four?
Because the Dhamma has two fulfillments: the Teacher and the disciple. Among these, disciples are threefold—by way of the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual.
Thus, there are four based on the distinction between those who can be cited as: "This Dhamma was received by me from this [source]."
Therefore he said, “I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, friends,” and so forth. And thus it is stated in the *Netti*: “There are four great authorities:

the authority of the Buddha, the authority of the Saṅgha, the authority of the Gaṇa, and the authority of the individual. These are the four great authorities. That which has the Buddha as its authority is the “authority of the Buddha.
This same method applies to the others as well. Therefore he said, “The Buddha and so forth... are the great authorities.”
“Neither should it be rejoiced in” means it should not be accepted; for the acceptance of a bond is called “hearing,” thus he said, “it should not be heard.
“Phrases and syllables” (padabyañjanāni) means both phrases (*pada*) and syllables (*byañjana*); the meaning is that they are phrases of meaning and phrases of expression.

They are called “phrases” (*pada*) because meaning is reached (*pajjati*) through them; syllables and so forth are “phrases of expression” (*byañjanapada*) because they are to be expressed (*pajjitabba*).

“Phrases” (*padāni*) refers to phrases of meaning, such as the introductory sections (*saṅkāsanādīni*). Some say: “In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, they are called ‘phrases consisting of phonemes’ (*byañjanapadāni*), because they are indeed phonemic phrases.

They are called “phonemes” (*byañjanāni*) because they manifest the meaning; thus they are “phrases of phonemes” (*byañjanapadāni*). They are called “phonemes” because the meaning is manifested by them;
thus, through the inclusion of both, they are “phrases of meaning” (*atthapadāni*). “In this place” (*imasmiṃ ṭhāne*) refers to this [place] where the Sutta was brought forth.
"In the passage": "The Pāḷi is stated" means that the entire Dhamma of the Pāḷi is stated. "The meaning is stated" means that the meaning of the Pāḷi is stated and demonstrated.
"The connection is explained" means that the linking of the subsequent teaching with the preceding teaching has been explained;
the relationship has been explained. "The sequence is explained" means that both the non-contradiction of what follows by what precedes and the point of distinction have been explained.
It has been explained. Thus, having correctly observed the textual teachings (pāḷidhamma) and so forth, grasping them thoroughly is "thorough learning";
therefore he said, "having grasped well. "They should be brought down into the Suttas" means they should be brought down by plunging into the Suttas with wisdom.
Since that plunging and bringing down consists of entering and penetrating therein, it is said, "they should be brought down."
"Showing by way of correlation is 'demonstration' (sandassana)"; thus he said, "they are to be correlated with the Vinaya.

In the investigation of the question, "What then is that Sutta, or what is the Vinaya?", the passage beginning with "And here... was stated to show that matter by way of the difference in the opinions of the teachers.
By "Vinaya," he refers to the text of the Vibhaṅga; for that [Vibhaṅga] is... [of] that which is designated as the Mātikā.
It deserves to be called "Sutta" because it indicates the meaning of the discourses (*sutta*). It is "Vinaya" because of its diverse methods and its distinguished method;

this refers to the *Khandhaka* recitation. Thus, when the *Sutta* and *Vinaya* are being encompassed in this way, even the *Vinayapiṭaka* is not fully included, because the *Parivāra* text is not comprised within it.
Alternatively, the *Suttanta* and *Abhidhamma Piṭakas* constitute the "Sutta."

Because meanings such as "indicating the purpose" (atthasūcanādi) are possible [in both cases]. "Even so" means even when the division into Sutta and Vinaya is stated thus: "The Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the Sutta, and the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya.
"They do not yet encompass it" means they do not yet grasp it in its entirety.
If one asks why, he says: "For that which is not named 'Sutta'... and so forth. Because this name "Sutta" [is not applied to it].

There exists Buddhist discourse such as the Jātaka and other works that were not included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti). Therefore, according to the method already stated, these do not encompass the three Piṭakas.

It is with the intention that the Suttanipāta, Udāna, and Itivuttaka—unlike the Dīghanikāya and other collections—are not included in the recitation because they lack the designation "Sutta" that those texts possess, that these [texts] are here taken together with the Jātaka and others. As for the Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka...
In this matter, the reason for its non-inclusion must be sought; or rather, what is the use of such a search?
Thus, every method of commentary has been rejected by way of demonstrating the Theravāda.
By asking "Does it exist?", he shows that there is indeed no word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) that does not have a name in the Suttas. Having rejected all of that—

Having refuted the interpretation stated in the commentary beginning with "‘Sutta’ means ‘Vinaya’" by saying, "This meaning is not intended here," [the author] says, "But the Vinaya is the cause," explaining that it is called *vinaya* because one is led away (*vineti*) from the defilements (*kilesa*) by means of it;
thus it is the method for the removal of defilements, and that itself is the cause. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
"For one possessed of lust" means for the state of being possessed of lust, that is, for the nourishment of sensual lust and the lust for existence.

"For the sake of conjunction" means for the sake of the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*). "For the sake of grasping" means for the sake of being associated with the four kinds of grasping (*upādāna*). "For the sake of great desire" means for the state of having great desire (*mahiccha-bhāva*).
"For the sake of non-contentment" means for the state of being discontented (*asantuṭṭha-bhāva*). "For the sake of indolence" means for the state of being lazy (*kusīta-bhāva*).

"For the sake of socializing" means for dwelling in the company of defilements (*kilesa-saṅgaṇika-vihāra*). "For the sake of accumulation" means for the threefold accumulation of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate toward the entire cycle of existence.

"For the sake of dissociation" means for the purpose of becoming dissociated from sensual lust and the like. "For the sake of non-clinging" means for the purpose of not grasping at any kind of kamma-existence.

"For the sake of fewness of wishes" means for the complete disappearance of wishing by way of fewness of wishes regarding requisites and so forth. "For the sake of contentment" means for the state of being contented in twelve ways.
"For the sake of the arousal of energy" means for the sake of both physical and mental energy.

For the purpose of undertaking [the practice]. "For seclusion" (*vivekāya*) means for the state of being secluded, through the accomplishment of seclusion from sense-desires (*kāmaviveka*), seclusion as a factor of that [path] (*tadaṅgaviveka*), and so forth.
"For diminution" (*apacayāya*) means for the diminution of the entire round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); the meaning is "for Nibbāna.
Thus, for one who practices wisely by way of learning, retaining, inquiring about, and attending to the Dhamma of the scriptures, there is the avoidance of states such as lust and so forth.
By acting as a cause, it leads to the state of dispassion and so forth;
this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, because it is held fast by virtue of preventing one from falling into the states of misery and the like, and because it subdues the defilements.
The meaning is that you should know this to be the Teacher’s instruction, because its practice proceeds in accordance with the advice of the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

He says, "In the Sutta," meaning "in the word of the Buddha contained within the Three Pitakas (Tipiṭaka)," because there is no word of the Buddha within the Three Pitakas that is devoid of the Truths (sacca).

He says, "In the Vinaya," meaning "in this cause for the subduing of lust and so forth," because it is by means of those words of the Sutta that the cause for the subduing of lust and so forth is revealed. And here, the entry into the Sutta occurs precisely by way of its inclusion within the word of the Buddha contained within the Three Pitakas.
"It must be understood as it is, not otherwise," he said, adding: "without appearing anywhere out of sequence in the suttas.

"Having peeled off the bark" means that just as one might forcibly peel away the bark, splinters, or outer skin of a large, healthy tree standing there, so too, while the Dhamma of the Dispensation remains healthy, [something] belonging to it [is removed] by means of mere phrasing.
Having manifested and illustrated faults such as internal contradictions that are like a discarded skin, he says:
"Such things are definitely included among the 'Gūḷhavessantara' [hidden or deceptive] and so forth; thus the meaning is 'they are not recognized.
Regarding "the subduing of lust and so on," because they do not appear in that form due to the sense of subduing lust and so on, they are to be discarded.
They are to be rejected and not accepted. "In all cases" means in all instances.
The commentary on the Mahāpadesa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Sañcetaniya Vagga is finished.
(19) 4. The Chapter on Brahmins (Brāhmaṇavagga).
1–3. Commentary on the *Yodhājīvasutta* and following suttas, numbers 181–183.
The first and subsequent suttas of the fourth chapter have their meanings already explained.
4. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta 184.
In the fourth [verse], "he grieves" (*socati*) means he grieves with the powerful sorrow arisen in the mind; the meaning is that he broods within through mental anguish.
"He is exhausted" (*kilamati*) means he is exhausted by the physical pain arisen in the body due to the influence of that very same sorrow. "He laments" (*paridevati*)...
Lamenting various things by way of uttering cries of distress, one wails with speech.
*Urattāḷin* means *urattāḷaṃ*; the meaning is "having struck the chest. Therefore he said, "having struck the chest. Regarding *kaṅkhā-vicikicchā*:
here, it is called *kaṅkhā* (doubt) because of doubting the object, thinking, "Is this indeed the fifth hindrance? What is this? [and] "This alone is better."

It is called "vicikicchā" because it is incapable of reaching a decision; that is, it "struggles (kicchati) while investigating the intrinsic nature of phenomena," or alternatively, it is so called because "investigation (cikicchā) has departed.
The commentary on the *Abhaya-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Brāhmaṇasacca-sutta* 185. Regarding the fifth [verse]:

"In this" (*ettha*) means in this section concerning the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*). "Anywhere" (*kvaci*) means in some place, at some time, or regarding some phenomenon (*dhamma*).
Alternatively, "anywhere" (*kvaci*) means internally or externally. "One's own self" (*attano attānaṃ*) refers to one's own person (*sakattānaṃ*), as in: "This... [and so forth].

By saying, "Indeed, sir, he is Brahmā, Mahābrahmā... the lord, the father of those who have been and those who will be," and so forth, [the Blessed One] spoke the words beginning with "of anyone" (kassaci) to show that he does not perceive a self as imagined by others, nor anything belonging to anyone.

In this context, "another" (parassa) refers to one who is grasped as another by birth or another by person. And as for the phrase "nor mine anywhere" (na ca mama kvacani), here the word "mine" (mama) [refers to the sense of ownership].
Regarding the phrase "not engaged with a non-existent basis," he said: "Setting aside the word 'mine' for a moment. "Of another" means of someone other than oneself.
There is indeed another person who stands for my sake; by virtue of him, everything succeeds for me.

Thus, showing that one does not see another as a self nor that [other] as something belonging to one's own self—according to the conceptualization of certain followers of wrong views—he said: "And nowhere," and so forth.

And herein, "I am not anywhere" means he does not perceive the existence of his own self anywhere. "Because of having nothing belonging to anyone" means he does not perceive even his own self as belonging to anyone else.
"And there is no 'mine'"—these two [phrases] should be connected as appropriate, with the word "there is" applied to each.
"And nowhere is there a self belonging to another" refers to the self of another.

He sees the non-existence of a self. He sees that there is no "mine-ness" in the self of another, thinking, "There is no 'mine' in the other's self," and thus he sees the non-self-nature of the other's self.

In this way, the conclusion is reached by grasping the emptiness of self and what belongs to self regarding the aggregates internally and externally—their nature as a mere heap of pure formations, and their emptiness according to the fourfold method.
The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇasacca Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Ummagga Sutta. 186.
In the sixth [verse], "is dragged along" means that the world, being subject to the mind, is dragged here and there. Of those very [factors] here...
"It should be understood as 'grasping' means that grasping belongs only to those who, not having fully understood the bases (*vastu*), fall under the power of the mind.
For those who have fully understood the aggregates (*skandha*) and abandoned the defilements (*kleśa*) do not fall under the power of the mind; rather, they bring the mind under their own control.
'Together with virtue' means together with the virtue of conduct and restraint. 'The preliminary practice'..."
Starting from the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) up to the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), one should practice the right way of conduct known as serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Ummagga Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta 187.
Regarding the phrase "the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha": here, *Vassakāra* is the name of that brahmin.
A *mahāmatta* is one endowed with great authority (*issariyamattā*). The term *issariyamattā* means by way of the measure of his authority.
The meaning here should be understood as "wealth" (*attha*), namely both sovereignty and material possessions;
for in the world, even the implements of enjoyment are called "measure" (*matta*). A great minister of the King of Magadha, or one in the kingdom of Magadha, is a "Magadhan great minister.
One whose residence is a village known as Tudi is "Todeyya. For this very reason he said, "of the resident of the village of Tudi. This refers to his being a resident of the village of Tudi.
And therein he should be regarded as being in the position of a ruler (*adhipatibhāva*).

For he presides over that village as its ruler, just as Soṇadaṇḍa did over [the village of] Taṇḍula, Kūṭadanta over Campā, and [Ambaṭṭha] over Khāṇumata. He was very wealthy, possessing a fortune of four hundred and fifty million.
"In the assembly" (*parisati*) means in the assembly, in a gathering of people; thus he said, "of the assembled assembly. "Well-pleased" (*abhippasanna*)...

In this context, the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of "approaching," which is why it says, "having surpassed, he was confident. The intended meaning is that, having surpassed the state that inspires confidence, he was confident even in a state that does not inspire confidence.
One who sees the purpose or goal of each respective task is an "insight into the goal" (*atthadasa*);

those who are sufficient, capable, and competent in such insight are "sufficiently insightful" (*alamatthadasa*); and those who excel over those who are sufficiently insightful are "surpassing the sufficiently insightful" (*alamatthadase atisayanti*).

They are more capable of seeing the goal. Therefore he said, "capable of seeing the goal," and so forth. One does not know either a true person (*sappurisa*) or a false person (*asappurisa*), because of failing to know the qualities of a true person and the qualities of a false person as they truly are. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Upaka Sutta 188.
In the eighth [verse], one "deserves hell" by way of rebirth, or is "bound to hell" by means of karma conducive to hell;
thus, he is a *nerayika*. Having arisen in the Avīci hell, he remains there for an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), which is designated as his lifespan.
"Fixed for an aeon" (*kappaṭṭho*). "Incurable" (*atekiccho*) means incapable of being cured by avoiding rebirth in hell. "As yet not exhausted" (*apariyādinnāva*) means precisely not yet consumed.

For even if one bhikkhu asks about the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), another about the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*), and so on up to the contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*), and no one looks toward another thinking, "I shall ask when this person has been asked," even though that is the case—
Their turn indeed becomes apparent, but the turn of the Buddhas does not become apparent.
Even before the shadow has passed the length of a span and four finger-breadths, the Blessed One teaches the fourteenfold contemplation of the body,
the ninefold contemplation of feelings, the sixteenfold contemplation of the mind, and the fivefold contemplation of phenomena.

Let alone these four. For if others were to ask questions concerning the four right efforts, others the bases of psychic power, others the five faculties, others the five powers, others the seven factors of enlightenment, and others the eight factors of the path, the Blessed One would explain those as well.
Let alone these eight. If others [were to ask] concerning the thirty-seven...
If people were to ask questions concerning the factors conducive to enlightenment, the Blessed One would explain them at that very moment.
Why? Because while the worldly masses speak one word, the Elder Ānanda speaks eight words;
and while the Elder Ānanda speaks one word, the Blessed One speaks sixteen words. Why? Because of the Blessed One’s tongue...
The teeth are soft; the lip-covering is well-polished; speech is unslurred; and the latency of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is light.
Therefore it is said: “The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is not exhausted; the phrasing and syllables of the Dhamma are not exhausted.

Therein, “teaching of the Dhamma” means the establishment of the lineage (tanti). Regarding “phrasing and syllables of the Dhamma,” here “Dhamma” refers to the Pāḷi. It is so called because it is traversed (pajjati).
That by which meaning is conveyed is a *pada* (word). A sentence (*vākya*) is also included within the word itself. That which manifests meaning is a *byañjana* (phoneme);
it is the syllable (*akkhara*). For when words and sentences are demarcated, that [syllable] manifests and makes clear their respective meanings.
By means of these successive words and phonemes, even though the Tathāgata speaks for an exceedingly long time, there is never an exhaustion of them.
He shows that [it] exists. "One who destroys virtues" means one whose nature is to destroy virtues. "Frivolous" means endowed with verbal frivolity.
The commentary on the Upaka Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Sacchikaraṇīya Sutta.
189. "By the mental body in the ninth" means by the co-nascent mental body. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sacchikaraṇīya Sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Uposatha Sutta*.
190. Regarding the tenth [case], the reduplicated expression “silent, silent” is stated according to the desire for deliberation; thus he says, “whichever way he looks around.
Here, the word *anu* in “having looked around” (*anuviloketvā*) is also a term expressing the desire for deliberation;
therefore, the meaning is “having looked around again and again,” that is, having opened his eyes adorned with the five types of clarity, here and there.
“Having looked” is what is meant. “Alam” means suitable or appropriate, as in such expressions as “alam eva nibbinditum” (enough for disenchantedness).
“Puṭosaṃ sambalaṃ” refers to provisions that are to be eaten after being carried by tying them in a bundle; the vowel *a* is changed to *o*.
Therefore he said “pātheyyaṃ” (provisions for the journey). The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Uposatha Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Vagga is finished.
(20) 5. The Mahāvagga.
1. Commentary on the Sotānugata-sutta 191.
Regarding the first [verse] of the fifth [chapter]: "Of those that have followed the stream" (*sotānugatānaṃ*) means having followed along the stream of confidence (*pasādasota*);
the meaning is "those that have become proficient and have reached the lips. And being such, having applied the ear of confidence, they are well-determined by the ear of knowledge (*ñāṇasota*).
He said, "They become names," and so forth, beginning with "the stream of confidence.
For some, the words previously learned are not well-mastered, clearly articulated, or properly defined.
When told, "Recite such-and-such a Sutta or Jātaka," they say, "I shall know it after having recited it, compared it, and investigated it thoroughly. For others, that...
That [consciousness] becomes proficient, like the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
when told, "Recite such-and-such a Sutta or Jātaka," it extracts that very [text] and recites it. With reference to this, it was said: "determined by the stream of knowledge.
The three genders are the feminine gender and so forth. The four terms are name and so forth. The seven case-endings are the nominative and so forth.
"Vaḷañjeti" means that one retains [the text] by reciting it aloud according to the sequence of the Pāḷi, following the connection between what precedes and what follows.
"Vacasā paricitā" means rehearsed orally according to the ten suttas, the ten chapters, and the ten fifties;

the meaning is that it has been rehearsed orally after observing, "The ten suttas have been traversed," "The ten chapters have been traversed," and so forth, by way of the chapters and the rest. By way of the chapters and so on...
For here, "familiarity through speech" is intended; it does not mean familiarity with a mere portion of a sutta or with the sutta alone by means of speech.
"Examined repeatedly with the mind" means scrutinized part by part and understood.
Or rather, for one who recites the Buddha’s word with speech and reflects upon it with the mind, it becomes manifest in various respects, like a great island.
It appears as something manifest, like a form that has been set on fire and left burning; it is with reference to this that it was said.
"Well-penetrated" means having been thoroughly penetrated according to reality, making it free from roots and free from thickets. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Sotānugata-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Ṭhānasutta 192.

In the second [verse], "by living together" means by dwelling with [him]. "Virtue should be known" means that one who dwells together or approaches [the person] should know whether he is "of good virtue or of bad virtue. And that, moreover, over a long period of time, not briefly.

And that virtue must be understood over a long period of time, not in a short one; for indeed, the manner of being self-restrained and the manner of having the sense faculties guarded cannot be demonstrated in two or three days.
"By attending to it" means that it can be known only by one who attends to it with the reflection, "I shall comprehend his virtue," and not by anyone else.
"By the wise" means that it can be known only by one who possesses wisdom, a person of intelligence.
For even when attending to it, a fool is unable to understand.
"By means of commerce" means by conversing with one another. "Whoever among men lives by commerce..."
“Know this, Vāseṭṭha: he is a merchant, not a brahmin.
Here, indeed, it is *vohāra* (conventional usage). In the passage, “There are four noble conventions and four ignoble conventions,” it refers to volition (*cetanā*).

In the passage, “A designation, a common name, a description, a conventional usage,” it refers to a description (*paññatti*). In the passage, “He would use that conventional usage merely as a conventional usage,” it refers to mere convention.
This refers to the conventional usage of speech. Here too, this very same [usage] is intended.

For the face-to-face account of one person does not agree with the behind-the-back account, nor does the behind-the-back account agree with the face-to-face account; likewise, the earlier account does not agree with the later account, nor does the later account agree with the earlier account.
It is possible to know by means of such speech alone: "This person is impure," as opposed to one who is pure in virtue.
However, the former accords with the latter, and the latter accords with the former.

What was spoken in the presence accords with what was spoken in the absence, and what was spoken in the absence accords with what was spoken in the presence. Therefore, demonstrating that one’s purity can be known through such speech, he spoke thus.
“Strength” (*thāma*) refers to the strength of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). For one who lacks the strength of knowledge, when calamities arise, he must grasp...
Not seeing what ought to be done—that is, what must be grasped—he wanders about like one who has entered a house without a door. Therefore he said:
"In times of adversity, monks, strength is to be known.
"By conversation" means by discussion; for the talk of one lacking wisdom floats away like a ball of snot in water, whereas that of the wise man [remains].
For one who speaks thus, inspired eloquence becomes infinite. Indeed, by the very movement of the water, it is known whether a fish is small or large.

"Destruction of kinsmen" (ñātivināsa) means the destruction of relatives through fear of thieves, disease, and so forth. "Calamity of wealth" (bhogabyasana) means the ruin of possessions; the meaning is the loss of wealth due to kings, thieves, and the like.
Therefore he said: "The same method applies to the second term as well. "The path of questions" (pañhummagga) means the seeking of questions.

The meaning is: "the investigation of the matter desired to be known. "Unsatisfying" (*atappaka*) means it does not bring contentment, like delicious food. "Gentle" (*saṇha*) means having a subtle nature.
The commentary on the *Ṭhāna-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta 193.

In the third [verse], "surpassing in action" (*karaṇuttariya*) means an action that is superior to other actions; since he has this as his characteristic, he is "one whose characteristic is surpassing in action. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sāmugiyasutta 194.

In the fourth [section], the "factors of striving for purity" (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) are those factors which constitute the primary exertion for the purity of a person. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Sāmugiyasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vappa Sutta 195.
In the fifth [verse], "with a closed heart" (*pihitatta*) means having stood after closing the gateway through which unwholesome states enter.
For one who stands having restrained the evil states that would otherwise proceed through an unclosed gateway is said to be "restrained by body" (*kāyasaṃvuta*).
"By fading away through final destruction" means by fading away characterized as absolute destruction; the meaning is "by non-arising cessation.
Is it the case that knowledge had previously arisen? Both of these should not be said.

Because the moments of abandoning, clear realization, and development are inseparable in time, ignorance is ceased by the arising of knowledge, just as darkness is [dispelled] by the lighting of a lamp.
Or rather, the state of cause and fruit may be spoken of by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

For just as the disappearance of darkness has the lighting of a lamp as its cause, so too the cessation of ignorance has the arising of true knowledge (*vijjuppāda*) as its cause. Furthermore, causal and resultant phenomena, though simultaneous, are conventionally expressed as if they were sequential, just as in the statement:
"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," which refers to the activity of arising immediately following the acquisition of the condition.
"Affliction" (*vighāta*) is so called because it afflicts both mind and body; it is suffering (*dukkha*).
"Burning" (*pariḷāha*) is so called because of its consuming nature. "Constant abodes" (*niccavihārā*) means abodes that occur at all times.

For, except during the moments of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) dwell at all times in this abiding in the equanimity of the sixfold base. "Having seen a form with the eye... [and so forth].
"Having seen a form with eye-consciousness. For the expression "having seen a form with the eye" is stated by way of a designation for its support (*nissaya-vohāra*).

This is indeed a discourse concerning the constituent parts (*sasambhārakathā*), as in the phrase "he pierces with a bow"; therefore, it should be understood that by means of the headword "support," the supported [consciousness] is being referred to.

"He does not become joyful through lust": even though he might become joyful at the moment of impulsion (*javana-kkhaṇa*) by way of worldly affection (*gehasita-pema*), [the text specifies this is not so].
It does not exist because it has been eradicated by the Path; nor does it arise as mental grief (*domanassa*) through the alteration of confidence (*pasāda*).

"He dwells equanimous and neutral" means that, by not looking on with indifference, he does not produce delusion (*moha*), but dwells equanimous and neutral precisely by way of the equanimity of knowledge (*ñāṇupekkhā*).
For one whose taints are destroyed remains neutral toward an object whether it be desirable, undesirable, or neutral, provided he does not look on with indifference.
In those who have not yet exhausted the taints, delusion arises through unwise attention;
by not allowing that to arise, and because it has been eradicated by the Path itself, he dwells equanimous by means of the equanimity of knowledge.
And this practice of his is said to be "accompanied by mindfulness and clear comprehension" because of the attainment of the fullness of mindfulness and the fullness of wisdom.
And here, by the phrase "he dwells equanimous at the six doors," the sixfold equanimity is described.
From the word "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*), however, four types of consciousness associated with knowledge are obtained, because clear comprehension is impossible without them.

From the expression "constant dwelling," even the eight great functional (*mahākiriyā*) types of consciousness are obtained, [even] at times when the conditions for the arising of knowledge are absent.

Because it demonstrates their occurrence. From the statement, "not being lustful, not being hateful," ten types of consciousness are obtained together with the smile-producing and the sustained-smile consciousnesses. For their occurrence by way of non-lustfulness and non-hatred is common to those as well.
But is it not the case here that these constant abidings are presented by way of the sixfold equanimity, according to the passage, "he dwells in equanimity"?

"How is joy obtained? "Through repetition. For although one whose taints are destroyed dwells frequently with equanimity toward both desirable and undesirable objects—because he does not abandon his own state of natural purity—nevertheless, when there is at times such a mental formation, that object which is desirable by its very nature [arises].
By way of grasping the specific nature of things as they truly are, the mind of an Arahant indeed continues to proceed accompanied by joy;
however, this is solely due to the force of previous habituation.
"The body" refers to the body of the five sense-doors; that which has its end within [the body] is "bodily" (*kāyantikā*), and thus it is "bodily" (*kāyantika*). Therefore he said:
“As long as the body with its five doors functions, so long does it proceed. This same principle applies here regarding the end of life (*jīvitantika*).

As for the phrase “having arisen subsequently”: having arisen after the mind-door feeling (*manodvārika-vedanā*) within this personal existence (*attabhāva*), it ceases prior to that [mind-door feeling];
therefore, in order to show the meaning established by implication in its own form, [the text says] “mind-door feeling...”
It is said: "Having first arisen, it ceases afterwards. Now, in order to explain that which was stated in brief, he says "For she," and so forth.
"Until thirty years" refers to the first stage of life. "At the time of fifty years" means from the first stage of life until the time of fifty years;
during that interval, she "remains" (ṭhitā), meaning she remains in an even state without undergoing increase or decrease.
It is "mild" (*manda*), meaning soft and not sharp. "Then" (*tadā*) refers even when [the person] is eighty or ninety years old, and also when [the faculty] has long been familiarized;
this is the intended meaning. "Shattered" (*bhagga*) means shattered by the loss of vitality, thus discolored.

"Only to the very core of the heart" (*hadayakoṭiṃyeva*) means that, instead of proceeding to the bases such as the eye, it goes only to the heart-base, which is the ultimate beginning and end of those [faculties]. "As long as" (*tāva*) means for as long as the feeling continues.
"By means of a large pond" means by means of a great lake (*mahātaḷāka*). "Endowed with five waterways" means connected with five channels for the entry and exit of water;
because it is completely full, [the water] flows out from here and there. "First, when the rain falls," and so forth, is the correlation of the similes.
"With reference to this feeling" means with reference to this aforementioned feeling pertaining to the mind-door that has reached its conclusion.
"With the breaking up of the body" means with the destruction of the personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Without going further" means without going to the next world.

"The cooling of feelings" means the absence of the feverish distress caused by the turmoil of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). And since this occurs solely through their complete non-occurrence, he said:
"They will be of a nature that does not occur."

With reference to the strong knowledge of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega-ñāṇa*) that has arisen in one who wishes to destroy their own personal existence (*attabhāva*), it is said: "Wisdom is like a pickaxe.
With reference to the meditative absorption (*jhāna-samādhi*) produced from that, it is said: "Concentration is like a basket.
And with reference to the knowledge of the commencement of insight (*vipassanā-ārambha-ñāṇa*) to be practiced by relying on that, it is said: "Insight is like a spade. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Vappa Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta, verse 196:
In the sixth [verse], "it heats" (*tapati*) thus it is "asceticism" (*tapa*); it refers to that which proceeds by way of devotion to self-mortification.
Energy (*vīriya*). Because of it, there is a loathing and dispassion for evil, which is characterized by an abundance of bodily rigidity;
thus he said, "by what is reckoned as the performance of difficult deeds," and so forth. Regarding the phrases "proponents of austerity and loathing" (*tapojigucchavādā*) and so on:

they preach austerity and loathing; they wander about grasping at that very thing as essential even with their minds; and they are devoted to various forms of self-mortification, clinging to that very thing with their bodies as well.
The meaning is "they dwell. "Of impure bodily conduct" means endowed with impure bodily conduct such as the taking of life and so forth.
"Of impure verbal conduct" means endowed with impure verbal conduct such as false speech and so forth.
"Of impure mental conduct" means [endowed] with impure mental conduct such as covetousness and so forth.
[They] are possessed [of these]. Granted that covetousness and the rest do indeed arise even at the time of the occurrence of unwholesome bodily conduct and verbal conduct;

however, at that time they belong to the side of volition (*cetanā*) or are not included in the conventional designation [of "conduct"]. Therefore, the application by way of covetousness and so forth was made specifically in the section on mental conduct (*manosamācāra*).
Alternatively, there is the absence of the status of verbal conduct and so forth for killing and the rest when they occur through another door [such as the body].

Just as in the case of those [faults] occurring at the other doors, although covetousness and the rest are not established as being bodily conduct and so forth, they are established solely as mental conduct;
therefore, covetousness and the rest are mentioned only in the section on mental conduct. For it has been said:
"Kamma operates at the doors; the doors themselves are not the operators of the doors."
"Therefore, through the doors [of sense-bases], actions are established as distinct from one another.
"Those of impure livelihood" means those possessed of a livelihood consisting of twenty-one types of wrong search, such as the practice of medicine, acting as a messenger, usury, and so forth.
And this is stated specifically with reference to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation, as in the passage: "And those recluses and brahmins..."
However, the application [of the term] should be understood according to outsiders and according to householders.
For even among householders, wrong livelihood is indeed found in other ways as well, through the violation of the laws of birth, family, and locality.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanāya*): here, "knowledge and vision" refers to the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of the fruit, and also omniscience.

Both reviewing knowledge and insight knowledge are included. For in the passage, "Friend, is it for the sake of purification of knowledge and vision that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?", it is path-knowledge that is called "knowledge and vision.
In the passage, "This is another superhuman state, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision, a state of ease attained," it is fruition-knowledge.
In the passage, “Knowledge arose in the Blessed One as well: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma has been dead for seven days,’” it is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
In the passage, “And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my final birth,’” it is the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
In the passage, “He directs his mind toward knowledge and vision,” it is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*). But here, “for the sake of knowledge and vision” refers to—
Knowledge of the path is called "vision and knowledge. Therefore he said, "for the sake of vision, which is designated as knowledge of the path.
It pierces without failing; thus, it is said "having made it unfailing, it pierces. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mallikādevī Sutta 197.
In the seventh [verse], "of little influence" (*appesakkha*) means of little power (*appānubhāva*).
That lack of influence is evident through the absence of both the attainment of lordship (*ādhipateyya*) and the attainment of a retinue (*parivāra*). Therein, demonstrating the absence of a retinue:
He said, “surrounded by attendants. “Mistresses” means those whose nature is to rule by the power of kamma that leads to lordship.
Since that mastery of hers became manifest through the condition of the attainment of great wealth, he spoke of it by way of its synonym, “wealth,” saying, “wealthy means mistresses.
She possesses great wealth both in land and in movable property; thus she is “of great wealth.”
Furthermore, demonstrating great wealth by means of the very wealth that is put to use, he said, "They are of great wealth through the wealth that is put to use.
*Īsā* means to rule; the meaning is "one who has overcome. A great *īsā* is a *mahesā*.

Because of their well-established status as great rulers (*mahesā*), they are called "of great influence" (*mahesakkhā*) because they cannot be described by others [as anything less]. Moreover, that state of being of great influence arises from the perfection of lordship and a retinue.
Because she is perceived [as such], it is said that she has a "great retinue.

She is "beautiful" (abhirūpā) because she possesses a form that exceeds [the norm] in its perfection of shape. "Perfection of shape" means the well-proportioned arrangement of the bodily parts, such as the hands and feet;
for through the perfection of the parts, the perfection of the whole is established. And "form" (rūpa) here refers to the body.
[The term] is used in such contexts as “he comes to be reckoned among those possessing beauty,” and so forth.

“Fitted for seeing” means she is fit to be seen because of her beautiful form; it is said that when she is being seen, one’s eyes delight in her, meaning she is to be looked upon even while setting aside other duties and distractions.
She is “gracious” (pāsādikā) because, while being seen, she gladdens the mind through joy. Therefore he said: “gracious by her appearance.”
"Excellence" (*pokkharatā*) is said to mean beauty; "excellence of complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatā*) means the excellence of complexion.
However, the ancients say that "lotus" (*pokkhara*) refers to the body, while "complexion" (*vaṇṇa*) refers simply to the skin tone.
According to their view, "complexion and lotus" are *vaṇṇapokkharāni*, and the state of these two is "excellence of complexion and lotus. Thus: "by supreme excellence of complexion and lotus."
The meaning should be understood as being both through a most excellent complexion and through the perfection of the body’s configuration. Therefore he said:
“both by complexion and by the body’s configuration. In this context, “by complexion” means by the element of color (*vaṇṇadhātu*).
“Body” refers to the collection of parts—such as hands, feet, neck, and head—distinguished by their specific arrangement; and that [body] is grasped here by way of its configuration.
He said: "By way of bodily configuration.
"Becomes enraged" means that, by way of anger itself, it clings to each respective point of origination like a crooked thorn or like the teeth of a sea-monster.
For [it clings] to the object which is the basis for the arising of anger and serves as the condition for resentment (*upanāha*).

"Provoking anger" refers here to the act of becoming incensed through the process of getting angry, not through the process of coveting. Among the terms beginning with "it becomes agitated" (*kuppati*), "anger" (*kopa*) is the initial arising;
"ill will" (*byāpāda*) is stronger than that because the mind becomes corrupted due to having acquired the habit of it.
Because it has acquired the habit to an even greater degree, it attains a state of strength as an adversary, being stronger than even that ill will.
*Patitthiyanā*. Regarding "food and drink" (*anna-pāna*) and so forth: it is called "food" (*anna*) because it is eaten; this includes both solid food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*).
It is called "drink" (*pāna*) because it is drunk; this refers to any kind of beverage. It is called "clothing" (*vattha*) because it is worn or covered;

this refers to undergarments and upper robes. "Vehicle" (*yāna*) means that by which one goes (*yāti tena*); this includes any means for the purpose of travel, such as umbrellas, sandals, carts, palanquins, and so forth. For even an umbrella serves to ward off the suffering of rain and heat.
Because it is the means for traveling the path, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). "Garland" (*māla*) refers to any flower, such as jasmine garlands and the like.
"Fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to any unguent, such as sandalwood paste and the like.
The commentary on the Mallikādevī Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Attantapa Sutta (198).

In the eighth [verse], *attā* refers to that wherein the conceit "I am" (*ahaṃmāna*) is established; it is the personal existence (*attabhāva*). However, in this context, that which is not another is the *attā*;

it is that self (*taṃ attānaṃ*). "Another" (*para*) means distinct from one's own self. "Seen" (*diṭṭha*) means in what has become directly perceived. "Phenomena" (*dhamma*) refers to the phenomena of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
For in that [body], there is a self, and there arises the view of a self and so forth; thus it is called "selfhood" (*attabhāva*). Therefore he said:
"In this very life" means "in this very selfhood. "Hunger" refers to craving, because it is the cause of physical hunger.
"Of the defilements that burn within" refers to those defilements that cause torment by generating distress and feverish agitation within one's own continuum.

He is *ludda* (cruel) because he causes others to weep by killing, slaughtering, and so forth. He is *dāruṇa* (terrible) because he tears apart body and mind through his state of causing affliction. He is *kakkhaḷa* (hard-hearted) because his heart is rigid. A *bandhanāgārika* is one appointed to a prison.
"By the consecration of a khattiya" means by the consecration to be performed for khattiyas.

A *santhāgāra* is a hall built as a place of assembly; it is a sacrificial hall (*yaññāgāra*). "With ghee-oil" means with oil mixed with ghee. For at that time, she [the earth] anointed her body with this "twin-fat" (*yamakasneha*).
He anoints. Having crossed over the state of a calf, he stands as a young bull (*vacchatara*).

"For the purpose of making an enclosure" means for the purpose of surrounding the altar with *dabba* grass together with new garlands. "On the sacrificial ground" means in the remaining place for sacrifice.
He said this because right practice in the Teaching is possible only for one who has cast far away pride, not for one whose nature is prideful.
“Because of having struck down conceit. “Because of being abundant” means because of their great quantity.
Intoxications based on wealth, health, and so forth are easily abandoned because their signs do not persist; however, intoxications based on lineage and learning are not so.

Even for those who have gone forth from the khattiya and brāhmaṇa castes, the priding themselves on birth and learning is difficult to abandon. Therefore he said: “For the most part... they harbor conceit.”
"Because of low birth" means because of being of inferior birth. "They are unable to stand firm" means they are unable to guard their virtue after having made it thoroughly pure;
for it is by way of virtue that one stands firm in the Dispensation. Alternatively, "to stand firm" means to stand firm in the supramundane state through the penetration of Truth.
For generally, those endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) are of good birth alone, not of bad birth.
"Completely pure" (*parisuddha*) means entirely purified in every respect due to the absence of defilements, because it demonstrates the absolute abandonment of lust and the other [hindrances].

"He gains faith" (*saddhaṃ paṭilabhati*) means he believes by way of the faith of ordinary worldlings (*pothujjanika-saddhā*). For those of a wise nature, the establishment of faith is preceded by the grasping of the excellence of the Dhamma, owing to their state of having the Dhamma as their authority and being confident in the Dhamma.

"Husband and wife" (*jāyampatikā*) refers to a householder and his wife. "Kāmaṃ... [desire]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with *kāmaṃ*; the translation reflects the portion available.)
When the term "husband and wife" (*jāyampatikā*) is used, it is understood as referring only to two people by way of the master of the house and the mistress of the house.

However, regarding a man who has many wives, what is there to say? It is stated as "two" in order to demonstrate that even cohabitation with a single woman constitutes a crowded confinement (*sambādha*).
[The word *saṅkiṇṇa* is used] in the sense of being "possessed of something" (*sakiñcana*) through passion and so forth, and in the sense of [being crowded] by fields, lands, and so forth.

In the sense of being a locus for the arrival of the stains of passion and so forth through the presence of obstacles, the state of being a place of arising is the same for both [the household life and renunciation];
thus, these two explanations are identical in meaning, differing only in phrasing. "In the sense of non-clinging" means in the sense of non-attachment, that is, by way of being unbound.
Thus, by way of being the locus for the occurrence of unwholesome and wholesome states, the household life and renunciation possess the characteristics of confinement and open space respectively.

Having shown this, he now says "But furthermore" (*apicā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that very occurrence of the wholesome (*kusalappavatti*) by way of its being a proper or improper occasion (*aṭṭhāna-ṭhānabhāvena*).

"A brief exposition" (*saṅkhepakathā*) means a commentary on the meaning without extracting each word individually. "Even for a single day" (*ekampi divasaṃ*) means even for the duration of a single day.
"Making it unbroken" (*akhaṇḍaṃ katvā*) means making it unimpaired by not committing even a minor offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭamatta*).
"Untainted by the stain of defilements" means having rendered it undefiled by way of the defilement of craving and so forth.

"Having clothed himself" means both having put on the lower garment and having wrapped himself in the upper robe. "House-dwelling" (*agāravāsa*) is a compound where the latter member has been elided; it is that which brings about the increase of the house, thus being "beneficial to the house.
"Mass of wealth" (*bhogakkhandho*) means a heap of wealth, a collection of wealth. "In the sense of binding" refers to [the attachment] through affection, such as for a son, a grandson, and so forth.
In the sense of being a bond by way of delimitation. They are known as "relatives" (*ñātī*) because they are recognized as "these are ours.

A "circle" (*parivaṭṭo*) is so called in the sense of revolving, such as through the succession of grandfather, father, sons, and so forth. Although the word *sikkhā* (training) is a general term, it is applied specifically here because of its proximity to the word *ājīva* (livelihood) and because it requires the specific qualities mentioned immediately above;
thus it is said: "the training of the bhikkhus, which is termed higher virtue" (*adhisīla*). In the sense of that which is to be practiced...
Training (*sikkhā*); that in which they live together is the livelihood (*sājīva*). "By way of the state of training" means by way of the training and by way of the livelihood associated with it.
"Fulfilling the training" means fulfilling the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).

"And not transgressing the livelihood" means not transgressing the training rules stated as "the body of names, the body of phrases, the body of terminology, and the body of phonemes," nor the word of the Blessed One.

The meaning is "having offered. And this very thing is called "training" (*sikkhanā*). In that regard, the non-transgression of the rules of conduct (*sājīva*) is the condition for the fulfillment of training (*sikkhāpāripūri*);
for it is through that [non-transgression] that the fulfillment of training occurs up to the attainment of the Path (*magga*).
"Anuppadātā" means a provider of support (*anubala*), or one who causes [the training] to proceed by way of following after it. But of what is there the following, and of what the proceeding?
Because it is stated as “of those who are united,” it is understood to mean “of the union. Therefore he said, “one who gives what is required for the union.
Furthermore, since through following along there is the placing, the protection, or the strengthening of the foundation of the union, he said, “seeing two people in harmony,” and so forth.
It is called an *ārāma* because they delight (*āramanti*) therein; it is a place where one should take delight.
However, since this meaning can be obtained even without the letter *ā*, it was said: "The Pāḷi reads *samaggarāmo* as well; this is the very same meaning. Regarding the word *ettha*:
"A chariot with faultless parts, a white canopy, and a single wheel rolls along;..."
“Behold him coming, free from distress, with the stream cut off and unbound”—this is from that verse.
Here, virtue is called “flawless. For this very reason it was said:
“Householder Citta, ‘flawless,’ venerable sir, is a designation for virtues. “Delicate” means soft due to lack of coarseness. Of the city...
In this context, the word *pura* should be understood as denoting those who dwell therein—just as in expressions such as “the village has arrived.
For this very reason, he says “of the city-dwellers. That which nourishes and increases the mind (*mana*) is *manāpa*. Therefore it is said: “causing the increase of the mind.
The passage beginning with “speaking at the proper time” demonstrates the practice of one who abstains from idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). For even speech that is connected with meaning—
Because speech that does not bring benefit through application at an improper time leads to harm, it conforms to speech that communicates what is disadvantageous;

therefore, it is said that "one who speaks at the proper time" (*kālavādī*) must avoid speaking at an improper time when abandoning idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). Even when speaking at the proper time, one must avoid what is untrue because it accomplishes both kinds of harm;
thus he says "one who speaks what is true" (*bhūtavādī*). And when speaking what is true, that which accomplishes welfare in this world and the next—
In order to show that this very [quality] is what should be spoken, it is said: "one who speaks of the goal" (*atthavādī*).
To show that even when speaking of the goal, one should not speak based solely on mundane phenomena (*lokīyadhamma*), but rather speak based on supramundane phenomena (*lokuttaradhamma*), it is said:
"one who speaks of the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*). And to show how the goal is based on supramundane phenomena, it is said: "one who speaks of the discipline" (*vinayavādī*).

For when the meaning is explained by way of the five trainings in restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the five trainings in abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*), it is based on the supramundane Dhamma because it serves as the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna.
Thus, it is shown that only when the meaning is explained as endowed with such specific qualities does it shine when there is skill in teaching;
it becomes effective in its function, and not otherwise. Therefore, [the Buddha] is described as "one who speaks words that possess a foundation" (*nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā*).
It has been stated. Now, in order to clarify that skill in teaching, he says "at the proper time" (*kālena*) and so forth.

For, having observed the distinctions in categorical and other forms of answering regarding the subject matter of speech as it has descended through questioning and so on, she—who clarifies, in accordance with each respective occasion, the setting aside [of questions], the demonstration of reasons and examples, and so forth—possesses a form that is both limited and circumscribed, yet which encompasses a vast, profound, noble, and supreme expansion of ultimate meaning.
One who establishes others in the Dhamma exactly as it is, in accordance with the power of their knowledge through discourse, is called "skilled in teaching"—
thus should the construction of the meaning here be understood.

Having thus analyzed the seven root training rules in their proper order, the abandoning of covetousness and so forth is achieved through the restraint of the sense faculties and the practice of vigilance.
In order to analyze that [term] as well—having extracted it by way of dividing it according to the conduct and virtue (ācāra-sīla)—the text proceeds;

and to explain its meaning, the words "from the destruction of seeds and the destruction of plants" (*bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā*) and so forth are stated. Therein, a "seed-group" (*bījagāma*) is a collection or multitude of seeds.
A "plant-group" (*bhūtagāma*) is a collection of trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, which have come into being, been born, and manifested. But are not trees and the like...

Because they lack consciousness, they are not living beings (*jīva*). This absence of consciousness should be understood from their lack of movement, their regrowth when cut, their possession of dissimilar types of matter, and their exclusion from the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Furthermore, since growth is found even in coral, stones, and salt, this is no reason for them to be considered living beings;
and as for their "perception of objects," that is merely a mental fabrication, like dreaming.

Just as in the case of Ciñcā and others, so too with those suffering from pregnancy cravings (*dohala*) and the like; why, then, is abstaining from the destruction of seeds and the community of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) desired?

Because it is befitting for a recluse (*samaṇa*) and because it protects the beings dwelling therein. For this very reason, it was said: "For people, O foolish man, perceive life in a tree," and so forth.
"Root-seed" (*mūlabīja*) means the root itself is the seed; or, that of which the root is the seed is "root-seed. This same method applies to the others as well.

"Knob-seed" (*phaḷubīja*) means a joint-seed (*pabbabīja*). The word "seed" (*bīja*), which is conventionally established for a solid fruit capable of sprouting due to its specific causal role in producing a similar fruit when combined with other conditions, is applied by extension to certain roots and so forth because they fulfill that same purpose.

It is stated as "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*) by qualifying it with the word "seed" (*bīja*) in order to exclude [the term] from its primary sense of "that which grows," just as in the cases of "form-form" (*rūparūpa*) and "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
But why, in this instance, is the "class of beings consisting of seeds" (*bījagāma*) specified while omitting the "class of beings consisting of elements" (*bhūtagāma*)?
This should not be viewed in that way; for have we not already said: "The root itself..."?

“Seed” (*bīja*) means root-seed (*mūlabīja*); it is also called “root-seed” because its root is the seed. Herein, by the first [term] the category of seeds (*bījagāma*) is indicated, and by the second, the category of beings (*bhūtagāma*).
This twofold category—both "root-seed" and "root-seed"—should be understood as being taught either by a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*) or by the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*).
For this very reason he says, “of the fivefold,” and so forth. “Of blue grass, trees, and so on.”
Of fresh grass and fresh trees, etc. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of medicinal plants, creepers, and so forth.

"One meal" (*ekabhatta*) means a single meal; one who has that is a "one-meal-eater" (*ekabhattika*). However, since such a person might also eat at night, he said "restrained from the night" (*rattūparata*) in order to exclude that possibility. Even so, one who eats after midday might still be considered a "one-meal-eater."
To prevent that [fault], it is said: “Abstaining from eating at improper times.
From the rising of the dawn until midday is called the time for eating as practiced by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones; any time other than that is the improper time (*vikāla*).
However, since eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase in the Commentary, [the period] “after midday has passed until the setting of the sun”...
"Food is called 'eating at the improper time,'" it is said.
Regarding the term *dārumāsaka*, the word "iti" indicates that it refers to such things as those which enter into common trade.

Since the meaning of "accepting" (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is understood to include having others take it for one and consenting to what has been set aside [for one's use], [the text says]: "He neither takes it himself, nor causes it to be taken..."
It is said: “One does not consent to what has been set down. Alternatively, there are three kinds of acceptance:
by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, acceptance by body is taking up; acceptance by speech is causing to take up;
and acceptance by mind is consenting. Taking all three kinds of acceptance together as one, it is called “acceptance.”
