Thus he said, “He does not learn it,” and so forth. This same method applies to the cases of receiving raw grain and so on as well.
Because secondary grains such as *nīvāra* are included within the category of primary grains such as *śāli*, it is stated that there are “seven kinds.
“I allow you, monks, five types of medicinal fats: bear fat, fish fat, crocodile fat, pig fat, [and human fat].”
Because it is stated that [the gift] is "like that of a donkey," this is called "specifically permitted" (*odissa-anuññāta*).
However, since it is stated that "it was received at the proper time," receiving is permissible when there is a requisite; thus he says, "except for what is specifically permitted.
Deceiving by means of suitability is "counterfeiting coins" (*rūpa-kūṭa*); the meaning is deceiving by means of a semblance. By a limb (*aṅga*), that is, by a part of one's own body.

Deception by means of the parts [of the measure] is *aṅgakūṭa*. Deception by means of taking [more than the allotted amount] is *gahaṇakūṭa*. Deception by concealing [the excess] is *paṭicchannakūṭa*. "He steps upon" (*akkamati*) means he presses down;
the connection is that he steps upon it at the initial stage. "The heart" (*hadaya*) refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as the *nāḷi* and so forth.
It is specifically the peak [of the liquid] that has been raised up when oil and other substances are being measured with the *nāḷi* and other measures.
The breaking of the topknot (*sikhābhedo*), which is its cutting off. "Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* and those residing at the Uttaravihāra.
"Killing" (*vadho*) means harming by means of blows with the fist, striking with a staff, and so forth; the meaning is "affliction.

For the word *vadha* is seen to have the sense of affliction as well, in such passages as "having repeatedly struck herself, she weeps. Just as in the case of the commonality of not being accepted [as an offering],...

Although there is a commonality in the nature of taking what is not given because it consists in seizing the property of another, women, boys, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth, are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing specific objects that should not be accepted by those who have gone forth.

Likewise, although there is a commonality in the nature of taking what is not given because it consists in seizing the property of another, false scales and so forth are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing specific instances of taking what is not given. It is not so, however, in the case of the category of killing living beings.
There is a purpose for mentioning "killing" again; it cannot be said that there is self-agency in that case and agency by another here, because of the statement:
"The volition that originates bodily and vocal application consists of six applications. Therefore, the meaning as previously stated is appropriate here.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "'Killing' means slaying. That too refers simply to striking.
And it can be understood that this was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), because the word "killing" (*māraṇa*) is seen to apply even to harming.

Showing that, when the robes and alms-food are respectively indicated as being merely for the maintenance of the body and the belly, it follows without distinction that all eight requisites have that same purpose, he said, “All these too,” and so forth. “These too” means...
Even those who possess nine requisites and so forth may be of few desires and contented; for it is not by that alone that one becomes full of great desire or discontented.
He dwells happily in the four directions; because the four directions themselves have become the locus of his happy dwelling, he is "four-directional" (*cātuddiso*).
Furthermore, he does not strike against beings or formations there with fear, and thus he is "without resistance" (*appaṭigho*).
He is "content" because he is satisfied by means of the twelve kinds of contentment. "With this or that" means with various superior and inferior things;
he is "enduring" because he overcomes external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal dangers such as sensual desire and other afflictions of body and mind.
He is "fearless" due to the absence of fear that causes bondage. He is "alone," without a companion.
Therefore, because it is like the horn of a rhinoceros (*khaggamiga*), the meaning is that one should "wander like a rhinoceros horn" (*khaggavisāṇakappo*).
A bird that has had its wings clipped or whose wings have not yet grown cannot fly;
thus, specifying it with the word "winged," the text says in the Pāḷi, "a bird possessed of wings. For one who [practices] the enjoyment of stored-up goods...
There is no laying down [of the robe] while one still has a longing for it; showing that this monk is of such a nature, he said, “This is the summary meaning here,” and so forth.
He said, “Ariya means faultless,” because they go away from those faults, or because they are far removed from them.
“Internally” means within oneself. “Faultless happiness” means non-material happiness, because it is free from the thorns of the defilements.

Restraint of the sense faculties is desired only for one who is established in the restraint of virtue as previously described, because that [restraint of virtue] is its foundation and because it serves as its protector;
thus it is said: "That bhikkhu, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue...
Regarding the remaining phrases, such as "he does not grasp at signs," and so forth—the summarized meaning here is as follows:
"Not seizing upon signs" means that he does not seize upon signs such as those of a woman or a man, or signs such as beauty which serve as a basis for the defilements;
he remains fixed upon the mere sight [of the object].

"Not seizing upon secondary characteristics" refers to the various modes—such as the hands, feet, smiles, laughter, speech, and glances—which are called "secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjana*) because they manifest the defilements in successive detail (*anu-anu byañjanato*).
It does not grasp at the mental aspect (*ākāra*). It grasps only that which is real (*bhūta*) therein. Regarding the phrase "on account of which" (*yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ*) and so forth:

for whatever reason—that is, due to that lack of restraint of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriyāsaṃvara*)—these states such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and the like would flow into this person who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained by the door of mindfulness, having left the eye-door open.
They would not follow after them. "He practices for their restraint" means he practices for the purpose of closing the door of that eye-faculty with the bolt of mindfulness.
And it is precisely while practicing in this way that one is said to "guard the eye-faculty" and "attain restraint over the eye-faculty.
This same method applies to the passages beginning with "having heard a sound with the ear," and so forth. Thus, this is [explained] in brief.

The virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla) should be understood as having the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and so forth that bind the defilements to form and the other [sense objects].
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*.

For it is because restraint of the sense faculties has the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and so forth regarding form and the rest that it is described as "the happiness of not being drenched by defilements," and so on.
The state of being unmoistened by defilements and the state of being undisturbed by them are also said to be his happiness.
"Advancing" (*abhikkamana*) means moving forward; "receding" (*paṭikkamana*) means returning.
Both of these are found within the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). In walking, for instance, one is said to "advance" when carrying the body forward.
Turning back is called "receding. Even while standing in one place, leaning the body forward is called "advancing," and drawing it backward is called "receding.
Even while seated, shifting toward the front part of the seat is called "advancing," and shifting toward the rear part of the seat is called "receding."
The same method applies even when lying down.

Regarding "clear comprehension of purpose" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) and so forth: one who knows thoroughly (*samantato*) or in every way (*pakārehi*), or who knows distinctly and specifically (*pakaṭṭhaṃ* or *savisesaṃ*), is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*).
The state of being clearly comprehending is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*); it is knowledge occurring in such a manner. Together with that which is reckoned as growth by way of the Dhamma...

That which proceeds with a purpose is "purposeful" (*sātthaka*); the clear comprehension of that which is purposeful, such as [the path] that has gone forth (*abhikkanta*), etc., is "clear comprehension of the purposeful" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
Clear comprehension of what is suitable—that is, what brings about one's own benefit—is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).

Clear comprehension regarding the range of activity, such as walking and so forth during the alms-round, and in other instances as well, regarding the range of activity known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) which is not abandoned, is "clear comprehension of the range of activity" (*gocara-sampajañña*).
Clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) regarding non-delusion in acts such as going forward is "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

In this context, when the thought to go forward arises, instead of proceeding merely by the power of that thought, one examines what is beneficial and what is not beneficial, thinking: "Is there any purpose for me in going there, or is there not?

This examination of what is beneficial is "clear comprehension of the purposeful" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*). And herein, "what is beneficial" refers to such things as seeing a shrine (*cetiya*), seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elders (*thera*), or seeing foulness (*asubha*).
This is growth by way of the Dhamma. For even upon seeing a cetiya or the Bodhi tree, one arouses joy with the Buddha as its object;
or, through seeing the Saṅgha, one arouses joy with the Saṅgha as its object, and by contemplating that very joy in terms of its exhaustion and passing away, one attains Arahantship.
Or, having seen elders and established oneself in their instruction, and then seeing a foul object, one arouses the first jhāna therein.
By comprehending that very same [body] through its dissolution and disintegration, one attains Arahantship; therefore, the vision of these [four postures] is called "purposeful.
Some, however, say: "Even material prosperity is indeed a purpose, because one practices for the support of the holy life (brahmacariya) by depending upon it.
Having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable regarding that movement, the discernment of suitability is "clear comprehension of suitability" (sappāya-sampajañña).
For example—firstly, visiting a shrine (cetiya) is indeed purposeful.

If, during a great festival for a shrine, assemblies gather within a radius of ten or twelve yojanas, both men and women, adorned and prepared according to their respective means, move about like figures in a painting.
Therein, greed arises toward desirable objects, aversion toward undesirable ones, and negligence toward that which is neither.
Delusion arises, or one incurs an offense involving physical contact, or there is an obstacle to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Thus, that place is unsuitable; it is suitable only when the aforementioned obstacles are absent. The same principle applies to the vision of the Bodhi tree.
Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if one has had a great pavilion constructed within a village and [performs the ceremony] throughout the entire night...
When people are listening to the Dhamma, there occurs both a gathering of people and an obstacle in the very manner already described.
Thus, that place is unsuitable; it is suitable only when there is no such obstacle. The same principle applies to seeing elders who are surrounded by large retinues.
Even the contemplation of the foul (asubha) is purposeful, because it serves as a cause for the attainment of the paths and fruits. For the sake of a tooth-stick...
The story of the young bhikkhu who went after taking a novice with him should be told here as the illustrative example.
Thus, even though it serves a purpose, the unattractive aspect of the female sex for a man is unsuitable, and the unattractive aspect of the male sex for a woman is likewise unsuitable;
rather, that which is of a similar kind is suitable. This discernment regarding what is suitable is called "suitability-awareness" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).

But for one who has thus acquired what is beneficial and suitable, having learned a "range" (gocara) consisting of a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects according to his own mental preference, the act of going on the alms-round while taking that very subject with him is called "clear comprehension of the range.
Furthermore, non-confusion regarding the forward steps and so forth is "clear comprehension of non-delusion. This should be understood as follows: here, a bhikkhu...
Whether walking forward or walking backward, unlike ordinary worldlings who—when walking forward and so forth—are deluded, thinking, "The self walks forward;
walking forward is produced by the self," or "I am walking forward;
walking forward is produced by me," he, being undeluded, [knows] by that very consciousness when the thought "I am walking forward" arises.
Together with the mind-originated air element, the air element arises producing intimation;
thus, by way of the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity, this skeletal structure designated as "body" moves forward.
As it moves forward in this manner, during the lifting of each individual foot, two elements—the earth element and the water element—become deficient and weak, while the other two become predominant.

In lifting up and carrying away, the two elements—the fire element and the air element—are weak and feeble, while the other two are predominant and powerful. It is the same with laying down and pressing down.
In that regard, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring during lifting up do not reach the stage of carrying away; likewise for carrying away.
Those occurring in the process of conveying do not reach the process of relinquishing; those occurring in relinquishing do not reach the process of depositing;
and those occurring in depositing do not reach the process of compression.
Right there, each joint by joint, each layer by layer, they break apart with a crackling sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan, becoming completely fused together. In that regard, what...
One approaches; whose approaching is it? In the ultimate sense, it is indeed the elements that go, the elements that stand, the elements that sit, and the elements that lie down.
For in each respective part, together with material form—“One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases.”
“The connection to the Avīci hell continues like the flow of a river.
Thus, non-confusion regarding advancing and so forth is called “clear comprehension of non-delusion” (*asammoha-sampajañña*). “Perfection of requisites” means the fulfillment of requisites.
“These four” refers to these four: restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), contentment, restraint of the sense faculties, and clear comprehension through mindfulness (*sati-sampajañña*).
The requisites for dwelling in the forest. "It becomes subject to criticism" means it becomes subject to criticism in the form of an accusation, such as:
"For this particular bhikkhu, there is merely a residence in the forest like that of animals or forest-dwellers, but there is no correct practice whatsoever suitable for forest-dwelling";
or [it refers to] forest-dwelling animals or people of a different class who are mere forest-dwellers.
One falls into a state of being censurable by way of misconduct. They cause one to hear terrifying sounds;
yet for those who do not flee even at that, they [the devas] place their heads... [etc. ...in their hands. It is "black" (*kāḷaka*) because it resembles a black spot;

it is the gross offense (*thullavajja*) designated as transgression. It is a "mole" (*tilaka*) because it resembles a mole; it is the minor offense (*aṇumattavajja*) designated as wrong thought. "That" refers to rapture (*pīti*). By virtue of its manifest nature...
He comprehends it as secluded by way of its presence and its destruction.
"Secluded" means secluded from people; therefore he said "empty. That, moreover, should be understood by the absence of the noise of people;
because sound is a thorn to jhāna, he said, "the meaning is 'little sound, little noise. "This very thing" refers precisely to the state of being noiseless.
A *vihāra* is an entire dwelling enclosed by a wall. An *aḍḍhayoga* is a long palace;

some also call it a "palace shaped like a garuḷa. A *pāsāda* is a square palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof. An *aṭṭa* is a specific type of multi-storied building, four or five stories high, suitable for repelling rival kings.
A *māḷa* is a specific type of building consisting of many corners but covered by a single roof-peak.
Another method: a *vihāra* is a long-faced palace (*pāsāda*). An *aḍḍhayoga* is a lodging with a roof covering only one side.
It is said that its wall on one side is higher, while on the other side it is lower; by this means, it becomes a one-sided-roofed structure.
A *pāsāda* is a long, square palace. A *hammiya* is a flat-roofed structure provided with a courtyard (*candika-aṅgaṇa*).
A "cave" (*guhā*) refers exclusively to a mountain cave. A "shelter" (*leṇa*) is a rock overhang with a closed door. A "pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*) is a bower of branches.

A dwelling that serves as a residence is "monastery lodging" (*vihārasenāsana*) in the sense of being a place to dwell. Beds and chairs such as the *masāraka* and so forth, together with the cushions to be spread upon them and the pillows, constitute "bed-and-chair lodging" (*mañcapīṭhasenāsana*) by association with the beds and chairs. [This includes] cotton cloth and so forth...
A "prepared resting place" (*santhatasenāsana*) is so called because it must be spread out upon the ground.

A "resting place as an open space" (*okāsasenāsana*) refers to a spot such as the foot of a tree that serves merely as a location for lying down or sitting, since it is not something artificially constructed;
it is already included by the term "resting place" itself, because the phrase "a secluded resting place" includes it through the general designation of "resting place."
If this is so, why was it called "arañña" (the forest)? To this he says, "But of this... and so forth.
That it is mentioned by way of the bhikkhunīs is said with reference to how it appears in the Vinaya; however, in the Abhidhamma as well, it is indeed stated:
"Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is 'arañña'. For therein, that which is not included within the precincts of a village—
That is described as "the forest" (*arañña*) in its literal sense. What was stated in the *Dhutanga-niddesa* is appropriate;
therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained therein. "At the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*) means near a tree. For this has been said:
"To the extent that at midday the shade spreads all around, or until the leaves fall in a windless place—to that extent [it is the root of a tree]."

Regarding "the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*): since the word *sela* (rock) is used without distinction as a synonym for mountain, it is stated that "a rock is a mountain," and not merely something made of stone.
For a mountain is of three kinds, including those made of earth and so forth.

A "cleft" (*vivara*) refers to a space resembling a chamber or the like, situated between two mountains standing very close to one another; or it may be within a single mountain itself. It is "like a hollow" (*umaṅgasadisa*).
“Like a thicket of reeds. A place not frequented by people means a place where people do not travel according to their ordinary course.
By the word “etcetera,” it is meant: “‘Forest retreat’ (vanapattha) is a designation for dwellings in forest thickets; ‘forest retreat’ is a designation for terrifying places;
‘forest retreat’ is a designation for places that cause the hair to stand on end; ‘forest retreat’ is a designation for remote border regions.”
This passage from the Canon includes the phrase: “‘Forest-dwelling’ (vanapattha) is not a designation for lodgings frequented by people.
“Uncovered” means not covered by any covering whatsoever, even by the branch of a tree.
“Having driven out” means having expelled. “Resembling a mountain slope or a cave” means resembling a mountain slope or resembling a cave.

Regarding "seeking alms-food" (*piṇḍapātapariyesana*), it is said that "alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) is used here by dropping the latter member of the compound; thus, he says, "having returned from seeking alms-food.
Regarding "the cross-legged posture" (*pallaṅka*): here the prefix *pari-* means "all around" (*samanta-to*).
Therefore, having placed the left thigh and the right thigh together and having joined the two feet together, the sitting is called "the cross-legged posture"; thus he says, "all around."
"Cross-legged posture" (*ūrūbaddhāsana*): sitting by way of binding the thighs is the *pallaṅka*.
"Having folded" means having both feet folded and drawn in so that the sitting is done in the manner of a *pallaṅka*.
He said "having bound" to indicate the making of such a connection between the two feet. It is the placing of the lower body straight.

Since it is understood that [the posture] is established by the word "sitting" itself, he says, "having placed the upper body straight," because here the word *kāya* refers specifically to the upper body.
To show both the actual form and the purpose of placing it straight, he says, "the eighteen," and so forth. "Not leaning" means not bending forward. "Not falling over" means...
It does not stray from the path nor leap over it; thus, through the attainment of successive excellence, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) proceeds toward growth and expansion.
Regarding the term *parimukhaṃ*, the prefix *pari-* here has the same meaning as the prefix *abhi-*, which is why he says "facing the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ*);
having turned away from external, manifold objects, [the mind] is directed toward the meditation subject alone.
The meaning is "having placed before. Or, showing that the prefix *pari-* has the sense of proximity, he says, "or having placed near the mouth.

And here, just as by such phrases as "he resorts to a secluded lodging," a lodging suitable for meditation is shown, so too by the word "sits" is shown a posture that belongs to neither the side of depression nor the side of agitation, but is peaceful.

“Having folded his legs crosswise” (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā) indicates the firmness of the sitting posture. “Having established mindfulness facing the front” (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) indicates the method for grasping the object of meditation.

*Pari* has the sense of grasping (*pariggaha*), as in the word *pariṇāyikā* (“guide”) and others. *Mukha* has the sense of an outlet (*niyyāna*), as in the phrase *suññatavimokkhamukhaṃ* (“the door to the liberation of emptiness”) and others.
...like that. For the meaning of "going out" (*niyyāna*) is the sense of departing from the opposite [of defilements];

therefore, "having established mindfulness with a well-ascertained going-out" means having made mindfulness such that it is entirely free from confusion and has abandoned confusion, having established it with supreme mindfulness and circumspection.
One covets, yearns for, and longs for by means of this, thus it is "covetousness" (*abhijjhā*); it is greed. "In the sense of breaking up" means in the sense of disintegration.
The meaning is: "in the sense of breaking up moment by moment. Regarding the phrase "by way of suppression" (*vikkhambhanavasena*):

here, "suppression" means non-arising and non-occurrence because [the defilements] have been thoroughly abandoned by their opposites. And the term "abandoned" is stated with reference to a state resembling what has been abandoned, since meditative absorption (*jhāna*) has not yet been attained.
Nevertheless, this [state] is not devoid of covetousness by its very nature, as is the case with eye-consciousness.
Rather, it is by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore he said: "It is not like eye-consciousness.
"The same method applies" means that while eye-consciousness is by its own nature free from covetousness and ill will, yet not because it has been suppressed by cultivation, this [mind] is not so;
for this mind is free from ill will, devoid of sloth and torpor, and unagitated, because it has been purified by cultivation.
The meaning is "and free from doubt. "The former state" refers to the condition of being pure and bright.

It is stated that "sloth is a sickness of the mind" and "torpor is a sickness of mental factors," because sloth is defined in the Abhidhamma as "that which at that time is the unfitness of the mind," and so forth, while torpor is defined as "that which at that time is the unfitness of the body," and so forth.

For mindfulness, in its mutual inseparability from the lightness of mind and body and so forth, is to be understood as their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), just as it is the specific condition for the respective excellence of the mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*)—namely, the absence of their respective deficiencies and so on.
Regarding the phrase "perceiving light" (*ālokasaññī*), he says: "Even at night... etc., demonstrating that this vowel *ī* indicates a meaning distinguished by an exceeding degree of presence.
"Endowed with": this refers to both mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).
"Having transcended" means having abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*). "How is this? How is this?"—such is "wavering" (*kathaṃkathā*), which is doubt (*vicikicchā*);
one who has this is a "waverer" (*kathaṃkathī*); one who is not a waverer is "non-wavering" (*akathaṃkathī*), meaning free from doubt.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the classification beginning with characteristics" (*lakkhaṇādibhedato*): here, by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the inclusion of conditions, decline, abandoners, and so forth should be understood.
For these too are to be seen according to their various classifications. Regarding the phrase "having cut them off, they cause them to fall":
here, "cutting off" and "causing to fall" mean precisely not allowing those types of wisdom that have not yet arisen to arise. Thus, [this refers] to the sublime and unsurpassed wisdoms.

Furthermore, the obstructive states that act as causes for the non-attainment of limited wisdom, and those which destroy the capacity for the other [superior wisdom], are called "weakening wisdom. Thus he concludes with the word "appento" (concluding).
The commentary on the Attantapasutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the *Taṇhā-sutta*, etc. (199–200).
In the ninth [sutta], it is said: “There are eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the internal, which stand pervading the three realms of existence.
Thus, because she possesses this net consisting of those various parts of herself, she is so called.

It is *jālinī* (the net-like). Therefore he says, “or three existences,” and so forth. Therein, “in this or that” means in each respective existence (*bhava*) or object (*ārammaṇa*). Furthermore, by the method of exposition beginning with “also,” he shows the meaning of the term *visattikā* (clinging) by citing a portion of the explanatory text (*niddesa-pāḷi*) starting with “rooted in craving” (*visamūlā*). This is the explanatory text here: “Rooted in craving, having craving as its source, originating from craving, and arising from craving; it clings to form, clings to feeling, clings to perception, clings to volitional formations, and clings to consciousness. Thus it is called ‘clinging. This is the meaning of the term *visattikā*. Therefore, it was said: “The world is bound by clinging. Thus, the meaning of the verse has been explained. Now, the commentary on the prose passage (*veyyākaraṇa*) will follow. Therein, the Blessed One first states the summary (*uddesa*) of the prose passage: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of sensual pleasures. “Clinging (visattikā): in what sense is it clinging? It is clinging because it is spread out; it is clinging because it is dispersed; it is clinging because it is extensive;
it is clinging because it invades; it is clinging because it scatters; it is clinging because it deceives; it is clinging because its root is poison;
it is clinging because its fruit is poison; it is clinging because its enjoyment is poison. Or else, it is clinging because it is vast.”
But that craving [is directed toward] forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; toward clans, groups, and dwellings; toward gain, fame, and praise; toward pleasure;
toward robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; toward the realm of sense-desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm;

toward existence in the sense-desire world, existence in the form world, and existence in the formless world; toward existence with perception, existence without perception, and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"In the one-constituent existence, the four-constituent existence, and the five-constituent existence—past, future, and present—it is 'clinging' (*visattikā*) because it is spread out and extended over things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

In this context, "spread out" (*visatā*) means extended by way of pervading the phenomena of the three planes, such as form and so forth. "Spread out" (*visaṭā*) is merely a restatement of the preceding term.
This is stated by changing the letter *ta* into the letter *ṭa*. "Visālā" means extensive. "Visakkati" means she endures.
For one who is lustful, even when struck by another on account of lust, endures it; or they say that "visakkana" refers to the quivering [of the mind].
"Visaṃharati" means that by showing the advantages of sensual pleasures in various ways, she causes [the mind] to turn away from renunciation through diverse modes.
It withdraws and contracts the mind; the meaning is that it carries away or brings about suffering (*visa*).
It is deceptive because it grasps the impermanent and so forth as permanent. It has suffering as its root because it is the cause of the karma that produces suffering;
or, it is "rooted in poison" (*visamūlā*) because feeling—which consists of the suffering of pain and so forth—is its root. It is "poison" (*visa*) because it is the origin of suffering.

"Visaphalā" means that its fruit is poison. Since there is an indulgence in the suffering of form and so forth through craving, and not in the Deathless (amata), it is called "indulgence in poison" (visaparibhogā).
In all cases, the derivation of the word should be understood according to its etymological analysis (nirutti).
However, to show the primary meaning here, it is further stated: "Or else, it is 'visaṭā'... and so forth.
“Tantaṃ” (the warp) is so called because it is stretched by weavers upon the loom-pins for the purpose of weaving cloth;

it is termed “that which is to be stretched” (*tanīyati*). However, since that thread is taken as being indeed entangled due to its state of being a continuous, tangled mass, he said, “become entangled like a warp.
To show in detail the meaning stated in brief, [he says] “Just as...”
The passage beginning with "nāmā" has been stated. "To bring together" (samānetuṃ) means to bring [the preceding and the following] into equality, that is, to make them even and straight.
Or, "tangled thread" (tantākula) refers to a thread that is indeed tangled; one who has become like a tangled thread is "born as a tangled thread" (tantākulakajāto).
From weaving comes "gulā"—this is the name for the ball of yarn belonging to a weaver, who has received the feminine name "gulā" due to his state of being entangled.
Because it is indeed difficult to discern whether [the thread] is from the top or from the bottom when it is bound on a spindle, he said:
"A *gulāguṇṭhika* is called a weaver’s sizing-thread.
A *sakuṇikā* is a *paṭapada-sakuṇikā*. For that dwells in a nest suspended from the branches of trees. That nest—

Having brought grass, fibers, and so forth from here and there, one weaves them in such a way that they cannot be joined at tip to tip or root to root, nor can they be separated, just like a *kañjiya* thread spun by a weaver. Therefore he said, “Just as,” and so forth.

Both of these—the *kañjiya* thread and the bird’s nest—are called “a ball of tangled wool. “In the same manner as before” refers to the passage beginning with, “In this very way, beings,” and so forth.

It is according to the method already stated. Granted that muñja and pabbaja grasses, even as they grow, fall down due to their length and remain in the forest tangled with one another in a state of utter confusion;

nevertheless, it was said, "Just as those [rope-grasses]," etc., in order to show that they are not so difficult to untangle when they have been made into ropes. The rest here is exactly according to the method stated below.
"Apāya" means non-prosperity; the meaning is that they are deprived of happiness or the causes of happiness.

"Because it is the destination of suffering" means because it is the place where the suffering of one bound for the states of loss (apāya) occurs. "From the height of happiness" means from prosperity. "Because of being fallen into ruin" means because of falling into a deformed state;
that is, because one has fallen in such a way that there is no height of happiness in that particular existence (attabhāva).
"Thus indeed is saṃsāra. But is it not the case that what was described by the words "the states of loss" and so forth is also saṃsāra? True, this is so;

however, the mention of the "states of loss" (apāya) and so forth is for the purpose of showing that hell and the other realms are characterized by excessive suffering. This point should be understood according to the maxim of "the cow and the calf" (the whole and its parts).
And "the succession of the aggregates" refers to the continuous arising of the five aggregates one after another in the relationship of cause and fruit.

“Proceeding without interruption” means proceeding without cessation. “All that” refers to all the suffering of the states of woe and the suffering of the round (saṃsāra) mentioned by the words “the states of woe,” and so forth.
“Like a ship tossed by the wind upon the great ocean” is said both to show the vastness of the place of wandering and to show the instability of that wandering.
This is a simile. It should be understood that the phrase "just as a yoked ox goes" is intended both to show the state of being overwhelmed and to show the difficulty of liberation.
Regarding "grasping as a whole," some say it is the common grasping of craving, conceit, and views;
however, it should be seen as grasping without making distinctions such as "it is thus," "it is so," or "it is otherwise. And "without making distinctions" means without comparison (*anupanidhāna*).
"Without making this distinction between similarity and dissimilarity" means without taking into account the comparison (*upanidhāna*).

For "thus" refers to non-comparison; whereas "in this way or otherwise" refers to comparison by way of similarity and dissimilarity. "Another mode" refers to a mode existing within the mental continuum of another.
"Exists" means it is always present. "Perishes" means it vanishes. "By way of doubt and discursive thought" [means] "What..."
"By way of reflection" means by way of such deliberation as: "Shall I come to be, or shall I not?

"By way of conceiving an aspiration" means by way of conceiving an aspiration such as: "O, may it be well for me to come to be. "Pure heads" (*suddhasīsā*): these are the common "heads" of craving, conceit, and views.
They are called "pure heads" because they do not depend on any specific distinction stated as "thus," "in this way," or "otherwise."
Thus it was said. In that context, when view is grasped by means of its "heads," craving—which is inseparable from it—is thereby shown.

By means of the four heads and the twelve head-based [factors] consisting of conceit and views, this very same craving is shown; thus he said: "In this way, these... should be understood as states of the wanderings of craving.
But is it not the case that the grasping of conceit and views is also intended here, since [it is said]: "By way of craving, conceit, and views..."?
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated that this is a 'grasping at a collection' (*samūhaggāha*); therefore, how can it be said that these are 'modes of craving' (*taṇhāvicarita*)?

It is replied: Even though views and conceit are mentioned, the designation "modes of craving" should be understood as being applied because those views and conceits—which are mutually dissociated—are nonetheless not dissociated from craving, since they are rooted in craving and dominated by it. The tenth [section] is self-evident.

201–210. In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], "asappurisa" means a base person. "One who destroys living beings" is a killer (*pāṇātipātī*). "One who takes what is not given" is a thief (*adinnādāyī*).
"One who engages in sexual misconduct" is an adulterer (*kāmesumicchācārī*). "One who speaks falsely" is a liar (*musāvādī*).
"One who stands in the habit of intoxication with spirits, wine, and liquors" is one addicted to intoxicants (*surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī*). Regarding killing living beings...
"Causes to undertake" means that just as one takes life oneself, so too one causes another to take hold of that very act.

The same method applies to the remaining [offenses] as well. "This is called" means that because such a person is possessed of unvirtuous conduct both by what he has done himself and by what has been done through his instigation—and is thus an heir to half of that—he is therefore called "one who is more of a non-person than a non-person."

It is said: "A true person" (*sappurisa*) means a supreme person (*uttamapurisa*). "A true person more excellent than a true person" means that because he is endowed with the virtue of morality (*sīla*) practiced by himself, and because he is an heir to half of what another does when exhorted by him, he is a supreme person even more excellent than a supreme person.
And in this context, regarding the immorality or morality performed by another, [it is understood] through his own command and...
One who has committed [an act] by means of vocal application is called "an heir to half of that" because they are an heir to the demerit or merit produced through the instigation of the command.
The second and subsequent [sections] have their meanings already explained.

221–231. The first [types] of the third [chapter] have meanings that are already evident. Regarding the "cintākavi" (poet by reflection) and so forth:

one should understand a *cintākavi* as a poet who composes by reflecting for a long time upon both the subject matter (*vatthu*) and its connection (*anusandhi*). A *sutakavi* (poet by what is heard) is one who composes by connecting what has been heard with what has not been heard after having heard something.
A *atthakavi* (poet by meaning) is one who, having considered some meaning, [composes] by way of its abbreviation, expansion, and so forth.
A *paṭibhānakavi* (a poet of inspired genius) is to be understood as one who, upon seeing any poem or drama composed by another,
creates something else similar to it through his own spontaneous and situational eloquence (*ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhāna*).

Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter]: "Black" (*kāḷaka*) means soiled; the meaning is that which causes the mind to become lusterless.
However, in this context, only that which has reached the level of a course of action (kamma-patha) is intended; thus he says, "the ten unwholesome courses of action.
Or, it is "dark" because it is the cause for birth in a dark state. Therefore he says, "having dark fruition.

Rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and wretchedness among humans is the dark fruition, which is described as its "state of darkness. "From producing" means from causing to be produced. "White" means bright, [referring to] the mind.
The meaning is: "it produces a state of luminosity. Or, it is "bright" because it is the cause for a bright rebirth. Therefore he said, "bright ripening" (*sukkavipāka*).
Bright ripening consists of rebirth in heaven and human excellence; this is what is called its "state of radiance.

However, according to the highest description, it is said to be "because of being produced in heaven," which means "because of causing [one] to be produced there. "Mixed karma" refers to that which occurs at times...
"Black ripens as black, white as white"—thus is action performed by way of mixture.
Having stated that it has a result of pleasure and pain, the passage beginning with "For mixed action... was spoken in order to show the mode of occurrence of that pleasure and pain therein.
The designation "black" and "white" for action is due to its being the cause of black and white birth-resorts; thus, because it leads to diminution, it is the destroyer of both.
Since even the "white" category (sukkapaññatti) is intended here for the karma that brings about the exhaustion of karma, he says:
“Both... this is the meaning here. In that context, “of both kinds of ripening” means of the ripening of both kinds as it has been attained.
For here, the ripening included within the state of prosperity (sampattibhava) is intended as “white” and “white ripening,” not the utterly pure ripening of the noble fruit (ariyaphala).

2. Commentary on the *Vitthārasutta*. 233.
In the second [sutta], "with affliction" (*sabyābajjha*) means with suffering; it is "with suffering" because of the suffering that must be produced by oneself.
The meaning is that it leads to suffering; this is what is meant. Among the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth:

the twelve unwholesome volitions (*akusalacetanā*) that have reached the state of "impulsion" (*copana*) by way of seizing and so on through the door of the body are called the "bodily formation free from affliction" (*abyābajjhakāyasaṅkhāra*).

Those same twelve [volitions] which, through the door of speech, bring about the occurrence of vocal utterance by way of the movement of the jaws are called the "verbal formation. [Those that occur] without reaching the impulsion of both [body and speech], in solitude...
The mental formation (*manosaṅkhāra*) is that which occurs at the mind-door for one who is thinking.

Thus, it should be understood that in all three doors, unwholesome volition (*cetanā*)—classified as bodily misconduct and so forth—is what constitutes formations (*saṅkhāra*). "He forms" means he accumulates;

and that accumulation, because it is established through the convergence of conditions, is like a gathering together into a mass. "The world with suffering" refers to the world of the states of misery (*apāyaloka*).

"Resultant contact" (*vipākaphassa*) refers to the occurrence of resultant [consciousness] there, expressed by way of the term "contact. "Hungry ghosts belonging to the intermediate state" (*vemānika-peta*) is stated because they constitute the majority;
however, for other beings in the states of misery (*vinipātika*) as well, there is pleasure at times and pain at times.

"For the abandoning of that" means for the purpose of establishing the state of non-arising for that aforementioned karma. "That volition" (*cetanā*) refers to the volition leading to diminution (*apacayagāminī*).
For this very reason it says: "The volition of the path leading to turning away (vivaṭṭagāminī) is to be understood.
The commentary on the Vitthāra Sutta is finished.

234–240. Regarding the phrase "In the third [case], O Bhante, 'the previous days' and 'the more previous days,'" here "the previous day" refers to yesterday, and "the more previous" refers to the day after that; thus he says, "starting from the day immediately preceding," and so forth.
In this way, within these two [contexts], the status of being "previous" and "more previous" is shown according to their respective order. Even though this is so, as for what is here...

“Earlier” (*purimatara*) is what is stated; from that point onward, whatever is proximate is “earlier,” and whatever is further is “earlier still” (*purimatara*), because the state of being “earlier still” is established in dependence upon the state of being “near” and “far,” just like the relationship between this shore and the far shore (*orapāra*).
The remainder is exactly as explained by the method already stated. The fourth and subsequent [sections] have their meanings self-evident.

10–11. Commentary on the *Samaṇa-sutta* and others. 241–2.

Regarding the tenth [sutta], the phrase “in the remaining passages as well” refers to the remaining passages such as “here, a second ascetic,” and so forth. For just as [in the passage] “quite secluded... [it was explained...]

The restriction established here by the words “from sensual pleasures” (kāmehi) is also applied to the phrase “secluded from unwholesome states” (vivicca akusalehi), because a restrictive sense is intended;
it is the same here as well. Therefore he said, “The second and so forth,” etc.

Since the state of being a recluse (samaṇabhāva) is defined in its primary sense by the attainment of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), four types of recluses are taught here according to those [fruits]. For in this context...
Only the four types of monks who have attained the fruits (*phalaṭṭhaka*) are intended here, because of the inclusion of the "monks who have stilled evil" (*samitapāpa*).

But why, in this context, are those standing on the path (*maggaṭṭha*) and those practicing for that purpose not included, as they were in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*? It is because of the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

For there, by showing that even insight (*vipassanā*) for the attainment of the path does not exist outside of this [teaching], let alone the paths and fruits, the Blessed One said: "Of the True Way... (*ñāyassa*).
It is said: "One who practices even a portion of the Dhamma—there is no ascetic outside of this [Dhamma].

Here, however, by taking the state of an ascetic only as it has reached its culmination, those ascetics established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭhaka*) alone are included; for one established in the fruit is more distinguished than one established in the path (*maggaṭṭha*), being a more worthy recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
This meaning is understood through the very difference in the teaching found in two suttas. "Empty" (*rittā*) means secluded (*vivittā*).
“Empty” means devoid of essence, because they lack the essence of those who have entered the path.

They are called “propositions” (*pavāda*) because people propound by means of them. He said, “four eternalist views,” and so forth, referring to the systems that indicate the various views of those who follow wrong paths.
In that context, there are four eternalist views: three by way of gain and one by way of reasoning; thus, there are four eternalist views.
A non-Buddhist who has attained knowledge of past lives, if of dull wisdom, recollects up to several hundred thousand births;
if of middling wisdom, ten eons of world-dissolution and evolution; if of sharp wisdom, forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, but not beyond that.
Recollecting in this way, he asserts: "The self and the world are eternal," whereas the rationalist [asserts] what is reached by reasoning.
Based on investigation and one’s own inspired intuition, one asserts: “The self and the world are eternal. Therefore it is said:
“Three [types of eternalism] arise from gain, and one from reasoning; thus there are four types of eternalist views.

A doctrine that proceeds by asserting that some among sentient beings and among conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are eternal is the “partial-eternalist view” (*ekaccasassatavāda*). Furthermore, that...

It is said that "there are four types of partial-eternalists" because they arise here after passing away from the states of existence of the Brahmakāyika, the Khiddāpadosika, and the Manopadosika gods, as well as through the arising of those who speculate [about the origin].
Regarding the phrase "four types of those who hold views on the finite and infinite":
here, *anto* (end) means that which one reaches (*amati*) or arrives at (*gacchati*) as a point of finality (*vosāna*), that is, a boundary (*mariyādā*). By way of its negation—

*Ananta* (infinite). *Anta* (finite) and *ananta* (infinite) together as "finite-infinite" (*antānanta*) are expressed by a general designation, or by the principle of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*), as in such cases as "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition.
Alternatively, "finite-infinite" refers to a doctrine associated with the finite and infinite, as in "the spears are moving.

Or it refers to that which is dependent upon the finite and infinite, as in "the beds are crying out. Since these [views] possess that [doctrine], they are called "finite-infinite-ists" (*antānantikā*). "The world is finite... [and so forth].

There are four proponents who maintain such views as: "The self and the world are infinite," "The self and the world are both finite and infinite," and "The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.

The first is stated with reference to one who perceives that very kasiṇa—of which the kasiṇa has not been expanded—as the self and the world; the second is stated with reference to one who has expanded the kasiṇa.

The third [view] is stated by expanding [the world] across; the fourth is stated by expanding upwards and downwards for one who has not expanded the kasiṇa; and the fourth is also mentioned by way of reasoning.

And here, it is appropriate that the first three views possess the quality of being "speculators on the finite and infinite" (antānantika), because they proceed by taking as their object both the finite and the infinite, and the finite-and-infinite [together];
but for the last [view], it is because it proceeds by way of negating both of those.

How is it "the view of finiteness and infinitude"? It is because it functions as a doctrine that negates both [of those views]. For even a doctrine that negates finiteness and infinitude has finiteness and infinitude as its object, since it functions by taking them as its basis.
"Amarā" means "does not die. What is it? It is the range of one who holds wrong views, which is without limits according to the method beginning with, "It is thus for me," and so forth.

It is both a view and speech. "Vividha-khepo" means distraction; because of the view of immortality (*amarā-diṭṭhi*) or because of speech, there is distraction, thus it is "endless equivocation" (*amarāvikkhepa*).
One who possesses this is an "endless equivocator" (*amarāvikkhepika*). Alternatively, *amara* is a species of fish;
as it darts about in the water by leaping up and so forth, it does not fall into the net. In the same way, this doctrine [flees] from here...

Because it runs about hither and thither and does not reach a firm conclusion, it is called "the elusiveness of the immortal" (*amarāvikkhepa*); those who possess this are the "Eloquents of the Elusiveness of the Immortal" (*amarāvikkhepikā*).
Since this doctrine proceeds in four ways due to being caused by a state of attachment to the practice of false speech, desire, fear, and delusion, it is said:
"There are four kinds of Eloquents of the Elusiveness of the Immortal."

"Arising by chance" (*adhicca-samuppanna*) refers to the view that takes as its object the mode of occurrence of the aggregates— designated as "self" and "world"— which arise without any cause such as prior intelligence or according to whim.
Because this view occurs in dependence upon that mode of occurrence and because it is concomitant with that mode, it is called "arisen by chance," just as one says, "the beds are crying out."
And [the phrase] “spears are moving. Because they possess that [view], they are the Fortuitous-Originists (*adhiccasamuppannika*).
It is said that there are “two types of Fortuitous-Originists” by way of their gains and by way of their reasoning.

A doctrine that proceeds as “there is perception” is the Doctrine of Perception (*saññivāda*); because they possess that, they are the Proponents of Perception (*saññivāda*). The fourfold group on form and the fourfold group on absolute happiness [are explained in the same manner].
By way of these four tetrads, there are sixteen theories of one who possesses perception (*saññivāda*).

Within these very [theories], by way of the first two tetrads, eight theories of one who possesses perception and eight theories of one who is neither percipient nor non-percipient (*nevasaññināsaññivāda*) are to be understood.
For while those views were held by those who grasped the self as "possessing perception" there, here they are held as "non-percipient" and "neither percipient nor non-percipient."

The seven doctrines of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) are so called because they establish the annihilation of a being while it remains in the state of a human, a sense-sphere deity (*kāmāvacara*), a fine-material-sphere being (*rūpāvacara*), or one of the four types of immaterial-sphere beings.

The five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbānavāda*) are so called because they proclaim the attainment of peace in this very life through the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure and through the enjoyment of the bliss of the fourfold fine-material jhānas.
"Present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to what is directly perceived; therein—
In this context, this is a designation for that which has obtained an individual existence (*attabhāva*). "Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means Nibbāna in the seen state;
the meaning is the subsiding of suffering in this very individual existence. They speak of that, thus they are "proponents of Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā*).
It is called a "method" (*ñāya*) because it is known, traversed, and penetrated; and because it is the cause for reaching Nibbāna, it is the Dhamma—thus he said, "of the method..."
"...of the Dhamma. But why is it that these [qualities] do not exist elsewhere, as in the statements "there is no ascetic outside of this [Dhamma]" and so forth?

Because they are not a field for them. For just as a mustard seed does not remain on the point of a needle, fire does not burn on the surface of water, and seeds do not sprout on a flat stone, even so, these ascetics do not arise among the external sectarian systems.
They arise only in this very dispensation. Why? Because of its being a "dry field.
Their lack of a field and their state as a dry field should be understood by way of the absence and presence of the Noble Path respectively. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, therein neither is there a recluse..."
In that [other] case, no ascetic is found; there, a second ascetic is not found; there, a third ascetic is not found;
there, even a fourth ascetic is not found. But in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there an ascetic is found, and a second [ascetic] is also found...
"Therein... there too... there yet again... there a fourth ascetic is found.
Indeed, Subhadda, in this Dhamma and Vinaya the Noble Eightfold Path is found. Right here, Subhadda, is an ascetic;
right here a second ascetic; right here a third ascetic; right here a fourth ascetic. The teachings of others are empty of true ascetics."
The absence and presence of the Noble Path should be understood through the absence and presence of perfectly pure virtue and the cultivation of perfectly pure serenity and insight.
Both of these are caused by the state of being ill-proclaimed or well-proclaimed, respectively; and that [ill-proclamation] is due to not having been proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Since a sectarian fold is not a field, whereas the Dispensation is a field, therefore...
Just as the lion, the king of beasts— with its well-tanned paws and a magnificent mane— does not dwell in a charnel ground or a heap of refuse,
but rather plunges deep into the Himalayas, which extend for three thousand leagues, and dwells only in the Jewel Cave;
and just as the elephant king Chaddanta is not born among the nine families of elephants, such as the Gocariya and others;
Just as the horse-king Valāhaka does not arise in a family of donkeys or mules, but arises only in the Sindha breed on the banks of the Indus;
and just as the heart-stealing jewel-treasure that grants all desires does not arise in a heap of refuse or among sand dunes and the like,
but arises only within the interior of a vast mountain;
Just as the king of makaras, Timirapiṅgala, does not appear in small lotus ponds but appears only in the great ocean, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep;

and just as the king of supaṇṇas, measuring one hundred and fifty yojanas, does not dwell in places such as the eraṇḍa forests near village gates, but dwells only after plunging into the great ocean at the Simbalidaha forest; so too [is it with the Tathāgata].
Just as Dhatarattha, the golden swan, does not dwell at the village gate in places such as pits,
but dwells only on Cittakūṭa surrounded by ninety thousand swans; and just as a universal monarch, the lord of the four continents, is not born into a low family,
but is born only into an unadulterated lineage of kshatriyas— so too it is with these ascetics.
Not even a single ascetic arises elsewhere in the sectarian abodes; rather, they arise only within the Buddha’s dispensation, which has been purified by the Noble Path.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic… empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics.
Regarding the eleventh [point], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Samaṇasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Kammavagga is finished.
(25) 5. The Chapter on the Fear of Offenses (Āpattibhayavagga).
1. Commentary on the Saṅghabhedaka-sutta 243.
Regarding the first [case] of the fifth [chapter], "in disputes, legal questions, and so forth":

this refers to these four—namely, the dispute-legal-question (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the accusation-legal-question (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the offense-legal-question (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the business-legal-question (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). Therein, "is it Dhamma" or "is it non-Dhamma"?
The dispute among monks who are quarreling over eighteen grounds is called a *vivādādhikaraṇa* (a legal issue arising from a dispute).

The accusation, as well as the censuring and the formal charge, of those who reproach [another] for failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), or for failure in conduct, view, or livelihood (*ācāra-diṭṭhi-ājīvavipatti*), is called an *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (a legal issue arising from an accusation). There are five [grounds] mentioned in the *Mātikā* and two in the *Vibhaṅga*.
The seven classes of offenses—this is called a legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).

The performance of the four types of formal acts, such as the seeking of permission from the Saṅgha and so forth—this is called a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Saṅghabhedaka-sutta is finished.
2–3. Commentary on the *Āpattibhayasutta*, etc. 244–5.

In the second [verse], it is called *bhasmaṃ* because it is scattered (*bhassati*) or thrown away due to its uselessness; thus, it means ashes or chaff. A bag or bundle for that is a "bag of ashes" (*bhasmapuṭa*). Therefore he said: "‘Bag of ashes’ means a bundle of chaff. The third [verse] has a self-evident meaning.
The commentary on the *Āpattibhayasutta*, etc., is concluded.
4–7. Commentary on the *Seyyāsutta*, etc. (246–9).
In the fourth [verse], *petā* refers to those who have gone to the state of the departed (*peccabhāva*).
Since they undergo death here and have their lives cut short in due time, it is said, "they are called *kālakatā*," meaning they are dead. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]
"Passed away into the state of a *peta*" means they have undergone rebirth by way of being born as a *peta*. Therefore he said:
"Or alternatively, those born in the realm of *petas* are called *petas*. They are unable to lie down on one side because of the arising of suffering.
By the phrase "excessive in heat," he shows the lion's fearless nature. The other timid animals [leave] their own lair...
Having entered, they lie down in whatever manner they please, preceded by agitation;
but the lion, being fearless by nature, lies down having established mindfulness, just like a mindful monk. Therefore he said, "two forepaws," and so forth.
Having placed two forepaws in one place by way of placing the right forepaw upon the left forepaw.

Just as in the method described in the final verse, here too the placing [of the mind] in one place should be understood; the observation of the standing-point should be understood by way of fearlessness alone.

Furthermore, the lion-like action described by the words "lifting up the head," etc., should be understood as being established through the nature of the dhamma that is fearless, like waking up without being terrified. The lion’s stretch should not be performed excessively in a single manner.
It is for the purpose of bringing about the fitness of the deposited bodily parts for activities such as movement.
The threefold uttering of the lion’s roar is for the purpose of warding off fear from lesser kings of beasts.
By the statement, "This, monks, is called the Tathāgata’s lying down," it is shown that the lying down in the fourth jhāna is the Tathāgata’s lying down.
He indicates this by the word "namely" (nāma). It is called a *seyyā* because one lies (*seti*) there, meaning it proceeds in a state of non-exertion;
thus, the fourth jhāna itself is the *seyyā*, hence "the fourth-jhāna-rest. But what is that fourth jhāna? It is the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*).
For, having stood upon that, having increased insight (*vipassanā*), and having gradually attained the supreme path, the Blessed One became a Tathāgata.
Regarding the word "born": this so-called "lying down" (seyyā) is not superior;

nevertheless, because it is stated in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* that "the Blessed One passed away immediately after the fourth jhāna," some maintain that only the attainment of the mundane fourth jhāna constitutes the Tathāgata’s lying down.
If this were the case, it would follow that the Tathāgata’s lying down occurs only at the time of his final passing away (*parinibbāna*).
And the Blessed One did not dwell frequently in the attainment of the worldly fourth jhāna.
Rather, it should be understood that the fourth jhāna occurring here functions by way of the supreme fruit (aggaphala).

In this regard, just as for beings lying down—characterized by the subsiding of sleep—occurs through the mind of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-citta), and that state is their natural condition resulting from their very birth and is their predominant mode of existence; even so...

The fourth jhāna, which is the culmination of the Blessed One’s possession of the noble birth and which constitutes the predominant mode of his conduct as the supreme fruit, should be understood as "the Tathāgata’s lying down.
The fifth and subsequent sections have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the *Seyyāsutta* and the others is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Discourse on Conventional Expression (Paṭhamavohārasutta) 250–253.
In the eighth [discourse], "of the ignoble ones" (*anariyānaṃ*) means of those who are not good, the base. "Conventional expressions" (*vohārā*) refers to transactions or verbal utterances;
that is, speaking in such a manner as, "I have seen this. And here, the meaning should be understood by way of the volition (*cetanā*) that originates each respective [act].
There is nothing further to be said regarding the ninth [sutta] and those that follow.
The commentary on the first Discourse on Designation is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Fear of Offenses is finished.
The Fifth Fifty is concluded. (26) 6.
The Chapter on Direct Knowledge (Abhiññāvagga): 1–3.
Commentary on the Discourses on Direct Knowledge, etc.
254–26. In the first [section] of the sixth [chapter], *samatha* is so called because it pacifies through opposition; thus he says "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatā*).

Because it sees by way of various modes such as impermanence and so forth, it is *vipassanā*, which is the knowledge that discerns formations (*saṅkhāra*). Therefore he says "the knowledge of insight that discerns formations" (*saṅkhārapariggaha-vipassanāñāṇa*).
In the second case, it is called "the ignoble search" because it is to be sought after by the ignoble;
or, it is the search of the ignoble because of its own inherent baseness. "The state of being worn out" means having the nature of decay. The third [search] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Abhiññā-sutta* and others is concluded.
4–10. Commentary on the *Mālukyaputta-sutta* and others, §§257–263.

In the fourth [discourse], "he disparages" means he rebukes; "he elevates" means he encourages. The passage beginning with "How... is commenced in order to clarify the manner of disparagement and the manner of elevation. The fifth and subsequent discourses are self-evident. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Mālukyaputta-sutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on Direct Knowledge (*Abhiññāvagga*) is finished.
Thus ends the Elucidation of Unexplained Points for the Commentary on the Four-Fold Group (*Catukkanipāta*) of the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the Commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
The second part is finished.
